The first mill in London to use the steam engines was so large and efficient that in one year it could produce more flour than the other mills in London combined. The ability to identify a person from a mere fingerprint is a powerful tool in the fight against crime. This is the most common criminal evidence, and often exceeds other methods of detection. Nowadays, older methods of inked fingerprinting, which can last for weeks, have given way to newer, faster techniques such as laser scanning fingerprints, but the principles remain the same. No matter which way you collect fingerprint evidence, every person who prints is unique. So what sets our fingerprints apart from our neighbours? A good place to start is to understand what fingerprints are and how they are created. A FINGERPRINT IS AN ARRANGEMENT OF SKIN RIDGES AND FURROWS AT THE FINGERTIPS. This lined skin develops fully during fetal development, when skin cells grow in the mothers uterus. These ridges are arranged into patterns and remain the same throughout human life. Other visible human characteristics, such as weight and height, change over time whereas fingerprints do not. The reason why each fingerprint is unique is that when a baby's genes combine with environmental influences, like temperature, it affects how the ridges on the skin grow. This causes the ridges to develop at different rates, bend and bend into patterns. As a result, no two people end up having the same fingerprints. Even identical twins have different fingerprints. It is not easy to map the journey of how the unique quality of the fingerprint was discovered. The moment in history that this happened is not entirely precious. HOWEVER, THE USE OF FINGERPRINTING CAN BE TRACED BACK TO SOME ANCIENT CULTURES, SUCH AS BABYLON AND CHINA, WHERE FINGERPRINTS WERE PRESSED ON POTTERY PLATES TO CONFIRM BUSINESS TRANSACTIONS. Whether people at this point really understood the full extent of the importance of fingerprints for identification purposes is another matter entirely. It is impossible to be sure whether the act was seen as a means of confirming identity or a symbolic gesture for binding a contract, when giving your fingerprint was like giving your word. Despite this uncertainty, there are those who have made a significant contribution to fingerprint analysis. History tells us that a 14th-century Persian physician stated early on that no two fingerprints are alike. Later, in the 17th century, the Italian physician Marcello Malpighi investigated the distinctive shapes of loops and spirals in fingerprints. In his honor, the medical world later named a skin layer after him. However, it was an East India Company employee, William Herschel, who came to see the true potential of fingerprinting. He took fingerprints from the local people as a form of signing contracts, to prevent fraud. His fascination with fingerprints motivated him to study them for the next twenty years. He developed the theory that fingerprints were unique to a person and did not change at all during his lifetime. In 1880 Henry Fowlds suggested that fingerprints could be used to identify convicted criminals. He wrote to Charles Darwin for advice, and the idea was referred to Darwin's cousin, Sir Francis Galton. GALTON EVENTUALLY PUBLISHED AN IN-DEPTH STUDY OF FINGERPRINT SCIENCE IN 1892. Although the fact that each individual has a completely unique fingerprint pattern has been well documented and accepted for a long time, this knowledge was not utilized for forensic purposes until the beginning of the 20th century. France labels criminals with a butterfly-de-lis symbol. The Romans tattooed mercenary soldiers to prevent them from becoming deserters. premise: A library at your fingertips several years ago, at the height of the dotcom boom, it was assumed that an advertising revolution, in which the printed word would be replaced by the computer screen, was just around the corner. It wasn't: for many, there's still not much to match the joy of cracking the spine of a good book and settling into an hour-and-two of reading. A recent flurry of activity from major technology companies including Google, Amazon, Microsoft and Yahoo! Indicates that the dream of bringing books online is still very much alive. The digitization of thousands of volumes of printing is not without controversy. On Thursday, November 3, Google, the world's most popular search engine, released a first chapter of books on Google Print, an initiative first launched a year ago. This collaborative effort between Google and some of the world's leading research libraries aims to make thousands of books available to search and read online free of charge. Although the books included so far are not covered by copyright, the plan has drawn the ire of publishers. Five major book companies are suing Google for copyright infringement over material it scanned, and despite running out of print, it is still protected by law. Google has said it will only publish short extracts from materials under copyright unless it is given explicit permission to publish more, but advertisers are not convinced. Ironically, many publishers are partnering with Google on a separate venture, Google Print Publisher, which aims to give readers an online taste of commercially available books. The searchable collection of extracts and book information is designed to entice readers to buy the complete books online or in printed form. In order not to faint, Amazon, the world's largest online retailer, has unveiled plans for its own foray into the mass e-book market. The company, which started ten years ago as an online book retailer, now sells a huge range of goods. Undoubtedly, Google, relatively new, needs to hit its core territory, Amazon revealed on Thursday that it will introduce two new services. Amazon Pages will allow customers to search for key terms in selected books and then buy and read online any part they want, from individual pages to chapters or entire works. Amazon Upgrade will give customers online access to books they have already purchased as hard copies. Customers will likely have to pay about five cents per page, with the large portion going to the publisher. Microsoft, too, has joined the online book cart. In late October, the software giant said it would spend about $200 million to digitize texts, up from 150,000 that are in the public domain, to avoid legal problems. It will do so in collaboration with the Open Content Alliance, a consortium of libraries and universities. (Yahoo! Pledged to make 18,000 books available online in collaboration with the same organization.) On Thursday, coincidentally the same day that Google and Amazon announced their initiatives, Microsoft released details of a deal with the British Library, the country's main reference library, to digitize about 25 million pages; these will be available through MSN Book Search, which will be launched next year. These companies hope to return to the levels of interest in e-books that were seen when Stephen King, the best-selling horror writer, published Riding the Bullet exclusively online in 2000. Half a million copies were downloaded in the first 48 hours after publication. This turned out to be a higher mark than tasting the following. While shoppers didn't hesitate to sit in front of a computer screen to read the latest novels, dedicated gadgets for reading e-books failed to catch on. Barnes & Noble, a leading American bookstore chain, began selling e-books aloud in 2000 but quietly unplugged the plug in 2003 as interest waned. The e-book market is growing again, albeit from a tiny base. According to the International Digital Advertising Forum, which compiles data from many of the world's leading publishers, in the third quarter of 2004, worldwide sales were 25% higher than the previous year. Unfortunately, this amounted to only a tiny split of $3.2 million among 23 publishers in an industry that brought in sales worth over $100 billion that year. Both retailers and advertisers think they will eventually be able to persuade consumers to do much more of their reading online. Some even hope they can become to online books what Apples iTunes is to online music. There are crucial differences between downloading fiction and downloading punk. Online music was driven from the bottom up: illegal file-sharing services became incredibly popular, and law firms later took over when pirates were forced to back down (by a wave of lawsuits); the legal providers are confident that more and more consumers will pay small sums for music rather than remain beyond the law. The iPod music player and the like have proven a fashionable and popular new way to listen to songs. The world of books has no parallel. So the commercial prospects for sellers of online books do not yet look very bright. They may get a lift from some new innovations. Being able to download only parts from books can help, for example: excerpts from manuals, textbooks, or cookbooks may entice certain customers; students may want to download the relevant sections of the course books; or readers may want to taste a book they then buy in printed copy. The ability to download reading material to hand-held electronic devices is increasingly common and 3G phones may encourage even more reception. In Japan, the value of e-books (mainly manga comic books) delivered to mobile phones has soared, though it will only be worth around $US6 billion ($51 million) in 2005, according to estimates
hypothesis: Being able to sample a book online before buying it may help sales.

premise: Neuroscientist reveals how to think differently In the past decade a revolution has taken place in the way scientists think about the brain. We now know that the decisions humans make can be attributed to the firing patterns of neurons in specific parts of the brain. These discoveries have led to a field known as neuroeconomics, which studies the brain's secrets to success in an economic environment that requires innovation and the ability to do things differently from competitors. A mind that can do so is iconoclastic. In short, an iconoclast is a person who does something that others say cannot be done. This definition implies that iconoclasts are different from other people, but more specifically, their brains differ in three different ways: perception, fear response, and social intelligence. Each of these three functions uses a different circuit in the brain. Opponents might suggest that the brain is irrelevant, that thinking in an original, even revolutionary way, is more a matter of personality than brain function. But the field of neuroeconomics was born out of the understanding that the physical workings of the brain place limitations on the way we make decisions. By understanding these constraints, we begin to understand why some people march to a different drum beat. The first thing to understand is that the brain suffers from limited resources. It has a fixed energy budget, about the same as a 40-watt bulb, so it has evolved to work as efficiently as possible. This is where most people are prevented from being iconoclasts. For example, when faced with information flowing from the eyes, the brain will interpret this information in the fastest way possible. That way he will rely on both past experience and any other source of information, like what other people say, to understand what he sees. It happens all the time. The brain takes shortcuts that work so well that we're rarely aware of them. We think our perceptions of the world are real, but they're just biological and electrical noises. Perception is not just a product of what your eyes or ears transmit to your brain. More than the physical reality of photons or sound waves, perception is a product of the brain. Perception is central in iconoclasm. Iconoclasts see things differently from other people. Their brains don't fall into effective traps like the average person's brain. Iconoclasts, either because they were born that way or through learning, have found ways around the perceptual shortcuts that plague most people. Perception is not something that is connected to the brain. It is a learned process, which is both a curse and an opportunity for change. The brain is faced with the fundamental problem of interpreting physical stimuli from the senses. Everything the brain sees, hears, or touches has multiple interpretations. The one chosen in the end is simply the best theory of mind. In technical terms, these hypotheses are based on the statistical likelihood of one interpretation over another and are heavily influenced by past experience, and more importantly for potential iconoclasts, by what other people say. The best way to see things differently from other people is to bombard the brain with things it has never encountered before. Novelty frees the perceptual process from the chains of past experience and forces the brain to make new judgments. Successful iconoclasts have a remarkable willingness to be exposed to what is fresh and different. Observing iconoclasts shows that they embrace novelty while most people avoid different things. The problem with novelty, however, is that it tends to activate the brain's fear system. Fear is a major obstacle to thinking like an iconoclast and stops the average person in its tracks. There are many types of fear, but the two that inhibit iconoclastic thinking and people usually find it difficult to deal with are fear of uncertainty and fear of public ridicule. These may seem like trivial phobias. But the fear of public speaking, which everyone must do from time to time, harms a third of the population. This makes it too common to be considered a mental disorder. It's simply a common version of human nature, one that iconoclasts don't let their responses inhibit. Finally, to be successful iconoclasts, people must sell their ideas to other people. This is where social intelligence comes in. Social intelligence is the ability to understand and manage people in a business environment. In the past decade there has been an explosion of knowledge about the social brain and how the brain works when groups coordinate decision-making. Neuroscience has discovered which brain circuits are responsible for functions like understanding what other people think, empathy, fairness, and social identity. These brain regions play key roles in whether people convince others of their ideas. Perception is also important in social cognition. The perception of enthusiasm, or someone's reputation, can make or break a deal. Understanding how perception fits into social decision-making shows why successful iconoclasts are so rare. Iconoclasts create new opportunities in every field from artistic expression to technology to business. They provide creativity and innovation that cannot be easily achieved by committees. The rules are not important to them. Iconoclasts face alienation and failure, but can also be a key asset to any organization. It is important for success in any field to understand how the iconoclastic brain works.

MALARIA-TYPE FEVER WAS RECORDED AMONG THE ANCIENT GREEKS BY WRITERS SUCH AS HERODOTUS WHO ALSO RECORDS THE FIRST PREVENTIVE MEASURES: FISHERMEN SLEEPING UNDER THEIR NETS. Treatments up to the nineteenth century were as varied as they were not effective. Spiders living in butter, purging and bleeding, and sleeping with a copy of the Iliad under the heads of patients are all recorded. The use of the first truly effective drug, an infusion from the bark of the cinchona tree, was recorded in 1636 but it was not until 1820 that quinine was produced, the active substance from the bark of the synchona and modern prevention became possible. Oliver Cromwell, the Protestant English leader who executed King Charles I, died of malaria as a result of his doctors refusing to give Catholic medicine! It is known that the malaria parasite, or plasmodium falciparum to give it its Latin name, has a life cycle that must pass through the Anopheles mosquito and human hosts in order to live. It can only reach its current form after humanity has mastered agriculture and lived in groups for that to happen. With two such different hosts, the life cycle of the parasite is remarkable. There is the sporozoite stage that lives in the mosquito. When a person is bitten by an infected Anopheles mosquito the parasite is transmitted to the person through the mosquito saliva. Just six such parasites may be enough to transmit the infection provided that humans' immune systems fail to kill the parasites before they reach the liver. There they become merozoites and multiply greatly, perhaps, to about 60,000 after 10 days and then spread throughout the bloodstream. Within minutes of this happening, they attack the red blood cells to feed on the iron-rich hemoglobin found inside. This is when the patient begins to feel sick. Within hours, they can eat up to 125 grams of hemoglobin, which causes anemia, fatigue, vulnerability to infection and lack of oxygen in areas such as the brain. Oxygen is transported to all organs by hemoglobin in the blood. The lack of oxygen leads to the cells blocking capillaries in the brain and the effects are very similar to that of a stroke with one important difference: the damage is reversible and patients can emerge from a malarial coma without brain damage. The merozoites now change into gametocytes that can be either male or female and it is this stage, with random mixing of genes generated, that can lead malaria to develop resistance to treatments. These resistant gametocytes can be transferred back to the mosquito if the patient is bitten, and they become zygotes. These zygotes divide and produce sporozoites and the cycle can begin again. The fight against malaria often seems to focus on the work of medical researchers trying to produce solutions like vaccines. But funding is low because, they say, malaria is a third-world condition and hardly bothers the rich and industrialized countries. It is true that malaria is, at root, a disease of poverty. The richer countries were able to eradicate malaria by expanding agriculture and so proper drainage so that mosquitoes could not reproduce, and by living in solid houses with glass windows so that the mosquitoes could not bite the human host. Campaigns in China's Hunan province, using insecticide-soaked netting around beds have reduced infection rates from more than a million a year to about 65,000. But the search for medical cures continues. About 15 years ago there were high hopes for DNA-based vaccines that worked well in experiments on mice. Some still believe that this is where the answer lies and soon too. Other researchers are not so sure and expect a wait of at least another 15 years before any significant development.

premise: Unusual beetle. Some of the most remarkable beetles are the dung beetles, which spend almost their entire lives eating and reproducing in manure. More than 4,000 species of these unusual creatures have evolved and adapted to the different climates of the worlds and the droppings of its many animals. AUSTRALIA'S NATIVE DUNG BEETLES ARE SCRUB AND FOREST DWELLERS, SPECIALISING IN COARSE POCKET DUNG AND AVOIDING THE SOFT CATTLE DUNG IN WHICH BUSH FLIES AND BUFFALO FLIES BREED. In the early 1960s George Bornemisa, then a scientist at the Australian governments' leading research organisation, the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO), suggested that dung beetles should be introduced into Australia to control the breeder flies. Between 1968-1982, the CSIRO imported insects from about 50 different species of dung beetle, from Asia, Europe and Africa, with the aim of adapting them to different climatic zones in Australia. Of the 26 species known to have successfully integrated into the local environment, only one, an African species released in northern Australia, has reached its natural limit. Introducing dung beetles into the pasture is a simple process: about 1,500 beetles are released, a handful at a time, to pat 2 fresh cows in the cow pasture. THE BEETLES IMMEDIATELY DISAPPEAR UNDER THE BURROWING PATS AND TUNNELS, AND IF THEY SUCCESSFULLY ADAPT TO THEIR NEW ENVIRONMENT, QUICKLY BECOME A PERMANENT AND SELF-SUSTAINING PART OF THE LOCAL ECOLOGY. Over time they multiply and within three or four years the benefits to pasture are obvious. Dung beetles work from the inside of the preach so that they are protected from predators such as birds and foxes. Most species burrow into the ground and bury dung in tunnels directly under the pats, hollowed out from the inside. Some large species native to France dig tunnels to a depth of about 30 cm below the dung tapeworm. These beetles produce sausage-shaped tumor cells along the tunnels. The shallowest tunnels belong to a much smaller Spanish species that buries dung in cells hanging like fruit from the branches of a pear tree. South African beetles dig narrow tunnels of about 20 cm below the surface of the wallpaper. SOME SURFACE-DWELLING BEETLES, INCLUDING A SOUTH AFRICAN SPECIES, CUT PERFECTLY SHAPED BALLS FROM PREACHING, WHICH ARE ROLLED UP AND ATTACHED TO THE BASES OF PLANTS. For maximum dung burial in spring, summer and autumn, farmers require a variety of species with overlapping active periods. In the cooler environments of Victoria state, the large French species (2.5 cm long) is adapted to smaller Spanish species (half that size) and mild climates. The former are slow to recover from the winter cold and produce only one or two generations of offspring from late spring to autumn. The latter, which reproduce rapidly in early spring, produce two to five generations per year. THE BALL-ROLLING SOUTH AFRICAN SPECIES, BEING A SUBTROPICAL BEETLE, PREFERS THE CLIMATE OF NORTHERN AND COASTAL NEW SOUTH WALES, WHERE IT USUALLY WORKS WITH THE SOUTH AFRICAN TUNNELING SPECIES. In warmer climates, many species are active for longer periods of the year. Dung beetles were initially introduced in the late 1960s with the aim of controlling buffalo flies by removing the droppings within a day or two and so preventing flies from reproducing. However, other advantages became apparent. After the beetle larvae have finished incarnating, the leftovers are a first-class source of fertilizer. The tunnels abandoned by the beetles provide excellent ventilation and water channels for root systems. In addition, when the new generation of beetles has left the nest, the abandoned burrows are an attractive habitat for soil-enriching earthworms. The digested dung in these burrows is an excellent food supply for the earthworms, which break it down further to provide essential nutrients to the soil. premise: A THEORY OF SHOPPING OVER A PERIOD OF A YEAR I TRIED TO EDIT AN ETHNOGRAPHY OF STREET SHOPPING IN AND AROUND NORTH LONDON. It was performed in collaboration with Alison Clark. I say tried because given the absence of community and the intense private nature of London households, this cannot be ethnography in the conventional sense. Nevertheless, through conversation, home presence, and accompanying landlords during their shopping, I attempted to come to an understanding of the nature of shopping through greater or lesser exposure to 76 households. My part in ethnography concentrated on the shopping itself. Alison Clark has since been working with the same households, but focuses on other forms of supply such as the use of catalogues (see Clark 1997). We usually first met these households together, but most of the material used in this specific article is derived from my subsequent fieldwork. After completing this essay, and researching some related shopping centers, we hope to write a more general ethnography of supply. It will also examine other issues, such as the nature of community and the implications for retail and the wider political economy. None of this, however, is part of the current article, which is primarily concerned with establishing the cosmological foundations of shopping. Determining that a household is included in the study means clarifying a wide range of degrees of involvement. The minimum requirement is simply that a landlord has agreed to be interviewed about his shopping, which would include the local shopping parade, shopping centres and supermarkets. At the other end are families we've known well during the year. The interaction will include formal interviews and a less formal presence at their homes, usually with a cup of tea. It also meant accompanying them to one or several events, which might include shopping trips or participating in activities related to the Clarks field of study, such as a meeting of a group delivering products to the home. Analyzing and writing the experience of an ethnography of shopping in north London, lead me in two opposite directions. The tradition of anthropological relativism leads to an emphasis on difference, and there are many ways in which shopping can help us clarify differences. For example, there are differences in the shopping experience based on gender, age, ethnicity and class. There are also differences based on the different genres of the buying experience, from mall to corner store. In contrast, there is a tradition of anthropological generalization about peoples and comparative theory. This leads to the question of whether there are fundamental aspects of shopping that point to a strong normativity that comes through research and is not completely dissipated by relativism. In this article I want to highlight the latter approach and argue that if not all, then most of the acts of shopping on this street present a normative form that must be addressed. In the later discussion of the shopping discourse I discussed the possibility that such a heterogeneous group of households could be fairly represented by a series of homogenous cultural practices. The theory I propose is certainly contrary to most literature on this subject. My basic premise, contrary to that of most consumption studies, whether they derive from economists, business studies or cultural studies, is that for most households on the street it is the act of shopping that has rarely been directed towards the person doing the shopping. Therefore shopping is not best understood as an individualistic or individualistic act related to the subjectivity of the buyer. Instead, the act of buying the goods is mainly directed to two other forms. The first of these expresses a relationship between the buyer and another specific person such as a child or spouse, present in the household, preferably or imagined. The second of these is a connection to a more general purpose that transcends any immediate benefit and is best understood as cosmological in that it takes the form of neither subject nor object but of the values to which people wish to devote themselves. It never occurred to me at any point while doing the ethnography that I should treat the subject of sacrifice as relevant to this study. In no sense could ethnography be treated as a test of the ideas presented here. The literature that seemed most relevant in the initial analysis of the London material was that on the subject of thrift discussed in Chapter 3. The crucial element in unlocking the sacrificial potential for understanding shopping came through reading the Bataiile. Bataille, however, was only the catalyst, since I would argue that it was the classical works on sacrifice and especially the basis of its modern study by Hubert and Maus (1964) that became the main basis for my interpretation. However, it is important in reading the following account to note that when I use the word victim, I am rarely referring to the colloquial sense of the term as it is used in the concept of the housewife sacrificing herself. Mainly the allusion is to this literature on ancient sacrifice and detailed analysis of the complex ceremonial sequence involving traditional sacrifice. The metaphorical use of the term may fill its place in a subsequent discussion, but it is secondary to the structure-level argument.

It turns out that it's not Florence's nose that makes her a leading drug rabid, but her unwavering concentration, plus a few other essential qualities. Florence could help neurobiologists understand both what they call attention processing, the brain mechanisms that determine what a person pays attention to and for how long, and its flip side, problems like attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). It is thought that 3 to 5% of children suffer from the condition in the US, where the incidence is highest, although often the diagnosis is controversial. Champness started by defining six essential traits that make a dog a detector. First, any good detector dog must love praise because it is the only tool available to trainers, but the dog must still be able to work long periods without it. Then he needs a strong hunting instinct and stamina to keep sniffing at the taxing rate of about 300 times a minute. The ideal detector is also fearless enough to handle the throngs of busy airports and the roaring engine rooms of cargo ships. The remaining two traits are closely related and cognitive in character. A good detector must be able to focus on the search mission for drugs, despite the distractions at any airport or dock. This is what neurobiologists call selective attention. And finally, with tens of thousands of hiding places for drugs, the dog must persevere and maintain focus for hours at a time. Neurobiologists call this sustained attention. Wendlow and Champness assess the dogs' abilities to concentrate by marking them on a scale of between one and five depending on the degree of focus on a toy thrown into a patch of grass. premise: Neuroscientist discovers how to think differently. In the past decade, there has been a revolution in the way scientists think about the brain. We now know that the decisions humans make can be attributed to the firing patterns of neurons in a particular part of the brain. These discoveries have led to a field known as neuroeconomics, which studies the brain's secrets to success in an economic environment that requires innovation and the ability to do things differently from competitors. A mind that can do this is an iconoclastic mind. In short, an iconoclast is a person who does something that others say cannot be done. This definition implies that iconoclasts are different from other people, but more specifically, their brains differ in three different ways: perception, fear response, and social intelligence. Each of these three functions uses a different circuit in the brain. Opponents might suggest that the brain is irrelevant, that thinking in an original, even revolutionary way, is more a matter of personality than brain function. But the field of neuroeconomics was born out of the understanding that the physical workings of the brain place limitations on the way we make decisions. By understanding these constraints, we begin to understand why some people march to a different drum beat. The first thing to understand is that the brain suffers from limited resources. It has a fixed energy budget, about the same as a 40-watt bulb, so it has evolved to work as efficiently as possible. This is where most people are prevented from being iconoclasts. For example, when faced with information flowing from the eyes, the brain will interpret this information in the fastest way possible. That way he will rely on both past experience and any other source of information, like what other people say, to understand what he sees. It happens all the time. The brain takes shortcuts that work so well that we're rarely aware of them. We think our perceptions of the world are real, but they're just biological and electrical noises. Perception is not just a product of what your eyes or ears transmit to your brain. More than the physical reality of photons or sound waves, perception is a product of the brain. Perception is central in iconoclasm. Iconoclasts see things differently from other people. Their brains don't fall into effective traps like the average person's brain. Iconoclasts, either because they were born that way or through learning, have found ways around the perceptual shortcuts that plague most people. Perception is not something that is connected to the brain. It is a learned process, which is both a curse and an opportunity for change. The brain is faced with the fundamental problem of interpreting physical stimuli from the senses. Everything the brain sees, hears, or touches has multiple interpretations. The one chosen in the end is simply the best theory of mind. In technical terms, these hypotheses are based on the statistical likelihood of one interpretation over another and are heavily influenced by past experience, and more importantly for potential iconoclasts, by what other people say. The best way to see things differently from other people is to bombard the brain with things it has never encountered before. Novelty frees the perceptual process from the chains of past experience and forces the brain to make new judgments. Successful iconoclasts have a remarkable willingness to be exposed to what is fresh and different. Observing iconoclasts shows that they embrace novelty while people avoid different things. The problem with novelty, however, is that it tends to activate the brain's fear system. Fear is a major obstacle to thinking like an iconoclast and stops the average person in its tracks. There are many types of fear, but the two that inhibit iconoclastic thinking and people usually find it difficult to deal with are fear of uncertainty and fear of public ridicule. These may seem like trivial phobias. But the fear of public speaking, which everyone must do from time to time, harms a third of the population. This makes it too common to be considered a mental disorder. It's simply a common version of human nature, one that iconoclasts don't let their responses inhibit. Finally, to be successful iconoclasts, people must sell their ideas to other people. This is where social intelligence comes in. Social intelligence is the ability to understand and manage people in a business environment. In the past decade there has been an explosion of knowledge about the social brain and how the brain works when groups coordinate decision-making. Neuroscience has discovered which brain circuits are responsible for functions like understanding what other people think, empathy, fairness, and social identity. These brain regions play key roles in whether people convince others of their ideas. Perception is also important in social cognition. The perception of enthusiasm, or someone's reputation, can make or break a deal. Understanding how perception fits into social decision-making shows why successful iconoclasts are so rare. Iconoclasts create new opportunities in every field from artistic expression to technology to business. They provide creativity and innovation that cannot be easily achieved by committees. The rules are not important to them. Iconoclasts face alienation and failure, but can also be a key asset to any organization. It is important for success in any field to understand how the iconoclastic brain works.

premise: Absenteeism in nursing: Research the length of absence from work is an expensive and disruptive problem for any organization. The cost of absenteeism in Australia stood at 1.8 million hours a day or $1400 million a year. The study reported here was conducted at the Prince William Hospital in Brisbane, Australia, where, prior to this time, some active steps were taken to measure, understand or manage the occurrence of absenteeism. Nursing absenteeism A common attitude among many nurses in the group selected for the study was that there was no reward or recognition for not taking advantage of the entitlement to paid sick leave that allowed them under their working conditions. Therefore, they believed they could also take the days off sick or otherwise. Similar positions were noted by James (1989), who noted that sick leave is seen by many workers as a right, like annual vacation leave. Miller and Norton (1986), in their survey of 865 nursing professionals, found that 73 percent felt they should be rewarded for not taking sick leave, because some workers always used their sick leave. Moreover, 67% of nurses believed that the administration is not sympathetic to the problems that shift work causes in the personal and social life of employees. Only 53% of respondents felt that every effort was made to schedule employees fairly. In another longitudinal study of nurses working in two Canadian hospitals, Hackett, Bycio, and Guion (1989) examined the reasons why nurses were absent from work. The most common reason mentioned for absence was a minor illness to myself. Other causes, in order of decreasing frequency, were illnesses in the family, family social dysfunction, work at home and bereavement. Method In an attempt to reduce the level of absenteeism among the 250 registered and registered nurses in the current study, Prince William's management has introduced three different, but may complete, strategies over 18 months. Strategy 1: Non-financial (material) incentives within the established wage and salary system Hospital funds could not be used to support this strategy. However, incentives could be obtained from local businesses, including free tickets to amusement parks, theaters, restaurants, etc. At the end of each faculty term, the department with the lowest absenteeism rate would win the award. Strategy 2: Flexible fair dispatching where possible gave staff the opportunity to set their work schedule within the limits of clinical needs. Strategy 3: Individual absenteeism and consultation Every month the managers would analyze the pattern of absence of staff with excessive sick leave (more than ten days a year for full-time employees). Typical patterns of potential voluntary absence such as absence before and after days off, excessive absence on weekends and overnight and individual days off were passed on to all ward nurses and then, as appropriate, followed up with action. The results of absenteeism rates in the six months preceding the incentive plan ranged from 3.69 percent to 4.32 percent. In the six months that followed, they ranged from 2.87 percent to 3.96 percent. That represents a 20 percent improvement. However, analyzing absenteeism rates on a year-to-year basis, the overall absenteeism rate stood at 3.60 percent in the first year and 3.43 percent the year after. This represents a 5% decrease from the first year to the second year of the study. It was not possible to prove a significant reduction in absenteeism over the two-year period. Discussion appears to be that the non-financial stimulus plan helps control absenteeism in the short term. As the program progressed it became more difficult to obtain prizes and this contributed to the programs losing momentum and finally ceasing. There were mixed results in wards as well. For example, in wards with staff who suffered from real long-term illness, there was little chance of winning, and to some extent the staff in those wards were understaffed. Our experience suggests that the long-term effects of incentive awards on absenteeism are questionable. During the study, the team was given a greater degree of control over their notes. This led to a significant improvement in communication between managers and staff. A similar effect was found from the implementation of the third strategy. Many of the nurses did not understand the impact that their behavior had on the organization and their colleagues, but there were also staff members who felt that talking with them about their absence was causing them and that often had a negative impact on the management-employee relationship. Conclusion Although there was some decrease in absenteeism rates, no single strategy or combination of strategies had a significant effect on absenteeism per se. Despite the disappointing results, our contention is that the strategies were not in vain. Shared ownership of absenteeism and a collaborative approach to problem solving facilitated improved collaboration and communication between management and staff. We believe that this improvement alone, although not tangibly measurable, has increased management's ability to manage the effects of absenteeism more effectively since this study.
hypothesis: Nurses in the Prince William Hospital study believed there were benefits in taking as little sick leave as possible.
label: c

premise: Adult Intelligence Over 90 years ago, Binet and Simon described two different methods for assessing intelligence. These were the psychological method (which concentrates mainly on intellectual processes, such as memory and abstract reasoning) and the pedagogical method (which concentrates on evaluating what a person knows). Binet and Simon's primary concern was to predict primary school performance independently of the individual student's social and economic background. As a result, they were satisfied with the psychological method, and they gave rise to an intelligence-assessment paradigm, which did not fundamentally change from their original tests. With few exceptions, the development of intelligence assessment devices for adults has progressed along the same lines of the Bint—Simon tests. Nevertheless, the difficulty of items was increased for older examinees. Thus, existing intelligence tests for adults were almost more formed from upward extensions of the original Bint—Simon scales. The Bint—Simon tests are quite effective in predicting school success in both primary and secondary education environments. However, they were found to predict far less success in postsecondary academic and occupational fields. Such a discrepancy raises fundamental questions about intelligence. One controversial question asks whether college success actually depends on currently used forms of measured intelligence, or that current measures of intelligence do not adequately sample the broader field of adult intellect. One possible answer to this question lies in questioning the preference of the psychological method over the pedagogical method for assessing the adult intellect. Recent studies in the fields of education, cognitive science, and adult development indicate that much of the adult intellect is indeed not adequately sampled by existing intelligence measures and may be better assessed using the pedagogical method (Ackerman, 1996; Gregory, 1994). Several lines of research have also converged on a redefinition of the adult intellect that places greater emphasis on content (knowledge) over process. Significant strides have been made in delineating knowledge aspects of intellectual performance that differ from traditional measures of intelligence (e.g., Wagner, 1987) and in demonstrating that adults' performance is strongly influenced by prior information on a subject and domain (e.g., Alexander et al., 1994). Even some older testing literature seems to indicate that knowledge measured by the Graduate Records Examination (GRE) is a similar or better indicator of future success in graduate school and graduate performance than traditional measures of ability (Willingham, 1974). Knowledge and intelligence When an adult is presented with a completely new problem (e.g., memorizing a random set of numbers or letters), the underlying intellectual processes are usually involved in predicting which people will succeed in solving problems. The dilemma for intellectual evaluation of adults is that rarely is an adult presented with a completely new problem in the real world of academic or occupational endeavors. Instead, the problems an adult is asked to solve almost necessarily rely heavily on his accumulated knowledge and skills - it's not building a house just by memorizing physics formulas. For an adult, intellect is better achieved by the tasks the person can perform and the skills he/she has developed rather than the number of digits that can be stored in working memory or the number of items of syllogistic thinking that can be correctly assessed. Thus, the content of intellect is at least as important as the processes of intellect in determining the real-world problem-solving effectiveness of adults. From the field of artificial intelligence, researchers discarded the idea of a useful general problem solver in favor of knowledge-based expert systems. This is because no amount of processing power can achieve proficiency at solving real-world problems without an extensive array of domain-relevant knowledge structures. Gregory (1994) describes the difference between concepts such as potential intelligence (knowledge) and kinetic intelligence (process). Similarly, Shank and Birnbaum (1994) say that what makes someone intelligent is what they know. One line of relevant educational research is from examining differences between experts and beginners suggesting that the typical expert is found to differ primarily from the novice in terms of experience and knowledge structures developed through the same experience rather than in terms of intellectual processes (e.g., Glaser, 1991). Further studies from developmental and gerontological perspectives have also shown that different aspects of adult intellectual functioning are largely determined by knowledge structures and less influenced by the types of process metrics, which have been shown to decrease with age across adult development (e.g., Schooler, 1987; Willis & Tosti-Vasey, 1990). CHANGING PARADIGMS BY CONSOLIDATING A VARIETY OF SOURCES OF RESEARCH EVIDENCE, IT IS CLEAR THAT OUR CURRENT METHODS OF ASSESSING MATURE INTELLECT ARE INSUFFICIENT. When faced with situations in which the intellectual performance of adults must be predicted (for example, continuing education or adult learning programs), we must begin to take into account what they know in addition to the traditional assessment of intellectual processes. Because adults are quite diverse in their knowledge structures (e.g., a physicist may know many different things than a carpenter), the challenge for future educational assessment researchers will be to develop batteries of tests that can be used to evaluate different sources of intellectual knowledge for different people. When adult knowledge structures are extensively tested with tests such as the Advanced Placement [AP] -and college-level exam program CLEP, it may be possible to improve things like predicting adult performance in specific educational endeavors, placing people, and adult educational counseling.
hypothesis: Better methods for measuring adult intelligence should be developed.

premise: Adults and children are often faced with statements about the alarming rate of tropical rainforest loss. For example, one graphic illustration to which children may readily relate is the estimate that rainforests are being destroyed at a rate equal to a thousand football fields every forty minutes - roughly the duration of a normal classroom period. In the face of the frequent and often vivid media coverage, children are likely to have formed ideas about rainforests - what and where they are, why they are important, what endangers them - independent of any formal tuition. It is also possible that some of these ideas will be misguided. Many studies have shown that children carry misconceptions about pure curriculum science. These misconceptions do not remain isolated but fit into a multifaceted, but organized conceptual framework, making it and the constituent ideas, some of which are erroneous, stronger but also amenable to change. These ideas may be developed by children who pick up ideas through popular media. Sometimes this information may be incorrect. It seems schools may not be providing an opportunity for children to re-express their ideas and so they are vetted and briefed by teachers and their friends. Despite the widespread coverage in the popular media of rainforest destruction, little official information is available about children's ideas in this area. The aim of the current study is to begin providing such information, helping teachers to shape their educational strategies to build on correct ideas and root out misconceptions and design programs in environmental studies in their schools. The study surveys children's scientific knowledge and their attitudes to rainforests. Middle school children were asked to fill out a questionnaire containing five open-form questions. The most frequent responses to the first question were self-evident descriptions of the term rainforest. Some children described them as moist, wet or warm. The second question concerned the geographical location of the rainforest. The most common responses were continents or countries: Africa (given by 43% of children), South America (30%), Brazil (25%). Some children also gave more general locations, like being near the equator. The responses to the third question concern the importance of the rainforest. The dominant idea, raised by 64% of students, was that rainforests provide animals with habitats. Fewer students responded that rainforests provide habitats for plants, and fewer mentioned the indigenous populations of the rainforest. More girls (70%) buildings (60%) raised the idea of the rainforest as a habitat for animals. Similarly, but at a lower level, more girls (13%) than buildings (5%) said that rainforests provide human habitats. These observations are generally consistent with our previous studies of students' views on the use and conservation of rainforests, in which girls were shown to be more sympathetic to animals and expressed views that seem to attach intrinsic value to non-human animal life. The fourth question touched on the causes of rainforest destruction. Perhaps encouragingly, more than half of students (59%) identified that human activities are those that destroy rainforests, some personalising the responsibility by using terms like us. About 18% of students specifically referred to tree-felling activities. One misconception, expressed by about 10% of students, was that acid rain is responsible for rainforest destruction; a similar proportion said that pollution destroys rainforests. Here, children confuse rainforest destruction with damage to Western European forests by these factors. While two-fifths of the students provided the information that rain forests provide oxygen, in some cases this response also adopted the misconception that rainforest destruction would reduce atmospheric oxygen, making the atmosphere incompatible with human life on Earth. In answer to a recent question about the importance of rainforest conservation, most children simply said we need rainforests to survive. Only a few of the students (6%) indicated that rainforest destruction may contribute to global warming. This is surprising given the high level of media coverage on this issue. Some children have expressed the idea that preserving the rainforest is not important. The results of this study suggest that certain ideas dominate children's thinking about rainforests. Students' responses point to some misconceptions in basic scientific knowledge of rainforest ecosystems, such as their ideas about rainforests as habitats for animals, plants and humans and the relationship between climate change and rainforest destruction. The students did not volunteer ideas that suggested they appreciated the complexity of the causes of rainforest destruction. In other words, they gave no indication of the range of ways in which rainforests are important or of the complex social, economic and political factors driving the activities that destroy the rainforests. One encouragement is that the results of similar studies on other environmental issues indicate that older children seem to be acquiring the ability to evaluate, evaluate, and evaluate conflicting opinions. Environmental education offers an arena in which to develop these skills, which are essential for these children as future decision makers.
hypothesis: The plight of the rainforest has been largely ignored by the media.

premise: Advantages of public transport. A new study conducted for the World Bank by Murdoch University's Science and Technology Policy Institute (ISTP) has shown that public transport is more efficient than cars. The study compared the rate of wealth poured into transportation by thirty-seven cities around the world. This included the public and private costs of building, maintaining and using a transportation system. The study found that the city of Perth in Western Australia is a good example of a city with minimal public transport. As a result, 17% of its wealth went into transportation costs. Some cities in Europe and Asia, however, spent only 5%. Professor Peter Newman, director of ISTP, pointed out that these more efficient cities were able to make a difference in attracting industry and jobs or creating a better place to live. According to Professor Newman, the greater Australian city of Melbourne is a rather unusual city in comparison of this kind. He describes it as two cities: a European city surrounded by a car-dependent city. Melbourne's large tram network has made the use of inner-city cars much lower, but the outer suburbs have the same car-based structure as most other Australian cities. The explosion in demand for accommodation in Melbourne's inner suburbs suggests a recent shift in many peoples preferences about where they live. Newman says it's a new, broader way to consider public transport issues. Previously, the argument for public transport was made on the basis of environmental and social justice considerations rather than economics. Newman, however, believes the study demonstrates that the car-dependent city model is inefficient and inadequate economically as well as environmentally. Bicycle use was not included in the study but Newman noted that the two most bike-friendly cities considered Amsterdam and Copenhagen were highly efficient, even though their public transport systems were affordable but not special. It is common for supporters of road networks to reject the models of cities with good public transport on the grounds that such systems will not work in their particular city. One objection is the climate. Some people say their city can't make more use of public transportation because it's too hot or too cold. Newman rejects this and points out that public transport has been successful in both Toronto and Singapore, and in fact, he has tested the use of cars against the climate and found zero correlation. When it comes to other physical attributes, the highway lobbies are on stronger ground. For example, Newman accepts that it would be difficult for a mountain city like Auckland to develop a really good rail network. However, he notes that both Hong Kong and Zurich have managed to succeed with their rail systems, heavy and light respectively, although there are few mountainous world cities. In fact, Newman believes the main reason for adopting one type of transport over another is politics: the more democratic the process, the more favoured public transport. He sees Portland, Oregon, as a perfect example of that. A few years ago federal money was awarded for the construction of a new road. However, local pressure groups forced a referendum on whether to spend the money on light rail instead. The rail proposal won and the tracks worked spectacularly. In the following years, more and more railway systems were introduced, dramatically changing the character of the city. Newman points out that Portland has roughly the same population as Perth and had a similar population density at the time. In Britain commute times to work have been stable for at least six centuries, as people avoided situations that required them to spend more than half an hour commuting to work. Trains and cars initially allowed people to live greater distances without taking longer to reach their destination. However, public infrastructure has not kept pace with urban sprawl, causing massive congestion problems that are now making travel times even higher. There is a widespread belief that increasing wealth encourages people to live farther away in a place where cars are the only sustainable transport. The example of European cities disproves this. They are often wealthier than their American counterparts but have not generated the same level of car use. In Stockholm car use has declined in recent years as the city has become larger and richer. A new study raises that point even more sharply. Developing cities in Asia, such as Jakarta and Bangkok, make more use of the car than wealthier Asian cities like Tokyo and Singapore. In cities that developed later, the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank discouraged the construction of public transport and people had to rely on cars that create the massive traffic jams that characterize those cities. Newman believes one of the best studies into how cities built for cars might be converted to rail use is the Urban Village Report, which used Melbourne as an example. He has found that pushing everyone into the city centre is not the best approach. Instead, the proposal advocated the creation of urban villages at hundreds of sites, mostly around railway stations. It was once assumed that improvements in telecommunications would lead to greater population dispersion because people were no longer forced into cities. However, ISTP teams research shows that the cities' population and job density increased or remained constant in the 1980s after decades of decline. The explanation for this seems to be that there is value in placing people working in related fields together. The new world will depend heavily on human creativity, and creativity flourishes where people meet face to face.
hypothesis: In Melbourne, people prefer to live in the outer suburbs.

premise: Adverts in the UK must meet standards set by the Advertising Standards Agency (ASA). This agency ensures that products are not falsely promoted and attaches a financial penalty for false statements. An example of this is post-production enhancement (PPE). PPE is a process in which images are digitally corrected after they have been taken. PPE is commonly used in skin care commercials; provides a smoother, younger, or healthier appearance than the product actually provides. Many companies find loop holes in ASA regulations regarding PPE by stating such a process was used in small print at the bottom of the image. Such promotions escape the regulations set by the Advertising Standards Agency but can still be misleading.

premise: Affordable fine art prices have dropped drastically. The art market is awash with good material, much of it from big-name artists, including Pablo Picasso and Andy Warhol. Many works are selling for less than one might expect, with items that would have earned 20,000 two years ago reaching just 5,000 to 10,000 this fall, according to Philip Hoffman, executive director of the Art Fund. Here, we summarize what seems cheap now, focusing on jobs in the 500 to 10.000 range. Picasso is one of the most iconic names in art, yet some of his ceramics and lithographs reached fewer than 1,000 each at Bonhams on Thursday. The low prices are due to the fact that he produced so many of them. However, their value steadily increased and his works would only become rarer as examples were lost. Nick McLaughton, chairman of Christies South Kensington, says that the biggest “affordable” category for leading artists is' multiple 'prints such as screen prints or lithographs in limited editions. At a Christie's sale this month, examples by Picasso, Matisse, Miro and Steinlen sold for less than 5,000 each. Alexandra Gill, head of prints at the auction house, says some of the prints are heavily handmade, or often coloured, by the artist, making them customisable. “Howard Hodgkin are a good example,” she says. There is still prejudice against prints, but for the artist it was another, equal, medium. Mr Hoffman believes that jobs of this kind are currently “as cheap as can be obtained” and will retain their value in the long term, though he admits their sheer number means prices are unlikely to rise anytime soon. It might be wiser to buy disposable real estate from lesser-known artists, he adds. For example, Christie's sale of art from the Lehmann Brothers collection on Wednesday will feature a valley with cornflowers in oil by Anthony Gross (22 of his works are held by the Tate), priced at 1,000 to 1,500. Large works by important Victorian painters are also available in this kind of price range. These pay off because their style is considered 'uncool', but they nonetheless delight a large traditional following. For example, the sale of 19th-century paintings at Bonhams on Wednesday has a Hampstead landscape by Frederick William Watts at between 6,000 and 8,000 and a study of three Spanish girls by John Benold Burgess between 4,000 and 6,000. There are proto-social realist works that also depict poverty, such as Uncared for by Augustus Edwin Mallaridi, 10,000 to 15,000 years old. Smaller auction houses offer a mix of eras and media. The sale on Tuesday at Chiswick Auctions in west London includes a 1968 screen print of Campbell's Tomato Soup by Andy Warhol, priced at 6,000 to 8,000, and 44 drawings by Augustus John, priced at 200 to 800 each. The latter were restored after the artist tore them down. Meanwhile, at the paintings and furniture sale at the Duke of Dorchester on Thursday there is a colourful block print of acrobats at play by Marc Chagall, between 100 and 200, and a lithograph of a mother and child by Henry Moore, between 500 and 700. A set of five watercolor landscape studies by Jean-Baptiste Camille Corot exceeds 1,500 to 3,000. Lucrative works by lesser-known artists and younger markets are less safe, but they have the potential to offer greater rewards if you catch an emerging trend. Speculating on such trends is high-risk, so it is worthwhile only if you like what you buy (you get something beautiful to keep, no matter what happens), can afford to lose the capital and benefit from the necessary research. A trend can be based on a country or region. China has surged, but other markets in Asia and the Middle East have yet to truly spring up. Mr. Horwich mentions some Iraqi paintings from the 1970s that he sold this year in Dubai. “They're part of a sophisticated scene that remains little known,” Hoffman says of Turkey and the Middle East. Meanwhile, Sotheby's Impressionist and Modern Art sale in New York includes a 1962 oil by Vietnam's Wu Cao Dam, a graduate of the École des Beaux Arts de l'Indochine in Hanoi and a friend of Chagall's, priced at $8000 to $12000 (5,088 to 7,632). The painting shows two girls strolling in traditional or dai dresses. Another way to make money is to try to spot talent in younger artists. The annual Paris Art Fair in Regent's Park provides an opportunity to shop from 170 contemporary galleries. Or you can bet on the future glory route of an artist based theme. For example, Gerald Laing's screen print of The Kiss (2007) showing Amy Winehouse and her ex-husband exceeds 4,700 at the malfunctioning fair.

premise: Almost everyone with or without a computer is aware of the latest technological revolution designed to forever change the way humans communicate, that is, the information highway, best exemplified by the ubiquitous Internet. Already, millions of people around the world are linked via computer simply by modem and address on the network, in much the same way that owning a phone connects us to almost anyone who pays a phone bill. In fact, because computer connections are made via the telephone line, the Internet can be perceived as a network of visual telephone links. It remains to be seen which way the information road heads, but many believe this is the educational hope of the future. The World Wide Web, a vast collection of Web addresses or sites, all of which information can be accessed, was primarily responsible for the rise in interest in the Internet in the 1990s. Before the World Wide Web, the “Web” was similar to an integrated collection of computerized typewriters, but the introduction of the 'Web' in 1990 made it possible not only to create text links but also graphs, images and even video. A website consists of a 'home page', the first screen of a particular website on the computer to which you are logged in, from which you can access other pages (or screens) related to the topic on the website and on thousands of other computers all over the world. This is achieved by a process called 'hypertext'. By clicking with a mouse device on different parts of the screen, a person connected to the “network” can go out for a walk, or browse through a screen, a person connected to the “network” can go out for a walk, or “surf” through a grid of pages to locate all the required information. Anyone can set up a website; promote your club, your institution, your company's products or simply yourself, that's what the internet and the internet are all about. Moreover, information on the Internet is not owned or controlled by a single organization. It is, perhaps, correct to say that no one and therefore everyone does not own the “network”. Because of the relative freedom of access to information, the Internet has often been criticized by the media as a potentially dangerous tool in the hands of young computer users. premise: Alternative Farming Practices in Oregon Onion growers in Eastern Oregon adopt a system that conserves water and keeps the topsoil in place, while producing the highest quality super colossal onions. Pear growers in southern Oregon have reduced their use of some of the most toxic pesticides by up to two-thirds, and are still producing top-quality pears. Range managers across the state have controlled the toxic tanzi rag with insect predators and saved the Oregon livestock industry up to $4.8 million a year. These are some of the results achieved by Oregon growers in collaboration with Oregon State University (OSU) researchers as they test new farming methods including integrated pest control (IPM). However, nationally, IPM did not provide results similar to those in Oregon. A recent report by the U.S. General Accounting Office (GAO) suggests that although integrated pest control can result in a dramatic reduction of pesticide use, the federal government lacks in effectively advancing this goal and implementing IPM. Farmers also blame the government for not making the new pest control options attractive. Wholesale changes in how farmers control pests on their farms are a costly business. Says Tony Brown, of the National Farmers Association. If farmers were given tax breaks to offset the expense, then they would willingly accept the new practices. The report goes on to note that although the use of the most dangerous pesticides has declined nationwide, they still account for more than 40 percent of all pesticides used today; and the national use of pesticides has increased by 40 million kilograms since 1992. Our food supply remains the safest and highest quality on the planet, yet we continue to overdose our farmland with potent and toxic pesticides and use less of the safe and effective alternatives, argued Patrick Leahy, who commissioned the report. Green action groups dispute the safety issue. There's no way that regular consumption of food products grown using toxic chemicals from nature found on today's farms can be healthy for consumers, noted Bill Buller, a spokesman for Green Action, one of the many lobbyists interested in this issue. The GAO report distinguishes Oregon apple and pear producers who have used the new IPM techniques with increasing success. Although Oregon is clearly ahead of the nation, scientists at OSU take the Government Accounting Office audit seriously. We must continue to develop effective alternative methods that will reduce environmental risks and produce high-quality products, said Paul Jepson, professor of entomology at OSU and new director of OSU's Integrated Plant Protection Center (IPPC). The IPPC brings together scientists from OSU's Agricultural Experiment Station, OSU Extension Service, the U.S. Department of Agriculture, and Oregon farmers to help develop agricultural systems that will conserve water and soil and reduce pesticides. In response to the GAO report, the Center placed even greater emphasis on integrating research and agriculture practices to improve Oregon agriculture environmentally and economically. The GAO report criticizes agencies for not clearly communicating the goals of the IPM, Jepson said. Our challenge is to greatly improve communication to and from growers, to learn what works and what doesn't. The work that comes from OSU researchers must be embraced in the field and not just fade out in scientific journals. In Oregon, growers and scientists are working together to drive new methods. For example, several years ago scientists at the OSus Malheur Experimental Station began testing a new drip irrigation system to replace old canals that wasted water and leached soil and fertilizer into streams. The new system reduced water and fertilizer use by half, kept topsoil in place and protected water quality. In addition, the new system produced crops of very large onions, rated super colossal and highly valued by the restaurant industry and food processors. Art Pimms, one of the researchers at Malheur comments: Growers are finding that when they adopt more environmentally benign practices, they can get excellent results. The new methods benefit the environment and give growers their success. OSU researchers in Malhor then tested mulching straw and found it successfully held the soil in place and kept the soil moist with less watering. In addition, and unexpectedly, the scientists discovered that the covered soil created a home for beneficial beetles and spiders that prey on onion thrips, a notorious pest in commercial onion fields, a discovery that could reduce the need for pesticides. 'I would never have believed we could replace the artificial pest control we had in the past and still maintain our good results, 'remarked Steve Black, a commercial onion farmer in Oregon, but instead we actually exceeded expectations. OSU researchers across the state have worked to reduce dependence on broad-spectrum chemical sprays that are toxic to many types of organisms, including humans. Consumers are rightly putting more and more pressure on the industry to change its reliance on chemical pesticides, but they still want a picture-perfect product, said Rick Hilton, an entomologist at OSU's Southern Oregon Research and Extension Center, where researchers are helping pear growers reduce the need for highly toxic pesticides. Perfect pears are an important product in Oregon and traditionally they have required a lot of chemicals. In recent years the industry has faced tough competition from overseas manufacturers, so any new method growers adopt must make sense economically as well as environmentally. Hilton is testing a growth regulator that interferes with the molting of codling moth larvae. Another study used pheromone devices to disrupt codling moth mating. These and other methods of combined pest control have allowed pear growers to reduce their use of organophosphates by two-thirds and reduce all other synthetic pesticides even further while still producing excellent quality pears. These and other statewide studies are part of the IPPC's effort to find alternative farming practices that benefit both the economy and the environment.

premise: Alternative transportation Transportation is a major issue in urban areas around the world. Rising fuel costs, environmental problems and traffic-clogged roads are some of the concerns that have led people to consider alternative forms of transport. Fuel-efficient cars and cars running on alternative energy sources are gaining increasing interest as people are more concerned about the costs of using gasoline. These costs include not only the ever-increasing price of filling a car fuel tank, but also the environmental costs of emitting massive amounts of car emissions into the atmosphere. Climate change is a topic of global concern. Closer to home, cities need to consider the effects on the health of their citizens. Car emissions have been linked to a range of health problems, particularly respiratory problems. For example, studies have linked childhood asthma and stunted lung growth to exposure to car exhaust in the air. Studies have also established links between car emissions and heart disease, certain cancers and immune system problems. The popularity of smaller, more fuel-efficient cars is on the rise. Hybrid vehicles are also becoming more common. These cars have two motors one battery-powered and one powered at in volume. The battery-powered engine causes the car to move from a standstill. Once the car reaches a certain speed, the banlin engine, which is more efficient at higher speeds, takes over to keep the car moving. There is also a growing interest in cars that are entirely battery-powered. These are cars that will be plugged into an electrical outlet for charging when not in use. Many see such vehicles as the car of the future. However, as long as the electricity is produced by coal-burning plants, as is often the case, these cars cannot be seen as using clean energy. Solar cars and hydrogen cars are other clean technologies that are gaining attention and hope for the future. CAR EMISSIONS ARE THE MOST SERIOUS SOURCE OF CONCERN, BUT THE SHEER NUMBER OF VEHICLES ON THE ROAD OVER 250 MILLION IN THE UNITED STATES ALONE AND OVER A BILLION WORLDWIDE HAS OTHER IMPLICATIONS, AS WELL. The roads and motorways built to accommodate the growing number of cars in use are a source of pollution in themselves. Pavement-covered soil cannot absorb rainwater, so engine oil and other pollutants are washed off the roads and into lakes, rivers and the ocean. Chemicals, herbicides, concrete, asphalt, paint and other materials used during road construction also contribute to environmental pollution. Personal comfort and health are also affected. While private cars are seen as a convenient way to get from place to place, congested roads mean traffic moves much slower, making travel difficult, especially during rush hour periods. And people who spend hours each day sitting in cars stuck in traffic are not standing, turning or doing any exercise, a condition that can lead to a variety of health problems. Thus, in addition to the development of passenger cars that run on alternative fuel sources, we must also examine alternative forms of transport. These will include walking, cycling, car travel and various types of public transport. The benefits of walking and cycling are obvious. They do not cause infection and improve physical health. Car pools The number of people sharing a ride in a private car means fewer cars on the road and allow riders to share the expenses involved. Buses for public transport, subway, passenger trainshave many advantages, as well. First, it may provide users with opportunities for physical activity because people need to get from their homes to the bus stations and train stations, and this is often done on foot. There are also mental health benefits, as resting on the train or bus while reading the newspaper or listening to music is much less stressful than driving your own car in rush-hour traffic. All these forms of transport reduce the number of cars on the roads and greatly reduce emissions. Looking to the future, cities should pay as much, or more, attention to public transportation and pedestrian and cyclist accommodation as to road construction and passenger car driver accommodation.
hypothesis: Electric cars do not pollute the environment.
