Fuel-efficient cars and cars running on alternative energy sources are gaining increasing interest as people are more concerned about the costs of using gasoline. These costs include not only the ever-increasing price of filling a car fuel tank, but also the environmental costs of emitting massive amounts of car emissions into the atmosphere. Climate change is a topic of global concern. Closer to home, cities need to consider the effects on the health of their citizens. Car emissions have been linked to a range of health problems, particularly respiratory problems. For example, studies have linked childhood asthma and stunted lung growth to exposure to car exhaust in the air. Studies have also established links between car emissions and heart disease, certain cancers and immune system problems. The popularity of smaller, more fuel-efficient cars is on the rise. Hybrid vehicles are also becoming more common. These cars have two motors one battery-powered and one powered at in volume. The battery-powered engine causes the car to move from a standstill. Once the car reaches a certain speed, the banlin engine, which is more efficient at higher speeds, takes over to keep the car moving. There is also a growing interest in cars that are entirely battery-powered. These are cars that will be plugged into an electrical outlet for charging when not in use. Many see such vehicles as the car of the future. However, as long as the electricity is produced by coal-burning plants, as is often the case, these cars cannot be seen as using clean energy. Solar cars and hydrogen cars are other clean technologies that are gaining attention and hope for the future. CAR EMISSIONS ARE THE MOST SERIOUS SOURCE OF CONCERN, BUT THE SHEER NUMBER OF VEHICLES ON THE ROAD OVER 250 MILLION IN THE UNITED STATES ALONE AND OVER A BILLION WORLDWIDE HAS OTHER IMPLICATIONS, AS WELL. The roads and motorways built to accommodate the growing number of cars in use are a source of pollution in themselves. Pavement-covered soil cannot absorb rainwater, so engine oil and other pollutants are washed off the roads and into lakes, rivers and the ocean. Chemicals, herbicides, concrete, asphalt, paint and other materials used during road construction also contribute to environmental pollution. Personal comfort and health are also affected. While private cars are seen as a convenient way to get from place to place, congested roads mean traffic moves much slower, making travel difficult, especially during rush hour periods. And people who spend hours each day sitting in cars stuck in traffic are not standing, turning or doing any exercise, a condition that can lead to a variety of health problems. Thus, in addition to the development of passenger cars that run on alternative fuel sources, we must also examine alternative forms of transport. These will include walking, cycling, car travel and various types of public transport. The benefits of walking and cycling are obvious. They do not cause infection and improve physical health. Car pools The number of people sharing a ride in a private car means fewer cars on the road and allow riders to share the expenses involved. Buses for public transport, subway, passenger trainshave many advantages, as well. First, it may provide users with opportunities for physical activity because people need to get from their homes to the bus stations and train stations, and this is often done on foot. There are also mental health benefits, as resting on the train or bus while reading the newspaper or listening to music is much less stressful than driving your own car in rush-hour traffic. All these forms of transport reduce the number of cars on the roads and greatly reduce emissions. Looking to the future, cities should pay as much, or more, attention to public transportation and pedestrian and cyclist accommodation as to road construction and passenger car driver accommodation.
hypothesis: Cycling has health benefits.
label: e

premise: Although commonly referred to as tidal waves, tsunamis are not caused by tides. A tsunami is a series of fast-moving waves created by disturbance above or below sea level. Although earthquakes are the most common cause of tsunamis, volcanic eruptions and landslides can also trigger tsunamis. Tsunamis can occur in any large body of water, however they usually occur in the Pacific Ocean. In open water, tsunamis travel at speeds of up to 800 mph, with wavelengths several hundred kilometers long but wave heights below one meter. As it approaches land, however, a tsunami slows down, its wavelength is compressed, and its height increases. In 2004, a catastrophic tsunami resulting from an earthquake in the Indian Ocean claimed more than 200,000 lives with 20-meter-high waves. While scientists cannot predict when a tsunami will occur, seismologists who monitor earthquakes in submarines can predict the arrival and impact of a tsunami using wave theory and measurement technology, thus allowing authorities to issue tsunami warnings.
hypothesis: Earthquakes occur most frequently in the Pacific Ocean.
label: n

premise: Although today is used to describe any movement to claim back territory for ethnic, linguistic, geographical or historical reasons, the term irredancy originally came from the Italian national movement Italia irredenta. Intended for non-redemptive Italy, Italian irredentism was an opinion movement rather than an official organization. It sought to unify ethnic Italian territories, like Trieste, Trentina and Istria, which were outside the borders of Italy at the time of Italian unification in 1866. The annexation of these Italian territories from Austria provided Italy with the strongest motive for participation in World War I. The Treaty of Versailles in 1919 satisfied most of Italy's Iredantist claims, however new borders outlined by the treaty gave rise to new Irdentist claims. The division of the German Empire into separate states created German minority populations in the new states Poland and Hungary. German Irdinate claims to these territories, as well as to Austria, resulted in World War II. The Treaty of Versailles created Yugoslavia to be a Slavic homeland, but ethnic and religious differences between Bosniaks, Serbs and Croats eventually led to war in the 1990s. The artificial political states created by the Treaty of Versailles in East Africa failed to take into account tribal boundaries, and therefore remained subject to Irrentistic claims. Similarly, boundaries set in the Near East are still disputed today.
hypothesis: Trieste, Trentina and Istria were re-united with Italy following the Treaty of Versailles.
label: n

Intended for non-redemptive Italy, Italian irredentism was an opinion movement rather than an official organization. It sought to unify ethnic Italian territories, like Trieste, Trentina and Istria, which were outside the borders of Italy at the time of Italian unification in 1866. The annexation of these Italian territories from Austria provided Italy with the strongest motive for participation in World War I. The Treaty of Versailles in 1919 satisfied most of Italy's Iredantist claims, however new borders outlined by the treaty gave rise to new Irdentist claims. The division of the German Empire into separate states created German minority populations in the new states Poland and Hungary. German Irdinate claims to these territories, as well as to Austria, resulted in World War II. The Treaty of Versailles created Yugoslavia to be a Slavic homeland, but ethnic and religious differences between Bosniaks, Serbs and Croats eventually led to war in the 1990s. The artificial political states created by the Treaty of Versailles in East Africa failed to take into account tribal boundaries, and therefore remained subject to Irrentistic claims. Similarly, boundaries set in the Near East are still disputed today.
hypothesis: Although originally an Italian movement, Iredantist claims are now made in other countries.

premise: Americans are currently choosing among many more options in many parts of life than has ever been possible before. To some extent, the opportunity to choose improves our lives. It's only logical to think that if a few choices are good, the better; people who care about having infinite possibilities will benefit from them, and those who don't can always just ignore the 273 cereal versions they've never tried. However, recent studies strongly indicate that psychologically, this assumption is wrong, with a percentage as low as 5% reporting that they are happy. Although some options are arguably better than none, more isn't always better than less. Recent studies offer insight into why many people end up dissatisfied and dissatisfied when their options expand. We started by distinguishing between maximizers (those who always strive to make the best choice possible) and providers (those who aim for good enough, whether there are better choices or not). In particular, we have compiled a system of statements on the maximization scale to diagnose people's tendency to maximize. Then we had several thousand people who rated themselves between 1 and 7 (total disagreement to total agreement) on statements like this since I never settle for second best. We also appreciated their sense of satisfaction with their decisions. We have not defined a sharp limit for separating maximizers from satisfiers, but in general, we think of people whose average scores are higher than 4 (the midpoint of the scales) as maximizers and those whose scores are lower than the midpoint as satisfiers. People who get the highest score on the test - the biggest maximizers engage in more comparisons of products than the lowest winners, both before and after they make purchasing decisions, and take them longer to decide what to buy. When vendors find an item that meets their standards, they stop looking. But maximizers exert enormous effort in reading labels, checking consumer magazines and trying out new products. They also spend more time comparing their purchasing decisions to those of others. We found that the biggest maximizers are the least satisfied with the fruits of their efforts. When they compare themselves to others, they benefit little from finding out that they have done better and a fundamental dissatisfaction from finding out that they have done worse. They are more likely to experience regret after a purchase, and if their purchase disappoints them, their sense of well-being takes longer to recover. They also tend to ponder or contemplate more than satisfy. Is it because maximizers are less happy in general than satisfiers? We tested this by having people fill out a variety of questionnaires known as reliable indicators of well-being. As expected, people with high maximization scores experienced less satisfaction with life and were less happy, less optimistic, and more depressed than people with low maximization scores. Indeed, people with extreme maximization ratings had depression scores that placed them at the limit of the clinical range. Several factors explain why more choice is not always better than less, especially for maximizers. High among these are opportunity costs. The quality of any given option cannot be assessed separately from its alternatives. One of the costs of choosing is the loss of opportunities that another option would have afforded. Thus, an opportunity cost of a beach vacation on Cape Cod may miss out on the great restaurants in Napa Valley. Early research on decision-making by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky showed that people react much more strongly to losses than to gains. If we assume that opportunity costs reduce the overall desire of the most preferred choice, then the more alternatives there are, the deeper our sense of loss will be and we will derive less satisfaction from our final decision. The opportunity costs problem would be better for a provider. The last good enough philosophy can survive thoughts of opportunity costs. Plus, the good enough standard leads to a lot less searching and testing of alternatives than the best standard of maximizers. With fewer options on the exam, a person will have fewer opportunity costs for subtraction. Just as people feel sorrow for the opportunities they have given up, they may also suffer regret at the possibility they were satisfied with. MY COLLEAGUES AND I DESIGNED A SCALE TO MEASURE TENDENCY TO FEEL REGRET, AND WE FOUND THAT PEOPLE WITH HIGH SENSITIVITY TO REGRET ARE LESS HAPPY, LESS SATISFIED WITH LIFE, LESS OPTIMISTIC, AND MORE DEPRESSED THAN THOSE WITH LOW SENSITIVITY. Not surprisingly, we also found that people with a high sensitivity to regret tend to maximize. Indeed, we think that concern about future regret is a key reason why people become magicians. The only way to be sure you won't regret a decision is by making the best decision possible. Unfortunately, the more options you have and the more opportunity costs you have, the more likely you are to experience regret. In a classic demonstration of the power of sunk costs, people were offered subscriptions to a local theatre troupe's season. Some were offered the tickets at full price and others at a discount. Then the researchers simply tracked how often ticket buyers did attend showings during the season. Full-price payers were more likely to show up at shows than discount-payers. The reason, the researchers argued, was that full-price payers would experience more regret if they didn't use the cards because not using the more expensive cards would constitute a greater loss. To increase the feeling of happiness, we can decide to limit our options when the decision is not decisive. For example, make a rule to visit no more than two stores when shopping for clothes.

MOST OF THE ART DISCOVERED SO FAR FROM THE ONGOING EXCAVATIONS COMES FROM THE ARCHAEOLOGICALLY IMPORTANT SERRA DE CAPIVERA NATIONAL PARK IN THE STATE OF PEAWI, AND IT IS CAUSING QUITE A BIT OF CONTROVERSY. The reason for the uproar? The art is dated to around 25,000 or possibly. According to some archaeologists, even 36,000 years ago. If true, this should challenge the broad field view that America was first settled from the north, via the Bering Strait from eastern Siberia around 10.000 BC. Just moving down to Central and South America in the thousands of years that followed. Before the designation of 130,000 acres as a national park, the rock art sites were difficult to reach and often dangerous to enter. In ancient times, this inaccessibility must have increased the importance of the sites, and indeed of the people who painted on the rocks. Wildlife and human figures dominate the art and are incorporated into often complex scenes involving hunting, supernatural creatures, fighting, and dancing. The artists depicted the animals that roamed the local ancient paintbrush forest. The large mammals are usually painted in groups and tend to show them a running position, as if trying to escape hunting parties. Processional lines of human and animal figures also seem to possess great impotence to these ancient artists. Could such lines represent family units or groups of fighters? On several panels, rows of stylized figures, some numbering up to 30 individual figures, were painted using the natural wavy contours of the rock surface, which evokes the outline of the second landscape Other interesting occurrences, but very rare, are scenes showing small human figures clinging and dancing around a tree, possibly involved in some ritual dance. Due to the favorable climatic conditions. The imagery on many panels is in an unusual state of preservation. Despite this, there are serious conservation issues that affect their long-term survival. The chemical and mineral amounts of the rock on which the images are placed is fragile and in some slabs it is unstable. In addition to the excretion of sodium carbonate on the rock surface, entire panel sections were broken off during the ancient and recent past from the main rock surface. These were then buried and sealed in sometimes ancient floor deposits. Perversely, this form of natural erosion and subsequent focusing has helped archaeologists date several key rock art sites. Of course, art dating is extremely difficult for the non-existence of plant and animal remains that might be scientifically dated. However, there are a small number of sites in the Serra de Capibra that give up their secrets through good systematic excavation. Thus, in Toca do Rocchiomo de Padre Forde. Along with painted toe fragments, crude stone tools were found. Also discovered were a host of scientifically datable sites of fireplaces, or hearths, the earliest dated to 46,000 BC. Arguably the oldest dates for human habitation in America. However, these conclusions tended to be without controversy. Visitors, mainly from North America, have suggested that the hearth may in fact be a natural phenomenon, the result of seasonal brushwood fires. Adding further silliness to the general debate is the fact that the artists in the National Hark area tended not to paint old motifs (as is often the case in rock art), making the relative chronology of the images or styles difficult. However, the variety of imagery and narrative that the paintings create from each of the many sites in the national park suggest that different artists probably made their art at varying times, and may have used each site for many thousands of years. With fierce debates raging about the dating, the origin of these artists is still very much open to speculation. The traditional view ignores the earliest dating evidence from South American rock art sites. In a revised scenario, some paleo-anthropologists now propose that modern humans migrated from Africa via the strong currents of the Atlantic Ocean about 63.000 years or more ago, while others suggest a more unlikely colonization coming from the Pacific Ocean. However, while the site hypothesis is plausible, there is still no supporting archaeological evidence between the South American coastline and the interior. Instead, it appears that there were several waves of human colonization in the Americas that occurred perhaps over a 60,000-100,000 year period, likely using the Bering Strait as a land bridge to cross the Americas. Despite the compelling evidence from South America, it stands alone: the earliest secure human evidence found so far in the North American state of Oregon dates back only to 12,300 years BC. So this is a fierce debate that may continue for many years to come. Yet the great rock art and its allied anthropology in northeastern Brazil, described here, play a huge and significant role in the debate.

premise: Essential Mediator has a strange irony about the blue whale. With adult adults up to 30 feet long and weighing nearly 200 tons, it is not only the largest animal in the world, but also the largest there has ever been. Yes, even the most impressive dinosaurs from the Jurassic period couldn't match this sleek, streamlined aquatic mammal in scale. So where's the irony? It lies in the fact that this huge animal feeds mainly on one of the smallest life forms in the oceans, a tiny crab known as krill. Krill lives in every ocean in the world. They therefore come in many varieties, although all of them have a similar shrimp-like appearance, with an exoskeleton divided into three parts, and with two large antennae on the front, and pairs of legs running along the underside. These creatures are distinguished from shrimps by their gills, which are mounted externally, and resemble rows of fibrous combs alongside their bodies. Another oddity is that their exoskeleton is usually transparent. This, and their small size, lead to the misleading conclusion that they are an immaterial presence, of little importance, until it is learned that an adult blue whale can consume nearly 40 million krill, weighing a total of 3,600 kg, in just one day. It is this, their sheer number, that makes these mysterious ghost-like crustaceans so important. Just looking at one species, the Antarctic krill, their collective weight (or biological mass) is estimated at about 500 million tons. In other words, it is more than twice the weight of all humans currently on Earth. Some scientists estimate that each year, up to half of that is eaten by whales, seals, penguins, squid and fish, illustrating that krill constitutes a vast food resource for other animals. The question is whether humans can actually get in. Antarctic krill is the largest species, at six centimeters. Most other species are about two inches long, and this makes them awkward to catch. Very fine fishing nets are needed, but they are difficult to drag in the water, quickly clogged and easily broken. In addition, when raised in large piles, the delicate krill crush each other, forcing their internal fluids out. They must also be peeled for the highest levels of fluoride in their exoskeleton, and finally, they must be prepared and frozen quickly because of the strong enzymes in their gut, which would otherwise cause rapid decay. It is problems like these that have limited the processed krill to be used primarily as fish food in aquariums or aquaculture, or bait in commercial fishing operations, but otherwise very much outside the public mind. Seafood-loving Japan is the only country in the world where few krills end up on the table. The cooked, peeled and frozen tail meat is sold on the market, and there is a low-grade krill paste used as a flavoring or coloring agent for food. These products originate from the small krill in the North Pacific, but it is the large Antarctic species that seems to offer the best commercial prospects, and perhaps a more appetizing meal. Most krill ships are therefore directed to waters around the Antarctic coast, but this is a remote area, subject to adverse weather conditions, making operations there difficult and expensive, as well as raising issues of the ecological consequences, especially given the importance of krill as the basis of the food chain in that pristine and unspoiled environment. To fully explore this food chain, however, it must be further reduced. Krill themselves are filter feeders, which use very fine comb-like appendages at the front of their bodies to extract microscopic organisms known as phytoplankton. These live in almost every body of water in the world, but only in the well-lit surface layers, since these organisms need exposure to sunlight, from which they obtain their energy. In the same way that plants on land are ultimately the basis of all food chains there, so is phytoplankton in the oceans. Since krill exist in such large numbers, then, logically, their main food source must be even more numerous. There are, in fact, so many phytoplankton that their collective photosynthesis accounts for up to half of the oxygen produced in the world. However, as with krill, the sheer number of phytoplankton lives unnoticed and is not observed. Their presence can only be inferred indirectly when they are pressed together by currents, where there can be correspondingly high concentrations of krill feeding on them. This can similarly result in the fact that the individual blue whales are usually found together, revealing one of nature's most remarkable and elusive food webs: from phytoplankton, to krill to the blue whale. In other words, from the smallest elements in nature, in two short steps leading to a mighty and awe-inspiring whale of the deep, the largest animal that ever existed. And the little ghost krill are the vital intermediary in this miraculous process.
hypothesis: Some dinosaurs were larger than the blue whale.

I couldn't see any sheep jumping over fences, there was nothing to count. Our memories are often linked in pictures, think of a wedding or Sunday at school. As a result, admits Neil, some aspects of his memory are terrible, but he is very good at remembering facts. And like others with aphantasia, he has trouble recognizing faces. When I think of my fiancée there is no image, but I definitely think of her, I know that today she has hair on the back, she is a brunette. But I don't describe a picture I'm looking at, I remember features on it, that's the weirdest thing and maybe it's a source of some regret. The reaction of his friends is very sympathetic: you are strange. But while Niall is very relaxed about his inability to imagine things, it causes distress for others. Meanwhile, Douglas Hofstetter of Indiana University said that EMI has created replicas that still rely entirely on the creative impulses of the original artist. premise: As their name suggests, Asian carp are not native to the United States, but these invasive fish have become the subject of a Supreme Court lawsuit. Introduced in the US in 1831, carps were originally intended for consumption although today they are not widely eaten. Populations have boomed in the Mississippi and Illinois rivers since the 1970s, when it is thought they fled fish farms in the Midwest during heavy floods. Carp consume only plankton, though copious amounts of it, and some species of Asian carp can grow to more than a hundred pounds. Not only are the fish a danger to recreational boaters, they also outcompete native species for food and space. Environmentalists fear that carp will penetrate the Great Lakes, using locks that connect the Mississippi to Lake Michigan, where they will damage the ecosystem. They also fear that by pushing out species like salmon, Asian carp will also harm the Great Lakes sport-fishing industry. The U.S. government currently spends $80 million a year on Asian carp control, using methods like toxins and underwater electrical barriers designed to repel carp. Evidence of carp in Lake Michigan has led anti-crepe activists to call for stronger measures, like blocking the locks on the Chicago Canal. Business interests strongly oppose the closure of this major shipping lane for economic reasons, and also argue that forcing canal traffic onto roads would cause pollution.
hypothesis: The anticarp activists are motivated by environmental concerns rather than by business interests.
label: c

After the cutting season, the spears are allowed to mature so that the plants can re-establish. The spears of cultivated varieties are much thicker than those grown in nature and the crown (shallow root ball) is much larger, but the taste of wild asparagus is better. premise: Attitudes to language are not easy to be systematic and objective about learning a language. The popular linguistic debate regularly degenerates into polemic and polemic. Language belongs to everyone, which is why most people feel they have a right to hold an opinion about it. And when opinions differ from each other, emotions can rise. Debates can start just as easily on points of easy use as on central policies of linguistic education. Furthermore, language is a very public behavior, so it is easy to specify and criticize various uses. No part of society or social behavior is exempt: linguistic factors influence how we judge personality, intelligence, social status, educational standards, work ability, and many other areas of identity and social survival. As a result, it is easy to offend and be offended when the use of language is attacked without emotion. In the most general sense, perspectivism is the view that one variety of languages has an inherently higher value than others, and that this should be imposed on the entire speech community. The view is offered particularly in relation to grammar and vocabulary, and often in reference to pronunciation. The preferred variety, in this account, is usually a variant of the 'standard' written language, especially as encountered in literature, or the formal spoken language that most closely reflects this style. It is said that the adherents of this variety speak or write 'correctly'; it is said that deviations from it are not true! All major languages have been studied prescriptively, especially in the 18th-century approach to writing grammars and dictionaries. The goals of these early grammarians were threefold: (a) they wanted to encode the principles of their languages, to show that there was a system underneath the apparent chaos of use, (b) they wanted a means of settling disputes over usage, and (c) they wanted to point out what they felt to be common errors, in order to 'improve' the language. The authoritative nature of the approach is best characterized by its reliance on the rules of grammar. Some uses are “prescribed,” to be studied and followed precisely; others are “forbidden,” to be avoided. In this early period there were no semi-means: usage was right or wrong, and it was the grammarian's job not only to document alternatives, but to express judgment on them. These attitudes are still with us, and they prompt widespread concern that linguistic standards should be maintained. However, there is an alternative point of view that deals less with standards than with the facts of linguistic use. This approach is summarized in the statement that it is the grammar's job to describe, not register and document the facts of linguistic diversity, nor attempt the impossible tasks of assessing language variation or stopping language change. In the second half of the 18th century, we already find supporters of this view, such as Joseph Fristy, whose Foundations of English Grammar (1761) insists that “the custom of speech is the original and only standard of any language! Linguistic issues, it has been argued, are not solvable by logic and legislation. And this concept has become the principle of the modern linguistic approach to grammatical analysis. Nowadays, the opposition between 'theorists' and 'perspectivists' has often become extreme, with both sides painting unrealistic pictures of the other. Descriptive grammarians have been portrayed as people who don't care about standards, because of the way they view all forms of usage as equally valid. Prescriptive grammarians have been shown to be blind adherents to historical tradition. The opposition was even presented in quasi-political terms - of radical liberalism versus elitist conservatism.
hypothesis: Our assessment of a person's intelligence is influenced by how he or she uses language.
label: e

premise: Bright light! BUG CITY, IN THE HEART OF AFRICA'S SAVANNAH, IS A CITY BUILT ENTIRELY FROM NATURAL AND BIODEGRADABLE MATERIALS, AND IS A MODEL OF SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT. Its curved walls, arches and graceful towers are also quite beautiful. It's not a human city, of course. It's a termite mound. Without termites and other nest-building insects, humans pay little attention to structures appropriate to their environment. However, as we grapple with climate change and resource depletion, interest in how insects manage their built environment is increasing, and we have much to learn. “The construction mechanisms and design principles that amplify the properties of possible insect nests are not well understood,” says Guy Thrulz of the Research Centre for Animal Cognition in France. It's not for lack of experience. Research on termite mounds dissipated in the 1960s, when Swiss entomologist Martin Lischer conducted groundbreaking studies on nests created by termites of the genus Macrotermes in the plains of South Africa. Lischer was the one who suggested that the chaotic mounds were actually superbly engineered ecological constructions. Specifically, he suggested an intimate connection between how the mounds were built and what the termites eat. MACROTHERM SPECIES LIVE ON CELLULOSE, A COMPONENT OF PLANT MATTER THAT HEMAKEN CANNOT DIGEST. In fact, neither can termites. They get around this by cultivating gardens for mushrooms, which can turn it into digestible nutrients. These areas must be well ventilated, their temperature and humidity closely controlled - no mean feat in the tropical climate where termites live. In Lischer's theory, heat from the metabolism of the fungi and termite bodies causes stagnant air, laden with carbon dioxide, to rise up a central chimney. From there it swings outward through the porous walls of the mound, while new air is sucked in at the base. THIS SIMPLE AND APPEALING IDEA HAS SPAWNED AT LEAST ONE ARTIFICIAL IMITATION: THE EASTGATE CENTRE IN HARARE, ZIMBABWE, DESIGNED BY ARCHITECT MICH PIERCE, WHICH BOASTS A TERMITE-INSPIRED VENTILATION AND COOLING SYSTEM. However, it turns out that few termite mounds if any go this way. Scott Turner, a termite expert at New Vera State University, and Rupert Soer a free-form engineer in Nottingham, UK, tested the design principles of Macrotermes mounds in Namibia. They found that the mound walls were warmer than the central nest, negating the kind of buoyant outward flow of CO^-rich air that Lisher suggested. INDEED, TRACKED GAS INJECTION INTO THE MOUND SHOWED LITTLE EVIDENCE OF CONSTANT AIRFLOW AND RECEPTION. Turner and Saar believe that termite mounds instead tap turbulence in the wind gusts that hit them. One breath of wind contains small swirls and currents that vary in speed and direction at different frequencies. The outer walls of the mounds are constructed to allow only vortices varying at low frequencies to penetrate deep within them. As the frequency range in the wind changes from gust to gust, the boundary between the stale air in the nest and the fresh air from outside moves within the walls of the mounds, allowing the two air bodies to be replaced. Essentially, the mound functions as a giant area. j This is very different from the way ventilation works in modern human buildings, where fresh air is blown in through vents to flush stale air out. Turner thinks there is something to be gleaned from the termites' j approach. “We could have turned the whole idea of the wall on its head,” he says. “We should not think of j-walls as barriers to stop the exterior from entering the inside, but rather design them as adaptive and porous interfaces that regulate the exchange of heat and air between the interior and the outside. Instead of opening a window to let in fresh air, the wall will be the one doing it, but it is filtered and carefully manages the way termite mounds do it. Turner's ideas were among many discussed at a workshop on insect architecture organized by Thraulz in Venice, Italy, last year. Its aim was to bind understanding from a range of disciplines, from insect behaviour specialists to practising architects. “Some real touchpoints have started to emerge,” Turner says. “There was a prevailing idea among biologists that architects could get a lot out of us. I think the opposite is also true. 'One issue was how adept termites are at adapting their buildings to local conditions. Termites in very hot climates, for example, embed their mounds deep in the soil - an incredibly effective way of regulating temperature. “The more we understand, this opens up a vast universe of new design principles inspired by biology,” Turner says. Such approaches are the opposite of modern human ideas of design and control, in which a central outline is pre-laid by an architect and carefully adhered to. But Turner thinks we could find ourselves adopting a more insect-like approach as technological advances make it doable.

premise: Because the UK government has never carried out a large-scale campaign to “put a Briton on the moon,” few know much about the British space programme. Unlike many other national space initiatives, the official focus of the British space programme has always been on unmanned satellite launches and, in fact, the UK has banned human space flight since 1986. All British astronauts who traveled in outer space during the ban did so with funding from non-governmental sources, either as “space tourists” or by acquiring American citizenship and joining the NASA program. However, interest in a British space program began much earlier. The British Interstellar Association, founded in 1933, prompted early research in the field and developed Britain's military interest in a space program. During the 1960s and 1970s, Britain launched a number of satellites and rockets: some on the Isle of Wight, some in Woomera, Australia, where a joint Australia-UK arms and space testing facility is located. More than 6,000 rockets have been launched from Woomera, including the Falstaff hypersonic rocket and the Black Arrow satellite launch rocket. The Ariel programme saw the UK develop and launch six satellites between 1962 and 1979, in collaboration with NASA; the last four spacecraft in this series were designed and built in the UK. At the time, Britain played no role in the “space race” between the world's two military powers that led to the first men setting foot on the moon, in a series of American-commanded missions that captured the world's imagination from 1969 to 1972. Since the rise of manned space flight, both the US and the Soviet Union (and later Russia) have included astronauts from Europe and other parts of the world on space missions. The official programme of satellite launches in the UK was cancelled in the early 1980s, but in 1985 the British National Space Centre was established to coordinate space activities in the UK. Today, the British Space Agency, founded in Wiltshire in 2010, has replaced the British National Space Centre and assumed responsibility for government policy and budgets for space exploration. Over the next twenty years, the agency aims to increase the size of the British space industry from 6 billion to 40 billion, and create over 30,000 jobs. Central to this programme is the new £40 million International Space Innovation Centre in Oxfordshire, which will study climate change and space systems security.

premise: Before the 20th century, relatively little was known about the atom. The idea that objects are made of smaller particles that cannot be smaller was described by two Greek philosophers; Lucipus and Democritus. They believed that if you continued to cut an object consistently, there would come a point when it would not be possible to cut it further. Therefore, the theory of the atom was established but could not be investigated further. In 1897, J. J. Thompson discovered the electron. He inserted a hot metal coil into an electric field, thus producing the first cathode ray. Importantly, he noticed that the cathode ray could be deflected by a magnetic field, when seen under a cloud chamber, and realized that it was negatively charged. Since the atom is neutral, it is proposed that there must be positively charged particles that give the atom total neutrality. J.J. THOMPSON INTRODUCED THE ATOMIC PLUMPODING MODEL THEORY; THAT POSITIVELY CHARGED PARTICLES AND NEGATIVELY CHARGED PARTICLES ARE MIXED TOGETHER IN AN INFINITELY SMALL REGION OF SPACE. In 1911 Ernest Rutherford performed the gold leaf experiment. He fired alpha particles at gold leaf and found that although most of the alpha particles passed, some were deflected. Occasionally he also saw a small spark in the collision. From this, he described that the atom cannot be a mixture of negatively and positively charged particles, but rather has a dense core of positively charged particles. He called these particles protons. He also realized that most of the atom is empty space. In 1932, James Chadwick performed an experiment that discovered the final component of the atom. In observing alpha decay, he noticed that one of the emitted particles was not deflected by a magnetic field, hence it was neutrally charged. He called this particle a neutron. Thus the Rutherford model of the atom was born; the protons and neutrons form the nucleus of the atom, whose electrons rotate in orbit.

premise: Bilingualism in children One misguided legacy of over a hundred years of writing about bilingualism is that children's intelligence will suffer if they are bilingual. Some of the earliest studies on bilingualism examined whether bilingual children were ahead or behind monolingual children2 on IQ tests. From the 1920s to the 1960s, the tendency was to find monolingual children ahead of bilingual on IQ tests. The conclusion was that bilingual children were mentally confused. Two languages in the brain, it was said, disrupted effective thinking. It has been argued that one developed language is superior to two semi-developed languages. The idea that bilinguals may have lower IQs still exists among many people, especially monolinguals. However, we now know that this early study was misguided and wrong. First, such research often gave bilinguals an IQ test in their weaker language, usually English. Had bilinguals been tested in Welsh or Spanish or Hebrew, a different result might have been found. The scrutiny of bilinguals was therefore unfair. Second, Lake was not compared to Lake. Bilinguals tended to come, for example, from a poor New York background or rural Welsh. Monolinguals tended to come from more middle-class urban families. Working-class bilinguals have often been compared with middle-class monolinguals. So the results would have been due more to differences in social classes than to language differences. The comparison between monolinguals and bilinguals was unfair. The latest research from Canada, the United States and Wales suggests that bilinguals equal at least monolinguals in IQ tests. When bilinguals have two well-developed languages (in the research literature called balanced bilinguals), bilinguals tend to show slight superiority in IQ tests compared to monolinguals. This is the received psychological wisdom of the moment and is good news for raising bilingual children. Take, for example, a child who can act in two languages in the school curriculum. This child is most likely to advance in IQ tests compared to owners of a similar monolingual language (same gender, social status, and age). Far from making people mentally confused, bilingualism is now associated with a slight degree of intellectual superiority. One note of caution should be sounded. IQ tests probably don't measure intelligence. IQ tests measure a small sample of the broadest concept of intelligence. IQ tests are simply paper-and-pencil tests in which only correct and incorrect answers are allowed. Is all intelligence summed up in such right and wrong, pencil and paper tests? Isn't there a wider range of intelligences that are important in daily functioning and in everyday life? Many questions need an answer. Do we define an intelligent person only as someone who scores high on an IQ test? Are the only intelligent people the ones who belong to high IQ organizations like MENSA? Is there social intelligence, musical intelligence, military intelligence, marketing intelligence, motor intelligence, political intelligence? Are all, or indeed all of these forms of intelligence, measured by a simple pencil-and-paper IQ test that requires a single, acceptable, and correct solution to each question? Defining what constitutes intelligent behavior requires personal value judgments about the type of behavior and which type of person is worth more. The current state of psychological wisdom regarding bilingual children is that when two languages are relatively developed, bilinguals have reasoning advantages over monolinguals. Take an example. A child is asked a simple question: How many uses can you think of offering a brick? Some children give only two or three answers. They can think about building walls, building a house and maybe that's it. Another child scribbles, pouring ideas one by one: blocks a rabbit hole, breaks a window, uses as a birdbath, as a plumbing line, as an abstract sculpture in an art exhibition. Studies in different continents of the world show that bilinguals tend to be more fluent, flexible, original and extended in their answers to this type of open-ended questions. The person who can think of several answers tends to be called a convergent thinker. They converge to a few generally accepted conventional answers. People who think of a lot of different uses for unusual items (e.g. brick, tin can, cardboard box) are called sprinklers. Differentiators like a variety of answers to a question and are imaginative and dominate their thinking. There are other dimensions of thinking in which roughly balanced bilinguals may have temporary and sometimes permanent advantages over monolinguals: increased sensitivity to communication, slightly faster movement in stages of cognitive development, and being less fixed in the sounds of words and more centered on the meaning of words. Such an ability to move away from the sound of words and correct the meaning of words tends to be a (temporary) advantage for bilinguals around the ages of four to six This advantage may be an initial advantage in learning to read and learning to think about language.
hypothesis: Bilinguals who are just starting to learn may pick up certain skills faster than monolinguals.

premise: Biodiversity Biodiversity seems to have become a favorite keyword for politicians, conservationists, protesters and scientists alike. But what exactly is it? The Convention on Biological Diversity, an international treaty for the conservation and distribution of the biological wealth of the planets, provides a well-worked definition: biodiversity includes every form of life, from the smallest bacterium to the largest animal or plant, the genes that give them their specific characteristics and the ecosystems from which they are separate. In October, the World Conservation Union (also known as the IUCN) published its updated Red List of Threatened Species, a reading of 11,167 creatures facing extinction 121 more than when the list was last published in 2000. But the new figures almost certainly downplay the crisis. About 1.2 million animal species and 270,000 plant species have been classified, but the welfare of only a fraction has been assessed. The resources are simply not available. The RJCN reports that 5714 plants are threatened, for example, but admits that only 4 percent of known plants have been assessed. And, of course, there are thousands of species that we have yet to discover. Many of these may also face extinction. It is important to develop a picture of the diversity of life on Earth now so that comparisons can be made in the future and trends can be identified. But it is not necessary to observe every type of organism in an area to get a snapshot of ecosystem health. In many habitats there are species that are particularly sensitive to changing conditions, and these can be used as indicator species in the media, usually it is large and charismatic animals such as pandas, elephants, tigers and whales that receive all the attention when discussing the loss of biodiversity. However, animals or plants much lower down the food chain are often the ones that are essential for conserving habitats in the process of saving the skins of those more luminous species. These are known as keystone species. By studying the complex feeding relationships within habitats, it is possible to identify species that have a particularly important impact on the environment. For example, members of the fig family are the main food for hundreds of different species in many different countries, so important that scientists sometimes call figs jungle burgers. A whole range of animals, from tiny insects to birds and large mammals, feed on everything from tree bark and leaves to flowers and fruit. Many fig species have very specific pollinators. There are several dozen species of fig trees in Costa Rica, and a different type of wasp has evolved to pollinate each of them. Chris Lyle of the Natural History Museum in London who is also involved in the Convention on Biological Diversity's global taxonomy initiative points out that if fig trees were affected by global warming, pollution, disease or any other catastrophe, the loss of biodiversity would be enormous. Similarly, sea otters play a key role in the survival of huge kelp forests along the coasts of California and Alaska. These marine rainforests provide a home to a wide variety of other species. Algae itself is the main food of purple and red sea urchins and in turn, the hedgehogs are eaten by predators, especially sea otters. They detach a hedgehog from the seabed then float to the surface and lie on their backs with the hedgehog's shell on their stomachs, smashing it with a stone before eating the contents. premise: Biological pest control The continued and reckless use of synthetic chemicals to control pests that pose a threat to agricultural crops and human health is proving counterproductive. Besides creating widespread ecological disturbances, pesticides have contributed to the emergence of a new strain of chemical-resistant and highly lethal superbugs. According to a recent study by the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), more than 300 species of agricultural pests have developed resistance to a wide range of potent chemicals. The disease-spreading pests, about 100 species of which have become immune to a variety of insecticides now in use, cannot be left behind. One glaring disadvantage of pesticide application is that while destroying harmful pests, they also wipe out many useful organisms that are not targeted, which keep the pest population growing. The result is what agroecologists call the treadmill syndrome. Because of their enormous reproductive potential and genetic diversity, many pests are known to withstand synthetic chemicals and bear offspring that have a built-in resistance to pesticides. The devastation that the walker syndrome can cause is well illustrated by what happened to Central American cotton farmers. In the early 1940s, basking in the glory of chemical-based intensive agriculture, farmers eagerly took up pesticides as a safe means of boosting crop yields. The insecticide was applied eight times a year in the mid-1940s, rising to 28 a season in the mid-1950s, following the sudden spread of three new strains of chemical-resistant pests. IN THE MID-1960S, THE SITUATION TOOK AN ALARMING TURN WITH THE OUTBREAK OF FOUR MORE NEW PESTS, WHICH NECESSITATED SPRAYING OF PESTICIDES TO THE POINT THAT 50% OF THE FINANCIAL EXPENDITURE ON COTTON PRODUCTION WAS DUE TO PESTICIDES. In the early 1970s, spraying often reached 70 times a season as farmers were pushed to the wall by invading genetically stronger insect species. Most pesticides currently on the market remain inadequately tested for cancer-causing and mutation-causing traits, as well as other negative health effects, says a study by environmental agencies in the United States. The U.S. National Resource Protection Board found that DDT was the most popular of a long list of hazardous chemicals used. In the face of increasing dangers from indiscriminate applications of pesticides, a more effective and more ecological strategy of biological pest control, which involves the selective use of natural enemies of the pest population, is rapidly gaining popularity - although, so far, this is a new field with limited potential. The advantage of biological control as opposed to other methods is that it provides a relatively low-cost perpetual control system with minimal harmful side effects. When handled by specialists, the biocontrol is safe, non-polluting and self-dispersing. The Commonwealth Institute of Biological Control (CIBC) in Bangalore, with its worldwide network of research laboratories and field stations, is one of the active, non-commercial research agencies engaged in pest control by pitting natural predators against parasites. CIBC also serves as a clearing house for the export and import of pesticide biomaterials worldwide. CIBC HAS SUCCESSFULLY USED THE SEED-FEEDING INVOICE, NATIVE TO MEXICO, TO CONTROL THE NASTY PARTHENIUM WEED, KNOWN TO EXERT AN INSIDIOUS INFLUENCE ON AGRICULTURE AND HUMAN HEALTH IN BOTH INDIA AND AUSTRALIA. Similarly, the Regional Research Laboratory in Hyderabad (RRL), supported by CIBC, is now trialling Argentine weevils to eradicate water hyacinth, another dangerous weed, which has become a nuisance in many regions of the world. According to Ms. Kaiser Jamil of RRL, Argentine weevil does not attack any other 74 plants and a pair of adult insects can destroy the weed in 4-5 days. CIBC is also perfecting the technique for breeding parasites that prey on Dyspene scale insects - notorious leafhoppers of fruit trees in the US and India. The extent to which biological control can be exercised effectively is proven by the following examples. In the late 1960s, when Sri Lanka's flourishing coconut plantations were hit by leaf-mining hispids, a larval parasite imported from Singapore brought the pest under control. A natural predator native to India, Neodumetia sangawani, has been found useful in controlling the Rhodes scale grass insect that devours forage grass in many U.S. regions. By using Neochetina bruci, a beetle native to Brazil, scientists from the Kerala Agricultural University freed a 12-kilometer-long trench from the grass clutches Salvinia molesta, commonly called African faiel in Kerala. About 30,000 hectares of rice fields in Kerala are infested with this weed.

According to a recent study by the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), more than 300 species of agricultural pests have developed resistance to a wide range of potent chemicals. The disease-spreading pests, about 100 species of which have become immune to a variety of insecticides now in use, cannot be left behind. One glaring disadvantage of pesticide application is that while destroying harmful pests, they also wipe out many useful organisms that are not targeted, which keep the pest population growing. The result is what agroecologists call the treadmill syndrome. Because of their enormous reproductive potential and genetic diversity, many pests are known to withstand synthetic chemicals and bear offspring that have a built-in resistance to pesticides. The devastation that the walker syndrome can cause is well illustrated by what happened to Central American cotton farmers. In the early 1940s, basking in the glory of chemical-based intensive agriculture, farmers eagerly took up pesticides as a safe means of boosting crop yields. The insecticide was applied eight times a year in the mid-1940s, rising to 28 a season in the mid-1950s, following the sudden spread of three new strains of chemical-resistant pests. IN THE MID-1960S, THE SITUATION TOOK AN ALARMING TURN WITH THE OUTBREAK OF FOUR MORE NEW PESTS, WHICH NECESSITATED SPRAYING OF PESTICIDES TO THE POINT THAT 50% OF THE FINANCIAL EXPENDITURE ON COTTON PRODUCTION WAS DUE TO PESTICIDES. In the early 1970s, spraying often reached 70 times a season as farmers were pushed to the wall by invading genetically stronger insect species. Most pesticides currently on the market remain inadequately tested for cancer-causing and mutation-causing traits, as well as other negative health effects, says a study by environmental agencies in the United States. The U.S. National Resource Protection Board found that DDT was the most popular of a long list of hazardous chemicals used. In the face of increasing dangers from indiscriminate applications of pesticides, a more effective and more ecological strategy of biological pest control, which involves the selective use of natural enemies of the pest population, is rapidly gaining popularity - although, so far, this is a new field with limited potential. The advantage of biological control as opposed to other methods is that it provides a relatively low-cost perpetual control system with minimal harmful side effects. When handled by specialists, the biocontrol is safe, non-polluting and self-dispersing. The Commonwealth Institute of Biological Control (CIBC) in Bangalore, with its worldwide network of research laboratories and field stations, is one of the active, non-commercial research agencies engaged in pest control by pitting natural predators against parasites. CIBC also serves as a clearing house for the export and import of pesticide biomaterials worldwide. CIBC HAS SUCCESSFULLY USED THE SEED-FEEDING INVOICE, NATIVE TO MEXICO, TO CONTROL THE NASTY PARTHENIUM WEED, KNOWN TO EXERT AN INSIDIOUS INFLUENCE ON AGRICULTURE AND HUMAN HEALTH IN BOTH INDIA AND AUSTRALIA. Similarly, the Regional Research Laboratory in Hyderabad (RRL), supported by CIBC, is now trialling Argentine weevils to eradicate water hyacinth, another dangerous weed, which has become a nuisance in many regions of the world. According to Ms. Kaiser Jamil of RRL, Argentine weevil does not attack any other 74 plants and a pair of adult insects can destroy the weed in 4-5 days. CIBC is also perfecting the technique for breeding parasites that prey on Dyspene scale insects - notorious leafhoppers of fruit trees in the US and India. The extent to which biological control can be exercised effectively is proven by the following examples. In the late 1960s, when Sri Lanka's flourishing coconut plantations were hit by leaf-mining hispids, a larval parasite imported from Singapore brought the pest under control. A natural predator native to India, Neodumetia sangawani, has been found useful in controlling the Rhodes scale grass insect that devours forage grass in many U.S. regions. By using Neochetina bruci, a beetle native to Brazil, scientists from the Kerala Agricultural University freed a 12-kilometer-long trench from the grass clutches Salvinia molesta, commonly called African faiel in Kerala. About 30,000 hectares of rice fields in Kerala are infested with this weed.

premise: Biological research refers to the search in the most remote areas of the world for genetic resources of commercial value. Bioprospecting is not a new phenomenon. The active ingredient in aspirin, for example, comes from willow bark, whose medicinal properties were known to the ancient Greeks. In recent years, however, the ethics of the practice have been debated. Opponents, who use the term biopiracy, see it as exploiting developing countries' resources and native medical knowledge for the benefit of the developed worlds. Pharmaceutical companies claim that drugs resulting from biological research could help thousands of people. Moreover, they do not patent native plants, but rather the techniques used to extract compounds from them. Despite these arguments, in 2005 the Indian government successfully revoked a US patent for the extraction of an antifungal agent from the neem tree. Central to the debate is the question of who owns global biodiversity. The United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) was established in 1993 to ensure that biological researchers would obtain consent and share the profits with the source country. The United States, on the other hand, has not approved the CBD. It is not only the pharmaceutical industry that has fallen from the sovereign rights to biological resources. In 2008, Mexican farmers won an appeal to revoke a U.S. patent on Mexican enola beans. Similarly, following a diplomatic crisis between India and the United States, a Texan company lost the right to patent basmati rice.
hypothesis: There have been cases when India has successfully revoked patents on its native flora.
label: e

premise: Birds have long been considered foolish, but laboratory research has shown that the bird group corvids including crows and jays are actually highly intelligent. Their ability to produce and use tools rivals that of chimpanzees. When hiding food stores, corvids demonstrate their episodic memory and future planning capacity; cognitive abilities previously thought to be unique to humans. Not only do corvids remember where they caught food, they remember when they stored it. If they are seen grabbing food, the corvids will return and re-hide it, unobserved by competitors. This expectation of theft shows that corvids recognize the state of mind of other people. Being the most social group of birds, corvids raise their young cooperatively and form long-term relationships. The social function of intellect theory, which postulated that social life was the impetus for the development of primate intelligence, is now applied to other species, such as corvids. Although they are capable of doing many of the same things as primates, corvids have smaller brains and lack the neocortex responsible for mammalian cognition. Instead, corvids have nidopalium, which scientists believe plays a similar role more efficiently. Primatic and corbid intelligence is sometimes used as an example of convergent evolution, whereby two unrelated species independently evolve the same adaptations to similar environmental conditions. But animal intelligence is a controversial subject, with no consensus about its definition. Some scientists argue that Corbid behavior can be explained by adaptive specialization and is not equivalent to primate intelligence, so convergent evolution does not apply.
hypothesis: The feeding behavior of corvids suggests that they have a certain awareness of what their competitors are thinking.
label: e

premise: Blighty. Are the British Isles, the UK, the UK and the UK the same thing? Well, no, actually. The British Isles is a non-political geographical term referring to an archipelago, or cluster of islands, comprising the two main islands surrounding England, Wales and Scotland and the entire island of Ireland, as well as all the numerous surrounding smaller islands. The United Kingdom is a shortened form of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, whereas Great Britain is England, Wales, and Scotland (and their adjacent islands) but not Northern Ireland, making the United Kingdom a geographical term but not a political entity. The neighbouring islands referred to include the Isle of Wight, the Isles of Scilly, the Isle of Anglesey (Ynys Mon in Welsh) and the Isles of Scotland (the Orkney and Shetland Islands and the Inner and Outer Hebrides). The term Great Britain is often used to mean Great Britain, although strictly speaking Britain covers England and Wales but not Scotland, because Great Britain derives from the Roman word Britain, which did not include the area now called Scotland, which was never conquered. To add to the confusion, the term British Isles encompasses the United Kingdom, the Channel Islands (Jersey and Guernsey) and the Isle of Man; the small islands are not part of Great Britain, the United Kingdom or the European Union but are self-governing British Crown dependencies. Finally, the term Ireland defines both a political entity, namely the Republic of Ireland (or Eyre), meaning Southern Ireland, and the geographical entity that is both Northern and Southern Ireland, the only land mass.
hypothesis: Jersey is not part of Great Britain but is part of the British Isles.

For Layard and others like him, it is clear that the purpose of governing is to promote a state of collective welfare. The only question is how to achieve this, and here positive psychology - a so-called science that not only identifies what makes people happy but also allows their happiness to be measured - can show the way. Equipped with this science, they say, governments can ensure happiness in society in a way they never could before. This is an incredibly crude and simple way of thinking, and for this reason it is increasingly popular. Those who think in this way are unaware of the vast philosophical literature in which the meaning and value of happiness have been studied and questioned, and write as if nothing of any importance was considered on the subject until it came to their attention. It was the philosopher Jeremy Bentham (1748-1832) who was more responsible than anyone else for the development of this way of thinking. For Bentham it was clear that the good of man consists of pleasure and the absence of pain. The Greek philosopher Aristotle may have identified happiness with self-realization in the fourth century B.C., and thinkers across the ages may have struggled to reconcile the pursuit of happiness with other human values, but for Bentham it was all metaphysics or mere fiction. Without knowing much about him or the school of moral theory that he founded - since they are of illiterate intellectual education and persuasion in the history of ideas - our supporters of positive psychology follow in rejecting as obsolete and irrelevant more or less all ethical reflection on human happiness so far. But as William Davies points out in his recent book “The Happiness Industry,” the view that happiness is the only obvious good is actually a way of limiting moral inquiry. One of the virtues of this rich, lucid and arresting book is that it places the current cult of happiness in a well-defined historical framework. Rightly, Davies begins his story with Bentham, pointing out that he was much more than a philosopher. Davis writes, 'Bentham's activities were those we might now link to a management consultant in the public sector. ' In the 1890s he wrote to the Home Office proposing that government departments be linked together through a system of 'call pipes', and to the Bank of England with a design for a printing device that could produce unfalsifiable banknotes. He drew up plans for a “frigidarium” to keep supplies like meat, fish, fresh fruit and vegetables. His celebrated design for a prison dubbed the 'Panopticon', where prisoners would be kept in solitary confinement while being visible at all times to guards, was adopted very nearly. (Surprisingly, Davies does not discuss the fact that Bentham intended his Panopticon not only as a model prison but also as a control device that could be applied to schools and factories.) Bentham was also a pioneer of the 'science of happiness'. If happiness is to be treated as a science, it must be measured, and Bentham suggested two ways in which this can be done. Seeing happiness as a complex of pleasurable sensations, he suggested that it could be quantified by measuring the human pulse rate. Alternatively, money can be used as a quantifiable standard: if two different goods have the same price, it can be argued that they produce the same amount of pleasure in the consumer. Bentham outlasted the latter measure. By associating money so closely with insider experience, writes Davies, Bentham 'set the stage for the entanglement of psychological research and capitalism that would shape twentieth-century business practices'. THE HAPPINESS INDUSTRY DESCRIBES HOW THE HAPPINESS SCIENCE PROJECT HAS BECOME AN INTEGRAL PART OF CAPITALISM. We learn a lot that is interesting about how economic problems are redefined and treated as psychological illnesses. In addition, Davies shows how the belief that one can objectively measure internal states of pleasure and dissatisfaction informed management and advertising studies. THE TENDENCY OF THINKERS LIKE J.B. WATSON, THE FOUNDER OF *BEHAVIOR*, WAS THAT HUMANS COULD BE SHAPED OR MANIPULATED BY POLICYMAKERS AND MANAGERS. Watson had no factual basis for his view of human action. When he became president of the American Psychological Association in 1915, he “never investigated even a single human being”: his studies were limited to experiments on white rats. However, Watson's reductive model is now widely applied, with 'behaviour change' becoming a goal of governments: in the UK a 'Behaviour Insights Team' has been set up by the government to investigate how people can be encouraged, at minimal cost to the public purse, to live in what are considered socially desirable ways. Modern industrial societies seem to need the possibility of increasing happiness to motivate them in their work. premise: Brightwell International Business College Tertiary Programme Support What is Tertiary Programme Support? Tertiary program support classes are focused English language classes available to international students already enrolled in a business program. Classes are offered twice a week on Wednesday afternoons from 14-16am and Friday mornings from 9.30-11.30am. Lecture classes begin in the week following orientation; however, tertiary program support classes begin during recruitment week. Why should you participate in support of a tertiary program? The classes are designed to help you get good grades on your assignments. They will not only help you improve your grammar and vocabulary and they will also ensure that you know how to write reports and assignments in the right way. Tertiary program support also teaches you how to use information sources for your projects and how to relate to those sources correctly. Do I have to participate? Tertiary program support classes are mandatory for all students who have an IELTS score of less than 6.0 in their first academic year. However, classes are available to all students who wish to attend. Since classes do not only focus on the English language, but also help students build their academic skills, we recommend that everyone attend a tertiary program support for at least the first semester. How much does it cost? There is no additional charge for attending classes. The Academic Skills Guide that accompanies the course and is mandatory is available at the campus bookstore for $25.95. The actual cost of the lesson is subsidized by the institute and is included in your course fees. More Seminars This Month: Library Orientation If you're having trouble finding the reference sources you need to write a quality assignment, we recommend signing up for Library Orientation. Until this discovery, it was estimated that the lynx - a large spotted cat with rough ears - died out in Britain at least 6,000 years ago, before the inhabitants of these islands began farming. But the 2006 find, along with three others in Yorkshire and Scotland, is compelling evidence that the lynx and the mysterious satellite were in fact one animal and the same animal. Had it not been for the animal's back to wear out over time, we could be safe, as there is no mistaking the lynx's grim tail. But even without this key feature, it's hard to see what else the creature could have been. The lynx is now becoming the totemic animal of a movement that is changing the British environment: the Rayldings. Reilding means mass restoration of damaged ecosystems. This involves letting trees return to irrigated places, allowing parts of the seabed to recover from blows and dredging, allowing rivers to flow freely again. Above all, it means bringing back missing species. One of the most striking findings of modern ecology is that ecosystems without large predators behave in completely different ways than those that guard them. Some drive dynamic processes that reverberate throughout the food chain, creating niches for hundreds of species that might otherwise struggle to survive. The killers are revealed to be bringing life. Such findings pose a major challenge to British conservationists, who have often chosen arbitrary assemblages of plants and animals and sought, with great effort and expense, to prevent them from changing. She tried to preserve the living world as if it were a jar of pickles, putting nothing and nothing out, while keeping nature in a state of arrested development. But ecosystems are not just collections of species; they are also the dynamic and changing relationships between them. And this dynamic often depends on large predators. At sea the potential is even greater: by protecting large areas from commercial fishing, we will be able to see again what 18th-century literature describes: vast shoals of fish pursued by fin and sperm whales, within sight of the English coast. This policy will also greatly increase catches in the surrounding sea; the fishing industry's insistence on scouring every inch of the seabed, without leaving any breeding reserves, could not hurt its interests any more. Revilding is a rare example of an environmental movement in which campaigners express what they are for rather than just what they oppose. One reason the renewed enthusiasm is spreading so quickly in Britain is that it is helping to create a vision more inspiring than the green movement's usual promise 'follow us' and the world will be a little less awful than it would otherwise be. 'The lynx poses no threat to humans: there is no known case of a human devouring people. It is a specialist predator of deer, a species that has exploded in Britain in recent decades, and hinders, by intensive browsing, attempts to re-establish forests. It will also wink Sica deer: an exotic species that is almost impossible for humans to control, since it hides in impenetrable plantations of young trees. The attempt to reintroduce this predator marries well with the aim of restoring forests to parts of our exposed and barren uplands. The lynx requires deep cover, and as such poses little risk to sheep and other animals, which should, as a condition of farm subsidies, be kept out of the forest. On a recent trip to the Cairngorm Mountains, I heard some conservationists suggest the lynx could be put there within 20 years. The lynx has now been reintroduced into the Jura Mountains, the Alps, the Vezges in eastern France and the Hertz Mountains in Germany, and has re-established itself in many more places. Europe's population has tripled since 1970 to about 10,000. Like wolves, bears, beavers, pigs, bison, elk and many other species, the lynx has managed to spread as agriculture has left the hills and people are finding that it pays more to protect charismatic wildlife than to hunt them, since tourists will pay for the chance to see it. Large-scale redevelopment is taking place almost everywhere - with the exception of the UK. Here, attitudes are just beginning to change. Conservationists are starting to accept that the old conservation jar model has failed, even on its own terms. Already, projects like Trees for Life in the Highlands are providing a clue to what might be to come. An organisation is being set up that will seek to speed up the spread of land and sea across the UK, and aims to reintroduce the rarest species into British ecosystems: hope.

Cinnamon has also been reported to have health benefits, and is considered to cure various diseases, such as digestion. Because the overland trade route allowed only small amounts of the spice to reach Europe, and because Venice had a virtual monopoly on the trade, the Venetians could set the price of cinnamon incredibly high. These prices, coupled with growing demand, sparked the search for new routes into Asia by Europeans eager to take part in the spice trade. In search of the high profits promised by the cinnamon market, Portuguese traders arrived on the island of Ceylon in the Indian Ocean towards the end of the 15th century. Before Europeans arrived on the island, the country organized the cultivation of cinnamon. During the peeling process, they curled the bark into a 'stick' shape that is still associated with the spice today. Salgama then gave the finished product to the king as a kind of tribute. When the Portuguese arrived, they had to increase production significantly, and so worked many other members of the Ceylon indigenous population, forcing them to work harvesting cinnamon. In 1518, the Portuguese built a fortress on Ceylon, which allowed them to defend the island, thus helping them develop a monopoly in the cinnamon trade and generate very high profits. In the late 16th century, for example, they enjoyed a tenfold margin when shipping cinnamon on an eight-day journey from Ceylon to India. When the Dutch arrived on the shores of South Asia in the early 17th century, they set their goal to displace the Portuguese as cinnamon kings. In 1640, the Dutch broke the 150-year Portuguese monopoly when they took over and occupied their factories. In 1658 they permanently expelled the Portuguese from the island, thus achieving control of the lucrative cinnamon trade. To protect their grip on the market, the Dutch, like the Portuguese before them, treated the native inhabitants harshly. Eventually, the Dutch began cultivating their own cinnamon trees to supplement the ever-small number of wild trees available for use. Then, in 1796, the English arrived in Ceylon, thus uprooting the Dutch from their control of the cinnamon monopoly.
