premise: Business planning What is a business plan? It's probably best described as a summary and assessment of your business idea, in writing. Preparing a business plan is the first and most important task for a business beginner. The plan should include details relating to the industry in which you operate, your product or service, marketing, production, personnel and financial strategies. What purpose does it serve? A business plan allows you to think about all the factors of the business, and solve potential problems before you get to them. This will identify strengths and weaknesses and help assess whether the business can succeed. It is a plan for the establishment, maintenance or expansion of a business. This is a work plan to use to compare your achievements to the goals you have set. It must provide information required by financial institutions when seeking financing. How to make a business plan Step 1: Collect information Collect as relevant information as possible about the industry in which you intend to operate (the number of businesses already operating, the size of their operations, where they are located). Use books, industry unions, and existing business owners to help you. Gather all possible information about the markets to which you are aiming (who buys, why he buys, what are the main qualities that the customer is looking for). Learn everything you can about the product (s) or services you intend to produce, distribute or offer. Step 2: Analysis Read all the material you have collected and decide what is relevant to your business idea. You may need to change your idea depending on what your research shows. The key question to ask is: Can you design a business that will earn enough to cover costs and pay wages and a reasonable profit to you as an owner? After completing Steps 1 and 2, you should have decided if there is a market for your product or service that is large enough and accessible enough to make your new business financially viable. Now you are ready to hand your plan to paper. Step 3: Formulate a strategy Decide how the business will operate. You must describe how the business will be run, and the staff and organizational structure that will be in place. Diagrams may be useful to show how these areas will work. Do not forget to include the responsibilities of each team. This is especially important if some of your team will be family members. There are three other parts that go together to create a comprehensive business plan: a marketing plan, which includes location, method of sale, packaging, pricing, and so on. In all these areas, you must be aware of consumer trends to make sure that your business does not become obsolete or irrelevant. Operational plan, which describes the day-to-day management of the business. You must include sources of supply, cost and quantities of materials, processes, equipment and methods to expand the services or products offered. FINANCIAL PLAN, WHICH IS A MASTER BUDGET FOR ACTION AND INCLUDES: CASH FLOW FORECAST BALANCE PROFIT AND LOSS STATEMENT SOURCES OF FINANCING SALES FORECAST AND TARGET. The financial aspects of the program are the most important and you should develop or access financial skills to make sure that this part of your plan is accurate and realistic. Don't forget the installation costs and the money needed to get through an initial period of low cash flow when calculating your first few years budget. Update your business plan Nothing stays constant in a business; circumstances change, markets change, fashions change, practices change. From time to time you should review your sources of information and re-evaluate your business plan. What's relevant when you start isn't necessarily so in five years. You may need to change goals and budgets if external factors (such as interest rates) change. Keep your information up to date and be prepared to change depending on the circumstances. A business plan should be thought of as flexible, not fixed. If you use these steps to develop a business plan, changing it according to the circumstances, you will be on the path to a successful business.
hypothesis: After the conclusion of a business plan, it will not be necessary to make any additional changes to it.
label: c

premise: Cave caves are natural underground spaces, usually those into which man can enter. There are three main types: the most common and widespread are those developed in soluble rocks, usually limestone or marble, by the underground movement of water; on the coast are those formed in cliffs usually by concentrated pounding of waves along joints and areas of crushed rock; and some caves are formed from basalt basalt, where the solid outer crust remains after the molten core has drained to form Rough tunnels, like those on Oakland's Little Basalt Mountains. Limestone of all ages, ranging from geologically recent times to more than 450 million years ago, is found in many parts of New Zealand, though not entirely cave. Many caves have been discovered, but there are still hundreds left to explore. The most notable limestone areas for caves are the hundreds of square kilometers of Te Kuiti Group (Oligocene) rocks from Fort Waikato southward to Mukao and from the coast inland to the Waipa Valley especially in the Waitomo District; and the Mount Arthur Marble (Upper Ordovichi) of the Northwest Nelson Mountains (fringed by thin strips of Oligocene limestone in the valleys and near the coast). Sedimentary rocks (including limestone) are usually laid in almost horizontal layers or beds that may be of any thickness, but most often 5-7.5 cm. These beds may accumulate to a total thickness of about one hundred meters. Pure limestone is brittle, and folding due to soil movements causes cracks along the partitions, and joints at angles to them. Rainwater seeps down through the soil and fractures in the underlying rocks to the water table, below which all voids and pores are filled with water. This water, which is usually acidic, melts the limestone along the joints, and once a passageway is opened, it is enlarged by the abrasive action of sand and pebbles carried by streams. Widespread resolution occurs between the seasonal boundaries of the water table. Erosion may continue to cut through the floor, or silt and pebbles may build floors and divert the courses of streams. Most of the caves still bear the stream that created them. Caves in the soft, well-flattened Oligocene limestones are generally horizontal in development, often with passages at several levels, and often of considerable length. Gardeners Gut, Waitomo, features two main levels and more than seven miles of passes. Cave plans show notable features, such as long, narrow, straight passages that follow common patterns like Broakory, Waitomo, or a number of parallel straights oriented in one or more directions like Te Anaroa, Rockville. Vertical sections of cave passages may be high and narrow following joints, as in Bor Cave, Waitomo; large and ragged in collapse chambers, as in Hollow Hill, Waitomo (length 233 m, width 59.4 m, and height 30.48 m); low and wide along substrate plains, such as Strike Blocks, Waitomo; or high vertical shafts worn in water, as the Rangatiawa shaft (91 meters). The Waitomo Caves in the hard and massive Mount Arthur marble (metamorphosed limestone) are mostly vertical in development, many reaching several hundred metres, the deepest known being Harwood Hole, Takaka (370 m). The unique beauty of the caves lies in the variety of minerals that are sometimes found completely covering walls, ceiling and floor. Stalactites (Gk. stalaktos, drips) are dependent growths of crystalline calcium carbonate (calcite) formed from solution by depositing trace amounts of calcite from seeping groundwater. They are usually white to yellow in color, but are sometimes brown or red. Where water evaporates faster than it drips, long thin straws form that can reach the floor or condense into pillars. If the water source moves across the ceiling, a thin curtain is formed, very much like a stage curtain. The lithites are stalactites that branch or curl. Stalagmites (Gk. stalagmos, the one that dripped) are conical or gnarled floor growths that are formed by splashing, if the water drips faster than it evaporates. These may grow towards the ceiling to form pillars of massive proportions. When calcite is deposited by water spreading thinly on the walls or floor, flowstone is formed and pools of water may build up their edges to form narrow walls of edging stone. Gypsum (calcium sulfate) is a white cave deposit of many crystal habits which are most likely dependent on moisture. The most beautiful form is the gypsum flower which is extracted from a spot on the cave wall in bundles of fibers that curl and split like a lily or orchid.
hypothesis: Stalagmites never grow very large.

From rough and curvy in Marilyn Monroe's days to thin and androgynous when Twiggy arrived on the London scene in the mid-Sixties, and then on to the towering Amazonian models of the Eighties and the heroin obsession chic and size zero of today, it's not just clothes coming in and out of fashion for women. The gainful idea of the perfect body for men, however, remains remarkably static: broad shoulders, large chests and arms, and rippling, visible abs and strong legs have long been the main components of a desirable male physique. However, a growing body of evidence suggests that this is changing. Rootsteins, a UK doll design company, has released its new male model, a Home Nouveau with a 27" attached waist. To put that in perspective, says one fashion reporter, I had a 27" waist when I was thirteen _ and I was really skinny. The company suggests that the homme nouveau will enhance the prevailing meatcake figure by carving a much more streamlined and curvy silhouette to suit the acute approach of a new generation. Elsewhere in the fashion industry, American Apparel is releasing a line of pants in sizes no larger than a 30-inch waist, squeezing most of the market for young men who have an average waistline greater than 5 inches. Skinny young men naturally begin to dominate the catwalks and magazine pages as well: no one wanted the big guys, said model David Gandy, describing how his muscular physique was losing him jobs. It was all skinny, androgynous looks. People would look at me very, very strangely when I went for hiccups. Achieving such a physique can be unattainable for those without the natural genetic make-up. 'I don't know that anyone would consider my body to be archetypal or exemplary to work towards, 'notes model Dabo McConville. You can't aim for it; it's defined by a vacuum of flesh, by what isn't. However, statistics indicate that this is not only an obsession of models, celebrities and the media more and more ordinary men are ready to make great efforts for a slim body. One indication is the growing number of men discovering surgical reconstruction. Male breast reduction has become particularly popular and, in 2009, the year-on-year growth rate for this procedure increased to 44% in the UK. Liposuction also remains popular in the market of male body reconstruction surgeries, with 35,000 such procedures performed on men every year. In addition, more men suffer from eating disorders than ever before. These are characterized by habitual eating habits, usually consuming insufficient or excessive amounts of food. Eating disorders damage the physical and mental state of people who suffer from them, and the desire to achieve unrealistic physiques is implicated as a factor. In 1990, only 10% of people with anorexia or bulimia were believed to be men, but this figure has steadily climbed to about a quarter today. About two in five binge eaters are male. Women still make up the majority of eating disorder sufferers, but the perception that it is a childhood problem has contributed to men being less likely to pursue treatment. In 2008, men's eating disorders were brought into the spotlight when former British Deputy Prime Minister, John Prescott, admitted he habitually ate junk food and then caused himself to vomit while in office. 'I never admitted it out of shame and embarrassment, 'he said. It was difficult for me as a person like myself to admit that I suffered from bulimia. In some ways, the slender male silhouette seems to complement, rather than displace, Ji Jo's physique. Mens Health, one of the only titles to make it through the swinging magazine market with sales increasing to a quarter of a million per issue, has a basic diet of bulky men on the cover that lure readers with the promise of big, strong muscles. Advertising executives and fashion editors suggest that in times of recession and political uncertainty, the image of the stronger male body again becomes desirable. Academic research supports this claim, suggesting that more feminine traits are desirable for men in comfortable and safe societies, while masculine physical traits are more attractive when survival returns to the individual. A study conducted at the University of Aberdeen, conducted on 4,500 women from more than 30 countries, found a striking correlation between levels of public health and the amount of personality women preferred among their men. In Sweden, the country considered to have the best healthcare, 68% of women preferred the men presented with female facial features. In Brazil, the country with the worst health care in the study, only 45 percent of women were prone to it. The results suggest that as health care improves, more masculine men fall ungraciously, the researchers concluded. In the end, wrote columnist Polly Vernon, we were left with two polarized ideals of male beauty. One is the sleek, thin silhouette that transmits innovative style and a rich and comfortable lifestyle. The second is the strong, muscular and austerity-resistant form that suggests a man can fend for himself with his bare hands. These ideals coexist by pulling men in different directions and encouraging them to believe that they must always pursue physical perfection, and at the same time undermining any firm conceptions about what physical perfection requires. As a result, achieving the ideal body becomes a useless and time-consuming task. Vernon concludes that this means less time for the more important things in life, and both sexes should resist the compulsive obsession with beauty.

Because the only truly child-oriented literature during this period was some instructional works to help with reading and general knowledge, plus the odd Puritan track as an aid to morality, the only course for avid child readers was to read adult literature. This still happens today, especially with thrillers or novels for adults that include more exciting graphic detail than is typically found in literature for younger readers. In the mid-18th century there were enough enthusiastic children's readers, and enough happy parents to give an answer to this matter, for publishers to specialise in children's books whose first aim was pleasure rather than education or morality. Influenced by Rousseau, who (1762) held that all books for children except Robinson Crusoe were a dangerous diversion, contemporary critics worried that children's literature should be instructive and uplifting. Among such voices stands out Mrs. Sarah Trimmer, whose guardian magazine of education (1802) carried the first regular reviews of children's books. premise: Chocolate Food of the Gods The story of chocolate begins with the discovery of America in 1492. Columbus was the first European to come into contact with cocoa. On August 5, 1502, on his fourth and final voyage to the Americas, Columbus and his crew met some natives in a canoe that contained beans from the cocoa tree. Columbus was amazed at how much value the Indians placed on them because he did not know that beans were used for currency. It is unlikely that Columbus brought these beans back to Spain and only about twenty years later did Cortez grasp the commercial possibilities when he found the Aztecs were using the beans to make the royal drink Chocolate. The Spanish, in general, did not like the bitter drink so Cortez and his followers made it tastier by adding cane sugar and later cinnamon and vanilla were added. Spanish monks released the secret home, and although the Spanish hid it from their neighbors for a century, finally the popularity of chocolate grew until it was the fashionable drink in the French court and the discerning choice of customers in London boardrooms. The cocoa beans are harvested from pods grown on the cocoa tree. THE PODS COME IN A VARIETY OF TYPES BECAUSE COCOA TREES ARE FREELY POLLINATED. These types can be reduced to three classifications. The most common is Forastero, which accounts for almost 90% of the world production of cocoa beans. It is easiest to cultivate and has a thick-walled pod and a pungent aroma. The rarest and most expensive are the Cariolo beans. These beans from the soft, thin pod have an aroma and delicacy that make them sought after by the best chocolate makers in the world. Finally, there is the Trinitario, which is believed to be a natural cross of varieties from the other two types. It has a great variety of characteristics but generally has a good taste and aromatic and the trees are particularly suitable for growing. The cocoa tree is definitely a tropical plant that thrives only in warm, rainy climates. Thus, its cultivation is limited to countries no more than 20 degrees north or south of the equator. The cocoa tree is delicate and very sensitive. It needs protection from the wind and requires a fair amount of shade in most conditions. This is especially true in the first two to three years of its growth. A newly planted cocoa seedling is often protected by another type of tree. It is normal to plant food crops for shade such as bananas, plantain, coconuts or coconuts. Rubber trees and forest trees are also used for shade. However, once established, the cocoa tree can grow in full sunlight, provided there are fertile soil conditions and intensive growth. With careful pruning and cultivation, the trees of most varieties will begin to bear fruit in the fifth year. With extreme caution, some varieties can be made to yield good crops in the third and fourth year. The process of turning cocoa into chocolate hasn't changed much since the Swiss made the big breakthroughs in the process in the late 19th century. First the beans (up to twelve varieties harvested from all over the world) undergo a process of fermentation and drying. They are then sorted by hand before cleaning and then roasting. Following winnowing removes the hard outer shells and leaves the so-called fingernails. A crushing and heating process known as the Hunts process is then used to remove almost half of the cocoa butter from the nails. This produces unsweetened chocolate (also called cooking chocolate). Basic edible chocolate is made from a blending of the unsweetened chocolate with some of the cocoa butter along with other ingredients such as vanilla sugar. The resulting product is then bound and this conching gives the chocolate that velvet texture that we know so well. The finished result is shaped, cooled, machine packed, distributed, sold and, of course, eaten! As far as production methods are concerned, manufacturers have absolutely free rein and have developed individual variations from the pattern. Each manufacturer seeks to protect its methods by performing certain actions in an atmosphere of security. No chef guards his favorite recipes more zealously than the chocolate maker keeps his formulas for blending the beans. Time intervals, temperatures and proportions are three critical factors that no company wants to disclose. Apart from the taste, one of the most pleasant effects of eating chocolate is the good feeling that many people experience after an addiction. Chocolate contains more than three known chemicals including caffeine, theobromine and phenylethylamine which are stimulants. Some researchers believe that chocolate contains pharmacologically active substances that have the same effect on the brain as marijuana and that these chemicals may be responsible for problems like the psychoses associated with craving for chocolate. However, eating too much of anything can cause health problems and as long as moderation is practiced, chocolate should not cause the average person any harm.

premise: Classification of societies Although humans have established many types of societies throughout history, sociologists and anthropologists tend to classify different societies by the degree to which different groups in society have unequal access to advantages like resources, prestige, or power, and generally refer to four basic types of societies. From the least to the most socially complex are clans, tribes, leaderships and states. TRIBE ARE SMALL-SCALE SOCIETIES OF HUNTERS AND GATHERERS, USUALLY OF LESS THAN A HUNDRED PEOPLE, WHO MOVE SEASONALLY TO TAKE ADVANTAGE OF WILD (UNDOMESTICATED) FOOD RESOURCES. Most surviving hunter-gatherer groups are of this type, such as the Hadza of Tanzania or the San of South Africa. Members of the clan are usually relatives, related by origin or marriage. The clans have no formal leaders, so there are no appreciable economic differences or disparities in status between their members. Because the clans are composed of mobile groups of hunter-gatherers, their sites consist primarily of seasonally occupied camps, and smaller, more specialized sites. Among the latter are killing sites or areas, places where large mammals are killed and sometimes slaughtered, and work sites, where tools are made or other specific activities are carried out. The base camp of such a group may prove rather immaterial residences or temporary shelters, along with residential waste. These tribe are usually larger than mobile hunter-gatherer groups, but rarely are more than a few thousand, and their diet or existence is largely based on cultivated plants and domesticated animals. Typically, they are settled farmers, but they may be nomadic with a very different mobile economy based on intensive exploitation of livestock. These are usually multi-community societies, where the individual communities are integrated into the larger society through kinship ties. Although some tribes have officials and even a capital or a seat of government, such officials lack the economic foundation necessary for efficient use of the settlement pattern typical of tribes is one of homesteads or inhabited agricultural villages. Characteristically, no single locality dominates any of the others in the area. Instead, the archaeologist finds evidence of isolated and permanently occupied houses or permanent villages. Such villages may consist of a collection of free-standing houses, like those of the first farms of the Danube Valley in Europe. Or they may be clusters of buildings grouped together, for example, the pueblo of the American Southwest, and the early farming village or small town of Cataluyuk in modern Turkey. These leaderships operate on the principle of ratingdifferences in social status between people. Different dynasties (a dynasty is a group claiming descent from a common ancestor) are ranked on a scale of prestige, and the senior dynasty, and hence society as a whole, is ruled by a chief. Prestige and rank are determined by the degree of close connection of the person to the chief, and there is no real stratification into classes. The manager's role is critical. Often, there is local specialization in craft products, and surpluses of these and of food products are periodically paid as a duty to the chief. He uses them to keep his guards, and may use them for redistribution to his subjects. The leadership usually has a center of power, often with temples, residences of the chief and his guardians, and craft specialists. Kingdoms vary greatly in size, but the range is usually between about 5000 and 20,000 people. premise: Collecting as a hobby. Gathering must be one of the most diverse human activities, and it's one that many of us psychologists find fascinating. Many forms of collecting have been defined with a technical name: an architectophile collecting teddy bears, a philatelist collecting postage stamps, and a daltiologist collecting postcards. Accumulating hundreds or even thousands of postcards, chocolate wrappers or anything else, takes time, energy and money that can surely be put to much more productive use. And yet there are millions of collectors around the world. Why are they doing this? Some people collect because they want to make money - this can be called an instrumental reason for collecting; that is, collecting as a means to an end. They will look for, for example, antiques they can buy cheaply and expect to be able to sell at a profit. But there could also be a psychological element - buying cheap and selling expensive can give the collector a sense of triumph. And as selling online is so easy, more and more people are joining. MANY COLLECTORS COLLECT TO DEVELOP THEIR SOCIAL LIFE, ATTEND COLLECTORS' GROUP MEETINGS AND EXCHANGE INFORMATION ABOUT ITEMS. It's a variant of joining a bridge club or gym, and similarly brings them into contact with like-minded people. Another motive for collecting is the desire to find something special, or a particular example of the item being collected, such as a rare early recording of a particular singer. Some may spend their whole lives searching for it. Psychologically, it can give purpose to a life that otherwise feels aimless. However, there is a danger that if the person is lucky enough to find what he is looking for, instead of celebrating his success, he may feel empty, now that the goal that propelled him on has disappeared. If you're thinking about collecting postage stamps, another potential reason for this - or, perhaps, the result of collecting - is its educational value. Stamp collecting opens a window to other countries, and to the plants, animals or famous people featured on their stamps. Similarly, in the 19th century many collectors amassed fossils, animals and plants from around the world, and their collections provided a vast amount of information about the natural world. Without those collections, our understanding would be vastly inferior to what it is. In the past - and also nowadays, albeit to a lesser extent - a popular form of collecting, especially among boys and men, was train spotting. This may include attempting to see each locomotive of a particular type, using published data identifying each, and marking each engine as it appears. Train people exchange information, these days often on a mobile phone, so they can figure out where to go, see a particular engine. As a by-product, many practitioners of the hobby become highly versed in train operations, or the technical specifications of various engine types. Similarly, people who collect dolls may go beyond increasing their collection, and develop an interest in the way dolls are produced, or in the materials used. These have varied over the centuries from the wood that was standard in Europe of the 16th century, through the wax and porcelain of later centuries, to the plastic of today's dolls. Or collectors might be inspired to learn how dolls reflect concepts of what children like, or should love. However, not all collectors are interested in learning from their hobby, so what we could call a psychological reason for collecting is the need for a sense of control, perhaps as a way of dealing with insecurity. One reason, conscious or not, why someone chooses to collect is to show the collector's individualism. Someone who decides to pick up something as unexpected as dog collars, for example, might convey their belief that they must be interesting themselves. And believe it or not, there is at least one dog collar museum, and it grew out of a personal collection. Of course, all hobbies give pleasure, but the common factor in collecting is usually passion: pleasure is to put it too delicately. More than most other hobbies, collecting can be utterly fascinating and can give a strong sense of personal fulfillment. To non-collectors this may seem an eccentric, if harmless, way to waste time, but potentially, collecting has plenty.

Rachel Holland demonstrates, mimicking the closing of the door silently behind her, smiling warmly, walking confidently past the carcass and shaking each interviewer's hand as she says her name. I want my place, and you have to give it to me! Before the 19th century, the only way to treat cancer was to physically remove the tumor from the body. This usually involves amputation or the removal of many tissues. Prisoners were beaten and forced to live in unsanitary conditions, while others were presented to an inquisitive public as a sideshow. There is little indication to suggest that other institutions established around the same time in other European countries have been much better. Even until the mid-twentieth century, mental institutions were regarded as places of isolation and punishment more than healing and consolation. In popular literature of the Victorian era that reflected real life events, people were often sent to the insane asylum as a legal means of permanently disposing of an unwanted heir or spouse. Later, in the mid-twentieth century, mental institutes regularly performed invasive brain surgery known as lobotomies on violent patients without their consent. The goal was to sedate the patient but ultimately produce a patient who was slightly more than a zombie. Such a procedure is well documented to devastating effect in one film Flying Over the Cuckoo's Nest. No wonder then that the shocking catalogue of treatment for the mentally ill has led to calls for change from social activists and psychologists alike. Improvements began to be seen in institutions from the mid-50s onwards, along with the introduction of community care for less severely ill patients. Community therapy is seen as a more humane and purposeful approach to dealing with the mentally ill. While institutionalized patients lived out their existence in prison, forced to comply with institutional regulations, the patients in the community were free to live relatively independent lives. The patient was never left solely alone because, theoretically, a variety of services could be accessed by the person. In its early stages, however, community care mostly consisted of help from the patients' extended family network. In recent years, such care has expanded to the provision of specialist community mental health teams (CMHT) in the UK. Such teams cover a wide range of services from rehabilitation to treatment and assessment at home. In addition, psychiatric nurses are at the disposal of prescription drugs and give injections. Thus, the patient receives the help he needs to survive in the everyday world while maintaining a degree of autonomy. Often, however, when a policy is put into practice, its failures are revealed. This is true of community care policy. While backup services may exist, a person may not call them when needed, due to unwillingness or inability to assess their personal situation. As a result, such a person may be alone at a critical stage of their illness, which can lead them to self-harm or even become a threat to other members of their community. While this may be an extreme scenario, there is also the issue of social alienation that needs to be considered. Community integration may not be sufficient to allow a person to find work, leading to poverty and isolation. Social exclusion can cause relapse because the person is left to fight mental health problems alone. The solution, therefore, is to ensure that the patient is always in contact with professional assistants and is not left alone to take care of himself. Always remember that while you can take the patient out of the institution, you cannot take the institution out of the patient. When asked about care in the community, there seems to be a division of opinion among the public and within the mental health profession itself. Dr. Mayala, an engaged clinical psychologist, is inclined to believe that while some patients may benefit from community care, the program is not for everyone. Sufferers of mild cases of mental illness stand to gain more from community care than those with more pronounced mental illnesses. I don't think it's a one-size-fits-all policy. But I also think there is a much better infrastructure of helpers and social workers in place now than in the past and the programme has a greater chance of success than in the past. Anita Brown, a mother of three, takes a different view. As a mother, I am very protective of my children. I suppose there must be assessment methods to ensure that dangerous people are not released among the public but I'm not in favour of that at all. I like to feel safe where I live, but more to the point, that my children are not under any threat whatsoever. Having worked in the field myself, I have seen how a patient can benefit from an independent life, away from an institution. It is clear that only people on their way to recovery would be suitable for consideration as participants in such a scheme. If you think about it, is it really fair to condemn a person for life in an institution when he can live a fulfilled and fairly independent life outside the institution?

premise: Changing our understanding of health to the concept of health has different meanings for different people and groups. These meanings of health have also changed over time. This shift is no more evident than in Western society today, when concepts of health and promoted health are challenged and expanded in new ways. For much of recent Western history, health was viewed in a purely physical sense. That is, good health has been linked to the smooth mechanical operation of the body, while poor health has been attributed to a breakdown in this machine. Health in this sense has been defined as the absence of disease or disease and is seen in medical terms. According to this view, creating health for people means providing medical care for the treatment or prevention of diseases and illnesses. During this period there was an emphasis on providing clean water, improving sanitation and housing. In the late 1940s the World Health Organization challenged this physically and medically directed view of health. They stated that “health is an absolute state of physical, mental and social well-being and is not merely the absence of disease” (WHO, 1946). Health and man were seen more holistically (mind/body/spirit) rather than just in physical terms. The 1970s were a whitewash of focusing on disease and disease prevention by emphasizing the importance of an individual's lifestyle and behavior. Specific behaviours seen as increasing disease risk, such as smoking, lack of fitness and unhealthy eating habits, were targeted. Creating healthcare means providing not just medical care, but health-promoting programs and policies that will help people maintain healthy behaviors and lifestyles. While this individualistic healthy lifestyle approach to health worked for some (the wealthier members of society), people who experienced poverty, unemployment, underemployment or little control over the conditions of their daily lives benefited little from this approach. This was mainly due to the fact that both the healthy lifestyle approach and the medial approach to health largely ignored the social and environmental conditions that affect people's health. During the 1980s and 1990s there was an increasing distancing from seeing lifestyle risks as the root cause of poor health. premise: Chelsea Rochman, an ecologist at the University of California, Davis, tries to answer a grim question: Is everything terrible, or are things just very, very bad? Rochman is a member of the working group of the National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis of Marine Waste, a collection of scientists investigating, among other things, the growing problem of marine debris, also known as ocean junk. Numerous studies have sounded alarm bells about the state of marine debris; in a paper recently published in the journal Ecology, Ruchman and her colleagues set out to determine how many of the perceived risks are real. Often, says Ruchman, scientists will end a paper by speculating about the broader effects of what they found. For example, research could show that certain seabirds eat plastic bags, and go on to warn that entire bird populations are at risk of dying out. “But the truth is that no one has yet tested these perceived threats,” says Ruchman. 'There wasn't a lot of information. 'Rochman and her colleagues examined more than a hundred papers on the impacts of marine debris published up to 2013. Within each article, they asked what threats scientists had investigated - 366 perceived threats in total - and what they had actually found. In 83 percent of cases, the perceived dangers of trash in the ocean were proven to be true. In the remaining cases, the working group found that the studies had weaknesses in design and content that affected the validity of their conclusions - they lacked a control group, for example, or used poor statistics. Remarkably, says Ruchman, only one well-designed study failed to find the effect he was looking for, an investigation of mussels that ingest microscopic pieces of plastic. The plastic passed from the muscles' stomachs into their blood streams, scientists found, and stayed there for weeks - but didn't seem to stress the mollusks out. Although mussels may be OK to eat garbage, the analysis also gave a clearer picture of the many ways in which ocean debris is troubling. As part of the studies they examined, most of the proven threats came from plastic waste, rather than from other materials such as metal or wood. Most of the hazards also included large pieces of debris - animals getting tangled in the bin, for example, or eating it and injuring themselves badly. But a lot of ocean debris is' microplastic ', or pieces smaller than five millimeters. These may be ingredients used in cosmetics and toiletries, fibers spilled by synthetic clothing in the wash, or the eroded remains of larger debris. Compared to the number of studies investigating large-scale debris, Ruchman's group found little research on the effects of these tiny parts. “There are still a lot of open questions for microplastics,” says Rochman, though she notes that more papers on the subject have been published since 2013, the cut-off point for the group's analysis. There are also, she adds, a lot of open questions about the ways in which ocean debris can lead to the death of sea creatures. Many studies have examined how plastic affects an individual animal, or the tissues or cells of that animal, rather than entire populations. And in the lab, scientists often use higher concentrations of plastic than is actually found in the ocean. None of this tells us how many birds or fish or sea turtles can die from plastic pollution - or how deaths in one species can affect that animal's predators, or the rest of the ecosystem. “We need to ask more ecologically relevant questions,” says Ruchman. Typically, scientists don't know exactly how disasters like a tanker accidentally spilling its entire cargo of oil and polluting huge areas of the ocean will affect the environment until after they happen. “We're not asking the right questions early enough,” she says. But if ecologists can understand how the slow impact of ocean trash is damaging ecosystems, they may be able to prevent the situation from worsening. Asking the right questions can help policymakers and the public understand where to focus their attention. The problems that seem or sound the most dramatic are not the best places to start. For example, the name of the “Great Garbage Patch in the Pacific” - a collection of marine debris in the northern Pacific - might conjure up a vast, floating garbage island. In reality, however, much of the debris is tiny or below the surface; a person can sail through the area without seeing any rubbish at all. A Dutch group called 'The Ocean Cleanup' is currently working on plans to put mechanical devices into the Pacific garbage area and similar areas to pump out plastic. But a recent paper used simulations to show that strategically placing the cleaning devices closer to shore would more effectively reduce long-term pollution. “I think it's very important to clear up some of these misconceptions,” says Ruchman. Among scientists as well as the media, she says, 'A lot of the images are about the trickery and the entanglement and all of that causes the perception that plastic waste is killing everything in the ocean. 'Investigating the existing scientific literature can help ecologists understand which problems really need to be addressed, and which ones are better for them - like the mussels - to absorb and ignore.
hypothesis: THE STUDIES THAT ROCHMAN SURVEYED HAVE ALREADY DEMONSTRATED THAT POPULATIONS OF SOME BIRDS WILL SOON BECOME EXTINCT.
label: c

premise: Children's literature for stories and poems intended for children has a particularly long history: lullabies, for example, were sung in Roman times, and some children's games and rhymes are almost as ancient. However as far as written literature was concerned, while there were stories printed before 1700 that children often exploited when they had the opportunity, such as translations of Aesop's fables, fairy tales and ballads and popular romances, these were not particularly aimed at young people. Because the only truly child-oriented literature during this period was some instructional works to help with reading and general knowledge, plus the odd Puritan track as an aid to morality, the only course for avid child readers was to read adult literature. This still happens today, especially with thrillers or novels for adults that include more exciting graphic detail than is typically found in literature for younger readers. By the middle of the 18th century there were enough enthusiastic children's readers, and enough happy parents to give an answer to this matter, for publishers to specialize in children's books whose first purpose was pleasure rather than education or morality. In Britain, a London merchant called Thomas Boreham produced Cajanus, the Swedish Giant in 1742, while the more famous John Newbury published a small beautiful pocket book in 1744. Its contents are beads, stories, children's games plus a free gift (ball and pillow) in many ways see the similar lucky designs of annuals for children this century. It is a tribute to Newberry's talent that he arrived at a winning formula quite quickly, to be pirated almost immediately in America. Such pleasant storylines would not last. Influenced by Rousseau, whose Émile Shalev (1762) held that all books for children except Robinson Crusoe were a dangerous diversion, contemporary critics worried that children's literature should be instructive and uplifting. Among such voices stands out Mrs. Sarah Trimmer, whose guardian magazine of education (1802) carried the first regular reviews of children's books. It was she who condemned the legends for their violence and general absurdity; her own stories, Wonderful Histories (1786) depicted talking animals that were always models of sense and generosity. So the moral story for children has always been threatened from within, given the way children derive entertainment from the most severe moralist. But the biggest blow to the improving children's book was to come from an unlikely source: an interest in folklore in the early 19th century. The two children's rhymes, selected by James Orchard Halliwell for the Folklore Society in 1842, and a collection of fairy tales by the erudite Brothers Grimm, quickly translated into English in 1823, soon surged in popularity among the young, quickly leading to new editions, each more child-focused than the previous. From now on younger children could expect stories written for their particular matter and with their limited life experience needs kept firmly in the foreground. What ultimately determined the reading of older children was not the availability of specialized children's literature as such but access to books that contained characters, such as young people or animals, with whom they could identify more easily, or action, such as exploration or combat, that placed few demands on adult adulthood or understanding. The final apotheosis of literary childhood as something to be protected from unpleasant realities came with the arrival in the late 1930s of child-centric bestsellers that intended entertainment in the most escapist way. In Britain, writers such as Enid Blyton and Richmel Crompton described children who were always free to experience the most unlikely adventures, safe in the knowledge that nothing bad could happen to them in the end. The fact that war broke out again during the course of her most popular books fails to register at all in the self-enclosed world populated by young Enid Blyton characters. The backlash against such dream worlds was inevitable after World War II, coinciding with the growth of paperback sales, children's libraries and a new spirit of moral and social concern. At the insistence of committed publishers and progressive librarians, writers slowly began to explore new areas of interest while shifting their plot settings from the middle-class world to which their mostly adult patrons had always previously belonged. The critical emphasis, during this development, was divided. For some, the most important task was to rid children's numbers of the social and exclusive prejudices that were no longer found acceptable. Others concentrated more on the positive achievements of contemporary children's literature. The fact that the authors of these works are now often recommended for the attention of adult readers as well as children echoes the 19th-century belief that children's literature could be shared across generations, rather than being a defensive barrier between childhood and the growth needed towards adult understanding.
hypothesis: Today, authors of children's books believe that their works should appeal to both children and adults.

premise: THINKING OF CHILDREN ONE OF THE MOST PROMINENT PSYCHOLOGISTS, CLARK HULL, ARGUED THAT THE ESSENCE OF LOGIC LIES IN ASSEMBLING TWO SEGMENTS OF BEHAVIOR IN SOME NEW WAY, WHICH HAD NEVER BEEN CARRIED OUT BEFORE, TO REACH A GOAL. Two of Clark Hull's followers, Howard and Tracy Candler, devised a test for children that was explicitly based on Clark Hull's principles. The children were given the task of learning to operate a machine to obtain a toy. To be successful they had to go through a two-stage sequence. The children were trained on each stage individually. The steps included just pressing one of the two correct buttons to get marble; and inserting the marble into a small hole to release the toy. The Candlers discovered that the children could learn the separate parts with sufficient ease. (All they had to do was put it in the hole.) But they didn't fit into most of them, to use Candler's terminology. They didn't press the button to get the marble and then proceeded without further help to use the marble to get the toy. So the Candlers concluded that they are incapable of deductive reasoning. The mystery at first seems to deepen when we learn from another psychologist, Michael Cole and colleagues, that adults in an African culture apparently cannot perform the Candler task. But this diminishes, however, when we learn that a task was designed that was completely analogous to Candler's but much easier for the African males to handle. Instead of a button-pressing machine, Cole used a locked box and two matchboxes of different colors, one of which contained a key that would open the box. It then becomes clear that the difficulty of integration is greatly reduced. premise: Food promotions for children are dominated by television advertising, and the great majority of this promotes the so-called “Big Four” of pre-candied cereals, soft drinks, confectionery and savoury snacks. In the past ten years advertising for fast food stores has grown rapidly. There is evidence that the dominance of television has recently begun to wane. The importance of strong global branding reinforces the need for multifaceted communications that integrate television with merchandise, connections and point-of-sale activity. The famous diet is sharply contrasted with that recommended by public health advisers, and themes of fun and fantasy or taste, rather than health and nutrition, are used to promote it to children. Meanwhile, the recommended diet receives little promotional support. There is ample evidence that children notice and enjoy food promotion. However, determining whether it really affects them is a complex problem. The review tackled this by examining studies that examined possible influences on what children know about food, their food preferences, their actual food behaviour (buying and eating) and their health outcomes (e.g. obesity or cholesterol levels). Most studies have examined food advertising, but few have examined other forms of food coding. In terms of nutritional knowledge, food advertising appears to have little effect on children's overall perceptions of what constitutes a healthy diet, but in some contexts it does have an impact on more specific types of nutritional knowledge. For example, seeing advertisements of soft drinks and cereals reduced the ability of primary-age children to correctly determine whether certain products contain real fruit or not. The review also found evidence that promoted food affects children's food preferences and their purchasing behaviour. A study of elementary school children, for example, found that exposure to advertising influenced which foods they claimed to like; and another showed that labeling and signage in vending machines affected what high school students bought. Several studies have also shown that food advertising can affect what children eat. One, for example, showed that advertising influenced the main squad's choice of a daily snack at game time. The next step, of trying to determine whether there is a link between food promotion and diet or obesity, is extremely difficult because it requires research done in real-world settings. Several studies have attempted this by using the amount of television viewing as a proxy for exposure to television advertising. They established a clear link between watching TV and diet, obesity and cholesterol levels. However, it is impossible to say whether this effect is caused by the advertising, the sedentary nature of watching television or the snacking that may occur while watching. One study solved this problem by taking a detailed diary of children's viewing habits. It showed that the more food advertisements they saw, the more snacks and calories they consumed. Thus the literature does indicate that food coding affects children's nutrition in a number of ways. It doesn't amount to a proof; as noted above in a study of this kind, irrefutable proof is simply not obtainable. Not all studies point to this conclusion either; several have found no effect. In addition, very few studies have attempted to measure how strong these effects are relative to other factors that influence children's food choices. However, many studies have found clear effects and they have used sophisticated methodologies that allow determining that i) these effects are not due only to chance; ii) they do not depend on other factors that may influence diet, such as eating habits or attitudes of parents; and iii) they occur at the brand and category level. Furthermore, two factors suggest that these findings actually underestimate the impact that food pruning has on children. First, the literature focuses primarily on television advertising; the cumulative effect of this combined with other forms of promotion and marketing may be significantly greater. Second, the studies examined direct effects on individual children, and downplayed indirect effects. For example, coding to fast food stores may not only affect the child, but also encourage parents to take them out for meals and reinforce the idea that this is normal and desirable behavior. This does not amount to proof of an effect, but in our view does provide sufficient evidence to conclude that an effect exists. The debate should now move to what action is needed, and in particular how the power of commercial marketing can be used to bring about improvements in young people's eating.
hypothesis: There is a lack of investigation into food-promoted practices other than television advertising.

premise: Clean and abundant fuels attracting record investments Renewable energy captured from wind, solar, earth's heat, tides and small dams is attracting record levels of investment as poor villagers and entire countries alike seek clean and bountiful ways to fuel economic growth. Global investment in renewable energy set a new record of $30 billion in 2004, according to a new report by the Renewable Energy Policy Network for the 21st Century (REN21). Technologies like wind, solar, biomass, geothermal and small hydro now provide 160 gigawatts of electricity-generating capacity at roughly four percent of the world's total, the report said. However, they are growing at rates of around 20-30 per cent a year, compared with two or three per cent for oil and gas. Renewable energy has become big business, said Eric Martinot, lead author of the study, Renewables 2005: Global Status Report. Martino, a senior fellow at the think tank Worldwatch based in Washington, and a lecturer at Tsinghua University in Beijing, said renewable energy had attracted some of the world's biggest companies, including General Electric, Siemens, Sharp and Shell's Royal Dutch. The report estimated that nearly 40 million households around the world heat their water using solar collectors, most of them installed in the past five years. Overall, the renewable energy industries provide 1.7 million jobs, most of them highly skilled and well-paid. Martino and another 100 researchers from more than 20 countries evaluated several renewable technologies: small hydro (meaning small dams), modern biomass (agricultural waste, for example), wind, solar, geothermal and biofuels like ethanol and biodiesel. These technologies now compete with conventional fuels in four separate markets: power generation, hot water and space heating, fuels for transportation, and rural (off-grid) energy supply. Renewable energy is gaining popularity because it is considered an infinite supply unlike oil, coal and gas and because it involves little or no pollution compared to the same fossil fuels. SCIENTISTS BLAME THE BURNING OF FOSSIL FUELS FOR RELEASING CARBON DIOXIDE AND OTHER GREENHOUSE GASES THAT TRIGGER GLOBAL CLIMATE CHANGE, WHICH IN TURN INTENSIFIES DROUGHTS IN SOME PARTS OF THE WORLD, FLOODS AND STORMS IN OTHERS AND THE SPREAD OF TROPICAL DISEASES TO TEMPERATE REGIONS. In addition, renewable energy may empower millions of poor and vulnerable people who lack access to reliable, affordable and clean modern energy services, U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan said in a message to the International Conference on Renewable Energy in Beijing, which opened Monday. Annan said the rise in oil prices has hit particularly hard in developing countries that import oil and highlights the need for alternative energy supplies. According to the REN21 report, government support for renewable energy is growing rapidly. At least 48 countries currently have some policy to promote renewable energy, including 14 developing countries. Typically, they include goals to ensure that renewable sources generated 5-30 percent of energy use in a given country around 2010-2012. The prospects for the renewable sectors appeared to have received another boost on Monday, when China announced it was raising its target to rely on renewable energy even though it acknowledged that coal would remain its main source of electricity for decades to come. Renewable energy should account for 15% of national consumption by 2020. China had previously aimed to obtain 10% of its energy from renewable sources by 2020. Mandates for blending biofuels into automotive fuels have been enacted in 20 states and provinces around the world, as well as in three key countries Brazil, China and India, the report said. The government leadership has ensured success in the market, according to REN21, which is made up of representatives of governments and NGOs. Market leaders in renewable energy in 2004 included Brawl in biofuels, China in solar hot water, Germany in solar power and Spain in wind energy, the report said. The world's fastest-growing energy technology is grid-connected solar photovoltaic (PV), whose existing capacity boomed by sixty percent a year between 2000-2004, covering more than 400,000 rooftops in Japan, Germany and the United States, the study suggests. Wind power came in second, with production capacity increasing by 28% last year with nearly 17 gigawatts installed as of 2004. Production of ethanol, biodiesel and other biofuels exceeded 33 billion liters in 2004, with ethanol sterilizing about three percent of the 1,200 billion liters of benzal produced worldwide. About $500 million is estimated to go to developing countries each year as development aid for renewable energy projects, training and market support, with the German Development Financing Group (GDFG), the World Bank Group and the World Environment Facility (GEF) providing most of these funds, and dozens of donors and other programs providing the rest, the report said. More than 4.5 million green electricity consumers in Europe, the United States, Canada, Australia and Japan purchased renewable electricity in 2004, the company added. Asia is seen as a huge market for renewable energy as it seeks to meet growing demand for electricity to feed rapid economic expansion against the backdrop of bulging oil prices.

The Department of Fisheries, which is responsible for monitoring fish levels in the River Thames, reported that the river has once again become home to 115 fish species including sea bass, flounder, salmon, smelt and breast. Porpoise was recently observed erupting in a river near central London. But things haven't always been so rosy. In the 1950s, sewage flows and industrial effluents killed the river. He was starved of oxygen and could no longer support aquatic life. Until the early 1970s, if you fell into the Thames, you would have to be transported to a hospital to have your stomach pumped. A clean-up operation began in the 1960s. In 1964 the Greater London Council (GLC) began work on greatly enlarged sewage works, which were completed in 1974. But the cleaning up of the Thames is not over. It is still ongoing, and it includes various governing arms and a wide range of non-governmental stakeholder groups, all of which represent a necessary aspect of the mission. In the case of London, the urban and non-urban London boroughs surrounding the course of rivers have their own reasons for keeping a nice river. And if their reasons do not hold a carrot attractive enough, the government also holds a persuasive stick. The Local Government Act of 2000 requires each local borough to prepare a community strategy to promote or improve the economic, social and environmental well-being of their area. And if your area includes a stretch of river, that means a sustainable river development strategy. Further legislation aimed at improving and sustaining the viability of the rivers was proposed. There is currently legislation protecting the River Thames, specifically or as part of a general environmental clause, in the Local Government Act, the Laws of London and the Act that created the post of Mayor of London. The result is a wide range of bodies officially tasked, in one way or another, with maintaining the Thames as a public convenience. For example, Transport for London the agency responsible for transport in the capital plays a role in regulating river use and river users. They are now responsible for controlling the effluent and rubbish coming from a craft that uses the Thames. This is done by officers in official vessels who regularly inspect vessels and do spot checks. Another example is how Thames Water (TW) has now been charged to reduce the amount of litter that finds its way into the tidal river and its tributaries. TWs director of environment and quality, Dr Peter Spillett, said: This project will build on our investment which has dramatically improved the water quality of the river. London should not be spoiled by waste that belongs in the bin rather than the river. Thousands of tons of trash reach the river every year, from poorly stored waste, people who throw waste from boats, and street trash that is smashed or washed into the river. Once the litter hits the water it becomes too heavy to burst again so the rivers act as a sink in the system. It consists of a huge cage that sits in the flow of water and collects the passing garbage. The device, moored just off the sea in front of the Royal Naval College in Greenwich, south-east London, is expected to catch up to 20 tonnes of floating debris every year. This machine, dubbed The Rash Muncher, are hoping to be the first of many, as the TW is now looking for sponsors to pay for more cages elsewhere along the Thames. Although they will all still have their roles, there is now a central department in the Environment Agency, which has the job of overseeing the Thames. This centralisation of responsibility will lead, it is hoped, to more effective control and enforcement.

premise: Climate change: An instant expert on climate change is with us. A decade ago it was conjecture. Now the future is unfolding before our eyes. The Canadian Inuit see it in the disappearing Arctic ice and permafrost. Residents of the shantytown in Latin America and South Asia see it in deadly storms and floods. Europeans see it as disappearing glaciers, forest fires and deadly heat waves. Scientists see it in tree rings, ancient corals and bubbles trapped in ice cores. These find that the world has not been as hot as it is now for a millennium or more. The three warmest years on record have all occurred since 1998; 19 of the 20 warmest since 1980. And the Earth has probably never warmed as fast as in the past 30 years - a period when natural influences on global temperatures, like solar cycles and volcanoes should have cooled us. Climatologists reporting for the United Nations Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) say we are seeing global warming caused by human activities. People are causing change by burning the vast natural reserves of coal, oil and natural gas. It releases billions of tons of carbon dioxide (CO2) every year, though the changes may have started at the dawn of agriculture, some scientists say. The physics of the greenhouse effect has been a matter of scientific fact for a century. CO2 is a greenhouse gas that traps the sun's radiation inside the troposphere, the lower atmosphere. It accumulated along with other man-made greenhouse gases, such as methane and chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs). Some studies suggest that cosmic rays may also be involved in warming. If current trends continue, we will raise carbon dioxide concentrations in the atmosphere to pre-industrial levels to double over the course of the current century. This will probably be enough to raise global temperatures by around 2C to 5C. Some warming is certain, but the extent will be determined by cycles that include melting ice, oceans, water vapor, clouds and changes in vegetation. Warming brings other unexpected changes. MELTING GLACIERS AND SEDIMENT CAUSE SOME RIVERS TO OVERFLOOD, WHILE EVAPORATION DRAINS OTHERS. Diseases are spreading. Some crops are growing faster while others are seeing yields reduced by disease and drought. Clashes over dwindling water resources can result in conflicts in many regions. As natural ecosystems such as coral reefs are disturbed, biodiversity is reduced. Most species cannot migrate fast enough to keep up, though others are already evolving in response to warming. Thermal expansion of the oceans, combined with melting ice on land, is also raising sea levels. In this century, human activity could trigger irreversible melting of Greenland's ice sheet. It would condemn the world to a sea level rise of six feet enough to flood lands occupied by billions of people. Global warming would be more pronounced were it not for the sulfur particles and other pollutants that shelter us, and because forests and oceans absorb about half of the carbon dioxide we produce. But the rate of accumulation of atmospheric CO2 has doubled since 2001, which suggests that nature's ability to absorb the gas could now be stretched to the limit limit. Recent studies suggest that natural CO2 reactors, such as peat bogs and forests, are actually beginning to release CO2. At the Earth Summit in 1992, the world agreed to prevent dangerous climate change. The first step was the Kyoto Protocol of 1997, which came into force during 2005. That would result in modest emissions reductions from industrialized countries. Many observers argue that deeper cuts are needed and developing countries, which have large and growing populations, will one day have to join in. Some, including the US Bush administration, say that scientific uncertainty about the pace of climate change is grounds for delaying action. The US and Australia renounced Kyoto. Most scientists believe we don't appreciate the dangers. In any case, according to the IPCC, the world needs to rapidly improve the efficiency of its energy use and develop non-carbon renewable fuels like: wind, solar, tidal and possibly nuclear energy. It also means developing new methods to convert this clean energy into motive power, such as hydrogen fuel cells for cars. Other less conventional solutions include ideas for preventing warming by mega-engineering the planet with giant mirrors to deflect the sun's rays, seeding the oceans with iron to create algal blooms or burying greenhouse gases under the sea. The bottom line is that we will need to reduce CO2 emissions by 70% to 80% simply to stabilize atmospheric CO2 concentrations and thus temperatures. The faster we do this, the less unbearably hot our future world will be.
hypothesis: Volcanoes can affect global climate.

premise: Coal is expected to continue to account for nearly 27% of global energy needs. However, with increasing international awareness of pressures on the environment and the need to achieve sustainable development of energy resources, how the resource is produced, transported and used is critical. A wide range of instruments and practices for pollution control exists in most modern mines and significant resources are invested in restoring mined lands. In addition, key research and development programs are dedicated to raising efficiency and reducing greenhouse gas emissions during coal consumption. Such measures help coal maintain its position as a major supplier of global energy needs. The coal industry was targeted by its critics as a significant contributor to the greenhouse effect. However, the greenhouse effect is a natural phenomenon involving an increase in global surface temperature due to the presence of greenhouse gases water vapor, carbon dioxide, tropospheric ozone, methane, and nitrous oxide in the atmosphere. Without the greenhouse effect, Earth's average surface temperature would have been as low as 33-35 degrees Celsius, or -15 degrees Celsius, life on Earth, as we know it today, would not have been possible. There is concern that this natural phenomenon is being altered by a greater accumulation of gases from human activity, possibly giving rise to further warming and changes in the Earth's climate. This additional accumulation and its prediction result have been called the enhanced greenhouse effect. However, there is considerable uncertainty about the enhanced greenhouse effect, particularly with respect to the extent and timing of a future increase in global temperature. Greenhouse gases arise from a wide variety of sources and their increasing concentration is largely related to the complex effects of population increase, improvement in living standards and lifestyle changes. From a current base of 5 billion, the United Nations predicts that the global population may stabilize in the twenty-first century between 8 and 14 billion, with more than 90% of the projected increase occurring in the developing countries of the world. The accompanying activities to support this growth, particularly for the required energy and food production, will result in a further increase in greenhouse gas emissions. The challenge, then, is to achieve a sustainable balance between population, economic growth and the environment. The main greenhouse gas emissions from human activities are carbon dioxide (CO2), methane and nitrous oxide. Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) are the only major contributor to the greenhouse effect that does not occur naturally, and comes from sources such as refrigeration, plastics, and manufacturing. The total contribution of coals to greenhouse gas emissions is thought to be about 18 percent, with about half of it coming from electricity generation. The global coal industry allocates extensive resources for research and development of new technologies and ways to capture greenhouse gases. Efficiency is expected to improve dramatically, hence CO2 emissions will decrease, through combustion and gasification techniques that are currently in pilot and demonstration phases. Clean coal is another way to improve fuel conversion efficiency. Investigations are being conducted on super-clean coal (3-5 percent ash) and ultra-clean coal (less than 1% ash). Superclean coal has the potential to improve the combustion efficiency of conventional crushed fuel power plants. Ultraclean coal will allow coal to be used in advanced power systems like coal-fired gas turbines, which, when operated in a combined cycle, have the potential to achieve much greater efficiency. The mining defendants point out that from an environmental standpoint, coal mining has two important factors in its favor. It makes only temporary use of the soil and does not produce toxic chemical waste. By carefully pre-planning projects, implementing pollution control measures, monitoring mining impacts, and restoring mining areas, the coal industry minimizes the impact on the neighboring community, immediate environment, and long-term land capacity. Dust levels are controlled by spraying roads and stock, and water pollution is controlled by strict separation of clean water runoff from runoff containing sediment or salt from the mine works. The latter is treated and reused for dust suppression. Noise is controlled by changing equipment and by the use of insulation and sound enclosures around machinery. Because mining activity represents only temporary land use, extensive restoration measures are taken to ensure that the soil capacity after mining meets agreed and appropriate standards, which in some cases are superior to the state of the soil before mining. When mining is underground, the surface area can be simultaneously used for forests, cattle grazing and crop growing, or even reservoirs and urban development, with little or no disruption to existing land use. In all cases, mining is subject to stringent control and approval processes. In open operations, however, the land is used exclusively for mining but land restoration measures are generally advanced with the development of the mines. When core samples are produced to assess the quality and quantity of coal at the site, they are also analysed to assess the ability of the soil or subsoil material to support vegetation. Top soils are stripped and grazed prior to mining for subsequent dispersal over rehabilitated areas. When mining ceases in one part of the open cut, the disturbed area is reshaped. Drainage inside and outside the site is carefully planned to make the new soil surface as stable as the local environment allows: dams are often built to protect the area from soil erosion and to serve as permanent water sources. Based on soil requirements, the soil is properly fertilized and replenished.

premise: Cod in trouble In 1992, the devastating collapse of cod stocks off the east coast of Newfoundland forced the Canadian government to take drastic measures and close the fishery. The disintegration of this vital fishery sounded a warning bell to governments around the world who were shocked that a relatively sophisticated, scientifically based fisheries management program, not dissimilar to their own, could have gone so wrong. The Government of Canada ignored warnings that the Taoiseach were using destructive fishing practices and refused to significantly reduce quotas, claiming the loss of jobs as too great a concern. In the 1950s the East Coast waters of Canada and the US provided 100,000 annual tons in cod catch which rose to 800,000 by 1970. This overfishing led to the seizure of only 300,000 tons by 1975. Canada and the US responded by passing legislation to expand their national jurisdictions over marine life resources to 200 nautical miles and catches naturally declined to 139,000 tonnes in 1980. However the Canadian fishing industry took over and restarted the fishery and the catch rose again until from 1985 it was Canadians who were landing more than 250,000 tonnes of northern cod per year. This exploitation destroyed the stocks and by 1990 the catch was so low (29,000 tonnes) that in 1992 (12% 000 tonnes) Canada had to ban all fishing in East Coast waters. In a fishery that has yielded for over a century catches of a quarter of a million tonnes, there remains biomass of less than 1700 tonnes and the fisheries department has also calculated that even with immediate recovery, stocks need at least 15 years before they will be healthy enough to meet previous fishing levels. The disastrous fishery came from massive investment poured into building giant granaries. The draggers haul vast nets held up by a combination of huge steel plates and heavy chains and rollers that plough the ocean floor. They drag anything in the way, cause enormous damage, destroy critical habitat and contribute to the destabilization of the northern cod ecosystem. The driggers focused on huge accumulations of cod while they were roosting, a time when the fish population is very vulnerable to capture. Excessive boating on spawning stock has become highly disruptive to the spawning process and ecosystem. In addition, literature activity resulted in physical dispersal of oocytes which led to higher fertilization failure. Physical and chemical damage to the larvae caused by the ship's action also reduced their chances of survival. These grains are now banned forever from Canadian waters. Canadian media often cite excessive fishing by overseas fleets, driven primarily by capitalist ethics, as the primary cause of fishing out of the North Atlantic cod stock. Many countries removed fish from Newfoundland's shores and all used deep-sea vessels, and many often blatantly exceeded the catch quotas and established treaty agreements. There is no doubt that non-North American fisheries were a contributing factor to the collapse of the cod stock, and that the capitalist dynamic that operated in Canada was too similar for the foreign ships and companies. But it is not possible to put all the blame there, no matter how easy it is to do it, since it does not relate to the management of resources. Who was to blame? Since the exploitation of fisheries in Newfoundland has been primarily directed by the government, we can argue that fishing is not a private area, as the fisherman does not have management rights normally associated with common property and property. The state appropriated the property, and made all management decisions. The fishermen are told who can fish, what they can fish, and basically, what to do with the fish once it is caught. In that context then, when a resource like the Newfoundland fishery crashes, it's more a tragedy of government negligence than a tragedy of the general public. Following the 92 ban on fishing for northern cod and most other species, some 30,000 people who had already lost their jobs after the introduction of the moratorium on northern cod in 1992, were joined by 12,000 more fishermen and factory workers. With more than forty thousand people without jobs, Newfoundland became an economic disaster zone, as processing plants closed, and vessels from the smallest dyke to the monster tugs were made idle or sold overseas at bargain prices. The costs to desperate individuals and communities now deprived of meaningful and sustainable employment are staggering.
