premise: Collecting ant specimens Collecting ants can be as simple as collecting stray ants and placing them in a glass jar, or as complicated as completing an exhaustive survey of all species present in an area and assessing their relative abundance. The exact method used will depend on the ultimate purpose of the collections. For taxonomy, or classification, long series, from a single nest, containing all castes (workers, including majors and juveniles, and, if present, queens and males), are desired, to allow determination of variation within species. For ecological studies, the most important factor is collecting identifiable samples of as many of the various species present as possible. Unfortunately, these methods are not always compatible. The taxonomist sometimes ignores entire species in favor of those currently studied groups, while the ecologist often collects only a limited number of specimens from each species, thus reducing their value to taxonomic investigations. To collect as wide a variety of species as possible, several methods should be used. These include manual collection, use of baits to attract the ants, soil debris sampling and the use of booby traps. Manual collection consists of searching for ants wherever they are likely to occur. This includes on the ground, under rocks, logs or other objects on the ground, in rotten wood on the ground or trees, in vegetation, on tree trunks and under bark. If possible, collections should be made from nests or foraging poles and at least 20 to 25 individuals should be collected. This will ensure that all individuals are of the same species, and thus increase their value for detailed studies. Since some species are mainly nocturnal, gathering should not be limited to daylight hours. Specimens are collected using an aspirator (often called a potter), forceps, a thin, damp paint brush, or fingers, if it is known that the ants do not sting. Individual insects are placed in plastic or glass tubes (1.5-3-0 ml capacity for small ants, 5-8 ml for larger ants) containing 75% to 95% ethanol. Plastic pipes with secure tops are better than glass because they are lighter and do not break as easily if handled improperly. BAITS CAN BE USED TO ATTRACT AND CONCENTRATE COLLECTIONS. This often increases the number of individuals collected and attracts species that are otherwise elusive. SUGARS AND MEATS OR OILS WILL APPEAL TO DIFFERENT SPECIES AND SHOULD BE USED VARIOUSLY. These baits can be placed on the ground or on the trunks of large trees or shrubs. When placed on the ground, the baits should be placed on small paper cards or other brightly colored flat surfaces, or in test tubes or vials. This makes it easier to identify ants and trap them before they can escape into the surrounding leaf litter. Many ants are small and search mainly in the leaf layer and other debris on the ground. Collecting these species by hand can be difficult. One of the most successful ways to collect them is to collect the leaf litter in which they search for food and extract the ants from it. This is most often done by placing leaf debris on a screen over a large funnel, often under some heat. When the leaf debris dries up from above, ants (and other animals) move downwards and eventually fall from the bottom and are collected in alcohol placed under the funnel. This method works especially well in rainforests and wetland areas. A method to improve the catch when using a funnel is to sift the leaf debris through a coarse screen before lowering over the funnel. This will concentrate the litter and remove larger leaves and twigs. It will also allow more malt to be sampled when using a limited number of funnels. The trap trap is another common tool for collecting ants. A trap can be any small container placed in the ground with the upper level with the surrounding surface and filled with a preservative. Ants are collected when they fall into a trap while foraging. The diameter of the traps can vary from about 18 mm to 10 cm and the number used can range from a few to several hundred. The size of the traps used is heavily influenced by personal preference (although larger sizes are usually better), while the number will be determined by the research being carried out. The preservative 46 used is usually ethylene glycol or propylene glycol, as alcohol will evaporate quickly and the traps will dry out. One advantage of traps is that they can be used for collection over a period of time with minimal maintenance and intervention. One disadvantage is that some species are not collected because they avoid the traps or do not usually encounter them while foraging.
hypothesis: Range is the key criterion for ecological collections.
label: e

premise: Early childhood computer games: Nintendos research and design process Designing computer games for young children is a daunting task for game producers, who for a long time have concentrated on enthusiasts of harder core games. This article chronicles the design and research process involved in creating the Nintendo DS for early childhood gamers. After talking to our producers who have a strong interest in designing for the DS, we finally agreed on three key goals for our project. First, understand the range of physical and cognitive abilities of preschoolers in the context of handheld system play; second, understand how preschoolers interact with the DS, especially how they master the various game forms and game mechanics offered by the games currently on the market for this platform; third, understand the expectations of preschoolers, parents regarding handheld systems as well as the contexts of purchase And a game within which a game takes place. The research team decided that home ethnographies with preschoolers and their families would yield a comprehensive database through which to give our producers additional information and insights, so we are beginning by performing 26 home ethnographies in three markets across the United States: an urban/suburban area on the East Coast, an urban/suburban area on the West Coast, and a suburban/rural area in the Midwest. Subjects in this study included 15 girls and 11 boys ranging from age 3 and three months to age 5 and 11 months. Also, because previous studies have shown the effects of older siblings on game play (demonstrated, for example, by more advanced motor coordination when using a computer mouse), households were employed in a combination of preschoolers with and without older peers. In order to understand experienced and new preschool users of the platform, we divided the sample so that 13 families owned at least one Nintendo DS and the others did not. For those households that did not own a DS, one was brought in for an interview for the child to play. This allowed us to see both the instinctive and intuitive movements of the new players (and of the more experienced players when playing new games), as well as the learned movements of the more experienced players. Each of these interviews took about 60 to 120 minutes and included the preschool-aged child, at least one parent, and often siblings and another caregiver. Three types of information were collected after each interview. Of all the older siblings and parents that were available, we collected data on: the buying decisions around the game systems in the household, the typical play patterns of the family, the levels of parental moderation in relation to computer games, and the most favorite games played by family members. We could also understand the ideology of gaming in these homes because of these home interviews: what types of spaces were used for the game, how the systems were installed, where handheld play took place in the house (as well as road play), and the number and type of games and game systems owned. The most important thing is that we collected the information for the game for each child. Before conducting the interviews, the research team discussed closely with home game producers to create a list of game mechanics and problems related to motor and cognitive abilities in preschoolers that were critical to their understanding prior to writing the games. These ranged from general skill issues related to game controllers to the effectiveness of in-game instructions to specific mechanics in current games that producers were interested in implementing for future early childhood titles. During the interviews, the facilitator gave preschool-specific guidance through a series of games so that he or she could observe the interaction and interrogate both the preschooler and his parents about feelings, attitudes, and frustrations that arose in the different circumstances If the subject in the experiment had previous exposure to the DS system, he or she was first asked to play his or her favorite game on that machine. This gave the researchers information about the current game skill related to the complexity of the chosen one, allowing them to see the child playing with mechanics that he or she was already familiar with. Among the 26 preschoolers, the scope of choice for the Nintendo DS was very wide, including the new Super Mario Bros., Sonic Prime. Nintendo, and the Tony Hawks proving ground. The interviewer watched the child play, noting preferences for game mechanics and motor interactions with the device, as well as the level of complexity of each game mechanic for the subject tested The researchers asked all preschoolers to play a specific game in consultation with our producers, The Little Mermaid: Arriles' Underwater Adventure. The game was chosen for two main reasons. First, it was one of the few games on the market with characters that appeal to this younger age group. Second, it incorporated a great variety of mechanics that emphasized the uniqueness of the DS platform, including the use of a microphone for exhaling or singing. The findings from this initial experiment were extensive. After reviewing the results and discussing the implications for game design with our internal game production team, we outlined the design needs and presented the findings to a company specializing in game design. We worked closely with the same experts to determine the game design for the two preschool-targeted DS games in development on what we collected. As the two DS games entered the development process, a constituent research course of action was established. Each time we developed new game mechanics, we brought preschoolers into our home utility lab to test the mechanics and evaluate both their simplicity and whether they were engaging. We tested alpha or beta versions of various game elements, in addition to examining the overall game structure. Once the full version of the DS game was ready, we went back to the field test with a dozen preschoolers and their parents to make sure that each of the game's components worked for the kids, and that the overall purpose of the game was understandable and the process was enjoyable for the players. We've also collected feedback from parents if they think the game is appropriate, engaging and worth the purchase.

premise: Consumer advice when buying shoes If you have a problem with shoes you recently bought follow this four-step plan. Step 1 Return to the store with proof of purchase. If you return damaged shoes at once, you have the right to insist on a refund. You're also likely to get one if you change your mind about the shoes and put them back right away. But if you are delayed or have had some use of shoes, the store may not refund you all your money. It depends on the condition of the shoes and how long you have them. If you are offered a bill of credit, you should not accept it. If you get it you usually won't be able to exchange it for cash later. Therefore, you may be left with an unwanted bill of credit, if you cannot find other shoes you want from the store. The store may want to send the shoes back to the head office for inspection. It's fair and can help sort things out but don't be turned away from the store that claims that it's the manufacturers responsibility. That's not true. The legal duty of the stores is to fix things. Step 2 If you seem to be getting nowhere, you can get help. You can get free advice from a Citizens Advice Bureau (get the address from your phone book), or from a local trading standards department. Again, refer to the telephone directory under the county, regional or borough council. In all these departments there are people who can advise you about defective goods and what to do with them. Step 3 Most stores are covered by the Footwear Code. If the store you are dealing with is covered, you can ask to send the shoes to a footwear inspection center for an independent opinion. The store has to agree with everything that the received report says. There is a charge of 21. You pay 7 and the store pays the rest (including postage). Step 4 As a last resort you can take your case to court. It's not as hard as it sounds. The small claims procedure for sums up to 1000 (750 in Scotland) is a cheap, easy and informal way to take legal action. The relevant forms are available from the county court nearest you or, in Scotland, from the sheriff court. You can get advice and newsletters from the Citizens Advice Bureau. Alternatively, some bookshops sell advice packs containing the relevant forms.
hypothesis: Legal advice and forms can be bought from some stores.
label: e

premise: Arctic pollution Our perception of the Arctic is that its distance from industrial centres keeps it pristine and clear of the impact of pollution. However, through a process known as cross-border pollution, the Arctic is receiving pollutants whose sources are thousands of miles away. Large amounts of pollutants are spilled into our atmosphere as well as our lakes, rivers and oceans on a daily basis. In the past 20 years, scientists have discovered a growing range of toxic pollutants in the north, including pesticides from agriculture, chemicals and heavy metals from industry, and even radioactive fallout from Chernobyl. These are substances that have invaded ecosystems almost worldwide, but are of particular concern in the Arctic. Originally, Arctic pollution was largely blamed for chemical leaks, and these leaks were thought to be small and localized. The consensus now is that pollutants from around the world are carried north by rivers, ocean currents and atmospheric circulation. Due to extreme conditions in the Arctic, including reduced sunlight, extensive ice cover and cold temperatures, pollutants break down much more slowly than in warmer climates. Pollutants can also be highly concentrated because of the significantly lengthened lifespan in the Arctic. Problems of spring runoff into coastal waters during the growth period of marine life are of critical concern. Spring algae bloom readily and absorb the concentrated pollutants released by spring melting. These algae are eaten in turn by zooplankton and a wide variety of marine life. The buildup of these pollutants increases with each step in the food chain or network and may affect northerners who eat marine mammals near the top of the food chain. Pollutants do not respect borders; cross-border pollution is the movement of pollutants across political boundaries, whether via air, rivers, or ocean currents. The eight Western countries, led by the 1989 Finnish initiative, established the Arctic Environmental Protection Strategy (AEPS) in which the participants agreed to develop an Arctic Monitoring and Assessment Program (AMAP). AMAP is establishing an international scientific network to monitor the current state of the Arctic in relation to specific pollutants. This monitoring program is extremely important because it will give a scientific basis for understanding the extent of the problem. In the 1950s, pilots travelling on weather reconnaissance flights in the Canadian High Arctic reported seeing bands of spring haze in the Arctic. It was during this period that the term arctic haze was first used, in reference to this smog of unknown origin. But it was not until 1972 that Dr. Glenn Shaw of the Geophysical Institute at the University of Alaska first presented ideas about the nature and long origin of Arctic haze. The idea that the source was long-term was very difficult for many to support. Every winter, cold, dense air settles over the Arctic. In the dark it appears that the Arctic is increasingly polluted by the accumulation of mid-latitude emissions from fossil fuel burning, smelting and other industrial processes. In late winter, the Arctic is covered with a layer of this haze the size of the African continent. When spring light reaches the Arctic, there is a smog-like haze, which makes the region, at times, look like pollution over cities like Los Angeles. This polluted air is a well-known and well-characterized feature of the Arctic environment in late winter. In America's northern Arctic, episodes of brown or black snow formed into land-based storm tracks that deliver gaseous pollutants and bound particles from Asian deserts and agricultural areas. Today it is known that the pollutants mostly originate from Europe and Asia. Arctic haze has been studied most extensively at Point Barrow, Alaska, throughout the Canadian Arctic and at Svalbard (Norway). Evidence from ice cores drilled from the Greenland ice sheet suggests that these haze particles did not always exist in the Arctic, but only began to appear in the last century. The Arctic haze particles appear to be similar to smog particles observed in more southern industrial areas, consisting mostly of sulfates mixed with carbon particles. It is believed the particles are formed when the gaseous sulfur dioxide produced by burning sulfur-carrying coal is irradiated in sunlight and oxidized to sulfur, a process catalyzed by trace elements in the air. These sulfate particles or droplets of sulfuric acid quickly trap the carbon particles, which also float in the air. Pure sulfate particles or droplets are colorless, so the darkness of the haze is believed to be caused by the carbon particles involved. The effect of haze on Arctic ecosystems, as well as the global environment, has not been adequately studied. The pollutants have only been studied in their spray form over the Arctic. However, little is known about what happens to them in the end. It is known that they are removed somehow. There is a good degree of likelihood that the pollutants will end up in the ocean, most likely the North Atlantic, the Norwegian Sea and possibly the Bering Sea, all three very important fisheries. Currently, the main issue among researchers is understanding the impact of Arctic haze on global climate change. The pollutants absorb sunlight and in turn heat the atmosphere. The global impact of this is currently unknown but the implications are quite strong.

The idea is that in each locality there should be only one pattern that best protects their wearers. These distant relatives of British Camberwell Beauty are found in abundance throughout Central and South America and the Caribbean. They are famous for their bright colors, poisonous bodies, and complex mimetic relationships. Although all ethomines are poisonous, their interest is to evolve to look like each other because predators that learn to avoid one species will also avoid others that resemble it. This is known as Mulerian mimicry. Mimicry rings may also contain insects that are not poisonous but are protected by appearance like a model species that is: an adaptation called Batesian mimicry. SO STRONG IS THE AVOIDANCE RESPONSE FROM EXPERIENCED PREDATORS THAT EVEN AN INCONGRUOUS IMAGINATION GIVES SOME PROTECTION. There will often be a whole series of species that mimic, with varying degrees of veracity, a focal or model species, says John Turner of the University of Leeds. The results of these frauds are some of the most refined examples of evolution known to science. In addition to color, many mimic copying behaviors and even the flight pattern of their model species. But why are there so many different imitation rings? One idea is that species that fly at the same height in the forest canopy evolve to look like each other. It has been suggested since the 1970s that the mimicry complexes are stratified according to flight altitude, DeVries says. The idea is that the color patterns of the wings are camouflaged against the different light and shadow patterns at each level in the canopy, providing a first line of defense, against predators. But the light patterns and wing patterns don't match up well, he says. And observations show that the insects do not move in altitude as the day progresses and light patterns change. Worse, according to DeVries, this theory does not explain why the model species flew at this particular altitude in the first place. They really flew that way. What he didn't get, however, was the explanation of light patterns. I thought, if this idea is really true, and I can see why it might help explain why there are so many different warning patterns in any one place. So maybe we can finally figure out how they can evolve in such a complex way. The work was complicated because of the huge diversity of species involved in Jeton Sacha. Not only were there 56 Ithomynean butterfly species divided among eight mimic rings, there were also 69 other insect species, including 34 day-flying moths and a fly, all in a 200-acre study area. Unlike many previous employees, he kept very precise notes of where exactly he caught his samples. The attention to detail paid off. Backloni found that the mimicry rings flew at two quite separate heights. Their use of the forest was quite unique, he recalled. For example, most members of the clear-winged mimicry ring would fly close to the forest floor, while most of the 12 species in the leopard-winged ring fly high up. Each imitation ring had its own characteristic flight altitude. However, being a practice rather than a theory, things have been a bit of a blur. They spend most of their time flying at a certain altitude. But they also spend a smaller proportion of their time flying at other altitudes, admits Clooney. Species were not stacked as rigidly as passenger planes waiting to land, but they seemed to prefer forest airspace. So far, so good, but he still hasn't explained what causes the different ethomine groups and their chromatic partners to fly in formations at these specific altitudes. Then Baccaloni had a brilliant idea. I started looking at the distribution of food plants of the ithomein larvae within the canopy, he says. For each, the Id records the height to which the host plant has grown and the height above the ground where the eggs or larvae were found. Once I brought them back to the field stations lab, it was just a matter of keeping them alive until they grew up and then hatched into adults I could identify.

premise: Can you pass me my glasses, please? The human eye was not designed for the years of intensive book learning prevalent today in modern society. The result is strain and deterioration in the eyes, often at a young age, but the same company has provided the obvious answer: corrective eyeglasses with lenses. The optical correction of poor vision in these devices, ubiquitous and always present, coming in all styles, colors and designs, is a stage that probably everyone will have to face at some point in their lives. It is not surprising that the first glasses were made by Catholic monks dedicated to writing, translating and copying well-written religious texts. In contrast to the general under-education and illiteracy of the time, these monks were proficient in many languages, and worked for years in scripts with poorly lit candles, an effort that took its toll on their eyesight. Thus, the earliest pictorial evidence of the use of glasses is a 1352 portrait of the Catholic cardinal, Hugh de Provence. However, the usefulness of spectacles had long since been realized by the population in general, and by 1300 the trade in lens grinding was widespread enough to require guilds and official regulations. Although popular and effective, no one was sure of the mechanics of it all. The first detailed mathematical explanation would not arrive until Johannes Kepler published his work on optics in 1604. Basically, glasses change the focal length of the eye lens. There are two main focus disorders: myopia and hyperopia. In the case of the first (myopia, in which it is difficult to see objects at a distance), concave lenses are used, which compensate for the refractive error in the eyes by pushing the focal point back, to the retina. Hyperopia (distance vision) uses convex lenses to do the opposite, bringing the focal point forward, to the retina. However, to accommodate the range of situations where clear vision is needed, from reading books and computer screens, to watching TV and driving cars, some glasses are equipped with more than one type of lens. The most common are bifocal lenses, with two distinct horizontal viewing areas. A conscious effort is therefore needed to focus through the lens band necessary to solve the visual challenge faced. A variation that helps with this are lenses that allow progressive transitions, rather than obvious changes between viewing angles. The simplest system of all is to have only a few pairs of glasses, saving them for specific tasks. Nowadays, lenses are often a plastic polycarbonate material, which offers lower weight and greater resistance to scratches, as well as the ability to filter out harmful ultraviolet and infrared rays from the sun. Similarly, the frames are flexible and lightweight, offering less friction and irritation to the skin. However, it cannot be said that glasses are convenient devices. Fat, dirt, sweat and steam can disperse them when eating or cooking, or from natural condensation due to temperature changes (for example when leaving a heated building to the colder outside). Glasses are embarrassing even during fast sports or labor work, break quite easily and are not cheap to repair. Obviously, therefore, contact lenses have considerable advantages. These are inserted directly above the pupil, and have the added benefit of perceived aesthetic appeal. Traditional glasses are sometimes seen as unfashionable, bearing associations of age or infirmity. The almost invisible contacts avoid this, which is perhaps one of the reasons why most wearers are women. However, by fully covering the pupil, contacts also offer better peripheral vision, and are better suited to less common visual impairments. Their disadvantage is the difficulty and inconvenience associated with putting them on and taking them off. They can also cause dryness and irritation. However, it is interesting to note that the modern era has seen eyeglasses become somewhat of a fashion accessory. Musicians Buddy Holly and John Lennon were so characterized by their glasses that their name was given to the style they wore. It is now even possible to buy glasses off the shelf, without an eye test, and profit from the need for quick solutions that people want in a busy society. Although they are a source of great income, the opticians recommend that people do proper eye examinations, not only to ensure the best results, but also for early detection of potential eye diseases, such as glaucoma, that may actually be the root cause of focus problems. Lace of the future may well be laser eye surgery. In this process, laser beams are used, usually to change the curvature of the cornea and thus provide long-term remedial benefits. Although it is simple enough and increasingly safe and affordable, given the subtlety of the eye, there remains little risk of failure and consequent vision problems, such as ghosting or halos. An interesting fact is that despite the growth of such surgery, and the use of contacts, traditional lenses remain as popular as ever. Nothing, it seems, can match the simple convenience of putting on a pair of glasses.
hypothesis: When glasses were invented, most people could read.
label: c

The ultimate goal is to prevent them from re-offending, an event technically known as criminal reoffending. This accurate assessment is a difficult subject, and it must be accepted that there are some people who can never be rehabilitated, the more we try. The term psychopath is often used here, one of the main determinants of this condition is an inability to learn from past mistakes. Thus, techniques to improve their behavior are unlikely to work. Obviously recidivism is highly correlated with this condition, but studies have shown that psychopathic prisoners tend to be released from prisons just as much as non-psychopathic ones. This is often explained by the fact that psychopathic people develop better strategies to mask their intentions, and become more adept at misleading others. Care and treatment only give them knowledge of criminal and judicial proceedings, which they can then twist to their advantage, commonly referred to as system cracking. Cases like these reveal the biggest problem in rehabilitation: the difficulty of reading the deepest intentions of human beings. However, the prisoners will be released, and as a result will need assistance to reintegrate them into society. This is most often done through parole, which involves the serving of the remainder of a sentence outside prison. This differs from probation, which is used in lieu of prison sentences, and consequently places greater limitations on the subject. A similar system is supervised release, when the subject faces the same limitations as probation, but only after serving the entire prison sentence. Whatever the case, the parole officer will supervise the released prisoner, offering support and assistance wherever possible. The decision on whether to grant parole normally rests with a parole board. The members may be judges, psychiatrists, criminologists and appointed citizens from the local community. The common factor is that they all have a good education, and are considered to have high moral standing. Again, trying to assess the psychological state of prisoners and what intentions are within them is problematic at best. These include the obvious, such as complying with the law, and contacting the parole officer at defined intervals, but may be more individual and specific, such as not using drugs and alcohol, and returning to the residence before a certain time (known as curfew). Ignoring all this, an arrest warrant is issued, the release time is stopped, and after that a discussion about the violation of parole is discussed. The Parole Board then makes a decision on whether to revoke the release (which sees the subject re-incarcerated) or allow the continuation of the release. As already mentioned, such decisions are not hard science, and mistakes can be made. That could make the release of parole a controversial issue and political baggage. It only takes one famous crime from a man on parole to violently mobilise public opinion against this system. Thus, the political will is often lacking, which has seen, for example, some US states abolish the parole system entirely, and others have done so for specific offences. Most often this is a response to public pressure, rather than a balanced assessment of the pros and cons. As always, the same argument applies without parole as an interim step, released prisoners may face an uphill struggle to avoid reoffending, which will cost society much more in the longer term. A more innovative method of encouraging rehabilitation is time off for good behavior. For each year of incarceration, it automatically assigns inmates who demonstrate good behavior a certain number of days. This means that year after year the good time is accumulated, resulting in the eventual release of perhaps a third of the penalty earlier. However, if prisoners commit more than a certain number of offences, or are particularly serious, they lose their time and must complete the full duration of their sentence.

premise: Pills Cure Everything: Myths or Reality? Browse the shelves of any health food store or pharmacy and you will find dozens of dietary supplements vitamins, antioxidants, minerals with a seemingly endless variety of homeopathic remedies. There is always something new, some wonder ingredient that offers the promise of a longer, healthier and happier life. There are extracts from every type of fruit and vegetable you can imagine, tomato, celery, carrots, papaya and cranberries along with green tea elixir, red wine extract and vitamins A-K in every color and shape. And all these supplements claim to help us in the constant fight against aging, cancer, cardiovascular disease and a plethora of other ailments. However, recent studies may show that this is too good to be true. How true are these claims? Vitamin tablets have been around forever, but antioxidants are the latest panacea; the question is, do they work? If the hype is true, then what antioxidants do is neutralize the free radicals in our bodies and later excrete them. Free radicals are atoms or molecules that have at least one unpaired electron and are therefore unstable and highly reactive. In animal tissues, they are believed to accelerate the progression of cardiovascular and age-related diseases, such as dementia and cancer. Antioxidants in fresh fruits and vegetables have been shown to combine with free radicals and neutralize them, preventing the oxidation that can lead to disease. An apple a day keeps the Rupaam away, eaten alongside four other servings of fresh fruits and vegetables! Obviously, those who eat more fruits and vegetables and the recommended daily intake is at least five servings are less prone to disease and live longer and healthier lives. Over the past 20-30 years, scientists have worked to isolate the active ingredients in fruits and vegetables that are considered antioxidants and conducted controlled tests of antioxidants, which have revealed that they do indeed appear to have the ability to stop some of the chemical processes that cause disease. Thus was born the multimillion-dollar industry of bottled antioxidants to supplement the diets of the busy and stressed. Antioxidants were first called into question during a large clinical trial in the US, in which a very common antioxidant, beta-carotene, also called pro-vitamin A (found in yellow and green vegetables, dairy and fish), was tested for its effectiveness against lung cancer in high-risk subjects. To the surprise and concern of the scientists who conducted the experiment, those people who took the supplement designed to reduce the risk of cancer had a significantly higher risk of developing lung cancer. This amazing discovery led to the abandonment of the experiments in the middle of the experimental process. Since that experiment in the mid-90s, other studies have similarly indicated that antioxidants and vitamin supplements are of questionable health value at best, and potentially harmful. It seems that even common vitamin supplements like vitamin C may, in large doses, actually worsen the risk of cardiovascular disease or cancer. As a result of these alarming studies, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and its European equivalent, the European Medical Agency (EMEA), made the decision to ban the manufacture and sale of a number of higher dose food additives currently on the market. Another aspect of the increasingly complex picture to consider is that recent research findings have also questioned some previously held beliefs about free radicals. It is possible, some scientists believe, that free radicals actually play a role in preventing disease. Professor Jennifer Horton of the University of West Wyoming is one of a number of scientists who have found that in small amounts, the free radicals may help stimulate the antioxidant systems in our bodies. It also turns out that free radicals may play a fundamental role in combating disease; recent studies at UIC suggest that they kill harmful bacteria and even cancer cells. Obviously, then, the use of bottled supplements with your diet is a practice to approach with caution; and essential to keep abreast of new developments in research. Ironically, those health-conscious people who already eat large amounts of fresh fruits and vegetables, whose diet excludes junk food and who get plenty of regular exercise and have less need for supplements tend to be the ones most likely to use them.
hypothesis: The FDA and EMEA have jointly funded a study on the safety of certain higher-dose vitamin supplements.
label: n

While steamships could make use of the fast and direct route between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea, the canal was of no use to sailing ships, which needed the stronger winds of much of the oceans, and therefore had to sail a much greater distance. While the global economy is expanding at a little more than 3% a year, the volume of trade has risen at a compound annual rate of roughly twice that. Foreign products, from meat to machinery, play a more important role in almost every economy in the world, and foreign markets are now luring businesses that have never cared much about sales beyond their countries' borders. What's behind this explosion in international trade? The general global decline in trade barriers, like tariffs and import quotas, is undoubtedly one explanation. The economic opening up of countries that have traditionally been small players is another. But one force behind the boom in imports and exports has gone almost unnoticed: the rapidly falling cost of getting goods into the market. Theoretically, in the world of trade, shipping costs are not important. It is assumed that goods, once they are produced, move instantly and at no cost from place to place. The real world, however, is full of frictions. Cheap labor may make Chinese clothes competitive in America, but if shipping delays tie up working capital and cause winter coats to arrive in spring, the trade could lose its advantages. At the beginning of the 20th century, agriculture and manufacturing were the two most important sectors almost everywhere, accounting for about 70% of total output in Germany, Italy and France, and 40-50% in America, Britain and Japan. International trade is therefore dominated by raw materials, such as wheat, timber and iron ore, or processed goods, such as meat and steel. But products of this type are heavy and bulky, and the cost of their transportation is relatively high. Countries still trade disproportionately with their geographic neighbors. Over time, however, world output shifted to goods whose value is unrelated to their size and weight. Today it is finished manufactured products that dominate the flow of commerce, and thanks to technological advances such as lightweight components, manufactured products themselves have tended to be lighter and less bulky. As a result, less transportation is required for each dollar of import or export. To see how this affects trade, consider the business of manufacturing disk drives for computers. Most of the world's disk drive production is concentrated in Southeast Asia. This is only possible because disk drives, although valuable, are small and light and therefore cost little to ship. Computer makers in Japan or Texas would not face bigger freight bills if they imported drives from Singapore instead of purchasing them in the local market. Distance is therefore not an obstacle to the globalization of the disk drive industry. This is even more true of the fast-growing information industries. Compact films and discs cost little to transport, even on a plane. Businesses can locate based on other considerations, such as the availability of labor, while worrying less about the cost of delivering their output. In many countries the deregulation has helped to jump-start the process. But behind the scenes, a series of technological innovations widely known as containerization and intermodal transportation led to rapid productivity improvements in cargo handling. Forty years ago, the export or import process involved very many handling steps, which risked parts of the shipment being damaged or stolen along the way. The invention of the container crane made it possible to load and unload containers without overturning the ship and the adoption of standard container sizes allowed the transport of almost any box in any ship. By 1967, dual-purpose ships, carrying loose cargo in hold* and containers on board, gave way to ships of all containers that transported thousands of boxes at a time. The shipping container has made ocean shipping a highly efficient and highly competitive business. But getting the cargo to and from the dock was a different story. National governments, in general, have kept a far firmer hand on truck and rail fares than on charges for sea freight. This, however, began to change in the mid-1970s, when America began deregulating its transportation industry. First airlines, then road and rail haulers, were freed from the restrictions on what they could carry, where they could haul it and what price they could charge. Large productivity gains were made. Between 1985 and 1996, for example, the railroads in America dramatically reduced their employment, route, and locomotive fleets while increasing the amount of freight hauled. The European railways also showed significant, albeit smaller, improvements in productivity. In America the period of huge productivity increases in transport may be almost over, but in most countries the process still has to go a long way. State ownership of railroads and airlines, regulation of freight rates, and tolerance of anticompetitive practices, such as cargo handling monopolies, all keep the cost of shipping unnecessarily high and discourage international trade. Lowering these barriers would help the world's economies move even closer.

Foreign products, from meat to machinery, play a more important role in almost every economy in the world, and foreign markets are now luring businesses that have never cared much about sales beyond their countries' borders. What's behind this explosion in international trade? The general global decline in trade barriers, like tariffs and import quotas, is undoubtedly one explanation. The economic opening up of countries that have traditionally been small players is another. But one force behind the boom in imports and exports has gone almost unnoticed: the rapidly falling cost of getting goods into the market. Theoretically, in the world of trade, shipping costs are not important. It is assumed that goods, once they are produced, move instantly and at no cost from place to place. The real world, however, is full of frictions. Cheap labor may make Chinese clothes competitive in America, but if shipping delays tie up working capital and cause winter coats to arrive in spring, the trade could lose its advantages. At the beginning of the 20th century, agriculture and manufacturing were the two most important sectors almost everywhere, accounting for about 70% of total output in Germany, Italy and France, and 40-50% in America, Britain and Japan. International trade is therefore dominated by raw materials, such as wheat, timber and iron ore, or processed goods, such as meat and steel. But products of this type are heavy and bulky, and the cost of their transportation is relatively high. Countries still trade disproportionately with their geographic neighbors. Over time, however, world output shifted to goods whose value is unrelated to their size and weight. Today it is finished manufactured products that dominate the flow of commerce, and thanks to technological advances such as lightweight components, manufactured products themselves have tended to be lighter and less bulky. As a result, less transportation is required for each dollar of import or export. To see how this affects trade, consider the business of manufacturing disk drives for computers. Most of the world's disk drive production is concentrated in Southeast Asia. This is only possible because disk drives, although valuable, are small and light and therefore cost little to ship. Computer makers in Japan or Texas would not face bigger freight bills if they imported drives from Singapore instead of purchasing them in the local market. Distance is therefore not an obstacle to the globalization of the disk drive industry. This is even more true of the fast-growing information industries. Compact films and discs cost little to transport, even on a plane. COMPUTER SOFTWARE CAN BE EXPORTED WITHOUT LOADING IT ONTO A SHIP, SIMPLY BY TRANSPORTING IT ON TELEPHONE LINES FROM COUNTRY TO COUNTRY, SO FREIGHT RATES AND CARGO HANDLING SCHEDULES BECOME INSIGNIFICANT FACTORS IN DECIDING WHERE TO PRODUCE THE PRODUCT. Businesses can locate based on other considerations, such as the availability of labor, while worrying less about the cost of delivering their output. In many countries the deregulation has helped to jump-start the process. But behind the scenes, a series of technological innovations widely known as containerization and intermodal transportation led to rapid productivity improvements in cargo handling. Forty years ago, the export or import process involved very many handling steps, which risked parts of the shipment being damaged or stolen along the way. The invention of the container crane made it possible to load and unload containers without overturning the ship and the adoption of standard container sizes allowed the transport of almost any box in any ship. By 1967, dual-purpose ships, carrying loose cargo in hold* and containers on board, gave way to ships of all containers that transported thousands of boxes at a time. The shipping container has made ocean shipping a highly efficient and highly competitive business. But getting the cargo to and from the dock was a different story. National governments, in general, have kept a far firmer hand on truck and rail fares than on charges for sea freight. This, however, began to change in the mid-1970s, when America began deregulating its transportation industry. First airlines, then road and rail haulers, were freed from the restrictions on what they could carry, where they could haul it and what price they could charge. Large productivity gains were made. Between 1985 and 1996, for example, the railroads in America dramatically reduced their employment, route, and locomotive fleets while increasing the amount of freight hauled. The European railways also showed significant, albeit smaller, improvements in productivity. In America the period of huge productivity increases in transport may be almost over, but in most countries the process still has to go a long way. State ownership of railroads and airlines, regulation of freight rates, and tolerance of anticompetitive practices, such as cargo handling monopolies, all keep the cost of shipping unnecessarily high and discourage international trade. Lowering these barriers would help the world's economies move even closer.

premise: Diabetes Here are some facts you probably didn't know about diabetes. It is the fastest growing disease in the world. It is the sixth leading cause of death in Australia. Over a million Australians suffer from it although 50% of them are still unaware of it. Every 10 minutes someone is diagnosed with diabetes. So much about the facts but what exactly is diabetes? Diabetes is the name given to a group of different conditions in which there is too much glucose in the blood. Here's what happens: the body needs glucose as its main source of fuel or energy. The body produces glucose from carbohydrate-containing foods such as carbohydrate-containing vegetables (such as potatoes or corn) and cereal foods (such as bread, pasta and rice) as well as fruits and milk. Glucose is carried in the body in the blood and the level of glucose is called glycemia. Glycaemia (blood sugar levels) in humans and animals must be neither too high nor too low, but just right. The glucose that circulates in the bloodstream now has to leave the blood and body tissues. This is where insulin comes into the story. Insulin is a hormone produced by the pancreas, a gland that sits just below the stomach. Insulin opens the doors that allow glucose to pass from the blood to the cells of the body where energy is generated. This process is called glucose metabolism. In diabetes, the pancreas cannot produce insulin or the insulin it produces is insufficient and cannot work properly. Without insulin doing its job, the glucose channels are closed. Glucose builds up in the blood leading to high blood glucose levels, which causes the health problems associated with diabetes. People refer to the disease as diabetes, but in fact there are two unique types of the disease. Type 1 diabetes is a condition characterized by high blood glucose levels caused by a complete lack of insulin. It occurs when the body's immune system attacks the insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas and destroys them. The pancreas then produces little or no insulin. Type 1 diabetes usually develops in young people but can occur in adults. Type 2 diabetes is the most common form of diabetes. In type 2 diabetes, either the body does not produce enough insulin or the cells ignore the insulin. Insulin is necessary so that the body can use sugar. Sugar is the basic fuel for cells in the body, and insulin takes the sugar from the blood into the cells. The diagnosis of diabetes often depends on what type the patient suffers from. In type 1 diabetes, the symptoms are usually sudden and sometimes even life-threatening hyperglycemia (high blood sugar levels) can lead to coma and is therefore often diagnosed quite quickly. In type 2 diabetes, many people have no symptoms at all, while other signs can go unnoticed, and are perceived as part of aging. Therefore, until symptoms are noticed, the blood glucose level for many people can be very high. Common symptoms include: being thirsty more than usual, passing more urine, feeling lethargic, always feeling hungry, for cuts that heal slowly, itching, skin infections, bad breath, blurred vision, unexplained weight change, mood swings, headaches, feeling dizzy and cramps in the legs. Currently there is no cure for diabetes, but there is a huge amount of research looking for a cure and providing excellent management techniques and products until a cure is found. Whether it's type 1 or type 2 diabetes, the goal of any diabetes treatment is to bring your blood glucose levels as close to the non-diabetic range as possible. For people with type 1 diabetes, this means insulin injections every day plus a healthy lifestyle. For people with type 2 diabetes, healthy eating and regular exercise may be all that's needed at first: sometimes tablets and/or insulin may be needed later. Ideally blood glucose levels are kept as close to the non-diabetic range as possible so frequent self-examination is a good idea. This will help prevent the short-term effects of very low or very high glucose levels in the blood, as well as the possible long-term problems. If someone is dependent on insulin, it must be injected into the body. Insulin can not be taken as a pill. Insulin will break down during digestion just like the protein in food. Insulin must be injected into the fat under your skin so that it enters your blood. Diabetes mellitus can cause serious complications for patients. When glucose builds up in the blood instead of entering the cells, it can cause problems. Short-term problems are similar in symptoms but long-term high blood sugar levels can lead to heart attacks, strokes, kidney failure, amputations and blindness. Your blood pressure and cholesterol outside the recommended range can also lead to problems like heart attack and stroke and in fact 2 out of 3 people with diabetes eventually die from these complications. Young adults aged 18 to 44 with type 2 diabetes are 14 times more likely to have a heart attack, and are 30 times more likely to have a stroke than their peers without diabetes. Young women account for almost all of the increase in heart attack risk, while young men are twice as likely to suffer a stroke as young women. This means that a huge number of people are going to have heart disease, heart attacks and strokes years, sometimes even decades, before they should.
hypothesis: Most diabetics develop heart problems or suffer a stroke.

Over a million Australians suffer from it although 50% of them are still unaware of it. Every 10 minutes someone is diagnosed with diabetes. So much about the facts but what exactly is diabetes? Diabetes is the name given to a group of different conditions in which there is too much glucose in the blood. Here's what happens: the body needs glucose as its main source of fuel or energy. The body produces glucose from carbohydrate-containing foods such as carbohydrate-containing vegetables (such as potatoes or corn) and cereal foods (such as bread, pasta and rice) as well as fruits and milk. Glucose is carried in the body in the blood and the level of glucose is called glycemia. Glycaemia (blood sugar levels) in humans and animals must be neither too high nor too low, but just right. The glucose that circulates in the bloodstream now has to leave the blood and body tissues. This is where insulin comes into the story. Insulin is a hormone produced by the pancreas, a gland that sits just below the stomach. Insulin opens the doors that allow glucose to pass from the blood to the cells of the body where energy is generated. This process is called glucose metabolism. In diabetes, the pancreas cannot produce insulin or the insulin it produces is insufficient and cannot work properly. Without insulin doing its job, the glucose channels are closed. Glucose builds up in the blood leading to high blood glucose levels, which causes the health problems associated with diabetes. People refer to the disease as diabetes, but in fact there are two unique types of the disease. Type 1 diabetes is a condition characterized by high blood glucose levels caused by a complete lack of insulin. It occurs when the body's immune system attacks the insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas and destroys them. The pancreas then produces little or no insulin. Type 1 diabetes usually develops in young people but can occur in adults. Type 2 diabetes is the most common form of diabetes. In type 2 diabetes, either the body does not produce enough insulin or the cells ignore the insulin. Insulin is necessary so that the body can use sugar. Sugar is the basic fuel for cells in the body, and insulin takes the sugar from the blood into the cells. The diagnosis of diabetes often depends on what type the patient suffers from. In type 1 diabetes, the symptoms are usually sudden and sometimes even life-threatening hyperglycemia (high blood sugar levels) can lead to coma and is therefore often diagnosed quite quickly. In type 2 diabetes, many people have no symptoms at all, while other signs can go unnoticed, and are perceived as part of aging. Therefore, until symptoms are noticed, the blood glucose level for many people can be very high. Common symptoms include: being thirsty more than usual, passing more urine, feeling lethargic, always feeling hungry, for cuts that heal slowly, itching, skin infections, bad breath, blurred vision, unexplained weight change, mood swings, headaches, feeling dizzy and cramps in the legs. Currently there is no cure for diabetes, but there is a huge amount of research looking for a cure and providing excellent management techniques and products until a cure is found. Whether it's type 1 or type 2 diabetes, the goal of any diabetes treatment is to bring your blood glucose levels as close to the non-diabetic range as possible. For people with type 1 diabetes, this means insulin injections every day plus a healthy lifestyle. For people with type 2 diabetes, healthy eating and regular exercise may be all that's needed at first: sometimes tablets and/or insulin may be needed later. Ideally blood glucose levels are kept as close to the non-diabetic range as possible so frequent self-examination is a good idea. This will help prevent the short-term effects of very low or very high glucose levels in the blood, as well as the possible long-term problems. If someone is dependent on insulin, it must be injected into the body. Insulin can not be taken as a pill. Insulin will break down during digestion just like the protein in food. Insulin must be injected into the fat under your skin so that it enters your blood. Diabetes mellitus can cause serious complications for patients. When glucose builds up in the blood instead of entering the cells, it can cause problems. Short-term problems are similar in symptoms but long-term high blood sugar levels can lead to heart attacks, strokes, kidney failure, amputations and blindness. Your blood pressure and cholesterol outside the recommended range can also lead to problems like heart attack and stroke and in fact 2 out of 3 people with diabetes eventually die from these complications. Young adults aged 18 to 44 with type 2 diabetes are 14 times more likely to have a heart attack, and are 30 times more likely to have a stroke than their peers without diabetes. Young women account for almost all of the increase in heart attack risk, while young men are twice as likely to suffer a stroke as young women. This means that a huge number of people are going to have heart disease, heart attacks and strokes years, sometimes even decades, before they should.

premise: Drinking filtered water The body consists mainly of water. This means that the quality of the water we drink daily has an important impact on our health. Filtered water is healthier than tap water and some bottled water. This is because it is free of contaminants, that is, substances that make it dirty or harmful. Substances that settle at the bottom of a glass of tap water and disease-carrying microorganisms (called bacteria or bacteria) are examples of contaminants. Filtered water is also free of toxic metals and chemicals that are common in tap water and even some brands of bottled water. Authorities know ordinary tap water is full of contaminants and they use chemicals, like chlorine and bromine to disinfect it. But such chemicals are hardly safe. Indeed, their use in water is associated with many different conditions and they are especially dangerous for children and pregnant women. For example, consuming bromine for a long time can cause low blood pressure, which can cause poisoning of the brain, heart, kidneys, and liver. Filtered water is usually clean of such water-disinfecting chemicals. Filtered water is also clean of metals, such as mercury and lead. Mercury has come to our drinking water mainly because the dental mixtures used by dentists have not been safely discarded for a long time. Scientists believe there is a link between mercury in water and many allergies and cancers as well as disorders, like ADD, OCD, autism and depression. Lead, however, usually finds its way into our drinking water because of pipe leaks. Of course modern pipes are not made of lead but pipes in older homes usually are. Lead is a known carcinogen and has been linked to pregnancy problems and birth defects. This is another reason why children and pregnant women must drink filtered water. The benefits of water are well known. We all know, for example, that it helps detoxify the body, so the purer the water we drink, the easier it is for the body to get rid of toxins. The result of drinking filtered water is that the body does not need to use as much of its energy for detoxification as when drinking unfiltered water. This means that drinking filtered water is good for our health in general. This is because the body can perform all its functions much more easily and this results in improved metabolism, better weight management, improved lubrication of the joints as well as effective hydration of the skin. There are many different ways to filter water and each type of filter targets different pollutants. For example, activated carbon water filters are very good at removing chlorine. Ozone water filters, on the other hand, are particularly effective at removing bacteria. For this reason, it is very important to know exactly what is in the water we drink so that we can decide what type of water filter to use. The Consumer Confidence Report (CCR) should be useful for this purpose. It is a certificate issued by public water suppliers every year, detailing the pollutants present in the water. If you know what these pollutants are, then it is easier to decide what kind of water filter to get.
hypothesis: The type of water you consume on a regular basis has a great impact on your overall health and well-being.

premise: Daydreamers all daydream sometimes. premise: Deer farming in Australia Deer are not native to Australia. They were introduced to the country during the nineteenth century as part of the acclimatization programs governing the introduction of exotic species of animals and birds into Australia. Six species of deer have been released in different locations. The animals dispersed and established wild populations in various locations around Australia, largely depending on their points of release into the wild. These animals formed the basis of the deer industry in Australia today. Commercial deer farming in Australia began in Victoria in 1971 with the capture of rossa deer from the Royal National Park, NSW. By 1985, only four species of deer, two from temperate climates (Red, Dora) and two tropical species (Russa, Chittle) were restricted to commercial farming. In late 1985, pressure from industry to increase the number of herds resulted in the development of import protocols. This resulted in the introduction of a large number of hybrids of red deer from New Zealand and North American elk directly from Canada. The cultivated national deer herd is now distributed in all states although most are found in New South Wales and Victoria. The number of animals farmed each year has continued to grow, despite the downward trend in venison prices since 1997. Worrying is the apparent increase in the number of female animals farmed and the number of intact herds committed to processing. With more than 40,000 animals farmed in 1998/99 and 60,000 in 1999/2000, there is a justified concern that the following years may see a dramatic decline in production. At least 85% of all venison produced in Australia is exported, mostly to Europe. At least 90% of all velvet rays produced are exported in an unprocessed state to Asia. PROGRAMS TO PROMOTE AUSTRALIAN DEER PRODUCTS CONTINUE TO HAVE A POSITIVE IMPACT ON SALES WHICH IN TURN POSITIVELY AFFECT THE PRICES PAID TO BREEDERS. The industry appears to be showing limited signs that it is emerging from a state of depression caused by internal and external factors that include: (i) the decline in the Asian currency; (ii) the lack of competitive advantage of the industry in impactful markets (particularly in relation to competition in New Zealand), and; (iii) within industry processing and marketing competition over limited product volumes of venison. Since the formation of the Australian Deer Breeders Association in 1979, the representative body for the industry has evolved through the Deer Farmers Association of Australia into the Deer Industry Association of Australia Limited (DIAA), which was registered in 1995. The industry has established two product development and marketing companies, Australian Deer Horn and Co-Products Pty Ltd (ADH) and Deer Industry Development Projects Pty Ltd, traded as the Deer Horn Industry Company (DIC). ADH collects and markets Australian deer horn and joint products on behalf of Australian deer farmers. IT PROMOTES THE HARVESTING OF VELVET RAYS ACCORDING TO THE STRICT QUALITY ASSURANCE PROGRAM PROMOTED BY THE INDUSTRY. The company also designs and coordinates regular velvet certification courses for Australian deer farmers. Estimates suggest that until the early 1990s the annual rate of increase in the number of farmed deer was up to 25%, but after 1993 this rate of increase probably declined to less than 10%. The main reasons for the decline in deer herd breeding rates during such a critical period for the market were: (i) severe drought conditions until 1998 that affected eastern Australia during 1993-96 and (ii) the consequent slaughter of a large number of breeding females, at very low prices. These factors have combined to reduce confidence in the industry. Lack of confidence has resulted in a decline in the new investments in the industry and a lack of willingness of established farmers to expand their herds. With the development of strong overseas markets for venison and velvet and the prospect of better seasons ahead in 1996, the trends described appear to have reversed significantly. However, the relatively small size of the Australian herd appears to impose undesirable limitations on the rate at which the number of herds can be expanded to meet the demands for products. Supply difficulties worsened when the supply of products, especially venison, was maintained by slaughtering young breeding females. The net result was the depletion of female breeding herds in the industry. The industry's schemes are funded by statutory levies on the sale of livestock for venison, the sale of velvet antlers and the sale of live animals to export markets. The industry has a five-year plan for 1996 2000 which includes animal nutrition, grazing quality, carcass quality, antler harvesting, advertising materials and technical bulletins. All of the projects generated a significant amount of information, complimenting similar work carried out in New Zealand and other deer farming countries. Major projects funded by levy funds include the Meat Market Project from 1992 to 1996. This initiative has resulted in a dramatic increase in international demand for Australian venison and an increase in domestic consumption of venison. In an effort to maintain existing venison markets in the short term and increase them in the long term, in 1997 the industry's top priority became increasing the size and production capacity of the national herd.

premise: Designed to last Can better design cure our throwaway culture? Jonathan Chapman, a senior lecturer at the University of Brighton, UK, is one of a new breed of sustainable designers. Like many of us, they are concerned about the huge waste associated with Western consumer culture and the damage it causes to the environment. Some, like Chapman, aim to create objects we want to keep rather than discard. Others are working to create more efficient or durable consumer products or products designed with recycling in mind. The waste involved in our fleeting relationship with durable consumer goods is tremendous. Household power tools, such as electric drills, are a typical example of such waste. No matter how much DIY the purchaser plans to do, the truth is that these things are thrown away after being used, on average, for only ten minutes. Most will serve the time of conscience, gathering dust on a shelf in the garage; people are reluctant to admit they've wasted their money. However, the end is inevitable for thousands of years at landfill waste sites. In design, manufacture, packaging, transportation, and disposal, an electric tool consumes many times its weight in resources, all for an active lifespan shorter than that of the average small insect. To understand why we have become so wasteful, we need to look at the underlying motivation of consumers. People hold onto things to give expression to who they are, and to show what group of people they feel they belong to Chapman says. In the world of mass production, however, this symbolism has lost much of its potency. For most of human history, people have had intimate contact with objects they used or valued. They often made the objects themselves, or family members passed them on. For more specialist artefacts, people relied on specialist manufacturers living nearby, whom they probably knew personally. Chapman notes that all these factors gave the objects a narrative history and emotional connection that today's mass production cannot match. Without these personal connections, consumer culture admires novelty. We know we can't buy happiness, but the opportunity to re-create ourselves with shiny, fresh products seems irresistible. When the novelty fades we simply renew the excitement by buying more new things: what John Thacra of Doors of Perception, a network for sharing ideas about the future of design, calls the new rule. As a sustainable designer, the Chapman solution is what he calls emotionally durable design. Think of your favorite old jeans. They just don't have the right feel until they've been worn and washed a hundred times, do they? It's like they're sharing the story of your life. You can fake that look, but it's not the same thing. Chapman says the gradual development of such a relationship turns our interactions with objects into something richer than a simple benefit. Swiss industrial analyst Walter Stahl, a visiting professor at the University of Surrey, calls this the bear factor. No matter how ragged and bloated we become a beloved Teddy, we are in no hurry to buy another one. AS ADULTS, OUR TEDDY BEAR CONNECTS US TO OUR CHILDHOOD, AND IT PROTECTS IT FROM OBSOLESCENCE STAHL SAYS THAT'S WHAT SUSTAINABLE DESIGN SHOULD DO. It's not just about making durable items that people want to keep. Sustainable design is a matter of correctly costing the entire production process, energy use and disposal. It's about systems design, culture shaping, says Tim Cooper of the Centre for Sustainable Consumption at Sheffield University in the UK. He thinks sustainable design is incredibly slow to take off, but says approaching environmental crises and resource depletion are pushing it to the top of the agenda. Thakkara agrees. For him, the roots of the imminent environmental collapse can be summed up in two words: weight and speed. We produce more stuff than the planet can sustain and use huge amounts of energy that spin more and more of it faster and faster. The information age was supposed to ease our economies and reduce our impact on the environment, but the opposite seems to be happening. We simply added information technology to the industrial age and accelerated the metabolism of the developed world, Thakara argues. Once you realize that, the cure isn't rocket science: reduce waste and energy use, stop moving things so much and use people more. Ezio Manzini, a professor of industrial design at the Polytechnico di Milano University, Italy, describes the process of transition to a post-jettisoning society as a mid-flight aircraft engine modification though, he believes it can be done, and he's not alone. Manzini says a crucial step will be to reshape our globalized world into what he calls the multi-local society. His vision is that every resource, from food to power generation, should as much as possible be sourced and distributed locally. These local hubs will then be connected to national and global networks to enable the most efficient use and flow of materials. So what would post-dumping consumerism look like? For starters, we will buy more and more sustainably designed products. This may be as simple as installing energy-efficient light bulbs, more efficient washing machines or choosing locally made groceries with less packaging. We spend less on material goods and more on services. Instead of buying a second car, for example, we might buy a car-sharing network. We will also buy less and hire much more: why own things that you hardly use, especially things that are expected to be constantly updated? Durable consumer goods will be sold with plans already in place for their disposal. Electronic products will be designed for recycling, with the extra cost added to the retail price as an upfront payment. As consumers become increasingly concerned about the environment, many large businesses are eagerly embracing sustainable design and brushing up on their green credentials to please their customers and stay one step ahead of competitors.
hypothesis: People often buy things that are rarely used and throw them away.
label: e

premise: Designing and shipping after the Restriction of Hazardous Substances Directive (RoHS) Almost two months after the EU ban on the use of six environmentally unfriendly materials came into force, designers have clear evidence that non-compliance with the Restriction of Hazardous Substances Directive (RoHS) means loss of sales. Palm Inc recently announced that its Treo 650 smartphone will no longer ship to Europe, as it does not meet RoHS requirements. And some Apple Computer Inc. products won't be sold in Europe for the same reason. The EU directive, which came into force on July 1, covers lead, mercury, cadmium, hexagonal chromium, polybrominated biphenyls and polybromic diphenyl ethers. Electronics suppliers around the world are working to eliminate these materials from almost all new products developed for the European market, adapting their manufacturing processes to a lead-free (Pb) environment. But this is just the beginning. Other countries, including China, Taiwan, and South Korea, and some U.S. states are creating their own green or RoHS-like legislation. This means that RoHS compliance must become an integral part of the designer development process, with RoHS testing at every stage: concept, development, prototype, first build, and volume production. Large companies will run the gamut from finding component stockpiles of certified green components to taking the proper care to prove compliance and developing processes that enable the higher temperature requirements of Pb-free production. And for designers, these are just the tip of the iceberg. A host of technical and reliability problems remained to be sorted out in the processing and soldering of Pb-free boards. What it comes down to is what Ken Stanwick, senior vice president at Design Chain Associates, calls a tribal lack of knowledge in designing RoHS-compliant systems. We had great tribal knowledge in regards to dealing with lead systems, but we didn't build up the same amount of knowledge for Pb-Free, he said. Any problem will be blamed on PB-free until it is settled. We need to understand tests that replicate more from the environment and different pressures that were going to be seen in this new system. Manny Marcano, president and CEO of EMA Design Automation Inc. (Rochester, NY), cited the impact of parts obsolescence, including the need to redesign old products and the resulting emphasis on component engineering at the expense of conceptual design. In contrast, the celestial body closest to the moon is dusty, barren, inhospitable, and dark. Technological innovations will be necessary, and the timing of the trip is absolutely critical. The different orbits of Mars and Earth mean that they come closest to each other every 26 months, but this event itself changes in a 15-year cycle. This means that only once in that period does the launch window open. This is not very little, but the tasks must necessarily leave at these times. Without the need to stand, there is almost no bending or pressure on the back or leg muscles. These gradually contract and weaken, while the bones lose their density, and the lungs their aerobic capacity. When they stay long enough in space, astronauts are unable to function properly. However, these individuals will need their full physical strength and alertness for the many operational roles required. These include docking in space, approaches and landing on Mars, remotely manipulating machines and dealing with any emergencies that arise. Another danger of such a duration in a hermetically sealed spacecraft is a disease. The human body constantly sheds waste material (sweat, skin flakes, hair, moisture, mucus and digestive products), all of which allow bacteria to multiply prolifically. Coughing and sneezing spray liquids into the air, which, without gravity to pull them down to surfaces, simply float as airborne particles in those dense confines, causing a slight exchange of bacteria between crew members. Bacterial infections and fungal attacks can be common, and the human immune system is weakened by microgravity. Thus, a long mission to Mars will require the best air cleaning system available, rigorous disinfection and hygiene procedures, plus an excellent supply of antibiotics. Arriving on Mars, the problems only increase. Staying on the planet for any significant length of time would be difficult. In the absence of a thick protective atmosphere or magnetosphere for burning or deflecting objects, respectively, astronauts would be exposed to potentially deadly UV radiation, micro-meteoroids, solar flares and high-energy particles, all of which regularly bombard the surface. Vessels and land capsules will need special shielding, which adds to the weight and expense. Construction of a dwelling will be time-consuming, difficult and dangerous. For a longer stay on Mars, the only solution, it seems, is to go underground. One of the most interesting discoveries in this respect is of possible cave entrances on the side of Arcia Mons, a large Martian volcano. Seven such entrances have been identified in satellite images, showing round holes similar to the collapse of cave ceilings. The hope is that these may lead to more extensive cave formations, or perhaps lava tubes, that offer the protection needed in such hostile terrain. Another advantage is the potential access to essential minerals and, most importantly, the possibility of frozen water. These sites therefore open the possibility of independent and permanent settlement on this planet. The most exciting option is to try it on the first trip in other words, making it a one-way journey. The advantage is that the duration of space travel is reduced instantly, reducing technological, biological and financial challenges. This very strong argument is offset to some extent by the difficulties in establishing a permanent presence, as well as the ongoing commitment required to it for example, in delivering food and supplies via unmanned spacecraft. Similarly, the psychological effects on these pioneers of permanent isolation from Barth and his community, as well as the crowding in enclosed Martian dwellings with the same members, raise issues of whether such a settlement is humanly possible. This raises the question of why to perform such tasks at all. The answer, according to supporters, is that it is our destiny. And today, people regularly engage in extreme sports, or work in dangerous professions, all of which significantly reduce their life expectancy.
