premise: Discovering the Lake A meteorite As the sun rose over picturesque Lake Bosomtaway, a team of Syracuse University researchers braced for another day of using state-of-the-art equipment to help unlock the mysteries hidden beneath the lake bottom. Nestled in the heart of Ghana, the lake contains an untapped repository of information that could help scientists predict future climate change by looking at evidence from the past. This information will also improve scientists' understanding of the changes taking place in the area affected by massive meteorite B. The project, led by Earth Sciences Professor Christopher Schultz of the College of Arts and Sciences and funded by the National Science Foundation (NSF), is the first large-scale effort to explore Lake Bosomtaway, formed 1.1 million years ago when a giant meteor crashed onto Earth. The resulting crater is one of the largest and best-preserved geological young craters in the world, says Schultz, who is collaborating on the project with researchers from the University of Arizona, the University of South Carolina, the University of Rhode Island and several Ghanaian institutions.\ Our data should provide information about what happens when an impact hits hard, pre-Cambrian, crystalline rocks that are billion years old,\ he says. C. Equally important is the fact that the lake, which is about 8 km in diameter, has no natural origin. The rim of the crater rises about 250 meters above the water surface. Streams flow into the lake, Schultz says, but the water comes out only by evaporation, or by seeping through the lake's sediments. For the past million years, the lake has acted as a tropical rain, filling and drying up with changes in precipitation and the tropical climate. The record of these changes is hidden in the sediment beneath the lake bed.\ The lake is one of the best sites in the world for studying Rupian climate change,\ says Schultz.\ The tropics are the heat engine for Earth's climate. In this process, a high-pressure air gun is used to create small pneumatic explosions in the water. The sound energy penetrates about 1,000 to 2,000 feet below the surface of the lake before bouncing back to the surface of the water. F. The reflected sound energy is detected by underwater microphones called hydrophones embedded in a 50-foot-long cable that is towed behind the boat as it crosses the lake in a carefully designed mesh pattern. On a good day, when everything was going as planned, the crew could collect data and return to the dock in the early afternoon. With the exception of a few relatively minor adjustments, the equipment and boat worked well. The problems that arose were mostly unscientific tree stumps, fishing nets, cultural barriers and occasional misunderstandings with local villagers. In the past, land scoured from the coastline by Mediterranean currents was replaced by sediment brought to the delta by the Nile River, but this no longer happens. PRIOR TO THE CONSTRUCTION OF THE DAMS, THE NILE FLOWED FREELY CARRYING MASSIVE AMOUNTS OF SEDIMENT NORTHWARD FROM THE INTERIOR OF AFRICA TO BE DEPOSITED ON THE NILE DELTA. So far, people have blamed the loss of delta land on the two major dams at Aswan in southern Egypt, which impede nearly all of the sediment that flowed down the river. PRIOR TO THE CONSTRUCTION OF THE DAMS, THE NILE FLOWED FREELY CARRYING MASSIVE AMOUNTS OF SEDIMENT NORTHWARD FROM THE INTERIOR OF AFRICA TO BE DEPOSITED ON THE NILE DELTA. It lasted 7,000 years, eventually covering an area of over 22,000 km² with layers of fertile silt. Annual floods brought new, nutrient-rich soil to the delta region, replaced what was washed away by the sea, and waived the need for fertilizers in Egypt's richest food-growing region. But when the Aswan dams were built in the 20th century to provide electricity and irrigation, and to protect Cairo's huge population center and surrounding areas from floods and annual droughts, most of the sediment with its natural fertilizer accumulated above the dam in the southern half, upstream of Lake Nasser, instead of moving into the delta. Now, however, it turns out there's more to the story. The sediment-free waters rising from the Aswan dams appear to pick up silt and sand as they erode the riverbed and banks on the 800-mile drive to Cairo. Daniel Jean Stanley of the Smithsonian Institution noticed that water samples taken in Cairo, just before the river entered the delta, indicated that the river sometimes carries more than 850 grams of sediment per cubic meter of water nearly half of what it carried before the construction of the dams. “I'm ashamed to say that the significance of this didn't hit me until after I read 50 or 60 studies,” Stanley says in Marine Geology. “There's still a lot of sediment going into the delta, but hardly any sediment goes out to sea to replenish the coastline. So this sediment must be trapped on the delta itself. 'When they're north of Cairo, most of the Nile's water is diverted to more than 10,000 miles of irrigation canals and only a small fraction reaches the sea directly through the rivers in the delta. The water in the irrigation canals is still or very slow and therefore cannot carry sediment, Stanley explains. The sediment sinks to the bottom of the canals and is then added to fields by farmers or pumped with the water into the four large freshwater lagoons located near the outer edges of the delta. So very little of it actually reaches the coastline to replace what is washed away by the Mediterranean currents. The farms in the delta plains and fishing and aquaculture in the lagoons make up much of Egypt's food supply. But by the time the rainfall came to rest in the fields and lagoons it was laden with municipal, industrial and agricultural waste from the Cairo region, home to more than 40 million people. “The pollutants are accumulating faster and faster,” Stanley says. Since then the concentration of mercury has increased significantly. Lead from engines using lead fuels and other industrial sources has also risen dramatically. These toxins can easily enter the food chain, affecting the output of fisheries and agriculture. Another problem is that agricultural waste includes fertilizers that stimulate an increase in plant growth in the lagoons and disturb the ecology of the region, with serious effects on the fishing industry. According to Siegel, international environmentalist organizations are beginning to pay more attention to the area, partly because of the erosion and pollution problems of the Nile Delta, but mainly because they fear the impact this situation could have on the entire ecosystem of the Mediterranean coast. But there are no easy solutions. In the immediate future, Stanley believes one solution would be to carry out artificial floods to flush out the delta's waterways, in the same way natural floods did before the construction of dams. However, he said, in the long run, it may be necessary to use an alternative process such as desalination to increase the amount of water available. “In my opinion Egypt has got to come up with a way for more water to flow through the river and the delta,” Stanley says. premise: Conceding that Saintly Image associations, so still believe, are separate from the government, staffed all by volunteers and spending every penny donated on the cause they support. And there is concern that such outdated perceptions could explode in the faces of charities as people begin to discover what the voluntary sector is really about. High-profile international programmes of awareness-raising activities, such as Make Pony History, have dragged the voluntary sector into the spotlight and shown charity workers business entrepreneurs as nothing less than angels of mercy. BUT WITH THE SPOTLIGHT COMES SCRUTINY, AND IF CHARITIES DON'T PRESENT COMPELLING CASES FOR POLITICAL CAMPAIGNING, SIX-FIGURE SALARIES AND PAYING EXPENSES OF CELEBRITIES WHO GO ON DEMANDING TRIPS TO REFUGEE CAMPS FOR FREE, THEY COULD BE BITTEN. If people become more sceptical about how charities use their donations, they will be less inclined to give money, says Nick Aldridge, director of strategy at the Association of Directors of Voluntary Organisations (ACEVO). A wide range of initiatives have been taken to ensure long-term confidence in the sector by explaining what charities are doing and publishing the data. But it's still hard to give donors a full picture because, unlike profit-driven businesses, charities cannot measure achievement solely on the bottom line. The Success in Funding report suggests that this may explain some of the communication difficulties faced by charities. However, it suggests that there are good reasons to try. Many funders, she argues, see high overhead expenses, for example, on premises, advertising and so on, treated appropriately, as a signal of an efficiently run organization, rather than a waste of resources. Detailed reporting can be an important component of efforts to increase transparency. Better information may also unlock more money by highlighting social problems and explaining what can be done to address them. Some charities are already taking steps in this direction. The Royal National Institute for the Deaf (RNID) has introduced an annual impact report, to tell people about the effects of its work in a broader sense than an annual report would normally allow. Each impact report looks back at what has been achieved over the past 12 months and also indicates the charity's targets for the coming year. We weren't good at educating the public on issues like why we do a lot of campaigning, he says. But the more high-profile the sector becomes, the more questions people will ask. She notes that the additional reporting and accounting requirements imposed on institutions across all sectors in recent years may have made them more transparent, but they have not made them more reliable. If we are to judge for ourselves, we need real communication in which we can question and observe, test and even challenge the evidence that others present. Presenting the evidence for what has been done, for all its shortcomings, may provide a better basis for placing trust or refusal than any number of brilliant publications that win unending success. Not everyone thinks the public needs to be fed spoonfuls of information to maintain trust. There is no evidence that there is a crisis of trust in charities, says Cathy Proa, research director at the Charities Aid Foundation. The facts support the claim. In a Charity Commission report published in November last year, the public gave charities 6.3 out of 10 on trust. Pharaoh believes key donors are more astute than they are shown. There's a heavy dependence on middle-class donors for charitable income, and I'd be astonished if they didn't realise that charities have to pay to have professional staff, she says. She believes the biggest threats to trust are the kind of scandals that hit the Scottish voluntary sector in 2003. Two high-profile charities, Breast Cancer Research (Scotland) and Moonbeam, were revealed to have spent some of their profits on their causes. The revelations have generated highly damaging media coverage. Even charitable Stewarts were astonished by how quickly the coverage snowballed when two bad stories turned into a sectoral crisis. Both of these events caused a media frenzy as journalists took every opportunity to undermine the sector, says Fiona Duncan, director of external affairs at Capability Scotland. After suffering the media backlash, Duncan launched Giving Scotland to redress the balance. Fourteen charities, plus the Scottish Council for Voluntary Organisations and the Institute of Fundraising Scotland, joined together to issue a communication restoring confidence in charities. The Scottish Executive pledged 30,000, and through donations from corporate supporters, the campaign was able to secure 300,000 worth of advertising for a two-week lightning campaign over Christmas 2003. Two months before the campaign began, the “Herald” newspaper published a survey that revealed that 52 percent of people were less likely to give because of the scandals. Giving Scotland conducted a similar survey in February 2004 and this time more than half the population said they were more likely to consider giving because of the campaign. We learned about strength in numbers and the importance of timing because it was Christmas, we were able to get good coverage,” Duncan says. It was an effective rearguard campaign. The many proactive initiatives now underway across the UK give charities the opportunity to prevent the situation from becoming so bad again, but their success will depend on whether they are willing to shed their sacred image and mobilise for the cause of creating a new and bolder situation.

premise: Do you look your age? It can be difficult to guess someone's exact age. A variety of factors may leave marks on our appearance: how much sleep we've had even the way we dress and our view of ourselves. The good news is that just as these factors can add years to your appearance, it follows that they can also take years off. We don't always have control over some of those social factors that can make us look younger, but there are other steps we can take to try to stop the ravages of age. Social Factors Last month the University of Southern Denmark released a report, The Impact of Environmental Factors on Facial Aging, that showed that the way we live can influence the age we look. In it, 1,826 twins were photographed and then ten sisters aged 25-46 years were asked to guess how old the models were. The results were intriguing. They showed that belonging to a high social class can make us look up to four years younger, and many other lifestyle factors have been shown to influence how we look. It was found that having children made men look a full year younger, although this had no effect on women, and the birth of four or more children eliminated the benefit. Depression and sun exposure were the biggest factors in making you look old ahead of your time. Depression amounted to up to three and a half years for the woman's perceived age (and 2.4 years for men). Sun exposure piled up for at least another year. Smoking lasts six months for a woman and a year for a man. Meanwhile, it was found that a high BMI (body mass index) takes a whole year off for both men and women. If you're not depressed, don't smoke and aren't too thin, you're actually doing well, says Professor Kara Christensen (married, three children, non-smoker), one of the authors of the reports. Professor Christensen's report concluded that it is more dangerous for our health to look a year older, than to be an actual year older. Nutrition is perhaps the biggest change we can make quite easily. There are four main factors that age us prematurely: smoking, too much alcohol, lack of fresh fruits and vegetables, and insufficient protein intake. You can immediately tell the smoker. It's not just the lines around the mouth and eyes, but smoking dries the body. Every time you inhale a cigarette, you're taking toxins into the body that need to be dispersed and eliminated by the liver and kidneys, and they depend on a lot of fresh water to carry toxins away. Most smokers don't drink nearly enough water. However, the really big and quick fix is to eat more fresh fruits and vegetables. You can see if someone is not eating enough, or any, fresh fruits and vegetables in a minute. The skin lacks freshness and transparency. This is because the skin is the last organ to benefit from the nutrients you eat as the brain, heart and lungs all get a first chunk. If someone's diet lacks fruits and vegetables, the skin will dry out. This is a sign that it is not possible to provide enough nutrients, so from an anti-aging point of view, it is important to have live, fresh food and raw food is essential. If you need to cook, steaming will retain at least some of the vitamins and minerals. The other really important thing, and one that we tend to miss in our diet-obsessed culture, is adequate intake of essential fatty acids (EFAs), from oily fish, nuts and seeds. EFAs are essential for extending lifespan because every cell in the body has a phospholipid bilayer that protects it, but they also give the skin a dewy, bouncy, youthful feel. One of the worst things you can do in terms of looking old is to go on a low-fat diet. Stress is another great one for adding years. We can help support the adrenal glands and thyroid, which take a hammering when stressed, by eating lots of fresh vitamin C and magnesium for the adrenal glands; and iodine, selenium, zinc and B vitamins to support the thyroid. Exercise We've come to think of exercise as a pure weight-loss pursuit and women tend to be quite afraid of lifting weights, but building lean tissue through weight-bearing exercise is key to keeping up the years. Exercise can help reduce the effects of aging by slowing the decline of type II muscle fibers. In general, type I muscle fibers are engaged in aerobic activities and type II with anaerobes. Type II responds to resistance work to improve muscle tone. With aging, there is a decrease in the frequency, duration and intensity of normal activity: we usually move less. So, these type II fibers deteriorate because they simply do not receive enough stimuli. Skin care Almost any skin cream promises to make you look younger. It is a promise that many are tempted to, but many end up disappointed. The problem is not that products don't work, but start too late and then don't spend enough money. A lot of people skip good skincare until they think they need it, and by then it's actually too late. In women, the skin around the eyes is the first to go, in men it is the hands. A good routine should start early because maintenance is much easier than repair. Your skin also becomes more transparent as you get older, so you need to adjust your makeup and hair color accordingly. Base should be lighter than you imagine, and shinier, and if you want to cover gray, don't be tempted to go for too dark hair color or color-block highlights are nice. Do not forget to apply a moisturizer around the back of the neck: this is the only part of the skin that is attached to the bone, so it is important that you take care of it to prevent falling.

Smoking lasts six months for a woman and a year for a man. Meanwhile, it was found that a high BMI (body mass index) takes a whole year off for both men and women. premise: Do literate women become better mothers? Children in developing countries are healthier and more likely to survive beyond the age of five when their mothers can read and write. Public health experts accepted this idea decades ago, but so far no one has been able to show that a woman's ability to read in itself improves her children's chances of survival. Most literate women learned to read in elementary school, and the fact that a woman received an education may simply indicate the wealth of her family or that she values her children more. Now a long-term study conducted in Nicaragua has eliminated these factors by showing that teaching reading to poor adult women, who would otherwise remain illiterate, has a direct impact on the health and survival of their children. In 1979, the Nicaraguan government established several social programs, including a national crusade for literacy. By 1985, about 300,000 illiterate adults from across the country, many of whom had never attended primary school, had learned to read, write and use numbers. During this time, researchers from the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine, the Central American Health Institute in Nicaragua, the National Autonomous University of Nicaragua and the Costa Rican Institute of Health interviewed nearly 3,000 women, some of whom had learned to read as children, some during the crusade for literacy and some who had never studied at all. The women were asked how many children they had given birth and how many died in their infancy. The research teams also tested the surviving children to find out how well fed they were. The researchers' findings were striking. At the end of the 1970s the infant mortality rate among children of illiterate mothers stood at about 110 deaths per thousand live births. At this point in their lives, mothers who later went on to learn to read had a similar level of child mortality (105/1000). However, among women educated in primary school, the infant mortality rate was significantly lower, standing at 80 per thousand. In 1985, after the end of the National Literacy Crusade, the infant mortality figures for those who remained illiterate and for those educated in primary school remained more or less unchanged. For those women who learned to read the campaign, the infant mortality rate stood at 84 per thousand, 21 points lower than for those women who were still illiterate. The children of the new mothers who were literate were better fed than those of women who could not read. Why are the children of literate mothers better? According to Peter Sandiford of the School of Tropical Medicine in Liverpool, no one knows for sure. Child health was not on the curriculum during the women's classes, so he and his colleagues are exploring other factors. They are working with the same group of 3,000 women, to try to find out whether reading mothers are making better use of hospitals and clinics, opting for smaller families, exercising more control over the home, learning modern child-care techniques faster, or whether they are simply more respectful of themselves and their children. The Nicaraguan study may have important implications for governments and aid agencies that need to know where to direct their resources. Sandiford says that there is growing evidence that female education, at any age, is an important health intervention in itself. The results of the study support the recommendation of world banks that education budgets in developing countries should be increased, not only to help their economies, but also to improve children's health. We've known for a long time that maternal education is important, says John Cleland of the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine. But we thought that even if we started educating girls today, married people should wait a generation for the proceeds. The Nicaraguan study suggests we might be able to get around that. Cleland cautions that the crusade in Nicaragua was special in many ways, and similar campaigns elsewhere may not work as well. It is notoriously difficult to teach adults skills that have no immediate impact on their daily lives, and many literacy campaigns in other countries have been far less successful. The crusade was part of a larger effort to bring better lives to people, Cleland says. Replicating these conditions in other countries will pose a major challenge for the development workers.

premise: PhD Sales. Pharmaceuticals is one of the most profitable industries in North America. But are the sales and marketing strategies of the pharmaceutical industry going too far? Several months ago Kim Schaefer, a sales representative for a major global pharmaceutical company, walked into a New York medical center to bring free information and samples of her company's latest products. That day she was lucky that a doctor was available to see her. The last rep offered me a trip to Florida. What do you have? Ask the doctor. He was only half-laughing. What was offered that day was a pair of tickets to a musical in New York. But on any given day, what Schaefer can offer is typical of today's pharmaceuticals: a car trunk full of promotional gifts and gadgets, a budget that can buy lunches and dinner for a small country, hundreds of free drug samples and the freedom to give a doctor $200 to prescribe her new product to the next six patients who fit the pharmaceutical profile. And she also has some $1,000 cash to offer in exchange for doctors' attendance at her company's next educational lecture. Selling drugs is a daily exercise in ethical judgment. Salesmen like Schaefer walk the line between the accepted practice of buying potential time with a free meal, and bribing doctors to prescribe their medications. They work in an industry that has been heavily criticized for its sales and marketing practices but find themselves in the middle of the old chicken or egg question that businesses won't use strategies that don't work, so are doctors to blame for the growing extravagance of pharmaceutical marketing? Or is it the industry's responsibility to decide the boundaries? The explosion in the sheer number of salespeople in the field and the amount of funding used to promote their causes is forcing a close examination of the pressures, effects, and connections between pharmaceutical representatives and doctors. Salesmen provide much-needed information and education to physicians. In many cases the glossy brochures, printouts of articles, and the prescriptions they provide are major sources of drug education for health care providers. With the huge investment the industry has placed in face-to-face sales, salespeople have essentially become experts in a single drug or group of drugs a huge advantage in getting the attention of busy doctors who need quick information. But the sales push rarely stops at the office. The flashy brochures and pamphlets left by sales representatives are often followed by dinners in expensive restaurants, meetings in warm, sunny places, and the flooding of gadgets for promotions. Rarely do patients watch a doctor write in a pen not equipped with a medication name, or see a nurse use a tablet that does not bear a pharmaceutical company logo. Pharmaceutical companies spend millions of dollars on promotional products like coffee mugs, T-shirts, umbrellas and golf balls. Money well invested? It's hard to tell. 'I got golf balls from one company and I use them, but that doesn't make me prescribe their medicine, 'says one doctor. I tend to think I'm not affected by what they give me. Free samples of expensive new drugs may be the most effective way to get doctors and patients to be loyal to the product. Salesmen hand out hundreds of dollars worth of samples every week worth $7.2 billion in one year. Although few comprehensive studies have been conducted, one University of Washington study investigated how the availability of drug sampling influenced what doctors prescribe. A total of 131 doctors self-reported their prescribing patterns The conclusion was that the availability of samples led them to divide and prescribe drugs that differed from their preferred drug choice. The bottom line is that pharmaceutical companies as a whole are investing more in marketing than in research and development. And the patients are the ones who pay in the form of sky-high prescription prices for every pen handed out, every free theater ticket and every steak dinner eaten. In the end, the fact remains that pharmaceutical companies have every right to make a profit and will continue to find new ways to increase sales. But as the world of medicine continues to grapple with what is acceptable and what is not, it is precious that companies must continue to be heavily scrutinized in their sales and marketing strategies.

premise: Don't wash away those fossils! Standard museum practice can wash away the DNA. Washing, brushing and varnishing of fossils, all standard conservation treatments used by many fossil hunters and museum curators alike greatly reduce the chance of recovering ancient DNA. Instead, the diggers should treat at least some of their bounty with gloves, and freeze samples while they're at, dirt and all, concludes a paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences today. Although many paleontologists know anecdotally that this is the best way to increase the chances of extracting good DNA, Eva-Maria Geigel of the Jacques Monod Institute in Paris, France, and her colleagues have now shown just how important conservation practices can be. That information, they say, should be taken home among the people who are actually in the field digging up bones. GEIGEL AND HER COLLEAGUES EXAMINED 3,200-YEAR-OLD FOSSIL BONES BELONGING TO A SINGLE INDIVIDUAL OF AN EXTINCT CATTLE SPECIES, CALLED OROX. The fossils were excavated at a site in France at two different times in 1947, and stored in a museum collection, or in 2004, and preserved under sterile conditions at 20 °C. The team's attempts to extract DNA from the 1947 bones all failed. However the newly excavated fossils have all yielded DNA. Because the bones were buried in the same period of time, and under the same conditions, the method of preservation had to be to blame, says Geigel.\ The amount of DNA fell apart in those 57 years as in the 3,200 years before,\ she says. Wash in, wash Because many paleontologists base their work on the shape of fossils alone, their conservation methods are not designed to preserve DNA, Geagle explains. The biggest problem is how you clean them. Fossils are often washed together on site in a large bathtub, which can allow water and contaminants in the form of contemporary DNA to seep into the pore bones.\ Not only is the authentic DNA washed out, but the contamination is washed in,\ Geigel says. Most ancient DNA experts know this already, says Hendrik Poinar, an evolutionary geneticist from McMaster University in Ontario, Canada. But that doesn't mean the best methods have become common among those who find the actual fossils. Obtaining fossils preserved with their DNA in mind relies on close ties between laboratory-based geneticists and the excavators, says paleontologist Svante P. Bo of the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig, Germany. And that only happens in exceptional cases, he says. P. Bo's team, which dealt with Neanderthal DNA sequencing, continually grapples with these problems.\ When you want to study human remains and ancient Neanderthals, there's a big problem of contamination with contemporary human DNA,\ he says. This does not mean that all museum specimens are fatally damaged, notes P bo. The Neanderthal fossils recently sequenced in his own laboratory, for example, were part of a museum collection treated in the traditional way. But P. Bo is keen to see samples of fossils from any major finds preserved in accordance with Geigel's recommendations for the case. Hot and Wet Geagle herself believes that in collaboration between bench and field researchers, properly preserving fossils can open avenues of discovery that have long been thought closed. Much human cultural development has occurred in temperate regions. DNA does not survive well in warm environments to begin with, and can disappear when fossils are washed and treated. For this reason, Geigel says, most ancient DNA studies have been done on permafrost specimens, like the woolly mammoth, or on remains protected from the elements in cold caves including cave bears and Neanderthal fossils. Better conservation methods, and a focus on fresh fossils, can increase DNA extraction from finer samples, Geigel says. And it could shed further light on the story of human evolution.

premise: Dummy pills There is an ongoing debate about the benefits and ethics of using placebos, sometimes called sugar pills. The placebo effect is well documented though not fully understood. This refers to the apparent benefits, both psychological and physiological, of taking a drug or receiving a treatment that you expect will improve your health, when in fact the tablet does not contain active ingredients and the treatment has never been proven. Any benefit that results from a placebo originates solely in the mind of the person taking it. The therapeutic effect can be real and measurable or perceived and imagined. The placebo effect is a headache for drug makers. By providing interactive courses that use the Internet infrastructure directly to one's personal computer and supporting the learner at their own pace, e-learning can, at times, be more effective than other conventional forms of training. The content of such training varies significantly but is commonly used to adopt new technologies, improve managerial capabilities, and improve financial planning.
hypothesis: One reason to cut back on conventional training is the increasing costs of personnel.

premise: Mental education. Educating a Mind by Bernie Neville is a book that looks at new and radical approaches to learning, describing the effects of emotion, imagination, and the unconscious on learning. One theory discussed in the book is the one proposed by George Lozanov, which focuses on the power of suggestion. Lozanov's teaching technique is based on the evidence that connections created in the brain through unconscious processing (which he calls nonspecific mental reactivity) are more durable than those created through conscious processing. Apart from the laboratory evidence of this, we know from our experience that we often remember what we caught on the periphery, long after we have forgotten what we began to learn. If we think of a book that we studied months or years ago, it will be easier for us to recall peripheral details: the color, the cover, the font, the table in the library where we sat while we studied it than the content on which we concentrated. If we think about a lecture that we listened to with great concentration, we will remember the appearance and behavior of the lecturers, our place in the hall, the failure of the merger, much more easily than the ideas we went to study. Even if these peripheral details are a little elusive, they are easily repeated in hypnosis or when we relive the event in the imagination, as in psychodrama. In contrast, the details of the lecture content seem to have disappeared forever. This phenomenon can be attributed in part to the common counter-approach to learning (extreme effort to memorize, stretching muscles, causing fatigue), but it also simply reflects how the brain works. That's why Lozanov made indirect teaching (suggestion) central to his teaching system. In Sogastopedia, as he called his method, consciousness is shifted from the curriculum to focus on something peripheral. The curriculum then becomes peripheral and takes care of the reserve capacity of the brain. The proposed approach to learning foreign languages provides a good illustration. In its last version (1980), it consists of reading vocabulary and text while the class listens to music. The first session is in two parts. In the first part the music is classical (Mozart, Beethoven, Brahms) and the teacher reads the text slowly and solemnly, paying attention to the dynamics of the music. Students follow the text in their books. Followed by several minutes of silence. In the second part they listen to baroque music (Bach, Corelli, Handel) while the teacher reads the text in an ordinary speech voice. During this time they close their books. During the entire session, their attention is passive; they listen to the music but do not attempt to learn the material. Prior to this, students were carefully prepared for the language learning experience. Through meeting with the satisfied staff and students, they develop the expectation that learning will be easy and pleasant and that they will successfully learn several hundred words of the foreign language during class. In an initial conversation, the teacher presents them with the material to be covered, but does not teach it. Also, students are instructed not to attempt to learn this during this introduction. A few hours after the two-part session, there is a follow-up lesson in which students are stimulated to recall the material presented. Again the approach is indirect. Students do not focus their attention on trying to remember vocabulary, but rather focus on using language for communication (e.g. through games or improvised dramatization). Such methods are no exception in language teaching. What distinguishes the sophotopedic method is that they are completely dedicated to aiding recall. It is assumed that the learning of material is automatic and effortless, achieved while listening to music. The task of teachers is to help students apply what they have learned consciously, thereby making it easily accessible to consciousness. Another difference from conventional teaching is the evidence that students can regularly learn 1000 new foreign language words during a featured session, as well as grammar and dialect. Lozanov experimented with teaching by direct suggestion during sleep, hypnosis, and trance states, but found such procedures unnecessary. Hypnosis, yoga, Silva's mind control, religious rituals, and faith healing are all linked to a successful proposal, but none of their techniques seem essential to this. Such rituals may be perceived as a placebo. Lozanov acknowledges that the ritual around suggestion in his system is also a placebo, but argues that without such a placebo people are unable or afraid to tap into the reserve capacity of their brains. Like any placebo, it must be given up on authority to be effective. Just as a doctor invokes the full power of an autocratic proposal by insisting that the patient take exactly this white capsule exactly three times a day before meals, Lozanov insists that the proposed session be carried out exactly in the prescribed manner, by trained and qualified subjunctive teachers. WHILE SOGESTOPAEDIA HAS GAINED SOME NOTORIETY THANKS TO SUCCESS IN TEACHING MODERN LANGUAGES, FEW TEACHERS ARE ABLE TO EMULATE THE SPECTACULAR RESULTS OF LUZANOV AND HIS ASSOCIATES. We can, perhaps, attribute mediocre results to an unsatisfactory placebo effect. The students did not develop the appropriate thinking system. They often have no motivation to learn using this method. They don't have enough faith. They do not consider it true teaching, especially since it does not seem to involve work that they have been taught to believe is essential to learning.
hypothesis: As an indirect benefit, students notice improvements in their memory.
label: n

premise: European transport systems 1990-2010 What were the trends and what are the prospects for European transport systems? It is hard to imagine vigorous economic growth without an efficient transport system. Although modern information technologies can reduce the demand for physical transportation by facilitating remote work and telephone services, the demand for transportation continues to grow. There are two key factors behind this trend. For passenger transport, the determining factor is the spectacular increase in car use. The number of cars on European Union (EU) roads saw an increase of three million cars every year between 1990 and 2010, and over the next decade the EU will see another significant increase in its fleet. As far as the transport of goods is concerned, growth is largely due to changes in the European economy and its production system. In the last twenty years, with the abolition of internal borders, the EU has moved from a stock economy to a flow economy. This phenomenon has been accentuated by the transfer of certain industries, especially labor-intensive ones, to reduce production costs, even though the production site is hundreds and even thousands of kilometers away from the final assembly plant or away from users. The strong economic growth expected in the countries candidate for entry into the European Union will also increase transport flows, in particular freight traffic on roads. In 1998, some of these countries already exported more than twice the 1990 volumes and imported more than five times the 1990 volumes. And although many candidate states have inherited a transportation system that encourages rail, the distribution among road bikes has tilted sharply in favor of road transport since the 1990s. Between 1990 and 1998 road freight increased by 19.4%, while in the same period rail freight decreased by 43.5%, although this could benefit the enlarged EU is still on average at a much higher level than in the existing member states. However, new sustainable binding development offers an opportunity for adapting the EU's common transport policy. This goal, agreed by the Gothenburg European Council, should be achieved by integrating environmental considerations into community policy, and changing the balance between means of transport is at the heart of its strategy. The ambitious target can only be fully achieved by 2020, but the proposed measures are nevertheless a first essential step towards a sustainable transport system that will ideally be in place in 30 years, that is, by 2040. In 1998, energy consumption in the transport sector was to blame for 28% of CO2 emissions, the leading greenhouse gas. According to the latest estimates, if nothing is done to reverse the traffic growth trend, CO2 emissions from transport can be expected to increase by about 50% to 1,113 billion tons by 2020, compared to the 739 billion tons recorded in 1990. Again, road transport is the main culprit because it alone accounts for 84% of CO2 emissions attributed to transport. Using alternative fuels and improving energy efficiency is therefore both an ecological necessity and a technological challenge. At the same time, greater efforts must be made to achieve modal shift. Such a change cannot be achieved overnight, all the more so after over half a century of steady deterioration in the road's favour. This reached a peak that today rail freight services are facing margins, with only 8% of the market share, and with international goods trains coping with an average speed of 18 mph. Three possible options have sprung up. The first approach would involve focusing on road transport solely through pricing. This option will not be accompanied by complementary measures on the other modes of transport. In the short term it may curb the growth in road transport through a better loading ratio of goods vehicles and the occupancy rate of passenger vehicles expected as a result of transport price increases. However, the lack of available means for reviving other means of transport will not allow more sustainable means of transport to take up the baton. The second approach also focuses on road transport pricing but is accompanied by measures to increase the efficiency of the rest of the roads (better quality of services, logistics, technology). However, this approach does not include investment in new infrastructure, and does not guarantee better regional cohesion. This could help achieve greater disconnection from the first approach, but road transport will retain the lion's share of the market and continue to concentrate on saturated arteries, despite being the most polluting of the situations. That is why it is not enough to ensure the necessary change of balance. The third approach, which is not new, involves a series of measures ranging from pricing to reviving alternative means of transport and targeting investments in the trans-European network. This integrated approach will allow the market shares of the other situations to return to 1998 levels and thus make a change of balance. It is much more ambitious than it seems, given the historical imbalance in favour of roads over the past fifty years, but will achieve a marked break in the link between road transport growth and economic growth, without placing limits on the mobility of people and goods.

The clay tablets were usually not burned; drying in the sun was apparently considered sufficient to preserve the text as long as it was in use. Fortunately, however, many tablets survived because they were accidentally fired when the buildings in which they were stored burned down. Writing in the script lasted about 3,000 years, in a vast line of inheritance that passed through Sumer, Akkad, Assyria, Nineveh, and Babylon, preserving for us fifteen languages in the region represented by present-day Iraq, Syria, and western Iran. The oldest texts recorded the transactions of tax collectors and merchants, receipts and bills of sale of a municipal company. They were associated with things like grain, goats and real estate. Later, Babylonian writers recorded the laws and kept other types of records. Knowledge gave strength. As a result, these writers were assigned their own, Nisaba, who was later replaced by the god Nevo of Borsipa, whose symbol is neither a weapon nor a dragon but something far more terrifying, the written stick. Handwritten texts on science, astronomy, medicine and mathematics abound, some of them offering remarkably accurate data. One tablet records the speed of the moon for 248 days; another tablet records an early sighting of Halley's Comet, between September 22 and September 28, 164 B.C. Further esoteric texts attempt to explain old Babylonian customs, such as the procedure for healing a sick person, which involved rubbing tar and plaster on the patient's door and sketching a design at the foot of the person's bed. What is clear from the vast body of texts (about 20,000 tablets were found in the library of King Ashurbanipal in Nineveh) is that the writers took pride in their writing and knowledge. The most distinct text, the Babylonian epic of Gilgamesh, deals with mankind's attempts to conquer time. In it, Gilgamesh, the king and warrior, is crushed by the death of his best friend and so embarks on adventures that predefine mythical heroes of ancient Greek legends such as Hercules. His goal is not just to survive his adversities but to make sense of that life. Remarkably, versions of Gilgamesh span 1,500 years, from 2100 BC to 600 BC, making the story the epic of an entire civilization. Egypt has given us the tradition of the writer not only as an educated person but as an artist and calligrapher. Scholars have identified about 6,000 separate hieroglyphic characters in use throughout the history of Egyptian writing, but it appears that there have never been more than a thousand characters in use during a single period. It still seems a lot to remember, but what was effectively lost was more than made up for in the beauty and richness of the texts. The writing is designed to impress the eye in the vastness of creation itself. Each symbol or glyph - a flowering reed (pronounced like\ i\), the owl (\ m\), the quail chick (\ w\), etc. - was a tiny work of art. Manuscripts were collected paying attention to the overall design. premise: Effort and Science to Win in Mexico, the Direction of Medicine and Applied Sciences of the National Commission for Deporta analyzes all aspects of sports science from the role of the auditory system in sporting achievements to the strength of the mind and its role in the ability to win. More recently, the focus has been assessing the visual acuity of cyclists and long-distance runners, but they also focus on the more traditional fields of sports research, among them psychology, nutrition, anthropology, biochemistry, and odontology. Ranging from a starting child athlete at age 9 to an older athlete, the facility in Deporta has attracted some of Mexico's most famous sporting and Olympic hopefuls. The study of elite athletes is now more scientific than ever says doctor Francisco Javier Squares, after each competition, the athletes are exposed to vigorous medical examinations and follow-up training in order to help us reach the personalized program. The modern athlete has become a big business, there is no longer a one-size-fits-all approach. For example, in the past two people who are both 1. 70 meters tall and weighing 70 kg would have received the same program of athletic conditioning now this idea is outdated. It may be that the first person has 35 kg of muscle and 15 kg of fat and the second person, despite the same height and weight, may have 30 kg of muscle and 20 kg of fat. Through a detailed scientific assessment here at our facility in Deporta, Squares says,... We are able to build a very specific training program for each individual. While many countries in the world are focused on elevating the glorious champion, the Mexican Olympic team is taking a slightly different approach. Psychologically, an athlete must bring to his efforts a healthy dose of humility. As Squares said, when an athlete wins in Mexico, it's always the result of a combined team effort with many people working behind the scenes to realize the sporting achievement. When an athlete stands on the podium, it is due to great effort on the part of many. As is often the case in some poorer countries, athletes and women are stifling in their development because of budgetary constraints. However, this was not a factor in consideration with the team in Mexico. The Mexican government has allocated a significant amount of money for the supply of the latest equipment and laboratories for sports research. In fact, the quality of Mexico's facilities puts them in line with countries such as Italy and Germany in terms of access to resources. One example of sophisticated equipment used in the Mexican facility is the hyperbaric chamber. This device is used to improve oxygen recovery after vigorous physical training. It does not change the molecular composition of oxygen. Increased pressure only allows oxygen to enter the tissues better. Due to the acquisition of our hyperbaric chamber, athletes are able to recover from intense training in a much shorter period of time. We typically use the room for 45- to 60-minute sessions daily or three times a week. During these periods between intense physical exertion and recovery, doctors are able to monitor for any weakness in how the heart responds. EEG had a major impact on our ability to measure the muscular endurance of the heart. In 1996 the life expectancy of an average Mexican stands at about 75 years. People are living longer and this is largely due to the advances of modern science. In the past, most tennis shoes were constructed of fabric and a solid rubber sole. These shoes had a poor build and caused hip and foot injuries. Today the technology of building shoes has changed radically. Now some shoes are injected with silicone and made of a more comfortable ergonomic construction. It helped not only the elite but also the recreational athlete and thus helps preserve the human body.

Fishermen in this area have known about the phenomenon for centuries. In fact, this is the time of year that they traditionally dedicate to taking care of their equipment and waiting for the return of cold water. The inhabitants of the region have given this phenomenon the name of El Nino, which is Spanish for\ the child\, since it occurs around the time of the celebration of the birth of the Christ child. While the countercurrent of the warm water usually lasts two months or less, there are cases where the disruption to the normal flow lasts for many months. In these situations, water temperatures are increased not only along the coast, but along thousands of kilometers offshore. Life on Earth uses about 25 of the 92 naturally occurring chemical elements, although only 4 of these elements oxygen, carbon, hydrogen, and nitrogen account for about 96 percent of the mass of living organisms. Thus, a first requirement for life may be the presence of most or all of the elements used by life. Interestingly, this requirement can be met in almost any world. Scientists have determined that all chemical elements in the universe except hydrogen and helium (and a tiny amount of lithium) were produced by stars. These are known as heavy elements because they are heavier than hydrogen and helium. Although all these heavy elements are quite rare compared to hydrogen and helium, they are found almost everywhere. Heavy elements are continually produced by stars and released into space by stellar deaths, so their amount compared to hydrogen and helium gradually increases over time. Heavy elements make up about 2 percent of the chemical content (by mass) of our solar system, the other 98 percent being hydrogen and helium. In some very old star systems, formed before the production of many heavy elements, the share of heavy elements may be less than 0.1 percent. However, in every star system studied there is at least some amount of all the elements used by life. Furthermore, as planets are small, solid objects formed in the early solar system that could accumulate and become condensing planets within a forming star system, they are necessarily made of heavy elements because the more common hydrogen and helium remain gases. Thus, planets everywhere should contain the elements necessary for life, which means that objects built from planets, moons, asteroids, and comets - also contain these elements. The nature of the formation of the solar system explains why Earth contains all the elements necessary for life, which is why we expect these elements to be present on other worlds throughout our solar system, galaxy, and universe. Note that this argument does not change, even if we allow life to be very different from life on Earth. Life on Earth is carbon-based, and most biologists believe life elsewhere may be carbon-based as well. However, we cannot completely rule out the possibility of life with another chemical base, such as silicon or nitrogen. The system of elements (or their relative proportions) used by other element-based life may be slightly different from that used by carbon-based life on Earth. But the elements are still products of stars and will still be present in planetesimals everywhere. No matter what types of life we seek, we will likely find the necessary elements in almost every planet, moon, asteroid and comet in the universe. A somewhat stringent requirement is the presence of these elements in molecules that can serve as ready-made building blocks for life, just as early Earth probably was an organic soup of amino acids and other complex molecules. The first two sources can only occur on worlds with atmospheres or oceans, respectively. But the third source would have to bring similar molecules to almost all worlds in our solar system. Studies of meteorites and comets indicate that organic molecules are common among both asteroids and comets. Because every body in the Solar System was hit repeatedly by asteroids and comets during the period known as the Heavy Bombardment (about 4 billion years ago), each body had to receive at least a few organic molecules. However, these molecules tend to be destroyed by solar radiation on surfaces that are not protected by atmospheres. Furthermore, while these molecules may remain intact beneath the surface (as they probably do in asteroids and comets), they probably cannot react with each other unless some kind of liquid or gas is present to move them. premise: Emerging tourism destinations The rise of emerging economies marks the third revolution the travel industry has undergone in the last 50 years. The second was the advent of the internet, which allowed millions to book flights, hotels, car hire and package tours without approaching a high street travel agent. Now fast-growing emerging economies - not only Dubai but also Bric countries (Brazil, Russia, India and China) and others, such as South Korea and Vietnam - are once again changing the world of travel, either as destinations or as sources of newly affluent travelers. Turkey was their most popular destination, followed by China and Egypt. The Chinese head the Vietnam visitors' table. The WTTC claims that travel and tourism is the world's largest industry in terms of its contribution to global GDP and employment. It predicts that employment will rise to 296 million in the coming decade. In fact, assessing the scope of the industry is not simple. When all travel and tourism are grouped together, so everything from airlines to coffee shops counts, it's no surprise that the WTTC total is so large. As a rule, restaurants do not register whether they serve tourists, business travelers or locals for a meal. In the next year or two, the travel industry is expected to find its longtime customers in rich Western countries a less reliable source of growth. Some of that extra buying power will go to travel, at home and abroad. Western companies are flocking to the developing world to prepare for these new tourists. premise: Endless harvest. More than two centuries ago, Russian explorers and fur trappers landed in the Aleutian Islands, a volcanic archipelago in the northern Pacific, and learned about a land mass that lies farther north. The indigenous inhabitants of the islands called this land mass Elisa, the Great Land; today we know it as Alaska. The forty-ninth state to join the United States of America (in 1959), Alaska is one-fifth the size of the 48 mainland states combined. It shares, with Canada, the second longest river system in North America and has more than half of the coastline of the United States. The rivers feed into the Bering Sea and Gulf of Alaska cold, nutrient-rich waters that support tens of millions of seabirds, and more than 400 species of fish, shellfish, crustaceans and mollusks. Taking advantage of this rich abundance, Alaska's commercial fisheries have evolved into some of the largest in the world. According to the Alaska Department of Fish and Hunting (ADF&G), commercial fisheries in Alaska landed hundreds of thousands of tons of shellfish and herring, and more than a million tons of land fish (cod, sole, perch, and pollock) in 2000. The true cultural heart and soul of Alaskan fishing, however, is salmon. Salmon, notes author Susan Ewing in Alaska's Great Nature Factbook, pumps through Alaska like blood through a heart, bringing rhythmic nourishment and circulation to land, animals and people. The expected abundance of salmon has allowed some local cultures to flourish, and the dying spits *feed bears, eagles, other animals and eventually the land itself. All five species of Pacific salmon are Chinook, or King; Chum, or Dog; Coho, or Silver; Sookie, or Red; Pink or Hump** in Alaskan waters, and 90% of all commercially caught Pacific salmon in North America are produced there. Indeed, if Alaska were an independent nation, it would be the largest producer of wild salmon in the world. During 2000, commercial tonnage of Pacific salmon in Alaska exceeded 320,000 tons, with a former ship value of over $260 million. Perceptions have not always been so healthy. Between 1940 and 1959, overfishing led to a crash in salmon populations so severe that in 1953 Alaska was declared a federal disaster area. With the start of statehood, however, the state of Alaska took over management of its fisheries, guided by a state constitution that requires Alaska's natural resources to be managed on a sustainable basis. During the same period, the statewide crop totaled about 25 million salmon. Over the following decades the average tonnage increased steadily as a result of this policy of sustainable management, until during the 1990s the annual harvest far exceeded 100 million, and on several occasions over 200 million fish. The main reason for such increases is what is known as abundance-based management in the season. There are biologists across the state who constantly monitor adult fish as they appear to spawn. The biologists sit in creek-side counting towers, studying sonar, watching from planes and talking to fishermen. Salmon season in Alaska is not predetermined. Fishermen know the approximate time of year when they will be allowed to fish, but on any given day, one or more field biologists in a particular area can stop the fishing. Even sport fishing can be stopped. It is this management mechanism that has allowed Alaskan salmon stocks and accordingly Alaskan salmon fisheries to thrive, even as salmon populations in the rest of the United States are increasingly considered threatened or even endangered. In 1999, the Marine Management Board (MSC) *** commissioned a review of the salmon fishery in Alaska. premise: English Heritage's Blue Plaque Scheme The Blue Plaque Scheme has been in operation for over 140 years and is one of the oldest of its kind in the world. The idea of establishing a memorial table was first proposed by William Ewart in the House of Commons in 1863. Emm had an immediate impact on the public imagination, and in 1866 the Society of Arts (later the Royal Society of Arts) founded a programme of formal panels. The society established its first plaque to the poet Lord Byron in 1867. In total, the Society of Arts established 35 panels; today, less than half of them survive, the earliest of which commemorates Napoleon III (1867). In 1901, the London County Council (LCC) Boards Scheme took over the London County Council (LCC), which established nearly 250 boards over the next 64 years and gave the scheme its popular appeal. Under the LCC, the blue plate design as we know it today was adopted, and the selection criteria are formalized. With the abolition of the LCC in 1965, the Boards Scheme passed to the Greater London Council (GLC). The plan changed little, but the GLC was keen to expand the range of people commemorated. The 262 panels erected by the GLC include those for figures such as Sylvia Pankhurst, an activist for women's rights; Samuel Coleridge-Thillor, composer of Hiawatha song; and Mary Seacole, the Jamaican nurse and Crimean War heroine. Since 1986, English Heritage has been administering the Blue Boards Programme. To date, English Heritage has erected nearly 300 panels, bringing the total number to more than 800. English Heritage receives about 100 proposals for blue plaques every year, almost all of which come from members of the public. The background of each case is very different. Each candidate has to meet basic selection criteria before they can be considered. Most importantly, they must have died for 20 years or passed the centenary of their birth, the earliest of them. This delay allows a person's reputation to mature and ensures that his fame will be long-lasting. Representatives of the English Heritage Blue Boards panel from various fields from around the country consider all proposals that meet the basic criteria; on average, about 1 out of 3 proposals are accepted. If a figure is rejected, bidders must wait another 10 years until their offer can be reconsidered. Detailed research is carried out on the surviving addresses of shortlisted candidates, using sources such as autobiographies, election ledgers and postal directories. Since only one plaque is allowed per person, the house to be commemorated must be chosen very carefully. Factors considered include the duration of residence and the candidate's achievements during the relevant years. A significant workplace can also be considered. Before a board can be erected, the owners and tenants of the building in question need to give their consent. Where listed buildings are concerned, consent for listed building is sought from the relevant local authority. If such consents are given, the board is designed, and then manufactured by a specialist manufacturer. Usually it is ready in about two months. Panels are laid in the fabric of the building, near the interior of the wall. The cost of manufacturing and installing a plaque is entirely borne by English Heritage. In total, it can take between two and five years from the initial proposal to the establishment of a board. The precise shape of the blue board, as we now see it, was a relatively late development, although certain guiding principles existed from the outset. The earliest tablets, erected in 1867, were blue. Their format, a circle with the name of the Arts Society worked into an around-the-edge format, was consistently used by the company over its 35 years of management. The manufacture of each slab is carried out by mixing and pouring a piece of thick clay into a casting mold. When dry enough, the plaster is removed and the outline of the inscription and border is transferred to the surface of the board and filled with white glaze. Blue glaze is then applied to the background before firing. This process produces gently raised figures and border, a distinctive feature of English Heritage plaques. After firing, the boards usually have a thickness of 2 inches (50 mm) and a final diameter of 19.5 inches (495 mm), although smaller diameter boards are sometimes used to withstand special circumstances. Extremely durable boards have been found and have an almost unlimited lifespan. Similar panels erected by the Society of Arts have lasted, perfectly legible, for over a century. Due to the slightly domed design, they are self-cleaning and practically do not require maintenance.

premise: Ergonomics is the scientific study of the interaction between people and machines. The domain aims to design equipment and environments best suited to the physical and psychological needs of users, thereby improving the efficiency, productivity and safety of a person using the device. A multidisciplinary field, ergonomics encompasses aspects of psychology, physiology, industrial design, and mechanical engineering. The domain is divided into three main areas. Physical ergonomics refers to the relationship between human anatomy and physical activity, for example the design of tools that minimize or eliminate muscle load. This field also examines how the physical environment affects performance and health. Cognitive ergonomics studies the mental processes involved in humans' interactions with systems, such as computer interfaces. In the design of the cockpit of an aircraft, for example, it is of vital importance that the control boards take into account human factors. Organizational ergonomics focuses on the optimization of socio-technical systems, such as team structure and work processes. More and more progressive organizations are looking for ways to improve ergonomics in the workplace. The advantage of this strategy is not only increased productivity but also reduced sick leave. In the United States, compensation for workers with repetitive strain injuries costs $20 billion annually.
hypothesis: Ergonomically designed control panel adapts to one's mental and physical needs.

premise: With the exception of duds, which are the shape of two interconnected triangles, all modern national flags are rectangular and their colors hark back to the days when flags were widely used for identification and communication. In many cases green represents Islam (along with the crescent moon) while the shape of the cross usually symbolizes a Christian nation. When we consider the mobility of our children, they can be driven to more places (and places farther away) than they can visit without access to a motor vehicle. However, allowing our cities to be dominated by cars is gradually eroding the independent mobility of children. Children have lost much of their freedom to explore their neighborhood or city without adult supervision. In recent surveys, when parents in some cities were asked about their own childhood experiences, most remembered that they had more, or far more, opportunities to go out alone, compared to their children today. They had more freedom to explore their environment. Children's independent access to their local streets may be important for their personal, mental and psychological development. Allowing them to know their neighborhood and community gives them a\ sense of place\. It depends on\ active exploration\, which is not provided when children are traveling in cars. (Such children may see more, but they learn less.) Not only is it important that children can get to local play areas on their own, but walking and cycling journeys to school and other destinations provide real play activities in themselves. These are very significant time and money costs for parents associated with transporting their children to school, sports and other places. As fewer children and adults use the streets as pedestrians, those streets become less sociable places. There are fewer opportunities for children and adults to have the spontaneous community. This in itself may exacerbate concerns related to assault and child abuse, as there are fewer adults available who know their neighbors' children, and can worry about their safety. As our roads become more dangerous, more parents drive their children to more places, thus contributing to increased danger levels for the remaining pedestrians. Instead, cover this cloth with another cloth and continue to apply pressure to the wound for 7 10 minutes. If the bleeding is from the ear, place a clean bandage over the ear, lay the victim on his side and allow blood to drain from the bandage.2 Lift the wound. Position the injured part of the body above the level of the heart if possible while applying direct pressure. 3 Know the pressure points. If direct pressure and elevation do not sufficiently slow down blood flow, find a pressure point. Large arteries found close to the surface of the skin supply blood to the head and each arm and leg. The most common pressure points used during first aid are located in the upper arms and in the creases above the upper legs. Apply pressure to the point of pressure closest to the wound so that the artery is pressed between the fingers and bone directly behind the artery. If you use the pressure point on a foot, you may need to use the heel of your hand instead of your finger.4 Turn to a tourniquet. In very rare cases, all of the above may fail. To prevent the victim from dying, you must apply a tourniquet. After applying a tourniquet, it should not be loosened or removed until the victim reaches medical help. If you use a tourniquet, write down somewhere on the victim the time it was applied, so that medical personnel know how long it has been in place. premise: The father of modern management is said that Peter Drucker invented the field of management before writing his first book on the subject, he knew of only two companies in the world with plans for the development of management. Ten years after the books were published, 3,000 companies taught the subject. Widely considered a pain in modern management,\ he has written 39 books and countless scholarly and popular articles examining how human beings are organized in all sectors of society the business, government, and nonprofit world. His writings predicted many of the major developments of the late twentieth century, including privatization and decentralization; the rise of Japan to a global economic superpower; the crucial importance of marketing; and the emergence of the information society with its need for lifelong learning. Drucker said writing is the foundation of everything he does. In 1937 he published his first book, written in Europe. The End of Economic Man: A Study of the New Totalitarianism examined the spiritual and social origins of fascism. In 1940, before the United States entered World War I, he wrote The Future of the Industrial Man, in which he presented his social vision for the post-war world. IN 1943, GENERAL MOTORS ASKED DRUCKER TO STUDY ITS MANAGEMENT METHODS. Drucker accepted and spent 18 months researching and writing the 1945 book. The concept of the corporation. The concepts Drucker introduced in the 1940s and 1950s persisted. In 1954 Drucker wrote his first book teaching people how to manage. The era of the practice of management, it introduced the concept/management by objectives. Management by objectives requires managers to set goals for those subject to theft and to come up with measures to measure results. Employees are then left alone to perform as they please and measure theft performance. Drucker wrote, “It is impossible to be effective unless a person decides first what he wants to achieve. He went on to explain that each worker should be given the tools to value himself, instead of being valued and controlled from the outside. Management by objectives has become an accepted business concept and is probably Drucker's most important contribution. Drucker posed challenges to young, middle, and senior management: “the very term middle management” becomes meaningless because some of them will have to learn how to work with people they have no direct control over, work across countries, and create, maintain, and operate systems - none of which are traditionally intermediate management tasks.\ Senior management faces the challenge of setting directions for an organization, of managing the fundamentals. Drucker interviewed managers and employees, visited factories, and attended board meetings. While the book focused on General Motors, Drucker continued to discuss the industrial corporation as a social institution and economic policy in the post-war era. He introduced previously unknown concepts such as collaboration between work and management, decentralization of management, and seeing workers as resources rather than as costs. Drucker saw people as a resource, and thought that they could satisfy more customers if they had more involvement in the jobs at the time and gained some satisfaction from doing them. Drucker argued that an industrial society allows people to pursue their dreams of personal achievement and equal opportunity - the need to run businesses by balancing a range of needs and goals, rather than subjecting an institution to a single value. This concept of management by objectives constitutes the key to his landmark 1954 The Practice of Management. He referred to decentralization as “a system of local self-government, in which the central management tells the heads of divisions what to do, but not how to do it. The young managers are given the freedom to make decisions and mistakes and learn from the experience. Senior leaders at General Motors disliked the book and discouraged their executives from reading it. Many other American executives have criticized Conception for its challenge to management authority. Drucker was not immune from criticism. The Wall Street Journal investigated some of his lectures in 1987 and reported that he was sometimes loose with facts. Drucker was wrong, for example, when he told an audience that English was the official language of all employees at the Mitsui Trading Company in Japan. And he was known for his visuals. Given the US government's recent involvement in financial firms, he was probably right in his predictions when he expected, for example, that the countries' financial centre would move from New York to Washington, others argue that one of Drucker's core concepts\ Management by Targets/ is flawed and has never been proven to work effectively. Specifically, critics say that the system is difficult to implement, and that companies often end up overemphasizing control, as opposed to fostering creativity, to meet their goals. Drucker hasn't shied away from controversy, either. Throughout his career, Drucker expanded his position that management is a liberal art, and he infused his management advice with interdisciplinary classes that include history, sociology, psychology, philosophy, culture, and religion. He also strongly believed that all institutions, including those in the private sector, had responsibility for society as a whole.\ The fact is,\ Drucker wrote in 1973,\ that in modern society there is no leadership group other than executives. If the managers of our great institutions, especially in business, don't take responsibility for the common good, no one else can or will.\ In his books, lectures, and interviews, the emergence of knowledge workers is just one of the demographic changes Drucker warns businesses to prepare for. Others include a decline in the birth rate in developed countries, a shift in population from rural to urban centers, changes in the distribution of disposable income, and global competitiveness. Drucker believes these changes will have a huge impact on businesses. Drucker held deep skepticism about macroeconomic theory and argued that economists of all schools fail to explain significant aspects of modern economies. Business/Gums\ have come and gone over the past 50 years, but Drucker's message continues to inspire executives. During the 1990s, Drucker wrote about social, political, and economic changes in the post-capitalist era, which he said are as profound as those of the Industrial Revolution. In his book Managing for the Future: The 1990s and Beyond (1992), Drucker discusses the emergence of the “knowledge worker” whose resources include specialized learning or skills instead of land, labor, or other forms of capital.
