Moreover, although the Green Revolution has greatly expanded global farm production since the 1950s, poverty has stubbornly persisted in Africa, Asia and Latin America. Sustained improvements in the productivity of large farms may play the primary role in boosting the food supply, but local efforts to provide cheap, individualized irrigation systems for small farms may offer a better way to lift people out of poverty. The Green Revolution was aimed at increasing the overall food supply, not raising the incomes of the rural poor, so it is not surprising that it did not exacerbate poverty or hunger. INDIA, FOR EXAMPLE, HAS BEEN SUPPLYING ITSELF WITH FOOD FOR 15 YEARS, AND ITS AGRA WAREHOUSES ARE FULL, BUT WITH MORE THAN 200 MILLION INDIANS A FIFTH OF THE COUNTRY'S POPULATION IS MALNOURISHED BECAUSE THEY CANNOT AFFORD THE FOOD THEY NEED AND BECAUSE THE SAFETY NETS IN THE COUNTRY ARE LACKING. In 2000, 189 countries committed to the Millennium Development Goals, which called for reducing global poverty by half by 2015. Yet with business as usual, we have no hope of achieving most of the Millennium Goals, no matter how much money rich countries contribute to poor ones. C THE SUPPLY-DRIVEN STRATEGIES OF THE GREEN REVOLUTION, HOWEVER, MAY NOT HELP SUBSISTENCE FARMERS, WHO MUST EXPLOIT THEIR STRENGTHS TO COMPETE IN THE GLOBAL MARKET. The average size of a family farm is less than four hectares in India, 1.8 hectares in Bangladesh and about half an acre in China. Combines and other modern farming tools are too expensive to use in such small areas. An Indian farmer selling surplus wheat grown on his one-acre plot could not compete with the highly efficient and subsidized Canadian wheat farms that typically span thousands of acres. Instead, subsistence farmers should take advantage of the fact that their labour costs are the lowest in the world, giving them a relative advantage in growing and selling high-value, intensively cultivated crops. Paul Pollack saw firsthand the need for small-scale strategy in 1981 when he met Abdul Rahman, a farmer in Bangladesh's Nuakhali district. Out of three quarter-acre plots of rain-fed rice fields, Abdel Dole could only grow 700 kg of rice annually and 300 kg less than he needed to feed his family. In the three months before the October rice harvest, Abdul and his wife were forced to watch silently while their three children survived on one meal a day or less. As Polk walked with him through the scattered fields he inherited from his father, Pollack asked what he needed to get out of poverty. Controlling water for my crops, he said, at a price I could afford. Soon Pollak learned of a simple device that could help Abdul achieve his goal: the tread pump. The pump, developed in the late 1970s by Norwegian engineer Gunnar Barnes, is operated by a man who walks instead on a pair of treads and two arm handles made of bamboo. Properly optimized and maintained, it can be operated several hours a day without tiring users. Each stepping pump has two cylinders made of engineering plastic. The diameter of the cylinder is 100.5 mm and the height is 280 mm. The pump is capable of working up to a maximum depth of 7 meters. Operation beyond 7 meters is not recommended to maintain the integrity of the rubber components. The pump mechanism has piston and foot valve assemblies. The action of treading creates alternate strokes in the two pistons that lift the water in pulses. F THE HUMAN-OPERATED PUMP CAN IRRIGATE HALF AN ACRE OF VEGETABLES AND COSTS ONLY $25 (INCLUDING PIPE DRILLING EXPENSES DOWN TO THE GROUNDWATER). Abdul heard about the tread pump from a cousin and was one of the first farmers in Bangladesh to buy one. He borrowed the $25 from David and easily repaid the loan four months later. He also improved the yield of one of his rice classes by watering it. His family ate some of the vegetables and sold the rest at the village market and made a net profit of $100. The cost of IDE's market creation activities was only $12 million, leveraged by an investment of $37.5 million from the farmers themselves. premise: Fordlandia's natural latex, or rubber, comes from the sap of rubber trees. Native to the Amazon region of South America, they had long been a Brazilian monopoly, and the flowering of wild rubber made many remote jungle towns rich, until thousands of the tree's seeds were smuggled in by Brit entrepreneur, Henry Wickham. These were used to establish plantations throughout British East Asia, where the trees, which faced none of their natural insect or fungal enemies, thrived. Thus the Brazilian rubber boom came crashing down, leaving control of the world supply to plantation owners in Malaysia (where to this day most of the world's natural rubber is produced). But in the late 1920s, the auto magnate, Henry Ford, had a vision. He believed in vertical integration, that is, a supply chain of automotive parts and products united through his ownership. As his factories produced hundreds of thousands of cars, each needing rubber tyres, Ford wanted to source rubber of his own and resented dealing with the interests of British plantations. That is why he decided to buy a huge area of rainforest in the Amazon, where he would transplant his workers and the American way of life, in order to create the largest rubber plantation on the planet. It will be called an ambitious, grandiose and doomed Fordlandia from the start. The first mistake was to hire a rather unreliable Brazilian to search for the best location in the Amazon, this man recommended a damp, rocky and barren series of hills near the Tapajos River, a tributary of the wide and mighty Amazon. In 1928, Ford blindly purchased a 10,000 km² franchise and immediately ordered the construction of a huge amount of infrastructure at enormous cost. For this came earthmoving equipment, tractors, stump pullers, trains, prefabricated dwellings, and food preparation equipment. The jungle on the surface was cleared, dozens of Fords workers were relocated, and from that wasteland sprang an instant slice of America, with a modern hospital, library, hotels, ice cream makers and row after row of prefabricated houses nestled along beautifully paved streets. The second big mistake was that, incredibly, Ford never thought to consult a skilled horticulturist. He naively assumed that his company's engineers, who had proved their worth in automobile manufacturing, would prove equally skilled in this agricultural endeavor. Thus, they planted the rubber trees thickly to each other, believing that they would nourish their home environment. However, in the Amazon jungle, wild rubber trees are actually few and far between protecting against the miraculous insect life that chew, drill, suck and bite. In such environments, monoculture farming approaches are dubious at best. Young Fords rubber trees appeared no sooner from the ground than they were attacked by caterpillars, ants, red spiders and, most significantly, South American leaf blight, which to this day limits the number of rubber plantations in the trees' homeland. The next problem was based on cultural differences. The newly planted fields needed hundreds of local workers who, though well paid, were expected to follow Ford's towering vision of a healthy lifestyle. Instead of the local custom to work before and after the middle of the hot day, Fords employees were forced to perform the company's standard 9 to 5 shift. Similarly, they were forced to eat American food and take part in weekend activities that were deemed healthy enough, like poetry reading and square dancing. Alcohol was strictly prohibited at work, in the housing estates or in Fordlandia's sphere of influence. AFTER A YEAR DENYING THEIR LOCAL CUSTOMS, THE MURDERED WORKERS HAD ENOUGH, AND A RIOT ENSUED THAT LEFT THE HAPLESS AMERICAN CREW RUNNING INTO THE JUNGLE TO ESCAPE INJURY. Everything was finally suppressed with the arrival of the Brazilian army. After three years, and with no significant amount of rubber to show for it all, Ford did what he had to do from the start - hire a skilled gardener, who eventually concluded that whichever way the rubber trees were planted, the soil was unsuitable for cultivating them. With such humiliating news, anyone less stubborn would have given up, and yet Ford purchased an additional tract of land about fifty miles downstream of the Tepajus River flatter, drier, better drained and better suited to machinery and started over. This time, Ford imported wear-resistant Malaysian rubber trees, and much more horticultural expertise. Still, 10 years later, in 1942, the operation could only produce a minuscule 750 tons of latex rubber. Ford factories had hoped for nearly 40,000. The final nail in the coffin was the development of synthetic rubber, and in 1945 it was time to admit defeat, though neither Ford did. By that time he was old and ill and had relinquished control of his company to his grandson, Henry Ford II, who closed the entire rubber operation. The holdings were sold back to the Brazilian government for a scant sum, leaving a loss of over $20 million (which would be 10 times that in today's terms) a complete and utter economic disaster.
hypothesis: Rubber trees are well suited to Malaysia.
label: c

Prisoners Margaret Dawson and Elizabeth Thackeray were among the first European women to ever set foot on Australian soil. A. Although many of the deported prisoners were barred from returning to Britain, others like Dawson, were, in theory, deported for a given period. In reality, however, the costs of trying to return to the mother country were far beyond the means of the majority. Many rewards were available to prisoners who demonstrated exemplary behavior, including land grants of 30 acres or more, tools for developing and farming the land, and access to inmate labor. First, genealogists need to consider who the information was provided by and what it was possible to verify that he or she knew. For example, a census record alone is considered unreliable because a reputable source of information cannot be found. A death certificate signed by an identified doctor, on the other hand, can be accepted as more reliable. In the case of bias or state of mind, researchers are advised to take into account that even when information is given by what can be considered a reliable source, there may have been motivation to be unreal to continue claiming a government benefit or avoiding taxation, for example. H. In general, data recorded at or close to the event under study are considered more reliable than records written at a later point in time, since while individuals may intend to give a true representation of events factual information may be incorrectly presented due to memory lapses and forgotten details. Finally, sources can be classified as original or derivative. The fireflies are a huge group containing over 2000 species, with new ones being discovered all the time. The feature that makes fireflies and glow worms so attractive is their ability to produce an often dazzling light display. The light is used by the adult fireflies as a signal to attract a mate, and each species must develop its own call sign to avoid being confused with other species glowing nearby. So within any one area each species will differ from its neighbors in some way, for example in its color or pattern of light, how long the light pulses last, the spacing between the pulses, and whether it appears in flight or from the ground. The almost magical light of the fireflies has attracted human attention for generations. It is described in an ancient Chinese encyclopedia written over 2000 years ago by a disciple of Confucius. Fireflies often appear in Japanese and Arabic folk medicine. All over the world they have inspired countless poems, paintings and stories. In Britain, for example, there are many anecdotes describing how glow worms were used for reading or were used as emergency bike lamps when cyclists' batteries failed without prior warning. Early travellers in the New World returned with similar stories, how Central American natives would collect a type of click beetle and release them indoors to light up their barracks. Girls threaded them around their feet to illuminate the forest paths at night. Fireflies very similar to the ones we see today have been found fossilized in rocks formed about 30 million years ago, and their ancestors probably glowed long before that. It is impossible to be sure exactly when and where the first firefly appeared. The highest concentrations of firefly species today are found in the tropics of South America, which may be that this is where they first evolved, or simply that they prefer the conditions there. Wherever they first arose, fireflies have since spread to almost all parts of the world. Today, members of the firefly family can be found almost everywhere outside the Arctic and Antarctic circles. As with many insects, the life of glowworms is divided into four distinct phases: the egg, the larva (equivalent to the larva of a butterfly), the pupa (or chrysalis), and the adult. The glow worm begins its life in the fall as a bright yellow egg. The freshly laid egg is extremely fragile but within a day its surface hardened into a shell. An egg usually takes about 35 days to hatch, but the exact time varies depending on temperature, from about 27 days in hot weather to more than 45 days in cold weather. By the time it is supposed to hatch, the glow worm's light organ is fully developed, and its glow signals that the egg will soon hatch. After leaving the egg, the larva slowly grows from a few millimeters to the size and shape of a match. The larval stage is the only time the insect can feed. The larva devotes much of its life to feeding and building up its food reserves so that as an adult it will be free to concentrate all its efforts on the task of finding a mate and reproducing. Throughout its time as a larva, about 15 months, the glow worm emits bright light. The larval light is much weaker than the adult females but can still be seen more than five meters away. In recent years, the pollution caused by millions of vehicles has dominated the debate on transportation. The problem has even convinced California as the home of car culture to curb traffic growth. But no matter how green they are, cars are unlikely to get us through crowded cities any faster. And persuading people to use trains and buses will always be an uphill struggle. Cars, after all, are popular for very good reasons, as anyone who has small children or heavy shopping knows. So politicians should be trying to lure people out of their cars, not force them out. There is certainly no shortage of alternatives. Perhaps the most attractive is the concept known as personal rapid transit (PRT), independently invented in the US and Europe in the 1950s. The idea is to go to one of many stations and hop into a computer-controlled car, which can get you to your destination along a network of instructional routes. You won't have to share your space with strangers, and with no traffic lights, pedestrians or parked cars to slow things down, PRT routes can carry far more traffic, without stopping, than any inner-city road. It's a wonderful vision, but the odds are stacked in front of the PRT for a number of reasons. The first cars traveled on existing roads, and only after they became popular and after governments began to earn revenue from them - a road network designed specifically for motor vehicles was built. Once on a road, the occupant would take over from the computer, and the term RUF vehicle comes from a Danish saying that means going fast will turn into an electric car. Passengers could drive to the Guidance Road, sit and read as they transported to the city. At work they would jump out and leave their vehicles to park themselves. Unlike PRT, such a system can grow organically, since each network will serve a large area around it and people nearby can buy it. And a dual-mode system may even win the support of car manufacturers, who can easily switch to the production of dual-mode vehicles. Of course, creating a new transportation system won't be cheap or easy. But unlike adding a dedicated bus lane here or expanding the underground railway there, an innovative system like Genesis can transform cities. Surely we can find a better way to get around?

premise: GREAT INVENTIONS THERE ARE SOME THINGS WE USE EVERY DAY. Can you imagine a world without zippers to fasten clothes? Have you ever wondered about the keyboard layout of a typewriter, which we see every day on the computer? These are just two of the many inventions that have made our lives easier. Maybe that's why we don't think about them much! The zipper What did we do before the invention of the zipper? In 1893, the world's first zipper was produced in Chicago. Although the inventor claimed that this was a reliable reinforcement for clothes, this was not the case. Chicago's zipper opened without warning, or jammed, and it quickly lost popularity. Twenty years later, a Swedish-born engineer named Sondbeck solved the problem. He attached tiny cups to the backs of the interlocking teeth, which meant that the teeth could be tangled more stably and reliably. Initially zippers were made of metal. They were heavy, and if they got stuck it was difficult to release them. Then came nylon zippers that were lighter and easier to use, and had smaller teeth. The fashion industry liked the new zippers much more because they do not distort the garment line or weigh lightly. They were also easier for the machinists to fit into the garment. Meanwhile, a new tightening agent appeared at the end of the twentieth century: Velcro. Velcro is another product made of nylon. Nylon is a very tough synthetic fiber first developed in 19305, and bears a name to remind the hearer of the two places where it was developed: New York for New York and LON for London. THE VELCRO IS MADE WITH VERY SMALL NYLON HOOKS ON ONE SIDE OF THE FASTENING WHICH CATCH TINY MOUSTACHES WITH A LOOP ON THE OTHER SIDE OF THE FASTENING. It is strong and durable. Velcro is used on clothing, luggage and footwear. It is quick and easy to fasten and unfasten, and has taken a large part of the share of zippers on the market. It is also used in ways where a zipper cannot be used, for example as an easily replaceable attachment on plaster casts, and to hold furniture fabrics in place. The typewriter and keyboard The keyboard of the modern typewriter is laid out in the most peculiar way. Why would someone place the letters on the left side of the top row of the keyboard in the order Q W E R T Y? The answer is simple: slow down the typist. But first, let's consider the history of the typewriter itself. In the 1860s, a newspaper editor named Christopher Scholes lived in Milwaukee, USA. Scholes invented the first of the modern typewriters, although there were patents for typewriter-like machines as early as 1714, when Queen Anne of England granted a patent to a man named Henry Mill for a machine that would put marks on paper so neat and precise that it could not be distinguished from the printing press. In 1829, across the Atlantic in Detroit USA, William Austin Burt took out a patent for a typewriter-like machine, four years before French inventor Javier Projean manufactured his machine designed to record words at a speed similar to someone writing with a pen. So the typewriter was not a new idea, although there was no successful realization of the idea before the Christopher Scholes machine. His typewriter became very popular, and soon people learned to type very quickly so quickly, in fact, that the keys got complicated. In manual typewriters the characters were set at the end of bars that rose to strike the paper when the key was pressed. In the first models, the keys were set in alphabetical order. When a fast typist listened to a word like federal, it was very likely that the nearby e and d keys would get tangled. Therefore, Soules began to find ways to slow down the typist. He looked for the letters most often used in English, then placed them far apart. For example, q and v, which are almost always used together in English, are separated by five intervening letters. The program worked, and the typist slowed down slightly. When computers came into use in the latter part of the twentieth century it was suggested that the keyboard should be rational. After all, it was no longer necessary to avoid the collision of manual typewriter keys. One new board included keys that produced letters that often appear together in English, like ing and th and ed, so that a word thing required two strokes to write instead of five. Although it made perfect sense, people had a very hard time learning to use a new keyboard, and the idea was scrapped. It is unlikely that the keyboard will ever change: as we approach the twenty-first century, the voice-activated computer, which is already in an advanced state of development, is becoming more and more accessible. It is very likely that soon we will have machines that take dictation while we talk to them, and the keyboard will be used for repairs.

premise: The migrations are large. Animal migration, however it is defined, is much more than just the movement of animals. Can this be loosely described as travel occurring at regular intervals? Often in an annual cycle that may include members of many sexes, and is rewarded only after a long journey. IT IMPLIES A HEREDITARY INSTINCT. Biologist Hugh Dingle identified five characteristics that apply, in varying degrees and combinations, to all migrations. These are prolonged movements that carry animals out of familiar habitats; they tend to be linear, not zigzag; they involve special behaviors relating to preparation (such as overfeeding) and arrival; they require special allocations of energy. And one more: Migrating animals maintain intense attention to the larger task, which keeps them undistracted from temptations and undeterred by challenges that would turn other animals aside. An Arctic tern, on its 20,000km flight from the extreme south of South America to the Arctic Circle, will not notice a nice stinking herring offered from bird-watching boats along the way. While local seagulls will hungrily dive for such handouts, the Sharon flies on. Why? The Arctic Sharon resists distraction because it is driven in the moment by an instinctive sense of something we humans find admirable: a greater purpose. In other words, she is determined to reach her destination. The bird senses that it can eat, rest and mate later. At the moment he is completely focused on the journey; his undivided intention is arrival. Arriving at some gravel coastline in the Arctic, on which other Arctic vermin have converged, will serve its larger purpose as shaped by evolution: finding a place, time and set of circumstances in which it can successfully hatch and give rise to offspring. But migration is a complex issue, and biologists define it differently, depending in part on what types of animals they study. Joe! Berger, of the University of Montana, who works on the American pronghorn and other large land mammals, prefers what he calls a simple, practical set-up suited to his beasts: movements from a seasonal home region away to another home region and back. Usually the reason for such seasonal movement back and forth is to search for resources that are not available in one area all year round. But daily vertical movements of zooplankton in the ocean upward at night to forage for food, downward by day to escape predators can also be thought of as migration. SO IS THE MOVEMENT OF APHIDS WHEN AFTER DEPLETING THE YOUNG LEAVES IN ONE FOOD PLANT, THEIR OFFSPRING FLY ON TO ANOTHER HOST PLANT, WITH NO APHID RETURNING TO WHERE IT STARTED. Dingle is an evolutionary biologist who studies insects. His definition is more complex than Bergers, noting the five features that distinguish migration from other forms of locomotion. They allow for the fact that, for example, aphids will become sensitive to blue light (from the sky) when it is time for takeoff on their great journey, and sensitive to yellow light (reflected from tender young leaves) when it is suitable to land. Birds will fatten themselves with heavy feeding before a long migratory flight. The value of its definition, Dingle argues, is that it focuses attention on what the phenomenon of wildebeest migration shares with the aphid phenomenon, and therefore helps guide researchers to understanding how evolution created them all. However, human behavior has a detrimental effect on animal migration. The pronghorn, which resembles an antelope, although they are unrelated, is the fastest land mammal in the New World. One population, which spends summers in the mountainous Grand Teton National Park in the western US, follows a narrow route from its summer range in the mountains, across the river and down to the plains. Here they await the frosty months, feeding mainly on loose brush blown by snow. These pronghorn are notable for the invariability of their migration path and the severity of its contraction in three bottlenecks. If they cannot pass through any of the three during their spring migration, they cannot reach the abundance of their summer pastures; if they cannot pass again in the fall, fleeing south to those wind-blown plains, they are likely to die trying to winter in the deep snow. Pronghorn, which depends on distance vision and speed to protect against predators, traverses high, open shoulders of land, where they can see and run. In one of the bottlenecks, wooded hills rise and form a V, leaving a corridor of open land only about 150 meters wide, filled with private houses. The increasing development leads to a crisis for the pronghorn, and threatens to strangle their passage. Conservation scientists, along with some biologists and land managers at the U.S. National Park Service and other agencies, are now working to preserve migratory behaviors, not just species and habitats. National Forest has identified the Pronghorn Trail, much of which runs on its land, as a protected migration corridor. But neither the Forest Service nor the Park Service can control what happens on private land in a bottleneck. And with certain other migratory species, the challenge is further complicated by far greater distances crossed, more jurisdictions, more borders, more dangers along the way. We need wisdom and determination to ensure that migratory species can continue their journey for some time longer.

premise: A growth model Shortly after the Second World War, development as we now understand it was triggered. Western governments and donors poured money into new agencies that started trying to stimulate the economies of underdeveloped countries. Because of this emphasis, it is now considered the growth model. Although we might expect that poverty reduction would be the central goal, the planners at this time were primarily concerned with industrial development. It was hoped that the benefits of this would trickle down to poor people through raising incomes and providing employment opportunities, thereby indirectly raising them above the privileged poverty threshold of a dollar a day. But the weaknesses of these assumptions were exposed when rates of poverty and economic growth were found to be rising in parallel in many countries. During the 1970s, a new trend took over the development of the drip. Instead of focusing on macroeconomic policies and large-scale industrial projects, planners shifted attention to the core requirements of individuals and communities. This became known as the Basic Needs Approach to Development. It was hoped that through the provision of services such as community sanitation and literacy programs, it would be possible to eradicate poverty from below. Economic growth was desirable but unnecessary basic needs redefined poverty from a lack of money to the inability to achieve the full human potential. The problem with basic needs programs, on the other hand, has been their expensive, resource-intensive nature, which involves continuous management and financing Since the 1980s, development planners have moved towards a sustainable livelihood approach, which emphasizes good livelihoods (material and social) that, most importantly, are independent and sustainable. Sustainable in this sense means that people are able to recover from the shocks and stresses of everyday life, exempting agencies from having to constantly monitor their lives. This approach emphasizes a perception of poverty that does not arise from the rich but from the poor themselves, who are considered the most appropriate location to determine the poverty indices that contribute to the multiple aspects of their deprivation. Although the sustainable livelihood approach has been criticized for lacking an environmental platform robust enough to respond to climate change, and for cutting off aspects of power and social status from being a part that can be challenged in development, it is now the preferred model for development projects. Although there is a certain linearity in the development practice trajectory, as paradigms shift in and out of fashion, vigorous scholarly debate persists around all approaches. The growth model, for example, is still defended by many theorists, especially economists. Those who believe in the growth model insist that nothing beats economic development as a tool for poverty alleviation for developing countries (though there is often less enthusiasm for its application to the post-industrial West). Many countries that explicitly focused on growth were able to make considerable breakthroughs in poverty reduction, even in the absence of a development plan; Japan and Germany followed this path after World War II, as did China from the 1970s. On the other hand, some countries with huge flows of funding for aid-based development projects, particularly those in sub-Saharan Africa, have struggled to make progress with meeting poverty reduction targets. However, there is good reason to be sceptical about the growth model, as evidenced by the many companies that have partially collapsed as a result prioritising economic growth over the work of human development. The experiences of many Eastern European countries with health and employment crises in the early 1990s are particularly traumatic examples of this. The growth model also suffers from an undemocratic method and technocratic, if not autocratic, underdeveloped countries often make policy decisions based on consultation with Western economists and institutions on how to produce growth. It dissolves the autonomy of the communities to make their own decisions about what matters to them, and what kind of society they would like to build. The transition to a sustainable livelihood approach is a positive move from the point of view of matters, since by acting on the principle that decisions should be made by those affected by them, it presents a role for local decision-making. It will be difficult, if not impossible, for any country in the near future to ignore economic growth as an indicator of development while continuing to meet development goals. However, it is important that we move away from seeing this type of growth as the main objective for development. Development is ultimately about people, and human development must be placed at the forefront; economic growth is simply one tool out of many that can help us along the way. We must also recognize that foreign advisers, whatever skills and knowledge they have, can sometimes be an obstacle; local autonomy must be respected for real development to occur. The growth model may have failed, but that doesn't make economic growth irrelevant. A sustainable livelihood approach offers beneficial and realistic alternatives. But it is folly to commit to a strictly defined and systematic program, less constricted thinking patterns will help us break the fashion cycle of development.

This will ensure your safety during training while avoiding injuries and/or other complications. It is imperative to follow the instructions of the doctor/fitness therapist before starting any training. Check out essential tips for gym safety. Check your fitness before starting any strength-training program. You may need to change or avoid lifting weights if you have muscle or joint problems, seizure disorders, heart disease, high blood pressure, previous injuries, or any other physical condition with the potential for danger. One of the cardinal principles of gym safety is to never exercise when you're tired or sick. You can aggravate your condition or hurt yourself. Warm up before each cardio workout, as it involves repetitive exercise and increases heart rate. The fingers should be stretched before carrying on top of the back, and the back should be narrowed. Birds walk on top of their legs with some stretching. Do not injure muscles without preparing them properly. Do not lift weights in a jerky way. This can lead to muscle injuries. Do your exercises in a slow and controlled manner. Increase the dumbbells gradually. Use safety collars when practicing squats, bench presses, curls and dumbbells. This will ensure that the weight plates do not slip and cause injury. Use a weight belt, wraps, straps, and gloves to support heavy lifts. It protects your lumbar region. Knee wraps prevent injury to your tendons and ligaments. Patches tend to get injured more easily. Start with some light cardiovascular activities, such as jogging, jumping jacks or brisk walking, just to get your muscles moving. Do not hold your breath while lifting weights, this can cause intra-abdominal pressure that can lead to a hernia. Breathe out as you strain and breathe in as you relax and let the weight drop. Repeat exercise routines steadily to enjoy the workout. Lift weights under control rather than exploding. Do not lean heavily on the stair rails. Leaning heavily on the stair rails will place unnecessary weight on your wrists and back. Unnecessary inclination can cause injuries to the wrists and back. Drink water while exercising. This prevents dehydration and helps better workout performance. Stop your fitness activities if you experience dizziness, fainting, or a change in heart rate. Any significant increase or decrease in blood pressure should not be ignored. A critical gym safety tip is to stop fitness activities if you feel pressure in your chest or shoulders and surrounding areas. Replace gym equipment in the right place after you're done with them. Leaving them around can hurt other gym members. Always use collars that prevent dumbbells from falling off the dumbbells. Keep your hands away from chains, cameras, pulleys and weight plates of exercise machines when in use. Use fitness equipment after wiping them. Wash your hands after exercise. This may reduce your chance of catching any virus.

Chemists in the US have successfully completed an 18-month experiment of the technique, which neutralises the acids in paper that cause book decay. The method was developed by the Dutch chemistry giant, Akzo, in collaboration with the U.S. Library of Congress. It can handle 1,000 books at a time at a fraction of the cost of digitization. World libraries and archives today are mostly filled with self-destructing books because of a new way of paper production introduced over a century ago. In this process, the wood pulp became the main source of the cellulose from which the paper was made, replacing the cotton or linen rags previously used. Unfortunately, book publishers were unaware that the slightly acidic nature of the wood pulp would ultimately threaten their work. The acid attacks the cellulose polymer of the paper, breaking it down into shorter and shorter pieces until the structure of the papers collapses. The only answer is to neutralize the acids in the newspaper by chemical means. This is usually done by unbinding the book, treating it page by page with a carbonate solution, and then re-binding it. The cost can be up to 200 per volume. The Akzos method can be performed without taking the cover off the book. On the face of it, DEZ appears to be the last chemical that needs to be brought into contact with paper. This volatile liquid bursts into flames when it comes into contact with air. However, it is not DeZs sensitivity to oxidation that is key to its use as a preservative, but rather its ability to neutralize acids by forming strong zinc salts. Because DEZ is volatile, it seeps into the pores in the paper. When it encounters an acid molecule, such as sulfuric acid, it reacts to form zinc sulfate and ethane gas. DEZ is such a strong base that it will react with any acid, including the weaker organic ones. It will also react with any water left in the paper to form zinc oxide. This is an added bonus for bookkeepers, as it buffers the paper from future attack by acidic gases from the atmosphere, such as sulfur dioxide. Not only will DEZ protect against acid attack, but it is also able to neutralize alkalis, which threaten certain types of paper, it can do this because zinc oxide is an amphoteric capable of reacting with acids or alkalis. For the process, the books are gently heated under vacuum for a day to remove residual moisture traces. The chamber is then flushed with dry nitrogen gas for five hours to remove the remaining air before introducing the DEZ at low pressure into the gas stream. DEZ passes for about eight hours. The unreactive DEZ is captured from the exit gases and recycled, while the ethane is burned. After completion of the process, the chamber is purified with nitrogen to remove residual DEZ. The whole process takes about three days. The cost for a book is about 2, significantly less than 40 for digitization. This work was originally funded by the US Library of Congress, which has over 10 million books now at risk. ACCORDING TO DICK MILLER, EXUS DIRECTOR OF BOOK PRESERVATION, TESTS HAVE SHOWN THAT THE METHOD CAN HANDLE HUNDREDS OF BOOKS AT A TIME. One million books a year could be extracted by the new process, for which Akzo was granted exclusive rights. The treated books are supposed to survive for centuries. Another national institution, the British Library, has launched a programme to adopt a book to help it meet the costs of processing the books. The British Library has so far raised over 80,000. premise: The future of helium in the air In recent years we have all been exposed to dire media reports regarding the imminent demise of global coal and oil reserves, yet the depletion of another major non-renewable resource continues without getting much press at all. Helium, an inert, odorless, monatomic element known to laypeople as the substance that makes balloons float and voices squeak when inhaled could disappear from this planet within a generation. Helium itself is not rare; in fact there is an abundant supply of it in the cosmos. In fact, 24 percent of our galaxy's fundamental mass is made up of helium, making it the second most abundant element in our universe. Because of its lightness, however, most helium disappeared from our planet many years ago. As a result, only a tiny proportion of 0.00052%, more precisely, remains in the Earth's atmosphere. Helium is a byproduct of thousands of years of radioactive decay from the elements thorium and uranium. The helium is mostly trapped in underground natural gas bunkers and is commercially extracted using a method known as fractional distillation. The loss of helium on Earth will greatly affect society. Resisting its conception as a novelty material for parties and gimmicks, the element actually has many essential applications in society. Probably the best known commercial use is in airships and in limp (non-flammable helium replaced hydrogen as the lifting gas du jour after the Hindenburg disaster in 1932, during which an airship burst into flames and crashed to the ground, killing several passengers and crew). But helium also helps in deep-sea diving, where it's mixed with nitrogen to reduce the dangers of inhaling ordinary, high-pressure air; as a detergent for rocket engines; and in its most common use, as a coolant for superconducting magnets in hospital MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) scanners. The possibility of losing helium forever poses the threat of a real crisis because its unique properties are incredibly difficult, if not impossible to replicate (certainly, no biosynthetic resin product comes close to approaching helium's point of feasibility, even as similar developments continue at pace for oil and coal). Helium is even cheerfully derided as a single element because it doesn't stick to other molecules like its cousin, hydrogen. According to Dr. Lee Sobotka, helium is the most noble gas, that is, it is very stable and does not react most often... It has a closed electronic configuration, the atom is very tightly bound. It is this greed of its electrons that prevents integration with other elements. Another important feature is the unique boiling point of helium, which is lower than that of any other element. Worsened global shortages could render millions of dollars of high-value, life-saving equipment utterly useless. The growing supply has already resulted in the postponement of research and development projects in physics laboratories and manufacturing plants around the world. There is a huge imbalance in supply and demand caused in part by the expansion of high-tech manufacturing in Asia. The source of the problem is the Helium Privatization Act (HPA), a U.S. law passed in 1996 that requires the U.S. National Helium Reserve to liquidate its helium assets by 2015 regardless of market price. Although intended to settle the original cost of the reserve by a U.S. Congress ignorant of its consequences, the result of this fire sale is that global helium prices are artificially inflated to the point that few can bother to recycle the material or use it discreetly. Inflated values also mean that natural gas extractors see no reason to capture helium. Much is lost in the extraction process. premise: How does the biological clock work? Our life expectancy is limited. Everyone takes it for granted biologically. Nothing lives forever! However, in this statement we think of artificially produced technical objects, products that are subjected to natural wear and tear during use. This leads to the result that at a certain time the object stops working and is not usable (death in the biological sense). But are the wear and loss of function of technical objects and the death of living organisms really similar or similar? Our dead products are static and closed systems. It is always the basic material that constitutes the object and which, in the course of natural things, wears out and matures. Aging in this case must occur according to the laws of physical chemistry and thermodynamics. Although the same law applies to a living organism, the consequence of this law is not inevitable in the same way. At least as long as a biological system has the ability to regenerate itself it can actually age without getting old; an organism is an open and dynamic system through which new material constantly flows. Destruction of old matter and creation of new material are therefore in constant dynamic equilibrium. The substance from which the organism is formed changes continuously. Thus, our body constantly replaces old material with new, just like a spring that more or less retains its shape and movement, but in which the water molecules are always different. Aging and death should therefore not be seen as inevitable, especially since the organism has many mechanisms for repair. In principle there is no need for a biological system to grow old and die. Nevertheless, limited life expectancy, aging and then death are fundamental characteristics of life. The reason for this is easy to identify: in nature, existing organisms adapt or are regularly replaced by new types. Due to changes in the genetic material (mutations), these have new characteristics and during their individual lives they are tested for optimal or better adaptation to environmental conditions. Immortality will interfere with this system - it needs space for a new and better life. This is the fundamental problem of evolution. Each organism has a life expectancy that is most typical. There are notable differences in life expectancy between different species, but within one species the parameter is relatively constant. For example, the duration of the average human life has hardly changed in thousands of years. Although more and more people are reaching advanced age as a result of developments in medical care and better nutrition, the typical upper limit for most remains 80 years. Another argument against the simple wear and tear theory is the observation that the time in which organisms age ranges from several days (even a few hours for single-celled organisms) to several thousand years, as in mammoth trees. If life expectancy is a genetically determined biological characteristic, it is logically necessary to propose the existence of an internal clock, which measures and controls in some way the aging process and which finally determines death as the last stage in a permanent plan. Similar to life expectancy, metabolic rate for different organisms has a constant mathematical relationship to body mass. Compared to life expectancy, this relationship is reversed: the larger the organism, the lower its metabolic rate. Again this relationship applies not only to birds, but also, similarly on average within the systematic unit, to all other organisms (plants, animals, unicellular organisms). Animals that behave energy-sparingly age especially, for example crocodiles and turtles. Parrots and birds of prey are often kept shackled. Thus they are not able to experience life and therefore they achieve a high life expectancy in captivity. Animals that save energy by hibernation or fatigue (e.g. bats or hedgehogs) live much longer than those that are always active. The metabolic rate of mice can be reduced by very low consumption of food (starvation diet). They may then live twice as long as their seventy well-fed members. Women are significantly older (about 10%) than men. If you look at the metabolic rate of both sexes you determine that the higher male metabolic rate roughly accounts for the lower male life expectancy. This means that they live life energetically - more intensely, but not for so long. From this it follows that economical use of energy reserves should prolong life. High-performance extreme sports may lead to optimal cardiovascular performance, but they certainly do not prolong life. Relaxation lowers the metabolic rate, as does adequate sleep and, in general, an equitable and balanced personality. Each of us can develop our own energy-saving plan with a little self-observation, critical self-control and, above all, logical consistency. Experience will show that living in this way not only increases life expectancy but is also very healthy. This final aspect should not be forgotten.
hypothesis: Wear theory applies to both artificial objects and biological systems.

premise: The hacking of Internet security, or rather the lack thereof, is the missile of today's computer user. Computer hackers write malicious computer software (or malware) that infects vulnerable computers and changes how they operate. Typically, these programs are downloaded from the Internet inadvertently with one click of the mouse. The consequences harm the user, ranging from a minor annoyance, for example, slowing down the speed of computers to a large financial loss for a person or company, when access to login and password details and fraud is generated. EXAMPLES OF MALWARE INCLUDE VIRUSES, WORMS, TROJANS (TROJANS), SPYWARE, KEYSTROKE LOGGING, SCARS SOFTWARE, AND DISHONEST ADWARE. A virus can be released when a user opens an email and downloads an attachment. The text part of the email cannot carry malware, but the attachment may contain a virus, for example in a macro (short program) embedded in a worksheet document, such as Excel. Viruses can replicate and if they spread to the host's boot sector files, they can leave the user with a blue screen of death. In these circumstances, the blue screen is accompanied by a message that a problem has been detected and Windows shuts down to prevent damage to your computer. While malware cannot physically damage the hard drive of computers, the boot sector information is destroyed and the computer is unable to function. In the worst case, the hard disk must be erased by reformation, before the operating system can be reinstalled, in which case every program and file will be lost. Unlike a virus, a worm can infect a computer without the user downloading an attachment, so it can spread through a computer network at tremendous speed. The ability of worms to replicate in this way means they can infect any contact in users' email address book and possibly every email contact on each recipient's computer. Instant messaging programs and social networking sites are at similar risk. A major characteristic of a worm is that it slows down the computer by consuming memory or hard disk space so that the computer eventually locks up. The word Trojan derives from the Trojan horse of Greek mythology who tricked the Trojans into allowing Greek soldiers to enter the city of Troy, hidden inside a wooden horse. Today a Trojan is a metaphor for malware that masquerades as useful software. Trojans are unable to replicate but they secretly interfere with the computer, allowing viruses and worms unlimited access to the system. Spyware tracks the internet browsing habits of computer users in secret. Some spyware simply tracks the number of visits consumers make to certain web pages and what they buy or spend, usually for marketing purposes. Keystroke logging is the main fraud activity linked to spyware. Here, private and confidential information is obtained from users' keystrokes, allowing criminals to acquire credit card details, or login names and passwords for online bank accounts. Some keyloggers operate legitimately to monitor employees' Internet use in the office or to track the browsing activities of children at home. Scareware is a type of extortion in which the victim is informed that the computer is infected with a virus, and for a fee he is offered a solution to fix the problem. The user is fooled into pressing the OK button and buys software unnecessarily because there is usually no virus. In one scam, a Scareware pop-up informs the victim that the computers registry contains critical errors when the problems are actually minor or even non-existent. Convinced by the pop-up ad, the victim buys the registry cleaner, which may not work or may even harm the computer registry. There are, of course, legitimate registry cleaners that will increase the speed of your computers. A real registry cleaner will usually be approved by a reputable company or recommended in a computer bulletin. Adware pop-up ads are similar to malware but are just a nuisance and not malware (unless dishonest), though they can still download programs that track your shopping habits and slow down your computer. The advertisements pop up automatically when the user opens the web browser and can be annoying because they hide information on the page that opens. One answer is to activate the Internet Explorers pop-up blocker in the privacy tab as this will block most automatic pop-ups. More effectively, a user can purchase an all-in-one security suite to block any malware. Security software automatically blocks and deletes any malware for a more secure web experience. Typically, the software will update itself every day as long as the computer is turned on.
hypothesis: Malware is usually downloaded from the Internet by mistake.

premise: Have researchers created synthetic life at the J. Craig Venter Institute? Researchers often insert a gene or two into an organism in order to make it do something unique. For example, researchers inserted the insulin gene into bacteria in order to make them produce human insulin. However, researchers at the J. Craig Venter Institute (JCVI) in Rockville, MD, have now created organisms containing a fully synthetic genome. This synthetic genome was designed by a computer, resulting in the creation of the first self-replicating species... That its parent is a computer,\ as Dr. Venter, the lead scientist on this project, said. Essentially, JCVI scientists took the genome of one bacterial species, M. mycoides, synthesized it from scratch and then transplanted it into another bacterial species, M. capricolum. DNA was synthesized as a series of cassettes, or pieces, spanning about 1,080 bases (the chemical units that make up DNA) each. These tapes were carefully assembled together and slowly introduced into the species M. capricolum. JVCI researchers also included several\ watermarks\ in the synthetic genome. Because DNA contains introns, which are non-expressed DNA ranges, as well as exons, which are expressed DNA ranges, much of the code can be modified without affecting the final organism. Also, the four bases of the DNA code - A, C, G, and T - can combine into triplets to encode 20 amino acids (the chemical units of which a protein consists), as well as start and stop instructions for gene expression. These amino acids are marked with individual alphabetic letters; for example, tryptophan is marked with the letter W. Thus, using the amino acid/alphabet, JCVI researchers were able to insert sequences of DNA specifically designed to spell out the names of study authors, project contributors, web addresses and even include quotes from James Joyce and Richard Feynman. Such engineering has helped clarify that the genome of M. capricolum is entirely synthetic and not the product of natural bacterial growth and replication. Over one million bases in total were introduced into M. capricolum. The end result was a bacterial cell that originated in M. capricolum, but behaved like and expressed the proteins of M. mycoides. This synthetic M. mycoides bacterium has also been able to replicate itself, a fundamental quality of life.65The demonstration that a fully synthetic genome can be used to start synthetic life promises other exciting discoveries and technologies. For example, photosynthetic algae can be implanted in the genome that would allow these organisms to produce biofuels. In fact, ExxonMobil's research and engineering firm has already signed an agreement with Synthetic Genomics, the company that helped fund JCVI's research team, to start just such a project. While some researchers agree that the technical achievement of the JCVI team is remarkable, detractors point to the difficulty of creating more complicated organisms from scratch. Other researchers point to the fact that some biofuels are already produced by microorganisms through the genetic engineering of just a handful of genes. And Dr. David Baltimore, a leading geneticist at CalTech, objected to the significance of the work done by the JCVI research team, stating that its lead researcher, Dr. Venter,\... Didn't create life, just imitated it. \

premise: Healthy food? The shelves of every supermarket are packed with probiotic yoghurts that can supposedly relieve constipation and ward off infections, butter substitutes that claim to reduce cholesterol, tomato extracts that keep skin looking youthful while preventing cancer, micronutrient-enhanced cereals essential for development and so on. Have food companies taken a higher standard of morality or are there other motivations for this concern than the health value of their produce? Food companies have taken into account the supposed health and nutritional benefits of their products for several reasons. Such products may appeal to both health-conscious shoppers and people who know they're eating unhealthily, but hope that a few vitamins here and a few probiotics there might make up for the junk. Best of all, from the perspective of food companies, these functional foods, which blur the line between foods and medicines, hold the promise of higher margins and faster growth. In Western Europe all this has attracted the attention of regulators on both sides of the Atlantic. They worry that some of these health claims may be misleading or unsupported by evidence, and are tightening the rules. On October 20, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) announced that it would overhaul the rules for nutritional claims on food labels and issue new standards early next year. She has already rebuked General Mills, the maker of Cheerios, a popular breakfast cereal, on the grounds that it has been clinically proven to lower cholesterol. The European Food Safety Authority is also striking, requiring companies to back health and nutritional claims in scientific studies. Hundreds of requests submitted to its scientific panel Functional food sales grew by 10.2% a year between 2006 and 2009, for example, while packaged food sales grew by 6.3%. This is why Nestlé, the world's largest food company, is making a big bet on functional food as a source of future growth. Many in the industry whine that these rules are heavy-handed, given that most of their products are perfectly safe and that some of the health claims go back decades or more. Requiring expensive studies to justify such claims would stifle innovation, they argue, and tilt the playing field against smaller companies, who would be unable to afford them. SURELY, THEY SAY, COMPANIES THAT FIND PROFIT IN ADDING IRON, IODINE, ZINC AND VITAMINS TO THEIR PRODUCTS, OR IN REDUCING LEVELS OF HIGH-FRUCTOSE CORN SYRUP OR SATURATED FAT, SHOULD BE APPLAUDED, NOT DENOUNCED. Many food brands started out as a means of reassuring customers that products are reliable. The desire to protect their brands gives food companies a strong incentive to ensure that their products are safe. But the situation now is that food companies claim that their products provide specific benefits - not just that they are safe to eat. Ordinary people cannot tell whether health claims made by food marketers are scientifically valid, so there is reason for regulatory scrutiny of such claims. What's more, although it's hard to imagine someone being hurt by eating too much cereal or yogurt, say, there is a risk of harm if health claims about functional foods encourage people to view them as substitutes for medications or lifestyle changes they may need. A few servings of veggies will do better than any probiotic yogurt. A lesson from the pharmaceutical industry is that industry-funded studies have a clear tendency to produce results that delight their sponsors. That's why food companies should register all studies and publish those with negative results as well. Clear guidelines about labeling are also important. To its credit, the FDA recently proposed rules that would force food companies to post all the important ingredients in their products on the front of packages, instead of choosing the healthy ones and keeping quiet about the fat, salt and sugar. The industry's claim that more scrutiny will kill innovation is incongruous. Those companies that make misleading claims will suffer; those willing to invest in appropriate scientific studies to back up their breakthroughs will benefit. And in pharmaceuticals, smaller companies seem to be innovating than larger companies. If food companies want to make the kinds of claims about their products that pharmaceutical companies make, they should be prepared to submit to similar scrutiny. Extraordinary claims, after all, require extraordinary evidence.
hypothesis: The food industry welcomes the new requirements from regulators.

premise: Health Intentions A century ago, the leading causes of death in the industrial world were infectious diseases like tuberculosis, influenza and pneumonia. Since the advent of antibiotics, vaccines and public health controls have reduced the impact of infectious diseases. Today, the leading killers are non-infectious diseases mainly related to lifestyle (diet, smoking and physical inactivity). The main causes of death in the United States in 1997 were heart disease, cancer, and stroke. Chronic health problems, such as obesity, non-insulin-dependent diabetes, and osteoporosis, which are not necessarily fatal but nonetheless debilitating, are steadily increasing. It is clear that economic and technical progress is not a guarantee of good health. Humans are qualitatively different from other animals because we manipulate the flow of energy and resources through the ecosystem to our advantage, and consequently to the detriment of other organisms. That's why we compete so successfully with other species. But with this success come some understandable failures, especially in terms of our health. According to physician Boyd Eaton and his fellow anthropologists, despite all our technological wizardry and intellectual advances, modern humans suffer from severe malnutrition. The human body evolved to eat a diet very different from the one most of us consume today. Before the advent of agriculture, about ten thousand years ago, people were hunter-gatherers, food changed with the seasons and climate and everything was obtained from local sources. Our ancestors rarely, if ever, ate cereals or drank the milk of other animals. Although ten thousand years seems a long time ago, 99.99 percent of our genetic material has already been created. We are therefore not well adapted to an agricultural diet of cereals and dairy products. At least 100,000 generations of people have been hunter-gatherers, only 500 generations have depended on agriculture, only ten generations have lived since the beginning of the industrial era and only two generations have grown up with highly processed fast food. Doctors Randolph Ness and George Williams write: Our bodies were designed over the course of millions of years for life spent in small groups hunting and gathering on the plains of Africa. Natural selection wasn't enough to modify our bodies to deal with fatty diets, cars, drugs, artificial lights and central heating. From this mismatch between our design and our environment stem many, perhaps most, preventable modern diseases. Do we really want to eat like prehistoric humans? Surely the cavemen weren't healthy? Was their life hard and short? Probably not. Archaeological evidence suggests that these hunter-gatherer ancestors were strong, robust, and thin with no sign of osteoporosis or arthritis even at more advanced ages. Paleolithic humans ate a diet similar to that of wild chimpanzees and gorillas today: raw fruits, nuts, seeds, vegetation, fresh untreated water, insects, and wild game meat low in saturated fats. Much of their food was harsh and bitter. Most important, like chimpanzees and gorillas, prehistoric humans ate a wide variety of plants estimated at between 100 and 300 different types in a single year. Today, even wealthy health-conscious Westerners rarely consume more than twenty to thirty different species of plants. The early human diet is estimated to have consisted of more than 100 grams of fiber per day. Today the recommended level of 30 grams is rarely achieved by most of us. Humans and lowland gorillas share a particularly similar digestive tract, the colon, but while gorillas draw up to 60 percent of their total energy from fermenting fiber in the colon, modern humans get only about 4 percent. When gorillas are brought into captivity and fed low-fiber diets containing meat and eggs, they suffer from many common human disorders: cardiovascular disease, ulcerative colitis, and high cholesterol levels. Their natural diet, rich in antioxidants and fiber, apparently prevents these diseases in nature, suggesting that such a diet may have serious consequences for our health. Not all agricultural societies have gone the same way. Many traditional farmers maintain the diversity of their diet by eating a variety of herbs and other plant compounds along with meat and grains. The Huasa people of northern Nigeria, for example, traditionally include up to twenty wild herbs in their grain-based soups, and peoples who have become highly dependent on animal products have found ways to counter the negative effects of such nutrition. While Africa's Maasai eat meat and drink blood, milk and animal fat as their only sources of protein, they suffer fewer heart problems than Westerners. One reason is that they always combine their live products with strong and bitter antioxidant herbs. In other words, the Maasai balanced the consumption of oxidizing and antioxidant compounds. According to Timothy Jones, it is not the high consumption of animal fat or the low consumption of antioxidants, that creates so many health problems in industrialized countries; it is the imbalance between the two. Eating the right foods and natural remedies requires sensitivity to subtle changes in appetite. Do I like something sweet, sour, salty, stimulating or soothing? What kind of hunger is that? And after consumption, has the need been achieved? Such subtleties are easily bypassed by artificially created superstimuli in processed foods that leave us unable to choose a healthy diet. We need to listen more carefully to our body's desires and take a deliberate role in maintaining our health before the disease begins.
hypothesis: Gorillas that live in the wild avoid most infectious diseases.

premise: High-tech crime-fighting tool. The crime-fighting technology is becoming more sophisticated and rightly so. The police need to be equipped for the 21st century. The hundreds of thousands of those who are in the database will never be charged with a crime. According to reports, the UK has more than 4 million CCTV (CCTV) cameras. There is an ongoing debate about the effectiveness of CCTV. Some evidence suggests that it is helpful in reducing shoplifting and car crime. It has also been used for the successful identification of terrorists and murderers. However, many argue that better lighting is just as effective at preventing crime and that cameras might root out crime. An internal police report said that only one crime was solved on every 1,000 cameras in London in 2007. In short, there is conflicting evidence about the effectiveness of cameras, so the debate is likely to continue. Professor Mike Peres, who has spent the past decade studying how design can contribute to reducing crime, said that in order for CCTV to have any impact, it must be used in a targeted way. For example, a program in Manchester records every license plate at the entrance to a shopping complex and alerts the police when it is found that one belongs to an untaxed or stolen car. This is an effective example of monitoring, he said. Most programs that simply continually document city centers that are often not observed do not yield results. CCTV can also have the opposite effect from the intended one, in that it gives citizens a false sense of security and encourages them to be careless with property and personal safety. Professor Peres said: “All the evidence suggests that CCTV alone does not have a positive effect on crime reduction and prevention at all. The weight of evidence suggests that investing is pretty much a waste of money unless you have lots of other things in place. 'He believes much of the increase has been driven by the marketing efforts of security companies promoting the crime-reduction benefits of their products. He described this as a “lazy approach to crime prevention” and said authorities should instead focus on how to change the environment to reduce crime. But in reality, that's not what's happening. Instead, police are considering using additional technology. Police forces have recently begun experimenting with cameras in their helmets. The footage will be stored on police computers, along with footage from thousands of CCTV cameras and millions of images from plate recognition cameras that are increasingly used to check drivers. And now a different kind of technology is being introduced. It's called a Microdrone and it's a toy-sized craft that hovers over streets or crowds to film the goings on below. The Microdrone has already been used to monitor rock festivals, but its supplier has also been in discussions to provide it to the Metropolitan Police and Soca, the serious organised crime agency. The drones are small enough for people on the ground to notice them when flying at 350 feet. They contain high-resolution video surveillance equipment and infrared night vision capability, so even in the dark they give their operators a bird's-eye view of locations while being virtually undetectable. The worrying thing is, who will get access to this technology? Merseyside Police are already using two devices as part of a pilot scheme to watch football crowds and city parks looking for anti-social behaviour. It's not just about crime detection: the West Midlands Fire Brigade is to hire a drone, for example, to get a better view of the scenes of fires and floods and to assist in rescue attempts; the Environment Agency is considering their use for monitoring the illegal fly drops and oil spills. The company that manufactures the drone says that it has no intention of licensing the equipment to individuals or private companies, which will hopefully prevent private security companies from getting their hands on them. But what about local authorities? In theory, this technology could be used against drivers. And where will the surveillance society end? There are already plans to introduce 'smart waters' containing a unique DNA code identifier that when sprayed on a suspect will stick to their clothing and skin and allow officers to identify them later. As long as high-tech tools are used in the fight against crime and terrorism, fine. But if it's another weapon to be used to invade our privacy then we don't want it.

Sufferers can fight back by making the most of any winter sunlight and by spending a few hours each day under special full-spectrum lamps. These provide more ultraviolet and blue-green light than regular fluorescent and tungsten bulbs. Some Russian scientists claim that children learn better after being exposed to ultraviolet light. In hot countries, working hours are often arranged so that workers can take a break, or even a siesta, during the hottest part of the day. Scientists are working to discover the links between weather and humans' moods and performance. It is generally believed that the weather is shortened by hot, inclement weather. There is no doubt that crimes against man rise in the summer, when the weather is warmer, and fall in the winter when the weather is colder. Studies in the United States have shown a link between temperature and street riots. The frequency of riots increases dramatically as the weather warms, peaking around 27-30C. But is this effect really due to a change in mood caused by the heat? Some scientists argue that trouble starts more often in hot weather just because there are more people on the street when the weather is good. Psychologists have also investigated how cold affects performance. The researchers compared divers working in freezing cold water at 5 degrees Celsius with others in water at 20 degrees Celsius (roughly the temperature of the swimming pool). The colder water aggravated the divers in simple arithmetic tasks and other mental tasks. But significantly, their performance was impaired once they were put into the cold water - before their bodies had time to cool down. This suggests that the low temperature did not directly slow mental functioning, but the feeling of cold distracted the divers from their tasks. Psychologists have conducted studies that have shown that people become less skeptical and more optimistic when the weather is sunny However, apparently this does not depend only on temperature. An American psychologist examined customers in a temperature-controlled restaurant. They gave bigger tips when the sun was shining and smaller tips when it wasn't, even though the temperature in the restaurant was the same. The relationship between weather and mood is made credible by the evidence for a link between behaviour and the length of daylight hours. This in turn may include the level of a hormone called melatonin, produced in the pineal gland in the brain. The amount of melatonin falls with greater exposure to daylight. Studies show that melatonin plays an important role in the seasonal behavior of some animals. For example, reindeer's food intake increases during the winter, peaking in February/March. It drops again to a low point in May, then rises to a peak in September, before dropping to another minimum in November. These changes appear to be triggered by altered melatonin levels. In the lab, hamsters gain more weight when the nights shorten and their melatonin levels drop. On the other hand, if they are given injections of melatonin, they will stop eating altogether. Time cues provided by the varying day and night lengths seem to trigger changes in animal behaviour - changes needed to cope with the cycle of seasons. People's moods have also been shown to be reactive throughout daylight hours. Skeptics might say that longer sun exposure puts people in a better mood because they associate this with the joyful feelings of holidays and freedom from responsibilities. However, the belief that rain and murky weather make people more unhappy is held up by a study in Belgium, which showed that a telephone counselling service receives more phone calls from people with suicidal feelings when it rains. When there is a thunderstorm brewing, some people complain that the air is heavy and that they feel nervous, funny and funny. They may be reacting to the fact that the air can be slightly positively charged when large thunderclouds produce the intense electric fields that cause lightning flashes. The positive charge raises the levels of serotonin (a chemical involved in sending signals in the nervous system). High levels of serotonin in certain areas of the nervous system make people more active and reactive and possibly more aggressive. When certain winds blow, like the Mistral in southern France and Fohn in southern Germany, mood can be affected - and the number of road accidents rises. This may be significant because the concentration of positively charged particles is greater than usual in these winds. In the UK, 400,000 ionizers are sold every year. These small machines increase the number of negative ions in the air in the room. Many people claim that they feel better in negatively charged air.

premise: How Private Universities Can Help Improve Public Universities There are many wealthy Germans. In 2003, it was estimated that private assets were worth US$5 trillion (US$5.6 trillion), half of which belonged to the richest tenth of the population. But with the money comes stinginess, especially when it comes to providing higher education. America devotes twice as much of its income to universities and colleges than Germany (2.6% of GDP, vs. 1.1%) largely because of higher private spending and larger donations. Next year's figures should be less embarrassing. In November, Klaus Jacobs, a German-born billionaire living abroad, announced that he would donate $200 million to the International University Bremen (IUB) in the largest gift ever. This saved IUB, Germany's only private and international university (with 30 programs and 1,000 students from 86 countries) from bankruptcy. It may also soften the country's still rigid approach to higher education. Higher education in Germany has long been almost entirely a government matter, not least because universities are designed to produce top civil servants. After 1945, the German states were transferred to responsibilities, deciding on details such as examination and admission rules. Reforms in the 1970s made the situation worse by strengthening, in the name of democracy, a layer of bureaucracy in the form of committees of self-government. Tuition fees were abolished in the name of access for all. But the rising number of students then met shrinking budgets, so the reforms returned. Today the number of college dropouts is among the highest in the rich world, making education the third most elite activity: only 22% of German youngsters get a degree, compared with 31% in Britain and 39% in America. German universities are low in the world rankings, so good students often go abroad. In the 1980s, it was hoped that private universities might make a difference. The University of Witten-Hardeka, founded in 1980, was the first. Teaching at IUB, which would soon change its name to Jacobs University, began in 2001. There are now 69 private (non-faith-based) institutions of higher education, compared with 24 a decade ago. There is increasing competition, particularly between business schools. At the same time the states are entering private enterprise into higher education. In 2003 Lower Saxony converted five universities into funds, with more autonomy. Others have gained more control over their budgets. Some states have also begun to charge tuition. And in October the jury declared the winners of the first round of the Excellence Initiative, a national competition between universities for extra cash. However, all this led to only minor improvements. Private universities educate only 3% of Germany's 2 million students, which is perhaps why they have trouble raising money. It also explains why many focus on lucrative subjects, like the Bocerius Law School in Hamburg. Others that depend on public funds. Only recently have wealthy people's funds made large investments, such as in the IUB or the Hertie School of Government in Berlin. Public universities, meanwhile, have not yet been given much autonomy. There is less direct control, but much more managed competition: a new bureaucracy to check the achievement of certain objectives. It is possible to avoid all this through price competition, but tuition, currently 1,000 a year on average, is centrally determined by each state. The Excellence Initiative is only a drop in the bucket. That's why Mr. Jacobs's contribution is important. For the first time, Germany will have a private university worth the name and with a solid economic base (if it continues its academic performance, that is: Mr. Jacobs has promised to donate 15 million a year over the next five years and another 125 million in 2011 to boost endowment, but only if things go well) If that works, other wealthy Germans may be tempted to invest in higher education as well. Nevertheless, private universities will play a small part in German higher education in the foreseeable future. This does not mean that public universities should be privatized. But they need more autonomy and an incentive to compete with each other, whether it's students, staff or donors. With luck, Jacobs' gift will not only make other German billionaires follow suit, but also help persuade countries to bail out their universities.

The Nutritional Information Initiative, launched last year, placed detailed labels on McDonald's packaging with data on calorie, protein, fat, carbohydrate and salt content.
