premise: How are deserts formed? Desert refers to a barren section of land, mainly in arid and semi-arid areas, where there is practically no precipitation, and the environment is hostile to any creature. Deserts have been classified in a number of ways, usually a combination of total precipitation, how many days the rains occur, temperature, humidity, and sometimes other factors. In some places, deserts have clear boundaries marked by rivers, mountains, or other landforms, while in other places, there are no clear boundaries between deserts and other landscape features. In arid areas where there is no vegetation cover protecting the soil, sand and dust storms will often occur. This phenomenon often occurs at the edges of the desert instead of within the deserts, where there are no longer any finer materials left. When a steady wind begins to blow, fine particles on the open ground will begin to vibrate. As the wind lifts, some of the particles are lifted into the air. When they fall to the ground, they hit other particles which will then be ejected into the air in turn, starting a chain reaction. There was enormous publicity about how severe desertification could be, yet the academic circuit never agreed on the causes of desertification. A common misunderstanding is that lack of precipitation causes desertification even the soil in some barren areas will soon recover after rain falls. In fact, more often than not, human activities are responsible for desertification. It is possible that the explosion in world population, especially in developing countries, is the main cause of soil degradation and desertification. As the population became denser, crop growth shifted to increasingly dry areas. It is particularly possible for these regions to go through periods of severe drought, which explains why crop failures are common. Growing most crops requires the natural vegetation cover to be removed first; when crop failures occur, large areas of land are devoid of plant cover and are therefore susceptible to wind and water erosion. During the 1990s, land areas underwent a population growth of 18.5%, mainly in very poor developing countries. Livestock breeding in semi-arid areas accelerates soil erosion and becomes one of the reasons for the advancement of desertification. In such areas where vegetation is dominated by grasses, animal husbandry is a key economic activity. Weeds are necessary for anchoring barren topsoil in a dry area. For centuries, nomads grazed their flocks and herds wherever grassland could be found, and oases offered opportunities for a more settled way of life. For some nomads, wherever they pass, the desert follows. Trees are of great importance when it comes to maintaining topsoil and slowing wind speed. In many Asian countries, firewood is the main fuel used for cooking and heating, prompting uncontrolled deforestation in dryland ecosystems. When too many trees are cut down, wind storms and dust storms tend to occur. What's worse, even conflicts and political wars can also contribute to desertification. To escape the invading enemies, the refugees will relocate entirely to some of the most vulnerable ecosystems on Earth. They bring with them their cultivation traditions, which may not be the right kind of practice for their new settlement. In the 20th century, in one of the countries of America there was a large part of farmland that turned into a desert. Since then, actions have been enforced so that such a phenomenon of desertification does not occur again. To prevent the reoccurrence of desertification, people are encouraged to find other livelihoods that do not rely on traditional land uses, that are not equally demanding on local lands and natural resources, but can still generate a sustainable income. Such livelihoods include, among other things, dry aquaculture for raising fish, crustaceans and industrial compounds derived from microalgae, greenhouse agriculture, and tourism-related activities. Another way to prevent the recurrence of desertification is to improve the economic prospects for life in city centers and places outside dry lands. Changing the general economic and institutional structures that generate new opportunities for people to support themselves will alleviate the current pressures accompanying desertification processes. In today's society, new technologies serve as a method of solving the problems that desertification brings. premise: How stores can exploit people's herd mentality to increase sales A trip to the supermarket may not seem like an exercise in psychological fightingbut it is. Shopkeepers know that filling a store with the scent of fresh bread makes people feel hungry and persuades them to buy more food than they intended. Inventing the most expensive products at eye level makes them sell faster than cheaper but less visible competitors. Now researchers are investigating how swarm intelligence (i.e. how ants, bees, or any social animal, including humans, behave in crowds) can be used to influence what people buy. At a recent conference on the simulation of adaptive behavior in Rome, Zishan-ul-Hasan Osmani, a computer scientist from the Florida Institute of Technology, described a new way to boost impulse buying through this phenomenon. Supermarkets are already encouraging shoppers to buy things they didn't realise they wanted: for example, by putting everyday items like milk and eggs at the back of the store, which forces shoppers to flick past other enticing products to reach them. Mr. Osmani and Ronaldo Menezes, also of the Florida Institute of Technology, set out to amplify this tendency to buy more by playing on the herd instinct. The idea is that if a particular product is perceived as popular, buyers are likely to choose it as well. The challenge is to inform customers about what others are buying. Enter smart cart technology. In Mr. Osmani's supermarket every product has a radio frequency identification tag, a sort of barcode that uses radio waves to transmit information, and each cart has a scanner that reads that information and transmits it to a central computer. When a customer walks past a merchandise shelf, a screen on the shelf tells him how many people currently in the store have chosen that particular product. If the number is high, he is more likely to choose it too. Mr Osmani's swarm movements model appeals to supermarkets because it increases sales without the need to give people discounts. And it gives buyers the satisfaction of knowing that they bought the right product, that is, the one that everyone bought. The model has not yet been widely tested in the real world, mainly because radio frequency identification technology is new and has only been experimentally installed in some supermarkets. But Mr Usmani says that both Wal-Mart in America and Tesco in Britain are interested in his work, and testing will begin in the spring. Other recent research on the power of social influence suggests that it is indeed possible to boost sales in this way. Matthew Slagnik of Columbia University in New York and his colleagues described the creation of an artificial music market in which about 14,000 people downloaded previously unknown songs. The researchers found that when people could see the songs ranked by how many times they were downloaded, they tracked the audience. When the songs were not ordered by rank, but were shown the number of times they were downloaded, the effect of social influence was still there but was less pronounced. People therefore follow the herd when it is easy for them to do so. In Japan a chain of convenience stores called Ranking RanQueen orders its products according to sales data from department stores and research companies. The stores sell only the most popular items in each product category, and the rating is updated weekly. Icosystem, a company in Cambridge, Massachusetts, also aims to take advantage of social media knowledge to improve sales. And the psychology that works in physical stores is just as strong online. Online retailers like Amazon are adept at telling shoppers which products are popular with like-minded consumers. Even in the privacy of your own home, you can still be part of the swarm.

premise: Humans have hunted whales for thousands of years, but in the 18th and 19th centuries whaling became an important industry, because of high demand for whale oil. Even after industrialization, whaling continued at unsustainable levels and in the mid-twentieth century whale populations declined greatly. The International Whaling Commission (IWC) was established in 1946 to ensure the conservation of whales and oversee the development of the whaling industry. In 1986, the IWC imposed a moratorium on commercial whaling to prevent the extinction of endangered whale species. As a result of the ban, whale stocks have recovered and therefore some countries support lifting the restrictions. Through loopholes in the moratorium, Japan, Norway and Iceland currently engage in commercial whaling and vigorously defend the practice as part of their cultural heritage. However, anti-whaling activists oppose whaling on ethical grounds. They argue that whales remain vulnerable, and that whales' intelligence gives them intrinsic value. The whaling debate is so intense that the IWC, which requires a 75% vote to overturn the ban, has come to a standstill. Even within countries that support a return to commercial whaling the issue is divisive. Not only has demand for whale meat declined, whale watching has become a popular tourist activity, and ending restrictions could threaten this lucrative industry.
hypothesis: Industrialization led to a reduction in demand for whale oil in the twentieth century.

It is held in a reservoir or lake behind a dam, and the force of water released from the reservoir through the dam rotates the turbine blades. premise: Hypnosis Is it real or just a circus trick? Hypnosis has been proven through several strictly controlled studies to reduce pain, control blood pressure, and even make warts disappear. But because very few studies have attempted to define the processes involved in practice, most scientists are skeptical of its power and uses. This scepticism prompted David Spiegel, professor of psychiatry at Stanford University School of Medicine, USA, and other researchers to closely examine what happens in the brain during hypnosis. Among scholars there are two schools of thought. One argues that hypnosis fundamentally changes the state of mind of the subjects: they go into a trance, which produces changes in brain activity. The other believes that hypnosis is simply a matter of hint and relaxation. Spiegel belongs to the First School and over the years has had a debate with two scientists on the other side, Irving Kirsch, a psychologist at the University of Connecticut, and Steven Coslin, a Harvard professor. Kirsch often uses hypnosis in his practice and does not deny that it can be effective. With hypnosis you do put people into changing situations, he says. But you don't need a trance to do that. To illustrate the point, Kirsch demonstrates how a subject holding a small object on a chain can cause it to swing in any direction by mere suggestion, with the chain responding to minute movements in the tiny finger muscles. You don't have to go into a trance for your subconscious and your body to act on suggestion, Kirsch says. The reaction is the result of your focus on moving the chain in a certain direction. Spiegel disagrees. One of his best-known studies found that when subjects were hypnotized and given suggestions their brainwave patterns changed, indicating that they had entered a trance. In one of his studies, people under hypnosis were told that their arms were numb, and then received mild electric shocks in the wrists. They did not flinch or react in any way, and their brain waves resembled those of people who had experienced a much weaker shock. In Kirsch's eyes this was not yet enough to prove the power of transatlantic, but Steven Coslin was ready to be convinced. Many external factors could have been responsible for the change in the subjects' mental state, but Coslin wondered, is something really going on in the brain? To find this out, Spiegel and Coslin decided to collaborate on a study that focuses on a part of the brain that is well understood: the circuit that is found to process the perception of color. Spiegel and Coslin wanted to test whether the subjects could activate the circuit by simulating color while under hypnosis. They selected eight people for an experiment conducted at Massachusetts General Hospital. Subjects were put into a scanner and shown a slide with coloured rectangles while their brain activity was mapped. Then they were shown a black and white slide and told to imagine that it had color. Both tasks were repeated under hypnosis. The results were striking. When the subjects actually saw the colored rectangles, the circle lit up on both sides of the brain; when they only had to visualize the color, the circle lit up only in the right hemisphere. In hypnosis, however, both sides of the brain became active, just as in normal vision; the imagination seemed to take on a hallucinogenic quality. After the experiment, Coslin was forced to admit, I am absolutely convinced now that hypnosis can amplify what mental imagery does. But Kirsch remains skeptical, saying, the experiments prove that people experience the effects of hypnotic suggestion but do not prove they enter a trance. He also claimed that subjects were told to see the card in color when they were hypnotized, but only imagine it in color when they were not. You're told to pretend you're having a different experience than offering to experience the experience. Spiegel, on the other hand, is first of all a clinician and another scientist. premise: Is there anyone out there? The search for extraterrestrial intelligence. The question of whether we are alone in the universe has haunted humanity for centuries, but now we may be on the verge of answering that question, as we search for radio signals from other intelligent cultures. This search, often known by the acronym SETI (Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence), is a difficult search. Although groups around the world have searched intermittently for three decades, it is only now that we have reached the level of technology where we can make a determined attempt to search all nearby stars for any sign of life. The main reason for the search is basic curiosity isthe same curiosity about the natural world that drives all pure science. We want to know if we are alone in the universe. We want to know if life evolves naturally if given the right conditions, or whether there is something very special about Earth that has nurtured the variety of life forms we see around us on the planet. The simple detection of a radio signal would suffice to answer the most basic question of all. In this sense, SETI is another cog in the mechanism of pure science that continually pushes the horizon of our knowledge. However, there are other reasons to be interested in whether life exists elsewhere. For example, we've had a civilization on Earth for perhaps only a few thousand years, and the threats of nuclear war and pollution in recent decades have told us that our survival may be tenuous. Will we last another two thousand years or will we wipe ourselves out? Since the lifetime of a planet like ours is several billion years, we can expect that if other civilizations did survive in our galaxy, their age would range from zero to several billion years. Thus, every other civilization we hear of may be much older, on average, than we are. The very existence of such a civilization would tell us that long-term survival is possible, and gives us some reason for optimism. It is even possible that the older civilization might pass on the benefits of its experience in dealing with survival threats such as nuclear war and global pollution, and other threats we have yet to discover. In discussing whether we are alone, most SETI scientists adopt two ground rules. First, UFOs (unidentified flying objects) are usually ignored because most scientists do not consider the evidence for them strong enough to bear serious consideration (though it is also important to keep an open mind in case truly compelling evidence emerges in the future). Secondly, we make a very conservative assumption that we are looking for a life form that is quite similar to us, because if it is radically different from us we may not recognize it as a life form, other than whether we are able to communicate with it. In other words, the life form we seek may well have two green heads and seven fingers, but it will still resemble us in that it has to communicate with its friends, take an interest in the universe, live on a planet orbiting a star like our sun, and, perhaps most limitedly, have chemistry, like us, based on carbon and water. Even when we make these assumptions, our understanding of other life forms is still very limited. We don't even know, for example, how many stars have planets, and we certainly don't know how likely life is to arise naturally, given the right conditions. However, when we look at the 100 billion stars in our galaxy (the Milky Way), and the 100 billion galaxies in the observable universe, it seems inconceivable that at least one of these planets does not have a life form; in fact, the most educated guess we can make, using what little we know about the conditions for carbon-based life, leads us to estimate that perhaps one in 100,000 stars may have a life-bearing planet orbiting it. That means our closest neighbors are maybe 100 light years away, which is almost the next door in astronomical terms. An alien civilization can choose many different ways of sending information across the galaxy, but many of them require too much energy, or they are severely weakened while traversing the vast distances across the galaxy. It turns out that for a given amount of transmitted power, radio waves in the 1000 to 3000 MHz frequency range travel the greatest distance, so all searches so far have concentrated on searching for radio waves in this frequency range. To date, several searches have been conducted by various groups around the world, including Australian searches using the Radio Telescope in Parks, New South Wales. So far there have been no revelations from some of the hundreds of stars being searched. THE SCOPE OF SEARCHES HAS INCREASED DRAMATICALLY SINCE 1992, WHEN THE U.S. CONGRESS VOTED NASA $10 MILLION A YEAR FOR TEN YEARS TO CONDUCT, A THOROUGH SEARCH FOR LIFE OFF EARTH. Much of the money in this project is invested in developing the special hardware needed to search for many frequencies at once. The project consists of two parts. Part one is a targeted search using the world's largest radio telescopes, the American-operated telescope in Arecibo, Puerto Rico, and the French telescope at Nancy in France. This part of the project is looking for the nearest 1000 likely stars with high sensitivity to signals at a frequency photographed 1000 to 3000 MHz. The second part of the project is an unintended search that tracks all of space at a lower sensitivity, using the smaller antennas of NASA's Deep Space Network. There is considerable debate about how we should react if we detect a signal from an alien civilization. Everyone agrees that we shouldn't respond right away. Apart from the impracticality of sending a reply over such great distances at short notice, it raises a host of ethical questions that the global community will have to address before any reply can be sent. Would the human race face the culture shock if faced with a superior and much older civilization? Fortunately, there is no urgency in this regard. The stars being tested are hundreds of light years away, so it takes hundreds of years for their signal to reach us, and another few hundred years for our answer to reach them. If so, it is immaterial whether there will be a delay of a few years, or decades, while the human race debates whether to reply, and perhaps formulates an answer carefully.
hypothesis: Foreign cultures may help the human race overcome serious problems.

The question of whether we are alone in the universe has haunted humanity for centuries, but now we may be on the verge of answering that question, as we search for radio signals from other intelligent cultures. This search, often known by the acronym SETI (Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence), is a difficult search. Although groups around the world have searched intermittently for three decades, it is only now that we have reached the level of technology where we can make a determined attempt to search all nearby stars for any sign of life. The main reason for the search is basic curiosity isthe same curiosity about the natural world that drives all pure science. We want to know if we are alone in the universe. We want to know if life evolves naturally if given the right conditions, or whether there is something very special about Earth that has nurtured the variety of life forms we see around us on the planet. The simple detection of a radio signal would suffice to answer the most basic question of all. In this sense, SETI is another cog in the mechanism of pure science that continually pushes the horizon of our knowledge. However, there are other reasons to be interested in whether life exists elsewhere. For example, we've had a civilization on Earth for perhaps only a few thousand years, and the threats of nuclear war and pollution in recent decades have told us that our survival may be tenuous. Will we last another two thousand years or will we wipe ourselves out? Since the lifetime of a planet like ours is several billion years, we can expect that if other civilizations did survive in our galaxy, their age would range from zero to several billion years. Thus, every other civilization we hear of may be much older, on average, than we are. The very existence of such a civilization would tell us that long-term survival is possible, and gives us some reason for optimism. It is even possible that the older civilization might pass on the benefits of its experience in dealing with survival threats such as nuclear war and global pollution, and other threats we have yet to discover. In discussing whether we are alone, most SETI scientists adopt two ground rules. First, UFOs (unidentified flying objects) are usually ignored because most scientists do not consider the evidence for them strong enough to bear serious consideration (though it is also important to keep an open mind in case truly compelling evidence emerges in the future). Secondly, we make a very conservative assumption that we are looking for a life form that is quite similar to us, because if it is radically different from us we may not recognize it as a life form, other than whether we are able to communicate with it. In other words, the life form we seek may well have two green heads and seven fingers, but it will still resemble us in that it has to communicate with its friends, take an interest in the universe, live on a planet orbiting a star like our sun, and, perhaps most limitedly, have chemistry, like us, based on carbon and water. Even when we make these assumptions, our understanding of other life forms is still very limited. We don't even know, for example, how many stars have planets, and we certainly don't know how likely life is to arise naturally, given the right conditions. However, when we look at the 100 billion stars in our galaxy (the Milky Way), and the 100 billion galaxies in the observable universe, it seems inconceivable that at least one of these planets does not have a life form; in fact, the most educated guess we can make, using what little we know about the conditions for carbon-based life, leads us to estimate that perhaps one in 100,000 stars may have a life-bearing planet orbiting it. That means our closest neighbors are maybe 100 light years away, which is almost the next door in astronomical terms. An alien civilization can choose many different ways of sending information across the galaxy, but many of them require too much energy, or they are severely weakened while traversing the vast distances across the galaxy. It turns out that for a given amount of transmitted power, radio waves in the 1000 to 3000 MHz frequency range travel the greatest distance, so all searches so far have concentrated on searching for radio waves in this frequency range. To date, several searches have been conducted by various groups around the world, including Australian searches using the Radio Telescope in Parks, New South Wales. So far there have been no revelations from some of the hundreds of stars being searched. THE SCOPE OF SEARCHES HAS INCREASED DRAMATICALLY SINCE 1992, WHEN THE U.S. CONGRESS VOTED NASA $10 MILLION A YEAR FOR TEN YEARS TO CONDUCT, A THOROUGH SEARCH FOR LIFE OFF EARTH. Much of the money in this project is invested in developing the special hardware needed to search for many frequencies at once. The project consists of two parts. Part one is a targeted search using the world's largest radio telescopes, the American-operated telescope in Arecibo, Puerto Rico, and the French telescope at Nancy in France. This part of the project is looking for the nearest 1000 likely stars with high sensitivity to signals at a frequency photographed 1000 to 3000 MHz. The second part of the project is an unintended search that tracks all of space at a lower sensitivity, using the smaller antennas of NASA's Deep Space Network. There is considerable debate about how we should react if we detect a signal from an alien civilization. Everyone agrees that we shouldn't respond right away. Apart from the impracticality of sending a reply over such great distances at short notice, it raises a host of ethical questions that the global community will have to address before any reply can be sent. Would the human race face the culture shock if faced with a superior and much older civilization? Fortunately, there is no urgency in this regard. The stars being tested are hundreds of light years away, so it takes hundreds of years for their signal to reach us, and another few hundred years for our answer to reach them. If so, it is immaterial whether there will be a delay of a few years, or decades, while the human race debates whether to reply, and perhaps formulates an answer carefully.

premise: His ecological logic If there were awards for tourism phrases that have been hijacked, diluted and misused then eco-tourism would have won the top prize. The term first emerged in the early 1980s reflecting an increase in environmental awareness and an understanding on the part of tour operators that many travellers wanted to believe that their presence abroad would not have a negative impact. It quickly became the hottest marketing tag a holiday could carry. Nowadays the eco-tourism label is used to cover everything from a two-week tour living with remote Indonesian tribes, to a one-hour speedboat trip through an Australian channel. In fact, any tour that involves cultural interaction, natural beauty spots, wildlife or a little soft adventure may be included in the dense eco-tourism folder. Certainly the original motivations behind the movement were honourable attempts to provide a way for those who care to make informed choices, but the lack of regulations and industry standard definition have left many travellers lost in the eco-tourism jungle. It is easier to understand why the eco-tourism market has become so crowded when we look at its broader role in the global economy. According to World Tourism Organization figures, ecotourism is worth $20 billion a year and accounts for a fifth of all international tourism. Add to this an annual growth rate of around five per cent and the pressure on many operators, both in developed and developing countries, to jump on the accelerating bandwagon is compelling. Without any widely recognized certification system, the consumer is left to question the credentials of an operator himself. It is a time-consuming process and many travelers usually take the operators' claims at face value, which only adds to the proliferation of fake eco-trips. However, there are a number of simple questions that will provide appropriate evidence of the company's commitment to minimising its impact on the environment and maximising the benefits to the local community of the tourist areas. For example, does the company use recycled or sustainable materials harvested locally to build its tourism assets? Do they pay fair wages to all employees? Do they offer employee training? It is common for city entrepreneurs to have tour companies in rural areas, which could mean that the money you pay ends up in the city and not in the community visited. By taking some extra time to explore the eco-tourism options, not only can your custom be guided to worthy operators, but you'll often find that the experience they offer is much more rewarding. The ecotourism business is still badly in need of a shake-up and a standardised approach. There are several organizations that have sprung up in the last ten years or so that try to educate travelers and operators about the benefits of responsible eco-tourism. The Ecological Tourism Association (TES), founded in 1990, is a nonprofit organization of travel industry, conservationists, and ecological professionals, whose goal is to make eco-tourism a true tool for conservation and sustainable development. Helping create structured economic value in wilderness environments and threatened cultures has arguably been one of the most notable achievements of the eco-tourism movements. TES organizes an annual initiative to further aid the development of the eco-tourism industry. This year it is launching Choosing Your Travel Makes a Difference, an educational campaign aimed at helping consumers understand the potential positive and negative impacts of their travel decisions. TES also offers guidelines for choosing an eco-trip and has established a register of approved eco-tourism operators around the world. A leading ecotourism operator in the UK is Tribes, which won in 1999 the Tourism Concern Award and the Independent Travellers' World Award for Most Responsible Tourism Operator. Amanda Marks, owner and manager of Tribes, believes the eco-tourism industry still has a way to go to put her house in order. So far, no ecotourism certification program has really worked, mainly because there has been no systematic way to check that certified companies are indeed complying with the code of practice. Amanda believes the most promising system is the recently relaunched Green Globe 21 program. The Green Globe 21 award is based on the sustainable development standards contained in Agenda 21 from the 1992 Earth Summit and was originally coordinated by the World Travel and Tourism Council (WTTC). The program is now an independent concern, though the WTTC still supports it. Until recently, tourism companies became charters and could use the Green Globe logo only for paying an annual retainer, hardly an appropriate standard. However, in November 1999 Green Globe 21 introduced an annual, independent inspection of operators wishing to use the logo. Miriam Keane, of Green Globe 21 marketing development, explains that current and new branches will now have one year to ensure that their operations meet Agenda 21 standards. If they fail the first inspection, they can only reapply once. The testing process is not a cheap option, especially for large companies, but the benefits of green globe status and the potential savings in operating costs that compliance with standards can bring should be significant. We have joint ventures with organisations around the world, including Australia and the Caribbean, that will allow us to effectively audit all partner operators,” says Miriam. The program also allows target communities to be certified on Green Globe 21. For a relatively new industry it is no surprise that ecotourism has gone through teething pains. However, there are signs that things are changing for the better. With a committed and unified approach by the travel industry, local communities, travelers and environmental experts can make eco-tourism a badge to be proud of and believe in.
hypothesis: Tourists have learned to carry out investigations on tour operators before using them.

Cans of moufanned worms in brine, or in tomato or chilli sauce are common in supermarkets. They can be eaten straight from the can. Fried into crispy snacks, or added as an ingredient to conventional dishes. Then comes the termite paste (you guessed it), a black smear with the look, smell and consistency, of an industrial solvent. Iron. Very rich. Then come the sperm-like larvae of some form of moth. Here, Peter hesitates. He finally comes out with suspicion, you get used to it. WHEN I NOD SKEPTICALLY, HE COMES OUT WITH A MUCH SAFER ONE, IN FACT, YOU EAT BUGS ALREADY, ALL THE TIME. premise: If it wasn't for nicotine, people wouldn't smoke tobacco. Why? Because of the more than 4000 chemicals in tobacco smoke, nicotine is the main one that acts on the brain, altering people's moods, appetite and alertness in ways they find pleasant and beneficial. Unfortunately, as you know, nicotine has a dark side: it is highly addictive. Once smokers get addicted to it, they must fix it regularly, sometimes several dozen times a day. Cigarette smoke contains 43 known carcinogens, which means long-term smoking can amount to a death sentence. In the United States alone, 420,000 Americans die each year from tobacco-related diseases. Breaking nicotine addiction is not easy. Each year, nearly 35 million people make a concerted effort to quit smoking. Unfortunately, less than 7% manage to abstain for more than a year; most start smoking again within days. SO WHAT IS NICOTINE AND HOW DOES IT IMPART ITSELF TO THE SMOKERS' BRAIN AND TO THE VERY BEING? The nicotine found in tobacco is a potent drug and smokers, and even some scientists, say it offers certain benefits. One is to improve performance. One study found that nonsmokers who received a nicotine dose typed about 5 percent faster than without it. To more or less extent, users also say that nicotine helps them maintain concentration, reduce anxiety, relieve pain and even dampen their appetite (thus helping with weight control). Unfortunately, nicotine can also produce harmful effects beyond addiction. In high doses, as is achieved from tobacco products, it can cause high blood pressure, distress in the respiratory and digestive systems, and increased susceptibility to seizures and hypothermia. First isolated as a compound in 1828, in its pure form nicotine is a clear liquid that turns brown when burned and smells like tobacco when exposed to air. It is found in several species of plants, including tobacco and, perhaps surprisingly, in tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplants (though in exceptionally low amounts that are not pharmacologically significant to humans). Simple as it may seem, the cigarette is a highly engineered nicotine delivery device. For example, when tobacco researchers discovered that much of the nicotine in a cigarette is not released when burned but remains chemically bound within the tobacco leaf, they began adding substances like ammonia to cigarette tobacco to release more nicotine. Ammonia helps keep nicotine in its basic form, which is more easily evaporated by the intense heat of the burning cigarette than the acidic form. Most cigarettes for sale in the U.S. currently contain 10 milligrams or more of nicotine. By inhaling smoke from a lit cigarette, the average smoker takes 1 or 2 milligrams of vaporized nicotine per cigarette. Today we know that only a tiny amount of nicotine is needed to fuel addiction. Studies show that manufacturers would need to reduce nicotine levels in a typical cigarette by 95% to prevent its power from becoming addictive. When a smoker puffs on a lit cigarette, smoke, including vaporized nicotine, is drawn into the mouth. The skin and oral mucosa immediately absorb a little nicotine, but the rest flows straight down to the lungs, where it easily diffuses into the blood vessels lining the walls of the lung. The blood vessels carry the nicotine to the heart, then pump it directly to the brain. While most of the effects a smoker is looking for occur in the brain, the heart also gets a hit. Studies have shown that a smoker of a first cigarette a day can raise his heart rate by 10 to 20 beats per minute. Scientists have discovered that a smoked substance reaches the brain faster than one that is swallowed, shaken (like powdered cocaine) or even injected. Indeed, a nicotine molecule inhaled in smoke will reach the brain within 10 seconds. Nicotine passes through blood vessels, which branch into capillaries inside the brain. Capillaries usually carry nutrients but they also easily contain nicotine molecules. Once inside the brain, nicotine, like most addictive drugs, triggers the release of chemicals associated with euphoria and pleasure. Just as it moves quickly from the lungs into the bloodstream, nicotine also diffuses easily through the walls of capillaries. It then migrates into the cavities surrounding ganglion cells and neurons that transmit nerve impulses throughout the nervous system. These impulses are the basis of our thoughts, feelings, and moods. To transmit nerve impulses to its neighbor, a neuron releases chemical messengers called neurotransmitters. Like nicotine molecules, the neurotransmitters drift into what is known as the synaptic space between neurons, ready to attach to the receiving neuron and thus transmit a chemical message that triggers an electrical impulse. The neurotransmitters bind to receptors on the surface of the receiving neuron. This opens channels in the cell surface through which ions, or charged atoms, of sodium enter. This creates a current across the membrane of the receiving cell, which completes the delivery of the message. Nicotine, a perfect mimic, competes with neurotransmitters to bind to receptors. It is conductive and like the vanquished chemical, opens ion channels that allow sodium ions to enter the cell. But there's a lot more nicotine around than the original transmitter, so a much larger current spreads across the membrane. This greater current causes increased electrical impulses to travel along certain neurons. With repeated smoking, the neurons adapt to this increased electrical activity, and the smoker becomes dependent on nicotine.
hypothesis: Despite the difficulties, according to the text more than thirty-five million people a year give up smoking.

In high doses, as is achieved from tobacco products, it can cause high blood pressure, distress in the respiratory and digestive systems, and increased susceptibility to seizures and hypothermia. Life itself was a constant, punishing search for food: some families raised manioc and other starchy crops in small garden plots evacuated from the forest, while the tribesmen scoured the land for small hunts and promising fish holes. When local resources were depleted, the tribe moved on. As for technology, Holmberg noted, the Siriono\ may be classified among the most handicapped peoples in the world\. Apart from bows, arrows, and crude digging sticks, the only tools Siriono seemed to have were two machetes worn the size of pocket knives. Although the lives of the Sirionos changed in the decades that passed, their image as Stone Age relics persisted. Indeed, in many ways the Sirionos embody the popular conception of life in Amazonia. To casual observers, as well as to influential naturalists and regional planners, the lush forests of Amazonia seem ageless, unconquerable, a habitat utterly inhospitable to human civilization. The apparent simplicity of Indian ways of life was thought to be an evolutionary adaptation to forest ecology, living proof that Amazonia could not - and could not - sustain a more complex society. Archaeological traces of much more elaborate civilizations have been dismissed as the ruins of invaders from outside the region, abandoned to decay in the uncompromising tropical environment. The popular perception of Amazonia and its indigenous inhabitants would be highly consequential if it were correct. But the human history of Amazonia in the last 11,000 years exposes this perception as a myth. premise: In November 1936, Crystal Palace, which had been moved since the Great Exhibition of 1851 to Sydenham Hill, burned to the ground. The building demolished in 1936 was very different from the one erected in Hyde Park for the Great Exhibition over eighty years earlier. Although all building materials were moved south to London after the six months of the exhibition, what was erected on Sydenham Hill was really a Beaux Arts form, rather than the greenhouse-like construction designed by Chatsworth House gardener Joseph Paxton. Some of the same features - public toilets, for example - that first appeared in the Crystal Palace during the Great Exhibition were also installed at the new site. But, the structure was modified and enlarged, so much so that it exceeded the boundaries of the new park intended for its construction. Moving Crystal Palace was a costly feat, and cost 1.3 million (96.5 million today), more than a million more than was required to build the original structure. The move put Crystal Palace into debt from which it never recovered. Although two separate railway stations were built to serve the permanent exhibition, in the 1890s the structure deteriorated badly. The palace was used in World War I as a naval training institution and was later the site of the First Imperial War Museum. Buckland's leadership in the 1920s and 1930s improved the gardens and returned visitors to the palace for regular exhibitions and fireworks shows, but a fire in 1936 prevented it from fully realising the palace's old glory. Nevertheless, as Buckland predicted, Crystal Palace are not forgotten today. In fact, the area of Peng Common and Sydenham Hill, where the structure was moved over 150 years ago, is now known as Crystal Palace.
hypothesis: A fireworks show started the fire that destroyed Crystal Palace.

premise: In casual language, the terms theory and model are often used interchangeably. Technically there is an important difference. Theories provide a general framework, but because of the generality of the specification, a theory cannot be shown to be useful or useless until it is fully defined in the form of a model. A model, on the other hand, needs to be formulated in a definition within the concepts, along with a set of assumptions about the concepts and the relationships between them. The appropriateness of a model should then be assessed with respect to a particular set of test data. The assessment may be made by conducting a properly designed set of empirical investigations, by rationally testing the model's assumptions with respect to the test data, or ideally both. In the strict sense, all models provide incomplete representations of the data to which they fit. Thus the significant question is not whether a model is correct or incorrect, but whether the model fits the data well enough to be useful in guiding the process. Statistical evidence and judgment play important roles in answering this question.
hypothesis: A model can exist in the absence of a theory.

premise: In ecological biology, a keystone species is a species of organism that exerts a disproportionately large influence on its environment, relative to its size and influence. The term keystone species was coined in 1969 by zoologist Robert Payne with the aim of explaining the relationship between a starfish species and its native environment. The classic example of a keystone species is the sea otter. Sea otters feed on sea urchins and other seaweed predators, maintaining their numbers and preventing them from damaging underwater kelp forests. Areas in the North Pacific devoid of sea otters are most often hedgehog averse, areas with large numbers of sea urchins, but few to no algae. The sea otter therefore protects seaweed forests from overgrazing by sea urchins, and maintains the ecological balance of their native environment.
hypothesis: Sea urchins are an example of a keystone species.
label: n

premise: In finance, due diligence may refer to the research and analysis process that occurs prior to an investment, takeover or business partnership. The potential investor typically uses internal resources or hires a consulting firm, specializing in due diligence and corporate investigations, to investigate the background of the company and the managers of the target company. The due diligence task typically includes reviewing press and SEC filings, reviewing regulatory and licensing issues, identifying liens and judgments, and disclosing civil and criminal litigation matters. Sophisticated investigators will also look for conflicts of interest, insider trading and press and public records identifying problems that may have occurred under the executives' supervision. The results of the investigation may be prepared in a due diligence report that the investor uses to understand the risks involved in the investment. premise: In law, trespass can be: the criminal act of entering someone else's land or property without the permission of the owner or lessee; it is also a civil legal tort that may constitute a valid cause of action for requesting judicial assistance and possibly damages through prosecution. In some jurisdictions trespass is an offence or offence covered by criminal law. In other jurisdictions, it is not considered a crime or punishment in nature, property is protected from trespass under civil law and privacy acts. In England and Wales, despite the prevalence of notices stating that trespassers will be prosecuted, unless trespassing is aggravated in some way, it will only be a civil error. Although criminal and civil trespass laws vary from jurisdiction to jurisdiction, most have the following aspects in common: Property owners and their agents (e.g., security guards) may use only reasonable force to protect their property. For example, placing bobby traps on a property to injure retainers or shooting at trespassers are generally strictly prohibited except in extreme circumstances. Not all people seeking access to property are trespassers. The law recognizes the rights of persons who have received explicit permission to be in the property (licensees) and persons who have a legal right to be in the property (invitees) not to be treated as trespassers. For example, a meter reader at a property for reading the meter is welcome, as is a traveling salesman, or a police officer seeking to execute a warrant.
hypothesis: Serious trespass is a civil error and offenders cannot be prosecuted.

premise: Insects, birds, and fish tend to be the creatures that humans feel most distant from. Unlike many mammals they do not engage in human-like behavior. Nor does the manner in which they swarm or flock together usually garners good press coverage: pacing like working ants may be a common visualization for city commuters, but it's a daunting image, not a positive one. But a new school of scientific theory suggests these swarms may have a lot to teach us. American writer Peter Miller explains, “I used to think that individual ants knew where they were going, and what they were supposed to do when they got there. But Deborah Gordon, a biologist from Stanford University, showed me that nothing an ant does makes sense except in terms of the colony as a whole. Which makes you wonder if, as individuals, we don't serve a similar role for the companies we work for or the communities we live in. Ants are not intelligent in and of themselves. However, as a colony, they make wise decisions. And, as Gordon discovered in the course of her research, there is no ant that makes decisions or gives orders. Take food collection, for example. No ant decides, there is a lot of food around today; a lot of ants have to go out to collect it. Instead, some forage ants emerge, and once they find food, they pick it up and return to the nest. At the entrance, they walk past reserve towers and send an exit signal. The faster the cultivators return, the more food there is and the rest of the foragers come out faster, until gradually the amount of food returned decreases. An organic calculation was made to answer the question, how many food growers does the colony need today? And if something goes wrong in a hungry lizard hanging around for an ant snack, for example, then a rush of ants returning without food sends waiting reserves a don't go out signal. But can such distributed control work in a human organization? Miller visited a Texas gas company that had successfully implemented formulas based on ant colony behavior to streamline its factories and route its trucks. He explains, if ant colonies created a reliable way to identify the best routes between the nest and their food sources, company executives thought, why not take advantage of that knowledge? So they invented a computer model, based on the principles of self-organization of an ant colony. Data is fed into the model about deliveries that need to be made the next day, as well as things like weather conditions, and it generates a simulation that determines the best route for the delivery trucks. Miller explains that he first realized the effect that swarm behavior could have on humans when he read a study on honey bees by Tom Seeley, a biologist at Cornell University. The honey bees choose as a group which new nest to move to. First, viewers fly in to explore multiple sites. When they come back they do a pitching dance to their place, and then other spectators will fly in and explore it. Many bees come out, but no one tries to compare all the sites. Each reports only one. The more they liked their nest, the more vigorous and longer their pitching dance and bees would choose to visit it. Gradually the volume of bees accumulates towards one site; this is a system that ensures that the best snowballs are supported on the site and the decision is made in the most democratic way. Humans, too, can make smart decisions using a variety of knowledge and a bit of friendly competition. 'The best example of shared decision-making that I witnessed during my research was a town meeting I attended in Vermont, where citizens met face-to-face to discuss their annual budget, 'Miller explains. For group decision-making to work well, you need a way to sort through the different options they offer; and you need a mechanism to narrow those options down. Citizens in Vermont control their municipal affairs by proposing proposals, or backing other proposals, until a consensus is reached through voting. As with bees, the broad sampling of options before making a decision will usually result in a compromise that is acceptable to everyone. The wisdom of the crowd makes smart decisions for the benefit of the group and leaves the citizens feeling represented and respected. The Internet is also an area where we increasingly exhibit swarm behavior, without any physical contact. Miller compares a wiki site, for example, to a termite mound. Indirect cooperation is the key principle behind information-sharing websites, just as it underpins the complex structures that termites build. Termites have no architects' blueprint or grand building plan. They simply sense changes in their environment, such as when the wall of mounds is damaged, changing the flow of air. They go to the site of change and drop a grain of earth. When the termite next finds this grain, they drop theirs too. Little by little, without any kind of direct decision-making, a new wall is being built. Termite mound, in this way, is quite similar to a wiki site. Instead of getting together and talking about what we want to post online, we just add to what someone perhaps a stranger on the other side of the world has already written. This indirect knowledge and skill-sharing is now finding its way into the corridors of power.
hypothesis: Travelers are often compared favorably with working ants.

Topology is a term that refers to the physical layout of a network or the architecture of its cable system. Cable problems can lead to a decline in the network. There are three basic types of LAN topology, which are the star, ring and bus, and each has its own advantages and disadvantages. With star topology each workstation has its own cable connected to a central hub. The signals go to the hub and then out to each of the workstations. A failure in one system will not affect any of the other workstations, but the failure of the hub will disconnect any computer. Star topology makes it easy to add more workstations, although only one computer can send and receive data from the hub at any one time. In ring topology, or a closed loop network, each workstation is connected to a common ring at an intersection. If one computer fails, it can bring down the entire network. In bus topology, the workstations are threaded together, with all computers connected to a backbone or bus cable; if two computers attempt to send a signal along the cable simultaneously a collision occurs; each collision slows down the network. Network faults are difficult to resolve with bus topology, because workstations share a cable, unlike the star and ring topologies.

premise: Internet security experts have long known that simple passwords do not fully protect online bank accounts from determined scam artists. Now research suggests that a popular secondary security measure provides little extra protection. The study, co-produced by researchers from Harvard and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, tested a technology called Web Authentication Images. In the system, now used by financial institutions like Bank of America, ING Direct and Vanguard, online banking customers are asked to choose a picture, like a dog or chess piece, that they will see every time they log into their account. The idea is that if customers don't see their image, they might be on a fake website, simulated to look like their bank's, and forbidden from entering their passwords. Harvard and MIT researchers tested this hypothesis. In October, they brought 67 Bank of America customers in the Boston area to a controlled environment and asked them to conduct routine online banking activities, like searching account balances. But investigators secretly pulled the photos. Of 60 participants who got this far into the study and whose results could be verified, 58 entered passwords anyway. Only two chose not to connect, citing security concerns. The premise is that site-authenticating photos increase security because customers won't enter their passwords if they don't see the right image, said Stuart Schechter, a computer scientist at the Lincoln Mi.Slow Lab. From the study we learned that the premise is correct less than 10 percent of the time. He added: 'If a bank asked me if they should deploy it, I would say no, wait for something better, 'he said. The system has some high-powered backers in the financial services world, many trying to comply with the new online banking regulations. In 2005, the Federal Financial Institutions Review Board, an interagency body of federal banking regulators, determined that passwords alone did not actually thwart intruders like identity thieves. It issued new guidelines, asking financial Web sites to find better ways for banks and customers to identify each other online. January 2007 was set as the compliance date, though the council has yet to begin enforcing the mandate. Banks knew immediately what they didn't want to do: ask customers to download new security software, or swipe hardware devices that feed them PIN codes that they could use to verify their identity. Both solutions would add an extra layer of security but, the banks believed, detract from the convenience of online banking. The image system, introduced in 2004 by a Silicon Valley company called PassMark Security, offered banks a painless addition to their security arsenal. Bank of America was among the first to adopt it, in June 2005, under the brand name SiteKey, asking its 21 million site users to choose an image from thousands of possible options and choose a unique phrase they would see every time they log in. SiteKey gives our customers a fairly easy way to authenticate Bank of America's website, said Sanjay Gupta, director of e-commerce at the bank. It was well received. However, Harvard and MIT researchers found that most online banking customers did not notice when SiteKey photos were missing. When respondents logged in during the study, they saw a site maintenance message on the screen in which their image and expressions should have been pictured. The error message also had a glaring misspelling, which further suggests something questionable. Mr. Gupta of Bank of America said he was not bothered by the survey results and stressed that Seitake had made the bank's Web site more secure. He also said the system was just one part of a larger security blanket. It's not like we're betting the bank on SiteKey, he said. Most financial institutions, like Bank of America, have other ways of knowing if a customer is legitimate. Banks often release a small piece of software, called a cookie, to a user's PC to associate the computer with a customer. If the client connects from another machine, he may be asked personal questions, like his mother's maiden name. Rachna Dhamija, the Harvard researcher who conducted the study, points out that scammers can use their dummy sites to ask customers these personal questions. She said the study proved that site authentication images are fundamentally flawed and, worse, may actually detract from security by giving users a false sense of security. In the end maybe that's why they adopted him. Sometimes the appearance of security is more important than the security itself.

premise: Investigating children's language for over 200 years, there has been interest in the way children learn to speak and understand their first language. Researchers carried out a number of small-scale studies, especially towards the end of the 19th century, using data recorded in parental diaries. However detailed and systematic investigation did not begin until the mid-decades of the 20th century, when the tape instrument came into routine use. This made it possible to keep a regular record of examples of children's speech, so that analysts could repeatedly listen to ambiguous extracts, thus producing a detailed and accurate description. Since then, the topic has attracted enormous multidisciplinary interest, mainly from linguists and psychologists, who have used a variety of observational and experimental techniques to deeply explore the process of language acquisition. Central to the success of this rapidly evolving field lies researchers' ability to devise satisfactory methods to elicit linguistic data from children. The problems that must be faced are quite different from those encountered when working with adults. Many of the linguists cannot use routine interrogation techniques with children. Certain types of experiments cannot be carried out, because aspects of children's cognitive development such as their ability to pay attention or remember instructions may not be advanced enough. Nor is it easy to get children to make systematic judgments about language, a task that is almost impossible under the age of three. And anyone who has tried to obtain even the most basic kind of data - a recording of a representative sample of a child's speech knows how frustrating it can be. Some children, it seems, are innately programmed to switch off as soon as they notice a recording device turned on. Since the 1960s, however, a number of sophisticated recording techniques and experimental designs have been devised. Children can be observed and recorded through one-way vision windows or through radio microphones, so that the effects of an investigator's presence in the same room the child is in can be eliminated. Large-scale sampling programs were carried out, with children sometimes enrolled for several years. Particular attention was paid to the design of experimental techniques well suited to the intellectual level and social experience of the child. Even pre-lingual infants have been brought in for research: acoustic techniques are used to analyze their voices, and their ability to perceive the world around them is monitored using special recording equipment. The result was a growing body of reliable data on the stages of language acquisition from birth to adolescence. There is no one way to learn the language of children. Linguistics and psychology have each brought their own approach to the subject, and many variations have been introduced to deal with the range of activities children engage in, and the large age range they present. Two main research paradigms are found. One of these is known as naturalistic sampling. A sample of a child's spontaneous use of language is recorded in a familiar and comfortable environment. One of the best places to make the recording is in the child's own home, but it is not always easy to maintain good acoustic quality, and the presence of the investigator or recording equipment can be a distraction (especially if the proceedings are filmed). Alternatively, the recording can be done at a research center, where the child is allowed to play freely with toys while conversing with parents or other children, and their observers and equipment are not intrusive. A qualitative, representative and naturalistic sample is generally considered an ideal figure for children's language learning. However, the method has a number of limitations. These examples are informative about speech production, but they give little guidance about children's understanding of what they hear around them. Moreover, examples cannot contain everything, and they can easily miss some important features of a child's linguistic ability. They may also not provide enough instances of a developing trait to allow the analyst to make a decision about how the child learns. For such reasons, the description of samples of children's speech should be supplemented by other methods. The other main approach is through experimentation, and the methods of experimental psychology have been widely applied to children's language research. The researcher formulates a specific hypothesis about the ability of children to use or understand an aspect of language and plans a relevant task for a group of subjects to perform. A statistical analysis of the subjects' behavior is made, and the results provide evidence that supports or falsifies the original hypothesis. Using this approach, as well as other methods of controlled observation, the researchers have come up with many detailed findings about the production and understanding of groups of children. However, the findings of these studies are not easy to generalize. What might be accomplished in a carefully controlled framework may not apply in the daily interaction load. Different types of subjects, experimental situations, and statistical procedures may produce different results or interpretations. Experimental research is therefore a slow and painstaking business; it may be years before researchers are convinced that all variables have been considered and the finding is genuine.

The digital revolution in music has allowed people to download, store and listen to songs on a tiny, portable device called an MP3 player. The process is quick and you can then have access to a library of thousands of songs that can fit in the palm of your hand. But experts say that continuously listening to loud music in these small music players can permanently damage hair cells in the inner ear, resulting in hearing loss. For example, outdated headphones have been replaced by smaller ones that fit neatly into the ear, instead of above them, which amplifies the sound. In addition, digital music is not distorted and maintains its clear sound, even in noisy settings, which encourages children to turn up the volume. Combine that with the fact that many kids will spend hours listening to their iPods, and you have the recipe for hearing loss. In another perspective, most MP3 players can reach levels of 120 decibels, which is more powerful than a chainsaw or lawnmower. When you consider 85 decibels is the maximum safe decibel level determined by hearing specialists during a workday, and that children will listen to music at decibel levels higher than this for long periods of time, hearing will always suffer. Besides hearing damage, there are other serious health risks. We live in a wireless age. Mobile calls can be made and received from anywhere and the Internet can be accessed without the need for cables. The benefits are enormous, bringing ease and comfort to our lives. Obviously mobiles and wireless technology are here to stay but are we paying the price for new technology? premise: Is there really a war on drugs? In our contemporary society, the media constantly bombards us with horror stories about drugs like crack-cocaine. From them, and probably from any other source, we learn that crack is instantly addictive anyway, we learn that it causes corruption, insane violence and almost always leads to death. The government tells us that we are preoccupied with the war on drugs and so it gives us various iconic models to loathe and hate: we learn to stereotype urban minorities as drug-burning wastelands and we learn to witch hunt drug users within our communities believing they represent moral sin and pure evil. I believe these headlines and ideals are ridiculous and based entirely on unnecessary and even harmful ideals promoted by the government to achieve goals other than those they claim. In an article by Craig Rennermans and Harry Levins titled Crack Attack: Politics and Media in America The Latest Drug Scare, the authors attempt to uncover and tackle some of the social problems that have resulted from the overexcitation of crack-cocaine as an epidemic problem in our country. Without detracting attention from the serious health risks for those few people who use the drug, Renerman and Levin demonstrate how minimally harmful the current epidemic is in practice. At the beginning of the article, the authors summarize the evolutionary history of crack-cocaine in the US. They specifically discuss how the crack-related deaths of two star athletes first gained wide attention to the problem in the mid-1980s. Since then, the government has reportedly used crack cocaine as a political scapegoat for larger inner-city problems of many countries. Thefts, violence and even socioeconomic depression have been blamed on crack. They argue that the government has invested considerably in studies whose results could be used to wage the constant war on drugs whereas to politicians, that war amounted to nothing more than a perceptual war on poverty and urban crime. Because politicians haven't had much other interest to discuss over the years, this aggressive attack on drugs has been held up as one of the only colorful means by which to generate debate, controversy and campaign fuel. In other words, when balancing the budget and maintaining an effective foreign policy became too boring to handle, Reinerman and Levin argue that the crack epidemic became the focus of politicians intent on luring the public interest into their flashy anti-drug campaigns. Finally, in addition to the media's excess attention on the war on drugs, Reinerman and Levin suggest that the constant coverage of crack in the news media was merely counterproductive to the ostensible purposes of any anti-drug program. With depictions of the crack high that glorify it considerably - the politically charged media campaigns to combat drugs have ironically acted somewhat as huge publicity campaigns to increase public awareness and stimulate the interests of daring junkies. While Reinerman and Levin are fairly adamant about their findings, they do retain a visible respect for the reality that crack had other causal factors and outcomes besides those described by them. Their main concern seems to be a call for putting a more realistic spotlight on the problem - so we can begin to deal with it as nothing more and nothing less than it needs to be. The war on drugs is indeed based on an exaggeration of facts. Although it is also evident that substances such as crack-cocaine may pose great health risks to those who use them, there is no widespread epidemic use of the drug nor does it validate the alleged myths that it causes such immediate destruction and destroys lives anyway. It is clear that we do indeed need to maintain a greater and more focused focus on the more important and common problems in society. Important energies and necessary funds are diverted from them to fight an almost imaginary battle against controlled matter. DEFINITIVELY, WE SHOULD ALLOW DRUGS LIKE CRACK-COCAINE TO GET THEIR PROPER ATTENTION AS SOCIAL PROBLEMS, BUT LET THEM GET NO MORE THAN THAT!
hypothesis: Drug users within the communities that won us over represent moral sin and pure evil.
label: c

premise: Is your child in school today? School attendance information for parents/carers Introduction Getting a good full-time education will give your child the best start in life. Studying at school regularly and accurately is essential if children want to make the most of the opportunities available to them. The law states that parents must ensure that their child attends regularly at the school where he/she is registered. What you can do to help make sure your child gets to school on time. This encourages habits of good time-keeping and reduces any possible disruption in class. If your child arrives after the prescription is closed for no good reason, this will be recorded as an unauthorized absence for that meeting. If your child has to miss school it is essential that you inform the school why, preferably on the morning of the first absence. (Your child's school will have an attendance policy explaining how this should be done.) If you know or think that your child is having trouble attending school, you should contact the school. It is better to do this sooner rather than later, since most problems can be dealt with very quickly. Authorized and Unauthorized Absence If your child is absent and the school does not accept an explanation from you, or considers that the explanation is not satisfactory, it will record your child's absence as unauthorized, that is, as avoidance. Most absences for acceptable reasons will be approved by your child's school: illness Unavoidable medical or dental appointments (if possible, schedule them after school or during school holidays) Interview with a potential employer or college Unusual family circumstances, such as bereavement and religious observance days. Your child's school will not authorize absenteeism for the following reasons: Shopping during school hours trips Holiday day trips Unagreed birthdays Caring for sick brothers or sisters or relatives.
hypothesis: Children must go to the school where they are enrolled.

premise: Is free internet access as universal a human right as access to clean water and health care? Many leading experts believe that 80% of the world's population that is not connected to the Internet should get access to information through a free low-bandwidth connection via mobile phones. The fifth of the Internet-connected world, however, faces a very different problem: an insatiable appetite for bandwidth exceeding availability. Bandwidth refers to the ability to transmit data over a channel. Emails, for example, require less bandwidth than video. Information jams arise when too many users try to transmit information at the same time, exceeding the capacity of the channels. The popularity of mobile internet devices means that demand for wireless channels is growing rapidly, but bandwidth supply is limited resulting in high charges for use. With bandwidth controlled by a handful of private providers, bandwidth is a subject of government debate in many countries, including the United States. Bandwidth providers support the introduction of tiered pricing structures, under which customers who pay higher tariffs will receive faster service. Critics believe that a tiered system violates the principle of net neutrality under which all data is treated as equal and would allow providers to profit from controlling a scarce resource. The providers claim that they are funding huge infrastructure updates like switching from copper wires to expensive optical fibres in order to improve services.
hypothesis: Supporters of network neutrality oppose the prioritization of certain Internet traffic.
label: e

premise: Is it any wonder there is a shortage of teachers? Daily, the press carries reports of schools going through four days just because they can't recruit enough teachers. But why? There is no simple answer. For starters, fewer students are entering teacher training courses when they leave school. But can you blame young people after the obstruction faced by the UK teaching profession over the past decade? The attack, unrelenting in the extreme, was on several fronts. Government inspectors, by chance or by design, fed the media with a constant stream of negative information about the teaching institutions of this country. Teachers also come in for a lot of the attacks from politicians. And the government wonders why there are problems in schools. The governments' clear contempt for the teaching profession was recently exposed by one of the most powerful men in government when she referred to schools as bog-standard comprehensives. Hardly the kind of comment that would inspire parents or career counselors seeking to direct the future of young people. Would you like to spend your working life in a dead-end profession? The government doesn't seem to want you to either. On the administrative side, most teachers are burdened by an ever-increasing flow of bureaucracy. Cynicism would lead me to believe that it prevents teachers from provoking disagreements because they erode from useless administrative exercises. Most teachers must then be cynical too! Abuse of teachers has spread, sadly, to young people in schools as evidenced by the recent catalogue of physical attacks on teachers. If adults have no respect for the teaching profession, young people can hardly be expected to think otherwise. The circle squares when, as well as qualified experienced and talented teachers, are expelled from the profession by the increased stress and pressure; fewer students turn to teacher training courses. Increased salaries are certainly welcome, but they are not the complete answer to a sector in crisis. ADDRESSING THE STATUS OF THE PROFESSION IN THE PUBLIC EYE IS VITAL TO ENCOURAGE EXPERIENCED TEACHERS TO STAY IN THE CLASSROOM AND MAKE IT AN ATTRACTIVE CAREER OPTION FOR PROSPECTIVE TEACHERS AGAIN. The relevant ministers should also go on a fact-finding mission and let school teachers know, rather than relying too much on consultants, what changes can be brought about to improve the quality of the education service. Initiatives in the field of education come surprisingly from politicians who know little about classroom practice or educational theorists who know even less, but are more dangerous because they work in the rarefied air of universities largely unaware of classroom practice. Making sure that no one with no recent classroom experience is employed as a teacher-coach at any tertiary institution will further enhance the teaching profession. If someone has no practical experience in the classroom, they cannot in all seriousness offer theories on the subject. Instead of giving them a sabbatical to write books or essays, lecturers at teacher-training institutions should be made to spend a year at the board or, these days, on the board. This will give them practical insights into current classroom practice. It was then possible for teachers to give students the opportunity to come and watch experts in the classroom: a much more worthwhile experience than the latter who sit and calculate ideas far from the classroom. So we will have fewer initiatives like the last government proposal to teach school thinking. Ostensibly, this is a commendable recommendation. But, as any practicing teacher will tell you, it's done in every classroom. Maybe someone should point out to the academic who thought up the program that the wheel has been around for a while. In the educational field, there is a surprisingly constant tension between education theorists and government officials on the one hand, who want to see teachers marching together for greater utopian abstraction and on the other practicing teachers. Any experienced classroom practitioner knows that the series of teaching and learning initiatives that subsequent governments have tried to impose on schools and colleges is not working.
hypothesis: The government approach in relation to teachers is of great interest to the general public.
label: n
