premise: Is there more to video games than people realize? Many people who spend a lot of time playing video games insist they have been helped in areas like confidence-building, presentation skills and debate. However, this way of thinking about video games is almost nowhere to be found in the mainstream media, which still tends to treat games as an odd mix of slightly menacing and alien. This lack of awareness has become increasingly inappropriate, as video games and the culture surrounding them have become very big business. Recently, the UK government published the Byron Report on the effects of electronic communications on children. Its conclusions lay a clear and rational basis for the study of the regulation of video games. The ensuing debate, however, descended into the same old squabble between partisan factions: preachers of mental and moral decay, and the innovative game designers. In between are the gamers, busy buying and playing while talking nonsense over their heads. Susan Greenfield, a well-known neuroscientist, describes her concerns in a new book. Each person's brain is the product of a mind that is personalized by the sum total of their experiences; with an increasing amount of our experiences from very early childhood occurring on screen rather than in the world, there is potentially a profound shift in how children's brains work. She suggests that fast-paced second-hand experiences created by video games and the Internet may inculcate a worldview that is less empathetic, more risk-taking and less contemplative than we tend to think of as healthy. GREENFIELDS'S PROSE IS FULL OF MIXED METAPHORS AND SELF-CONTRADICTIONS AND IS PERHAPS THE WORST ENEMY OF HER ATTEMPTS TO PERSUADE. This is unfortunate, because no matter how much technophiles may snore, it articulates common fears that have a basis in fact. Unlike even their immediate predecessors, the latest electronic media is simultaneously associated with home and work, their mobility blurs the boundaries between these spaces, and video games are at their forefront. A generational gap has opened up that is in many ways deeper than the corresponding changes associated with radio or television, more alienating for those who are unfamiliar with new technologies, more absorbing for those who are. So how do our legislators regulate something that is too fluid to be fully understood or controlled? Adam Martin, lead programmer of an online games developer, says: Computer games teach and people don't even notice they are learning. But isn't the type of learning that takes place in games rather narrow? A large part of gaming addiction comes from the fact that when you play you master a set of challenges. But humanity's greater understanding of the world comes mostly through communication and experimentation, through answering the question of what if? Games also excel in this provision. Steven Johnson's thesis is not that electronic games constitute great popular art, but that the average level of mass culture steadily demands more intellectual engagement on the part of consumers. Games, he points out, produce satisfaction through the complexity of their virtual worlds, not by their robotic predictability. Testing the nature and limits of laws of such imaginary worlds has more in common with scientific methods than pointless addiction, while the complexity of the problems children encounter in games exceeds that of anything they might find at school. Greenfield argues that there are ways of thinking that playing video games simply can't teach. She has a point. We should never forget, for example, the unique ability of books to engage and expand the human imagination, and give us the means to more fully express our situation in the world. Intriguingly, the video game industry is now growing in ways that have more in common with an old-fashioned world of ancillary pastimes than with a cyber future of lonely, isolated obsessives. Games in which friends and relations gather around a console to compete in activities are growing in popularity. The agenda is increasingly set by the concerns of mainstream consumers what they consider acceptable to their children, what they want to play at parties and generations ago. These trends embody a familiar but important truth: Games are human products, and are under our control. This does not mean that we still fully master or understand them, but it should remind us that there is nothing inevitable or incomprehensible about them. No matter how deeply it may be felt, instinctive fear is an inappropriate response to technology of any kind. Until now, the dire predictions made by many traditionalists about the death of outdated narratives and imaginative thought at the hands of video games could not be sustained. Television and cinema may suffer, economically, from interactive media. But literacy standards haven't dropped. Young people still enjoy sports, going out and listening to music and most studies including a recent $1.5 million study funded by the US government indicate that even pre-teen teens are not in the habit of blurring gaming worlds and real worlds. But the sheer pace and scale of the changes we face leaves little room for complacency. Richard Battle, a British author and games researcher, says The Times is changing: Accept it; embrace it. Just as today, we have no living memories of a pre-radio era, we will soon live in a world where no one alive experiences growing up without computers. For this reason we must try to examine what we are going to lose and gain, before it is too late.
hypothesis: Susan Greenfields's way of writing has become more complex over the years.

Books became major vehicles for artistic expression, and the artists who produced them, especially calligraphers and painters, enjoyed a high status, and their workshops were sponsored by princes and their courtiers. Before 900 AD, manuscripts of the Qur'an (the book containing the teachings of the Islamic religion) appear to have been the most common type of books produced and decorated, but after this date a wide variety of books were produced for a wide spectrum of patrons. Most of them were produced for sale on the open market, and cities boasted special souks (markets) where books were bought and sold. THE MOSQUE OF MARRAKECH IN MOROCCO IS KNOWN AS KOTUVIER, OR THE MOSQUE OF THE BOOKSELLERS, AFTER THE NEARBY MARKET. Paper manufacturing was introduced to the Islamic countries from China in the eighth century. Within fifty years, the government in Baghdad was using paper for documents. The introduction of the paper sparked a conceptual revolution whose results have barely been studied. premise: Floating islands are not known for their mobility but sometimes this happens. Natural floating islands have been documented in many parts of the world (Burns et al 1985). Longevity studies in lakes were carried out by Hesser, and in rivers and the open sea by Bohey (Smithsonian Institution 1970). They can form in two common ways: landslides of peat soils (usually vegetated) into lakes or seawater or as flooding of peat soils (usually bound by roots of woody vegetation) after storm surges, river floods, or lake level rises. The ability of the living part of a floating island to maintain its equilibrium in the face of destructive forces, such as fire, wave attack or hijacking and falling while riding sea or sweltering waves is a major obstacle. In general, floating islands passing through the ocean are likely to be short-lived; wave washing gradually eliminates enough of the islands' freshwater reservoir to dilute ground air and kill vegetation around the edges, which in turn causes erosion and reduces buoyancy and horizontal mobility. The forces acting on a floating island determine the speed and direction of movement and are very similar to those acting on floating mobile ice floes during the partially open water season (Peterson 1965). Unlike such ice rafts, many floating islands carry vegetation, possibly including trees used as sails. Burns et al examined the acting forces and concluded that relatively low wind speeds were required to mobilize free-floating islands with vegetation two meters or more high. Seeing islands floating in the sea is a rare event; such a thing is unplanned, short-lived and usually undocumented. On July 4, 1969, an island about 15 meters in diameter and 10-15 trees 10-12 meters high was included in the daily notice to seamen as posing a navigational hazard between Cuba and Haiti. McWhirter described the island as probably... Like it's being held by a mangrove-type mat; there was some soil on it but it looked pretty thick around the bottom, like there's dead foliage, grass-like stuff or something on the island itself. The trees came out of it. The trees seemed to come straight out of the brown layer on the surface. No roots were seen. By July 14 the island had apparently fallen apart and the parts partially submerged so that only the upper tree trunks were above water. By July 19, no trace of the island had been found after an intensive six-hour search. Another example though freshwater, can be found in Victoria, Australia in the Floating Islands of Pirron Yaluk. Descriptions of how the floating islands were created have been given by local residents. These accounts have not been disputed in the scientific literature. Prior to 1938, the lake was an intermittent marsh that usually dried up in the summer. A drainage ditch was dug at the lowest point of the swamp in the northern part of its perimeter. This likely encouraged the development or enlargement of a peat mat on the floor of the outlet. Potatoes were grown in the center of the socket where the peat rose into a light mound. The peat was lit in a fire in 1938 that burned from the dry ends towards a central damp section. A track was laid through the bog last century and pavement work was carried out in 1929/30. This trail restricted the flow between the outlet and its former southern arm. These roadworks, plus the collapse and partial filling of the North Drainage Canal, created drainage conditions conducive to the transition from a swamp to a permanent lake. The transformation from swamp to lake was dramatic, and occurred in the winter of 1952 when rainfall of about 250 mm was well above average. The peat was very buoyant and the central elevated section isolated by the fire, broke away from the rocky basalt floor as water levels rose in winter. The main island broke up into several smaller islands that slowly drifted up to 200 meters in the lake boundaries and ranged in size from 2 to 30 meters in diameter. Subsequent years experienced average or above average rainfall and water levels were maintained. A realignment of the highway in 1963 completely blocked the outlet's former southern exit, further improving its ability to retain water. The road surface also provided an additional runoff source for the outlet. Anecdotal evidence suggests that the islands floated undisturbed for 30 years after their formation. Typically they moved between the northwest and NE sides of the lake in response to prevailing winds. In 1980, the Rural Water Commission issued a nearby motel a home license to remove water from the lake and occasionally water is taken for firefighting purposes. The most significant amount taken for firefighting was during severe fires in February 1983. Since then, the Pirron-Yaluk Islands have ceased to float, and this is thought to be associated with a drop in water levels of about 600 mm over the past 10-15 years. The islands either ran aground on the bed or the lagoon or vegetation attached them to the bed. Floating islands have attracted attention because they are rare and their behavior has provided not only explanations for events in myth and legend, but also a great space for discussion and speculation among scientific observers and others.

premise: It is much easier to motivate employees in a growing organization than in a declining one. As organizations expand and add personnel, opportunities for advancement, salary increases, and the excitement of being associated with a dynamic organization create feelings of optimism. Management is able to use growth to entice and encourage employees. When an organization is reduced, the best and most mobile employees tend to leave voluntarily. Unfortunately, they are the ones that the organization can least afford to lose those with the highest skills and experience. The underage workers remain because their job options are limited. Morale also suffers during the decline. People fear they may be the next to resign. Productivity often suffers, as employees spend their time sharing rumors and providing each other with moral support instead of focusing on their work. For those whose jobs are secure, pay raises are rarely possible. Wage cuts, which have not been heard during periods of growth, can even be imposed. The challenge for management is how to motivate employees in such reduced conditions. The ways to deal with this challenge can be divided into six key points, described below. There is plenty of evidence to support the motivational benefits that result from carefully matching people to jobs. For example, if the job is running a small business or an autonomous unit within a larger business, high achievers should be sought. However, if the position to be filled is a managerial position in a large bureaucratic organization, a candidate should be selected who has a high need for power and a low need for affiliation. Therefore, high-achievers should not be put in jobs that are incompatible with their needs. High-achievers will do best when the role provides moderately challenging objectives and where there is independence and feedback. However, it should be borne in mind that not everyone is motivated by jobs with high independence, variety and responsibility. The literature on goal-setting theory suggests that managers should ensure that all employees have specific goals and take notes on how well they are on those goals. For those with high achievement needs, usually a minority in some organization, the existence of external goals is less important because high achievers already have intrinsic motivation. The next factor to be determined is whether the objectives should be assigned by a manager or set collectively in collaboration with the employees. The answer to this depends on perceptions of goal-making and the culture of organizations. If opposition to goals is expected, the use of participation in goal setting should increase acceptance. However, if participation is incompatible with culture, goals must be assigned. If participation and culture are incompatible, employees are likely to perceive the participation process as manipulative and will be adversely affected by it. Regardless of whether goals are achievable or good in management's perceptions of employee competence, if employees consider them unattainable they will reduce their effort. Managers must be confident, then, that employees feel confident that their efforts can lead to performance goals. For managers this means that employees must have the capacity to carry out the work and must treat the evaluation process as valid. Because workers have different needs, what serves as reinforcement for one may not be for another. Managers can use their knowledge of each employee to personalize the rewards over which they have control. Some of the more obvious rewards that managers assign include salary, promotions, autonomy, the scope and depth of the role and the opportunity to participate in setting goals and making decisions. Managers should make the rewards contingent on performance. Rewarding non-performance factors will only reinforce those other factors. Key rewards such as salary increases and promotions or progress towards achieving employees' specific goals should be allocated. Depending on how to maximize the impact of rewards, managers should look for ways to increase their visibility. Eliminating the secrecy around pay by openly communicating everyone's pay, advertising performance bonuses and allocating annual pay rises in a lump sum instead of distributing them over a full year are examples of actions that will make rewards more visible and possibly more motivating. The way rewards are distributed should be transparent so that employees understand that rewards or outcomes are equitable and equal to the inputs given. On a simplistic level, experience, abilities, effort, and other obvious inputs should account for differences in pay, responsibilities, and other obvious outcomes. The problem, however, is complicated by the existence of dozens of inputs and results and the fact that groups of workers attach different degrees of importance to them. For example, a study that compared clerical and manufacturing workers identified nearly twenty inputs and results. Clerical workers considered factors such as the quality of work performed and knowledge of work near the top of their list, but these were at the bottom of the list of production workers. Similarly, production workers thought the most important inputs were intelligence and personal involvement in performing the tasks, two factors that were quite low in officials' importance ratings. There were also important, albeit less dramatic, differences on the outcome side. For example, production workers rated the progress highly, whereas clerical workers rated the progress in the bottom third of their list. Such findings suggest that one person's capital is an inequality of others, and thus an ideal should probably consider different inputs and outcomes depending on the group of workers.

The first of these crates arrived at a San Francisco mail center and, after being accidentally dropped, promptly exploded, killing all 15 present. Point taken. However, it was soon discovered that when frozen (at about five degrees), the nitro was much less sensitive to shock. The problem was then in thawing it back into a liquid form, at which point it became even more unstable. Again, the increasing death toll will attest to this fact. However, nitroglycerin always remained in demand, being the first practical mining explosive to be produced. Before that, gunpowder was used, but it was limited and bulky. Gopoder is a low explosive, meaning it burns from layer to layer, producing gases that expand at less than the speed of sound. Nitro is a high explosive, meaning it explodes, meaning it is triggered to react by the nearly propelling shock wave, producing gases that expand more than the speed of sound. Gunpowder could not effectively shatter rock (though it was suitable for bullets and artillery shells). Only nitro could really do the job, and a Swedish chemist, Alfred Nobel, was interested. Noble Enterprises moved primarily from iron and steel production to the almost exclusive production of cannons, armaments, and gunpowder, and he saw the commercial value in making nitroglycerin manageable. He began experimenting at considerable cost. In 1864, his younger brother and several workers were killed in an explosion at the factory. Instead, Noble built a new factory in the remote hills of Germany, determined to find the answer. At first he tried to combine nitro with conventional gunpowder, marketing the final product as blasting oil, but accidental explosions continued. His factory was destroyed again, on two occasions! THE BREAKTHROUGH FINALLY CAME WHEN THE NOBLES COMPANY MIXED LIQUID NITROGLYCERIN WITH INERT ABSORBENT SILICATE SAND, KNOWN AS DIATOMIC SOIL. It was produced by grinding diatomite, a rock found around the local hills. It resembles a volcanic sponge, being very light and very porous, but in fact it is the fossilized remains of diatoms, a hard-shelled algae. This combination immediately made the nitro less dangerous to handle, and by being solid, more convenient to pack and transport. Noble patented his invention in 1867 called dynamite, based on Dina the Greek word for power. In its best known form, dynamite is created in short sticks wrapped in paper consisting of three introductory quarters to a quarter of diatomaceous earth, but it will always remain dangerous to manufacture, store and use. Over time, the nitro can seep out, crystallize on the outside of the sticks or gather at the bottom of the storage boxes, with all the instability that comes from having raw nitro. Nevertheless, in an era of extensive railroad and tunnel construction, the product would earn Noble a large fortune. Yet while high explosives serve a laudable purpose in peacetime engineering projects, Noble's fortune was also based on weapons of death and destruction, and the public knew it. Noble himself was very troubled, especially given the events that took place when his brother Ludwig died. The French newspapers mistakenly thought it was Alfred's own death, and published an obituary. Alfred happened to be in France at the time, and one can only wonder from his reaction when he read of his own death! However the obituary was harsh and protective, calling Noble the merchant of death, someone who got rich by finding ways to kill more people faster than ever before. Certainly it was this event that influenced him, in 1895, to write a new last will, a year before his death. It will surprise everyone and change the course of history. When Alfred Nobel died, unmarried and childless, at the age of 63, he noted that apart from a few small inheritances, his vast fortune (about $200 million in today's money) would be devoted to establishing the Nobel Prizes. These will be awarded annually to whoever bestows the greatest benefit to humanity in physics, chemistry, peace, medicine and literature. The Nobel strategy worked, as Nobel Prizes are now considered among the most prestigious in the world. Few think all that money comes from nitroglycerin, dynamite, gunpowder and armaments manufacture, the indirect cause of incalculable human carnage.

premise: Is it your choice or is it really? We are constantly required to process a wide range of information to make decisions. Sometimes, these decisions are trivial, like which jam to buy. Other times, the stakes are higher, like deciding which symptoms to report to the doctor. However, the fact that we are used to processing large amounts of information does not mean that we are better at it (Chabris & Simons, 2009). Our sensory and cognitive systems have systematic ways of failing that often, perhaps happily, we are unaware of. Imagine you're strolling through your local city park when a tourist comes up to you and asks for directions. During the conversation, two men carrying a door pass between the two of you. If the person asking for directions switched places with one of the people carrying the door, would you notice? Studies suggest you might not. Harvard psychologists Simmons and Levi (1998) conducted a field study using this exact dataset and found that the change in identity was not noticeable by 7 (46.6%) of the 15 participants. This phenomenon has been called change blindness and refers to the difficulty viewers have to notice changes in visual scenes (e.g. changing the person), when the changes are accompanied by another visual disturbance (e.g. the passage of the door). Over the past decade, the phenomenon of change blindness has been replicated many times. Particularly noteworthy is an experiment by Davies and Hain (2007) that investigated whether change blindness affects eyewitness recognition. Specifically, the participants were presented with video hacking legislation. In the video, a man enters the house, goes through the different rooms and puts valuables in a backpack. However, the identity of the burglar changed after the first half of the film while the initial intruder was not in sight. Of the 80 participants, 49 (61%) did not notice a change in the identity of burglars, suggesting that change blindness may have serious consequences for criminal proceedings. To most of us, it seems strange that people can miss such obvious changes while paying active attention. However, to perceive these changes, attention must be focused on the changing feature. In the study described above, participants likely did not expect the change to happen, so it is possible that their attention was focused on the valuables the burglar stole, rather than the intruder. Based on change blindness research, scientists have concluded that we perceive the world in far less detail than previously thought (Johansson, Hall, & Sikstrom, 2008). Instead of keeping track of all the visual details around us, we seem to focus our attention only on those attributes that are currently significant or important, ignoring those that are irrelevant to our current needs and goals. Thus, at any given time, our representation of the world around us is crude and incomplete, allowing for changes or manipulations to go undetected (Chabris & Simons, 2010). Given the difficulty people have to notice changes in visual stimuli, one wonders what would happen if these changes were concerned with the decisions people make. To test choice blindness, Hall and colleagues (2010) invited supermarket customers to taste two different types of jams and teas. After participants tasted or smelled both samples, they indicated which one they preferred. Then, they were allegedly given another sample of their preferred choice. In half of the trials, however, these were samples of the jam or tea that were not selected. As expected, only about a third of the participants recognized this manipulation. Based on these findings, Hall and colleagues proposed that choice blindness is a phenomenon that occurs not only for choices involving visual material, but also for choices involving taste and smell information. Recently, the phenomenon has also been replicated for choices involving auditory stimuli (Sauerland, Sagana, & Otgaar, 2012). Specifically, participants had to listen to three pairs of voices and decide for each pair which voice they found more sympathetic or more criminal. The voice was presented again; however, the result was manipulated for the other voice duo and the participants were presented with the unselected voice. In replicating Hall and colleagues' findings, only 29% of participants recognized this change. Markelbach, Jelichick, and Peters (2011) investigated choice blindness for intensity ratings of your own psychological symptoms. Their participants had to rate the frequency with which they experienced 90 common symptoms (e.g. anxiety, lack of concentration, stress, headaches, etc.) on a 5-point scale. Before a follow-up interview, the researchers inflated the ratings to two symptoms by two points. For example, when participants rated their feelings of shyness, as 2 (i.e. occasionally), it was changed to 4 (i.e. all the time). This time, more than half (57%) of the 28 participants were blind to symptom rating omission and accepted it as their symptom intensity rating. This demonstrates that blindness is not limited to recent preference choices, but can also occur with intensity and frequency. Taken together, these studies suggest that choice blindness can occur in a wide variety of situations and can have serious implications for medical and judicial outcomes. Future research is needed to determine how, in these situations, choice blindness can be avoided.

premise: Kangaroo culling is a controversial issue in Australia, where the government has implemented culls to control populations. The issue is particularly emotive because of the kangaroo's status as a national symbol, with some detractors seeing the wreckage as an attack on Australia's identity. Although they are native to Australia, kangaroos threaten the grassland ecosystem in some areas. Overgrazing causes soil erosion and thus threatens the survival of certain rare species of lizard. Furthermore, in overpopulated areas, food shortages cause kangaroos to damage wheat crops. Protesters generally oppose the elimination on the grounds that it is inhumane. Instead, they prefer relocating kangaroos to suitable new habitats, or sterilizing the animals in overpopulated areas. Sterilization, however, would have no immediate impact on the limited resource problems and soil degradation through grazing. Not only is relocating large numbers of kangaroos an expensive task, critics believe it could traumatize the relocated kangaroos and ultimately threaten the new habitat.
hypothesis: Sterilizing kangaroos will not immediately alleviate problems from their overgrazing.
label: e

In the opening pages of Aspirin: The Amazing Story of a Panacea, Diarmuid Jeffries describes this little white pill as one of the most amazing creations in medical history, a drug so incredibly diverse that it can relieve headaches, ease your aching limbs, lower your temperature and treat some of the deadliest human diseases. Its properties have been known for thousands of years. Ancient Egyptian physicians used extracts from the willow tree as an analgesic, or analgesic. Centuries later, the Greek physician Hippocrates recommended willow bark as a remedy for labor pains and as a fever reducer. But it was only in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries that the chemical salicylates found in the willow tree became the subject of serious scientific investigation. The race continues to identify the active ingredient and replicate it synthetically. At the end of the nineteenth century, a German company, Friedrich Bayer & Co. managed to create a relatively safe and effective chemical compound, acetylsalicylic acid, which was renamed aspirin. The end of the nineteenth century was a fertile time for experimentation, partly because of the hunger among scientists to answer some of the great scientific questions, but also because these questions were the means by which to answer. One scientist in a lab with a few chemicals and a test tube can make significant breakthroughs whereas nowadays, to map the human genome for example, needs an army of researchers, a bank of computers and millions and millions of dollars. But an understanding of the nature of science and scientific inquiry is not sufficient in itself to explain how society regenerates. In the nineteenth century, scientific progress was closely linked to the Industrial Revolution. It was a time when people often had the means, motive and determination to take an idea and make it a reality. In the case of aspirin that happened partly a series of minor, often unrelated advances, that were violated by broader economic, medical and scientific developments of the century, leading to one final major breakthrough. The link between big money and pharmaceutical innovation is also a significant one. The continued shelf life of aspirin was assured because for the first 70 years of its life, huge sums of money were invested in promoting it as a regular everyday painkiller. In the 1970s, other painkillers, such as ibuprofen and acetaminophen, entered the market, and pharmaceutical companies then focused on advertising these new drugs. But just at the same time, discoveries were made regarding the beneficial role of aspirin in preventing heart attacks, strokes and other afflictions. Were it not for these findings, this pharmaceutical wonder may have disappeared. So the link between big money and drugs is strange. Commercial markets are necessary for developing new products and ensuring they stay around long enough for scientists to do research on them. But commercial markets are just as likely to kill certain products when something more attractive comes along. In the case of aspirin, a potential miracle cure existed for over 70 years without anyone investigating how it obtained its effects, since they made more than enough money from it as it was. IF IBUPROFEN OR PARACETAMOL HAD ENTERED THE MARKET JUST A DECADE EARLIER, ASPIRIN MIGHT NOT BE HERE TODAY. It would be just another forgotten drug that people didn't bother to research. None of the recent discoveries of aspirin's benefits have been made by the big pharmaceutical companies; they've been made by scientists working in the public sector. The reason for this is very simple and direct, Jeffries says in his book. Pharmaceutical companies will only pursue research that is going to provide financial benefits. There is no more profit in aspirin. It's incredibly cheap with tiny profit margins and has no more patent, so anyone can produce it. In fact, there's almost a motive for pharmaceutical companies to ramp up the drug further, he argues, because it could put them out of business by preventing the sale of their more expensive brands. So what's the solution to the lack of commercial interest in examining the therapeutic benefits of aspirin? More public money is going to clinical trials, Jefferies says. If I were the Ministry of Health I would say it is a very cheap drug. There could be a lot of other things we can do with it. We need to spend a lot more money trying to find out. Jeffrey's book that tells not only the story of a panacea but also examines the nature of innovation and the role of big business, public money and regulation reminds us why research like this is so important.

premise: Away from the recent wintry waters floods in Central Europe's rivers have been among the worst since the Middle Ages, and as winter storms return, the spectre of the floods returns too. Just weeks ago, the Rhône River in southeastern France burst its banks, driving 15,000 people from their homes, and worse could be on the way. Traditionally, river engineers have gone on Plan A: get rid of the water quickly, drain it from land and go down to sea in high-sided rivers that have been re-engineered as high-performance drains. But as they grew they dug urban drains, as wide and straight as they formed the rivers, and as much as they built the banks, the floods kept coming back and taunting them, from the Mississippi to the Danube. Arid when the floods arrived, they looked worse than ever. No wonder engineers are turning to Plan B: dump the destructive power of water by dispersing it into fields, forgotten lakes, flood plains and aquifers. Back in the days when rivers followed a more tortuous path to sea, floodwaters lost momentum and volume while meandering across flood plains and swaying in wetlands and interior doors. But today the water tends to make an uninterrupted journey to the sea. And this means that when it rains in the territories, the water drops all at once. Worse, every time we close more flood plains, the rivers flowing farther downstream become more violent and uncontrollable. DICKS ARE ONLY AS GOOD AS THEIR WEAKEST LINK AND THE WATER WILL FIND IT WITHOUT MISTAKE. In trying to turn the complex hydrology of rivers into the simple mechanics of a water pipe, the engineers often created danger where safety was guaranteed, intensifying the floods they intended to end. Take the Rhine, the most engineered river in Europe. For two centuries, German engineers wiped out its backwaters and cut it off from its flood plain. Today, the river has lost 7% of its original length and runs up to a third faster. WHEN IT RAINS HEAVILY IN THE ALPS, THE PEAK FLOWS FROM SEVERAL OVERLAPPING TRIBUTARIES IN THE MAIN RIVER, WHERE THEY ONCE ARRIVED SEPARATELY. And as four-fifths of the lower flood plain of the Lower Rhine has been blocked, the water is rising higher and higher. The result is more frequent floods that cause greater damage to homes, offices and roads sitting in the flood plain. The same thing happened in the US in the mighty Mississippi, which drains the second largest river basin in the world into the Gulf of Mexico. The European Union is trying to improve rain forecasts and model more accurately how heavy rains swell rivers. That may help cities prepare, but it won't stop the floods. To do that, say hydrologists, you need a new approach to engineering not just rivers, but the entire landscape. The UK Environment Agency - which received an extra $150 million a year for expenditure following floods in 2000 that cost the country $1 billion - puts it this way: the focus is now on working with the forces of nature. Concrete walks loom outside, and new wetlands: incoming. To help keep London's feet dry, the agency is breaking the banks of the Tamas upstream and reflooding 10 square miles of ancient flood plain at Otmore outside Oxford. Closer to London it has taken out $100 million of new marshland and an aid channel across 16 miles of flood plain to protect the town of Maidenhead, as well as the ancient playing fields of Eton College. And near the south coast, the agency is digging ditches to reconnect old meanders on the River Cookmere in East Sussex that were cut off by floodbanks 150 years ago. The same thing is happening on a much larger scale in Austria, in one of Europe's largest river restorations to date. Engineers are regenerating flood plains along 60 miles of the Drava River as it emerges from the Alps. They also widen the riverbed and route it back to abandoned meanders, bull lakes and backwaters hanging in prairies. premise: A wild Khmer Rouge high school Tul Sui sits on a dusty road on the outskirts of Phnom Penh, Cambodia. In 1976, the Khmer Rouge renamed the secondary school S-21 and made it a center of torture, interrogation, and execution. Of the 14,000 people known to have entered, only seven survived. Not only did the Khmer Rouge meticulously transcribe the interrogations of prisoners; they also meticulously photographed the vast majority of prisoners and created a remarkable photographic archive. Each of the nearly 6,000 returned S-21 portraits tells a story of shock, resignation, confusion, defiance, and horror. Although the most frightening images that emerged from Cambodia were those of the mass graves, the most haunting were the portraits taken by the Khmer Rouge at S-21. Today, S-21 Prison is known as the Tule Slang Museum of the Genocide. Inside the gates, it looks like any high school; five buildings face a grassy courtyard with pull poles, green lawns and lawn bowling alleys. The classrooms on the ground floor in one building remain to be seen as they were in 1977. The Spartan interrogation rooms are furnished only with a school desk and chair set facing a steel bed frame with cuffs at each end. On the far wall appear harrowing photographs of bloated, crumbling corpses chained to bed frames with pools of wet blood below. These were the sights that greeted the two Vietnamese photojournalists who first discovered S-21 in January 1979. In another building, the walls are lined with thousands of S-21 portraits. At first glance, the photograph of a shirtless young man seems typical of prison photos. Closer examination reveals that the number tag on his chest was securely attached to his pectoral muscle. With a bruised face and a locked chain around his neck, a boy stands with his arms by his sides and looks straight at the camera. A mother with her baby in her arms stares at the camera with a look of indignant resignation. The photographs and confessions were collected with the aim of proving to Khmer Rouge leaders that their orders had been carried out

premise: Kitchen pollution in the house. Scientist Brett Singer is a vegetarian. So why does he fry burgers? Singer and his team of indoor air researchers at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (Berkeley Lab) have found dangerous levels of nitrogen dioxide and carbon monoxide in a surprisingly large portion of California home kitchens. What's more, their research has shown that the most common device to reduce this internal air problem, engine covers vary greatly in performance. In a small, nondescript building in a parking lot on the Berkeley Lab site, Singer's group set up a test kitchen to conduct a battery of cooking experiments. By frying burgers and green beans with a variety of hoods operating in different settings, the researchers are collecting important data on the effects on air quality, as well as developing a standardized test for hoods that could ultimately allow consumers to evaluate and compare their effectiveness. In a study of Southern California homes published in Environmental Health Perspectives, Singer's group found that a significant proportion of residences exceed outdoor air quality standards for several pollutants on a weekly basis as a result of cooking with gas burners. If those were conditions that were out, the EPA (Environmental Protection Agency) would have been dismissed. But since it's in people's homes, there's no regulation requiring anyone to fix it, Singer said. Reducing people's exposure to pollutants from gas stoves should be a public health priority. Berkeley Lab's team of indoor air quality researchers is the oldest and most comprehensive in the nation and has contributed to many of the standards and building codes currently in place for both homes and industrial buildings, such as schools and offices. In recent years, as more attention has been paid to making buildings more energy efficient, which often means making them tighter, or less leaky, to reduce heating and cooling costs, ventilation has become increasingly important. Without proper ventilation, indoor air quality can suffer and cause serious health problems. A previous Berkeley Lab study found that the cumulative health consequences of poor indoor air quality that cooking is the primary but not the only source of are as significant as those of all the traffic accidents or infectious diseases in the United States. In a recent study led by Logue, the team analyzed extensive data from several sources to understand how common it is that homes in California experience indoor air pollution at dangerous levels. They estimated that 60 percent of homes in the country that cook at least once a week with a gas stove could reach pollutant levels that would be illegal if found outdoors. That equates to 12 million Californians routinely exposed to nitrogen dioxide levels exceeding federal outdoor standards, 10 million exposed to formaldehyde in excess of federal standards and 1.7 million exposed to carbon monoxide in excess of environmental air standards in a typical winter week. These contaminants can come both from the cooking burners, especially the gas burners, but to a lesser extent from electric burners and also from the cooking itself. The main health effect of nitrogen dioxide, which is also found in the vapors of any type of combustion, is an increased likelihood of respiratory problems. Exposure to carbon monoxide is most severe for those with cardiovascular disease because it can enter the bloodstream and reduce the supply of oxygen to the body's organs and tissues. The internal contaminant that scientists believe may be most harmful to human health is particulate matter, including fine particles, which are less than 2.5 micrometers in diameter, and ultrafine particles, smaller than 1 micrometer. They are produced by gas and electric burners and by cooking. They can be very harmful because they can get into the lungs and, for the smaller particles, enter the bloodstream or other tissues. Electric burners produce ultra-fine particles primarily by repelling dust, Singer explained. It's the same process with your toaster, resistance cooker or radiator if you haven't used it in a while. After you turn it on, you can smell it\ u001f. You smell the chemicals that have evaporated. Once in the air, they recondense into these ultrafine particles. This is the chemistry lab in your kitchen. Singer recommends using hoods while cooking. If each of these homes used a hood that is exhausted from the outside and even moderately efficient, the number of homes exceeding the standards would drop by more than half, he said. Still, Singer's previous studies have found that engine lids vary greatly in their capture efficiency, or efficiency in removing contaminants. premise: Cormilda College is a unique school located near Darwin in the Northern Territory of Australia. FOR 20 YEARS, UNTIL 1989, CORMILDA COLLEGE OPERATED AS A GOVERNMENT-RUN LIVING SCHOOL FOR ABORIGINAL HIGH SCHOOL STUDENTS. IN 1989 IT WAS PURCHASED FROM THE GOVERNMENT BY TWO CHRISTIAN CHURCH GROUPS AND SINCE THEN IT HAS EXPANDED GREATLY, AND INCLUDES A DAY SCHOOL AS WELL AS PENSIONERS (RESIDENTIAL STUDENTS) IN YEARS 8—12. Although 320 students from the total number of colleges are Aboriginal students, drawn mainly from isolated communities across the Northern Territory, Cormilde also has a waiting list of non-Aboriginal students. With a current enrollment of 600, the number of students is expected to grow to 860 by 1999. Central to the school's mission is the encouragement of individual excellence, which has resulted in programs designed specifically for the student population. Specialist support programs enable traditional Aboriginal students, who often use a second language, to understand and succeed in the core curriculum. A GIFTED AND TALENTED PROGRAM WAS INTRODUCED, WHICH INCLUDES A SPECIAL PROGRAM FOR THE TERTIARY ASPIRATIONS OF ABORIGINES AND TORRES STRAIT RESIDENTS, AS WELL AS AN ADAPTIVE EDUCATION UNIT. Furthermore, in Years 11 and 12, students can choose to follow the Northern Territory Standard Courses, or those of the International Baccalaureate (LB.). To provide appropriate pastoral care as well as an appropriate academic structure, three separate sub-schools were established. Pre-High School: For Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students aged 8-10 who are in secondary school but have difficulty reading and writing. Supported High School: For Aboriginal students and Torres Strait Islander residents who are of secondary school age and operate at secondary school levels 8—12 who need second language specific literacy and literature support. High School: For students of multicultural years 8-12. Students remain in their sub-schools for classes in the major subject areas of English, Mathematics, Social Education and Science. This arrangement takes into account both varied literacy levels and the learning styles and cultural understandings appropriate for traditional Aboriginal second language users. In elective subjects chosen by the students which include Indonesia, Music, Art, Drama, Science for Life, Commerce, Geography, Modern History, Woodwork, Metalwork, Economics and Law Studies the students mix based on interest in the subject. TO HELP DEVELOP THE ABORIGINAL EDUCATION PROGRAM, A SPECIAL CURRICULUM SUPPORT UNIT WAS ESTABLISHED. One of its functions is to repackage school courses so they can be taught in ways that suit students. The education program offered to Aboriginal students uses an approach that begins with the experiences of the students themselves and gradually builds a bi-cultural understanding. IN ONE COURSE, INTRODUCING WESTERN EUROPEAN CULTURE THROUGH TRADITIONAL STORYTELLING, STUDENTS ARE HELPED TO BUILD A COMMON FOUNDATION FOR APPROACHING THE ENGLISH LITERATURE CURRICULUM. Based on the oral culture of traditional Aboriginal communities, they become acquainted with traditional stories of other cultures, orally and in writing. In a Year 10 primary course, Theory of Learning, concepts from Aboriginal culture are placed side by side with European concepts so that students can use their knowledge base to help bridge the cultural gap. Another project of the support unit was the publication of several books, the most popular, Cormilda Zepers. The idea of Cormilda Capers was conceived when it became clear that there was a lack of fascinating material for adolescent readers in schools. One of the stories in the book, Bullman's Lots Hits the Big Smoke, tells of the adventures of the Cormilde students on their first visit to Sydney, Canberra and Snow Country. By focusing on experiences that directly impacted the lives of students at the college, and on ideas and issues of immediate interest to Aboriginal students, Cormilda Capers has won enthusiastic support within and outside the school.

premise: Land of the rising amount. Japan has a significantly better record in terms of average mathematical achievements than England and Wales. Large sample international comparisons of student achievement since the 1960s determined that not only did Japanese students at 13 have better average achievement scores, but there was also a greater proportion of low achievers in England, where, incidentally, the variability in achievement scores was much greater. The percentage of gross national product invested in education is quite similar in both countries, so how is higher and more consistent achievement in mathematics achieved? High schools in Japan cover three years of schooling, from seventh grade (age 13) to ninth grade (age 15). Almost all students at this stage attend state schools: only 3% are in the private sector. The schools are generally modern in design, located away from the road and spacious inside. The classrooms are large and the students sit at individual tables in rows. Classes last a standard 50 minutes and are always followed by a 10-minute break, which gives students a chance to let off steam. Teachers begin with a formal speech and mutual bowing, then concentrate on teaching the entire class. The classes are usually large at about 40 and are not streamed. Students remain in the same classroom for all classes throughout the school and develop a class identity and considerable loyalty. The students attend the school in their neighborhood, which in theory removes a ranking by school. In practice in Tokyo, because of the relative concentration of schools, there is some competition to get into the better school in a particular area. Traditional ways of teaching form the basis of the lesson and the remarkably quiet classes take their own notes on the points raised and the examples demonstrated. Everyone has their own copy of the textbook provided by the central education authority, Monbusho, as part of the idea of free compulsory education until the age of 15. These textbooks are overall small, presumably cheap to produce, but well designed and logically developed. (One teacher was particularly eager to introduce color and images into math textbooks: he felt it would make them more accessible to students who had grown up in a cartoon culture.) Besides approving textbooks, Monbusho also decides on the most central national curriculum and how it is delivered. All classes follow the same pattern. At first, students put homework solutions on the board, then teachers comment, correct or expand as needed. Students indicate their homework themselves: this is an important principle in Japanese education as it allows students to see where and why they made a mistake so that they can be avoided in the future. No one cares about mistakes or ignorance as long as you're willing to learn from them. After the homework has been discussed, the teacher explains the topic of the lesson, slowly and with a lot of repetition and expansion. Examples are presented on the board; questions from the textbook go through first with the class, then the class is assigned questions from the textbook to perform individually. Only rarely are supplementary worksheets distributed in math class. The impression is that the logical nature of textbooks and their comprehensive coverage of various kinds of examples, combined with the relative homogeneity of the class, make the worksheets redundant. At that point the teacher would turn around and make sure all the students were coping well. It is amazing that large and involved classes in mathematics could be maintained throughout their compulsory studies from 6 to 15. Teachers say they give individual help at the end of class or after school, and schedule additional work if necessary. In the observed lessons, each wrestler will be helped by the teacher or quietly ask for help from their neighbor. A carefully nurtured class identity makes students eager to help each other anyway, it's in their best interest because the class moves forward together. That rarely seems to be enough help to allow slow learners to keep up. However, the Japanese attitude to education runs along the lines of if you work hard enough, you can do just about anything. Parents are kept closely informed of their children's progress and will play a part in helping their children keep up with class, sending them to Joko (private evening tuition) if extra help is needed and encouraging them to work harder. It seems to work, at least for 95 percent of the school population. So what are the main contributing factors to the success of mathematics teaching? Obviously the approaches matter. Education is highly valued in Japanese culture; mathematics is recognized as an important compulsory subject throughout schooling; and the emphasis is on hard work along with an emphasis on accuracy. Other relevant points relate to the supportive attitude of a class towards slower students, the lack of competition in the classroom and the positive emphasis on self-learning and improving individual standard. And the view of repeated boring lessons and the study of the facts by heart, sometimes quoted in relation to Japanese lessons, may be unfair and unjustified. No bad math classes were observed. They were mostly good and one or two were inspirational.
hypothesis: There is a wider range of achievement among English students studying maths than among their Japanese counterparts.
label: e

premise: Language diversity One of the most influential ideas in the study of languages is that of universal grammar (UG). It was introduced by Noam Chomsky in the 1960s, and is widely interpreted as meaning that all languages are essentially the same, and that the human brain is born ready for language, with a structured program capable of interpreting the common rules that underlie each mother tongue. For five decades this idea prevailed and influenced work in linguistics, psychology and cognitive science. To understand a language, it is implied, you must weed out the vast diversity of languages and find their common human core. Since the theory of UG was proposed, linguists have identified many universal language rules. However, there are almost always exceptions. It was once believed, for example, that if a language had syllables that begin with a dot and end with a consonant (VC), it would also have syllables that begin with a consonant and end with a dot (CV). This universal lasted until 1999, when linguists showed that Arraneta, spoken by Indigenous Australians from the area around Alice Springs in the Northern Territory, has VC syllables but no CV syllables. Other non-universal universals describe the basic rules of connecting words. Take the rule that every language contains four basic word classes: nouns, verbs, adjectives, and proverbs. Work over the past two decades has shown that several languages do not have an open class of proverb, which means that new proverbs cannot be easily created, unlike English where any adjective can be turned into a proverb title, for example soft to soft. Others, like Lao, spoken in Laos, have no adjectives at all. More controversially, some linguists argue that some languages, like Straits Salish, spoken by natives from northwestern regions of North America, do not even have distinct nouns or verbs. Instead, they have a single type of words that will include events, objects and qualities. Even indisputable universals have apparently been found lacking. This includes recursion, or the ability to place infinitely one grammatical unit within a similar unit, like Jack thinks Mary thinks that... The bus will arrive on time. It is widely considered the most essential characteristic of human language, one that distinguishes it from the communication of all other animals. However Dan Everett of Illinois State University recently published a controversial work that showed that the Amazonian pygmy does not have this quality. But what if the very diversity of languages is key to understanding human communication? Linguists Nicholas Evans of the Australian National University in Canberra, and Stephen Levinson of the Max Planck Institute for Psychophysics in Nijmegen, Netherlands, believe that languages do not share a common set of rules. Rather, they say, their sheer diversity is a defining feature of human communication something not seen in other animals. While there is no doubt that human thinking influences the form language takes, if Evans and Levinson are right, language in turn shapes our brains. This suggests that humans are more diverse than we thought, with our brains having differences depending on the language environment we grew up in. And that leads to a disturbing conclusion: every time a language goes extinct, humanity loses an important piece of diversity. If languages don't obey one set of common rules, then how are they formed? Instead of universals. You get standard engineering solutions that languages adopt over and over again, and then you get exceptions. Says Evans. He and Levinson argue that this is because any given language is a complex system shaped by many factors, including culture, genetics, and history. There are no absolutely universal features of language, they say, only tendencies. And it is a combination of strong and weak tendencies that characterizes the bio-cultural mix that we call language. According to both linguists, the strong tendencies explain why many languages exhibit common patterns. A variety of factors tend to push language in a similar direction, such as brain structure, the biology of speech, and communication efficiency. Widely shared linguistic elements may also be those that build on a type of specifically human thinking. For example, the fact that before we learn to speak we perceive the world as a place full of things that cause actions (agents) and things that actions done to them (are handled) explains why most languages deploy these grammatical categories. Weak tendencies, however, are explained by the uniqueness of different languages. Evans and Levinson argue that many aspects of the particular natural history of a population may influence its language. For example, Andy Butcher of Flinders University in Adelaide, South Australia, observed that Indigenous Australian children have by far the highest incidence of chronic middle ear infection of any population on the planet, and that most indigenous Australian languages lack many sounds common in other languages, but are difficult to hear with middle ear infection. Whether this condition shaped the sound systems of these languages is unknown, Evans says, but it is important to consider the idea. premise: Learning lessons from the past Many past societies have collapsed or disappeared leaving behind monumental ruins like the ones my poet imagined in his sonnet, Ozymandias. By breakdown, I mean a drastic reduction in human population size and/or political/economic/social complexity, over a considerable area, for an extended period of time. By these standards, most people would consider the following past societies as famous victims of full-fledged collapses rather than mere minor declines: the Anasazi and Cahokia in the borders of the modern US, the Mayan cities in Central America, the Mucha and Tiwanaku societies in South America, Nordic Greenland, Mycenaean Greece and Minoan Crete in Europe, Great Zimbabwe in Africa, Angkor Wat and the Indus Harappan Valley Cities in Asia, and Easter Island in the Pacific. The monumental ruins left behind by those past societies hold a fascination for all of us. We admire them when, as children, we first learn about them through photographs. As we grow up, many of us plan vacations in order to experience them firsthand. We feel drawn to their often spectacular and haunting beauty, and also to the mysteries they pose. The rubble scales attest to the former wealth and power of their builders. However, these masons disappeared, abandoning the large structures they had created in such an effort. How can a company that was once so mighty eventually collapse? It has long been suspected that many of those mysterious abandonments were caused at least in part by ecological problems: people inadvertently destroying the environmental resources on which their societies depended. This suspicion of unintentional ecological suicide (ecocide) is confirmed by discoveries made in recent decades by archaeologists, climatologists, historians, paleontologists and palynologists (pollen scientists). The processes by which past societies undermined themselves by damaging their environments fall into eight categories, whose relative importance differs from case to case: deforestation and habitat destruction, land problems, water management problems, overhunting, overfishing, impacts of introduced species on native species, human population growth, and increased influence of people. These past crashes have tended to follow somewhat similar courses comprising variations on the theme. Writers find it tempting to draw analogies between the course of human societies and the course of individual human life to talk about birth, growth, peak, old age, and eventual death. But that metaphor proves wrong for many companies in the past: they declined rapidly after peaking in numbers and power, and these rapid declines must have surprised and shocked their citizens. It is clear that this trajectory, too, is not a route that all past societies have followed unchanged until its completion: different companies have collapsed to different degrees and in slightly different ways, while many companies have not collapsed at all. Today, many people feel that environmental problems overshadow all other threats to world civilization. These environmental problems include the same eight that undermined past societies, plus four new ones: human-caused climate change, the buildup of toxic chemicals in the environment, energy shortages and full human utilization of the planet's photosynthetic capacity. But the severity of these contemporary environmental problems has been vigorously debated. Are the risks greatly exaggerated, or, on the contrary, are they underestimated? Will modern technology solve our problems, or is it creating new problems faster than it solves old problems? When we deplete one resource (e.g. wood, oil, or ocean fish), can we count on being able to replace some new resource (e.g. plastics, wind and solar energy, or farmed fish)? Isn't the rate of human population growth decreasing, one that was already on the way for the world's population to settle in a certain manageable number of people? Such questions illustrate why these famous collapses of past cultures have taken on more significance than just that of a romantic mystery. Maybe there are some practical lessons we can learn from all these past breakdowns. But there are also differences between the modern world and its problems, and those past societies and their problems. We should not be naïve to the point of thinking that exploring the past will yield simple, directly transferable solutions to our societies today. We differ from past societies in some ways that put us at low risk from them; some of these aspects often mentioned include our powerful technology (i.e. its beneficial effects), globalization, modern medicine, and greater knowledge of past societies and distant modern societies. We also differ from past societies in some ways that put us at greater risk than them: again, our powerful technology (i.e., its unintended destructive effects), globalization (such that now a problem in one part of the world affects all the rest), the dependence of millions of us on modern medicine for our survival, and our much larger human population. Maybe we can still learn from the past, but only if we think carefully about its lessons.
hypothesis: We must be careful when making comparisons between past and present.

Will modern technology solve our problems, or is it creating new problems faster than it solves old problems? When we deplete one resource (e.g. wood, oil, or ocean fish), can we count on being able to replace some new resource (e.g. plastics, wind and solar energy, or farmed fish)? We should not be naïve to the point of thinking that exploring the past will yield simple, directly transferable solutions to our societies today. We also differ from past societies in some ways that put us at greater risk than them: again, our powerful technology (i.e., its unintended destructive effects), globalization (such that now a problem in one part of the world affects all the rest), the dependence of millions of us on modern medicine for our survival, and our much larger human population. premise: Less TV, less violence and aggression Cutting back on TV, videos and video games reduces acts of aggression among schoolchildren, according to a study by Dr. Thomas Robinson and others from Stanford University School of Medicine. The study, published in the January 2001 issue of Archives of Pediatrics and Adolescent Medicine, found that third- and fourth-graders who took part in a curriculum to reduce television video and use video games engaged in fewer acts of verbal and physical aggression than their peers. The study took place at two similar elementary schools in San Jose, California. Students at one school underwent an 18-lesson, six-month program designed to limit their media use, while the others did not. Both groups of students had similar reports of aggressive behavior at the start of the study. After the six-month program, however, the two groups had very real differences. The students who reduced their TV time engaged in six fewer acts of verbal aggression in an hour and rated 2.4 percent less than their classmates as aggressive after the program. ACTS OF PHYSICAL VIOLENCE, PARENTAL REPORTS OF AGGRESSIVE BEHAVIOR, AND PERCEPTIONS OF AN AVERAGE, FRIGHTENING WORLD ALSO DIMINISHED, BUT THE AUTHORS SUGGEST FURTHER RESEARCH TO SUBSTANTIATE THESE RESULTS. Although many studies have shown that children who watch a lot of television are more likely to act violently, this report further verifies that television, videos, and video games actually cause the violent behavior, and is among the first to evaluate a solution to the problem. Teachers at the Intervention School included the program in their existing curriculum. Early classes encouraged students to track and report the time they spent watching television or videos, or playing video games, to motivate them to limit these activities themselves. After the initial classes came TV-turn-off, an organization that encourages less TV viewing. For ten days, students were challenged to go without television, videos or video games. After that, teachers encouraged students to stay on a seven-hour-a-week media allowance. Almost all students attended Turnoff, and most remained under their budget in the following weeks. Additional classes encouraged children to use their time more selectively, and many of the final lessons had students themselves advocating reducing screen activities. This study is not the first to find a link between television and violence. Nearly all 3,500 research studies on the subject in the past 40 years have shown the same relationship, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics. Among the most notable studies is Dr. Leonard D. Arons, who found that exposure to childhood television violence is the strongest predictor of aggressive behavior later in life even in violent behavior in childhood. The more violent television subjects watched at age eight, the more severe their aggressive behaviour was even 22 years later. Another study by Dr. Brandon S. Centerwell found that murder rates rise after television viewing. In the United States and Canada, murder rates doubled 10 to 15 years after television was introduced, after the first television generation grew up. Centerwall tested this pattern in South Africa, where television broadcasts were banned until 1975. Homicide rates in South Africa remained relatively stable from the mid-1940s to the mid-1970s. In 1987, however, the murder rate rose by 130 percent from its level in 1974. Homicide rates in the United States and Canada have meanwhile declined. The Centerwalls study implies that the medium of television, not just the tent, promotes violence, and Dr. Robinson's current research supports this conclusion. The Turnoff did not refer specifically to violent television, nor to the ensuing allotment period. Reducing television in general reduces aggressive behavior. Even non-violent TV is more violent than real life and may lead viewers to believe that violence is funny, meaningless and a viable solution to problems. Also, watching TV in any content robs us of the time to interact with real people. Watching too much television may hinder the skills and patience we need to get along with others without resorting to aggression. Television, as a medium, advocates aggression and violence. The best solution is to turn it off.

premise: Lost for words. Many minority languages are on the danger list in the Navajo Native American nation, which spans four states in the American Southwest, the mother tongue is dying out. Most of its speakers are middle-aged or elderly. Although many students take classes in Navajo, the schools are run in English. Street signs, supermarket products and even their own newspaper are all in English. Not surprisingly, linguists doubt that native speakers of Navajo will remain a century from now. The Navajo are far from alone. Half of the world's 6,800 languages are expected to disappear within two generations, meaning one language lost every ten days. Never before has Earth's linguistic diversity diminished at such a rate. “Right now we're going to three or four languages that dominate the world,” says Mark Pagel, an evolutionary biologist from the University of Reading. “It's a mass extinction, and it's hard to know if we'll ever come back from the loss.” Isolation breeds linguistic diversity: as a result, the world is convoluted in languages spoken by only a few people. Only in 250 languages there are more than a million speakers, and at least 3,000 have fewer than 2,500. Not necessarily those little languages are going to disappear. Navajo is considered endangered even though it has 150,000 speakers. What makes a language endangered is not just the number of speakers, but their age. If it is spoken by children it is relatively safe. The critically endangered languages are those spoken only by the elderly, according to Michael Krauss, director of the Elask Native Languages Center, in Fairbanks. Why do people reject the language of their parents? It starts with a crisis of trust, when a small community finds itself alongside a larger, wealthier society, says Nicholas Ostler, of the British Foundation for Endangered Languages, in Bath. “People lose confidence in their culture,” he says. 'When the next generation reaches their teens, they may not want to be squeezed into the old traditions. Change is not always voluntary. Often, governments try to kill a minority language by banning its use in public or discouraging its use in schools, all to promote national unity. The former American policy of running Indian reservation schools in English, for example, effectively put languages like Navajo on the list of dangers. But Selikoku Mopwin, head of the linguistics department at the University of Chicago, argues that the deadliest weapon is not government policy but economic globalization. “Indians have not lost pride in their language, but they have had to adapt to socio-economic pressures,” he says. “They can't refuse to speak English if most commercial activity is in English.” But are languages worth saving? At the very least, there is data loss for the study of languages and their development, which relies on comparisons between languages, both living and dead. When unwritten and unrecorded language disappears, it is lost to science. Language is also intimately linked to culture, so it may be difficult to preserve one without the other. “If a person switches from Navajo to English, he loses something,” Moffon says. “Moreover, the loss of diversity may also deprive us of different ways of looking at the world,” Pagel says. There is increasing evidence that language learning produces physiological changes in the brain. “Your brain and mine are different from the brain of someone who speaks French, for example,” Pagel says, and that can affect our thoughts and perceptions. “The patterns and connections we create between different concepts may be constructed by the linguistic habits of our community.” So despite the best efforts of linguists, many languages will disappear over the next century. But a growing interest in cultural identity may prevent the most dire predictions from coming true. “The key to fostering diversity is for people to learn their ancestral tongue as well as the dominant language,” says Doug Wallen, founder and president of the Endangered Language Foundation in New Haven, Connecticut. “Most of these languages wouldn't survive without a great deal of bilingualism,” he says. In New Zealand lessons for children have slowed the erosion of the Maori and rekindled interest in the language. A similar approach in Hawaii has yielded about 8,000 new speakers of Polynesian languages in recent years. In California, 'trainee' programs provided life support for several indigenous languages. Volunteer 'trainees' mate with one of the last living speakers of a Native American language to learn a traditional skill like basket weaving, with exclusive instruction in the endangered language. After about 300 hours of training they are usually fluent enough to pass the language on to the next generation. But Moffwin says preventing language dying is not the same as giving it new life by using it every day. “Keeping a rim is more like preserving fruit in a jar,” he says. However, conservation can bring back language from the dead. There are examples of languages that have survived in written form and then been resurrected by later generations. But written form is essential for this, so the mere possibility of revival has led many speakers of endangered languages to develop writing systems in which it did not exist before.
hypothesis: National governments could do more to protect endangered languages.

premise: Low-cost lamps illuminate rural India Until three months ago, life in this modest village without electricity would have stopped after sunset. In his mud-and-clay house, three children of Ganpat Jadhab used to study in the dim, smoky glow of a kerosene lamp, when their monthly fuel quota of four gallons dried up in just two weeks, they had to strain their eyes using the light from a cooking fire. All this changed with the installation of low-cost, energy-efficient lamps powered entirely by the sun. The lights were installed by the Grameen Surya Bijli Foundation (GSBF), an Indian NGO focused on bringing light to rural India. Some 100,000 Indian villages still have no electricity. The GSBF lamps use LED light-emitting diodes four times more efficient than a normal lamp. After a $55 installation cost, solar power lights the lamp free of charge. LED lighting, like cell phones, is another example of a technology whose low cost could allow the rural poor to jump into the 21st century. Up to 1.5 billion people nearly 80 million in India alone light their homes using oil as the main means of lighting. The fuel is dangerous, dirty, and although it is subsidised consumes almost four per cent of the budget of typical rural Indian households. A recent report by the Medium Technology Development Group suggests that indoor air pollution from such lighting media causes 1.6 million deaths worldwide every year. It is estimated that LED lamps, or rather white LEDs, produce almost 200 times more useful light than a kerosene lamp and almost 50 times the amount of useful light from a conventional lamp. This technology can light up an entire rural village with less energy than that used in a single standard 100-watt bulb, says Dave Irvin-Halliday, professor of electrical engineering at the University of Calgary, Canada and founder of the Light up the World (LUTW) Foundation. LUTW, founded in 1997, has used LED technology to bring light to nearly 10,000 homes in remote and weakened corners of some 27 countries like India, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Bolivia and the Philippines. The technology, which is not yet widely known in India, is faced with some scepticism here. LED systems are revolutionizing rural lighting, but this is not a magical solution to global energy problems, says Ashok Junjunwala, head of the Department of Electrical Engineering at the Indian Institute of Technology, Madras. In a scenario where nearly 60 percent of India's rural population uses 180 million tons of biomass a year for cooking using primitive wood stoves that smoke and provide only 10-15 percent efficiency in cooking - Jhunjunwala emphasizes the need for a clean energy source, not only for lighting but also for other domestic purposes. The Indian government launched in April an ambitious project to bring electricity to 112,000 rural villages over the coming decade. However, the remote locations of the village would make it difficult to achieve this goal. A.K. Lakhin, chairman of the Indias Rural Electricity Corporation, says the Indian government recognizes the potential of LED lighting powered by solar technology, but has expressed reservations about its high costs. Had only LEDs not been imported but manufactured locally, he says, and in large quantity. The lamps installed in nearly 300 homes by GSBF cost nearly half the price of other solar lighting systems. Jasjeet Singh Chada, the founder of the NGO, currently imports his LEDs from China. He wants to set up an LED manufacturing unit and a solar panel manufacturing unit in India. If produced locally, the cost of its LED lamp may drop to $22, as they will not be charged heavy import duties. We need close to $5 million for that, he says. Mr Chada says he has also asked the government to exempt the lamps from such functions, but to no avail. An entrepreneur who made his money from plastics, Chada, poured his money into the project and provided the initial installations free of charge.
