premise: Myths about public speaking The fear of public speaking arises not only from what a person does not know or understand about public communication, but also from misconceptions and myths about public gatherings. These misconceptions and myths persist among professionals as well as among the general public. Persistent myths about public communication simply increase fear in people and prevent their development into competent public speakers. Perhaps the most persistent myth about public communication is that it is a special activity reserved for extraordinary events. After all, public speeches are not done so often. There are only a few special events during the year where even an outgoing professional person will stand behind a lectern to make a public speech, and many professionals can count on one hand the number of public speeches given in a career. Undoubtedly, therefore, public communication is a rare activity reserved for particularly important events. This argument, of course, ignores the true nature of public media and the nature of the events in which it occurs. To contact people who do not know well, to solve problems, to share understanding and points of view, to support points of view or to seek stimulation, means to engage in public speaking. Public communication, then, is a familiar everyday activity that takes place in streets, restaurants, meeting rooms, court rooms, parks, offices, factories and gatherings. Contrary to the widespread misunderstandings, public speaking is not an unusual activity reserved for special occasions and confined to the podium or platform. Rather it is, and should be developed as a daily activity that occurs wherever people meet. A related misconception regarding public communication is the belief that the public speaker is an exceptionally gifted person with innate abilities and tendencies given by God. While most professionals would reject the idea that public speakers are born, not Christians, they never feel that effective public media has developed extraordinary personal talents to an extraordinary degree. At the heart of this misconceptionlies the myth of public speaking as a special activityis an overly narrow view of what a public person is and does. Development as an effective public communicator begins with the understanding that it is not necessary to be a nationally renowned professional platform speaker, a speaker for a fee, to be a competent public person. The public speaker is an ordinary person who is faced with the need to be a public person and uses common abilities. A less common but severe misconception of public speaking is expressed in the belief that public speeches have a lasting purpose. A public speech is something perceived as a historical event that will be part of an ongoing and generally available public record. Some of the public speeches are faithfully recorded, transcribed, reproduced and become part of widely available historical documentation. These instances are rare compared to the thousands of unrecorded public speeches heard every day. Public communication is usually situation-specific and transient. Most audiences succeed if they remember up to 40 percent of what a speaker says immediately after the speaker finishes; even less is retained as time passes. This fact is also reassuring and challenging for the public caller. On the one hand, it suggests that there is room for human error in public statements; on the other, it challenges the speaker to overcome the poor listening habits of most audiences. Finally, professional people, perhaps more than other groups, often subscribe to the misconception that public communication must be an exact science that, if done properly it will succeed. The problematic consequence of this reasoning is that if public communication fails, it is because it was improperly prepared or carried out. This argument unfortunately ignores the uncertainty of human interaction. Public speakers achieve their goals through their listeners, and the only truly predictable aspect of human listeners is their unpredictability. Moreover, public messages may succeed despite inadequate preparation and terrible delivery. It should be added that professional people often mismanage their concerns about public communication. However, once an understanding of what public gatherings assume and require, once the myths that impair the growth of a public person are unburdened, the development as a competent public communicator can properly begin.

Road traffic was extremely scarce within the county, and alternative means of transportation were restricted to donkeys in the north of the county. People relied mostly on the trails, which were slippery and dangerous during the rains. Before solutions could be proposed, the problems had to be understood. Little was known about the transportation requirements of rural households, so Phase I, between December 1985 and December 1987, focused on research. Improving the road network was deemed necessary to ensure the import and export of goods to the province. These improvements were made using methods that were heavily dependent on labor. In addition to improving roads, these methods provided training in operating a mechanical workshop and bus and truck services. However, the difference from the conventional approach was that this time consideration was given to the needs of local transport outside the road network. Most goods were transported on trails providing shortcuts up and down the hillside, but the trails posed a real safety risk and made the journey on foot even more arduous. It made sense to improve the paths by building stairs, railings and bridges. The use of bicycles was limited by their high cost and lack of spare parts available. The bulls were not used at all but donkeys were used by some households in the northern part of the county. MIRTP focused on what would be most appropriate for Makata residents in terms of what was available, how much they could afford and what they were willing to accept. Even the introduction of low-cost means of transportation was difficult because of the general poverty of the district. The locally produced wheelbarrows were still too expensive for all but a few households. Modifications to the original design by local carpenters cut production time and costs. Other local carpenters were trained in the new design so they could respond to requests. Nevertheless, a locally made wooden wheelbarrow that costs around 5000 Tanzanian shillings (less than $20) in a macta, and is about a quarter of the cost of a metal wheelbarrow, is still too expensive for most people. Donkeys, imported into the province, became more common and conducive, in particular, to the transportation of crops and goods to market. Those who bought donkeys are mostly from wealthier households, but with increased supply through domestic breeding, donkeys should be cheaper. Meanwhile, local initiatives are promoting the rental of existing donkeys. However, it should be noted that a donkey, which costs 20,000 Tanzanian shillings less than a bicycle, is still an investment equal to the average income of households for half a year. This clearly illustrates the need for complementary measures if one wants to help the rural poor. It was easy to criticize the MIRTP for using in the early stages a top-down approach, in which decisions were made by experts and officials before being transferred to communities, but it was necessary to start the process from the level of the provincial government authorities. It was difficult to respond to requests from villagers and other rural residents without the support and understanding of the district authorities. Today, no one in the county is arguing about the importance of improved trails and cheap means of transportation. But this is the result of dedicated work over a long period, particularly on the part of the officers in charge of community development. They played a vital role in raising awareness and interest among the rural communities. The concept of integrated rural transport is now firmly established in Tanzania, where a centralised programme of rural transport is about to begin. premise: Making every drop count a The history of human civilization is intertwined with the history of the ways we have learned to manipulate water resources. As towns gradually expanded, water was brought in from increasingly remote sources, leading to sophisticated engineering efforts like dams and aqueducts. At the height of the Roman Empire, nine main systems, with an innovative layout of pipes and well-built sewers, provided the inhabitants of Rome with water per capita as much as is supplied in many parts of the industrial world today. In the course of the Industrial Revolution and the population explosion in the 19th and 20th centuries, the demand for water rose dramatically. Unprecedented construction of tens of thousands of monumental engineering projects designed to control floods, protect clean water supplies and provide water for irrigation and hydropower, has brought great benefits to hundreds of millions of people. Food production has kept pace with population growth largely because of the expansion of artificial irrigation systems that allow 40 percent growth of global food. Nearly a fifth of all electricity generated worldwide is produced by turbines that are rotated by the power of falling water. C However there is a dark side to this picture: despite our progress, half of the world's population still suffers, with water services inferior to those available to the ancient Greeks and Romans. As the UN report on access to water in November 2001 reiterated, more than a billion people lack access to clean drinking water; some two and a half billion lack adequate sanitation services. PREVENTABLE WATER-RELATED DISEASES KILL AN ESTIMATED 10,000 TO 20,000 CHILDREN EVERY DAY, AND RECENT EVIDENCE SUGGESTS THAT WE ARE FALLING BEHIND IN EFFORTS TO SOLVE THESE PROBLEMS. D The consequences of our water policy go beyond the danger of human health. Tens of millions of people have been forced to move from their homes often with no warning or little compensation to make way for reservoirs behind dams. More than 20% of all freshwater fish species are now threatened or endangered because dams and water withdrawal have destroyed the ecosystems of the free-flowing rivers in which they thrive. Some irrigation methods impair soil quality and reduce agricultural productivity. Groundwater aquifers are being pumped out faster than they are replenished naturally in parts of India, China, the US and elsewhere. And disputes over shared water resources have led to violence and continue to raise local, national and even international tensions. E Early in the new millennium, however, the way resource planners think about water is starting to change. premise: Making Time for Science Chronobiology may sound a bit futuristic like something from a science fiction novel, perhaps but it's actually a field of study concerning one of the oldest processes that life on this Earth has ever known: short-term time rhythms and their effect on flora and fauna. It can take many forms. Marine life, for example, is affected by tidal patterns. Animals tend to be active or inactive depending on the position of the sun or moon. Many creatures, including humans, are mostly diurnal meaning, they like to go out during sunlight hours. Nocturnal animals, such as bats and possums, prefer to forage for food at night. A third group is known as carposcular: they thrive in the low light of dawn and dusk and remain inactive at other hours. When it comes to humans, chronobiologists are interested in the so-called circadian rhythm. This is the complete cycle that our body is directed to go through naturally in the passage of a twenty-four-hour day. Apart from sleeping at night and waking up during the day, each cycle involves many other factors such as changes in blood pressure and body temperature. Not everyone has the same circadian rhythm. Night people, for example, often describe how they find it very difficult to operate during the morning, but become alert and focused by the evening. This is a benign variation within circadian rhythms known as chronotype. Scientists have limited capabilities to create resistant changes in chronobiological requirements. Recent therapeutic developments for humans such as artificial light machines and the administration of melatonin can reset our circadian rhythms, for example, but our bodies can tell the difference and health suffers when we violate these natural rhythms for extended periods of time. Plants seem more inflexible in this respect; studies prove that vegetables grown in season and ripened on the tree are much higher in essential nutrients than those grown in greenhouses and laser-ripened. Knowledge of chronobiological patterns can have many pragmatic implications for our daily lives. While contemporary life can sometimes be seen as doubling down on biology, who needs circadian rhythms when we have caffeine pills, energy drinks, shift work and cities that never sleep? Keeping in sync with our body clock is important. The average urban dweller, for example, wakes up in the glare time of 6.04 in the morning, which researchers say is too early. One study found that even an increase at 7.00 in the morning has detrimental effects on health unless exercise is carried out for 30 minutes afterwards. The optimal moment was reduced to 7.22 m; muscle pain, headache, and mood swings were reported as lowest by the study participants who woke up then. Once you're up and ready to hit the road, what then? If you are trying to shed a few extra pounds, dietitians are adamant: never skip breakfast. It confuses your circadian rhythm and puts your body into starvation mode. The recommended course of action is to follow an intense workout with a carbohydrate-rich breakfast; on the contrary and the weight loss results are not so noticeable. A great morning for the vitamin break too. The absorption of supplements in the body does not depend on time, but naturopath Pam Stone points out that the extra boost at breakfast helps us get energy for the coming day. To improve absorption, Stone suggests adapting supplements to foods in which they are soluble and avoiding caffeinated beverages. Finally, Stone cautions to take care of storage; high potency is best for absorption, and heat and moisture are known to dilute the potency of an additive. Espresso after dinner is becoming a tradition that Italians have to thank for, but to prepare for a good night's sleep we are better off curbing caffeine consumption as early as 3pm with a half-life of seven hours, a cup of coffee containing 90 mg of caffeine taken at this time can still leave 45 mg of caffeine in your nervous system at ten o'clock that evening. It is essential that by the time you are ready to sleep, your body gets rid of all traces. Evenings are important to relax before going to bed; however, dietitian Geraldine Giorgio warns that carbohydrate fasting after five is a cultural myth more than a chronobiological requirement. This will deprive your body of vital energy needs. However, overloading the intestines can lead to indigestion. Our digestive tracts do not close completely overnight, but their work slows to a crawl as our bodies prepare for sleep. A modest snack intake should be completely sufficient.
hypothesis: Circadian rhythms identify how we do different things on different days.

premise: Many people are aware that high cholesterol contributes to heart disease, but they would be surprised to learn that cholesterol performs vital functions in the human body. A lipid produced in the liver and found in the membranes of animal cells, cholesterol is used to repair tissue and digest fat, as well as to produce hormones, bile salts and vitamin D. However, problems arise when excess cholesterol accumulates on the walls of blood vessels, thus interfering with blood flow. A person's blood cholesterol count consists of two different types of cholesterol: low-density lipoprotein (LDL), sometimes called bad cholesterol, and high-density lipoprotein (HDL), known as good cholesterol. While HDL transports cholesterol from the arteries to the liver, LDL carries cholesterol from the liver to the arteries where it accumulates. Although some foods of animal origin, such as meat, shellfish, cheese and eggs, are rich in dietary cholesterol, it is actually the consumption of saturated fats found in red meat, full-fat dairy products, cakes and biscuits that increase the levels of bad cholesterol. Conversely, eating polyunsaturated fats and soluble fiber can lower LDL.
hypothesis: To maximize blood flow in the arteries, HDL levels must be minimized.
label: c

Works with partner organizations in Africa, Latin America and India to support the economic lives of street children. The purpose of this article is to share some of the lessons that S.K. And our partners have learned. Background Typically, children do not come to the streets for one reason, but from a combination of factors: a lack of adequate funding in schools, the demand for income at home, family breakdown and violence. The street may be attractive to children as a place to find adventurous play and money. Yet it is also a place where some children are exposed, with little or no protection, to exploitative employment, urban crime and abuse. Children who work on the streets are typically involved in unskilled and labor-intensive tasks that require long hours, such as shining shoes, carrying goods, guarding or washing cars, and informal surveillance. Some may also earn income through begging, or through theft and illegal activities. At the same time, there are street children who take pride in supporting themselves and their families and often enjoy their work. Many children may choose entrepreneurship because it allows them a degree of independence, is less exploitative of many forms of paid employment, and is flexible enough to allow them to participate in other activities such as education and household tasks. S. Kay Street Business Partnerships has worked with partner organizations in Latin America, Africa and India to develop innovative opportunities for street children to earn income. S.K. I's bicycle courier service first started in Sudan. The participants of this enterprise were provided with bicycles, which they used for the delivery of parcels and messages, and that they were required to pay for them gradually from their wages. A similar plan was taken in Bangalore, India. Another successful project, The Shoe Shine Collective, was a partnership program with the YW C. A. in the Dominican Republic. In this project, participants were loaned money to purchase shoeshine boxes. They were also given a place of sale to store their equipment, and facilities for individual savings plans. The Youth Skills Organizing Initiative in Zambia is a joint program with the Red Cross Society and Y.W.C. Street Boys are supported to start their own small business through business training, life skills training and access to credit. Ideally, potential participants will be involved in the organizations' programs for at least six months, and trust and relationship-building have already been established. Participant involvement was essential to developing relevant programs. When children had a central role in determining procedures, they were more likely to obey them and enforce them. It is critical that all loans be linked to training programmes that include the development of basic business and life skills. There are huge benefits to involving parents or guardians in the program, when such relationships come out. Home visits allow staff to know where participants live and understand more about each person's situation. Small loans are initially provided for the purchase of fixed assets such as bicycles, shoe-brushing kits and basic building materials for a market stall. In the 17th century, human-operated screw presses were introduced that could strike up to 30 coins per minute. With the advent of the Industrial Revolution, machines powered by steam were available and a private mint was opened in Birmingham by entrepreneur Matthew Bolton. He secured contracts for pennies and two coins, and produced coins of much higher quality than the tower, which lacked space for steam-powered presses. A decision was made to move facilities from the tower to Tower Hill, where the Royal Mint began production in 1810. The new presses were able to strike up to 100 coins per minute. Coins in the United Kingdom were circulated in various parts of the British Empire, and after World War I the Royal Mint sought orders from countries all over the world. IN 1964 THE GOVERNMENT DECIDED TO ADOPT A DECIMAL SYSTEM OF CURRENCY AND A NEW ROYAL MINT WAS BUILT READY FOR DECIMALISATION ON 15 FEBRUARY 1971. The new mint was built at Llantrisant in South Wales in 1967 and the first phase was opened by the Queen on 17 December 1968. A state-of-the-art foundry was later installed, followed by departments of engraving, toolmaking and testing along with a special section for prominent proof coins for the collector market. The original site on Tower Hill was knocked down after the Llantrisant facility had a variety of stamping facilities. Tower Hill struck its last coin in November 1975.

premise: Mobile money transfers The ping of a text message has never sounded so sweet. In what is touted as a world first, Kenya's largest mobile operator allows subscribers to send cash to other phone users via SMS. The service, known as M-Pesa, or Mobile Money, is expected to revolutionize banking in a country where more than 80% of people are excluded from the formal financial sector. Besides cash transfer, a highly sought after service among urban Kenyans that supports relatives in rural areas Safaricom network customers will be able to save up to 50,000 shillings (370) in a virtual account on their devices. M-Pesa, developed by Vodafone, which holds a 35% stake in Safaricom, was officially launched in Kenya two weeks ago. More than 10,000 people have signed up for the service, with about 8 million shillings transferred so far, most of them in minuscule denominations. Safaricoms executives are confident growth will be strong in Kenya, and further across Africa. We're actually giving people ATM cards without them having to open a real bank account, said Michael Joseph, chief executive of Safaricom, who called the money transfer concept the next big thing in cell telephony. M-Pesas is simple. No need for a new device or SIM card. To send money, you transfer the cash to a registered agent usually a retailer who credits your virtual account. You then send between 100 shillings (74p) to 35,000 shillings (259) via text message to the desired recipient even to someone on another mobile network who redeems it at an agent by entering a secret code and presenting ID. A commission of up to 170 shillings (1.25) is paid by the recipient but it compares favourably with fees levied by the major banks, whose services are too expensive for most of the population. Mobile phone growth in Kenya, as in most of Africa, has been staggering, even among the rural poor. By June 1999, Kenya had 15,000 mobile subscribers. It now has nearly 8 million out of a population of 35 million, and the two operator networks are extensive as access to banks is restricted. Safaricom says it is not so much competing with financial services companies but filling a void. Over time, M-Pesa will allow people to borrow and return money, and make purchases. Companies will be able to pay salaries directly to employees' phones something that has already attracted the interest of larger employers, such as the tea companies, which often have to pay their employees in cash because they do not have bank accounts. There are concerns about security, but Safaricom insists that even if someone's phone is stolen, the PIN system prevents unauthorized withdrawals. Mr Joseph said the only danger was sending cash to the wrong mobile number and the recipient would cash it straight away. The project has been closely watched by mobile operators around the world as a way to target the multibillion-pound international cash transfer industry long dominated by companies such as Western Union and Moneygram. Remittances sent from nearly 200 million migrant workers to developing countries totaled 102 billion last year, according to the World Bank. The GSM Association, which represents more than 700 mobile operators worldwide, believes it could double by 2012 if transfers via SMS become the norm. Vodafone has entered into a partnership with Citigroup that will soon allow Kenyans in the UK to send money home via text message. The charge for sending 50 is expected to be about 3, less than a third of what traditional services charge.
hypothesis: M-Pesa can only be used by people who use one telephone network.
label: c

They are the urge to acquire, the urge to connect, the urge to understand and the urge to protect. The drive to purchase must comply with the drive to purchase to optimize the acquisition aspect as well as the achievement element. Thus the manner in which exceptional performance is recognized, the kind of benefits provided to polish the career trajectory. But sometimes a written letter of appreciation generates more motivation than a thousand-dollar check, which can serve as the invisible force to boost business involvement. The impulse to affirm the urge to bond is also key to motivating motivation. There are many types of relationships between people, such as friendship, family. In a company, employees also want to be an essential part of the company. They want to belong to society. Employees will be motivated if they find personal belonging to the company. Meanwhile, the greatest commitment will be achieved by the employee provided that the force of motivation within the employee influences the direction, intensity and persistence of the decision and behavior in the company. The urge to understand The urge to understand drives many employees to higher performance. For years it has been known that setting stretching goals can greatly affect performance. Organizations need to ensure that the different job roles provide employees with a simulation that challenges them or allows them to grow. Employees don't want to do meaningless things or monotonous work. If the work did not provide them with personal meaning and fulfillment, they would leave the company. The drive for defense The drive for defense is often the most difficult lever to pull. This impulse manifests itself as a quest to create and promote justice, fairness and the ability to express ourselves freely. The studies show that the urge to bond is primarily related to the realization of commitment, while the urge to understand is primarily related to the amount of effort employees put into jobs. The impulse to acquire can be provided by a reward system that ties rewards to appearances, giving the best people opportunities to get ahead. For the purpose of driving defense, research on merging Company P and Company H shows that employees at the former company show an unusually cooperative attitude. The key to motivating employees successfully is to comply with all drives. Each of these drives is important if we are to understand employee motivation. These four motivations, while not necessarily the only human motivations, are those that are central to a unified understanding of modern human life.

premise: Motivation for employees in difficult conditions It is much easier to motivate employees in a growing organization than in a declining organization. As organizations expand and add personnel, opportunities for advancement, salary increases, and the excitement of being associated with a dynamic organization create feelings of optimism. Management is able to use growth to entice and encourage employees. When an organization is reduced, the best and most mobile employees tend to leave voluntarily. Unfortunately, they are the ones that the organization can least afford to lose those with the highest skills and experience. The underage workers remain because their job options are limited. Morale also suffers during the decline. People fear they may be the next to resign. Productivity often suffers, as employees spend their time sharing rumors and providing each other with moral support instead of focusing on their work. For those whose jobs are secure, pay raises are rarely possible. Wage cuts, which have not been heard during periods of growth, can even be imposed. The challenge for management is how to motivate employees in such reduced conditions. The ways to deal with this challenge can be divided into six key points, described below. There is plenty of evidence to support the motivational benefits that result from carefully matching people to jobs. For example, if the job is running a small business or an autonomous unit within a larger business, high achievers should be sought. However, if the position to be filled is a managerial position in a large bureaucratic organization, a candidate should be selected who has a high need for power and a low need for affiliation. Therefore, high-achievers should not be put in jobs that are incompatible with their needs. High-achievers will do best when the role provides moderately challenging objectives and where there is independence and feedback. However, it should be borne in mind that not everyone is motivated by jobs with high independence, variety and responsibility. The literature on goal-setting theory suggests that managers should ensure that all employees have specific goals and take notes on how well they are on those goals. For those with high achievement needs, usually a minority in some organization, the existence of external goals is less important because high achievers already have intrinsic motivation. The next factor to be determined is whether the objectives should be assigned by a manager or set collectively in collaboration with the employees. The answer to this depends on perceptions of goal-making and the culture of the organization. If opposition to goals is expected, the use of participation in goal setting should increase acceptance. However, if participation is incompatible with culture, goals must be assigned. If participation and culture are incompatible, employees are likely to perceive the participation process as manipulative and will be adversely affected by it. Regardless of whether the objectives are achievable or in management's perceptions of the employee's competence, if employees consider them unattainable they will reduce their effort. Managers must be confident, then, that employees feel confident that their efforts can lead to performance goals. For managers this means that employees must have the capacity to carry out the work and must treat the evaluation process as valid. Because workers have different needs, what serves as reinforcement for one may not be for another. Managers can use their knowledge of each employee to personalize the rewards over which they have control. Some of the more obvious rewards that managers assign include salary, promotions, autonomy, the scope and depth of the role and the opportunity to participate in setting goals and making decisions. Managers should make the rewards contingent on performance. Rewarding non-performance factors will only reinforce those other factors. Key rewards such as salary increases and promotions or progress towards achieving the employee's specific goals should be allocated. Depending on how to maximize the impact of rewards, managers should look for ways to increase their visibility. Eliminating the secrecy around pay by openly communicating everyone's pay, advertising performance bonuses and allocating annual pay rises in a lump sum instead of distributing them over a full year are examples of actions that will make rewards more visible and possibly more motivating. The way rewards are distributed should be transparent so that employees understand that rewards or outcomes are equitable and equal to the inputs given. On a simplistic level, experience, abilities, effort, and other obvious inputs should account for differences in pay, responsibilities, and other obvious outcomes. The problem, however, is complicated by the existence of dozens of inputs and results and the fact that groups of workers attach different degrees of importance to them. For example, a study that compared clerical and manufacturing workers identified nearly twenty inputs and results. Clerical workers considered factors such as the quality of work performed and knowledge of work near the top of their list, but these were at the bottom of the list of production workers. Similarly, production workers thought the most important inputs were intelligence and personal involvement in task performance, two factors that were quite low in officials' importance ratings. There were also important, albeit less dramatic, differences on the outcome side. For example, production workers rated the progress highly, whereas clerical workers rated the progress in the bottom third of their list. Such findings suggest that one person's capital is another's inequality, and thus an ideal should probably consider different inputs and outcomes depending on the group of workers.

Therefore, high-achievers should not be put in jobs that are incompatible with their needs. High-achievers will do best when the role provides moderately challenging objectives and where there is independence and feedback. The literature on goal-setting theory suggests that managers should ensure that all employees have specific goals and take notes on how well they are on those goals. The next factor to be determined is whether the objectives should be assigned by a manager or set collectively in collaboration with the employees. The answer to this depends on perceptions of goal-making and the culture of the organization. If opposition to goals is expected, the use of participation in goal setting should increase acceptance. Among the many reasons cited are low compensation, inadequate benefits, poor working conditions and morale, and compromised employee attitudes (Maroudas et al., 2008). This was succinctly summarized by Michel et al. (2013): 'Providing support to employees gives them the confidence to do their jobs better and the motivation to stay in the organization. 'Hospitality organizations can therefore improve the motivation and retention of employees through the development and improvement of their working conditions. These conditions are inherently related to the work environment. While it appears that employees' responses to their job characteristics may be influenced by a tendency to view their work environment negatively, there is no evidence to support this hypothesis (Spector et al., 2000). There is a strong relationship between employees' perceptions and certain factors in their work environment that are separate from the job itself, including company policies, wages, and vacations. In a real sense, the services of hotel workers represent their industry (Schneider and Bowen, 1993). This representation has generally been limited to guest experiences. This suggests that there was a dichotomy between the guest environment provided in luxury hotels and the working conditions of their employees. Therefore, it is essential for hotel management to develop HRM practices that allow them to inspire and retain talented employees. This requires an understanding of what motivates employees at different management levels and at different stages of their careers (Enz and Siguaw, 2000). This suggests that it is helpful for hotel managers to understand which practices are best for increasing employee satisfaction and retention. Herzberg (1966) proposes that people have two main types of needs, the first being extrinsic motivational factors relating to the context in which the work is carried out, rather than the work itself. These include working conditions and job security. When these factors are not positive, job dissatisfaction can arise. Significantly, however, just fulfilling these needs does not result in satisfaction, but only a reduction in dissatisfaction (Maroudas et al., 2008). Employees also have internal motivational needs or motivations, which include factors such as achievements and recognition. Unlike external factors, motivating factors may ideally result in job satisfaction (Maroudas et al., 2008). For example, Tews, Michel and Stafford (2013) conducted a study that focused on staff from a theme restaurant chain in the United States, it was found that enjoyable activities had a positive effect on performance and managers' support for fun had a positive effect on reducing turnover. Their findings support the view that fun may indeed have a beneficial effect, but that the framing of that fun must be carefully aligned with both organizational goals and employee characteristics. “Managers must learn how to achieve the delicate balance of allowing employees the freedom to enjoy work while maintaining high levels of performance” (Tews et al., 2013). Those particularly suited to the hospitality industry include providing adequate breaks during the working day, staff functions involving families and providing health and wellbeing opportunities.

premise: Multitasking debate Can you do them at the same time? Talking on the phone while driving isn't the only situation where we've been worse at multitasking than we might like to think we are. New research has identified a bottleneck in our brains that some say means we are fundamentally incapable of true multitasking. If experimental findings reflect real-world performance, people who think they're multitasking probably just don't succeed in all of their parallel occupations or at best, except one. Practice may improve your performance, but you will never be as good as when you focus on one task at a time. The problem, according to Renee Marois, a psychologist at Vanderbilt University in Nashville, Tennessee, is that there's a sticking point in the brain. To demonstrate this, Marois devised an experiment to locate it. Volunteers watch a screen and when a certain image appears, a red circle, say, they have to press a key with their index finger. Circles of different colors require clicks from different fingers. A typical response time is about half a second, and the volunteers quickly reached their peak performance. Then they learn to listen to different recordings and respond by playing a specific sound. For example, when they hear a bird chirp, they should say ba; an electronic sound should trigger a line, and so on. Again, no problem. An ordinary person can do this in about half a second, with almost no effort. The trouble comes when Marois shows volunteers a photo, then almost immediately plays them a sound. Now they are confused. If you view an image and play a sound at the same time, one task is deferred, he says. In fact, if the second task is presented within half a second or so that it takes to process and respond to the first, it will simply be delayed until the first is completed. The greatest delays in duplicate tasks occur when both tasks are displayed at the same time; delays gradually shorten as the interval between task presentation lengthens. There are at least three points where we seem to be getting stuck, says Marois. The first is simply to identify what was being looked at. This can take a few tenths of a second, during which we are unable to see and identify the second item. This limitation is known as the attentional blink: experiments have shown that if you maintain a certain event and a second event appears unexpectedly at any time within that crucial window of concentration, it may register in your visual cortex but you won't be able to act on it. Interestingly, if you do not look forward to the first event, you have no problem responding to the second. What exactly causes the attention blink is still a matter of debate. A second limitation is in our short-term visual memory. It is estimated that we can track about four items at a time, less if they are complex. A deficiency in this ability is thought to explain, in part, our staggering inability to detect even enormous changes in otherwise identical scenes, the so-called changes blindness. Show people pairs of nearly identical pictures, say, aircraft engines in one picture disappeared in the other picture and they won't be able to spot the differences. However, again, there is disagreement as to what really is the essential limiting factor. Does it boil down to a shortage of storage capacity, or does it have to do with how much attention the viewer pays? A THIRD LIMITATION IS THAT CHOOSING A RESPONSE TO INHIBIT STIMULUS WHEN YOU SEE A CHILD ON THE ROAD, FOR EXAMPLE, OR TO ANSWER WHEN YOUR MOTHER TELLS YOU ON THE PHONE THAT SHE'S THINKING OF LEAVING YOUR FATHER ALSO REQUIRES BRAINPOWER. Choosing a response to one of these things will delay by a few tenths of a second your ability to respond to the other. This is called the bottleneck theory of reaction selection, first proposed in 1952. But David Meyer, a psychologist at the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, isn't buying the bottleneck idea. He thinks the interruption of dual tasks is just evidence of a strategy used by the brain to prioritize multiple activities. Meyer is known as an optimist by his friends. He has written papers with titles like near-perfect time-sharing performing dual tasks: opening the central cognitive bottleneck. His experiments showed that with enough practice at least 2000 attempts some people can perform two tasks simultaneously as competently as they perform them one after the other. He suggests that there is a central cognitive processor that coordinates all of this, and what's more, he thinks he uses discretion sometimes he chooses to delay one task while completing another task. Marois agrees that practice can sometimes erase interference effects. He found that with just one hour of practice each day for two weeks, the volunteers show a huge improvement in managing his two tasks at once. Where he disagrees with Meyer is in what the brain does to achieve it. Marois speculates that practice may give us the opportunity to find less crowded circles to perform a task, such as finding reliable back streets to avoid heavy traffic on major roads, making our response an unconscious task. After all, there are plenty of examples of subconscious multitasking that most of us routinely engage in: walking and talking, eating and reading, watching TV, and folding the laundry. It's probably not surprising that in general, we get worse at multitasking as we get older. According to Art Kramer of the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, who studies how aging affects our cognitive abilities, we are talking in our twenties. Although the decline is slow during the 30s of our lives and on until the 50s of our lives, it is there; and after 55 it becomes more agile. In one study, he and colleagues asked young and older participants to perform a simulated driving task while talking. He found that while younger drivers tended to miss background changes, older drivers failed to notice things that were most relevant. Similarly, older subjects had more difficulty paying attention to the more important parts of a scene than younger drivers. However, it's not all bad news for the over-55s. Kramer also found that older people can benefit from the practice. Not only did they learn to perform better, brain scans showed that underlying this improvement was a change in the way their brains become active. While it's clear that often practice can make a difference, especially as we get older, the basic facts remain sobering. We have this impression of an all-powerful complex mind, says Marois, and yet we have very degrading and crippling limits. For most of our history, we've probably never had to do more than one thing at a time, he says, and so we haven't evolved to be able to. But maybe we will in the future. We may yet look back one day at people like Debbie and Alon as ancestors to a new breed of true multitaskers.

In addition, it can be argued that the practice of interpreting or reading each medium follows different conventions. In many cases, the architectural style of the building further reinforces this idea. In addition, a collection as large as that of London's National Gallery is housed in several rooms, each with dozens of works, each of which may be worth more than anything the average visitor has. Moreover, considering the value of the original work within the framework of its treasury impresses the viewer that because these works were originally produced, they were assigned enormous monetary value by a person or institution more powerful than themselves. It is clear that nothing the viewer thinks of the piece will change that value, so today's viewer is deterred from trying to extend the same kind of spontaneous, immediate, self-contained reading that would have originally met the piece. This displacement effect is further amplified by the sheer volume of exhibits. A fundamental difference between paintings and other art forms is that there is no set time when viewing a painting. Conversely, the audience is encouraged by an opera or play over a certain length of time, which is the duration of the show. Similarly, novels and poems are read in a set temporal sequence, while the picture has no obvious place to start watching, or in which to end. Thus works of art themselves encourage us to see them superficially, without appreciating the richness of detail and work involved. As a result, the dominant critical approach becomes that of the art historian, a specialized academic approach dedicated to discovering the meaning of art in the cultural context of its time. Again, this seems to be paid to the same spontaneous and participatory criticism, which can be found in abundance in criticism of works of classical literature, but absent in most art history. premise: Natural Pesticide in India A dramatic story about cotton farmers in India shows just how devastating pesticides can be to people and the environment; and why today's agriculture is so dependent on pesticides. This story also shows that it is possible to stop using chemical pesticides without losing a crop to destructive insects, and it explains how to do it. THE STORY STARTED ABOUT 30 YEARS AGO, A HANDFUL OF FAMILIES MIGRATED FROM GUNTUR DISTRICT IN ANDHRA PRADESH, SOUTHEAST INDIA, TO PONOKOLA, A COMMUNITY OF ABOUT 900 PEOPLE FARMING PLOTS OF BETWEEN TWO AND 10 ACRES. The foreigners from Guntur brought cotton culture with them. Cotton sought out farmers by promising to put in more money than the mixed crops they had already grown to eat and sell: millet, sorghum, groundnuts, pigeon peas, mung beans, chillies and rice. But growing cotton meant the use of pesticides and fertilizers until then was a mystery for the largely illiterate farmers of the community. When cotton production began to spread in the state of Andhra Pradesh. The high value of cotton made it a particularly attractive crop, but growing cotton required chemical fertilizers and pesticides. Because most farmers were poor, illiterate and with no previous experience of using agricultural chemicals, they had to rely on small-scale local agribusiness traders for advice. The merchants sold them seeds, fertilizers and pesticides on credit and also secured the purchase of their crops. The dealers themselves had little technical knowledge about pesticides. They were merely relaying promotional information from multinational chemical companies that supplied their products. At first, cotton yields were high, and pesticide spending was low because cotton pests had not yet moved in. Farmers have never earned so much! But within a few years, cottonwood pests like ballworms and aphids hit the fields, and farmers saw how rapid the evolution of the insects could be. Repeated spraying killed the weaker pests, but left those most resistant to pesticides to reproduce. As pesticide resistance increased, farmers had to apply more and more pesticides to achieve the same results. AT THE SAME TIME, THE PESTICIDES KILLED BIRDS, WASPS, BEETLES, SPIDERS AND OTHER PREDATORS THAT ONCE PROVIDED NATURAL PEST INSECT CONTROL. Without these predators, the pests could destroy the entire crop if no pesticides were used. Eventually, farmers mixed cocktails of pesticides containing up to ten different brands and sometimes had to spray their cotton frequently up to twice a week. They were really hooked! THE VILLAGERS HESITATED, BUT ONE OF THE ELDERS OF THE VILLAGE OF PONOKOLA DECIDED TO RISK TRYING THE NATURAL METHODS INSTEAD OF PESTICIDES. His son collapsed from acute pesticide poisoning and survived but the hospital bill was staggering. The SecuRes team trained this village on how to protect its cotton crop using a toolkit of natural practices that the India Centre for Sustainable Agriculture put together in collaboration with scientists from Andhra Prades State University. They called the toolkit pesticide-free management or NPM. The most important resource in the NPM toolkit was the neem tree (Azadirachta indica) common in most of India. A neem tree is a broad-leaved evergreen tree related to the mahogany. It protects itself from insects by producing an abundance of natural pesticides that act in a variety of ways: with an arsenal of chemical defenses that repel egg-laying, interfere with insect growth and, most importantly, disrupt the ability of crop-eating insects to sense their food. In fact, neem has traditionally been used in India to protect stored grains from insects and to produce soaps, skin creams and other health products. To protect crops from insects, neem seeds are simply ground into a powder that is soaked overnight in water. The solution is then sprayed onto the crop. Another preparation, neem cake, can be mixed into the soil to kill soil pests and diseases, and is used as a nitrogen-rich organic fertilizer. Neem trees are grown locally, so the only cost is the labor to prepare neem for application in the fields. The first farmers' experiment with NPM was a complete success! His harvest was as good as that of farmers who used pesticides, and he earned much more because he did not spend a single rupee on pesticides. Inspired by this success, 20 farmers tried NPM the next year. SECURE PLACED TWO WELL-TRAINED TEAMS IN PUNOKOLA TO TEACH AND HELP EVERYONE IN THE VILLAGE, AND THE VILLAGE WOMEN PUT PRESSURE ON THEIR HUSBANDS TO STOP USING TOXIC CHEMICALS. Families who no longer exposed themselves to pesticides began to feel much better, and the rapid improvements in income, health, and general well-being quickly sold everyone the value of NPM. By 2000, all farmers in Ponocola were using NPM, not only for cotton but also for their other crops. H. The suicide epidemic has come to an end. And with the money, health and energy that returned when they stopped poisoning themselves with pesticides, villagers were inspired to start more community and business projects. The women of Ponocola created a new source of income by collecting, milling and selling neem seeds for the NPM in other villages. Villagers bailed out their children with contracts and gave them special six-month pick-up courses to return to school. Fighting pesticides, and winning, have boosted rural solidarity, self-confidence and optimism about the future. When merchants tried to punish NPM users by paying less for NPM cotton, farmers banded together to form a marketing cooperative that found fairer prices elsewhere. The leadership and cooperation skills that the citizens of Ponocola developed in the NPM struggle helped them tackle other challenges, such as water purification, building a cotton gin that would add value to cotton before selling it, and convincing the state government to support the NPM in resisting multinational pest control corporations.

premise: Nature on display in American zoos The first zoo in the United States opened in Philadelphia in 1874, followed by the Cincinnati Zoo the following year. By 1940, there were zoos in more than 100 American cities. The Philadelphia Zoo was more thoroughly designed and better funded than most of the hundreds of zoos that would later open, but in its landscape and its mission to educate and entertain it embodied ideas on how to build a zoo that remained consistent for decades. Zoos arose in the late nineteenth century during the transition of the United States from a rural, agricultural state to an industrial nation. The population more than doubled between 1860 and 1900. As more middle-class people lived in cities, they began to seek new relationships with the natural world as a place for recreation, self-improvement, and spiritual renewal. Cities have established systems of public parks, and nature tourism has already become even more fashionable with the establishment of national parks. Nature is considered good for people of all ages and classes. The study of nature was incorporated into school curricula, and collecting natural history became an increasingly popular pastime. At the same time, the fields of research formerly considered natural history have grown into separate fields like taxonomy, experimental embryology, and genetics, each with its own specialists and structures. As laboratory research gained prestige in the zoology departments of American universities, the gap between professional and amateur scientific activities widened. Previously natural history was open to enthusiasts and was easily popularized, but research required access to microscopes and other equipment in laboratories, as well as advanced education. The new zoos distinguish themselves from migratory animal displays by stating their mission as the education and advancement of science, in addition to recreation. Zoos introduced zoology for the non-specialist, at a time when the intellectual distance between amateur naturalists and laboratory-oriented zoologists was increasing. They attracted a wide audience and quickly became a feature of any growing, forward-thinking city. They were symbols of civic pride at an importance level with art museums, natural history museums and botanical gardens. Most American zoos were founded and operated as part of the Public Parks Administration. They depended on municipal funds, and they did not charge an entrance fee. They tended to assemble as many different mammal and bird species as possible, along with several reptiles, presenting one or two specimens from each, and they competed with each other to be the first to introduce a rarity, like a rhinoceros. In the constant effort to attract the public for repeat visits, certain types of display have come in and gone out of fashion; for example, dozens of zoos have built special islands for their large monkey populations. In the 1930s, the Works Progress Administration funded millions of dollars of construction at dozens of zoos, for the most part, the animal collections were organized by species and a combination of enclosures according to a fairly loose classification scheme. Although many histories of individual zoos describe the 1940s through the 1960s as a period of stagnation, and in some cases there was neglect, new zoos continued to be established throughout the country. In the 1940s and 1950s, the first zoos designed specifically for children were built, some with the attraction of farm animals. An increasing number of zoos have tried new ways to organize their displays. In addition to the traditional approach of displaying similar types together, zoo planners had a new approach of placing animals in groups according to their continent of origin and designing exhibits showing animals from particular habitats, for example, polar, desert, or forest. During the 1960s, some zoos arranged some displays according to animal behavior; the Bronx Zoo, for example, opened the World of Darkness exhibit of nocturnal animals. Paradoxically, at the same time as zoo displays began incorporating ideas about the ecological relationships between animals, big cats and primates continued to be displayed in the bathroom as cages lined with tiles. In the 1970s, a new wave of reform emerged. Popular movements for environmentalism and animal welfare drew attention to endangered species and to zoos that did not provide adequate care for their animals. More projects were undertaken by research scientists and zoos began employing full-time veterinarians as they stepped up captive breeding programs. Many zoos that were supported entirely by municipal budgets began to enlist private financial support and charge admission fees. In the prosperous eighties and nineties. Zoos have built realistic landscape immersion exhibits, many of them around the theme of the tropical rainforest. Increasingly, conservation has moved to the forefront of the zoo's agenda. Although zoos were popular and pervasive institutions in the United States in the early twentieth century, historians have paid little attention to them. Zoos may have been overlooked because they were and still remain multipurpose institutions, and as such they fall among the categories of analysis that historians often use. In addition, their stated goals of recreation, education, advancement of science, and protection of endangered species often clashed. Zoos occupy a difficult middle ground between science and show, high culture and low and remote forests and the hamlet city landscape, and urban wildlife and people.

premise: Nature or nurture? Several years ago, in one of the most fascinating and disturbing experiments in behavioral psychology, Stanley Milgram of Yale University tested 40 subjects from all walks of life for their willingness to obey instructions given by a 'leader' in a situation where subjects might feel personal aversion to the actions they were called to perform. Specifically, Milgram told each “subject teacher” volunteer that the experiment was for the noble purpose of education, and was intended to test whether punishing students for their mistakes would have a positive effect on students' learning ability or not. Milgram's experimental setup consisted of placing the teacher subject in front of a panel of thirty switches with labels that ranged from '15 volts electrical (mild shock) 'to '450 volts (severe shock hazard)' in phases of 15 volts each. The teacher-subject was told that whenever the student gives an incorrect answer to a question, a shock should be given, starting from the lowest level and increasing in severity with each successive wrong answer. The supposed “student” was in reality an actor hired by Milgram to simulate receiving shocks by emitting a spectrum of groans, screams, and writings along with an assortment of statements and phrases defending both the experimenter and the experimenter. Milgram told the teacher subject to ignore the student's reactions, and administer whatever level of shock was required, in accordance with the rule governing the experimental situation of the moment. As the experiment evolved, the student would deliberately give incorrect answers to the questions posed by the teacher, thus bringing various electrical penalties, even up to the danger level of 300 volts or higher. Many of the taught subjects shied away from providing the higher levels of punishment, and turned to Milgram with a questioning look and/or complaints about the continuation of the experiment. IN THESE SITUATIONS, MILGRAM CALMLY EXPLAINED THAT THE TEACHER SUBJECT SHOULD IGNORE THE STUDENT'S CALLS FOR MERCY AND CONTINUE THE EXPERIMENT. If the subject is still averse to continuing, Milgram said that it is important for the purpose of the experiment to carry out the procedure to the end. His last argument was 'You have no other choice. You have to move on.” What Milgram was trying to find out was the number of teachers-professions who would be willing to administer the highest levels of shock, even in the face of strong personal and moral aversion against the experiment rules and experimental conditions. Before conducting the experiment, Milgram explained his idea to a group of 39 psychiatrists and asked them to predict the average percentage of people in a normal population who would be willing to give the highest shock level of 450 volts. The overwhelming consensus was that almost all teacher professionals would refuse to obey the experimenter. The psychiatrists felt that “most subjects would not go beyond 150 volts” and they expected that only four percent would rise to 300 volts. Moreover, they thought that only a crazy margin of roughly one in 1,000 would give the highest shock of 450 volts. What were the actual results? Well, more than 60% of teachers continued to comply with Milgram up to the 450 volt limit in rehearsals of the experiment in other countries, the percentage of obedient teacher professions was even higher, reaching 85% in one country. How can we explain this huge gap between what calm, rational, knowledgeable people predict in the comfort of their studies and what stressed, confused but cooperative “teachers” actually do in a real-life laboratory? Man's first inclination may be to argue that there must be some sort of built-in animal aggression instinct triggered by the experiment, and that Milgram's tea subjects merely followed a genetic need to discharge this extinguished initial impulse onto the pupil by administering the electric shock. A hard-nosed modern sociobiologist might even go so far as to argue that this aggressive instinct evolved as a beneficial trait, having been of survival value to our ancestors in their struggle against the hardships of life on the plains and caves, eventually finding its way into our genetic makeup as a remnant of our ancient animal ways. An alternative to this idea of genetic programming is to see the teachers-subjects' actions as a result of the social environment in which the experiment was performed. As Milgram himself noted, 'Most subjects in the experiment see their behavior in a larger context that is both beneficial and beneficial to society in its search for scientific truth. The psychological laboratory has a strong claim to legitimacy and inspires trust and confidence in whoever appears there. An action such as victim shock, which in isolation looks bad, takes on a completely different meaning when placed in this framework. Thus, in this explanation the subject merges his unique personality and personal and moral code with that of larger institutional structures, while giving up individual qualities such as loyalty, self-sacrifice, and discipline to the service of malevolent authority systems. Here we have two radically different explanations for why so many professional-teachers were willing to give up their sense of personal responsibility for the sake of an institutional authority figure. The problem for biologists, psychologists and anthropologists is to find out which of these two polar explanations is more likely. It is, in essence, the problem of modern sociobiology to discover the extent to which rigid genetic programming dictates, or at least biases greatly, the interaction of animals and humans with their environment, namely their behavior. In other words, sociobiology is concerned with elucidating the biological basis of all behavior.
hypothesis: In sociological explanation, personal values are stronger than authority.

premise: Networking as a concept has acquired what is in fact an unjustified atmosphere of modernity. It is regarded in the corporate world as an essential tool for the modern businessman, since they go around the world drumming up business for themselves or the corporation. The idea was worn as a badge of distinction, and not just in the business world. People can be divided basically into those who keep personal knowledge and contacts to themselves, and those who are willing to share what they know and indeed their friends with others. An insecure person, for example someone who has difficulty sharing information with others and is unable to bring people together, including friends, does not make for a good network. The classic network is someone strong enough within themselves to connect different people including close friends with each other. For example, a businessman or academic may meet someone who may be a valuable contact in the future, but currently that person may benefit from meeting another associate or friend. It takes a fairly confident person to bring these people together and allow a relationship to develop independently of himself. From the point of view of non-networks such a development may be intolerable, especially if it occurs outside their control. The unfortunate thing here is that the initiator of the relationship, if he knew this, would be the one who would be most beneficial. And why? Because all things being equal, people move within circles and that person has the potential to be sucked into ever-increasing spheres of new connections. They say if you know eight people, you're in touch with everyone in the world. It does not take much common sense to realize the potential of any type of venture since a person is able to rely on the experience of more and more people. Unfortunately, the creation of new contacts, business or other, while it brings success, causes problems. It expands the world of details. It's really not a bad thing altogether, but it puts more pressure on the network admin through the need to maintain an increasingly large circle of people. The most convenient way out is, perhaps, to eliminate old contacts, but this will be anathema to our network worker since it will defeat the entire purpose of the network. Another problem is the reaction of friends and associates. A lean spread gives a person less time for others who might have been closer to it in the past. In the workplace this can cause tension with jealous colleagues, and even with superiors who might be tempted to rein in more successful inferiors. Jealousy and jealousy can turn out to be very harmful if faced with a very insecure manager, since this person may seek to strangle someone's career or even block it completely. The answer here is to let their superiors share in the glory; throw them a few crumbs of comfort. It's called leadership from below. In the current business climate, companies and organizations need to cooperate with each other in order to expand. As globalization grows rapidly, societies need to be able to sprawl not just over countries but continents. While people may resist this development, for the moment it is here to stay. Without cooperation and connections, specialist companies will not survive long. Computer components, for example, need to be compatible with the different machines that exist on the market and to achieve this, companies need to work in collaboration with others. No business or institution can afford to be an island in today's environment. In the not so distant past, it was possible for companies to go it alone, but now it is more difficult to do this. The same goes for the academic world, where ideas have been jealously guarded. The opening of universities and colleges to the outside world in recent years has greatly benefited industry and educational institutions. The stereotypical academic is one who moves in a rarefied atmosphere and lives a life of sometimes spectacular isolation, a prisoner of his own genius. This type of person does not easily fit into the modern network format. Yet even this lonely world is changing. IVORY TOWERS REMAIN INCREASINGLY FREQUENT AS EDUCATION EXPERTS FORM LINKS WITH OTHER BODIES; SOMETIMES TO STARTLING EFFECT AS IN SILICON VALLEY IN AMERICA AND AROUND CAMBRIDGE IN ENGLAND, WHICH NOW HAS ONE OF THE MOST CONCENTRATED CLUSTERS OF HIGH-TECH COMPANIES IN EUROPE. It's the network callers, the wheeler-dealers, movers and movers, call them what you will, who carry the world on. The world of Neanderthals shook between 35,000 and 40,000 BC; they were replaced by Homo sapiens with the networking skills that separate us from other animals: understanding, abstraction of thought and culture, which are inextricably linked to survival planning and productivity in humans. They say the meek will inherit the earth. But will they?
hypothesis: Networking is not a modern idea.
label: e

premise: Neuroaesthetics An emerging discipline called neuroaesthetics seeks to bring scientific objectivity to the study of art, and has already given us a better understanding of many masterpieces. The blurred imagery of impressionist paintings seems to stimulate the amygdala in the brain, for example. Because the amygdala plays a crucial role in our emotions, this finding may explain why many people find these parts so exciting. Could the same approach also shed light on abstract twentieth-century works, from geometric blocks of Mondrian paint, to Pollux's seemingly random arrangements of paint splashing on canvas? Skeptics believe that people claim to like such works simply because they are famous. We definitely have a tendency to follow the crowd. When asked to make simple perceptual decisions such as fitting a shape to its rotated image, for example, people often choose a completely wrong answer if they see others doing the same. It's easy to imagine that this mentality would have an even greater impact on a fuzzy concept like artistic appreciation, where there is no right or wrong answer. Angelina Holly-Dolan, of Boston College, Massachusetts, responded to this debate by asking volunteers to view pairs of paintings or works by famous abstract artists or doodles of babies, chimpanzees and elephants. They were then forced to judge what they preferred. A third of the paintings received no captions, while many were incorrectly marked volunteers might think they were watching a chimp with messy brushstrokes when they actually saw an acclaimed masterpiece. In each set of experiments, volunteers typically preferred the work of well-known artists, even when believed to be by an animal or child. It seems that the viewer can sense the vision of the artists in the paintings, even if they cannot explain why. Robert Pepperell, an artist based at Cardiff University, creates obscure works that are neither entirely abstract nor clearly representative. In one study, Pepperell and his collaborators asked volunteers to decide how strong they considered a piece a work, and whether they saw anything familiar in the piece. The longer it took them to answer these questions, the more they rated the piece under review, and the greater their neural activity. The brain seems to see these images as riddles, and the more difficult it is to decipher the meaning, the more rewarding the moment of recognition. And what about artists like Mondrian, whose paintings consist entirely of horizontal and vertical lines enveloping blocks of paint? Mondrian works are deceptively simple, but eye-tracking studies confirm that they are carefully composed, and that simply rotating a piece radically changes how we see it. With the original, the volunteers' eyes tended to stay longer in certain places in the image, but with the altered versions they would fly across a piece more quickly. As a result, the volunteers viewed the altered versions as less enjoyable when they later rated the work. In a similar study, Oisin Vartanian of the University of Toronto asked volunteers to compare original drawings to those he had altered by moving objects within the frame. He found that almost everyone preferred the original, be it a Van Gogh still life or an abstract by Miró. Vartanian also found that changing the composition of the paintings reduced activation in those brain regions associated with meaning and interpretation. In another experiment, Alex Forsythe of the University of Liverpool analysed the visual complexity of different artworks, and its results suggest that many artists use a central level of detail to please the brain. Too little and the work is boring, but too much leads to a kind of perceptual overload; according to Forsythe. Moreover, attractive works are both abstract and representational, showing signs of repeated motifs of fractals repeated on a different scale. Fractals are common throughout nature, for example in the forms of mountain peaks or tree branches. It is possible that our visual system, which has developed in the great outdoors, makes it easier to process such patterns. It is also intriguing that the brain seems to process movement when we see a handwritten letter, as if we were reproducing the writers' moment of creation. This has led some to wonder whether Pollux's works feel so dynamic because the brain reproduces the energetic actions the artist used while painting. This could depend on our brain's mirror neurons, which are known to mimic other actions. However, it will be necessary to test the hypothesis thoroughly. We may even be able to use neuroaesthetic studies to understand the lifespan of some works of art. While the fashions of the period may shape what is popular today, works best adapted to our visual system may be most likely to linger once the trends of previous generations have been forgotten. It's still early days in the field of neuroaesthetics and these studies are probably just a taste of what's to come. However, it would be foolish to reduce the appreciation of art to a set of scientific laws. The importance of the style of a particular artist, his place in history and the artistic environment of his time should not be underestimated. Abstract art offers both a challenge and the freedom to play with different interpretations. In some ways, it's not that different from science, where we're constantly looking for systems and deciphering meaning so we can see and appreciate the world in a new way.
hypothesis: Some ideas about the relationship between mirror neurons and art appreciation require further validation.

The NYLSO is an amateur orchestra for mature players of violin, viola, cello, and contrabass. If you played a string instrument when you were younger and would like to start over, or if you are studying as an adult and would like the opportunity to play in a group of similar people, then NYLSO is for you! Our goal is to create a fun, supportive and non-competitive environment for adults aged 18 to 80+ who wish to participate in collective music creation. Participants should have basic music reading skills and a willingness to commit to the group, but are not required to audition. It is recommended to study your device for at least one year. If you've ever been paid to play your instrument, have recently graduated with a degree in performing, or you've been playing continuously since grade school, you may decide we're not the right team for you. How we work: We know that New Yorkers are busy people. It's okay if you miss an entire rehearsal period when an emergency arises. In the end, however, too many absences disrupt the functioning of the group and make it difficult to perform the pieces. The sessions are held in six-week rehearsal cycles, with two-hour rehearsals taking place once a week. We work with the goal of producing one to three very informal concerts of friends and family per year. Our professional conductor/facilitator acts as a coach and conductor during rehearsals. Substitute conductors also join to teach various segments, providing groups of players with valuable experience working with different approaches and styles. Everyone is encouraged to play to their full potential, whatever that may be, but please recognize that although we have a conductor, her role is not to provide one-on-one guidance during rehearsals. NYLSO is a self-supporting collective; we receive no other funding. The cost is $80 per six-week cycle. The payments apply to rehearsal space costs, conductors' fees and music photography. Materials you will need in rehearsals: you will need an instrument, a portable music stand and any other relevant accessories. You should bring a folder to keep your music together and a soft lead pencil with an eraser for writing in changes. Music is provided.

BUT THE POLITICAL URGE TO SIGN SOMETHING EVERY FOUR OR FIVE YEARS HAS ONLY BEEN INTERRUPTED, RATHER THAN SILENCED, BY THAT FAILURE. In 2007, the EU marks the 50th anniversary of another treaty - the Treaty of Rome, its founding treaty. Government leaders have already agreed to celebrate it ceremoniously, reaffirming their commitment to an increasingly close union and to the fundamental ideals of European unity. Then, according to the bureaucratic planners in Brussels and Berlin, emphatically ignoring the possibility of a public rejection, the whole thing would be signed, signed and a new constitution handed down in 2009-2010. That didn't happen in 2005—06. Defensive, cynical and destructive, the leaders of the eurozone's three biggest countries - France, Italy and Germany - stumbled towards their undisputed goals. They saw no reason to resort to any kind of European policy and the EU, as a result, barely functioned. But by mid-2007 all three would disappear, and this fact alone would change the European political landscape. The result is that the politics of the three major continental countries, the bureaucratic momentum and the economy of recovery will all be matched to give a boost towards integration in 2007. That doesn't mean Momentum will be irresistible or even popular. The UK government, for example, will almost certainly not want to go with the flow, beginning another chapter in the long history of confrontation between Britain and the rest of Europe.
