premise: Counting One of the first great intellectual achievements of a young child is learning to speak, followed by learning to count. From earliest childhood we are so tied to our number system that it is a feat of imagination to consider the problems faced by early humans who have not yet developed this facility. Careful consideration of our number system leads to the belief that rather than being a fixture that comes naturally to man, it is one of the great and remarkable achievements of humankind. It is impossible to study the sequence of events that led to the development of the concept of number. Even the earliest tribes had a counting system that, if not advanced, was sufficient for the tasks they had to perform. Our ancestors didn't have much use for actual numbers; instead their considerations were more similar than the type Is that enough? Instead of how much? When they were engaged in collecting food, for example. However, when early humans first began to reflect on the nature of things around them, they found that they needed the idea of a simple number to keep their thoughts in order. As they began to settle, breed plants and herd animals, the need for a sophisticated number system became paramount. One will never know how and when this ability to count evolved, but it is certain that counting evolved well until humans created even semi-permanent settlements. Evidence of early stages of arithmetic and counting can be easily found. The indigenous peoples in Tasmania were able to count only one, two, many; those of South Africa counted one, two, two and one, two, two and one, and so on. But in real situations the number and words are often accompanied by gestures to help resolve any confusion. For example, when using a system of one, two, many types, the word plural means, look at my hands and see how many fingers I show you. This basic approach is limited in the range of numbers it can express, but this range will usually suffice when dealing with the simpler aspects of human existence. The inability of some cultures to handle large numbers isn't really surprising. European languages, when studied for their previous version, are very poor in the number of words and phrases. THE ANCIENT GOTHIC WORD FOR TEN, TACHUND, IS USED TO PHRASE THE NUMBER 100 AS TACHUND TACHUND. By the seventh century, the word teon had become interchangeable with the Tachund or Hund of the Anglo-Saxon language, so 100 was noted as hund teontig, or ten times ten. The average person in 7th century Europe did not know the numbers as we know them today. In fact, to be a witness in a court of law a person had to be able to count to nine! Perhaps the most fundamental step in developing a sense of number is not the ability to count, but to see that a number is really an abstract idea instead of a simple attachment to a set of certain objects. It must have been within the reach of the earliest humans imaginable that four birds are distinct from two birds; however, it is not an elementary step to link the number 4, as related to four birds, to the number 4, as connected to four rocks. Number association as one of the attributes of a specific object is a major obstacle to the development of true number sense. When the number 4 in the brain can be written down as a specific word, regardless of the object to which it is referred to, the person is ready to take the first step towards developing a system of notations for numbers and from there to arithmetic. Traces of the first stages in the evolution of numbers can be seen in several languages alive today. The number system of the Chesimchian language in British Columbia contains seven separate word groups for numbers according to the type of item counted: for counting flat objects and animals, for round objects and time, for people, for long objects and trees, for canoes, for measurements and counting when no particular object is narrated. The latter appears to be a later development whereas the first six groups present remnants of an older system. This variety of number names can also be found in some common languages like Japanese. Mixed with the development of number sense is the development of counting ability. Counting is not directly related to the formation of a number concept because counting can be done by matching the counted items to a group of pebbles, corn grains, or counters fingers. These aids were indispensable to very early people who would have found the process impossible without some kind of mechanical assistance. Such aids, although different, are still used even by the most educated in today's society due to their convenience. All counting ultimately involves reference to something other than the things being counted. At first it may have been grains or pebbles, but now it's a sequence of memorized words that happen to be the names of the numbers.

Careful consideration of our number system leads to the belief that rather than being a fixture that comes naturally to man, it is one of the great and remarkable achievements of humankind. It is impossible to study the sequence of events that led to the development of the concept of number. Even the earliest tribes had a counting system that, if not advanced, was sufficient for the tasks they had to perform. Our ancestors didn't have much use for actual numbers; instead their considerations were more similar than the type Is that enough? Instead of how much? When they were engaged in collecting food, for example. However, when early humans first began to reflect on the nature of things around them, they found that they needed the idea of a simple number to keep their thoughts in order. As they began to settle, breed plants and herd animals, the need for a sophisticated number system became paramount. One will never know how and when this ability to count evolved, but it is certain that counting evolved well until humans created even semi-permanent settlements. Evidence of early stages of arithmetic and counting can be easily found. For example, when using a system of one, two, many types, the word plural means, look at my hands and see how many fingers I show you. premise: Old dogs and new tricks The first days of an animal's life play a major role in shaping its future. Cormorant birds are used in China and Japan for catching fish using a traditional method of river fishing that dates back thousands of years. A CORMORANT DIVES UNDERWATER CATCHING A FISH, THEN CLINGS TO A BAMBOO POLE THAT THE FISHERMAN IS HOISTING INTO THE BOAT. It is easy to train a cormorant to behave this way because the bird was drowned on the fisherman instead of its natural mother. The fisherman drowns the cormorant on himself by appearing to the chick as it hatches from the egg. The young bird mistakes the fisherman as the mother bird and bonds with him, responding to his voice and later swimming alongside his boat. This following reaction is nature's way of preventing young birds from straying from their mother. The stamping process lasts a period of up to two days after hatching. After this sensitive period, the effect of imprinting remains unchanged for the duration of the bird's life and cannot be reversed. Dogs, cats, sheep, horses and other animals undergo a process of stamping similar to birds. In the case of dogs, the sensitive period lasts up to 12 weeks. During this period, the puppy can drown both on its natural mother and on humans. Puppies are born blind and deaf, and naturally stay close to their mothers so they don't need an immediate follow-up response. The sensitive period lasts from the second week to the fourteenth week of life. It is critical that a dog socializes with other dogs, family pets, and people within this time frame. If the underlying social behavior is not embedded in the puppy by the fourteenth week it will lead to behavioral problems later in life that are difficult to change. A puppy should be left with its natural mother and litter for several weeks before socializing with people. If a puppy is taken from its natural mother too early and taken care of by people, it considers humans its natural friends and dogs as complete strangers. Dogs that have only socialized with people may be aggressive towards another person's dog or even attack it. Conversely, a dog that has been kept with the mother and litter for too long will not treat humans as companions and is more likely to be aggressive towards people and bite them. Dogs that are not properly socialized with both dogs and people can be difficult to control and will not respond to taming. Negative experiences with humans during the imprinting phase can have lasting effects on a dog. It's a cliche, but bad behavior in a dog is usually the fault of its owner. A rescue dog that has been neglected and abused by its owner may remain nervous and afraid of humans. It is possible for a dog to overcome behavioral problems derived from stamping but it requires a lot of training and may not be completely successful. Negative behaviors are often inadvertently reinforced when a dog gains more attention because of its bad behavior than for behaving well. In obedience training, the dog is taught to respond to basic commands such as sit, stay, drop, and release. In one training technique, the owner shouts a command for example, sit back and if the dog acts accordingly he is rewarded with his favorite toy and receives verbal praise. The dog associates the act of sitting with praise from his owner and learning to obey. It is better to avoid punishment and negative experiences to ensure a safe, happy and obedient dog. Even an old dog can teach new tricks, or at least new behaviors, with daily workouts. Not all dog behavior can be explained by stamping and taming. Generations of captive breeding domesticated dogs so they could live in people's homes as pets, or as working animals. Dogs were selectively bred to enhance or suppress their natural abilities to suit human needs. For example, Border Collie and Belgian Shepherd Dogs are purebred to stimulate sheep and protect them, more so when a dog has been drowned on the flock. Spaniels and retrievers are used as gun dogs to retrieve hunting birds for hunters. Smell dogs such as the Beagle and Foxhound are used to their unusually acute sense of smell when sniffing and tracking prey such as rabbits and foxes. Some dogs, such as pit bull terriers, were deliberately bred for fighting and can make dangerous pets. It is worth remembering that all dogs have been domesticated from wolves, so any dog has the potential to bite the hand that feeds it, no matter how well socialized and trained it is.

premise: Uxbridge Although more than 100 km separate the English cities of Oxford and Cambridge, their universities are linked by the term Uxbridge. It is a name that can be applied to the university or both. Traditionally, a degree at Uxbridge has symbolised the pinnacle of academic achievement. Cities such as Birmingham, Liverpool, Bristol and Manchester had their own universities, but these were not as valued as Oxbridge and were given the Ghanaian title of red-brick universities. In recent times, the name Uxbridge has also become a derogatory term. Some people believe that Uxbridge is part of a social class system that favours the privileged few, born of wealth or high social status, at the expense of the less well-off, socially disadvantaged, though equally gifted students. While Oxford and Cambridge encourage applications from applicants living in deprived areas, only 1 in 100 of the poorest students at universities in England received an education at Uxbridge in 2010, far lower than the proportion of poorer students at red-white universities. It cannot be disputed that a disproportionate number of Oxbridge participants went to a toll-paying private school rather than a free state school. Nationally, only 1 in 15 students receive a private education, yet nearly half of the students in Uxbridge attended a private school. Fee-paying schools have higher staff-to-student ratios, so their students receive more tuition and achieve higher grades than students from state sector schools. It is no surprise that pupils with an education paid for by their parents are 20 times more likely to be offered a place at Uxbridge. There is no reason to believe that the best students in the state sector are less intelligent than those in the private sector. Given the same educational opportunities and living circumstances, students of the state sector can achieve equally high grades. The failure of the best students to achieve their potential can often be linked to difficult home lives, lack of motivation or peer pressure from less academic students. The achievement gap between university applicants from toll-paying schools and state schools is maintained when Oxbridge graduates are rewarded with the most lucrative jobs, giving them the chance to send their children to the best schools. Viewed from the perspective of life chances, Uxbridge helps maintain the social divide in which the rich get richer and the poor stay poor. Some people would argue that this Uxbridge advantage is a symptom of social stratification rather than a cause of it. After all, parents cannot be blamed for wanting the best education for their children and Uxbridge cannot be held responsible for the failure of state schools to achieve the necessary grades. There is no evidence to suggest that Uxbridge selects pupils on anything other than merit. Indeed, on some issues the application process includes admissions and fitness tests that help ensure an even playing field. Perhaps then, the state sector should encourage and support more applications from their best students to the best universities. Alternatively, the low ambition of some parents of pupils may not drive gifted pupils forward and upwards, or it could be that some pupils from ordinary backgrounds are not suited to the idea of studying at Uxbridge. Students who don't feel they will fit in at Uxbridge can still make the most of their talents by attending one of the country's many excellent universities. The inequality in our society does not begin and end at Uxbridge. The best state schools are usually found in the most affluent areas. Injustices can arise when parents move to secure a place for a child in a more desirable school and thus they force another child into a low-performing school. Other parents, the better-off, though not necessarily wealthy, would pay for their children to be educated at a private school to avoid having to move home. Either way, the desire to provide children with the best possible education outweighs any sense of social justice. Unless remedies can be found for the gap in educational standards in the pre-university years, it is unrealistic to believe that Uxbridge contributes in any substantive way to a lack of social mobility. A place in Uxbridge should be seen as an opportunity for self-improvement and learning to the highest standards, whatever the social background.
hypothesis: There are few good schools in the state sector.

premise: Power from the Earth Geothermal power refers to the production of electricity by using heat sources located far below the surface of the earth. As you know, if a deep hole was drilled in the ground, you would soon encounter a particularly hot and molten rock. At depths of 30 to 50 km, temperatures exceeding 1000° C prevail. Obviously, access to such temperatures would provide a wonderful source of geothermal power. The problem is that such depths are hard to reach: drilling of about 30 miles or more is simply too expensive in today's technology. Fortunately, warm enough temperatures are available at considerably shallower depths. In some areas, where the earth's surface has changed over timefor example, volcanic activity temperatures exceeding 300° C can be found at depths of only 1 to 3 km, which can be accessed in a feasible way. Some of these areas are potentially ideal for generating electricity by geothermal means. Geothermal power generation can be explained as a steam power system that uses the Earth itself as a boiler. When water is sent to a depth of 1 to 3 km, it returns to the surface as steam and is able to generate electricity. Electricity produced in this way hardly produces carbon dioxide or other waste materials. If the steam and hot water are routed back underground, power generation can be semi-permanent in nature. Furthermore, geothermal energy can provide a stable supply of electricity unlike other natural energy sources like solar power and wind energy, both of which rely heavily on weather conditions. Accordingly, electricity generation using geothermal energy is four to five times more efficient than using solar power. As for wind energy, geothermal energy is twice as economical. Only the hydroelectric power generation approaches the cost of generating electricity from each is about the same. Although geothermal power generation appears to be a highly attractive option, development has been slow. The world's first successful attempt at geothermal electricity generation was achieved in Italy in 1904. Electricity generation in Japan first began in 1925 in the town of Beppu. Since then, countries as diverse as Iceland and New Zealand have joined the list of countries that use this valuable energy source. In 2000, the city of Beppu hosted the World Geothermal Congress, whose aim was to promote the adoption of geothermal energy production worldwide. The International Geothermal Community at the 2000 World Geothermal Congress called on countries' governments to commit to strong commitments for the development of their indigenous geothermal resources for the benefit of their people, humanity and the environment. However, a number of factors still hinder the development of geothermal power generation. First, it has a low energy density which makes it unsuitable for large-scale production where, for example, it needs to produce over 1,000,000 kW. Second, the cost is still high compared to the most common sources of energy production today: fossil fuels and atomic energy. Another consideration is the amount of risk involved in the successful construction of a new geothermal power generation facility. The drilling that must take place between 2,000 and 3,000 m below the surface must be accurate to only a few meters from one side or the other of the targeted location. To achieve this, extensive surveys, drilling expertise and time are required. It is not uncommon for a project to span ten years from its planning stage to the start of operations. The extent of the risks involved is clear. Although it has long been considered a resource-poor nation, Japan, which is thought to have about 10% of the world's geothermal resources, may well have considerable advantages for exploiting geothermal power. It has one of the longest-running power plants using geothermal energy. The station, built in 1966, pointed the way to the future when the country was affected by the two global oil shocks in the 1970s. There are now about 17 factories operating across the country responsible for a total output of over 530,000 kW. This figure, though impressive, accounts for only 0.4% of total electricity generation in Japan. Clearly, then, further progress must be made in the development of geothermal energy. As long as costs remain high compared to other energy sources, geothermal energy struggles to match the efficiency of existing power sources. More research and innovation in the field, as well as government support and a sense of urgency, are needed to help propel geothermal energy towards its promising future.
hypothesis: It could take a decade to develop a single geothermal power plant.
label: e

premise: Psychometrics Psychometrics involves psychological and educational assessment of the subject through the measurement of attitudes, personality, abilities, and knowledge. The field has two main focuses; the creation of measuring instruments and procedures and the development and improvement of the existing methodology that is operated. The concept of psychometric testing, introduced long before the establishment of IQ testing and other recent methodologies, was first explored by Francis Galton who developed the first test procedures supposedly related to intelligence; however, his measurement tools were actually based on physical and physiological metrics rather than the brain test itself. The measurements included the physical strength, height and weight of the subjects recorded and results used to assess the intelligence of the subjects. Although the approach was unsuccessful, the studies Galton conducted were to influence the work of future researchers. Approaches to measuring intelligence, defined as the relative ability of the brain to think, reason, plan conceptually, solve problems, understand, and learn, were later developed by pioneers such as Charles Spearman. Significant contributions to its early development were also made by Wilhelm Wendt, L. Thurston, Ernst Heinrich Weber, and Gustav Fechner. The best-known traditional approach to the development of psychometric devices for measuring intelligence is the Stanford-Binet IQ test, originally developed by French psychologist Alfred Binet. The researchers define intelligence as separate from other traits such as personality, character, creativity and even knowledge and wisdom for their evaluation. Intelligence testing methods are not intended to determine a level of genetic intelligence separate and unaffected by the environment to which the person is exposed in life; but rather to measure the intelligence of the individual seen as a result of both nature and nurture. Psychometrics is now a useful and widely used tool used to measure abilities in academic fields such as reading, writing, and mathematics. IQ tests are commonly used to test intelligence, although some believe that this test is unfair and does not truly represent the intellect of the subjects since people may excel in different areas of thinking. Psychologist Howard Gardner, working on this assumption, introduced the concept of individual cognitive profiling in 1983 in his book Frameworks of Mind: The Theory of Multiple Intelligences. He believes that one child may perform excellently in one aspect, but fail in another and that his overall performance should be taken into account in several intellectual areas. Gardner first identified seven different types of intelligence, these are; linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, body-kinesthetic, musical, interpersonal, and intrapersonal. In 1999 after further research he added an eighth element to the equation; naturalistic intelligence, and at the time of writing investigates the possibility of a ninth; this is existential intelligence. The first intelligence as defined by Gardner in the theory of multiple intelligences, linguistic intelligence, refers to the ability of individuals to process and communicate written and spoken words. Such people are said to excel at reading, writing, storytelling, learning a foreign language, and memorizing words and dates. The logical-mathematical category is associated with the ability of a person to think logically, think scientifically, make deductions, and commit negligence in mathematical calculations. Spatial intelligence is associated with vision and spatial judgment; such individuals have been observed to have strong visual memory and the potential to excel in artistic subjects. Those who exhibit a predisposition to the third classification, body-kinesthetic intelligence, often learn best by physically practicing an action rather than by reading or seeing. Musical intelligence, as the name implies, refers to the ability to define differences in tempo and timbre; people with musical intelligence are often able to sing, play musical instruments, and compose music at a high level. Because there is a high level of audio-related competence, it is said that many in this category learn well in a lecture mode where they are required to listen attentively to information. Interpersonal intelligence refers to people's ability to communicate and empathize with others; typically extroverts, they learn well through discussion, debate, and interaction with others, the last of the original 7 categories identified by Gardner, intrapersonal intelligence, fits the opposite description of interpersonal intelligence; such individuals work best independently. According to Gardner they are capable of high levels of self-reflection and are often perfectionists. However, a number of psychometric experts oppose Gardner's views and have reservations about the validity of his theories. First, some detractors dispute the overall definition of intelligence used in Gardner theory. They believe that, in fact, certain categories such as interpersonal or intrapersonal intelligence relate more to personality than to cognitive performance. The newly identified naturalistic intelligence, which refers to an affinity for the natural world and an ability to cultivate and nurture, has been completely rejected by many as nothing more than a hobby. Doubts have been raised that others, such as musical intelligence, are in reality talents. A recent criticism attached to the theory is that some believe that intelligences cannot be treated as separate entities since some individuals may function equally well in what can be considered diverse domains; linguistic and logical-mathematical for example. However Gardner argues that his theories are sound, since an identified and separated part of the brain is responsible for controlling aspects related to each of the different types of intelligence. Despite criticism received from some of his contemporaries, Gardner's theories are highly respected and often applied in the education world as a tool for identifying children's different abilities and potential career paths. For example, those who show linguistic abilities are said to be ideal in positions that include writing, politics, and teaching; logical mathematical thinkers suitable for careers in science, mathematics, law, medicine, and philosophy. It is said that those who display spatial intelligence are suitable for careers such as art, engineering or architecture; while people with a penchant for body-kinesthetic intelligence may excel in fields such as athletics, dance or creating crafts. Strengths in the field of musical intelligence are said to often lead to success as a singer, conductor or musician. Those who display strong interpersonal skills have been recognized as often making effective politicians, managers, diplomats, and social workers; while those who show dominant intrapersonal intelligence say they are better suited to professions that involve greater self-reflection and lower levels of interaction with the outside world like writing, philosophy, or theology.

premise: Language Learning Objectives: The Australian Senate Inquiry into National Language Policy The Australian Parliament's Senate Inquiry Report on National Language Policy in Australia proposed five targets for non-English language learning in Australian schools. First point The first point refers to what might be called the more stringent utilitarian reasons for learning a language: acquiring mastery of a language other than English for the purpose of direct communication. The communication in question may be of an informal nature, such as that which occurs during trips abroad, or between members of different groups in Australian society in a variety of social situations. To a large extent, however, the purpose of learning this language relates to the language of languages other than English in various fields of employment, such as interpretation and translation, international trade, diplomacy and defence. Professor M. Halliday, a witness to the inquiry, warned against placing too heavy an emphasis on utilitarian goals, stating that practical arguments should not be limited which are in some sense dishonest if you tell someone: If you spend all this time learning a language you will immediately go and find a use for it. The committee agrees that, in isolation, practical arguments tend to give an incomplete picture of the value of language learning. In the early school years, for example, utilitarian goals may be less important than they are at a tertiary level where employment considerations strongly influence. Point two The second objective concerns the relationship between language and the cultural context from which it emerges. Many submissions have emphasized the value of the language learning experience as a means of understanding other cultures, hence developing sensitive and tolerant intercultural attitudes. This proposal is applied to cultures both in Australia and overseas. Thus, it has been argued that language learning can contribute in important ways both to harmonious community relations within Australia and to understanding the cultural values of other countries. It has also been argued that language provides the key to key historical cultures, like the cultures of classical antiquity that exerted a profound influence on Western tradition. During the hearings, Dr David Ingram of the Australian Federation of Modern Language Teachers' Associations referred to evidence giving some empirical support to the claim that the language learning experience fosters the development of a better understanding of other cultures. The committee has no difficulty accepting the proposal. However, she believes that the measure of success achieved may depend largely on the teaching methodology adopted, and the degree of commitment of teachers to the cause of cultural awareness and sensitivity. Third point The third objective relates to the role of language learning is the preservation of ethnic languages and cultures in Australia. The submissions argue that a key element of Australia's multiculturalism policy is recognition of the value of the cultural heritage of the different groups in Australian society. Since language and culture are inextricably intertwined, the preservation of cultural heritage necessarily involves the preservation of the languages associated with them. In the case of Aboriginal communities this issue takes on a special note of urgency because in many cases Aboriginal cultures and languages are on the verge of total disappearance. The aim in this context, therefore, is not only to help preserve cultural and reef heritage but to help preserve that heritage from extinction. A PROMINENT FOURTH POINT AMONG THE LANGUAGE LEARNING GOALS DESCRIBED IN THE SUBMISSIONS WAS THE FOURTH POINT: THE DEVELOPMENT OF STUDENTS' GENERAL COGNITIVE AND LINGUISTIC ABILITIES. The educational outcomes at stake here have been described in a number of ways. Professor M. Halliday, for example, spoke of language learning as an educational exercise of first importance, as developing thinking. Another submission addressed the development of a more pointed and critical awareness of the nature and mechanism of language. Professor Klein pointed to research conducted specifically in Canada which, he said, indicates that bilinguals are superior to monolinguals in logical thought and conceptual development, verbal intelligence and divergent thinking. Fifth point Finally, several submissions have talked about the role of language learning is the general development of personality. To a large extent, this objective establishes and summarizes aspects of those that have already been covered. The possibility of direct communication with speakers of another language, for example, offers an opportunity to expand personal horizons. A similar outcome can be expected from the encounter with another culture made possible through language learning. When the language spoken is the child's mother tongue, the language of an immigrant group or an aboriginal language, another factor arises. In this context, it has been argued, language learning contributes significantly to the development of personal self-esteem, since the introduction of language into school encourages children with this language background to appreciate it and value it as an asset. As a result, their appreciation of their family value as well as their own worth may rise. The Commission believes that the submissions were correct in drawing attention to these personal development issues. Naturally, the benefits of learning the language spoken here are less easy to quantify than those involved in the objectives discussed earlier. Nevertheless, the Commission believes that if taught properly, languages can play an important role in helping young people establish their identity and develop their personal and social personalities.
hypothesis: There is evidence to suggest that learning a language does not necessarily promote a better understanding of cultures.

premise: Paleolithic Cave Paintings In any investigation of the origins of art, attention is focused on the cave paintings created in Europe during the Paleolithic period (about 40,000-10,000 years ago) such as those depicting bulls and other animals at Lesko Cave in France. Being the most preserved and striking signs of what has been a global creative explosion, how do we begin to explain their appearance? Instinctively, we might want to update the earliest human artists by assuming they painted for the sheer joy of painting. The philosophers of classical Greece recognized this as a crucial feature of human beings:\ to savor works of imitation\ to enjoy the very act and triumph of representation. If we were close to a real lion or snake, we might feel scared. But a well-executed image of a lion or snake will give us pleasure. Why do we assume that our Paleolithic ancestors were different? This simple acceptance of art for art's sake has a certain appeal. Thinking of Lascaux as a gallery allows it to be a kind of special viewing place where you can display the handicrafts of talented artists. It is likely that everyday existence in parts of Paleolithic Europe may not have been so difficult, with plenty of prepared food and therefore the leisure time for art. The problems in this explanation, however, are different. FROM THE OUTSET, THE MULTITUDE OF ARCHAEOLOGICAL DISCOVERIES, WHICH INCLUDES SOME OF THE WORLD'S COUNTLESS ROCK ART SITES THAT CANNOT BE DATED, SERVED TO HIGHLIGHT AN INCREDIBLY LIMITED REPERTOIRE OF SUBJECTS. The images that are repeated are of animals. Human figures are unusual, and when they do appear, they are rarely made with the same attention to the form accorded to the animals. If Paleolithic artists simply sought to represent the beauty of the world around them, wouldn't they have left a much greater variety of images of trees, flowers, of the sun and stars? Another question for art theory for art's sake is posed by the high prevalence of Paleolithic imagery that appears not to mimic any reality whatsoever. These are geometric shapes or patterns made up of points or lines. Such marks may be found isolated or repeated over a specific surface but also scattered across more familiar shapes. A good example of this can be seen in the geologically spectacular cave of Peche Merle, in the Lot region of France. Here we come across some beloved animals from the powerful pair of horses of the Paleolithic repertoire. But above and around the outline of the horses there are multiple dark spots, overlooked by the otherwise naturalistic representation of animals. What imitates such a pattern? There's also the location factor. The Lasco Caves may be thought of as underground galleries, but many other paintings have been found in hollows that are completely unsuitable for any kind of tight viewing corners that would surely have been awkward even for artists to penetrate, let alone anyone wanting to see the art. Finally, we may question the idea that the Upper Paleolithic period was a paradise where food came easily, leaving humans ample time to amuse themselves with art. For Europe it was still the Ice Age. An estimate of the basic food level then necessary for human survival was judged to be 2200 calories per day. This consideration, combined with the severe emphasis on animals in cave art, has convinced some archaeologists that the primary motive behind Paleolithic images must be in the primary activity of Paleolithic people: hunting. Hunting is a skill. Tracking, stalking, persecuting and killing the prey are difficult, sometimes dangerous activities. What if the process could be made easier by art? In the early decades of the twentieth century, Father Henri Breuil argued that the cave paintings were all about\ sympathetic magic\. The artists diligently strove to make their animal images evocative and realistic because they tried to capture the spirit of their prey. What could have caused their teaching attention to create such naturalistic and familiar images? According to Breuil, the artists may have believed that if a hunter was able to create a real figure of some animal, then this animal was almost captured. If so, the pictures had a magical ability to confer success or luck in hunting.
hypothesis: There is more variety in the way humans are depicted in cave art than in the way animals are.

Bank reconciliation checks the accuracy of cash register entries against bank statements. The differences between the bank columns in the cash book and the bank statement may reflect errors made by the business or by the bank; however, they can usually be explained by checks the business has written that have not yet been presented to the bank or equally by undisposed deposits. A small cash book is used to maintain office floats, for example 50, to pay for various office items like stamps, stationery and travel expenses. The small cash overflow reduces the need to write checks to small items and then make many accounting entries. However, payments received in the form of banknotes and coins should be paid to the bank in the usual way and not into the small cash box. Ideally, receipts should be provided for small cash claims and a small cash voucher produced for paid-in funds. In this way the sum of receipts, vouchers and small cash in the box should always be equal to the float (50). When the buoyancy drops, the payments recorded in the tiny cash book add up and the corresponding amount is withdrawn from the bank to complete the flotation to its original level.

premise: The phases of the Moon travel a distance of about 382,400 km, the Moon takes just over twenty-nine days to complete its orbit around the Earth. During this lunar cycle, many different phases of the Moon are visible from Earth, although the Moon itself never changes shape. The cyclical period of the Moon is determined by the extent to which the Sun illuminates the Moon on the side facing the Earth. Just like the Earth, the Moon is sphere-shaped, and therefore always half-illuminated by the Sun. However, because the Moon and Earth are in synchronous rotation, we can only see the near side of the Moon. The side we don't see is called the far side, or the dark side, a term that is often misunderstood. The dark side refers to the mystery of this invisible side, not the amount of light it receives. Both the near side and the far side of the Moon receive about the same amount of sunlight. Although we see a slightly different moon from Earth each day, its repeated cycle is both predictable and functional. There are eight phases of the Moon, each of which has a unique name signifying how much of the Moon is visible from Earth. THE EARLY STAGES ARE SAID TO BE DIMMING, OR GRADUALLY INCREASING IN SIZE. The first phase is called a new moon. At this time the Moon is arranged between the Earth and the Sun. The illuminated side of the moon faces the sun, not the earth, so the earth appears to have no moon at all. As the Moon begins to slowly move eastward from the Sun, it becomes slightly more visible. After the new moon, the phase of the waxing crescent begins. At this point, the moon appears to be less than half lit. The first quarter occurs when half of the moon is visible. It is called the first quarter, not because of its size, but because it represents the end of the first quarter of the lunar cycle. THE NEXT STEP IS CALLED WAX HUMPING AND REPRESENTS A MOON THAT IS LARGER THAN A HEMISPHERE, BUT NOT QUITE COMPLETE. This phase is accompanied by a full moon, which occurs when the illuminated side of the moons faces the Earth directly. When the moon begins to decrease again, it is said to be decreasing. The phases in the second half of the cycle look the same as the first, except that the opposite half of the Moon's near side is illuminated, so the Moon appears to be shrinking rather than growing. After the waning gibbons comes the last quarter, when half the moon is visible, and finally the waning crescent. IN THE NORTHERN HEMISPHERE, WHEN THE MOON DIMS, MOONLIGHT RISES FROM RIGHT TO LEFT. The opposite occurs in the Southern Hemisphere. Like the sun, the moon is an accurate tool for measuring time. A complete cycle of the moon is called lunation. A full cycle of the moon usually lasts a little less than one calendar month, so the phase of the moon that begins a month usually repeats just before the month ends. When two full moons occur in one calendar month, the other is called a blue moon. This phenomenon occurs approximately once every 2.7 years. Within one cycle, the age of the moons from the last day of the new moon is calculated. For example, the moon is about fifteen days old in the phase of the full moon. The moon can also be used to calculate the time of day. Just like the Sun, the Moon rises and sets each day and is visible on the Earth's horizon. In a new moon, the moon and sun flow and set at almost the same time. When the moon begins to wax, or move farther in its orbit, it rises about an hour later each day. In a full moon, the moon rises at about the same time as the sun sets and sets as the sun rises. Therefore, the moon is out in the daytime as often as at night although it is not always easy to see it in daylight. The Islamic calendar is based on the phases of the moon. The beginning of each new month in the Islamic calendar begins when the waxing crescent first appears in the night sky. The major phases of the moon, which include new moon, first quarter, full moon, and last quarter are published in the almanacs for each month. The phases can also be found on many calendars in the Western world. Despite the world's fascination with the moon, its phases are not entirely unique. The planets Venus and Mercury have similar phases; however, unlike the Moon, these planets can never be on the opposite side of Earth from the Sun. To see the equivalent of the full moon phase of these planets, we would need to have the ability to see through the Sun.

premise: Plant Smells Everyone is familiar with fragrant flowers, and many people have heard that floral scents help a plant attract pollinators. This common perception is mostly true, but it is surprising how little scientific evidence for it exists. Of course, not all flowers are pollinated by biological factors for example, many types of grass are wind-pollinated, but weed flowers may still emit volatiles. In fact, plants emit organic molecules all the time, although they may not be obvious to the human nose. As for flower smells that we can detect in our noses, bouquets that attract moths and butterflies usually smell sweet, and those that attract certain flies look rotten to us. The release of volatile substances from plant parts of the plant is recognized, although until recently the physiological functions of these chemicals were less clear and received much less attention from scientists. When a pine tree trunk is damaged - for example, when a beetle tries to dig into it - it secretes a very smelly resin. This resin consists mostly of terpenehydrocarbons with a backbone of 10, 15 or 20 carbons that may also contain oxygen atoms. The heavier C20 terpenes, called diterpenes, are glue-like and can cover and paralyze insects as they clog the hole. This defense mechanism is as ancient as it is effective: Many samples of fossilized resin, or amber, contain the remains of insects trapped inside. Many other plants emit volatiles when they are damaged, and in some cases the emitted signal helps protect the plant. For example, (Z) _3_ hexanyl acetate, known as volatile green leaf because it is emitted from many plants when injured, discourages females of the moth Heliothis virescens from laying eggs on injured tobacco plants. Interestingly, the profile of the emitted tobacco volatiles is different at night than during the day, and the nocturnal mixture, which is rich in several (Z) _3_hexen_i-olesters, is most effective at repelling the night-active H. virescens moth. Volatiles induced by herbivores are often used as indirect defenses. These breeders exist in a variety of plant species, including maize, beans and the model plant species Arabidopsis thaliana. Plants not only emit volatile in an acute form, on the site where caterpillars, mites, aphids or similar insects eat them but also usually from undamaged parts of the plant. These signals attract a variety of predatory insects that prey on the plant-eaters. For example, some parasitic wasps can detect the volatile signature of a damaged plant and lay their eggs inside the offending larva; eventually, the wasp eggs hatch, and the nascent larvae feed on the larva from the inside out. The growth of infected larvae lags considerably, in favor of the plant. Similarly, volatiles released by plants in response to the laying of herbivore eggs can attract parasites of the eggs, thus preventing them from hatching and avoiding an attack by hungry herbivores that would have appeared. Plant volatiles can also be used as a form of currency in some very indirect protection schemes. In the rainforest understory Leonardoxa Africana, ants of the species Petalomyrmex phylax patrol young leaves and attack any herbivorous insects they encounter. The young leaves emit high levels of the volatile compound methyl salicylate, a compound that ants use as a pheromone or as an antiseptic in their nest. Methyl salicylate appears to be both an attractant and a reward offered by the tree to induce ants to perform this valuable deterrent function. Floral scent has a strong impact on the economic success of many agricultural crops that rely on insect pollinators, including fruit trees like the cherry, apple, apricot, and bee-pollinated peach, as well as tropical vegetables and plants such as papaya. Pollination affects not only crop yield, but also the quality and efficiency of crop production. Many crops require most, if not all, eggs for fertilization for optimal size and shape of the fruit. This problem has been exacerbated by recent disease epidemics that have killed many honey bees, the main insect pollinators in the United States. One of the means by which plant breeders circumvent the pollination problem is by growing self-compatible, or apomyctic, varieties that do not require fertilization. Although this solution is sufficient, its disadvantages include close genetic uniformity and consequent susceptibility to pathogens. Some breeders tried to improve honeybees' foraging by spraying odorant compounds on orchard trees, but this approach was expensive, had to be repeated, had toxic effects on the soil or local biota, and ultimately proved ineffective. The poor effectiveness of this strategy likely reflects the inherent limitations of the locally applied artificial compounds, which clearly fail to convey the appropriate message to bees. For example, general spraying of the volatile mixture cannot tell insects exactly where the bloom is located. Clearly a more refined strategy is needed. The ability to enhance existing floral scent, create a de novo scent, or modify odor characteristics, all of which can be achieved by genetic engineering, will allow us to manipulate the types of insect pollinators and the frequency of their visits. Furthermore, the metabolic engineering of fragrance may increase crop protection against pathogens and pests. Genetically manipulating the scent would also benefit the flower industry. Ornamental plants, including cut flowers, foliage, and potted plants, play an important aesthetic role in human life. Unfortunately, traditional breeding has often produced varieties with improved vase life, shipping characteristics, color and shape while sacrificing desirable perfumes. The loss of smell among ornamental plants, which have a global value of more than $30 billion, makes them important targets for genetic manipulation of floral fragrance. Some work has already begun in this area, as several groups have created petunia and carnation plants expressing the linalool synthase gene from C. These experiments are still preliminary: for technical reasons, the gene is ubiquitously expressed in the plant, and although the transgenic plants did produce small amounts of linalool, the level was below the detection threshold of the human nose. Similar experiments in tobacco used genes for other monoterpene synthases, such as the one that produces limonene, but yielded similar results. The next generation of experiments, already underway, includes sophisticated programs targeting the expression of odor genes specifically for flowers or other organs such as specialized glands that can store antimicrobial compounds or herbivore repellents.

Traditionally, the man's role was to be the breadwinner of the family providing the funds to pay for food and shelter. However, due to the many new and unique responsibilities placed on families, in many cases men and women fathers and mothers were forced into the workforce. In general, the reasons for both being involved in the workforce revolve around the need to add to the family's current financial base. To a lesser extent, the need to interact with adults in a stimulating work environment is another popular reason. Whatever the reasons which may be, for many families, the decision of a father and mother to move out of the home and join the workforce has led to a number of adverse effects within the home which in turn affect their performance as employees. Many researchers agree that attitudes towards work are transferred to family life. This leakage can be positive or negative. Positive spillover refers to the spread of satisfaction and positive stimulation at work resulting in high levels of energy and satisfaction at home. If the amount of research is to be taken as an indication, it seems that positive spillover is not a dominant phenomenon in the workplace with most studies focusing on the effects of negative spillover. Often noting the incompatible nature of work and family life, the study focuses on problems and conflicts at work that have the effect of draining and preoccupying the individual, making it difficult for him to participate fully in family life. Social scientists have devised a number of theories in an attempt to explain the work-family dynamic. Compensation theory is one that is widely used. He posits that the relationship between work and family is negative in that he points out that high involvement in one area always the work domain leads to low involvement in the other. As a person progresses in career, the requirements usually change from moderate to more demanding and if the advanced worker has younger children, this change in work responsibilities will usually manifest itself in the form of less time spent with the family. Scholars subscribing to this theory note that the drain on family time is significantly associated with conflict between work and family with an escalation in conflict as the number of family members increases. The human condition is a state of change. In studying work-family dynamics, it can be clearly seen that as the pattern of adult development for men and women differs and as family and career demands change, individuals may link work and family roles differently at different stages in their lives. Thus, the relationship between work and family is constantly changing over the course of a person's life. The developmental approach therefore adopts a psychological-developmental framework to explore the dynamics of the relationship between individual, family, and career developments throughout the life of an employee. Interpersonal climate influences the motivation of family and work-related activities in the family and workplace. Within the family, the sense of appreciation by the spouse directly influences one's self-determination, and at the same time in the workplace, the feeling of autonomy support by one employer has shown an effect on self-determined motivation towards work-related activities. Studies built on the theory of self-determination indicate that if people have a high level of self-determination, they decide which activities to devote themselves to and thus participate in a positive way, making it difficult for family alienation to occur. Segmentation theory proposes that work and family are actually two completely separate domains and people are able to maintain a clear delineation between the two. Theorists who relate to this view argue that the emotions, attitudes, and behaviors of the recruits in the two different environments are separate and will not affect work or family. While this theory certainly applies to some, apparently not all men and women are able to neatly divide the two experiences. Winthrop notes that although a woman may enter the workforce, studies have shown that in the context of the family, the care of her husband and children as well as in residence is still in the domain of women. This type of idea is related to the old saying; the place of the woman is in the home. She is seen as the one who takes care of all household duties whereas, stereotypically, the man is the one who brings home the food for the family. The extent to which this is felt is definitely based on social expectations and behavioral norms. Perhaps the most positive relationship that could be established between work and conflict was in relation to irregular working hours. Factors such as the need to work weekends, the need to work more than nine hours a day or having to work during vacation periods have all been added to the dynamics of the conflict. In addition, rank or position and thus employees' expectations and time requirements showed a negative impact on family and work relationships. Many have conducted empirical research in relation to work-family conflict and job satisfaction with significantly varying outcomes. However, one recognized result that few researchers dispute is that when conflict arises between work and family, job satisfaction decreases.

premise: Pollution in the Gulf pouring water into the sea sounds harmless enough. But in Florida Bay, a large, shallow stretch between the southern tip of the Everglades and the Florida Keys, it is proving highly controversial. That's because researchers are divided on whether it will help or hinder the plants and animals living in the bay. What is at risk is the future of the bays and extensive beds of seagrasses. These grow on the muddy floor of the bays and serve as nurseries for larvae of shrimp, lobsters and fish many of which are important sport and commercial fishing species. Also at stake is an impressive array of coral reefs that stretch along the Florida Keys and make up the third largest barrier reef in the world. Since the 1980s, coral cover has declined by 40%, and a third of coral species have disappeared. This had a detrimental effect on the animals that depend on the reef, such as crustaceans, turtles and nearly 600 fish species. What causes such ecological change is a matter of much debate. And the answer is of no small consequence. This is because America's government plans to devote $8 billion over the next 30 years to revitalizing the Everglades. Seasonal freshwater streams to the Everglades are due to be restored in order to improve the health of the areas. But then they will flee to the Gulf. Joseph Zinnam, a marine ecologist from the University of Virginia, thinks this is a good idea. He believes that a shortage of fresh water in the Gulf is his main problem. The blame, he said, lies in a century of drainage in the Everglades aimed at turning the wetlands into farmland and areas for development. This caused the flow of fresh water into the Florida Gulf to dwindle, making the waters in the bay, overall, saltier. This, he claims, kills the seagrasses, and as these rot, nutrients are released that feed the microscopic plants and animals living in the water. This, he says, is why the bays that were once clear water often resemble pea soup. And in a vicious circle, this murky bloom blocks sunlight, causing more seagrasses to die and even more turbidity. Brian Lapointe, a marine scientist at the Harbor Branch Oceanography Institute in Fort Pierce in Florida, disagrees. He thinks seagrasses can tolerate salinity levels much higher than what the bay actually exhibits. Furthermore, he notes that when freshwater flow through the Everglades was experimentally increased in the 1990s, it led to massive plankton blooms. Freshwater flowing from well-fertilized farmland, he said, had caused a five-fold increase in nitrogen levels in the Gulf. It was like pouring petrol on a fire. The result was mass mortality of seagrasses because of increased turbidity from plankton. Dr. Lapointe adds that because corals only thrive in waters where nutrient levels are low, restoring nitrogen-rich freshwater would cause more damage to the reef. It's a plausible theory. The water flowing from crops grown on 750,000 acres of heavily fertilized farmland at the northern edge of the nitrogen-rich Everglades, half of which ends in a bay. But Bill Kruczynski, of America's Environmental Protection Agency, is convinced that nitrogen from farmland is not the main problem. Some coral reefs away from any nitrogen pollution are dying and, oddly, some are thriving. Dr. Kuczynski thinks increasing nutrients coming from local sewage discharges from thousands of septic tanks along the Florida Keys are part of the problem. Such claims and counterclaims make it difficult to predict the impact of the rehabilitation program. If increased salinity is the main problem, ecology of the bays will benefit from the Everglades restoration project If, on the other hand, nitrogen is the problem, increasing freshwater flow could make matters much worse. If this second hypothesis turns out to be true, the cure is nitrogen removal from farmland or sewage discharges, or perhaps both, neither of which will be easy. Man-made wetlands, currently built to reduce the flow of phosphate into the bay - also from fertilisers - will need an algae culture (a sort of containable algal bloom) to add to them to cope with discharges from farmland. It will be expensive. So does replacing the septic tank with a proper sewer - one estimate puts the cost at $650 million. Either way, it is clear that when, on December 1, 3,000 square miles of sea around the reef are designated as a protective zone by the deputy commerce minister, Sam Bodman, it will do nothing to protect the reef from pollution. Some argue, however, that there is a more fundamental flaw in Bay's plans: the very idea of returning it to a utopian ideal before man caused its damage. No one knows what Florida Bay was like before the 1950s, when engineers cut the biggest canals in the Everglades and took most of the water. Dr Kruczynski suspects it was more like an estuary. The bay that many people want to recreate could have been nothing more than a changing phase in the history of the bays. These arguments not only threaten to create ecological but also economic problems. The Florida Keys economy depends on tourism - the local tourism industry has an annual turnover of $2.5 billion. People come for fishing boat trips, for mint viewing, or for diving and snorkeling to watch exotic colored corals. If the plan to restore the Everglades worsens the problems in the bay and the reef, it could prove a very costly mistake.
hypothesis: Everyone agrees that pouring water into the sea is not harmful enough even in the Florida Bay Area.

premise: Pottery production in ancient Akrotiri Excavations at the prehistoric Akrotiri site, on the Aegean coast, have revealed much about the technical aspects of pottery production, indisputably one of the basic industries of this Greek city. However, much less is known about the socio-economic context and how production is organized. The bulk of the pottery found in Akrotiri are locally produced, and date to the end of the fifteenth century BC. He clearly fulfilled a huge variety of requirements for settlements: more than fifty different types of pots can be distinguished. The pottery found includes a wide variety of functional types like storage jars, smaller containers, pouring vessels, cooking pots, drinking vessels and so on, all related to specific activities and which were manufactured and distributed with these activities in mind. Given the large number of forms produced and the relatively high degree of standardization, it is assumed that most, if not all, of Akrotiri's pottery was produced by specialized craftsmen in a non-domestic context. Unfortunately, neither potters' workshops nor kilns were found in the excavated area. The reason for this may be that the ceramic workshops were found on the periphery of the site, which has not yet been excavated. In any case, the presence of the pottery, and the consistent repetition of the same types in different sizes, indicate production on an industrial scale. Akrotiri potters appear to have responded to pressures beyond their own households, namely to the increasing complexity of regional distribution and exchange systems. WE CAN IMAGINE THEM AS FULL-TIME CRAFTSMEN WORKING PERMANENTLY IN A CRAFT AT A HIGH RATE OF PRODUCTION SUCH AS POTTERY PRODUCTION, SUSTAINING THEMSELVES ENTIRELY FROM THE INCOME OF THE THEN CRAFT. In view of the above, one can begin to speak in terms of mass-produced pottery and the existence of organized workshops of craftsmen in the period 1550 to 1500 BC. However, how pottery production was organized in Akrotiri remains an open question, as there is no real documentary evidence. All our knowledge comes from the ceramic material itself, and from the tentative conclusions that can be drawn from it. The invention of the units of quantity and of a numerical system for their circulation was of capital importance for a society oriented to exchange such as that of Akrotiri. Despite the lack of written records, the archaeological evidence reveals that concepts of measurement, both of weight and of number, were formulated. Standard measures may have already been followed, such as those evidenced by a cascading series of lead weights manufactured in disk form found at the site. The existence of capacity units in the Late Bronze Age is also evidenced by the marking of units of measure for liquid wine on excavated containers. It must be recognized that the function of pottery plays a very important role in determining the characteristics then. The intended function affects the choice of clay, the manufacturing technique and the shape and size of the pots. For example, large storage jars (pithoi) will be needed to store goods, while smaller containers will be used for transportation. In fact, the length of a man's arm limits the size of a smaller pot to a capacity of about twenty lines; it is also the maximum that a man can comfortably carry. The different sizes of the container thus represented standard quantities of merchandise, which is a fundamental component of the exchange function. Akrotiri merchants handling goods such as wine were able to easily determine the amount of wine they transported by the number of containers carried in ships then, since the capacity of each container is known to be 14-18 liters. (We can make here a parallel to the current practice in Greece of selling oil in 17kg cans.) Therefore, we can assume that their shape, capacity and sometimes decoration are indicative of the goods contained in them. Because individual transactions would typically involve different quantities of a given commodity, a variety of standard types of vessels would be needed to meet the requirements of merchants. H. In attempting to recover capacity systems by measuring the volume of excavated pottery, a rather generous range of tolerances must be allowed. Potters of that time seem to have had specific vessel sizes in mind, and attempted to reconstruct them using specific type and quantity of clay. However, it will be quite difficult for them to achieve the exact size required each time, without any mechanical means of regulating the symmetry and thickness of the wall, and some potters will be more skilled than others. In addition, variations back on types and size may also occur because of unforeseen circumstances during the injection process. For example, instead of destroying the entire pot if the clay in the rim contained a piece of gravel, a potter might produce a smaller pot simply by cutting the rim. Even when there is no discernible external difference between pots designed to contain the same amount of merchandise, differences in their capacity can actually reach one or two liters. In one case, it seems that the deviation from the required size is up to 10-20 percent. The increasing demand for standardized exchanges, closely related to commercial transactions, was perhaps one of the main factors that led to the standardization of pottery production. Thus, the entire ceramic production and exchange network depended on specific regional economic conditions, and would reflect the socio-economic structure of the prehistoric Akrotiri.

Prediction is a much more pernicious science than discovery. These non-destructive waves travel faster through the Earth's crust than the damaging and destructive secondary waves and can therefore provide valuable, albeit brief, early warning. This effect of different speed waves can be compared to the relationship between light and sound; we see lightning before we hear thunder. Some people believe that animals can detect P-waves and that this is what causes them to start behaving strangely. These diseases affect the structure of brain tissue and are all fatal and incurable. Not all prions are dangerous; in fact, prion-like proteins are found naturally in many (possibly all) plants and animals. Because of this, scientists reasoned that such proteins could give some evolutionary advantage to their host.

Potential water wars are likely to be in areas where rivers and lakes are shared by more than one country, says Mark Evans, a UN employee. Evans predicts that population growth and economic development will lead to nearly one in two people in Africa living in countries facing water shortages or so-called water stress within 25 years. Water scarcity is defined as less than 1,000 m³ of water available per person per year, while water pressure means less than 1,500 m³ of water available per person per year. The report says that by 2025, 12 more African countries will join the 13 already suffering from water stress or water shortages. What makes the water issue even more pressing is that demand for water will grow faster and faster as larger areas are put into crops and economic development. Evans adds that the strong possibility that the world is experiencing climate change also adds to this urgency. How to tackle water shortages is at the forefront of the battle between environmentalists on the one hand and governments and construction companies on the other. At the recent World Summit for Sustainable Development in Johannesburg, activists continued their campaign to halt dam construction, while many governments were outraged by a vocal minority thwarting their plans. One of the UN's eight development goals is to reduce by half the proportion of people without sustainable access to safe drinking water by 2015. How to ensure that happens was one of the big themes of the summit. Much of the text on this issue had already been agreed, but one of the unresolved issues in the implementation plan was whether the water target would be expanded to cover sanitation. The risks arising from water-borne diseases in the absence of sanitation facilities means that the two goals are closely linked. Only American negotiators opposed extending the targets to include sanitation due to the financial commitment involved. However, Evans says the US is about to agree to this extension. This agreement could give the UN an opportunity to show that in one key area the global development agenda in Johannesburg has made progress. But implementation is always more difficult, as South Africa has experienced in its water program. In the face of the continuing rise in unemployment, paying for water and other utilities has the potential to quickly undo high achievements of governments in delivery since 1994. It is also the way to ensure adequate water supply and its management that will increasingly become a political battleground in South Africa. However, there are major projects proposed elsewhere in South Africa that might be stalled by activists who might put pressure on funding agencies like the World Bank. Griff says her group will campaign during the summit against the proposed Scoifram Dam, to be built near Frenchhawk to supply more water to Cape Town. Instead of relying on building a new dam, the city should ensure that the water is used wisely at all times and not just during dry periods, Griff says. Another battleground for her group is over privatizing the water supply, she says. The water supply, she insists, is best handled in the public interest by responsible government. There is growing hope from technological advances to tackle water shortages. This is an agricultural production that occupies about 90% of the water consumed for human purposes, says the UN. To reduce agricultural demand for water, the International Institute of Water Management in Sri Lanka is researching ways to obtain more crop per drop through the development of drought-resistant crops, as well as through better water management techniques. One of the research sites of the institutes is the Limpopo River basin. According to the director-general of the institutes, Frank Reisberman, rice growers in China use a quarter of the water in concrete made for those in South Africa. The institute hopes that the green revolution in crop productivity will soon match the blue revolution in improving water utilization in agriculture.

premise: Project management, the system of organizing resources to achieve a long-term final goal, is severely contrasted with process-based operations, such as traditional banking. When such process-based industries, which can be characterized by the functional execution of immediate tasks, embark on a project, a clash of civilizations almost inevitably arises. But as the corporate world moves towards an increasingly project-based model, executives in process-based businesses need to be educated in project management. Social life, indeed, would be impossible if we did not understand to some extent the motives and attributes of those we meet, and did not react to them; and it is clear that we are accurate enough for most practical purposes, although we recognize that misinterpretations arise especially easily on the part of others who judge us! Errors can often be corrected as we progress. But every time we cling to a definite decision about a person, which cannot be easily corrected through their feedback, the shortcomings of our judgments become apparent. The hostess who mistakenly thinks the Smiths and the Joneses will get along well together can do little to restore her party's success. A school or business may be saddled for years with unwanted staff, because the selection committee that interviewed him for fifteen minutes did not evaluate his personality. Just because the process is so familiar and taken for granted, it sparked little scientific curiosity until recently. Playwrights, writers and artists over the centuries have excelled at portraying character, but rarely stopped to ask how they, or we, know people, or how accurate our knowledge is. However, the popularity of unscientific systems like Lavater's physiognomy in the eighteenth century, Gaels phrenology in the nineteenth and of handwritten interpretations by graphologists, or palm readings by gypsies, show that people are aware of weaknesses in their judgment and want better diagnostic methods. This belief is hardly justified: since the main objective of psychology was to establish the general laws and principles underlying behavior and thinking, rather than applying them to concrete problems of the individual person. Many professional psychologists still consider it their primary role to investigate the nature of learning, perception, and motivation in the abstract or average person, or in lower organisms, and consider it premature to put such young science to practical uses. They would disavow any supreme skill in judging their fellow men. Indeed, being more aware of difficulties than the non-psychologist, they may be more reluctant to commit to definite predictions or decisions about other people. Nevertheless, to an increasing extent psychologists are moving to other educational, occupational, clinical and applied fields, where they are called upon to use their expertise for purposes such as the adaptation of education or work to the child or adult, and the person to the job, therefore a large part of their activity consists of personality assessment. The success of psychologists in assessing personality has been limited, compared to what they have achieved in the areas of competencies and training, and as a result most people continue to rely on non-scientific assessment methods. In recent times a huge amount of work has been done on personality tests, and on carefully controlled experimental studies of personality. Personal investigations by Freudian psychologists and others have an even longer history. And yet psychology seems no closer to providing society with practical techniques that are reliable and accurate enough to gain general acceptance. The correctness of the methods of psychologists in the field of assessing personality and the value of their work are under constant fire from other psychologists, and it is far from easy to prove their worth. The growth of psychology has apparently helped responsible members of society to become more aware of the difficulties of evaluation. But there's no point telling employers, educators and judges how inaccurately they diagnose the personalities they have to deal with, unless psychologists are confident they can provide something better. Even when university psychologists themselves appoint a new staff member, they almost always resort to the traditional techniques of assessing candidates through interviews, past records and testimonials, and probably make at least as bad appointments as other employers. However, a large amount of experimental development of better methods has been carried out since the 1940s by groups of psychologists in the armed services and civil service, and by organizations like the (British) National Institute of Industrial Psychology and the American Institute of Research.
