premise: Pulling strings to build pyramids No one knows exactly how the pyramids were built. Marcus Cheon reckons the answer may hang in the air. The pyramids of Egypt were built more than three thousand years ago, and no one knows how. The accepted picture is that tens of thousands of slaves hauled stones on sleds. But there is no evidence to back this up. Now a Californian software consultant named Maureen Clemmons has suggested that kites may have been involved. While perusing a book about the monuments of Egypt, she noticed a hieroglyph that showed a line of men standing in strange poses. They were holding what looked like ropes that led, through some mechanical system, to a giant bird in the sky. She wondered if perhaps the bird was actually a giant kite, and the men were using it to lift a heavy object. Curious, Clemmons contacted Morteza Garib, a professor of aeronautics at the California Institute of Technology. He was fascinated by the idea. Coming from Iran, I have a keen interest in Middle Eastern science, he says. He, too, was struck by the photo that sparked Clemmons' interest. An object in the sky probably had wings that were too short and wide for a bird. There certainly exists the possibility that it was a kite, he says. And since he needed a summer project for his student Emilio Graf, investigating the possibility of using kites as heavy lifters seemed like a good idea. Garib and Graaf set themselves the task of lifting a 4.5-meter stone pillar from horizontal to vertical, using no energy source other than wind. Their initial calculations and wind tunnel experiments in a scale model convinced them that they would not need strong wind to lift the 33.5 tonne pillar. Even a modest force, if sustained over time, will do. The key was to use a pulley system that would increase the applied force. So they erected a tent-shaped scaffold directly over the edge of the horizontal pillar, with pulleys hanging from the top of the scaffolding. The idea was that as one end of the pillar rose, the base would roll across the earth on a cart. Earlier this year, the team put Clemmons' implausible theory to the test, using a 40-square-foot rectangular nylon sail. The kite lifted the pillar clear of the ground. We were absolutely stunned, says Garib. As soon as the sail opened to the wind, tremendous force was generated and the column was raised to vertical in just 40 seconds. The wind was blowing at a slight speed of 16 to 20 miles per hour, just over half of what they thought would be needed. What they failed to reckon with was what happened when the kite opened. There was a tremendous initial force five times greater than the steady-state force, Garib says. 'That idiot means kites can lift huge weights, 'Garib realized. Even a 300-ton column could have been raised to vertical with about 40 men and four or five sails. So Clemmons was right: the builders of the pyramids could have used kites to lift massive stones into place. Whether they did indeed do so is another matter, says Garib. There are no pictures showing the construction of the pyramids, so there is no way of knowing what really happened. The evidence for using kites to propel large stones is no good or worse than the evidence for the brute force method, Garib says. Indeed, the experiments have left many experts unconvinced. The evidence for kite lifting doesn't exist, says Wilke Wendrich, an associate professor of Egyptology at the University of California, Los Angeles. Others feel there is more of a case for the theory. Harnessing the wind would not have been a problem for talented sailors like the Egyptians. And they are known to have used wooden pulleys, which can be strong enough to bear the weight of massive stone blocks. In addition, there is physical evidence that the ancient Egyptians were interested in flight. A wooden object found on the staircase pyramid in Saqqara looks oddly like a modern glider. Although it is dated to several centuries after the construction of the pyramids, its sophistication suggests that the Egyptians may have developed ideas of flight for a long time. And other ancient civilizations certainly knew about kites; as early as 1250 BC, the Chinese used them to deliver messages and throw burning debris at their enemies. Experiments may even have practical uses nowadays. There are many places around the world where people do not have access to heavy machinery, yet they know how to handle wind, sailing and basic mechanical principles. Grieve has already been approached by a civil engineer in Nicaragua, who wants to erect buildings with adobe roofs supported by concrete arches on a site that heavy equipment cannot reach. His idea is to build the arches horizontally, then lift them into place using kites. We gave him some design cues, Garib says. I was just waiting for him to report back. So whether or not they were actually used to build the pyramids, it seems that kites may make sensible construction tools in the 21st century AD.
hypothesis: Clemmons found a strange hieroglyph on the wall of an Egyptian monument.

premise: Reading the screen Does electronic communication aggravate illiteracy and make our children stupid? On the contrary, says Colin McCabe, they have the potential to make us read and read and truly write. The debate around literacy is one of the most charged in education. On the one hand there is an army of people convinced that the traditional skills of reading and writing are declining. On the other hand, a host of progressives protest that literacy is far more complicated than simple technical mastery in reading and writing. This latter role has been supported by most relevant academic work over the past 20 years. These studies argue that literacy can only be understood in its social and technical context. In Renaissance England, for example, far more people could read than they could write, and within reading there was a distinction between those who could read a pattern and those who could manage the more difficult task of reading a manuscript. An understanding of these earlier periods helps us understand today's crisis in the debate about literacy. There seems to be evidence that there has been an overall decline in some aspects of reading and writing you only have to compare today's tabloid newspapers to those of 50 years ago to see a clear decline in vocabulary and simplification of syntax. But the picture is uneven and does not easily demonstrate the simple distinction between literate and illiterate that has been considered sufficient since the mid-19th century. While reading a certain amount of writing is as critical as it ever was in industrial societies, it is doubtful whether a full extended conception of either is as necessary as it was 30 or 40 years ago. While print retains much of its authority as a source of topical information, television is increasingly usurping this role. The ability to write regular letters has been undermined by the telephone and studies suggest that for many people the only use for writing, outside of formal education, is collecting shopping lists. The decision of some car manufacturers to issue their instructions to machinists as a video package rather than as a guide may be taken to mark the end of any automatic link between industrialization and literacy. On the other hand, it's also the case that an increasing number of people are making a living from writing, which is better rewarded than ever before. Schools are generally seen as institutions where school rules for film, television, and recorded sound have almost no place; but it is not clear that this objection is appropriate. While you don't need to read and write to watch TV, but you definitely need to be able to read and write to create programs. Those who work in the new media are not illiterate. The traditional objections between the old and new media are inadequate for understanding the world that a young child now encounters. The computer re-established a central place for the word written on the screen, which had previously been entirely devoted to the image. There is even anecdotal evidence that children master reading and writing to go online. There is no reason why the new and old media cannot be integrated into schools to provide the skills to become economically productive and politically privileged. However, there is a crisis in literacy and it would be foolish to ignore it. Realizing that literacy may decline because it is less central in certain aspects of daily life is not the same as agreeing to this state of affairs. The production of school work with the new technologies can be a significant stimulus to literacy. How should these new technologies be introduced into schools? It is not enough to call computers, camcorders and editing suites in every classroom; unless they are properly integrated into the educational culture, they will stand unused. Evidence suggests that this is the fate of much of the information technology used in the classroom. Similarly, although media studies are now part of the national curriculum, and more and more students are now being required to take these courses, teachers are left unsure of both methods and objectives in this area. It's not the fault of the teachers. The entertainment and information industries should be drawn into a debate with educational institutions to determine how best to integrate these new technologies into the classroom. Many people in our era are drawn to the pessimistic perception that new media destroys old skills and erodes critical judgment. It is possible that earlier generations were more literate, but if you take the pre-19th century meaning of the term it was only true for a small part of the population. The word literacy is a 19th-century coinage to describe a divorce of reading and writing from the full knowledge of literature. The educational reforms of the 19th century yielded reading and writing skills that can be separated from full participation in cultural heritage. The new media now points to not only a futuristic cyber economy, it is also making our cultural past available to the nation as a whole. Most children's access to these treasures is initially through television. It's doubtful whether our literary heritage was available or sought by more than about 5 percent of the population; it certainly wasn't available to more than 10 percent. But the new media joining the old, through the civil service tradition of British broadcasting, is now making our literary tradition available to everyone.
hypothesis: Literacy levels are not as easy to analyze as it used to be.

premise: Increase in IEA temperatures The average air temperature on Earth has risen this century, as has the temperature of sea surface water. Because water expands as it warms, a warmer ocean means higher sea levels. We cannot say with certainty that the temperature rise is due to the greenhouse effect; the heating may be part of a natural variability over a long time scale that we have not yet recognized in our 100 short recording years. That is assuming, however, that the accumulation of greenhouse gases is responsible, and that warming will continue. Scientists and residents of low-lying coastal areas would like to know the extent of future sea level rise. This calculation is not easy. Models used for the purpose treated the oceans as passive, stationary, and one-dimensional. Scientists assumed the heat was simply dissipating into the sea from the atmosphere. Using basic physical laws, they predict how much of a known volume of water will expand to a given increase in temperature. But the oceans are not one-dimensional, and recent work by oceanographers - using a new model that takes into account several subtle aspects of the sea - including vast and complex ocean currents - suggest that sea level rise may be less than some previous estimates predicted. An international forum on climate change, in 1986, produced data for probable sea level rises of 20 cm and 1.4 m, equivalent to atmospheric temperature rises of 1.5 and 4.5 °C respectively. Some scientists estimate that ocean warming resulting from temperature increases by 2050 will raise sea levels by between 10 cm and 40 cm. This model only takes into account the effect of temperature on the oceans; it does not address changes in sea level caused by melting of ice sheets and glaciers, and changes in groundwater storage. When we add estimates of these, we arrive at data of total sea level rises of 15 cm and 70 cm respectively. It is not easy to try to accurately model the enormous complexity of the constantly changing oceans, with their large volume, massive currents and sensitivity to the influence of land masses and the atmosphere. For example, consider how heat enters the ocean. Does it just\ dissipate\ from the warmer air vertically into the water, warming only the surface layer of the sea? (Warm water is less dense than cold, so it won't spread downward). Conventional models of sea-level rise considered this to be the only method, but measurements showed that the rate of heat transfer to the ocean by vertical diffusion is much lower in practice than the data many models have adopted. Much of the early form, for simplicity's sake, ignored the fact that water in the oceans moves in 3D. By movement, of course, scientists do not mean waves, which are too small to consider them, but the movement of massive amounts of water in huge streams. To understand the importance of this, we must consider another process - progress. Imagine smoke rising from a chimney. On a still day it will spread slowly in all directions through diffusion. However, with a strong directional wind, everything will change downwind, this process is a progression - transporting features (mainly heat and salinity in the ocean) by the movement of air or water bodies, rather than by conduction or diffusion. A massive ocean current called the Girs makes the movement. These currents have a much greater capacity to store heat than the atmosphere. Indeed, only the upper 3m of the ocean contain more heat than the entire atmosphere. THE ORIGIN OF THE JAYERS LIES IN THE FACT THAT MORE HEAT FROM THE SUN REACHES THE EQUATOR THAN THE POLES, AND NATURALLY HEAT TRENDS MOVE FROM THE FIRST TO THE LAST. Warm air rises at the equator, and draws more air beneath it in the form of winds (\ trade winds\), which along with other air movements, provide the primary force driving ocean currents. The water itself is heated at the equator and moves towards the pole, distorted by the rotation of the Earth and influenced by the positions of the continents. The resulting extensive circular motions between about 10' and 40' north and south are clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere. They flow towards the east at southerly latitudes in the equatorial zone. They then flow towards the Poles, along the eastern sides of the continents, as warm currents. When two different water masses meet, one time will move below the other, depending on their relative density in the deactivation process. Density is determined by temperature and salinity. Convergence of water of different density from the equator and poles at the depth of the oceans results in sustained investment. This means that water moves vertically as well as horizontally. Cold water from the Poles moves as depth - it is denser than warm water until it appears on the surface in another part of the world in the form of a cold stream. Section 8. HOW GREENHOUSE EFFECTS WILL CHANGE OCEAN TEMPERATURES OCEAN CURRENTS, IN 3D, FROM A “GIANT” CONVEYOR BELT, WHICH DISTRIBUTES HEAT FROM THE THIN SURFACE LAYER TO THE INTERIOR OF THE OCEANS AND AROUND THE WORLD. Water may take decades to circulate in these three-dimensional sectors in the locomotive mile of the ocean, and centuries in the deep water. With the increased atmospheric temperatures due to the greenhouse effect, the oceans' conveyor belt will carry more heat to the interior. This reduction transfers heat much more efficiently than simple diffusion. Because warm waters expand more than cold when heated, scientists assumed that sea levels would rise unevenly around the world. Today it is believed that this inequality cannot last, since winds will act to continuously disperse the spread of water. Of course, if global warming changes the strength and distribution of winds, then this process cannot occur, and sea levels may rise in some areas more than others.
hypothesis: The surface layer of the oceans is warmed by the atmosphere.

premise: Robots Since the dawn of human ingenuity, people have invented increasingly cunning tools to deal with dangerous, boring, burdensome or just plain nasty work. This compulsion culminated in robotics, the science of granting various human abilities to machines. The modern world is increasingly populated with quasi-intelligent gizmos whose presence we barely notice but whose ubiquitous creeping presence has removed much human labor. Our factories are buzzing to the rhythm of robot assembly arms. Our banking is done at automated acceptance terminals that politely thank us for the transaction. Our subway trains are controlled by tireless robot drivers. Our mine shafts are dug by automatic moles, and our nuclear accidents like those at Three Mile Island and Chernobyl are cleaned by robots that are fit to withstand radiation. Such is the extent of uses envisaged by Karel Kapek, the Czech playwright who coined the term robot in 1920 (the word robot means forced labour in Czech). As progress accelerates, the experiment becomes an exploit at a record rate. Other innovations promise to expand the capabilities of human operators. Thanks to the incessant miniaturization of electronics and micromechanics, there are already robot systems that can perform certain types of brain and bone surgeries with sub-millimeter precision far greater than skilled doctors can achieve with their hands alone. At the same time, techniques of long-distance control will keep people even further away from danger. In 1994 a ten-foot-tall robotic NASA explorer named Dante, with video camera eyes and spider-like legs, mingled on the ominous rim of an Alaskan volcano while technicians 2,000 miles away in California watched the scene by satellite and controlled the descent of Dantes. But if robots are to reach the next level of labor-saving service, they will need to operate with less human oversight and be able to make at least some decisions for themselves goals that pose a formidable challenge. Although we know how to tell a robot to deal with a specific error, says one expert, we still can't give a robot enough common sense to reliably interact with a dynamic world. Indeed the search for true artificial intelligence (Al) has yielded very mixed results. Despite a spasm of initial optimism in the 1960s and 1970s, when it seemed that transistor circuits and microprocessors might be able to operate in the same way as the human brain by the 21st century, researchers have recently expanded their predictions by decades if not centuries. What they found, in an attempt to model thought, is that the human brain's roughly one hundred billion neurons is far more competent and human perception far more complicated than previously imagined. They have built robots that can detect the mismatch of a machine board in a fraction of a millimeter in a controlled factory environment. But the human mind can glimpse the rapidly changing scene and immediately ignore the 98 percent irrelevant, focusing immediately on hunting through a winding forest or the one suspicious face in a stormy crowd. The most advanced computer systems on the planet cannot come close to this kind of capabilities, and neuroscientists still don't know exactly how we do it. Nevertheless, when information theorists, neuroscientists, and computer experts combine their talents, they find ways to get some life-like intelligence from robots. One method forgoes the linear and logical structure of conventional electronic circuits in favor of the messy, ad hoc arrangement of real brain neurons. There is no need to program these neural networks. They can teach themselves by a system of feedback signals that reinforce electrical pathways that produced correct responses and, conversely, erase connections that produced errors. Eventually the network connects to a system that can pronounce certain words or distinguish certain shapes. In other fields researchers are struggling to fashion a more natural relationship between people and robots in the expectation that machines will one day take on some of the tasks now done by humans, for example, in nursing homes. This is especially important in Japan, where the percentage of elderly citizens is growing rapidly. So experiments at Tokyo Science University created a life-size soft plastic model face robot of a female head with a video camera embedded in the left eye as a prototype. The researchers' goal is to create robots that people feel comfortable around. They concentrate on the face because they believe facial expressions are the most important way to convey emotional messages. We read these messages by interpreting phrases to decide whether a person is happy, scared, angry or nervous. Thus the Japanese robot aims to detect emotions in the person it looks at by sensing changes in the spatial arrangement of the person's eyes, nose, eyebrows and mouth. He compares these configurations with a database of standard facial expressions and guesses the emotion. The robot then uses an ensemble of tiny pressure pads to adjust its plastic surface for an appropriate emotional response. Other labs take a different approach, one that doesn't try to mimic human intelligence or emotions. Just as computer design has moved away from a single central computer in favour of multiple individual workstations and individual processors have been replaced by arrays of smaller units that break down a major problem into parts that are solved simultaneously many experts are now investigating whether swarms of semi-intelligent robots can produce collective intelligence that is greater than the sum of its parts. That's what hives and ant colonies do, and some teams are betting that legions of species of creatures can be sent working together like an ant colony to explore the climates of planets or test pipelines in hazardous industrial situations.
hypothesis: Robots are capable of making fine visual judgments.

premise: Raise Mary Rose. How a sixteenth-century warship was recovered from the seabed. On July 19, 1545, an English and French fleet engaged in a naval battle off the coast of southern England in the area of water called the Solent, between Portsmouth and the Isle of Wight. Among the English ships was a warship called the Mary Rose. Built at Portsmouth some 35 years earlier, she had had a long and successful fighting career, and was a favourite of King Henry VIII. Reports of what happened to the ship vary: while witnesses agree that she was not damaged by the French, some argue that she was outdated, too overloaded and sailed too low in the water, others that she was improperly handled by an undisciplined crew. What is indisputable, however, is that the Mary Rose sank in the Solent that day, taking at least 500 men with her. After the battle, attempts were made to recover the ship, but these were unsuccessful. Mary Rose came to rest on the seabed, lying on her right (right) side at an angle of about 60 degrees. The hull (hull) served as a trap for sand and mud carried by Solent currents. As a result, the starboard side quickly filled in, leaving the exposed port side (left) to be eroded by marine organisms and mechanical degradation. Because of the manner in which the ship sank, almost the entire starboard half survived intact. During the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, the entire site was covered with a layer of hard gray clay, which minimized further erosion. Then, on June 16, 1836, some fishermen in the Solent discovered that their gear had been caught on an underwater blockage, which turned out to be Mary Rose. Diver John Dean happened to be exploring another sunken ship nearby, and the fishermen approached him and asked him to release their gear. Dean dived down and found the equipment caught on a tree protruding slightly from the seabed. On further exploration, he uncovered several more trees and a bronze gun. Dean continued to dive at the site on and off until 1840, bringing back several additional guns, two bows, various lumber, part of a pump, and other small artifacts. The Mary Rose then faded into a fog for another hundred years. But in 1965, military historian and amateur diver Alexander McKee, in conjunction with the British Sub-Aqua Club, initiated a project called Solent Ships. While on paper this was a plan to examine a number of known ruins in the Solent, what McKee really hoped for was to find the Mary Rose. Ordinary search techniques were not satisfactory, so McKee entered into a collaboration with Harold A. Edgerton, a professor of electrical engineering at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. In 1967, Edgerton side-scan sonar systems revealed a large object of unusual shape, which McKee believed to be Mary Rose. Further excavations revealed stray pieces of wood and an iron gun. But the climax of the operation came when, on May 5, 1971, part of the ships' frame was uncovered. McKee and his team now knew for certain that they had found the wreck, but were not yet aware that it also contained a treasure trove of beautifully preserved artefacts. Interest in the project grew, and in 1979 the Mary Rose Foundation was established, with Prince Charles as president and Dr. Margaret Roll its archaeological director. The decision of whether or not to salvage the wreck was an easy one, although an excavation in 1978 showed that the body might be able to be raised. While the original aim was to raise the body if at all possible, the operation did not receive approval until January 1982, by which time all the necessary information was available. An important factor in the attempt to save Mary Rose was that the remaining body was an open shell. This led to an important decision: namely to carry out the lifting operation in three very clear steps. The body was attached to the lifting frame by means of a net of screws and lifting wires. The problem of pumping the body backwards and downwards into the mud was overcome by using 12 hydraulic jacks. These lifted it several inches over a period of several days, as the lifting frame slowly rose up its four legs. Only when the body hung freely from the lifting frame, clear of the seabed and from the suction effect of the surrounding mud, did the rescue operation progress to the second phase. At this point, the lifting frame was fixed to a hook attached to the crane, and the hull was completely raised from the seabed and moved underwater to the lifting cradle. This required precise positioning to locate the legs into the jacking guides of the lifting cradle. The lifting cradle was designed to fit the body using archaeological survey drawings, and was fitted with airbags to provide additional cushioning for the shell's delicate wooden frame. The third and final stage was to lift the entire structure into the air, then the body was also supported from below. Finally, on October 11, 1982, millions of people around the world held their breath as the wooden skeleton of Mary Rose was raised from the water, ready to be returned home to Portsmouth.

premise: RESTORING A DAMAGED REPUTATION IN 2009 IT WAS REVEALED THAT SOME OF THE INFORMATION PUBLISHED BY THE UNIVERSITY OF EAST ANGLIA'S CLIMATIC RESEARCH UNIT (CRU) IN THE UK, RELATING TO CLIMATE CHANGE, WAS INACCURATE. Furthermore, it was argued that some of the relevant statistics were withheld from publication. The ensuing controversy affected the reputation not only of that institution, but also of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), with which the CRU is involved, and of climate scientists in general. Even if the allegations regarding misconduct and incompetence were ultimately proved largely untrue, or limited to a few people, the damage was done. The perceived wrongdoings of some people have raised doubts about the many. The response of most climate scientists was to cross fingers and hope for the best, and they kept a low profile. Many no doubt hoped that subsequent independent investigations into the IPCC and CRU would draw a line under their problems. However, while these are likely to help, they are unlikely to undo the damage caused by months of hostile news reports and attacks from critics. The damage done should not be underestimated. As Ralph Caesaron, president of the US National Academy of Sciences, wrote in an editorial in the journal Science: Public opinion has moved towards the view that scientists often try to suppress alternative hypotheses and ideas and that scientists will withhold data and try to manipulate some aspects of peer review to avoid dissent. He concluded that the perceived misbehavior of even a few scientists could diminish the credibility of science as a whole. A public opinion poll conducted in early 2010 found that the proportion of people in the U.S. who trust scientists as a source of information about global warming has dropped from 83 percent in 2008 to 74 percent. Another survey conducted by the British Broadcasting Corporation in February 2010 found that only 26 percent of British people now believe climate change is confirmed as man-made, down from 41% in November 2009. Regaining the trust and confidence of the public is never easy. To bend over and hope for the best current strategy in climate science makes that almost impossible. Far better to learn from the successes and failures of organizations that have faced similar blows to their public standing. In fact, climate science needs professional help to rebuild its reputation. It could be worse than following the advice given by Leslie Gaines-Ross, reputation strategist at public relations (PR) firm Webef Shandwick, in her recent book Corporate Reputation: 12 Steps to Maintaining and Restoring Reputation. Gaines-Ross's strategy is based on her analysis of how various organizations responded to crises, like desktop printer company Xerox, whose business plummeted during the 1990s, and the U.S. National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) after the Columbia shuttle disaster in 2003. The first step she suggests is to take the heat leader first. In many cases, CEOs who publicly accept responsibility for corporate failures can begin to reverse the free fall of their company's reputation, but not always. If the leader is at least partly responsible for the fall from grace, it can be almost impossible to convince critics that a new direction can be described with the same person at the helm. This is the dilemma facing the heads of the IPCC and CRU. Both were blamed for their organisations' problems, not least in the way they dealt with critics, and both were subjected to public calls for their removal. However both organisations seem to believe they can repair their reputations without a leadership change. The second step described by Gaines-Ross is to communicate tirelessly. However, many climate researchers avoided the media and the public, at least until the official investigations finished their reports. This comment may be understandable, but it has come back. Journalists following the story have been unable to find speakers willing to defend climate science. In this case, no comment is usually interpreted as a silent, collective admission of guilt. However, staying visible is just a start; climate scientists should also be careful what they say. They must understand that they face doubts not only about the published results, but also about their behavior and sincerity. It simply would not work for scientists to continue to appeal to the weight of evidence, while refusing to discuss the integrity of their profession. The damage was amplified by a perceived reluctance to admit even the possibility of mistakes or wrongdoings. The third step suggested by Gaines-Ross is don't underestimate your critics and competitors. This means not only recognizing the skill with which opponents of climate research have carried out their campaigns through Internet blogs and other media, but also acknowledging the validity of some of their criticisms. It is clear, for example, that climate scientists need better standards of transparency, to allow scrutiny not only by their peers, but also by critics outside the world of research. It's also important to get in touch with these visitors. This does not mean giving up outlandish arguments based on prejudice rather than evidence, but rather there is a duty to help the public understand the causes of climate change, as well as the options for avoiding and dealing with the consequences. To begin the process of building trust in their profession, climate scientists need to keep track of these three seeps. But this is just the beginning. Gaines-Ross reckons that it usually takes a company four years to salvage and restore a broken reputation. Winning back the public's trust is a marathon, not a sprint, but you can't win at all if you don't get to the start line

premise: Red list of threatened species reveals global extinction crisis The planet's most severely endangered animals and plants are disappearing at breakneck speed since 1996, the world's largest international conservation organisation reported today. One in four mammal species and one in eight bird species face a high risk of extinction in the near future, in almost all cases because of human activity. The total number of threatened animal species increased from 5,205 to 5,435. The 2000 IUCN Red List of Threatened Species is published every four years by the World Conservation Union IUCN. The Red List is considered the most authoritative and comprehensive assessment of the state of global biodiversity. The IUCN, founded in 1948, brings together 77 countries, 112 government agencies, 735 NGOs, 35 offshoots and about 10,000 scientists and experts from 181 countries in a global partnership. Based on all these sources of information, the Red List report uses scientific criteria to classify species into one of eight categories: Extinct, Extinct in the Wild, Critically Endangered, Endangered, Vulnerable, Lower Risk, Data Deficient, and Underestimated. A species is classified as threatened if it falls in the categories Critically Endangered, Endangered or Vulnerable. The fact that the number of critically endangered species increased from mammals from 169 to 180; birds from 168 to 182 was a jolting surprise, even to those already familiar with today's growing threats to biodiversity. These findings should be taken very seriously by the world community, says Marita von Bieberstein Koch-Woeser, director general of the IUCN. The magnitude of the risk, presented by movements into the higher risk categories, has increased, although the overall percentage of threatened mammals and birds has not changed much in four years, the IUCN found. Primates such as monkeys and apes showed the greatest increase in the number of threatened mammals from 96 to 116 species. It has been found that many changes are caused by habitat loss and hunting habitat, particularly the bush meat trade. The number of critically endangered primates increased from 13 to 19. Endangered primates number 46 today, compared with 29 four years ago. Russell Mittermeyer, president of Conservation International and chairman of the IUCNs' Primate Expert Group, says the Red List is a solid record of the global extinction crisis, revealing only the tip of the iceberg. Many wonderful creatures will be lost in the first decades of the 21st century unless we greatly increase levels of support, involvement and commitment to conservation, he warns. Human and financial resources must be mobilized 10 to 100 times the current level to deal with this crisis, reads the Red List analysis. Indonesia, India, Brazil and China are among the countries with the most threatened mammals and birds, while the plant species are declining rapidly in South and Central America, Central and West Africa and Southeast Asia. Habitat loss and habitat deterioration affect 89 percent of all threatened birds, 83 percent of mammals, and 91 percent of threatened plants assessed. Habitats with the highest number of threatened mammals and birds are lowland tropical rainforests and mountains. Freshwater habitats are extremely vulnerable with many threatened species of fish, reptiles, amphibians and invertebrates. Freshwater turtles, which are heavily exploited for food and medical use in Asia, have gone from 10 to 24 critically endangered species in the past four years. Hunting of these species is neither regulated nor managed, and harvest levels are too high for the species to sustain, the IUCN warns. As populations disappear in Southeast Asia, there are signs that this trade is increasingly shifting to India, and further afield to the Americas and Africa. The report indicates an extremely severe deterioration in the condition of river-dwelling species mainly due to water development projects and other habitat changes. One of the main threats to species inhabiting the lake is introduced species. A systematic analysis of the status of these species will be carried out in three years. BirdLife International has produced the global status analysis which is a key component of the Red List. The most significant changes have been in albatrosses and paterels, with an increase from 32 to 55 threatened species. 16 albatross species are threatened today compared to just three in 1996, as a result of long-line fishing. Of the five remaining albatross species, four are now virtually threatened. Threatened penguin species have doubled from five to ten. These increases reflect the increasing threats to the marine environment, the IUCN reports. Birdlife International has launched an international campaign titled, Saving the Albatross: Keeping the World's Seabirds Off the Hook to Reduce Accidental Seabird Catch Through Long Line Fishing, while adopting appropriate mitigation measures. The Philippines, another biodiversity hotspot, has lost 97 percent of its original vegetation and has more critically endangered birds than any other country. The IUCN Red List includes 5,611 species of threatened plants, many of which are trees. The total number of threatened plant species in the world is still small relative to the total number of plant species, but this is because most plant species have not yet been assessed for their threat level, says the IUCN. The only major plant group that has been comprehensively assessed is the conifers, of which 140 species, 16 percent of the total, are threatened. Estimates conducted by the Nature Conservancy, which have not yet been incorporated into the Red List, indicate that one-third of North American plant species are threatened. In the last 500 years, human activity has forced 816 species into extinction or extinction in the wild. One hundred and three extinctions have occurred since 1800, indicating an extinction rate 50 times greater than the natural rate. Many species are lost before they are discovered. A total of 18,276 species and subspecies are included in the 2000 Red List. About 25 percent of reptiles, 20 percent of amphibians and 30 percent of fish, mostly freshwater, assessed so far are listed as threatened. Because only a small fraction of these groups have been assessed, the percentage of threatened species could be much higher, the IUCN says. As well as classifying species according to their extinction risk; the Red List provides information on species range, population trends, major habitats, major threats and conservation measures, both already existing and those needed. This allows insight into the processes driving extinction. The publication of the 2000 Red List comes a week before the Second World Conservation Congress in Amman, Jordan, where IUCN members will meet to define global conservation policies for the next four years, including ways to tackle the growing extinction crisis.

premise: Reducing electricity consumption in the background The Isle of Ig Island is located off the west coast of Scotland, and is reached by ferry from the mainland. For the island community of about a hundred inhabitants, it was always expensive to import products, materials and skilled labor from the mainland, and this encouraged a culture of self-satisfaction and careful use of resources. Today, although the island now has the most modern amenities, CO2 emissions per household are 20% lower than the UK average, and electricity consumption is 50% lower. When Aig planned its electricity grid, which was turned on in February 2008, it soon became clear that to drive down capital construction costs it would be necessary to manage demand. It would also allow the island to generate most of its electricity from renewable sources, mainly water, wind and solar power. This aim was overseen by the Ig Heritage Trust (EHT). Eigg technology manages electricity demand primarily by limiting the immediate power that can be used to five kilowatts (kilowatts) per household and ten kilowatts per business. If use exceeds the limit, the power supply is cut off and maintenance staff should be invited to come and turn it on again. All households and businesses have energy monitors, which display the current and cumulative power consumption, and sound an alarm when consumption reaches a user-defined level, usually set several hundred watts below the actual limit. The result is that Ig residents have a keen sense of how much power different appliances use, and are careful to minimise energy consumption. Demand is also managed by warning the entire island when renewable energy production is lower than demand, and diesel generators operate to back it up what is known as a red light day, as opposed to green light days when there is enough renewable energy. Residents are taking steps to temporarily reduce electricity demand even further, or postpone demand until renewable energy production increases. Energy use on the island has also been reduced through improved wall and loft insulation in homes, new boilers, solar water heating, car sharing and small, energy-saving measures in households. New energy supplies are being developed, including sustainably harvested forests to supply wood for heating. Eigg Heritage Trust installed insulation at all its properties at no cost to tenants, while private properties paid for installing their own insulation. The same applies to installations of solar water heating, although not all trust assets have accepted this so far. The foundation also runs a green grants program, in which residents can claim 50 percent of the cost of equipment to reduce carbon emissions, up to a limit of 300. The purchases included bicycles, solar water heating, secondary glazing, thicker curtains and greenhouses for growing food locally, rather than importing it. Environmental benefits Prior to the installation of the new electricity grid and renewable energy generation, the majority of households in Eigg used diesel generators to provide electricity, resulting in significant carbon emissions. The houses were also poorly insulated and had old and inefficient oil-burning boilers, or used coal for heating. The Ig Heritage Foundation's work to reduce energy use has resulted in significant reductions in carbon emissions from households and businesses on the islands. The average annual use of electricity per household is just 2,160 kilowatt-hours (kWh), compared to the UK average in 2008 of 4,198 kWh. Domestic carbon emissions fell by 47%, from 8.4 to 4.45 tonnes a year. This compared with average UK household emissions of 5.5 to 6 tonnes a year. Emissions should decline further over the next few years as the supply of wood for heating increases. Social benefits The completion of the Igs electricity network has made a significant difference to the inhabitants of the islands, freeing them from dependence on diesel generators and providing them with a stable and affordable electricity supply. Reliable electricity supply has resulted in improvements in other areas, for example, better treatment of drinking water in some homes, and eliminating the constant noise of diesel generators. Improved home insulation and heating have also yielded benefits, making it cheaper to keep homes at a comfortable temperature. One of the incentives for limiting electricity use, rather than charging different amounts depending on use, was to make access to energy equitable. Each household has the same quota of five kilowatts, regardless of income, so the available resources are distributed evenly across the islands' population. Economic and occupational benefits The Igs electricity network supports four part-time maintenance jobs on the island, and residents have also been employed in construction work improving Trust-owned homes and other buildings. Also, the start of the organized harvesting of trees for heating created a number of forestry jobs for residents. A part-time Green Project Manager role was also created. A wider economic impact resulted from a reliable and affordable electricity supply, which allowed a number of new businesses to be established, including restaurants, shops, guest houses and self-catering accommodation. As Ige became known for cutting carbon emissions and protecting the environment, an increasing number of visitors came to the island to learn about his work, which brought additional economic benefit to residents

premise: Reflection in the mirror Probably the first mirrors were simply pools of water that reflected the image of the one who looked into it. The sight of nature, although cheap and accessible, must have been quite frustrating with the slightest disturbance on the surface of the water that made it difficult to see clearly. It is not entirely clear when the first man-made mirrors were produced, but mirrors made of brass are mentioned in the Bible, and later bronze mirrors were in common use among the ancient Egyptians, Romans and Greeks. In addition to bronze, the Greeks and Romans experimented with polished silver for the manufacture of simple mirrors. Crude forms of glass mirrors were first produced in Venice in 1300. Small sheets of glass were cut from discs made in the spinning process. When this glass was raised with a tin or lead coating, a mirror was created. In the early periods of their development, mirrors were rare and expensive. France had glass factories but only in Venice, Italy was the secret of mirror disposal known. The chemical process of coating a glass surface with metallic silver was discovered by the German chemist Justus von Liebig in 1835, and this advance inaugurated the modern techniques of mirror production. By the end of the 17th century, mirrors were manufactured in Britain and mirror manufacturing subsequently developed into an important industry in many other European countries. People wore them in their hats, or placed them like jewels in their rings. The company glittered and shone like the firmament. A little later, America was gripped by the mirror craze, only this time they were interested in larger mirrors. In house after house in residential districts and eastern cities one could find one long mirror after another placed between two front living room windows. In the manufacture of mirrors today, plate glass is cut to size, and all defects are removed by polishing with a blush. The glass is scrubbed and washed with a reduction solution before applying the silver. THE GLASS IS THEN PLACED ON A CAST-IRON HOLLOW TABLE, COVERED WITH FELT AND KEPT BY STEAM. A solution of silver nitrate is poured onto the glass and left undisturbed for about an hour. Silver nitrate is reduced to metallic silver and a shiny silver deposit is gradually formed. The deposit is dried, coated with shellac and dyed. Therefore, most of today's mirrors consist of these layers. Glass is used from above because it is smooth, clear and protects the reflecting surface. A mirror should be very smooth in order for the best reflection to occur. Mirrors may have planar or curved surfaces. A curved mirror is concave or convex, depending on whether the reflecting surface faces toward or away from the center of curvature. Curved mirrors in normal use have surfaces of various shapes. Perhaps the most common is spherical. Spherical mirrors produce images that are enlarged or reduced, by mirrors for applying facial makeup and by rear-view mirrors for vehicles. Cylindrical mirrors are another common type of shape. These focus a beam of light parallel to linear focus. A paraboloid mirror is a mirror often used to focus rays parallel to a sharp focus, as in a telescope mirror, or to produce a parallel beam from a source at its focus, such as a searchlight. A less common but useful form is the ellipsoid. Such a mirror will reflect light from one of two foci to the other. While the mirror is the focus of the production, the frame plays an important albeit slightly less important role as an anchor by which the mirror is affixed to its correct position. From the end of the 17th century onwards, mirrors and their frames played an increasingly important role in the decoration of rooms. The early frames, complementing the shiny binocular appearance, were usually of ivory, silver, ebony or tortoiseshell or were coated in walnut, olive, and bornum. Embroidery frames and beads were also found. CRAFTSMEN SUCH AS GREENLING GIBBONS OFTEN PRODUCED ELABORATELY CARVED MIRROR FRAMES TO FIT AN ENTIRE DECORATIVE ENSEMBLE. Soon the tradition of incorporating a mirror into the space above the cabinet was established: many of the early versions of these mirrors, usually called mantels, were enclosed in glass frames. The architectural structure of which these mirrors formed part became increasingly elaborate. Focusing heavily on the effect created by mirrors, 18th century designers such as the English brothers Robert and James Adam created fireplace units stretching from the fireplace to the ceiling. Overall, mirror frames reflected the general taste of that era and were often modified to accommodate changes in the taste frames generally were cheaper and therefore more easily replaced than the mirror itself. At the end of the 18th century, painted decoration largely replaced carving on mirrors, the frames decorated with floral patterns or classical ornaments. At the same time, the French began to produce round mirrors. USUALLY SURROUNDED BY A NEOCLASSICAL GILDED FRAME THAT SOMETIMES SUPPORTED CANDLESTICKS, THESE MIRRORS ENJOYED GREAT POPULARITY UNTIL THE 19TH CENTURY. Improved skill in mirror manufacturing also enabled the introduction of the cheval glass, a full-length independent mirror, supported on a four-legged frame. These were mainly used for dressing purposes, although occasionally they had a decorative function. Newer and cheaper techniques for making mirrors in the 19th century led to a great spread in their use. Not only were they regularly incorporated into furniture like wardrobes and sideboards, they were also used in everything from high-powered telescopes to decorative schemes in public places. Their popularity continues today. Through them, babies are able to develop awareness of their individuality through mirror games. This type of emotional reflection stimulates babies to move different parts of their body and even promotes verbal utterances.

It is not entirely clear when the first man-made mirrors were produced, but mirrors made of brass are mentioned in the Bible, and later bronze mirrors were in common use among the ancient Egyptians, Romans and Greeks. In addition to bronze, the Greeks and Romans experimented with polished silver for the manufacture of simple mirrors. Crude forms of glass mirrors were first produced in Venice in 1300. Small sheets of glass were cut from discs made in the spinning process. When this glass was raised with a tin or lead coating, a mirror was created. In the early periods of their development, mirrors were rare and expensive. France had glass factories but only in Venice, Italy was the secret of mirror disposal known. The chemical process of coating a glass surface with metallic silver was discovered by the German chemist Justus von Liebig in 1835, and this advance inaugurated the modern techniques of mirror production. By the end of the 17th century, mirrors were manufactured in Britain and mirror manufacturing subsequently developed into an important industry in many other European countries. People wore them in their hats, or placed them like jewels in their rings. The company glittered and shone like the firmament. A little later, America was gripped by the mirror craze, only this time they were interested in larger mirrors. In house after house in residential districts and eastern cities one could find one long mirror after another placed between two front living room windows. In the manufacture of mirrors today, plate glass is cut to size, and all defects are removed by polishing with a blush. The glass is scrubbed and washed with a reduction solution before applying the silver. THE GLASS IS THEN PLACED ON A CAST-IRON HOLLOW TABLE, COVERED WITH FELT AND KEPT BY STEAM. A solution of silver nitrate is poured onto the glass and left undisturbed for about an hour. Silver nitrate is reduced to metallic silver and a shiny silver deposit is gradually formed. The deposit is dried, coated with shellac and dyed. Therefore, most of today's mirrors consist of these layers. Glass is used from above because it is smooth, clear and protects the reflecting surface. A mirror should be very smooth in order for the best reflection to occur. Mirrors may have planar or curved surfaces. A curved mirror is concave or convex, depending on whether the reflecting surface faces toward or away from the center of curvature. Curved mirrors in normal use have surfaces of various shapes. Perhaps the most common is spherical. Spherical mirrors produce images that are enlarged or reduced, by mirrors for applying facial makeup and by rear-view mirrors for vehicles. Cylindrical mirrors are another common type of shape. These focus a beam of light parallel to linear focus. A paraboloid mirror is a mirror often used to focus rays parallel to a sharp focus, as in a telescope mirror, or to produce a parallel beam from a source at its focus, such as a searchlight. A less common but useful form is the ellipsoid. Such a mirror will reflect light from one of two foci to the other. While the mirror is the focus of the production, the frame plays an important albeit slightly less important role as an anchor by which the mirror is affixed to its correct position. From the end of the 17th century onwards, mirrors and their frames played an increasingly important role in the decoration of rooms. The early frames, complementing the shiny binocular appearance, were usually of ivory, silver, ebony or tortoiseshell or were coated in walnut, olive, and bornum. Embroidery frames and beads were also found. CRAFTSMEN SUCH AS GREENLING GIBBONS OFTEN PRODUCED ELABORATELY CARVED MIRROR FRAMES TO FIT AN ENTIRE DECORATIVE ENSEMBLE. Soon the tradition of incorporating a mirror into the space above the cabinet was established: many of the early versions of these mirrors, usually called mantels, were enclosed in glass frames. The architectural structure of which these mirrors formed part became increasingly elaborate. Focusing heavily on the effect created by mirrors, 18th century designers such as the English brothers Robert and James Adam created fireplace units stretching from the fireplace to the ceiling. Overall, mirror frames reflected the general taste of that era and were often modified to accommodate changes in the taste frames generally were cheaper and therefore more easily replaced than the mirror itself. At the end of the 18th century, painted decoration largely replaced carving on mirrors, the frames decorated with floral patterns or classical ornaments. At the same time, the French began to produce round mirrors. USUALLY SURROUNDED BY A NEOCLASSICAL GILDED FRAME THAT SOMETIMES SUPPORTED CANDLESTICKS, THESE MIRRORS ENJOYED GREAT POPULARITY UNTIL THE 19TH CENTURY. Improved skill in mirror manufacturing also enabled the introduction of the cheval glass, a full-length independent mirror, supported on a four-legged frame. These were mainly used for dressing purposes, although occasionally they had a decorative function. Newer and cheaper techniques for making mirrors in the 19th century led to a great spread in their use. Not only were they regularly incorporated into furniture like wardrobes and sideboards, they were also used in everything from high-powered telescopes to decorative schemes in public places. Their popularity continues today. Through them, babies are able to develop awareness of their individuality through mirror games. This type of emotional reflection stimulates babies to move different parts of their body and even promotes verbal utterances.
hypothesis: The first man-made mirrors were made of bronze.
label: c

premise: Research using twins. For biomedical researchers all over the world, twins offer a valuable opportunity to break down the influence of genes and the natural and nurturing environment. Because identical twins come from one fertilized egg that splits in two, they share almost the same genetic code. Any difference between them and one younger-looking skin twin, for example, must be due to environmental factors like less time spent in the sun. Alternatively, by comparing the experiences of identical twins to those of fraternal twins, who come from separate eggs and share on average half of their DNA, researchers can quantify the extent to which our genes influence our lives. If identical twins are more similar to each other in relation to the disease than fraternal twins, then the vulnerability to the disease must be rooted at least in part in heredity. These two lines of research investigating the differences between identical twins to pinpoint the influence of the environment, and comparing identical twins with siblings to measure the role of inheritance have been crucial to understanding the interplay of nature and nurture in determining our personality, behavior, and vulnerability to disease. The idea of using twins to measure the influence of heredity dates back to 1875, when English scientist Francis Galton first proposed the approach (and coined the phrase 'nature and nurture'). But twin studies got a surprising twist in the 1980s, with the arrival of studies on identical twins who were separated at birth and reunited as adults. Over two decades 137 sets of twins eventually visited Thomas Bouchard's laboratory in what became known as the Minnesota Study of Twins Raised Apart. Numerous tests were carried out on the twins, and each was asked more than 15,000 questions. Bouchard and colleagues used this mountain of data to identify how much twins were affected by their genetic makeup. Key to their approach was a statistical concept called heredity. In broad terms, the heritability of a trait measures the extent to which differences between members of a population can be explained by differences in their genetics. And everywhere Bouchard and other scientists looked, they seemed to have found the invisible hand of genetic influence that helps shape our lives. Recently, however, twin studies have helped lead scientists to a radical new conclusion: that nature and nurture are not the only fundamental forces at work. According to a recent field called epigenetics, there is also a third factor at play, one that in some cases serves as a bridge between the environment and our genes, and in others acts by itself to shape who we are. Epigenetic processes are chemical reactions related neither to nature nor to cultivation but represent what the researchers called a 'third component'. These responses affect how our genetic code is expressed: how each gene is strengthened or weakened, even turned on or off, to build our bones, brains and all other parts of our bodies. If you think of our DNA as an enormous piano keyboard and our genes as keys each key signifying a section of DNA responsible for a particular character, or trait, and all the keys that combine to make us who we are then epigenetic processes determine when and how each key can be hit, changing the melody that sounds. One of the ways in which the study of epigenetics has revolutionized our understanding of biology is by revealing a mechanism by which the environment directly influences genes. Animal studies, for example, have shown that when a rat experiences stress during pregnancy, it can cause epigenetic changes in the fetus that lead to behavioral problems as the rodent grows. Other epigenetic processes seem to occur randomly, while others are normal, such as those that guide embryonic cells as they become heart, brain or liver cells, for example. Geneticist Daniela Reid has worked with many twins over the years and thought deeply about what twin studies have taught us. “It's very clear when you look at twins that a large part of what they share is connected,” she says. “A lot of things about them are absolutely identical and immutable. But it is also clear, when you know them, that other things about them are different. Epigenetics is the source of many of these differences, in my opinion. Reed credits the work of Thomas Bouchard for today's rise in twin studies. “He was the trailblazer,” she says. “We forget that 50 years ago it was thought that things like heart disease were entirely caused by lifestyle. Schizophrenia was thought to result from impaired motherhood. Twin studies have allowed us to contemplate more with what people are actually born with and what is caused by experience. 'However, adds Reed, recent work in epigenetics promises to take our understanding even further. “What I like to say is that nature writes things in pencil and some things in pen,” she says. Things written with a pen can't be changed. It's DNA. But things written in pencil you can. It's epigenetics. Now that we're actually able to look at the DNA and see where the pencil writings are, it's kind of a whole new world. '

premise: Rogue smell theory gets boost A controversial theory of how we smell, which claims our fine sense of smell depends on quantum mechanics, has been given the thumbs up by a team of physicists. Calculations by researchers from University College London (UCL) show that the idea that we smell odor molecules by sensing their molecular vibrations makes sense in terms of the physics involved. It's still a way to prove that the theory, proposed in the mid-1990s by biophysicist Luca Turin, is correct. But it should make other scientists take the idea more seriously.\ It's a big step forward,\ says Torino, who has now set up his own perfume company Flexitral in Virginia. He says that since he published his theory, it has been ignored and not criticized.\ Most scientists have assumed that our sense of smell depends on receptors in the nose that detect the shape of incoming molecules, which triggers a signal to the brain. This molecular “lock and key” process is thought to be behind a wide range of the body's detection systems: how certain parts of the immune system detect invaders, for example, and how the tongue recognises particular flavours. But Torino argued that the smell didn't seem to fit that picture well. Molecules that look almost identical can smell very differently like alcohols, which smell like spirits, and thiols, which smell like rotten eggs. And molecules with very different structures can smell similar. Most strikingly, some molecules can smell different from animals, if not necessarily to humans simply because they contain different isotopes (chemically identical atoms but of different mass). TURIN'S EXPLANATION OF THESE STINKING FACTS GIVES RISE TO THE IDEA THAT THE OLFACTORY SIGNAL IN OLFACTORY RECEPTOR PROTEINS IS TRIGGERED NOT BY THE SHAPE OF AN ODOR MOLECULE, BUT BY ITS VIBRATIONS, WHICH CAN CAUSE AN ELECTRON TO JUMP BETWEEN TWO PARTS OF THE RECEPTOR IN A QUANTUM-MECHANICAL PROCESS CALLED TUNNELING. This electron movement can initiate the olfactory signal sent to the brain. This would explain why isotopes can smell different: their vibrational frequencies change if the atoms are heavier. Torino's mechanism, says Marshall Stoneham from the UCL team, is more akin to identifying a skate card than a key that fits a lock. Electron tunneling with the help of vibration can undoubtedly occur It is used in an experimental technique to measure molecular vibrations.\ The question is whether this is possible in the nose,\ says Stoneham's colleague, Andrew Horsfield. Stoneham says that when he first heard about the Turin idea, while Torino himself was from UCL, I didn't believe him\. But, he adds, because it was an interesting idea, I thought I had to prove it couldn't work. I did some simple calculations, and it was only then that I began to feel that Luca might be right.\ Now Stoneham and his co-workers have done the work more thoroughly, in an article to be published soon in Physical Review Letters. The UCL team calculated the electron jump rates at a receptor even though it has an odour molecule attached to it. This rate depends on various properties of the biomolecular system that are unknown, but the researchers could estimate these parameters based on values typical of molecules of this type. The key issue is whether the jump rate with the odorant in place is significantly greater than that without it. The calculations show that this is what means that detecting an odor in this way seems theoretically possible. But Horsfield stresses that this is different from Turin's proof of idea.\ So far things seem plausible, but we need appropriate experimental verification. We begin to think about what experiments can be carried out.\ In the meantime, Torino continues forward with his hypothesis.\ At Flexitral we designed fragrances solely on the basis of their calculated vibration,\ he says.\ Our success rate in detecting fragrances is two orders of magnitude better than competitors.\ At the very least, he puts his money where his nose is.

premise: Role set Each person in any situation occupies a role in relation to other people. The particular person with whom the person is concerned in analyzing each situation is usually given the name of a focal person. He has the focal role and can be seen sitting in the middle of a group of people, with whom he communicates in some way in this situation. This group of people is called his set of roles. For example, in the family situation, a set of roles of individuals may be shown as in Figure 6. The set of roles should include all those with whom a person has more than trivial interactions. Defining the role The definition of each individual role in each situation will be a combination of the job expectations that the members of the role group have from the focal role. These expectations are often defined occupationally, sometimes even legally. The job definitions of lawyers and doctors are clearly defined both legally and culturally. The job definitions of, say, a movie star or a bank manager, are also quite clearly defined in cultural terms, perhaps too clearly. People often find it difficult to escape the role that cultural traditions have defined for them. Not only with doctors or lawyers, the required job behavior is so limited that if you are in that role over time it ends up becoming part of you, part of your personality. Thus, there is a certain probability that all accountants will be similar or that all blondes are similar - they are forced to do so by the expectations of their duties. It is often important that you clarify what your specific role is at a given time. The means to do this are called, quite clearly, role signs. The simplest job marks are uniforms. The number of stripes on your arm or pips on your shoulder is a very precise role definition that allows you to do certain things that are very prescribed in certain situations. Imagine yourself investigating a stranger on a dark street at midnight without wearing the role signs of a policeman! In social circumstances, attire was often used as a role mark to indicate the nature and degree of formality of each encounter and occasionally the social status of the people present. The current trend to blur these role marks in clothing is probably democratic, but it also makes some people very insecure. Without role marks, who knows who has what role? Place is another role sign. Managers often behave very differently outside and inside the office, even to the same person. They use a change of position to indicate a change of position, for example, from a boss to a friend. Indeed, if you want to change your duties you must find an external sign that you are doing so or you will not be allowed to change - the subordinate will continue to hear you as his boss no matter how much you try to be his friend. In very significant cases of changing roles, for example from a soldier in the ranks to an officer, from a bachelor to a married man, the change of role should have a very clear sign, hence rituals. It is interesting to see, for example, some reduction in the emphasis given to marriage ceremonies. This can be taken as an indication that there is no longer such a large change in the role from a bachelor to a married person, so there is no need for a public change in sign. In organizations, signs and office furniture are often used as role signs. These and other requirements for status are often flouted, but they may serve a purpose as a sort of uniform in a democratic society; roles without signs often lead to confused or differing expectations of the role of the focal person. ROLE AMBIGUITY ROLE AMBIGUITY ARISES WHEN THERE IS SOME UNCERTAINTY IN THE MINDS, WHETHER OF THE FOCAL PERSON OR OF MEMBERS OF HIS ROLE-SET, AS TO EXACTLY WHAT HIS ROLE IS AT ANY GIVEN TIME. One of the decisive expectations that shape the definition of the role is that of the individual, the person who is the focus himself. If his occupation of the position is unclear, or if he differs from that of the others in the set of roles, there will be a degree of role ambiguity. Is it bad? Not necessarily, as the ability to shape their role is one of the freedoms that many people desire, but the ambiguity may lead to role stress that will be discussed later. The virtue of job descriptions is that they reduce the ambiguity of that role. Unfortunately, role descriptions are rarely full role definitions, except at the lower end of the scale. At middle and higher levels of management, they are often a list of official jobs and duties that say little about the more subtle and informal expectations for the job. The result is therefore to give the person the uncomfortable feeling that there are things left unsaid, that is, to increase the feeling of ambiguity in the roles. When looking at the ambiguity of roles from the other side, from the point of view of the members of the role set, a lack of clarity in the role of the focal person can cause insecurity, insecurity, irritation, and even anger among the members of his role set. One list of principal roles identified the following: manager, planner, policymaker, expert, rewards and penalties controller, counselor, friend, teacher. If it is not clear, through role signs of one type or another, which role is currently the executive role, the other party may not respond in the appropriate way we may, in fact, hear a completely different message if the person in focus speaks to us, for example, as a teacher and we hear it as a principal.

Pierre de Rosetta (Rosetta Stone) is dated to 196 BC when the Macedonians ruled Egypt. The stone has great historical value because it is carved in the same text written in both ancient Egyptian scripts (hieroglyphs and demotic) and in Greek. At the time of the discovery, Egyptian hieroglyphic writing could not be understood, and by comparing the symbols to the Greek text it was eventually deciphered. This allowed researchers to understand the significance of Egyptian hieroglyphs dating back almost 4,000 years. Napoleon was defeated by the British fleet at the Battle of the Nile in 1798 and he left Egypt two years later. The Rosetta Stone, along with other antiquities, was delivered to the British under the terms of the Treaty of Alexandria in 1801. It was exhibited in the British Museum and to this day remains one of the most popular exhibitions. In 1802 Thomas Young, an English academic, translated some of the words in the demotic part of the stone. Despite this early success, he made little progress with the hieroglyphic symbols, which proved to be confusing. He realized that the symbols used a combination of alphabet letters and phonetic sounds to convey the same meaning as classical Greek writing. The stone was made on the first anniversary of the coronation of the Boy Kings in 197 BC and takes the form of a decree. He confirms Ptolemy V's rightful place as king of Egypt and instructs the priests to worship him and erect temples. It lives in the far north of Australia and off the coast of Queensland, but is found as far north as the Murray River in western New South Wales. The taipan is an aggressive hunter, moving quickly through grassy areas with ease. Finding its prey by smell, the reptile hurls itself at the victim, causing several quick bites. Like most other venomous snakes, the taipan uses its venom sparingly. Since they do not consider a person a prey, they are known to strike and bite without releasing venom at all, which does not lead to side effects. premise: Student life at Canterbury College. Most courses at Canterbury College last only four days a week, leaving one day free for independent study. The atmosphere at the college is that of an adult environment in which a mutually respectful relationship between students and teachers is encouraged. Canterbury is a student city with a number of institutes of further and higher education. The town centre is just a five-minute walk from the college and easily accessible during lunch or school breaks. Canterbury College has developed strong international connections over the years and, as a result, many students have the opportunity to visit and work in a European country during their studies. The Student Union and SRC all students are automatically members of the Canterbury College Student Union (CCSU) and can attend meetings. The union is very active and is run by an executive committee elected by students in the fall term. The president is elected each summer term to provide continuity for the next academic year. Representatives from each field of study make up the Student Representative Council (SRC) which allows each student a say in union affairs. IN ADDITION TO REPRESENTING STUDENTS INTERNALLY IN THE COLLEGE ON THE ACADEMIC COUNCIL AND WITH A SUBCOMMITTEE OF THE COLLEGIATE CORPORATION, THE CCSU ALSO BELONGS TO THE NATIONAL STUDENT UNION REPRESENTING NATIONAL STUDENT INTERESTS. The Union also organizes and supports entertainment, sports activities and excursions. Student Facilities Learning Resource Center (LRC) The Corey Learning Resource Center provides easy access to a wide variety of printed and audiovisual learning materials that can help students in courses. There is enough space for quiet independent study and there are also areas for group work. Resources provided include books, periodicals, audio and video tapes, and CDs. Interlibrary loans are available locally and nationally through the British Library. All students are encouraged to use the Open Access Information Technology Center located on the first floor. It has a variety of computing, word processing, and desktop publishing software. A bookshop A branch of Waterstones Bookstores is located on campus, where you can buy a range of stationery, drawing supplies, artists materials and books, as well as many other useful items you will need. The Children's Center at the college children's center has places for under 5 years of age when some subsidized places are available to students. Places are limited, so, if you are interested, apply early to book a place by contacting Linda Baker at the college's phone number. This dining room provides refreshments from 08.30 to 19.00 with hot meals served three times a day. Healthy eating options are available. This cafe is open during regular college hours and serves light snacks and drinks. Proceeds from the cafe are transferred to the Student Association. Crypt Restaurant This is a tutorial restaurant that offers good quality cuisine in a pleasant environment. Meals are very affordable and you are invited to sample skillful dishes of the students when the restaurant is open to the public during the week. Reservations can be made by calling 01227511244. Chapel View Restaurant This is another tutorial restaurant and has been established as a quick service facility offering a selection of snacks and main courses at a modest price

However, it was equally possible to imagine the same evidence of daily life on exposed cliffs or hills, on trees or animal skins, and near rivers and coastlines.
