Thus, prehistoric people are characterized as cavemen, who are considered to have a tendency to live in these places only because that is where most of the evidence is taken. This caveman effect is an example of what is known as sampling bias one of the biggest problems when doing any kind of statistical data collection. Surveys, for example, are popular because they are easy to manage and relatively cost-effective, especially if they are conducted remotely by technical means, such as telephone, mail, email, or the Internet. Surveys are also suitable for obtaining an unusually large number of respondents, which in theory allows for a greater chance of sampling all variations of the target population. You can also fix them with regular questions and answers (such as check the box or closed questions). This allows easy collection, analysis and presentation of results, all in the air of precision that mathematics brings. Such surveys, however, have been shown to be notoriously unreliable because of the difficulty of obtaining representative samples. In other words, the sampling is biased, or biased in favor of certain outcomes. Let's look at some examples. If people are called on cell phones, this immediately excludes those who prefer landlines, so the sample of respondents may be those with more technical knowledge, and few data based, for example, on technical issues (how often do you use the Internet? ). If calling home homes during the daytime, most workers during the day will be excluded. Those who will be answered are more likely to be the unemployed, the disabled, the elderly and the elderly, who skew data based on, for example, work-related topics (how important is work in your life? ). No matter how large the sample size, sample bias can nullify the results immediately. One of the more subtle sampling biases is known as self-selection. No matter how rigorously respondents are chosen to be random and typical of the target population, those who choose to respond will differ from those who do not. In general, respondents who are willing to spend time providing answers obviously want to say something, whereas those who choose not to answer probably don't. Thus, any survey in which many respondents do not answer, do not give clear answers, or only give superficial or thoughtless answers, is immediately invalidated, since opinionated viewpoints are disproportionately represented. The latter is such an immediate and obvious problem that it has given rise to techniques to maximize the possibility of accumulating responses. One of the more effective is to give respondents an advanced warning (often via the mail), highlighting the time, nature of the survey and the manner of delivery, as well as expressing appreciation for assistance. Interviewers themselves must be sufficiently trained in proper techniques for asking questions, and with plenty of salespeople and rogue artists, interviewers must provide an introduction about themselves, their company and the nature of the interview, fully and with considerable honesty, in order to gain the trust of those they speak to. Even so, sampling bias can easily arise because of the number of variables present, since it only takes one to skew the data. If you take samples from a specific location say, Square Corner, then it could be that this location is in the business district, excluding ordinary employees from the sample. It could be near a restaurant district, except for those who cook more often for themselves. If there is a health club nearby, most respondents may be much healthier than the average of the population. If it is on a university campus, designed to survey university students, is it near the Faculty of Engineering or Arts? Part-time or full-time schools? Are they rich or poor? Male or female? What about race, color, gender, religion, socio-economic background, and first language? The list goes on and on. One method of dealing with this is to make sure that all targeted groups are represented, if only slightly, and make mathematical extrapolations to correct the bias. For this to work, the degree of underrepresentation must be precisely quantified, and it is assumed that the unrepresented respondents are indeed typical of their type. If, for example, one strives to find the opinion of the population regarding the outcome of an election, but one woman for every four men can be interviewed, it will be possible to multiply the women's answers by four, and thus it can be assumed (carefully and under many conditions) that the gender sampling bias has been corrected. But that assumes that all other variables that exhibit bias were often excluded from a very problematic assumption.
hypothesis: Larger survey samples can reduce sampling bias.

premise: The secret of Thailand's success? It's a question that officials here in Asia are increasingly posing: Why are your economies so vibrant? Explanations include young and swelling populations, declining debt, growing cities, emerging middle-class consumer sectors, developing markets and of course (the rise of China. The idea is that the more opportunities women have, the more vibrant economies are and, as a result, there is less need to rack up huge public debt to boost growth. It's an idea reinforced by a new survey by MasterCard International Inc., which compares the socioeconomic level of women to men in Asia-Pacific countries. The index uses four key indicators: labor force participation, college education, management roles and above-median income. Which Asian nation hosts when it comes to the advancement of women? Thailand. It received a score of 92.3 out of a possible 100, and according to the MasterCards index, 100 equals gender equality. The survey was based on interviews with 300 to 350 women in thirteen countries and national statistics. Malaysia came second with a score of 86.2, while China came third with 68.4. The average score in Asia was 67.7. At the bottom of the list is South Korea (45.5), followed by Indonesia (52.5) and Japan (54.5). Perhaps this is a strange coincidence, but the MasterCards' findings fit quite well with two important issues in Asia: economic leadership and debt. They travel the four globes, combing jungles, forests and savannas. But they're not looking for ancient artifacts, lost treasure or undiscovered graves. Just backpacks. It may lack the romantic allure of archaeology or the smell of danger that accompanies going after big game, but seed hunting is an increasingly serious business. Some are looking for seeds for Propure owners in hiring biotech companies, pharmaceutical companies and private corporations in search of species that will yield the drugs or crops of the future. Others are collecting to preserve, and working to halt the sad slide to extinction faced by so many plant species. Among the pioneers of this botanical treasure hunt was John Tredescant, an English royal gardener who brought back plants and seeds from his travels abroad in the early 16th century. Later, the English botanist Sir Joseph Banks who was the first director of the Royal Botanic Gardens at Kew and travelled with Captain James Cook on his travels towards the end of the 18th century - was so driven to expand his collections that he sent botanists around the world at his expense. Those tumultuous days of exploration and discovery may have ended, but they have been replaced by an urgent need to preserve our natural history for the future. This modern task motivates hunters like Dr. Michail van Selgren, a kind-hearted Dutchman who often wears a wide-brimmed hat in the field - he could easily be considered the Indiana Jones cinematic hero. He and three other seed hunters work for the Millennium Seed Bank, an 80 million [pound sterling] international conservation project aimed at protecting the world's most endangered wild plant species. The groups headquarters are in a modern glass-and-concrete structure on a 200-acre estate at Wickhurst Place in the West Sussex village. Inside its underground vaults are 260 million dried seeds from 122 countries, all stored at a temperature of -20 Celsius to survive for centuries. Among the 5,100 species represented are nearly all of the UK's 1,400 native seed-bearing plants, the most complete collection of any flora in the country. The Millennium Seed Bank, overseen by the Royal Botanic Gardens, is the world's largest wild plant repository. It aims to collect 24,000 species by 2010. The reason is simple: thanks to the efforts of mankind, about 25% of the world's plants are on the verge of extinction and may disappear within 50 years. were now responsible for habitat destruction on an unprecedented scale, and over the past 400 years the extinction rates of plant species have been 70 times greater than those noted by the geological record as normal. Experts predict that over the next 50 years another billion hectares of wilderness will be converted into farmland in developing countries alone. The consequences of this loss are enormous. Besides supplying basic food crops, plants are a source of many machinery and the main supply of fuel and building materials in many regions of the world. They also protect the soil and help regulate the climate. However, worldwide, plant species are being driven to extinction before their potential benefits have been discovered. The World Conservation Association has listed 5,714 threatened species that will surely be much higher. In the UK alone, 300 wild plant species are classified as endangered. The Millennium Seed Bank strives to ensure that even if a plant goes extinct in the wild, it will not be lost forever. Stored seeds can be used to help restore a damaged or devastated environment or in scientific research to find new benefits to society - in medicine, agriculture or local industry - that would otherwise be lost. Seed banks are an insurance policy to protect the world's plant heritage for the future, explains Dr Paul Smith, another Kew seed hunter. Seed conservation techniques were originally developed by farmers/he says. Storage is the foundation of what we do, preserving seeds until you can use them just like in agriculture, Smith says there's no reason why any plant species should go extinct, given today's technology. But he admits the biggest challenge is finding, naming and _ classifying all the world's plants. And someone needs to collect those seeds before it's too late. There aren't many people out there who do that, he says the key is getting to know the flora from a particular area, and that knowledge takes years to acquire. There are about 1,470 seed banks scattered around the world, with a total total of 5.4 million specimens, of which perhaps two million are not distinct duplicates. Most preserve genetic material for use in agriculture to ensure crop diversity; others aim to preserve wild species, although only 15 percent of all bank plants are wild. Imperial College London examined crop collections from 151 countries and found that while the number of plant samples increased in two-thirds of countries, the budget was cut by a quarter and remained static by a further 35%. The U.N. Food and Agriculture Organization and the International Agricultural Research Advisory Group have since established the World Conservation Fund, which aims to raise $260 million to protect seed banks forever.

premise: In search of the Holy Trinity for energy Neely Cross, the EU's competition commissioner, did not mince her words when she reported on European energy markets on Wednesday, January 10th. European energy companies have failed to invest in grids and so customers are suffering. The vertically integrated energy companies such as Electricite de France (EDF) or Germany's E. ON, widely referred to as national champions, are essentially acting like domestic monopolies. SHY OF COMPETITION, EAGER FOR ARTIFICIALLY HIGH PRICES, THEY HELP BLOCK EFFICIENT PRODUCTION, TRANSMISSION AND DISTRIBUTION OF ENERGY ON THE CONTINENT. Energy prices vary greatly across Europe. Ms. Cross wants to see cheaper energy, and intends to push suppliers to sell their distribution network and get them to invest more in transportation systems so that more energy in the form of gas, or electricity, for example, can flow easily across borders. It is incredibly difficult, for example, for gas-poor Germany to import from the neighbouring, gas-rich Netherlands. The companies that control national markets have, so far, had little interest in improving interconnections, which would mean lower prices for consumers across the continent. Ms. Cross, of course, will have trouble getting her way. The European Commission, which on the same day presented its recommendation to improve EU energy policy, also wants to see the separation of ownership, the legal separation between energy suppliers and carriers, something that the combined energy companies and interested governments, notably in France and Germany, are obliged to fiercely oppose. Complicating the matter is a debate over the security of energy supplies in Europe. Much has been made of the risk to Western Europe becoming too dependent on Russian gas exports. Russia under Vladimir Putin tends to use energy exports as a blatant foreign policy tool, especially when it tries to bully countries in its hinterland. Last year Russia cut off gas shipments to Ukraine, which also affected supplies in Central and Western Europe. This week it blocked oil exports passing through Belarus to Europe, though that quarrel was soon resolved. The risk is that concerns about security of supply may be used shockingly by those in Europe who oppose the kind of liberalisation that Ms Cross has encouraged. Companies like E. ON and EDF might argue that only protected national champions are able to guarantee supply, by cutting long-term deals with powerful foreign suppliers. The committee disagrees. Such deals are too often politically motivated and far from transparent. The defense was tried long enough and apparently did not work for the internal market, nor did these companies promise the best deals to consumers from the Russians. In contrast, the Commission's new policy proposes, ideally, breaking up these companies into suppliers and distributors. (As the second best solution, especially for France and Germany, it recommends the management of the networks by a third party.) Properly independent managers of Europe's energy grids would have a strong incentive to build interconnected pipelines and power lines across borders. For the gas market another means of ensuring competition and security would be finding a wider range of suppliers, for example by building more terminals for importing liquefied natural gas. It would likely also mean lower prices, if the example of liberal Britain over the past ten years is anything to go by. Whether any of this is likely to happen soon, however, is another matter. The Commission also calls on European governments to agree on a joint effort to reduce carbon emissions by at least 20% by 2020 (compared to 1990 levels). If America is willing to play football, the Commission proposes to reduce emissions by up to 30%. Achieving each of the targets means the promotion of cleaner cars, a more efficient emissions-trading system in Europe, wider use of public transport and a sharp increase in the use of renewable energy sources, like wind and solar power. All this is laudable enough, but will also require political horse-trading because leaders of European governments are due to meet in March to discuss the various energy proposals to avoid commitments that could hurt domestic energy companies or make European companies less competitive than rivals in America, Asia and elsewhere.

premise: Pouring light on it There are three main types of bulb for illuminating a room: incandescent, fluorescent and most recently the light-emitting diode (LED) bulb. All three bulbs have advantages and disadvantages when it comes to purchase price, operating costs and environmental impact. The traditional incandescent bulb has been in use for more than 100 years. This is done by suspending a thin coil of tungsten wire between two electrodes. When a current flows through the wire it reaches a temperature of more than 2,000 degrees Celsius and glows a warm white. The bulb is filled with argon, an inert gas, to prevent the wire from evaporating. Traditional light bulbs are not very efficient, converting less than 10% of the energy into light with the rest as heat, making them too hot to handle. Most household bulbs are rated at 40, 60 or 100 watts. Mass production of fluorescent light bulbs began in the 1940s. The standard size is 1.2 m in length and 2.5 cm in diameter. The tube contains a small amount of mercury and the inner surface of the glass has a phosphorus coating. There are two electrodes, one at each end of the tube, but no wire in between. INSTEAD, MERCURY ATOMS ABSORB THE ELECTRICAL ENERGY AND EMIT ULTRAVIOLET (UV); THIS LIGHT IS NOT VISIBLE UNTIL IT HITS THE PHOSPHORUS COATING ON THE GLASS, WHICH EMITS VISIBLE WHITE LIGHT. Fluorescent bulbs are five times more efficient than incandescent lamps. A 20-watt fluorescent tube will produce a similar amount of light to a 100-watt bulb and operates much cooler, helping to give it 10 times the lifespan of a bulb. The bright light produced by standard fluorescent bulbs makes them an ideal choice for offices and factories, rather than homes, where the incandescent bulb has traditionally dominated. However, it seems that the newer compact fluorescent lamps (CFL) will make the old bulbs extinct. Global warming is the main reason. Compared to an incandescent bulb, a single energy-saving fluorescent lamp will save about one ton of carbon dioxide emissions over its lifetime, as well as reduce consumers' electricity costs. NOT EVERYONE LIKES THE NEW CFLS, WHICH HAVE THE FOLLOWING DRAWBACKS: THEY'RE TEN TIMES THE PRICE OF TRADITIONAL BULBS; FLICKERING CAN OCCUR WITH DIMMER SWITCHES; THEY NEED TO HEAT UP TO GIVE FULL BRIGHTNESS; AND THEY EMIT A BLUISH, LESS NATURAL LIGHT THAT CAN STRETCH THE EYE. Traditional bulbs are safer to dispose of because they are free of mercury, which is a neurotoxin. The mercury is safe inside a sealed CFL but it is released into the atmosphere if the bulb is broken. Mercury can build up in the body to attack the brain and central nervous system. The reduced carbon footprint of CFLs compared to traditional bulbs may be exaggerated. While it is true that traditional light bulbs convert 90% of electricity into heat instead of light, this heat is not wasted. The light bulb helps keep the house warm so that less fuel is burned; for example, less gas or oil. If you replace all your bulbs with CFLs it can be very expensive in the short term and save less energy than you might imagine if your home is properly insulated or you live in a cold climate. If you live in a warm climate, switching to a CFL will reduce your carbon footprint and the cost of your electricity bills, but the savings will be less than you might expect if daylight hours are long and nights are short. CFLs are themselves under threat from the latest generation of light-emitting diodes (LEDs). LEDs have been around since the 1920s but only recently have they become bright enough for room lighting. The most common applications to date have been traffic lights, solar garden lights and car brake lights; infrared LEDs are used in television remote controls. LEDs are electronic components that emit photons of light when the current is applied. Lights for the home are made by grouping several LEDs into one bulb. Although more expensive than CFLs, LEDs last up to six times as long and twice as efficient, producing the same amount of light from half the electrical power (half the carbon emissions). Other advantages of LED lighting include: instant activation, meaning no heating time; no problems with frequent on/off, which shorten the life of fluorescent bulbs; no glass to break because the LED is made of hard transparent plastic; and they are free of toxic mercury.

When heated to about 1500 °C (C) it becomes a molten mass that hardens as it cools slowly. The first successful method of making clear, flat glass included spinning. This method was very effective because the glass did not touch any surfaces between being soft and becoming hard, so it remained completely flawless, with a 'fire finish'. However, the process took a long time and was labor-intensive. Nevertheless, the demand for flat glass was very high and glass manufacturers around the world were looking for a method to make it continuously. The first continuous film process involved squeezing molten glass through two hot rollers, similar to an old barbecue. This made it possible to make glass of almost any thickness without a break, but the rollers would leave both sides of the glass marked, and then they would have to be ground and polished. This part of the process rubbed off about 20 percent of the glass, and the machines were very expensive. The buoyancy process for making flat glass was invented by Alistair Pilkington. This process allows the production of transparent, dark and coated glass for buildings, and clear and dark glass for automobiles. Pilkington experimented with improving the melting process, and in 1952 the idea came to him to use a bed of molten metal to create the flat glass, completely eliminating the need for cylinders inside the floating bath. The metal had to melt at a low temperature from the point of hardening of the glass (about 600° C), but could not boil at a temperature below the temperature of the molten glass (about 1500° C). The best metal for the job was tin. The rest of the idea relied on gravity, which ensured that the molten metal surface would be perfectly flat and horizontal. As a result, when pouring molten glass onto the molten tin, the bottom of the glass will also be perfectly flat. If the glass was kept warm enough, it would flow over the molten tin until the top surface was also flat, horizontal, and completely parallel to the bottom surface. Once the glass cooled to 604C or less it was too difficult to mark and could be moved out of the cooling zone by rollers. The glass settled to a thickness of six millimeters because of surface tension interactions between the glass and the tin. Luckily, 60 percent of the flat glass market at that time was for six-millimeter glass. Pilkington built a pilot plant in 1953 and in 1955 persuaded his company to build a full-scale factory. However, it took 14 months of non-stop production, costing the company 100,000 a month, before the plant produced any usable glass. Moreover, once they were able to produce marketable flat glass, the machine was put out of service to prepare it for years of continuous production. When it started again it took another four months to fix the process again. They finally succeeded in 1959 and today there are floating factories all over the world, with each one capable of producing about 1000 tons of glass every day, non-stop for about 15 years. Floating plants currently produce glass of almost optical quality. Several processes - smelting, distillation, homogenization - occur simultaneously in the 2000 tons of molten glass in the furnace. They occur in separate regions in a complex glass flow driven by high temperatures. This amounts to a continuous melting process, lasting up to 50 hours, that delivers glass smoothly and continuously to the floating bath, and from there to a coating area and finally to a heat treatment area, where stresses generated during cooling are released.42The principle of floating glass has not changed since the 1950s. However, the product changed dramatically, from a single thickness of 6.8 mm to a range between a sub-millimeter and 25 mm, from a film often damaged by inclusions and bubbles to near-optical perfection. To ensure the highest quality, testing is carried out at each stage. Occasionally, a bubble is not removed during distillation, a grain of sand refuses to melt, shaking in the tin puts ripples on the glass film. Automated online testing does two things. First, it exposes faults in the upstream process that can be fixed. The test technology makes it possible to make more than a hundred million measurements per second across the film, detecting defects that the naked eye will not be able to see. Second, it allows downstream computers to navigate cutters around flaws. premise: Sleep apnea Sleep apnea is a common sleep disorder. This affects a number of adults similar to the percentage of the population suffering from diabetes. The term breathing is of Greek origin and means without breathing. Sufferers of sleep apnea stop breathing repeatedly while they sleep. This can happen hundreds of times during the night, each gasp lasting between 10 and 30 seconds. In extreme cases, people stop breathing for more than a minute at a time. There are three different types of sleep breathing, with obstructive sleep breathing being the most common. Obstructive sleep apnea pain (OSA), which affects 90 percent of sleep apnea sufferers, occurs because of obstruction of the upper airway. A person's breathing stops when air is somehow prevented from entering the trachea. The most common sites for capturing air include the nasal passage, tongue, tonsils, and obulae. Fatty tissue or tight muscles in the back of the throat can also cause blockage. Central sleep respiratory pain has a different root cause, although the consequences are the same. In sleep central breathing pain, the brain forgets to send the signal that tells the muscles it's time to breathe. The term central is used because this type of respiratory pain is related to the central nervous system and not to the blocked air flow. The third type of sleep breathing pain, known as mixed pulse, is a combination of the two and is the rarest form. Fortunately, in all types of breathing, the brain eventually signals the person to wake up so that breathing can resume. However, this persistent pattern of disturbed sleep is hard on the body and results in very little rest. SLEEP BREATHING PAIN IS ASSOCIATED WITH SEVERAL RISK FACTORS, INCLUDING BEING OVERWEIGHT, MALE, AND OVER FORTY YEARS OF AGE. However, like many disorders, sleep apnea can affect children and in many cases has been found to be the result of a person's genetic makeup. Despite being so common, this disorder often goes undiagnosed. Many people experience symptoms throughout their lives without realizing they have a serious sleep disorder. Often, it is not the person suffering from sleep apnea who notices the repeated episodes of sleep disorders, but a partner or family member who sleeps nearby. The cessation of air is usually accompanied by heavy snoring, loud enough to stimulate others from sleep. Those who live alone are less likely to have an early diagnosis, although other symptoms such as headaches, dizziness, irritability and exhaustion may prompt a person to seek medical advice. If left untreated, sleep apnea, which is a progressive disorder, can cause cardiovascular problems, and increase the risk of heart disease and stroke. Sleep apnea pain is also blamed in many cases of poor driving and poor job performance. In order to diagnose sleep apnea, patients are usually sent to a sleep center for a polysomnography examination. This test monitors brain waves, muscle tension, breathing, eye movement and oxygen in the blood. Audio monitoring for snoring, gasping, and episodic awakening was also done during a polysomnogram. Non-invasive solutions to treat sleep breathing pain include simple lifestyle changes. In many cases, symptoms of sleep apnea can be eliminated when patients try to lose weight or avoid alcohol. People who sleep on their back or stomach often find that their symptoms disappear if they try to sleep on their sides. Sleep experts also claim sleeping pills interfere with the natural performance of the throat and mouth muscles and suggest patients stop all sleep medication for a trial period. When these treatments are unsuccessful, sleep apnea sufferers can be fitted with a CPAP mask, worn at night over the mouth and nose, similar to an oxygen mask. CPAP stands for Continuous Positive Airway Pressure. In extreme cases, especially when facial deformities are the cause of sleep breathing pain, surgery is necessary to make a clear passage to air. Many different types of surgery are available. The most common form of surgery used to combat sleep respiratory pain is opholo-palato-peringoplasty (UPPP). This procedure involves removing the avula and excess tissue around it. UPPP helps about 50% of patients who undergo the procedure, while the other half continue to rely on the CPAP machine even after surgery. Another type of surgery called mandibular myotomy involves removing a piece of the jaw and adjusting the tongue. By reconnecting the tongue to a position about ten millimeters forward, air is able to flow more freely during sleep. This gentle procedure is performed only by surgeons with expertise in facial surgery and almost always manages to eliminate air obstruction. The latest surgical procedures use radio frequencies to shrink the tissue around the tongue, throat and soft palate.

premise: So what is it that decides whether a language should last or be threatened with extinction? The number of languages spoken in the world is expected to continue to decline dramatically but what determines the winners and losers? Surprisingly some commentators argue that along with languages spoken by very small communities the really big languages like English are also facing extinction. The case against the small linguistic community is clear; if there is no one left to speak a language then that language dies. The case against a dominant language, apparently all-conquering, like English is less evident and is therefore much more interesting. As more and more of the world speaks English it is inevitable, the argument goes, that it will break down first into dialects and then into separate languages linked only by their shared linguistic heritage. This is a moot point because it goes against the view that dialects need isolation before they can be formed (without isolation, speech is standardized by the dominant language proclaimed through international science, engineering, medicine and business and print and digital media around the world and this squeezes dialects).

Typically, infection occurs through direct contact with secretions from an infected person. Its spread is also possible from contaminated particles in the air, such as those that occur when someone coughs or sneezes. However, it should be clarified that the risk is not great simply from being in the same room as an infected person, because the influenza virus, unlike other respiratory viruses, does not dissolve in the air. Within 4-6 hours after someone contracts the flu, the virus multiplies in infected cells and the cells explode and spread the virus to other nearby cells. The spread lasts up to 72 hours, the exact duration depends on the response of the body's immune system and the strength of a particular flu strain. The range of human reactions to the influenza virus has been of interest to scientists for many years. This is because the effect can vary between no infection and a rapid and deadly spread of the virus to many people. One area of research that has received particular attention is the individual's immune system response. When a person's immune system is healthy, the virus is attacked when it enters the body, usually in the respiratory tract. This reduces the severity of the disease. In contrast, people with compromised immune systems (typical of the young, where it is not fully developed, or in the old and sick, where it does not work effectively), often suffer the worst effects. One of the body's responses to the flu is the creation of antibodies that recognize and destroy this particular strain of influenza virus. What fascinates most researchers in the field is that the human body seems able to store these antibodies throughout life in the event of a future attack from the same or similar strains of influenza. While researching these antibodies, scientists turned their attention to what was perhaps the world's worst flu epidemic. The actual number of deaths is disputed, but the outbreak in 1918 killed between 20 and 50 million people. It is also estimated that a fifth of the world's population may be infected. Through tests done on some of the survivors of the 1918 outbreak, it was discovered that 90 years later, they still had antibodies to this flu strain, and some were actually still producing the antibodies. Work now focuses on why these individuals survived in the first place, with one theory being that they were actually exposed to an earlier and similar strain, and therefore developed immunity to the 1918 strain. It is hoped that in the near future we will be able to isolate the antibodies and use them to vaccinate people against further outbreaks. However, influenza vaccination is an inaccurate measure. At best, the vaccine protects us from the flu variations that doctors expect that year. If their predictions are wrong in a particular year, the vaccine will not prevent us from becoming infected. This is further complicated by the fact that there are two main types of flu, known as influenza A and influenza B. Influenza B causes less concern because its effects are usually less severe. However, influenza A has the power to alter its genetic makeup. Although these genetic changes are rare, they create entirely new strains of flu against which we have no protection. It has been suggested that this is what happened immediately before the 1918 outbreak, with studies indicating that there had been genetic modification in China. In 2005, another genetic change was recorded in the influenza A virus, giving rise to the H5N1 strain, also known as bird flu, or bird flu. Typical of such new varieties, we have no way to fight it and many people infected with it die. Perhaps more worrying is that it is a species that was only previously found in birds but that changed its genetic composition in a way that allowed it to be transmitted to humans. Much of the fear surrounding this virus is that it will change again, developing the ability to pass from person to person. If this change does happen, scientists and doctors can reasonably expect a mortality rate similar to that which occurred in 1918, and given that we can now travel quickly and more easily between countries, infecting many more people than was previously possible, it could be several times worse.

So, like the British, Shiras presented his expedition as a search for knowledge: he would return fossils, make meteorological measurements and explore unknown parts of the continent. However the government response was cool, and Shirasa struggled to raise funds. Fortunately, a few months later, former Japanese Prime Minister Shigenobu Koma came to the rescue of Shirases. With Kumas' backing, Shirasa gathered enough money to buy and equip a small ship. He eventually also acquired a scientist named Trotaru Takeda. He would sail to New Zealand, then arrive in Antarctica in February, during the southern summer, then proceed to the Pole the following spring. However, it was not to be. Few doubted Shiras' courage, but most thought the expedition was ill-prepared because the Japanese had only light sleds for transportation across the ice, made of bamboo and wood. premise: Team monitoring is an issue especially for managers The only type of team monitoring that is not subject to regulation is where one person watches another. Once any recording begins, even if it is manual, monitoring is subject to the Data Protection Act and employees must be told if the surveillance is taking place and why. The information collected should be secure, and the affected teams have the right to see information related to them. While a person's consent is not required, he or she should be consulted regarding the processing of personal information (monitoring data is interpreted as personal), and monitoring methods cannot cause unnecessary stress. However, covert surveillance can be used without consultation, but only in particularly serious circumstances, such as when a member of staff is suspected of dishonesty. In that case, the covert surveillance (e.g. hidden cameras) must be in targeted areas and at times when dishonest behavior is expected - any other information should be ignored.
hypothesis: The Data Protection Act cannot be circumvented when tracking staff.

premise: Stem cells are cells that can regenerate and differentiate into specialized cell types. Because of their potential to replace diseased or damaged human tissue, stem cells are seen by scientists as key to developing new treatments for a wide range of conditions, including degenerative diseases and genetic diseases. Treatments based on adult stem cells - from sources like cord blood - have been successfully developed, but what makes stem cell research controversial is the use of embryonic stem cells. Not only do embryonic stem cells reproduce faster than adult stem cells, they also have wider differentiation potential. The main opponents of stem cell research are pro-life, who believe that human life should not be destroyed for the sake of science. Supporters of stem cell research object to this crucial point by saying that no human life can be seen in the embryo, and that medical advances justify the destruction of embryos. Furthermore, stem cell research utilizes the thousands of excess embryos created for IVF treatment. The issue is particularly divisive in the United States, where federal funding is not available to create new embryonic stem cell lines, though recent legislation has opened up government funding for continued research on embryonic stem cells created through private funding. While many governments ban the production of embryonic stem cells, it is allowed in countries including the UK, Sweden and the Netherlands.
hypothesis: The bioethical debate over embryonic stem cell research centers on whether it is the destruction of human life.
label: e

premise: Stairs A thousand years ago, stair wells were fundamental to life in the driest regions of India. Although many have been neglected, recent restoration has restored them to their former glory. Richard Cox travelled to north-west India to document these magnificent monuments from a bygone era. During the sixth and seventh centuries, the inhabitants of the modern states of Gujarat and Rajasthan in northwestern India developed a method of obtaining access to clean and fresh groundwater in the dry season for drinking, bathing, watering livestock and irrigation. However, the significance of this stepwell invention goes beyond its utilitarian application. Unique to the region, stair wells are often architecturally complex and vary greatly in size and shape. During their heyday, they were places of gathering, leisure, relaxation and worship for villagers of all castes except the lowest castes. Most staircases are found dotted around the desert regions of Gujarat (where they are called vav) and Rajasthan (where they are known as Bauri), while a few also survive in Delhi. Some were located in or near villages as public spaces for the community; others were placed alongside roads as resting places for travellers. As their name suggests, stair wells consist of a series of stone steps that descend from ground level to the water source (usually an underground aquifer) as it recedes following rains. When the water level was high, the user had to descend only a few steps to reach it; when it was low, it would be necessary to negotiate several levels. Some of the wells are vast, open craters with hundreds of cobblestone steps each sloping side, often in layers. OTHERS MORE ELABORATE, WITH LONG STAIRCASE PASSAGES LEADING TO THE WATER THROUGH SEVERAL FLOORS BUILT OF STONE AND SUPPORTED BY PILLARS, THEY ALSO INCLUDED PAVILIONS THAT PROTECTED VISITORS FROM THE UNRELENTING HEAT. But perhaps the most impressive features are the intricate decorative sculptures that adorn many stairwells, showing activities from fighting and dancing to everyday acts like women combing their hair and devouring butter. Over the centuries, thousands of wells were built across northwest India, but most have now fallen unused; many are abandoned and dry, as the groundwater has been diverted for industrial use and the wells no longer reach the water table. Their situation has not been helped in recent dry periods: southern Rajasthan suffered an eight-year drought between 1996 and 2004. However, several important sites in Gujarat have recently undergone major restoration, and the state government announced in June last year that it plans to restore the stair wells across the state. In Patten, the ancient state capital, the stair well of Rennie Key and B (Queens Stapwell) is perhaps the current best example. It was built by Queen Udayamaty in the late 11th century, but was swept away following a flood during the 13th century. But the Archaeological Survey of India began reconstructing it in the 1960s, and it is currently in pristine condition. 65 meters long, 20 meters wide and 27 meters deep, Rani Ki Webb features 500 separate sculptures carved in niches throughout the monument, depicting deities like Vishnu and Parvati in various incarnations. Incredibly, in January 2001, this ancient structure survived a devastating earthquake measuring 7.6 on the Richter scale.48 Another example is Surya Kund in Mudra, northern Gujarat, near the Temple of the Sun, built by King Bhim I in 1026 in honor of the sun god Surya. It is actually a tank (cond means reservoir or pond) rather than a well, but displays the hallmarks of stair well architecture, including four sides of stairs descending to the bottom in a stunning geometric structure. THE TERRACES HOUSE 108 SMALL, INTRICATELY CARVED TEMPLES BETWEEN THE STAIRCASE SYSTEMS. Rajasthan also has plenty of wells. The ancient city of Bondi, 200 miles south of Jaipur, is known for its architecture, including its stair wells. One of the larger examples is Raniji Ki Bauri, built by the queen of the region, Nathbatji, in 1699. At 46 metres deep, 20 metres wide and 40 metres long, the intricately carved monument is one of 21 illuminations commissioned in the Bondi area by Nathbatji. In the ruined ancient city of Abhenri, about 95 miles east of Jaipur, lies Chand Bauri, one of India's oldest and deepest wells; aesthetically, it is perhaps one of the most dramatic. The Bauri, built around 850 AD near the Mata Grid Temple, features hundreds of glazed staircases extending along three of its sides, descending steeply by 11 floors, resulting in a striking geometric pattern seen in the distance. On the fourth side, covered verandahs supported by ornate pillars overlook the stairs. Still in public use is Namrana Ki Bowery, located just off Jaipurdehli Expressway. Built around 1700, its nine storeys deep, with the last two levels under water. On the ground level there are 86 columnar openings from which the guest descends 170 steps to the deepest water source. Today, after years of neglect, many of these monuments to medieval engineering have been saved by the Archaeological Survey of India, which recognized the importance of preserving them as part of the country's rich history. Tourists flock to wells in far-flung corners of northwest India to gaze in wonder at these architectural marvels from 1,000 years ago, which serve as a reminder of both the sophistication and art of ancient civilizations and also of the value of water to human existence

premise: Study finds internet fraud countermeasures ineffective Internet security experts have long known that simple passwords do not fully protect online bank accounts from determined scam artists. Now research suggests that a popular secondary security measure provides little extra protection. The study, co-produced by researchers from Harvard and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, tested a technology called Web Authentication Images. In the system, now used by financial institutions like Bank of America, ING Direct and Vanguard, online banking customers are asked to choose a picture, like a dog or chess piece, that they will see every time they log into their account. The idea is that if customers don't see their picture, they might be on a fake website, surprised to look like their banks, and don't have to enter their passwords. Harvard and MIT researchers tested this hypothesis. In October, they brought 67 Bank of America customers in the Boston area to a controlled environment and asked them to conduct routine online banking activities, like searching account balances. But investigators secretly pulled the photos. Of 60 participants who got this far into the study and whose results could be verified, 58 entered passwords anyway. Only two chose not to connect, citing security concerns. The premise is that site-authenticating photos increase security because customers won't enter their passwords if they don't see the right image, said Stuart Schechter, a computer scientist at the Lincoln Mi.Slow Lab. From the study we learned that the premise is correct less than 10 percent of the time. He added: 'If a bank asked me if they should deploy it, I would say no, wait for something better, 'he said. The system has some high-powered backers in the financial services world, many trying to comply with the new online banking regulations. In 2005, the Federal Financial Institutions Review Board, an interagency body of federal banking regulators, determined that passwords alone did not actually thwart intruders like identity thieves. It issued new guidelines, asking financial Web sites to find better ways for banks and customers to identify each other online. January 2007 was set as the compliance date, though the council has yet to begin enforcing the mandate. Banks knew immediately what they didn't want to do: ask customers to download new security software, or swipe hardware devices that feed them PIN codes that they could use to verify their identity. Both solutions would add an extra layer of security but, the banks believed, detract from the convenience of online banking. The image system, introduced in 2004 by a Silicon Valley company called PassMark Security, offered banks a painless addition to their security arsenal. Bank of America was among the first to adopt it, in June 2005, under the brand name SiteKey, asking its 21 million site users to choose an image from thousands of possible options and choose a unique phrase they would see every time they log in. SiteKey gives our customers a fairly easy way to authenticate Bank of America's website, said Sanjay Gupta, director of e-commerce at the bank. It was well received. However, Harvard and MIT researchers found that most online banking customers did not notice when SiteKey photos were missing. When respondents logged in during the study, they saw a site maintenance message on the screen in which their image and expressions should have been pictured. The error message also had a glaring misspelling, which further suggests something questionable. Mr. Gupta of Bank of America said he was not bothered by the survey results and stressed that Seitake had made the bank's website more secure. He also said the system was just one part of a larger security blanket. It's not as if you bet the bank on SiteKey, he said. Most financial institutions, like Bank of America, have other ways of knowing if a customer is legitimate. Banks often release a small piece of software, called a cookie, on a user's computer to associate the computer with a customer. If the client connects from another machine, he may be asked personal questions, like his mother's maiden name. Rachna Dhamija, the Harvard researcher who conducted the study, points out that scammers can use their dummy sites to ask customers these personal questions. She said the study proved that site authentication images are fundamentally flawed and, worse, may actually detract from security by giving users a false sense of security. RSA Security, the company that bought PassMark last year, has a lot of great data on how SiteKey instills trust and confidence and good feelings into their customers, Ms. Demija said. premise: Tips and Study Techniques If you often find yourself struggling with your studies, here are some useful study tips and techniques that can help you... When it comes to studying or learning, each student prefers his distinct pattern corresponding to his speed, grasping ability, and other academic abilities. However, there are certain learning techniques that can help the learning process to a great extent. Taking notes in class, reviewing the notes, rewriting the study material can seem too intimidating at times, here is a step-by-step guide that may help you if you are in the process of converting your own study plan. First of all you need to acquire some useful study habits to follow a good study plan. Here are study habits that can help you: Attending classroom knowledge classes is interactive as well as important. The amount of knowledge that can be grasped in the classroom is very valuable for students. Be sure to attend classes regularly so you don't miss the important points and topics mentioned in class. Teachers often mention important topics and topics that may be helpful when cracking the tests and exams in the classroom. Attending classes will help you understand and remember each concept clearly and clarify any doubts you have on the subject. No amount of reading or self-study can match the level of interactive learning that is a distinct feature of classroom encounters. Keeping notes organized and comprehensive Yes Keeping your notes is another essential element of learning. One simple process for getting comprehensive notes is to include the following steps: Make class notes while reviewing the notes during self-study, make your own additions to summarize your understanding of a topic of further research to include more data for your comments. A well-organized set of comprehensive notes is the key to learning correctly. Also make sure the notes are clean in terms of writing and presentation; avoid scribbles in your final comments. It is always best that you type in your notes and save them online or take prints. A soft copy of your notes always works well because you can take prints if and when required and on top of that you never have to worry about losing your notes. However, do not worry if you do not have a computer or if you prefer to write you notes on paper, you can also save files or notebooks. Self-study and research It is a common misconception that self-study can only begin after studying a specific topic or chapter in the classroom. You need to start preparing for class in advance whenever you can. After attending classes, it is extremely important to have time to review the notes that you took during the lesson as well as try to read more about the topic yourself. Whether it's reference books, or e-books, try looking for more information about your subject so that you have a comprehensive view of the topics being studied under your syllabus. Often while reading and self-study, it happens that you encounter doubts or questions that did not occur to you in class. Try to answer these questions yourself with the help of books or the Internet, however, in case you cannot find and answer write down these questions so that you remember to clarify the questions in your next lesson. Group Discussions Discussions and Conversations Yes, one of the important habits that must be acquired to improve the study process is to indulge in group discussions, discussions or simple conversations about the topics you are studying. Group discussions can be a great way to broaden your perspective on important issues because group discussions give each member of the group a chance to voice their understanding, which may not necessarily be similar. Group discussions are therefore a healthy and informal way to exchange information and discuss issues. Many teachers encourage the group discussion technique in their classroom as well. A regular planning process may seem convenient It is always preferable to have a weekly or daily program so that sudden changes in class schedules or any other changes can be taken into account accordingly. Balanced research No matter how shocking people are to the planning process and schedules, it is a well-known fact that having a clear and detailed plan makes it easier for a person to reach the goal. According to your convenience, make a daily/weekly/monthly planner for your studies. Although monthly planning is, there are certain types of students who burn the oil at midnight, taking it out every day. The learning process should be such that it leaves enough space for the student to indulge in leisure and relaxation activities. Always set a schedule that won't harm your sleep, your health, your sports/leisure activities, and other routine tasks. Studying a single topic in a row (like a whole week or so), can be boring, so plan a schedule to help you move from one subject to another in enough time. Build the right attitude Students are usually too caught up in grades, percentages, and the whole grade system. Always remember that if you study with the aim of acquiring knowledge, the grades will be brighter by default. However, if you are only aiming for the high grades, there is a chance that you will get the grades, but miss out on acquiring comprehensive knowledge on a particular subject. Always study with the right attitude, and you will never have to worry about your grades. Knowledge is far beyond grades and percentile notation.

premise: Studying in the UK Why is the UK now home to over a quarter of a million international students? Students come to study in the UK from all over the world, from over 180 countries of the European Union, Australia and New Zealand, USA, Asia, Africa, Middle East, Far East, South America... Some British universities have students from 100 countries. There are now more than 270,000 international students in the UK. Of that number, about 75% are education courses, with 130,500 (a nearly equal number of men and women) studying full-time undergraduate courses. Why do they come to UK universities? First, because they receive a quality certification that is recognized throughout the world. Thousands of international students have used their skills in the UK to get a good job. Second, if English isn't their first language, they'll probably be perfectly fluent by the time they graduate! ANOTHER REASON FOR STUDYING IN THE UK IS THE EASE OF THE UKIELTS APPLICATION SYSTEM. Instead of applying to several different universities or colleges, passing their admissions tests and paying their application fees, students can do it all in one form. They can choose up to six courses by sending the form to the Universities and Colleges Admissions Service (UCAS) whose staff deal with applications for them. If the pupil schools, colleges or the nearest British Council offices have access to the system, they can even fill out the form electronically over the internet. It's a big decision to learn a long way from home. But students can be assured of great support in the UK. Universities and colleges take care of their students. There are personal tutors, counselors, study skills counselors, and financial advisors to help with any problem. There are also priests or representatives of major religions. In addition, there are medical services, and if a course lasts more than six months, students are entitled to free medical care within the framework of the National Health Service. All students are allowed to use these services. However, many institutions also have international student counsellors. Students can contact them with any questions before coming; they will probably arrange transportation service from major airports for arriving students and organize welcome events. International students can also go see them at any time during their courses. For students with families, childcare facilities are often provided at an affordable cost. There is no obligation to use any of these services. If a student is independent and has no problems, he will not come knocking on his door! But it can be comforting to know they're there. Campuses are safe places to live, as in general most towns in the UK. As anywhere else, there are areas in some cities that are best avoided after dark, but you will be advised on this. Universities and colleges ensure that student residences are secure, and in most places transportation is provided at night for female students. Students will be able to take part in a variety of social and sporting activities. There are team and individual sports at all levels; and clubs and societies covering every interest from drama to politics, watersports to backgammon, discussions to social work and voluntary. Student unions organise discos and gigs, and run pubs, bars and dining venues. The clubs are run by students for students and are always well advertised at the beginning of the academic year. Joining one or two companies is a great way to meet other students from the UK and other countries. There are thousands of courses to choose from. Some students opt for a vocational program. Agriculture and related subjects, engineering, law and business studies are popular with international students. Others choose an academic subject like history or politics. The choice is almost limitless. And what do international students do at the end of their courses? Some stay to do graduate work. (20 percent of students on UK graduate courses are from abroad.) The majority return home, armed with their skills in Britain. If an English student is not yet good enough to enroll in a degree course, he or she may want to spend some time first in an English language course. There are many to choose from, some of which are held in universities and colleges, some in private language schools. The British Council can offer advice on choosing the right one. Some students may need additional academic skills. In such cases a student can consider taking a Foundation Access Course or IELTS (General Training) IA, run by many of the UK's higher education institutions. Fees may seem high at first, but when you consider the following points, the costs at universities and colleges in the UK compare well with the costs in other English-speaking countries. Most courses in the UK are at least one year shorter than those in other countries. COURSE FEES INCLUDE: ALL TUITION FEES (EXCEPT BOOKS AND EQUIPMENT); GENERALLY, FREE USE OF COMPUTING, EMAIL, AND INTERNET FACILITIES; LANGUAGE LEARNING IF ONE WISHES TO LEARN ANOTHER LANGUAGE (AND ENGLISH LANGUAGE SUPPORT IF NECESSARY); USE OF FREE OR INEXPENSIVE SPORTS FACILITIES; AND A STUDENT WILL NOT PAY JUST TO ATTEND LECTURES. Much teaching will be done in small groups. In addition, the teaching staff is ready to provide additional help if the student needs it and the student can go see them outside of the scheduled course hours. In summary, there are a number of key benefits to studying in the UK. First, the standards at higher institutions in the UK are generally higher than others, and a student will receive an internationally recognised qualification. Secondly, a student will meet students from all over the world, and gain an advantage in building international connections. Third, most universities and colleges provide accommodation for first-year international students and a variety of other services not provided to international students in many other English-speaking countries. Finally, the application system is simplified, saving the cumbersome processes required by many other countries.

premise: Such a fascinating game It is one of the most popular games in the world, played by millions of people at home, in clubs, on the Internet, in correspondence and tournaments. This is chess, a modest arrangement in which two players stare at a checkered board with 64 squares arranged in an eight-by-eight grid, and examine their 16 pieces each as the first move is played. When the king of opponents is destroyed, the game is over, but between the beginning and the end, a multitude of elegant, intricate and fascinating moves and combinations can unfold. The origins of chess lie in northwestern India, around the 6th century. At that time there was a game known as Katuranga, which meant four divisions, when these divisions were those of the army, represented by the infantry, cavalry, elephants and chariots. These parts were to eventually become the tabernacle, the knight, the bishop, and the rook, respectively, in the modern descendant of the game. Around 600 AD, Katuranga spread to Persia, then, after the Muslim conquest of that region (beginning around that time), the game gained ground throughout the Islamic world, from where it eventually spread to Europe. Around 1200 AD, Southern Europe began to change the rules, and within 300 years the game had become the one we play today. The queen has long replaced the previous vizier and became the most powerful creation, while the tabernacles were given the opportunity to advance two squares in the first move in order to speed up the game. These new laws quickly spread throughout Western Europe, creating the game now known as Western Chess or International Chess, to distinguish it from older or regional versions of the game. As for the players themselves, One World thinks the best of them are necessarily smart, with unusually high IQs; however, research has failed to confirm this link. Some studies have shown that good chess players may have a strong IQ, but there appears to be no direct correlation between this and chess ability. Paradoxically, the academically brilliant may even be less able at chess, and vice versa. Apparently, there are other factors involved, such as spatio-visual insight and subliminal memory, that are not necessarily picked up by conventional intelligence tests, are easily noticeable, or even useful in real life. But there are non-mental factors which clearly play a role. No one can doubt that raw talent is needed, but even the best and brightest must systematically go through at least 10 to 15 years of theoretical study and competitive practice before they reach World Championship levels. American chess genius Bobby Fischer was only 13 when he produced the game of the century, but he was not world champion until he was 29. The Russian chess player, Garry Kasparov, was the youngest ever world champion, at the age of 22, but began dedicated state-sponsored training from the age of ten onwards, with personal chess coaches. All this shows the permanent place that chess has in Western culture, which also means that this region has produced, historically, all the greatest players. However, interest in chess is now growing in the East, although there is one problem is the tough competition it faces with local board games, such as Xiangqi and Gu. These are more popular by a wide margin, but relative to China for example, with its huge population and state-sponsored training, it is fast becoming a major chess power. The reigning world champion in women's chess is Chinese, and the country performs well in the Chess Olympiads. The future of the game in this country really looks bright. Talking about the future inevitably leads to the topic of computer chess. Serious chess machines began to emerge in the 1970s and 1980s, but their abilities were far below those of the top human players. Progress, although slow, was steady, and with increasing memory and faster processing, it was inevitable that one day a computer would be able to match humans. Yet this is only by a brutal passage of all possible moves, millions a second, deeper and deeper into the position. The final movement choices give the appearance of intuition and long-term strategy, when in fact they are simply based on thoughtless and directionless material counting. In 1989, the Deep Thought computer scored several victories against top human players, though the world champion at the time, Garry Kasparov, easily defeated the machine in a few neat matches. In 1996, however, IBM brought out the next-generation computer, Deep Blue, and placed it in a game with the same player. Despite managing to score the first win facing the reigning world champion, by losing three and drawing two of the remaining matches, she lost the match. However, a rematch the following year saw Kasparov facing an even better machine, Deeper Blue. This time, the computer won 3 1/2 2 1/2. And they're only getting better. As impressive as these results seem, most people agree that it's akin to a forklift that beats lifting weights somehow not a valid competition, and has little meaning. Yes, computers can beat games, but creativity and intelligence are still the province of human players. These factors, as well as the tense psychological struggle of the minds and personalities involved, along with the limitless artistry of the positions themselves, will always make chess such a fascinating game.

premise: The fickle heart of the sun may leave us cold. There is a dimmer switch inside the sun that causes its brightness to rise and fall in timescales of about 100,000 years - exactly the same period as between the ice ages on Earth. So says a physicist who created a computer model of our star's core. Robert Ehrlich of George Mason University in Fairfax, Virginia, designed the effect of temperature fluctuations in the sun's interior. According to the standard view, the temperature of the Sun's core is held constant by the opposing pressures of gravity and nuclear fusion. However, Ehrlich believed that slight variations should be possible. He took as his starting point the work of Attila Grandfire of the Konkuli Observatory of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences. In 2005, Grandfire and a collaborator, Gabor Aguston, calculated that magnetic fields in the core of the Sun might produce small instabilities in the solar plasma. These instabilities will cause local fluctuations in temperature. Ehrlich's model shows that while most of these fluctuations cancel each other out, some reinforce each other and turn into long-term temperature changes. The preferred frequencies allow the Sun's core temperature to oscillate around its average temperature of 13.6 million Kelvin in cycles lasting 100,000 or 41,000 years. Ehrlich says that random interactions within the sun's magnetic field can reverse the fluctuations from one cycle length to another. These two timescales are instantly recognizable to anyone familiar with Earth's ice ages: in the last million years ice ages have occurred roughly every 100,000 years. Before that, they occurred roughly every 41,000 years. Most scientists believe that the ice age is the result of subtle changes in the Earth's orbit, known as Milankovich cycles. One such cycle describes how the Earth's orbit gradually changes shape from a circle to a slight ellipse and back about every 100,000 years. The theory says this changes the amount of solar radiation the Earth receives, triggering the ice age. HOWEVER, A PERSISTENT PROBLEM WITH THIS THEORY HAS BEEN ITS INABILITY TO EXPLAIN WHY THE ICE AGE CHANGED FREQUENCY A MILLION YEARS AGO.\ IN MILENKOVICH, THERE IS CERTAINLY NO GOOD IDEA WHY THE FREQUENCY SHOULD CHANGE FROM ONE TO THE OTHER,\ SAYS NEIL EDWARDS, A CLIMATOLOGIST AT THE OPEN UNIVERSITY IN MILTON KEYNES, UK. The transition problem is also not the only one faced by Milankovich theory. Ehrlich and other critics argue that the temperature changes caused by Milenkowitz cycles simply are not large enough to drive the Ice Age. However, Edwards believes the small changes in solar heating produced by Milankovich cycles are then amplified by feedback mechanisms on Earth. For example, if sea ice begins to form because of a slight cooling, carbon dioxide that would otherwise find its way into the atmosphere as part of the carbon cycle is locked up in the ice. This weakens the greenhouse effect and the earth cools further. According to Edwards, there is no lack of such mechanisms.\ If you add their effects together, there is more than enough feedback to make Milankovich work,\ he says.\ The problem now is to identify which mechanisms are at work.\ This is why scientists like Edwards are still unwilling to give up the current theory.\ Milankovich cycles give us ice ages roughly when we watch them occur. Their cores are much smaller than that of the Sun, so Ehrlich believes the oscillation periods could be short enough that they can be observed. premise: Sunday is a fun day for modern Britons In a new study, sociologists from the University of Essex analysed the typical British Sunday, and found we get up later and do fewer chores than we did 40 years ago and are far more likely to go shopping or have fun than to cook lunch on Sunday. Academics at the university's Institute for Social and Economic Research asked 10,000 people to keep a detailed diary of how Sundays were spent in 2001. The results were then compared with 3,500 diaries written in 1961, a treasure trove of information uncovered in two egg boxes and a tea box in the BBC basement by the director of ISERs, Professor Jonathan Gershoni. The contrast between the two eras could not have been more pronounced. Forty years ago, Sunday mornings were a storm of activity when men and women especially women were discovered in their weekly chores and cooked up a storm in the kitchen. Women rarely allowed themselves leisure until the afternoon, after cleaning the dishes. In 1961, more than a fifth of all men and women in Britain sat at a table at 2pm, presumably going into a roast with all the trimmings on. Then there will be an additional load to the table between 5pm and 6pm. For drinking tea. Since the arrival of brunch, the gastropub and the all-you-can-eat Sunday buffet at the local curry house, such institutions have become extinct. Today we are herding all day. You only have two free days a week. You don't want to waste one because there's nothing to do but watch TV. Sunday leapfrogged Saturday in the fun stakes. On Saturdays you recover from the week. Sundays are the last weekend stronghold that you want to get as much out of the day as possible before you have to go back to work. According to the researchers, being able to trace around B&Q made the most dramatic difference to our Sundays. In 1961, adults spent an average of 20 minutes a day shopping; in 2001, it was 50 minutes. Shopping was previously a gender-segregated activity that would take place during the week, while the husband was at work. Now it's men as much as women, Gershoni said. Everyone is more likely to relax or do Sunday morning shopping these days than scrub the floor or place shelves. Men now stay in bed longer, and get up not, as before, to work at home, but to shop or engage in other outdoor leisure activities. Men do about the same amount of unpaid work around the house as once a Sunday, yet it spreads throughout the day, rather than cramming in the morning. Women are doing this much less than 40 years ago. Indeed, men and women were quite different genders in 1961, with regard to how Sundays were spent, with men far more likely to be out of the house in the pub or playing football before lunch. For women, leisure happened only in the afternoon. But by 2001, the forms of men's and women's Sundays were much more similar, says the report. Sunday for me is just to hold the weekend and try to avoid the Monday. An ideal Sunday would involve getting up and having a nice lunch. Sometimes we cook, but more often I go out for a roast or a banger and mash in a gastropub. If it's a nice day, there's nothing better than sitting outside in the beer garden, reading one tabloid Sunday papers and one broadsheet with Guinness, especially cold. Sunday is often a chance to visit other parts of London, as long as it's not too far away. I use Sundays to go clothes shopping, or to the movies. I often go to Camden Market, as I love the international foods on offer and look for deals and vintage clothing. Jonathan Bentley Atchison (25, Clapham, London, works in media) I'm usually at home preparing my Sunday lunch. Some friends go out to eat, but my husband Mark loves a roast, so we don't. After that, I do the laundry, like every day, and then I take my daughter Grace to the netball and watch her play. Mark Potter was around last Sunday, he was tidying up the garage. He works six days a week, so on Sunday he stays home. I don't like shopping on Sunday because every man and his dog are out. I don't work, so I can do it in a week. I tend to watch TV and relax. When summer comes, we go to barbecue at the homes of family or friends. Growing up, my dad would do the landscaping and paint the fences while my mom would do housework. Hazel Helous (42, Manchester, housewife, married with three children) When we were at home I would go out to the garden, and my late wife Rose would cook the Sunday lunch and do the housework. I was an engineer, and Rose worked full-time as a supermarket manager. In 1961 we had just moved to Bristol, and I spent Sunday maintaining the new house. The washing and ironing had to be done it was an atmosphere of working together. Sometimes we would go spend the day with Rose's sister or other relatives. In 1961, it was the first time I had a new car, so we spent time in the village or garden centres. Now, I get up on Sundays and spend a few hours reading newspapers. Brian Jones (79, pensioner, Frampton Cottrell, near Bristol)
hypothesis: Mrs Hallou's husband does not do household chores on Sundays.

The results were then compared with 3,500 diaries written in 1961, a treasure trove of information uncovered in two egg boxes and a tea box in the BBC basement by the director of ISERs, Professor Jonathan Gershoni. The contrast between the two eras could not have been more pronounced. Forty years ago, Sunday mornings were a storm of activity when men and women especially women were discovered in their weekly chores and cooked up a storm in the kitchen. Women rarely allowed themselves leisure until the afternoon, after cleaning the dishes. In 1961, more than a fifth of all men and women in Britain sat at a table at 2pm, presumably going into a roast with all the trimmings on. Then there will be an additional load to the table between 5pm and 6pm. For drinking tea. Since the arrival of brunch, the gastropub and the all-you-can-eat Sunday buffet at the local curry house, such institutions have become extinct. Today we are herding all day. You only have two free days a week. You don't want to waste one because there's nothing to do but watch TV. Sunday leapfrogged Saturday in the fun stakes. On Saturdays you recover from the week. Sundays are the last weekend stronghold that you want to get as much out of the day as possible before you have to go back to work. According to the researchers, being able to trace around B&Q made the most dramatic difference to our Sundays. In 1961, adults spent an average of 20 minutes a day shopping; in 2001, it was 50 minutes. Shopping was previously a gender-segregated activity that would take place during the week, while the husband was at work. Now it's men as much as women, Gershoni said. Everyone is more likely to relax or do Sunday morning shopping these days than scrub the floor or place shelves. Men now stay in bed longer, and get up not, as before, to work at home, but to shop or engage in other outdoor leisure activities. Men do about the same amount of unpaid work around the house as once a Sunday, yet it spreads throughout the day, rather than cramming in the morning. Women are doing this much less than 40 years ago. Indeed, men and women were quite different genders in 1961, with regard to how Sundays were spent, with men far more likely to be out of the house in the pub or playing football before lunch. For women, leisure happened only in the afternoon. But by 2001, the forms of men's and women's Sundays were much more similar, says the report. Sunday for me is just to hold the weekend and try to avoid the Monday. An ideal Sunday would involve getting up and having a nice lunch. Sometimes we cook, but more often I go out for a roast or a banger and mash in a gastropub. If it's a nice day, there's nothing better than sitting outside in the beer garden, reading one tabloid Sunday papers and one broadsheet with Guinness, especially cold. Sunday is often a chance to visit other parts of London, as long as it's not too far away. I use Sundays to go clothes shopping, or to the movies. I often go to Camden Market, as I love the international foods on offer and look for deals and vintage clothing. Jonathan Bentley Atchison (25, Clapham, London, works in media) I'm usually at home preparing my Sunday lunch. Some friends go out to eat, but my husband Mark loves a roast, so we don't. After that, I do the laundry, like every day, and then I take my daughter Grace to the netball and watch her play. Mark Potter was around last Sunday, he was tidying up the garage. He works six days a week, so on Sunday he stays home. I don't like shopping on Sunday because every man and his dog are out. I don't work, so I can do it in a week. I tend to watch TV and relax. When summer comes, we go to barbecue at the homes of family or friends. Growing up, my dad would do the landscaping and paint the fences while my mom would do housework. Hazel Helous (42, Manchester, housewife, married with three children) When we were at home I would go out to the garden, and my late wife Rose would cook the Sunday lunch and do the housework. I was an engineer, and Rose worked full-time as a supermarket manager. In 1961 we had just moved to Bristol, and I spent Sunday maintaining the new house. The washing and ironing had to be done it was an atmosphere of working together. Sometimes we would go spend the day with Rose's sister or other relatives. In 1961, it was the first time I had a new car, so we spent time in the village or garden centres. Now, I get up on Sundays and spend a few hours reading newspapers. Brian Jones (79, pensioner, Frampton Cottrell, near Bristol)
