premise: Sunset for oil business The world is about to run out of oil. Or maybe not. It depends on who you believe... Members of the Departments Analysis Centre (ODAC) recently met in London and presented technical data supporting their bleak forecast that the world is dangerously close to running out of oil. The leading lights of this moment, including geologists Colin Campbell, rejected rival views presented by the U.S. Geological Survey and the International Energy Agency that contradicted their findings. Dr Campbell even condemned the astonishing display of ignorance, denial and obfuscation on the part of government, industry and academics on this issue. So is the oil really running out? The answer is easy: yes. No one seriously disputes the idea that oil is, for all practical purposes, an unrenewable resource that will run out sometime, be it years or decades. The harder question is determining when exactly oil will start to become scarce. And an answer to that question involves augmenting the Hubberts record. Mr. King Hubert, a Shell geologist of legendary status among depletion experts, predicted in 1956 that oil production in the United States would peak in the early 1970s and then decline slowly, in something resembling a bell-shaped curve. At the time, his prediction was controversial, and many rubbished it. AFTER 1970, HOWEVER, EMPIRICAL EVIDENCE PROVED HIM RIGHT: OIL PRODUCTION IN AMERICA DID PEAK AND HAS BEEN DECLINING EVER SINCE. Dr. Huberts' analysis relied on the observation that oil production in a new region usually increases rapidly at first, as the easiest and cheapest reserves are exploited. Over time the stockpiles age and go into decline, and so lifting oil becomes more expensive. Oil from this region then becomes less competitive relative to other fuels, or oil from other regions. As a result, production slows down and generally tapers off. This, he claimed, caused a bell-shaped curve. His successful prediction encouraged a new generation of geologists to apply his methodology on a global scale. Chief among them are the experts at ODAC, who fear that the world peak in production will come in the coming decade. Dr Campbell used to argue that the record should have already been reached; now he thinks he is right around arriving. Heavyweights have now joined this sombre chorus. KENNETH DEFIZ OF PRINCETON UNIVERSITY ARGUES IN A LIVELY NEW BOOK (THE VIEW FROM THE HUBERTS SUMMIT) THAT GLOBAL OIL PRODUCTION MAY PEAK AS EARLY AS 2004. This strongly contradicts the central thinking. THE GEOLOGICAL SURVEY OF AMERICA PREPARED AN EXHAUSTIVE STUDY OF OIL DEPLETION LAST YEAR (IN PART TO REFUTE DR CAMPBELLS' ARGUMENTS) THAT POSTPONED PEAK PRODUCTION BY SEVERAL DECADES. The IEA has just been considering its new global energy forecast, which predicts enough oil to comfortably meet demand for 2020 from remaining reserves. Rene Dahan, one of ExxonMobil's top executives, goes further: with a promise characteristic of the world's largest energy company, he insists the world will be bathed in oil for another 70 years. Who's right? To understand these opposing views, it's worth looking back at the sorry history of oil forecasting. Doomsters have been predicting dry wells since the 1970s, but so far oil is still flowing. Almost all the predictions for 2000 made after the oil shocks of the 1970s were overly pessimistic. America's Department of Energy thought oil would reach $150 a barrel (at 2000 prices); even Exxon predicted a $100 price. Michael Lynch of DRI-WEFA, an economic consulting firm, is one of the few oil dramatists who generally gets things right. In a new paper, Dr. Lynch analyzes these historical predictions. He finds evidence of both bias and repeated errors, suggesting that methodological errors (rather than just bad data) were the problem. In particular, he hits out at forecasters who have used Hubert-style analysis relying on fixed estimates of how much recoverable oil there will eventually be underground, in the parlance of the industry: that figure, he insists, is actually dynamic, since improvements in infrastructure, knowledge and technology raise the amount of recoverable oil. It points to what will probably determine whether the pessimists or optimists are right: technological innovation. The first camp tends to underestimate claims of future technological revolutions in areas like deepwater drilling and improved recovery. Dr. Depace captures this mindset of the end of technology very well. He argues that because the industry has already spent billions on developing technology, this makes it difficult to request new technology today, since most wheels have already been invented. However, techno-optimists argue that the technological revolution in oil has only just begun. Average recovery rates (how much of the known oil in the reservoir can actually be brought to the surface) are still only around 30-35%. Industry optimists believe that new techniques on the drawing board today could raise that figure to 50-60% within a decade. Given the industry's remarkable track record in innovation, it may be foolish to bet against it. It's the result of adversity: The nationalizations of the 1970s forced Big Oil to develop reserves in expensive and inaccessible places like the North Sea and Alaska, undermining Dr. Hubberts's assumption that cheap reserves are first developed. The investments received upstream have lowered the cost of finding and developing the wells over the past two decades from over $20 per barrel to around $6 per barrel. The cost of oil production fell by half, to below $4 a barrel. Such miracles won't be cheap, however, as much of the world's oil is now produced in aging fields that are rapidly diminishing. The IEA concludes that global oil production should not peak in the next two decades if the necessary investments are made. So how much is needed? If oil companies are to replace lost output in these aging fields and meet the world's growing demand for oil, the agency estimates that they must invest $1 trillion in non-OPEC countries in the coming decade alone. That's no small figure.
hypothesis: Oil may last longer than other energy sources.

premise: THE ART OF HEALING AS IN SO MANY, THE MEDICINE OF THE TANG DYNASTY LEFT ITS EUROPEAN COUNTERPART IN THE SHADOW. She flaunted her national health service, leaving behind the teachings of the incomparable Sun Simiao. If there was no further evidence of China's sophistication in the Tang era, then a look at Chinese medicine would suffice. At the western end of the Eurasian continent the Roman Empire was gone, and there was no new place to claim the status of the cultural and political center of the world. In fact, for several centuries, this center happened to be the capital of the Tang Empire, and Chinese medicine under the Tang was well ahead of its European counterpart. The organizational context of health and healing was built to an extent that it had no priority in Chinese history and found no parallel elsewhere. AN IMPERIAL MEDICAL OFFICE WAS INHERITED FROM PREVIOUS DYNASTIES: IT WAS IMMEDIATELY RESTRUCTURED AND STAFFED WITH DIRECTORS AND DEPUTY DIRECTORS, CHIEF AND ASSISTANT MEDICAL DIRECTORS, PHARMACISTS AND CURATORS OF MEDICINAL HERB GARDENS AND OTHER STAFF. In the first two decades after the formation of its reign, the Tang administration established major and several provincial medical colleges with professors, lecturers, clinical pharmacists, and pharmacists to train students in one or all of the four departments of medicine, acupuncture, physical therapy, and exorcism. Doctors were given positions in a government medical service only after passing certification tests. They were paid depending on the number of drugs they performed in the past year. In 723 Emperor Xuanzong personally composed a general formula of prescriptions recommended to him by one of his imperial pharmacists and sent it to all provincial medical schools. An Arab traveler, who visited China in 851, noted with surprise that prescriptions from the emperors' formulas were posted on bulletin boards at a crossroads to improve the welfare of the population. The government was concerned with protecting the general population from potentially harmful medical practice. The Tang legal code was the first in China to include laws dealing with harmful and heterodox medical practices. For example, treating patients for money without adhering to standard procedures was defined as fraud combined with theft and had to be tried in accordance with the legal laws on theft. If such treatments resulted in the death of a patient, the healer would have to be banned for two and a half years. In the event that a doctor deliberately failed to practice according to the standards, he was to be tried in accordance with the laws on intentional homicide. Even if no damage was done, he was to be sentenced to sixty strokes in a heavy stick. In fact, physicians engaged in the Tang period had access to an abundance of pharmaceutical and medical texts, the plans of which ranged from purely pragmatic advice to highly sophisticated theoretical considerations. Concise descriptions of the location, morphology, and functions of human body organs stood side by side in libraries with books allowing readers to calculate the daily, seasonal, and annual climatic conditions of sixty-year cycles and to understand and predict their effects on health. Several Tang authors wrote large collections of prescriptions, continuing a literary tradition documented since the 2nd century BC. The two most notable works read here were those of Sun Simiao (581—682? ) Wang Tao (c. 670-755). The latter was a librarian who copied more than six thousand formulas, classified in 1,104 parts, from sixty-five older works and published them under the title Wciitai miyao. Twenty-four sections, for example, were devoted to ophthalmology. They reflect the Indian origin of much Chinese knowledge on eye diseases and especially on cataract surgery. Sun Simiao was the most prominent physician and writer not only of the Tang dynasty, but of the entire first millennium AD. He was an intellectual and a doctor of broad education; his worldview incorporated concepts of all three major currents competing in his time Confucianism, Taoism, and Buddhism. Sun Simiao gained fame during his lifetime as a clinician (he was summoned to the imperial court at least once) and as the author of prescriptions worth thousands of gold (Qianjinfang) and his sequels. In contrast to developments in the 12th century, doctors relied on individual prescriptions and substances to treat their patients' illnesses. The theories of systematic correspondences, typical of the acupuncture tradition, have not yet been extended to cover pharmacology. Sun Simiao rose to the pantheon of Chinese popular Buddhism around the 13th century. He was revered as the most important god of medicine. He gained this extraordinary role in Chinese collective memory not only because he was an outstanding clinician and writer, but also because of his ethical concerns. Sun Simiao was the first Chinese writer known to have authored an elaborate medical ethical code. Although it is based on Buddhist and Confucian values, its deontology resembles the Hippocratic Oath. It initiated a debate about the mission of medicine, its professional obligations, its social status, and moral justification that lasted until the arrival of Western medicine in the 19th century. Despite or more likely because of its long prosperity and political stability, the Tang dynasty did not add significantly new ideas to the interpretation of disease, health, and healing. Medical thought reflects human anxieties; changes in medical thought always occur in the context of new existential fears or of fundamentally altered social circumstances. Nevertheless, medicine was a most fascinating element of Tang civilization and it left a rich legacy for the centuries that followed.

premise: The Department of Ethnography The Department of Ethnography was established as a separate department within the British Museum in 1946, offering 140 years of gradual development from the original Department of Antiquities. Ife deals with the people of Africa, the Americas, Asia, the Pacific and the Persians of Europe. While this includes complex kingdoms, as in Africa, and ancient empires, like those of the Americas, the main focus of attention in the twentieth century was on small-scale societies. Through its collections, the Departments' specific interest is to document how objects are created and used, and to understand their importance and significance to those who produce them. Such objects can include both the unusual and the everyday, beautiful and banal. The collections of the Department of Ethnography include about 300,000 objects of art, about half of which are the product of the current century. The department has a vital role in providing information on non-Western cultures to visitors and researchers. To this end, the focus of collecting has often been less on individual objects than on groups of materials that allow the presentation of a wide range of cultural expressions of society.60 Much of the latter collection has been carried out in the field, sometimes by museum staff working on general anthropological projects in collaboration with a variety of national governments and other institutions. The material collected includes great technical series - for example, of textiles from Bolivia, Guatemala, Indonesia and the islands of West Africa - or of types of objects such as boats. The latter include working examples of corals from India, reed hogs from Lake Titicaca in the Andes, kayaks from the Arctic, and canoes excavated from several countries. THE FIELD ASSEMBLIES, LIKE THOSE FROM SUDAN, MADGASKET, AND YEMEN, INCLUDE A WHOLE RANGE OF MATERIAL CULTURE REPRESENTING PRIMARILY ONE PEOPLE. It may cover the life needs of an African shepherd or on an Arab farmer, ritual objects, or even occasionally airport art. Again, the MightReading series of acquisitions represents decades of fieldwork documenting social experience as reflected in the variety of clothing and jewelry styles, tents and camel traps from various Middle Eastern countries, or in evolving preferences in personal decoration and attire from Papua New Guinea. Of particular interest are a series of collections that continue to document the development of ritual and material forms for which the department already holds early (if not the earliest) collections created after first contact with Europeans. The importance of these purchases goes beyond the objects themselves. They arrive at the museum with a record of the social context, ideally including photographic records. Such purchases have multiple purposes. Significantly they document future change. Most people think of the cultures represented in the collection in terms of the absence of advanced technology. In fact, traditional practices rely on a sustained abundance of technological ingenuity. Limited resources and ecological constraints are often overcome by personal skills that would be considered exceptional in the West. Of growing interest is how much of what we might see as disposables are recycled and reused elsewhere. With the independence of much of Asia and Africa after 1945, it was assumed that economic progress would quickly lead to the disappearance or assimilation of many small-scale societies. Therefore, it was felt that the museum should acquire materials that represent people whose material art or culture, ceremonial or political structures are at the point of irreversible change. That approach has changed with the realization that marginalized communities can survive and adapt in the steeple of partial integration in a notoriously volatile world economy. Since the seventeenth century, with the emergence of trade companies exporting manufactured textiles to North America and Asia, the import of cheap goods has often contributed to the destruction of local skills and indigenous markets. On the one hand, modern imported goods may be used in an everyday setting, while on the other hand other traditional objects may still be required for ritually significant events. In this regard, trade and exchange are impaired. Like the Third Estate, Sauby wrote, the Third World is nothing, and it wants to be something. The term therefore implies that the Third World is exploited, as the Third Estate was exploited and that, like the Third Estate, its fate is revolutionary. Three years later the French economist François Peroux launched a new journal, on problems of underdevelopment, with the same title. In the late 1950s the term was often used in French media to refer to the underdeveloped countries in Asia. Africa, Oceania and Latin America. Today's politicians and social commentators, however, now use the term developing world in a politically correct effort to dispel the negative connotations of the Third World. Countries in the developing world have a number of common features: distorted and highly dependent economies dedicated to producing primary products for the developed world; traditional rural social structures; high population growth and widespread poverty. However, the developing world is sharply differentiated, as it includes countries of different levels of economic development. And despite the poverty of the village and urban flock towns, the elites who control most Third World countries are wealthy. This integration of conditions in Asia, Africa, Oceania and Latin America is related to the absorption of the developing world into the international capitalist economy, by way of conquest or indirect control. The main economic result of Western domination was the creation of a world market, for the first time in history. By establishing sub-economies linked to the West throughout the developing world, and by introducing other modern institutions, industrial capitalism has disrupted traditional economies and indeed societies. This disruption led to underdevelopment. Because the economies of underdeveloped countries have been adapted to the needs of industrialized nations, they often include only a few modern economic activities, such as mining or growing plantation crops. Control of these activities often remains in the hands of large foreign companies. Prices for developing-world goods are typically set by large buyers in the economically dominant countries in the West, and trade with the West provides nearly all of the developing worlds' revenues. Throughout the colonial period, absolute exploitation greatly limited the accumulation of capital in foreign-controlled countries. Even after decolonization (in the 1950s, 1960s and 1970s), the economies of the developing world grew slowly, or not at all, largely due to deteriorating terms of trade the relationship between the cost of goods a nation must import from abroad and its income from the exports it sends to foreign countries. They say trade conditions deteriorate when the cost of imports rises faster than revenue from exports. premise: The Falkirk Wheel a unique engineering feat. The Falkirk Wheel in Scotland is the first and only rotating boat lift in the world. Opened in 2002, it is central to the ambitious £84.5m Millennium Link project to restore navigational capacity across Scotland by reconnecting the historic waterways of the Port and Clyde and Union canals. The main challenge of the project lies in the fact that the Port and Clyde Canal is located 35 metres below the level of the Union Canal. Historically, the two canals were joined near the town of Falkirk by a sequence of 11 locks closed sections of canal in which it was possible to raise or lower the water level to be lowered over a distance of 1.5 km. It was dismantled in 1933, thus breaking the link. When the project was launched in 1994, the British Waterways Authority was keen to create a dramatic twenty-first-century landmark that would not only form a fitting commemoration of the millennium, but also an enduring symbol of the region's economic regeneration. Many ideas were submitted for the project, including concepts ranging from an egg wheel to tilted tanks, from giant sight relays to overhead monorails. The eventual winner was a plan for the giant revolving steel boat lift that should become the Falkirk Wheel. The unique shape of the structure is claimed to have been inspired by various sources, both man-made and natural, most notably a double-headed Celtic axe, but also the enormous rotating propeller of a ship, the rib cage of a whale or the spine of a fish. THE VARIOUS PARTS OF THE FALKIRK WHEEL WERE BUILT AND ASSEMBLED, LIKE ONE GIANT TOY BUILDING SET, AT BUTTERLEY ENGINEERING'S STEEL MILLS IN DERBYSHIRE, ABOUT 400 MILES FROM FALKIRK. The team there carefully assembled the 1,200 tons of steel, carefully adjusting the parts to an accuracy of just 10mm to ensure a perfect final fit. In the summer of 2001, the structure was dismantled and transported on 35 lorries to Falkirk, before they were all screwed onto the ground again, and finally raised into place in five large sections using a crane. The wheel would have to withstand enormous and constantly changing pressures as it rotated, so to make the structure stronger, the steel sections were bolted and not welded to each other. Over 45,000 screw holes were fitted to their bolts, and each screw was fastened by hand. The wheel consists of two sets of opposite axe-shaped arms, connected at a distance of about 25 meters apart to a fixed central spine. Two completely opposite water-filled gondolas, each with a capacity of 360,000 litres, are installed between the ends of the arms. These gondolas always weigh the same, whether they carry boats or not. This is because according to Archimedes' displacement principle, floating objects transfer their own weight in water. So when a boat enters the gondola, the amount of water coming out of the gondola weighs just as much as the boat. This keeps the wheel balanced and so, despite its enormous mass, it spins 180 in five and a half minutes using very little power. It takes just 1.5 kilowatt-hours (5.4 MJ) of energy to spin the wheel about as much as boiling eight small household water kettles. Boats that need to be lifted enter the canal basin at the level of the Port and Clyde Canal and then enter the lower wheel gondola. Two hydraulic steel gates are raised, to seal the gondola from the water in the canal basin. The water between the gates is pumped out. A hydraulic clamp, which prevents the wheel arms from moving while the gondola is anchored, is removed and allows the wheel to turn. In the central machine room an array of ten hydraulic motors begins to rotate the central axis. The axle connects to the outer arms of the wheel, which begin to rotate at a speed of 1/8 revolution per minute. When the wheel rotates, the gondolas are kept in an upright position by a simple gear system. Two eight-metre-wide wheels surround a fixed inner cogwheel of the same width, connected by two smaller wheels travelling in the opposite direction to the outer wheels to ensure that the gondolas always remain straight. When the gondola reaches the top, the boat goes straight to the aqueduct located 24 meters above the canal basin. The remaining 11 meters of lift needed to reach the Union Canal are achieved using a pair of locks. It was not possible to build the wheel to raise boats above the full 35-metre differential between the two canals, due to the presence of the historically important Antonine Wall, built by the Romans in the 2nd century AD. Boats travel under this wall through a tunnel, then through the locks, and finally to the Union Canal.

premise: The inventive invention gap, as I define it here, consists not only of ideas for new technologies like the computer or drought-resistant crops, but, more fundamentally, of ideas for better institutions and social arrangements, like efficient markets and empowered governments. How much and what kind of ingenuity society requires depends on a variety of factors, including the goals of the company and the circumstances in which it must achieve those goals whether it has a young or aging population, an abundance of natural resources or a shortage of them, a mild climate or punishment, whichever is the case. How much and what kind of ingenuity society provides also depends on many factors, such as the nature of human invention and understanding, the rewards that economics affords producers of useful knowledge, and the intensity of political resistance to social and institutional reforms. A good supply of the right kind of invention is essential, but it is obviously not enough on its own. We know that wealth creation, for example, depends not only on the adequate supply of useful ideas but also on the availability of other, more conventional factors of production, such as capital and labor. Similarly, prosperity, stability and justice generally depend on the resolution, or at least containment, of major political struggles over wealth and power. In our economies, however, ingenuity often replaces labor, and an increase in the physical plant stock is usually accompanied by a growth in the inventory of invention. And in our political systems, we need great ingenuity to establish institutions that successfully manage struggles for wealth and power. It is clear that our economic and political processes are intimately entangled in the production and use of ingenuity. The countless cumulative changes of the past century in our societies across the planet, in our technologies, and in our interactions with the surrounding natural environments have accumulated to create a qualitatively new world. Because these changes have slowly accumulated, it is often difficult for us to recognize how deep and sweeping they are. They include much larger and denser populations; a much higher per capita consumption of natural resources; and much better and more available technologies for the movement of people, materials, and especially information. Taken together, these changes have sharply increased the density, intensity, and pace of our actions with one another; they have greatly increased the burden we impose on our natural environment; and they have helped shift power from national and international institutions to individuals and subgroups, such as special political interests and ethnic factions. As a result, people in all walks of life, from our political and business leaders to all of us in our day to day, must deal with far more complex, urgent and often unpredictable circumstances. Managing our relationship with this new world requires vast and growing amounts of social and technical ingenuity. As we strive to maintain or increase our prosperity and improve our quality of life, we must make much more sophisticated decisions, and in less time, than ever before. When we improve the performance of any system, from our cars to the planner network of financial institutions, we tend to make it more complex. Many of the natural systems critical to our well-being, like the global climate and oceans, are extraordinarily complex to begin with. We often cannot predict or manage the behavior of complex systems with great precision, because they are often very sensitive to the smallest changes and disturbances, and their behavior can move from one state to another abruptly and dramatically. In general, as the man-made and natural systems we depend on become more complex, and as our demands of them increase, the institutions and technologies we use to manage them must become more complex, further increasing our need for ingenuity. The good news, however, is that the remarkable changes of the last century in our societies and technologies have not only heightened our need for ingenuity; they have also resulted in a huge increase in its supply. The growth and urbanization of human populations has combined with remarkable new communications and transportation technologies to expand interactions between people and produce larger, more integrated and efficient markets. These changes, in turn, greatly accelerated the creation and delivery of beneficial ideas. But this is critical but we should not jump to the conclusion that the supply of invention always increases in accordance with the requirement of our invention: while it is true that need is often the mother of invention, we cannot always rely on the right kind of ingenuity appearing when and where we need it. In many cases, the complexity and speed of operation of today's vital economic, social, and arid ecosystems outweigh the perception of the human mind. Few of us have more than a preliminary understanding of how these systems work. They remain fraught with countless unknown unknowns, making it difficult to deliver the invention we need to solve problems related to these systems. In this book, explore a wide range of other factors that will limit our ability to deliver the ingenuity required in the coming century. For example, many people believe that new communication technologies strengthen democracy and make it easier to find solutions to our societies, collective problems, but the story is less clear than it seems. The crushing of information in our daily lives shortens our attention span, limits the time we have to reflect on critical public policy issues and makes policy arguments more superficial. The modem markets and science are an important part of the story of how we deliver ingenuity. Markets are extremely important, as they give entrepreneurs an incentive to generate knowledge. As for science, although it seems to face no theoretical limits, at least in the foreseeable future, practical constraints often slow its progress. The cost of scientific research tends to rise as it delves deeper into nature. And the rate of progress of the sciences depends on the characteristic of the phenomena of nature that it studies, simply because some phenomena are more difficult to understand fundamentally than others, and therefore the production of useful new knowledge in these fields can be very slow. As a result, there is often a critical time lag between recognizing between a problem and delivering sufficient ingenuity, in the form of technologies, to solve that problem. Progress in the social sciences is exceptionally slow, for reasons that are not yet understood; but we desperately need better social knowledge to build the sophisticated institutions that the world requires today

At this time, it was called Poona - after a place in India - and from about 1860 it became popular in England. There, netting was first introduced in 1867, and the modern scoring system began to develop, although there were many disagreements about the rules between the players, and there was no official organization to govern the sport. All this changed in 1887. The name 'Badminton' was introduced after a famous party at a country house of that name in the same year. Although it happened again in 1988, it was 1992 before badminton was played as a fully recognised Olympic sport - when the mixed pairs were added in 1996. premise: The Iron Bridge was the first iron bridge of its kind in Europe and is universally recognized as a symbol of the Industrial Revolution. The Iron Bridge crosses the River Severn at Caulbrookdale, in the west of England. It was the first cast-iron bridge to be successfully erected, and the first large cast-iron structure of the industrial era in Europe, although the Chinese had expert iron casters centuries earlier. Rivers used to be the equivalent of today's highways, in that they were widely used for transportation. The River Severn, which begins its life in the Welsh mountains and eventually enters the sea between Cardiff and Bristol, is the longest navigable river in Britain. It was ideal for transportation purposes, and special boats were built to navigate the water. In the middle of the eighteenth century the Søren was one of the busiest rivers in Europe. Local goods, including coal, iron products, wool, grain, and cider, were shipped by river. Among the commodities that came upstream were luxuries like sugar, tea, coffee and wine. In places, the banks of the river were lined with docks and the river was often overloaded with loading or unloading boats. In 1638, Basil Brooke patented a steel-making process and built a furnace at Caulbrookdale. It later became the property of Abraham Darby (known as Abraham Darby I to distinguish him from his son and grandson of the same name). After serving an apprenticeship in Birmingham, Darby opened a business in Bristol, but he moved to Coalbrookdale in 1710 with an idea that coal sourced coal could provide a more economical alternative to coal as fuel for iron production. This led to cheaper and more efficient iron production from the abundant supply of coal, iron and limestone in the region. His son, Abraham Darby II, was a pioneer in the manufacture of cast iron, and had the idea of building a bridge over the Soren, since ferry stores of all kinds across the river, especially the large quantities of fuel for the furnaces at Coalbrookdale and other surrounding ironworks, were fraught with considerable expense and delays. However, his son Abraham Darby III (born 1750) was the one who in 1775 organized a meeting to plan the construction of a bridge. It was designed by a local architect, Thomas Pritchard, who had the idea to build it out of iron. Sections were poured over the winter of 1778-9 to a 7-foot-wide bridge with a span of 31 feet, 12 feet above the river. Construction took three months during the summer of 1779, and amazingly, no one was injured during the construction process, a feat almost unheard of even in large modern civil engineering projects. Work on the approach roads continued for another two years, and the bridge was opened to traffic in 1781. Abraham Darby III financed the bridge by commissioning paintings and engravings, but he lost much on the project, which cost almost double the estimate, and he died, leaving immense debts in 1789, aged only 39. The district did not flourish any longer, and during the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries factories were closed. Since 1934 the bridge is only open to pedestrians. The Iron Bridge, universally recognized as a symbol of the Industrial Revolution, now stands at the heart of the Iron Bridge Channel World Heritage Site. It has always been a mystery how the bridge was built. Despite its pioneering technology, no eyewitness reports describing the iron bridge being erected are known and certainly no plans have survived. However, recent discoveries, studies and experiments shed new light on how it was constructed, challenging the assumptions of recent decades. In 1997, a small watercolor sketch by Elias Martin was discovered in the Swedish capital Stockholm. Although there are plenty of early views of the bridge by many artists, this is the only one that shows it actually under construction. Until recently it was assumed that the bridge was built from both banks, with the internal supports tilted across the river. This would have allowed river traffic to continue uninterrupted during construction. But the photo clearly shows footage of the raised bridge from a river barge. This contradicts everything that historians have assumed about the bridge, and it is even thought that the picture could have been faked since no one else was discovered. So in 2001 a half-scale model of the bridge was built, to see if it could have been built in the manner depicted in the watercolour. The results tell us much more about how the bridge was built. We now know that all the major castings were made separately because they are all slightly different. The bridge was not welded or bolted together like metal bridges nowadays. Instead it was installed together using a complex system of joints normally used for wood, but this was the traditional way in which iron structures were connected at the time. The construction of the model demonstrated that the painting shows a very realistic method of building the bridge that could work and was most likely the method used. Now only one mystery remains in the story of the Iron Bridge. The Swedish watercolor sketch was apparently torn from a book that would have contained similar drawings. It was painted by a Swedish artist who lived in London for 12 years and travelled the UK painting what he saw. No one knows what happened to the rest of the book, but perhaps the other sketches still exist somewhere. If they are ever found they could provide further valuable evidence of how the Iron Bridge was built.

It was the first cast-iron bridge to be successfully erected, and the first large cast-iron structure of the industrial era in Europe, although the Chinese had expert iron casters centuries earlier. Rivers used to be the equivalent of today's highways, in that they were widely used for transportation. The River Severn, which begins its life in the Welsh mountains and eventually enters the sea between Cardiff and Bristol, is the longest navigable river in Britain. It was ideal for transportation purposes, and special boats were built to navigate the water. In the middle of the eighteenth century the Søren was one of the busiest rivers in Europe. Local goods, including coal, iron products, wool, grain, and cider, were shipped by river. Among the commodities that came upstream were luxuries like sugar, tea, coffee and wine. In places, the banks of the river were lined with docks and the river was often overloaded with loading or unloading boats. In 1638, Basil Brooke patented a steel-making process and built a furnace at Caulbrookdale. It later became the property of Abraham Darby (known as Abraham Darby I to distinguish him from his son and grandson of the same name). After serving an apprenticeship in Birmingham, Darby opened a business in Bristol, but he moved to Coalbrookdale in 1710 with an idea that coal sourced coal could provide a more economical alternative to coal as fuel for iron production. This led to cheaper and more efficient iron production from the abundant supply of coal, iron and limestone in the region. His son, Abraham Darby II, was a pioneer in the manufacture of cast iron, and had the idea of building a bridge over the Soren, since ferry stores of all kinds across the river, especially the large quantities of fuel for the furnaces at Coalbrookdale and other surrounding ironworks, were fraught with considerable expense and delays. However, his son Abraham Darby III (born 1750) was the one who in 1775 organized a meeting to plan the construction of a bridge. It was designed by a local architect, Thomas Pritchard, who had the idea to build it out of iron. Sections were poured over the winter of 1778-9 to a 7-foot-wide bridge with a span of 31 feet, 12 feet above the river. Construction took three months during the summer of 1779, and amazingly, no one was injured during the construction process, a feat almost unheard of even in large modern civil engineering projects. Work on the approach roads continued for another two years, and the bridge was opened to traffic in 1781. Abraham Darby III financed the bridge by commissioning paintings and engravings, but he lost much on the project, which cost almost double the estimate, and he died, leaving immense debts in 1789, aged only 39. The district did not flourish any longer, and during the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries factories were closed. Since 1934 the bridge is only open to pedestrians. The Iron Bridge, universally recognized as a symbol of the Industrial Revolution, now stands at the heart of the Iron Bridge Channel World Heritage Site. It has always been a mystery how the bridge was built. Despite its pioneering technology, no eyewitness reports describing the iron bridge being erected are known and certainly no plans have survived. However, recent discoveries, studies and experiments shed new light on how it was constructed, challenging the assumptions of recent decades. In 1997, a small watercolor sketch by Elias Martin was discovered in the Swedish capital Stockholm. Although there are plenty of early views of the bridge by many artists, this is the only one that shows it actually under construction. Until recently it was assumed that the bridge was built from both banks, with the internal supports tilted across the river. This would have allowed river traffic to continue uninterrupted during construction. But the photo clearly shows footage of the raised bridge from a river barge. This contradicts everything that historians have assumed about the bridge, and it is even thought that the picture could have been faked since no one else was discovered. So in 2001 a half-scale model of the bridge was built, to see if it could have been built in the manner depicted in the watercolour. Meanwhile, a detailed archaeological, historical and photographic survey has been done by the Iron Bridge Museum Trust, along with a three-dimensional CAD model (computer-aided design) by English Heritage. The results tell us much more about how the bridge was built. We now know that all the major castings were made separately because they are all slightly different. The bridge was not welded or bolted together like metal bridges nowadays. Instead it was installed together using a complex system of joints normally used for wood, but this was the traditional way in which iron structures were connected at the time. The construction of the model demonstrated that the painting shows a very realistic method of building the bridge that could work and was most likely the method used. Now only one mystery remains in the story of the Iron Bridge. The Swedish watercolor sketch was apparently torn from a book that would have contained similar drawings. It was painted by a Swedish artist who lived in London for 12 years and travelled the UK painting what he saw. No one knows what happened to the rest of the book, but perhaps the other sketches still exist somewhere. If they are ever found they could provide further valuable evidence of how the Iron Bridge was built.

premise: The Nature and Objectives of Archaeology Archaeology is in part the discovery of the treasures of the past, in part the painstaking work of the scientific analyst, in part the activation of the creative imagination. He toils in the sun digging in the Middle East, he works with the Inuit living in the snows of Alaska, and he explores the sewers of Roman Britain. But that's also the painstaking task of interpretation, so that we can understand what these things mean for the human story. And this is the preservation of world cultural heritage from looting and careless damage. Archaeology, then, is both an exercise in the field and an intellectual pursuit in research or in the laboratory. That's part of its big attraction. Its rich blend of danger and detective work has also made it the perfect tool for writers and filmmakers, from Agatha Christie with Murder in Mesopotamia to Steven Spielberg with Indiana Jones. Far from reality, such depictions capture the essential truth that archaeology is an exciting journey in search of knowledge about ourselves and our past. But how does archaeology relate to disciplines such as anthropology and history, which also deal with the human story? Is archaeology itself a science? And what is the responsibility of the archaeologist in today's world? Anthropology, at its most extensive, is humanity's study of our physical characteristics as animals and our unique non-biological characteristics that we call culture. Culture in this sense includes what the anthropologist, Edward Taylor, summed up in 1871 as “knowledge, belief, art, morality, custom and all other abilities and habits acquired by man as a member of society”. Anthropologists also use the term 'culture' in a more restricted sense when they refer to the “culture” of a particular society, that is, the non-biological characteristics unique to that society, which distinguish it from other societies. Anthropology is therefore a broad discipline so broad that it is usually divided into three smaller disciplines: physical anthropology, cultural anthropology, and archaeology. Physical anthropology, or biological anthropology as it is also called, concerns the study of human biological or physical characteristics and how they evolved. Cultural anthropology or social anthropology analyzes human culture and society. Two of its branches are ethnography (the first-hand study of individual living cultures) and ethnology (which aims to compare cultures using ethnographic evidence to derive general principles about human society). Archaeology is the “past time of cultural anthropology”. WHILE CULTURAL ANTHROPOLOGISTS WILL OFTEN BASE THEIR CONCLUSIONS ON THE EXPERIENCE OF LIFE WITHIN CONTEMPORARY COMMUNITIES, ARCHAEOLOGISTS INVESTIGATING SOCIETIES MOVED PRIMARILY THROUGH THEIR MATERIAL REMAINS THE BUILDINGS, TOOLS, AND OTHER ART OBJECTS THAT COMPRISE WHAT IS KNOWN AS THE MATERIAL CULTURE LEFT OVER FROM FORMER SOCIETIES. Nevertheless, one of the most important tasks for the archaeologist today is to know how to interpret material culture in human terms. How were these pots used? Why are some apartments round and others square? Here the methods of archaeology and ethnography coincide. Archaeologists in recent decades have developed 'ethnoarchaeology', in which, like ethnographers, they live among contemporary communities, but with the specific aim of studying how such societies use material culture, how they make their tools and weapons, why they build their settlements where they do, and so on. Moreover, archaeology has an active role in the field of conservation. Heritage studies constitute an evolving field, in which it becomes clear that world cultural heritage is a diminishing resource with different meanings for different people. If, then, archaeology deals with the past, in what way does it differ from history? In the broadest sense, just as archaeology is an aspect of anthropology, so too is part of history by which we mean the entire history of mankind from its beginning over three million years ago. Indeed, for more than ninety-nine percent of that vast time period, archaeology exploring past material culture is the only significant source of information. Conventional historical sources only begin with the introduction of written records around 3,000 BCE in western Asia, and much later in most other parts of the world. A common distinction is between pre-history, meaning the period before written records and history in the narrow sense, meaning the study of the past through written evidence. For archaeology, which studies all cultures and periods, whether with or without writing, the distinction between history and prehistory is a convenient dividing line that recognizes the importance of the written word, but in no way diminishes the importance of the useful information contained in oral history. Because the purpose of archaeology is the understanding of humanity, it is a humanistic study, and because it deals with the human past, it is a historical discipline. But it differs from written history research in a fundamental way. The material the archaeologist finds does not directly tell us what to think. Historical records make statements, offer opinions, and pass judgments. The artifacts the archaeologists discover, however, tell us nothing directly by themselves. In this respect, the archaeologist's practice is quite similar to that of the scientist, who collects data, conducts experiments, formulates a hypothesis, tests the hypothesis against additional data, and then, in conclusion, invents a model that seems best to summarize the pattern observed in the data. The archaeologist must develop a picture of the past, just as the scientist needs to develop a coherent view of the natural world.

premise: Oxford School of Drama Annual Acting Course This is an intensive course designed for those who have completed their academic studies and already have experience in theatre or film. premise: The role of Swiss Postbus Schweiz Postbus Ltd. is the largest of the 78 bus companies in the country. Run by the Post Office's Automotive Services Department, it carries over 120 million passengers annually and is carefully integrated with other public transport services: trains, boats and mountain cableways. The Swiss transport system is similar to the tree, with the larger branches representing federal and private railways, the smaller branches being the buses, and the twigs being the municipal transport operators that operate trams, city buses, boats, chair lifts, and so on. But the trunk that holds the tree together is the vast post-boss network, without which the entire network would not have functioned. There is no inhabited place in Switzerland that cannot be reached by any public transport. Federal law and the Swiss constitution stipulate that any village with a population over 40 is entitled to regular bus services. The frequency of these services is directly related to population density. Schedules are made up four years in advance, and rarely change. If a new route is to be introduced, the population of the affected area is invited to vote in a referendum. Sometimes, postbuses are the sometimes only major links between settlements. These cars, often with trailing in tow to increase their capacity, are a common sight in high-altitude areas, and some of their distinctive sound of Rossini and William Tell Overthorn, which the drivers play on three-tone pillar beams with electric compressors at every road turn is one of the most familiar Swiss sounds. The tri-tone horns can still be used to talk to post offices (and each other) remotely. By changing the combination of sounds, a driver can announce a post1 departure, a post arrival, a special post arrival and so on much more romantic and often more reliably than radios or mobile phones. This musical language began in the mid-nineteenth century, when coach drivers could also blow their horns a certain number of times as they approached the station to indicate the number of horses that needed to be fed, which gave the station manager time to prepare the fodder. The history of the postbus begins in 1849, when the Swiss postal service became a monopoly. The role of modern day yellow buses was then played by horse-drawn carriages (or in winter by sleds, to travel on snow), which were the same color. By 1914, eight years after the first engines were introduced, there were still 2,500 horses, 2,231 carriages (or carriages) and 1,059 sleds in service. After World War I, Switzerland Post acquired a fleet of military trucks converted into post-bosses, but it was not until 1961 that the last horse-drawn coach was replaced by a motorized version. Today, the Swiss Post Office boasts one of the most advanced bus fleets in the world, including fuel cell models and the world's first driverless bus. It was launched in 2015 in the town of Sion, the capital of the canton of Valais, one of the 26 cantons, or administrative regions, that make up the country. Postbuses often travel to places that other means of transportation cannot reach. That's why most drivers see themselves as educators and tour guides. Although it is not in their job description, they will most likely point to the sights cascading, gullies and so on and are always ready to stop for a photo opportunity. The longest postbus journey in Switzerland, and one of the highest, crosses four mountain passes and an eight-hour hike undertaken by a single postbus. The route passes through several cantons; two languages (German and Italian); all four seasons ranging from blazing sunlight to heavy rains and snow; and countless places of interest, one of the passes, the Gotthard, is often described as the Peoples Way, probably because it connects the German-speaking Canton of Uri with Italian-speaking Ticino. Similar to Switzerland itself, postbuses speak all four languages of the country: German, French, Italian and Romansh and by law, their automated intercom messages are given in the language of the canton where the bus currently passes. Regardless of their previous driving experience, drivers undergo a lot of training. During the first year, they have, drive postbuses under the supervision of a more experienced driver. Only after two years of safe driving in the valleys can they be pronounced ready for a mountain bus. Some routes are not busy at all, with the bus often carrying only two or three passengers at a time. But for most people living in small mountain villages, the postbus is paramount. He not only carries villagers to town and back, he takes village children to and from school, delivers mail, transports milk from the village farm to the valley, collects rubbish from the village (Swiss laws do not allow dumping anywhere in the mountains), and brings building materials to households. It takes elderly villagers to the shops and carries their shopping up the hill to their homes. More a friend than just a means of transportation, for residents of mountain villages the postbus is an essential part of life.

premise: Absolute fire bans Total fire bans affect everyone. Whether you live in the city, suburbs or in the country, you need to know when one is declared and what it means you can't do. What is a total fire ban? A total fire ban prohibits: lighting any fire in the open air any other open-air activity that may start a fire. Covert areas such as patios, pergolas and cabins that are open or partially open to the weather are considered open air. When will a total fire ban be announced? The decision to impose a ban is based on the weather forecast and local conditions. A total fire ban will be declared on days when the fires are expected to threaten lives and property. How will I know when a total fire ban has been announced? When a ban is announced it will be: on the DFES website www. dfes. wa. gov. au in the total fire ban information line 1800 709 355 which is broadcast on ABC local radio and other media published to subscribers through DFES websites automated RSS feeds posted on the Dfess Twitter account displayed on local government roadside fire danger rating signs. How long has a total fire ban been in place? The ban will normally be in effect from 12.01 am to 23.59 on the day it is announced; however, if weather conditions change significantly, times may change. What are the penalties for ignoring a total fire ban? You can be fined up to 25 000$ and/or jailed for 12 months for ignoring the ban.

premise: Transition cake for the eloquent What is transition care? Transitional care is for older people who have received medical care but need more help for recovery, and time to make a decision about the best place for them to live in the longer term. Transitional care can only be accessed directly from the hospital. Transition therapy focuses on individual goals and treatments and is only available for a limited time. It offers access to a suite of services that may include: low-intensity care such as physical therapy (exercise, mobility, strength and balance) and podiatry (foot care) access to a social worker nursing support for clinical care such as personal wound care Who provides transition care services? Transitional care is most often provided by NGOs and subsidized by the government. If your circumstances allow it, it is expected that you will contribute to the cost of your treatment. The daily care fee is set by the organization that provides your transit care services (your service provider). They have to explain these fees to you, and the amount charged should form part of the agreement between you and the service provider. The fee is calculated on a daily basis. Where do I get transitional care? Transition therapy is provided in your home or residential setting. This setting can be part of an existing elderly care home or from a health facility such as a separate wing of a hospital. What if I already receive services through another program? If you already receive subsidized residential care in an elderly care home, but need to go elsewhere for transitional care, your place in the aging home will be saved until you return.

premise: Hard sums and psychology In their first years of learning math at school, kids all over the world usually have to learn the schedule, also called the multiplication table, which shows what you get when you multiply numbers together. Children have traditionally learned their schedule by switching from 1 times 1 to 12 times 12 is 144. The time tables have been around for a very long time. The oldest known tables that use base 10 numbers, the base now used everywhere in the world, are written on bamboo strips dating from 305 BC, found in China. However, in many European cultures the schedule is named after the ancient Greek mathematician and philosopher Pythagoras (570-495 BC). And so it is called the Pythagorean table in many languages, including French and Italian. In 1820, in his book The Philosophy of Arithmetic, mathematician John Leslie recommended that young students remember the schedule up to 25 x 25. Nowadays, however, educators generally believe that it is important for children to memorize the table up to 9 x 9, 10 x 10 or 12 x12. The current aim in the UK is for school pupils to know all their schedules up to 12 x 12 by the age of nine. However, many people do not know them, even as adults. Recently, some politicians have been asked arithmetic questions of this kind. For example, in 1998, Schools Minister Stephen Byres was asked the answer to 7 x 8. He misanswered and said 54 rather than 56, and everyone laughed at him. In 2014, a young boy asked UK Chancellor George Osborne the exact same question. Because he passed A-level maths and was in charge of Britain's economic policy at the time, you'd expect him to know the answer. However, he simply said, I have established it a rule in life not to answer such questions. Why would a politician refuse to answer such a question? It's certainly true that some amounts are much harder than others. Studies have shown that learning and remembering sums that include 6,7,8 and 9 tend to be more difficult than remembering sums that include other numbers. And it's even harder when 6,7,8 and 9 are multiplied by each other. Studies often find that the hardest tally is 68, with 78 not far behind. However, although 78 is a relatively difficult sum, it is unlikely that George Osborne did not know the answer. So there must be another reason why he refused to answer the question. The answer is that Osborne was put in place and he didn't like it. It is known that when there is a lot of pressure to do something right, people often find it difficult to do something that they usually find easy. When you put someone on the spot and ask a question like that, it causes stress. A person's heart beats faster and their adrenaline levels rise. As a result, people will often make mistakes that they would not normally make. It's called strangulation. Choking often happens in sports, for example when a footballer takes a decisive penalty. In the same way, the boys' question put Osborne under great pressure. He knew it would be a disaster for him if he got the answer to such a simple question wrong and feared he might suffocate. And that's why he refused to answer the question. premise: Addiction to TV 2 Excessive craving does not necessarily involve physical substances. Gambling can become compulsive; sex can become obsessive. One activity, however, stands out for its prominence and as a wholethe most popular pastime in the world, television. Most people admit to having a love relationship with it. They complain about the couch's boob tube and potatoes, then they settle in their couches and grab the remote control. Parents are usually worried about their children's (if not their own) viewing. Even scholars who study television for a living marvel at the psychics holding them personally. Percy Tannenbaum of the University of California, Berkeley wrote: Between life there have been more awkward moments and countless occasions when I engage in conversation in a room while a television set is on, and I cannot for the life of me stop occasionally peering at the screen. This happens not only during boring conversations but during fairly equally interesting conversations. b. Scientists have been studying the effects of television for decades, and generally focus on whether watching violence on television correlates with real-life violence. Less attention has been paid to the basic allure of the small screen - the medium, as opposed to the message. The term TV addiction is inaccurate and loaded with value judgments, but it captures the essence of a very real phenomenon. Psychologists and psychiatrists formally define substance dependence as a disorder characterized by criteria that include spending a lot of time using a substance; using it more often than the person intends; thinking about reducing use or making repeated unsuccessful efforts to reduce use; giving up important social, family, or occupational activities to use it; and reporting withdrawal symptoms when stopping use Beau. All these criteria can apply to people who watch a lot of television. That doesn't mean watching TV, per se, is problematic. Television can teach and entertain; it can reach aesthetic heights; it can provide much-needed distraction and escape. The difficulty arises when people feel strongly that they don't need to watch as much as they do and yet find themselves strangely unable to reduce their viewing. Some knowledge of how the medium exerts its pull may help heavy viewers gain better control over their lives. The amount of time people spend watching TV is staggering. On average, people in the industrialized world devote three hours a day to half their leisure time, and more than any individual activity saves work and sleep. At this rate, someone who lived to be 75 would have spent nine years in front of the tube. For some commentators, this dedication simply means that people enjoy television and make a conscious decision to watch it. But if that's the whole story, why are so many people experiencing concerns about how much they watch? In Gallup polls in 1992 and 1999, two in five adult respondents and seven in ten teenagers said they spent too much time watching television. Other surveys have consistently shown that about 10 percent of self-addicted adults are addicted to television. What is it about TV that has such a hold in the US? In part, the attraction seems to stem from our biologically directed response. The intentional response, first described by Ivanpavlov in 1927, is our instinctive visual or auditory response to any sudden or new stimulus. It's part of our evolutionary heritage, a built-in susceptibility to movement and potential predatory threats. In 1986, Byron Reeves of Stanford University, Esther Thorson of the University of Missouri and their colleagues began investigating whether the simple features of television cuts, edits, zooms, repetitions, sudden noises trigger the intentional response, thus keeping attention on the screen. By watching how brain waves were influenced by formal features, the researchers concluded that these stylistic tricks could indeed elicit involuntary responses and derive their attentional value through the evolutionary significance of motion detection... The form, not the content, of television is unique. The intentional response may explain in part common viewer comments such as: If a TV is on, I just can't keep my eyes off it, I don't want to watch as much as I do, but I can't help it, and I feel mesmerized when I watch TV. In the years since Reeves and Thorson published then-pioneering work, researchers have delved deeper. Annie Leng's research team from Indiana University showed that heart rate decreases for four to six seconds after intentional stimulation. In ads, action sequences, and music videos, formal features often arrive at a rate of one per second, thus triggering the directed response continuously. Lang and her colleagues also investigated whether formal features affect people's memory of what they saw. In one of their studies, participants watched a program and then filled out a score sheet. Increasing the frequency of edits (defined here as the change from one camera angle to another in the same visual scene) improved memory recognition, presumably because it focused attention on the screen. Increasing the frequency of cuts to a new visual scene - had a similar effect but only up to a point. If the number of cuts exceeded 10 in two minutes, the recognition decreased sharply. Producers of educational television for children have found that formal features can help learning. But increasing the rate of cuts and edits ends up putting a strain on the brain. premise: Desert rot Despite its name, dry rot is anything but dry; it needs water to grow. Wood is made up of cellulose and lignin, and the fungus transfers the cellulose to its sugar constituents and eventually to carbon dioxide and water, which the fungus absorbs. The affected wood takes on a dull brown appearance, dries out and quickly loses mechanical strength. Dry rot can threaten the structure of the building because it can spread beyond its source to penetrate walls and bricks. In the short term, wood affected by dry rot can be removed and the nearby tree treated with a chemical fungicide. However, prevention is better than cure, and dry rot will not grow in an environment with less than 20 percent humidity. Wet rot is more common in buildings than dry rot but is a much less serious problem because it cannot spread into the brickwork. Like dry rot, wet rot cannot grow in dry wood. Usually both dry and wet rot can be attributed to a definite source of rainwater ingress into the building, for example broken tiles, gutters or bricks. Painting trees with a primer and top layer can stop the penetration of water into the tree, thereby preventing the germination of wood rot spores. However, an intact paint surface can mask fungal infiltration that may have entered the tree in an exposed surface, for example where the wood is embedded with wet bricks. The presence of dry rot can be confirmed by checking with a screwdriver, when the wood will easily give way, and also by tapping with a hammer, when it will sound hollow.

premise: Teens trying to change the world, one purchase at a time When classes end here at Fairwater Street School, eighth-graders ignore the mall down the street and head straight to a place they consider much cooler: the local natural food grocery store. There they gather in groups of ten or more sometimes, overwhelmed by a marketing atmosphere linking attractiveness with good eating. When it comes time to buy something even as small as a chocolate treat, they feel good to know that a farmer somewhere probably got a good price. Food is something you need to stay alive, says eighth-grader Emma Lewis. Paying farmers well is really important because if we didn't have unprocessed food, everyone married would live on sweets. Moral eating, as it is described, is becoming a priority for teenagers as well as adults in their early 20s. What started a decade ago as a concern on college campuses to eschew clothes produced in factories overseas has spawned a parallel phenomenon in the food and beverage industries. Here, young buyers are leveraging their dollars with the goal of reducing pesticide use, limiting deforestation and making sure farmers aren't left with little on payday. Once again, college campuses are setting the pace. Students at 30 colleges helped persuade administrators to make sure all cafeteria coffee came with a fair trade label, which meant bean pickers in Latin America and Africa received wages higher than current prices. Their counterparts on 300 other campuses are pushing to follow suit, according to the United Students for Fair Trade in Washington, D.C. Coffee is just the beginning. Bon Appetit, an institutional food service provider based in California, relies on organic produce and local produce. Each year since 2001, more than 25 colleges have asked the company to bid on their food service contracts. Although Bon Appetit deliberately limits its growth, its collegial client list has grown from 58 to 71 in the same period. It's really only in the last five years that we've seen college students worried about where their food is coming from, says Maisie Genzler, Bon Appetit's director of strategic initiatives. Before that, students were excited to receive candied cereals. To reach a younger group that often doesn't drink coffee, fair trade importer Equal Exchange gilded our cocoa line in 2003 and chocolate bars in 2004. The gains in both sectors justified the project, says Equal Exchange's co-president, Hove Everts. What's more, dozens of schools have contacted the firm to use its products in fundraising and classroom teaching tools. Children are often the ones who storm the family for recycling and other environmentally friendly practices, says Mr Everts. So, it's a due audience. The concerns of today's young food shoppers seem to reflect in some ways the idealism that inspired earlier generations to join boycotts in solidarity with farm workers. Today's efforts differ in that young consumers say they don't want to make sacrifices. They want quality products and competitive prices that don't require exploiting workers or the environment. They will gladly reward companies that deliver. One activist who shares that sentiment and hears it again and again from her colleagues is Summer Rain Oakes, a college graduate and fashion model who promotes stylish fair trade clothing. 'I'm not going to buy something that can't stand on its own or looks bad just because it's socially responsible, 'says Ms Oakes. My generation came to terms with the fact that everyone was a consumer, and we all buy something. So if I have to buy food, what are the consequences? The desire to improve the world's biggest problems can be frustrating, especially for those who feel ineffective because they are young. Marketers are finding that teens resent this sense of helplessness and are pushing products that make young shoppers feel like they're making a difference, says Michael Wood, vice president of Teenage Research Unlimited. His example: Atos Water from Starbucks, which donates five cents from every bottle sold to water purification centers in developing countries. It is a very easy way for young people to contribute. All they have to do is buy bottled water, says Mr Wood. Buying products or supporting companies that give them ways to support global issues is one way for them to get involved, and they really appreciate it. Convenience also drives consumer activism. Jo Cornu, national coordinator of Students United for Fair Trade, says she first got into trouble about five years ago as a high school student when she spent time hanging out at coffee shops. 'Buying coffee with an eco-friendly label was a very easy way for me to express what I believed in, 'she says. For young teenagers, consumption is their first foray into activism. At Fairweather Street School, Emma Lewis teamed up with classmates Kayla Kleinman and Therese LaRue to sell fair trade chocolate, cocoa and other products at school fundraisers in November. When the amount reached $8,000, they realized they were striking a chord. Some adults are quick to point out the limitations of ethical consumption as a tool for doing good deeds and personal growth. Gary Lindsay, director of Children's Ministries, encourages fair-trade purchases, but he also arranges for children to collect toys for artisan children and save coins for a project to build playgrounds in Tanzania. He says it helps them learn to enjoy helping others even when they don't get anything tangible in return. When do we earn, how much do we really give? Is it really sacrifice? Mr Lindsay is asking for Fair Trade products, he says: These things are great when they've been given opportunities like this every now and then, but I think we expect that we're going to have to derive something from everything we do is a very selfish approach.
hypothesis: Bon Appetit used to sell candied breakfast cereals.

What started a decade ago as a concern on college campuses to eschew clothes produced in factories overseas has spawned a parallel phenomenon in the food and beverage industries. Students at 30 colleges helped persuade administrators to make sure all cafeteria coffee came with a fair trade label, which meant bean pickers in Latin America and Africa received wages higher than current prices. Their counterparts on 300 other campuses are pushing to follow suit, according to the United Students for Fair Trade in Washington, D.C. Coffee is just the beginning. Bon Appetit, an institutional food service provider based in California, relies on organic produce and local produce. Although Bon Appetit deliberately limits its growth, its collegial client list has grown from 58 to 71 in the same period. It's really only in the last five years that we've seen college students worried about where their food is coming from, says Maisie Genzler, Bon Appetit's director of strategic initiatives. Before that, students were excited to receive candied cereals. Today's efforts differ in that young consumers say they don't want to make sacrifices. They want quality products and competitive prices that don't require exploiting workers or the environment. premise: The Australian political scene is dominated by two major parties who have quite different political agendas. However, the policies of the Australian Labor Party and the Liberal Party have become much harder to differentiate in recent years. In fact, it would be correct to say that both parties are made up of conservative, moderate and radical elements, so the general public is often confused which party to vote for. However, it is common to find that an Australian will lean to support either of these two parties and remain loyal to that party for life. The Labour Party was formed in the early twentieth century to protect the interests of the common worker and give trade unions political representation in Parliament. The party has always had strong links with the unions, and it advocates a conception of a welfare society in which people who are less fortunate than others are financially, and otherwise, assist in their quest for a more equitable share of the economic pie. The problem is that such socialist political agendas are extremely expensive to implement and maintain, especially in a country that, although relatively wealthy, is vast and with a small, working population base hence paying taxes. Welfare companies tend to go bankrupt unless government spending is kept under control. The Liberal Party, on the other hand, argues that the best way to ensure the distribution of wealth in the country is to allow more freedom for its creation. This, in turn, means more opportunities, jobs created etc, and therefore more wealth available to everyone. However, the manner in which the poor will participate in this distribution of wealth (beyond being given, at least in theory, the opportunity to create it) is less well understood. Practice, of course, may turn into nonsense even the best theoretical intentions, and often the less politically powerful intentions are handled poorly under governments that implement “free-for-all” policies. It's no wonder that given the two main options offered to them, Australian voters are increasingly turning their attention to the smaller political parties, which claim to offer more balanced policies, often based on one key contemporary issue. So, for example, in the last election there was the No Aircraft Noise Parry, popular in city areas, and the Green Party, which deals almost exclusively with environmental issues.
