premise: The benefits of being bilingual. According to recent data, most of the world's population is now bilingual or multilingual, having grown up speaking two or more languages. Previously, such children were considered at a disadvantage compared to their monolingual peers. However, over the past few decades, technological advances have allowed researchers to examine in depth how bilingualism communicates and alters cognitive and neurological systems, thus identifying some distinct advantages of being bilingual. Studies show that when a bilingual person uses one language, the other is active at the same time. When we hear a word, we don't hear the whole word at once: the sounds come in sequential order. Long before the word is finished, the language system of the brain begins to guess what that word could be. If you hear 'can', you'll likely trigger words like 'candy' and 'candle' as well, at least in the earlier stages of word recognition. For bilingual people, this activation is not limited to a single language; auditory input activates corresponding words regardless of the language to which they belong. Some of the most compelling evidence for this phenomenon, called 'language activation', comes from studying eye movements. A Russian-English bilingual who was asked to “pick up a marker” from a set of objects would look more at a stamp than at someone who does not know Russian, because the Russian word for “stamp,” marka, sounds like the English word he or she heard, 'mark'. In such cases, common language activation occurs because what the listener hears can map words in both languages. However the need to deal with this ongoing linguistic competition can cause difficulties. For example, knowing more than one language can cause speakers to name images more slowly, and can increase the states 'tip of the tongue', when you can almost, but not quite, conjure up a word in the head. As a result, the constant juggling of two languages creates a need to control how well a person accesses the language at any given time. For this reason, bilingual people often perform better in tasks that require conflict management. In the classic Stroop task, people see a word and are asked to name the word's font color. When the color and the word match (i.e., the word 'red' is printed in red), people correctly read the color faster than when the color and the word do not match (i.e., the word 'red' is printed in blue). This happens because the word itself ('red') and its font color (blue) collide. Bilingual individuals often excel at tasks like this, which exploit the ability to ignore competing perceptual information and focus on the relevant aspects of the input. BILINGUALS ARE BETTER AT TRANSITIONING BETWEEN TWO TASKS; FOR EXAMPLE, WHEN BILINGUALS HAVE TO SWITCH FROM CLASSIFYING OBJECTS BY COLOR (RED OR GREEN) TO CLASSIFYING THEM BY SHAPE (CIRCLE OR TRIANGLE), THEY DO SO FASTER THAN MONOLINGUALS, REFLECTING BETTER COGNITIVE CONTROL WHEN THEY NEED TO MAKE RAPID CHANGES IN STRATEGY. It also appears that the neurological roots of bilingual advantage extend to brain regions more traditionally associated with sensory processing. When monolingual and bilingual adolescents listen to simple speech sounds without intervening background noises, they show very similar brainstem responses. When researchers play the same sound to both groups in the presence of background noises, however, the neuronal response of the bilingual listeners is significantly larger, reflecting better encoding of the fundamental frequency of the sound, a feature of sound that is closely related to the perception of pitch of sound. Such improvements in cognitive and sensory processing may help a bilingual person process information in the environment, and help explain why bilingual adults acquire a third language better than monolingual adults master a second language. This advantage may be rooted in the skill to focus on information about the new language while reducing interference from the languages they are already familiar with. Research also suggests that bilingual experience may help maintain the sharpness of cognitive mechanisms by recruiting alternative brain networks to compensate for those damaged during aging. Older bilinguals enjoy improved memory relative to monolingual people, which could lead to real-world health benefits. In a study of more than 200 patients with Alzheimer's disease, a degenerative brain disease, bilingual patients reported showing initial symptoms of the disease an average of five years later than monolingual patients. In a follow-up study, the researchers compared the brains of bilingual and monolingual patients respectively for the severity of Alzheimer's symptoms. Surprisingly, the brains of the bilinguals had more physical signs of disease than their monolingual counterparts, even though their behavior and external abilities were identical. If the brain is an engine, bilingualism may help it go farther on the same amount of fuel. Moreover, it seems that the benefits associated with a bilingual experience begin very early. IN ONE STUDY, RESEARCHERS TAUGHT SEVEN-MONTH-OLD BABIES RAISED IN MONOLINGUAL OR BILINGUAL HOMES THAT WHEN THEY HEARD A TATTOO SOUND, A DOLL APPEARED ON ONE SIDE OF THE SCREEN. In the middle of the study, the doll began to appear on the opposite side of the screen. In order to receive a reward, the infants had to conform to the rule they had learned; only the bilingual infants were able to successfully learn the new rule. This suggests that for very young children, as well as for older people, navigating in a multilingual environment confers benefits that go far beyond language.
hypothesis: Bilingual people consistently read pictures faster than monolingual people.
label: c

premise: The Birth of Scientific English Science The world is now dominated by a small number of languages, including Japanese, German and French, yet English is probably the most popular world science language. This is not just because of the importance of English-speaking countries like the US in scientific research; the scientists of many non-English speaking countries are finding that they need to write their research articles in English to reach a wide international audience. Given the prominence of scientific English today, it may seem surprising that no one actually knew how to write science in English before the 17th century. Before that, Latin was considered the French language1 for European intellectuals. The European Renaissance (14th-16th century or so) is sometimes called the 'revival of learning', a period of renewed interest in the 'lost knowledge' of the classical period. But at the same time, researchers began to test and expand this knowledge. Europe's emerging nation-states have developed competitive interests in world exploration and trade development. Such an expansion, which should take the English language west to America and east to India, was supported by scientific developments such as the discovery of magnetism and hence the invention of the compass improvements in cartography and perhaps the most important scientific revolution of which were all the new theories of astronomy and the movement of the Earth in relation to the planets and stars, developed by Copernicus (1473-1543). England was one of the first countries where scientists enthusiastically embraced and published Copernican ideas. Some of these scholars, including two interested in the language John Wallis and John Wilkins assisted in the founding of the Royal Society in 1660 to promote empirical scientific research. Across Europe, academies and similar societies arose and created new national scientific traditions. In the early stages of the scientific revolution, most publications in national languages were popular works, encyclopedias, educational textbooks, and translations. The original science was not done in English until the second half of the 17th century. For example, Newton published his mathematical treatise, known as the Principia, in Latin, but published his later work on the properties of light opticians in English. There were several reasons why original science continued to be written in Latin. The first was simply a matter of audience. Latin suited an international audience of scholars, while English reached a wider audience socially, but more locally. Hence popular science is written in English. A second reason for writing in Latin may, perversely, be a concern for secrecy. Open publication had dangers in putting initial ideas into the public domain that had not yet been fully exploited by their 'author'. This growing concern with intellectual property rights was a characteristic of the period in which it reflected both the humanistic notion of the individual, the rational scientist who invents and discovers through private intellectual work, and the growing connection between original science and commercial exploitation. There was a social distinction between 'scholars and gentlemens' who understood Latin, and tradesmen who lacked classical education. And in the middle of the 17th century it was common for mathematicians to keep their discoveries and proofs secret, by writing them in ciphers, in obscure languages, or in private messages deposited in a sealed box with the Royal Society. Some scientists may have felt more comfortable with Latin precisely because its audience, though international, was socially limited. Doctors most strongly held on to Latin as an “inner language.” A third reason why the writing of original science in English was delayed may have to do with the linguistic inadequacy of English in the early modern period. The English were not well equipped to handle scientific arguments. First there was a lack of the necessary technical vocabulary. Second, it lacks the grammatical resources required to represent the world in an objective and impersonal way, and to discuss the relationships, such as cause and effect, that may hold between complex and hypothetical entities. Fortunately, several members of the Royal Society had an interest in the language and were engaged in various linguistic projects. Although a proposal in 1664 to establish a committee for the improvement of the English language came in exception, members of the society did much to foster the publication of science in English and to encourage the development of an appropriate writing style. Many members of the Royal Society also published monographs in English. One of the first was by Robert Hook, the Society's first curator of experiments, who described his experiments with microscopes in micrography (1665). This piece is largely narrative in style, based on a transcript of oral demos and lectures. In 1665 a new scientific journal, Philosophical Transactions, was inaugurated. Possibly the first English-language international scientific journal, it encouraged a new genre of scientific writing, that of short, focused descriptions of particular experiments. The 17th century was therefore a formative period in the establishment of scientific English. In the following century, much of this momentum was lost as German established itself as the leading European language of science. It is estimated that by the end of the 18th century 401 German scientific journals had been established compared to 96 in France and 50 in England. However, in the 19th century Scientific English again enjoyed significant lexical growth as the Industrial Revolution created the need for a new technical vocabulary, and new, specialized, professional societies were established to promote and publish in the new disciplines.
hypothesis: The most important scientific development of the Renaissance period was the discovery of magnetism.

premise: The concept of childhood in Western countries The history of childhood has been a turbulent topic in social history since the most influential book Hundreds of Childhood, written by the French historian Philippe Tele, appeared in 1960. He argued that childhood is a concept created by modern society. Whether childhood is itself a recent invention has been one of the most debated issues in childhood history. Historian Philip Aries argued that children were considered miniature adults, with all the intellect and personality that implies, in Western Europe during the Middle Ages (until about the end of the 15th century). After reviewing photographs and diaries from the Middle Ages, he concluded that there was no distinction between children and adults because they share similar leisure and work activities; however, this does not mean that children have been neglected, abandoned or despised, he argued. The idea of childhood corresponds to the awareness of the peculiar nature of childhood, which distinguishes the child from the adult, even the young adult. Therefore, the concept of childhood should not be confused with affection for children. Traditionally, children have played a functional role in contributing to family income in history. In these circumstances, children were considered beneficial. Back in the Middle Ages, 5- or 6-year-olds did necessary chores for their parents. During the 16th century, 9- or 10-year-olds were often encouraged or even forced to leave their family to work as servants for wealthier families or trade apprentices. In the 18th and 19th centuries, industrialization created a new demand for child labor; therefore many children had to work for a long time in mines, workshops and factories. The question of whether long working hours would interfere with the growing bodies of children began to confuse social reformers. Some have begun to understand the potential of systematic studies to monitor how much these early savings might affect children's development. The concerns of the reformers gradually affected the working condition of children. For example, in the United Kingdom, the Factory Act of 1833 marked the emergence of legal protection of children from exploitation and was also associated with the rise of schools for factory children. Due partly to factory reform, the worst forms of child exploitation were gradually eliminated. The influence of trade unions and economic changes also contributed to development by leaving certain forms of child labor unnecessary during the 19th century. Initiating children to work as useful children was no longer a priority, and childhood was considered a time for play and education for all children instead of a privileged minority. Childhood was increasingly understood as a more extended stage of dependency, development, and learning with the age delay to the start of full-time work - nevertheless, work continued to play a significant, if less vital, role in children's lives in the late 19th and 20th centuries. Finally, the useful child has become a controversial concept during the first decade of the 21st century, especially in the context of worldwide concern from the large number of children engaged in child labor. The half-time schools established under the 1833 Factory Act allowed children to work and attend school. However, a significant proportion of children never attended school in the 1840s, and even if they did, they dropped out by the age of 10 or 11. At the end of the 19th century in Britain the situation changed dramatically, and schools became the core of the concept of ordinary childhood. It is no longer a right for children to attend school and all children are expected to spend a substantial part of their day in the classroom. After arriving at school, children's lives could be separated from home life and the adult world of work. In this way, the school becomes an institution dedicated to shaping the minds, behaviors and morals of the young. Besides, education dominated the management of children's waking hours through hours spent in the classroom, homework (growth of after-school activities) and the importance attributed to parental involvement. Industrialisation, urbanisation and mass education pose new challenges to those responsible for protecting children's welfare as well as promoting their learning. An increasing number of children are treated as a group with unique needs, and are organized into groups in light of their age. For example, teachers need to know some information about what to expect from children in their classes, what types of instruction are appropriate for different age groups and what is the best way to assess children's progress. Also, they want tools that allow them to sort and select children according to their abilities and potential.
hypothesis: In the 20th century, almost all children had to go to school with a full-time schedule.

premise: The Myth of Creativity It is a myth that creative people are born with their talents: gifts from God or nature. Creative genius, in fact, is latent within many of us, without us realizing it. But how far do we have to travel to find the way to creativity? For many people, a long way. In our daily lives, we have to perform many actions out of habit to survive, such as opening the door, shaving, getting dressed, going to work and so on. If this were not the case, we would most likely become mentally desensitized. So ingrained are our habits, though this varies from person to person, that sometimes when a conscious effort is made to be creative, an automatic response takes over. We may try, for example, to go to work in a different route, but end up in our usual way. By then it's too late to go back and change our minds. Another day, maybe. The same goes for all other areas of our lives. When we solve problems, for example, we may look for different answers, but we often find ourselves walking the same well-trodden paths. Therefore, for many people, their actions and behavior are located in inalienable lumps, their brains clogged with the cholesterol of normal actions, preventing them from acting freely, thereby strangling creation. Unfortunately, the struggle for survival of humans has become a tyranny and the obsessive desire to give order to the world is an example of this. Witness people's attitude to time, social mores, and the multitude of rules and regulations by which the human mind is now limited. The basis for maintaining creative ability begins at school. School, later university then work, teach us to regulate our lives, imposing a continuous process of restrictions that grows exponentially with the advancement of technology. Is it surprising then that creative ability seems so rare? He's trapped in a prison we set up. However, even here in this hostile environment, the foundations for creativity are laid; because embarking on the creative path is also in part the use of laws and regulations. Such restrictions are needed so that once they are learned, they can be broken. The truly creative mind is often perceived as completely free and uninhibited. But a better image is that of a mind, which can be free whenever it wants, and one that recognizes that rules and regulations are parameters, or barriers, that must be raised and knocked down again at will. An example of how the human mind can be trained to be creative might help here. People's brains are just like tense muscles that need to loosen them up and unlock potential. One strategy is the erection of artificial barriers or obstacles in solving a problem. As a form of stimulation, participants in a task can be forbidden to use certain solutions or follow certain lines of thought to solve a problem. In this way, they are committed to exploring unfamiliar territory, which could lead to some amazing discoveries. Unfortunately, the difficulty with this exercise, and with creation itself, is convincing people that creation is possible, shrouded as it is in so many myths and legends. There is also an element of fear involved, subliminal as it may be, since deviating from the security of thought patterns is very similar to madness. But, open Pandora's box and a whole new world will unfold before your eyes. Lifting barriers into place also plays a major role in helping the brain control ideas instead of letting them randomly collide. Parameters serve as containers for ideas and thus help the brain to correct them. When the brain thinks laterally and two ideas from different areas of the brain come or come together, they form a new idea, much like atoms that float around and then form a molecule. Once the idea is formed, it must be contained or it will fly away, so fleeting is its passage. The brain has to hold it in place for a while so it can recognize it or read it again. Then the parameters can serve as channels along which ideas can flow, develop and expand. When the mind has brought the idea to fruition by thinking it through to its conclusion, the parameters can be lowered and the idea can be allowed to float and come into contact with other ideas.
hypothesis: The act of creation is associated with madness.
label: e

Bakelite was a good insulator and was resistant to water, acids and moderate heat. When cooled with liquid nitrogen at 196° C (high temperature compared to other superconductors), this material loses all its electrical resistance, and can levitate (lift) in a magnetic field. Instead, GR sees gravity as a distortion in the fabric of space and time, which permeates the entire cosmos. As such, any claim to protecting objects from gravity is to defy Einstein himself. Although the average IQ is by definition 100, IQ scores have risen by one standard deviation (15-16 points) per generation. Therefore, if new test participants take an older version of the test, the average score will be higher than 100. Many theories attempt to explain the Flynn effect, which include dietary changes, improvements in education, and the increasingly stimulating environments in which we all live.

premise: The forgotten forest found only in America's Deep South, longleaf pine forests have been reduced to about 3 percent of their former range, but new efforts are being made to restore them. The beauty and biodiversity of the long pine forest are well-kept secrets, even in his native south. However, it is among the richest ecosystems in North America, rivaling tall grass prairies and the ancient forests of the Pacific Northwest in the number of species it harbors. And like the other two disappearing wildlife habitats, Longleaf is also critically endangered. In long-leaved pine forests, growing trees are widely scattered, creating a park-like open environment, more like savanna than forest. The trees are not as dense as to block the sun. This openness creates a forest floor that is among the most diverse in the world, where plants such as many floral grass roses, trumpet pitcher plants, Venus fly traps, lavender ladies and pine egg buttons grow. Up to 50 different species of wildflowers, shrubs, grasses and ferns have been catalogued in just one square metre. Nearly 92 million acres of long-leaved forest once flourished from Virginia to Texas, the only place in the world where it is found. However, by the beginning of the 2nd century, almost all of it was written, paved or farmed into oblivion. Only about 3 percent of the original range still supports long-leaved forest, and only about 10,000 acres of it are old uncut growth, the remainder being forest that has regrown after felling. According to estimates, 100,000 of these acres are still disappearing every year. However, a quiet movement to alleviate this trend is winding down across the region. Governments, private organizations (including the NWF) and individual conservationists are looking for ways to protect and preserve the remaining long leaves and to plant new forests for future generations. Understanding how to restore pine forests will also allow biologists to help the plants and animals that depend on this habitat. Nearly two-thirds of the declining, threatened, or endangered species in the southeastern United States are associated with long leaves. Longleaf's total destruction is only part of their story, says Mark Danaher, biologist for the Francis Marion National Forest in South Carolina. He said the deaths of these animals and plants were also linked to the lack of fire, which once swept through southern forests on a regular basis. Fire is absolutely critical for this ecosystem and the species that depend on it, Danaher says. Name almost every species that appears on Longleaf and you can find a connection to fire. The Bachmans sparrow is a secretive bird with a beautiful song echoing across the long flat trees. It sticks its nest on the ground beneath clumps of barbed wire and small blue grass on the open lower floor. But as soon as the fire has been absent for several years, and thickets of bushes begin to grow, the sparrows disappear. Gopher tortoises, the only land deer east of the Mississippi, are also abundant in long leaves. A keystone species for these forests, its burrows provide homes and safety for more than 300 species of vertebrates and invertebrates, ranging from diamond-backed eastern rattlesnakes to gopher frogs. If the fire is suppressed, however, the turtles suffocate. If we lose fire, says Bob Mitchell, an ecologist at the Jones Center, we lose wildlife. Without fire, we also lose long leaves. Fire knocks down oaks and other hardwood trees that can grow and flood long forests. They're firewoods, Mitchell says. They developed in the lightning capital of the eastern United States. And not only lightning strikes set fire to the forest. Native Americans also lit bonfires to keep the forest open, Mitchell says. So did the early pioneers. They helped create the long pine forests we know today. Fire is also changing how nutrients flow in long-leaved ecosystems, in ways we are only beginning to understand. For example, researchers have discovered that frequent fires provide extra calcium, which is critical for egg production, to endangered red woodpeckers. Frances James, a retired avian ecologist from Florida State University, has studied the small black-and-white birds for more than two decades in Florida's sprawling Apalachicola National Forest. Realizing that female woodpeckers laid larger clutches in the first breeding season after their territories burned, she and her colleagues went looking for answers. 'We've learned that calcium is hidden in woody shrubs when the forest isn't burning, 'says James. But when there's a fire, a pulse of calcium moves down into the soil and up into the long leaf. Eventually, this calcium makes its way up the food chain to an ant species that dwells in trees, which is the favorite food of red cockatoos. The result: more calcium for birds, leading to more eggs, more young and more woodpeckers. Today, fire serves as an essential management tool for the preservation of its long-leaved and wildlife. Most of these fires are prescribed burns, deliberately set with a drip torch. Although the public is often opposed to any type of fire and the accompanying smoke with it these frequent low-intensity burns reduce the risk of catastrophic flare-ups. Forests are going to be burned, says Amadou Diop, NWFs southern forest restoration manager. It's just a question of when. With prescribed burns, we can choose the time and place. Diop heads a new effort by the NWF to restore Longleaf. It's a species we need to get back to, he says. Educating landowners about the benefits of growing long leaves is part of the plan, he adds, which will start soon in nine Southern states. Right now, most of the long leaves are on public lands, says Jerry McCollum, president of the Georgia Wildlife Federation. Private land is where we need to work, he adds, noting that more than 90 percent of the area in the historical range of long leaves falls in this category. Interest among private landowners is growing throughout the South, but restoring long leaves is not an easy task. The herbaceous layer, the understory of wire grasses and other plants must be recreated. In areas where the land has not been chewed up by agriculture, but has been converted into loblolly or cut pine plantations, the seed bank of the long leaf forest generally remains viable underground. Over time, this original vegetation can be coaxed back. Where agriculture has destroyed the seeds, however, the wire weed must be replanted. Currently, the expenditure is prohibitive, but researchers are looking for low-cost solutions. However, the return of long leaves is not intended for myopia. Few of us will be alive when the pines planted today become mature forests in 70 to 80 years. But this does not stop lovers of long leaves. Today, it is difficult to find long seedlings for purchase, says one of the private landowners. Everyone wants them. Longleaf is in regeneration.
hypothesis: Few can live to see the replanted forest reach maturity.
label: e

premise: The future of fish across the ocean has changed completely since the first commercial fishermen cast the nets of hooks over a thousand years ago. Fishing intensified with the centuries, but even in the nineteenth century it was still felt, rightly, that the abundant sea resources were often beyond the reach of fisheries, so there was no need to restrict fishing or create protected areas. The twentieth century heralded an escalation in fishing intensity unprecedented in the history of the oceans, and modern fishing technologies leave fish nowhere to hide. Today, the only sanctuaries from fishing are the ones we deliberately create. Unfortunately, the sea passes far behind the land in terms of terrain and the quality of protection provided. For centuries, as fishing and commerce expanded, we held to the idea that the sea was different from land. We still see it as a place where people and nations should be free to come and go as they please, as well as a place that should be free for us to exploit. Perhaps this is why we are so reluctant to defend the sea. On land, protected areas proliferated as human populations increased. Here, compared to the sea, we have made more progress in our struggle to preserve the richness and diversity of wildlife and landscapes. 12% of the world's land is now in protected areas, while the corresponding figure for the sea is only three-fifths of one percent. Worse, most marine protected areas allow for continued fishing. Areas that are not limited to any exploitation cover something like five thousand of the total area of the global sea. Today we belatedly realize that natural refuges from fisheries have played a critical role in sustaining fisheries and maintaining healthy and diverse marine ecosystems. This does not mean marine reserves can rebuild fisheries on their own and other management measures are also needed for this. However, places that are not restricted to fishing form the final and most important part of our fisheries management reform package. They underpin and enhance all of our other efforts. But there are limits to the defense. Reserves cannot recover what is dead. We will never be able to revive extinct species worldwide, and rehabilitating locally extinct animals may require reintroduction from other locations, if natural dispersal from the remaining populations is insufficient. We also see, in cases such as the northern cod in Canada, that fisheries can shift marine ecosystems to different countries, where different mixtures of species prevail. In many cases, these species are less desirable, as the main fisheries have gone or are much reduced in number, and changes may be difficult to undo, even with a complete moratorium on the fishery. The Mediterranean Sea sailed by Ulysses, the legendary king of ancient Greece, supported abundant monastic seals, numerous wood turtles. Their disappearance through hunting and overfishing has completely rebuilt the food webs, and recovery is likely to be much harder to achieve than their extermination. This means that the sooner we act to protect marine life, the more certain our success will be. For some people, creating marine reserves is an admission of failure. According to their logic, reserves should not be necessary if we have done our job properly in managing the uses we make of the sea. Many fisheries managers are still wedded to the idea that one day their models will work, and politicians will listen to their advice. Just give the approach time, and success will be theirs. How much time do we have? This approach has been tried and refined over the past 50 years. There have been few successes that have brought the executives' hats off, but a growing litany of failure. The Common Fisheries Policy, an EU instrument for managing fisheries and aquaculture, exemplifies the worst pitfalls: flawed models, flawed advice, ill-advised recommendations from government bureaucrats and then the disregard of much of that advice by politicians. When it all went wrong, as it inevitably should have, Europe sent its boats to other countries to obtain fish for far less than they were actually worth. We are squandering the wealth of the oceans. If we don't break out of this cycle of failure, humanity will lose a major source of protein, and much beyond. Disrupting natural ecosystem processes, such as water purification, nutrient cycling and carbon storage, could have consequences for human life itself. We can go a long way to avoid this catastrophic mistake of simply managing common sense. Marine reserves are at the heart of the reform. But they would not be enough if they were applied only here and there to reinforce the crumbling structure of rational fisheries management that scientists predicted in the Forties and Fifties. They should be placed centre stage as a fundamental basis for everything we do in the oceans. Reserves are a first resort, not a last resort when all else fails.

The fence is the Australian version of the Chinese Wall, but even longer, erected to keep out hostile intruders, in this case hordes of yellow dogs. The empire she guards is that of wool growers, the world's second-largest sheep herd sovereigns, after about 123 million heads and keepers of China's four billion dollar wool export business. Never mind that more and more conservationists, politicians, taxpayers and animal lovers say that such a barrier would never be possible today on ecological grounds. With parts of it almost a century old, the dog fence has become, as conservationist Lindsay Fairweather admits, an icon of the ingenuity of the Australian frontier. To appreciate this extraordinary outback monument and meet the people whose livelihoods depend on it, I spent part of an Australian autumn travelling the wire. It is known by various names in different states: the dog fence in South Australia, the border fence in New South Wales and the barrier fence in Queensland. I would call it simply the fence. For most of its stunning length, this epic fence winds like a river across a landscape, unless it rains heavily, there are hardly any rivers. The eccentric route, determined mostly by property lines, provides a sampling of Outback topography: the fence runs over sand dunes, across salt lakes, up and down rock-strewn hills, through dense bushes and across barren plains. This marks the traditional line of separation between cattle and sheep. Inside, where the dingoes are legally classified as vermin, they are horned, poisoned and trapped. The adaptable dingo spread quickly and in a short time became the top predator, killing all of its marsupial competitors. Standing about 22 centimetres at the shoulder slightly higher than a coyote wildebeest, the dingo is Australia's largest land predator. The wool growers' war against the dingo, similar to the sheep rancher rage against coyotes in the US, began not long after the first European settlers came down in 1788 and brought a cargo of sheep with them. Dingoes officially became outlaws in the 1830s when governments placed a bounty on their tadpoles. Today the prizes for problem dogs that kill sheep inside the fence can reach $500. As pioneers penetrated the interior with their flocks of sheep, fences replaced the shepherds until at the end of the 19th century thousands of miles of barrier fencing crisscrossed the vast grasslands. It is estimated that since the sheep arrived in Australia, the number of dingoes has increased a hundredfold. Although dingoes have been exterminated from parts of Australia, an educated guess puts the population at more than a million. This marks the difference between profit and loss. But the fence casts a much wider ecological shadow because it has become a kind of land dam, diverting the flow of animals inside and out. For Sturt and other early explorers, it was a rare occurrence to see kangaroos. Now they are everywhere because without a local predator the kangaroo population has exploded inside the fence. Kangaroos are now cursed more than dingoes. They became rivals of sheep, competing for water and grass. Park officials, who recognize that the fence is to blame, respond to the kangaroo surplus by saying the fence exists, and we must live with it.

premise: The history of glass From our earliest origins, man made use of glass. Historians have discovered that a type of natural glass - obsidian - formed in places like the mouth of a volcano as a result of the intense heat of a melting sand eruption - was first used as tips for spears. Archaeologists even found evidence of man-made glass dating back to 4000 BC; it took the form of glazes used to coat stone beads. It was not until 1500 BC, however, that the first hollow glass container was created by covering a sand core with a layer of molten glass. Glass blowing became the most common way of making glass containers from the 1st century BC. The glass made during this period was highly colored due to the impurities of the raw material. In the 1st century AD, methods were developed to create colorless glass, which was then minted by the addition of coloring materials. The secret of glass production was taken throughout Europe by the Romans during this century. However, they retained the skills and technology required to make glass closely, and it was only after their empire collapsed in 476 AD that knowledge of glassmaking spread throughout Europe and the Middle East. From the 10th century onwards, the Venetians gained a reputation for technical skill and artistic ability in glass bottle making, and many of the craftsmen in the city left Italy to set up glass factories across Europe. A major milestone in the history of glass occurred with the invention of lead crystal glass by the English glassmaker George Ravenscroft (1632-1683). He attempted to counter the branching effect that sometimes occurred in blown glass by introducing lead into the raw materials used in the process. The new glass he created was softer and easier to decorate, and had a higher refractive index, which added to its luster and beauty, and it proved invaluable to the optical industry. Thanks to Ravenscroft's invention, optical lenses, astronomical telescopes, microscopes, and the like were made possible. In Britain, the modern glass industry began to develop only after the repeal of the Excise Act in 1845. Prior to that time, heavy taxes were imposed on the amount of glass melted in the greenhouse, and were levied continuously from 1745 to 1845. Joseph Paxton's Crystal Palace at the Great Exhibition in London of 1851 marked the beginning of glass as a material used in the building industry. This revolutionary new building encouraged the use of glass in public, domestic and horticultural architecture. Glass manufacturing techniques have also improved with the advancement of science and the development of better technology. From 1887 onwards, glass production evolved from the traditional mouth-blowing to a semi-automatic process, after factory owner HM Ashley introduced a machine capable of producing 200 bottles per hour in Castleford, Yorkshire, England - three times faster than any previous manufacturing method. Then in 1907, the first vending machine in the US was developed by Michael Evans - founder of the Owens Bottling Machine Company (later the major manufacturers Evans-Illinois) - and installed in its factory. Evans' invention can produce an impressive 2,500 bottles an hour. Other developments came quickly, but it was not until World War I, when Britain was cut off from vital glass suppliers, that glass became part of the scientific sector. Before that, glass was seen as a craft rather than an exact science. Today, glass production is a big business. It has become a modern high-tech industry operating in a highly competitive global marketplace where quality, design and service levels are critical to maintaining market share. Modern glass plants are capable of producing millions of glass containers a day in many different colors, with green, brown and clear remaining the most popular. Few of us can imagine modern life without glass. It appears in almost every aspect of our lives - in our homes, in our cars and whenever we sit down to eat or drink. Glass packaging is used for many products, many drinks are sold in glass, as well as many food products, as well as medicines and cosmetics. Glass is an ideal material for recycling, and with consumers' growing concern for green issues, glass bottles and jars are becoming increasingly popular. Glass recycling is good news for the environment. This saves used glass containers that are sent to landfill. Since less energy is required to melt recycled glass than to melt raw materials, this also saves fuel and production costs. Recycling also reduces the need for quarrying raw materials and thus saves precious resources.
hypothesis: Concern for the environment leads to increased demand for glass containers.

In addition to its historical interest, testing the studio system growth may offer clues as to the types of struggles that accompany the growth of any new medium. In fact, it may be intriguing to examine what changes occurred during the Hollywood studio's growth, and compare those changes to contemporary struggles in which production companies are trying to define and dominate emerging industries, such as online film and interactive television. The industry's transition away from silent films began in the late 1920s. The 1927 Warner Bros. film “The Jazz Singer” was the first to feature synchronized speech, and with it came a period of industry turmoil. Studios now had proof that talkie films would make them money, but the financial investment that would require making these types of films, from new camera equipment to new screening facilities, made studios hesitant to invest at first. Ultimately, the power of cinematic sound to move audiences and also enhance story convinced studios that it was worth investing in flicks. Overall, the use of sound in cinema was well received by the audience, but there were still many technical factors to consider. Although the full integration of sound in the films was completed by 1930, it would take them a little longer to regain their elegance and stylistic skill. Now the camera had to be wrapped in a large, bulky and non-movable soundproof box. In addition, the actors struggled, having to direct their speech to microphones awkwardly hidden in giant plants, telephones or even costumes. Vertical integration is the other key element in the rise of the Hollywood studio system. The major studios realized they could increase their profits by handling every stage of film life: production (making the film), distribution (getting the film out to people), and exhibition (owning the cinemas in the major cities where first films were shown). Five studios, the Big Five, operated to achieve vertical integration in the late 1940s, owned vast real estate on which elaborate sets could be built. In addition, these studios determine the exact terms of film release dates and patterns. Warner Bros., Paramount, 20th Century Fox, MGM and RKO formed this exclusive club. The three small studios Universal, Columbia and United Artists also created pictures, but each lacked one of the crucial elements of vertical integration. Together, these eight companies acted as a mature oligopoly, essentially running the entire market. During the Golden Age, studios were remarkably consistent and stable enterprises, largely due to long-serving management chiefs of notorious film moguls who ruled their kingdoms with iron fists. At MGM, Warner Bros. and Columbia, the same men ran their studios for decades. The rise of the studio system also depended on treating the stars, which were built and utilized to suit the studios' image and schedule. On the other hand, studios have had to cultivate flexibility, in addition to consistent factory output. Examining how each production company tried to differentiate itself led to loose characterizations of individual studios' styles. In 1948, independent film producers and exhibitors finally won their fight against the monopolistic behavior of the major studios. In the United States versus Paramount's federal decree from that year, studios were ordered to give up their theaters in what is commonly referred to as an eviction that opens the market to smaller producers. When the Bretton Woods fixed rate regime ended in 1971, economists imagined that a new era of freely floating exchange rates would keep imports and exports in roughly balance, thus eliminating large trade deficits and the need to borrow abroad to cover them. Whatever the description, it stems from what should be considered the most unique fruit on the planet - durian, a Southeast Asian favorite, commonly called the king of fruits. Its title, in many ways, is deserved. As the fruit goes, it's huge and impressive. The spikes are so sharp that even holding the massive object is difficult. This leads to wonder why nature designed such a smelly fruit in such uncomfortable packaging. Nature, on the other hand, is smarter than one might think. For starters, that pungent smell allows easier identification by animals in the thick tropical forests of Brunei, Indonesia and Malaysia, where the wild durian originates. When the pod falls, and the bark begins to crack, wild deer, pigs, orangutans and elephants are easily pulled out, navigating from hundreds of feet away directly to the tree. The second wise fact is that because the internal seeds are quite large, the durian tree needs correspondingly larger animals to eat, swallow and transport these seeds away, hence the use of this tough spiny cover. Only the largest and strongest animals can get through it. And what are they looking for? Upon opening the large pod, one is shown in one of white fibrous gravel in which lie pockets of soft yellowish flesh, divided into lobes. Each lobe holds a large brown seed inside it. Although these seeds themselves can be cooked and eaten, this is the surrounding meat on which all the fuss is created. One of the best descriptions comes from the British naturalist, Alfred Wallace. His experience, written in 1856, is typical of many, and certainly mine. At first he struggled hard to overcome the unpleasant aroma, but after eating it outside the doors he discovered that the meat has a rich sticky smoothness, neither acidic nor sweet nor juicy; and yet he does not want any of these qualities, since it is in itself perfect. He immediately became a happy Dorian foodie. Exactly! In fact, the taste can vary considerably depending on the stage of ripeness and storage methods. In southern Thailand, the people prefer younger durian, with a firmer texture and milder flavor, while in Malaysia, the preference is to allow the durian to naturally fall off the tree, then ripen further during transportation. The result is a buttery texture and a very individual aroma, often slightly fermented. Whatever the case, it is this soft creamy consistency that easily allows durian to blend in with other Southeast Asian delicacies, from sweets and cakes, to modern milkshakes and ice cream. It can also appear in meals, mixed with vegetables or chilli, and lower-grade durian (otherwise unsuitable for human consumption) fermented into a pulp, used in a variety of local rice dishes. The market is mainly other Asian countries, although interest is growing in the West because Asian immigrants take their tastes and eating preferences with them, for example, in Canada and Australia. The fruit is seasonal and local, the sale of durian pods is usually done by weight. These can fetch high prices, especially in the more affluent Asian countries, and especially when you consider that less than a third of that heavy backpack contains the edible pulp. In the true spirit of Alfred Wallace, there are certainly a large and growing number of happy Dorian eaters out there.

premise: The Kyoto Protocol is an international agreement written by the United Nations with the aim of reducing the effects of climate change. This agreement sets targets for countries in order to be able to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions. These gases are believed to be responsible for causing global warming as a result of recent industrialization. The protocol was written in 1997 and each country that signed the protocol agreed to reduce their emissions to its specific target. This agreement could only be legally binding when two conditions were met: when 55 countries agreed to be legally bound by the treaty and when 55% of emissions from industrialized countries were accounted for. The first condition was met in 2002 however countries such as Australia and the United States refused to be bound by the agreement so the minimum of 55% of emissions from industrialized countries was not met. Only after Russia joined in 2004 did it allow the protocol to come into force in 2005. Some climate scientists have argued that the combined target of a 5.2% reduction in emissions from industrialized countries will not be enough to avoid the worst consequences of global warming. In order for us to have a meaningful impact, we will need to strive to reduce emissions by 60% and get larger countries like the US to support the agreement.
hypothesis: Greenhouse gas emissions from Australia and the United States represent 45% of emissions from industrialized countries.
label: c

premise: Lack of sleep It is estimated that the average man or woman needs between seven and a half to eight hours of sleep a night. Some can get by on a lot less. Baroness Thatcher, for example, reportedly managed to get by on four hours of sleep a night when she was Prime Minister of the United Kingdom. Dr Jill Wilkinson, senior lecturer in psychology at the University of Surrey and co-author of Psychology in Counselling and Therapeutic Practice, states that healthy people who sleep less than five hours or even two hours every 24 hours are rare, but represent a considerable minority. Recent beliefs are that the main purposes of sleep are to allow the body to rest and regenerate, allowing time for repairs and tissue regeneration. One supporting evidence for this theory of rest and repair is that the production of the growth hormone somatotropin, which helps tissues regenerate, peaks while we sleep. Lack of sleep, on the other hand, can damage the immune system, confuse thinking, cause depression, promote anxiety and encourage irritability. Researchers in San Diego deprived a group of men of sleeping between Sam and Lam on just one night, and found that their body's natural levels of protection against viral infections dropped significantly when measured the next morning. Sleep is essential for our physical and emotional well-being and there are few aspects of everyday life that are not disturbed by the lack of it, says Professor William Ragelson of the University of Virginia, an expert on insomnia. Because it can seriously undermine the functioning of the immune system, sufferers are vulnerable to infection. For many people, lack of sleep is rarely a matter of choice. Some have trouble falling asleep, others stay asleep until morning. Despite the popular belief that sleep is one long event, studies show that on an average night there are five sleep phases and four cycles, during which the sequence of phases repeats. In the first light phase, the heart rate and blood pressure decrease and the muscles relax. In the next two stages, sleep becomes deeper and deeper. In the fourth stage, usually coming after an hour, sleep is so deep that if awakened, the sleeper would be confused and confused. At this time, sleepwalking can occur, with an average episode lasting no more than 15 minutes. In the fifth stage, the rapid eye movement (REM) phase, the heartbeat quickly returns to normal levels, brain activity accelerates to daytime elevations and above and the eyes continually move under closed eyelids as if the sleeper is looking at something. At this time, the body is almost paralyzed. This REM phase is also the time when we dream. Sleep patterns change with age, which is why many people over 60 develop insomnia. In America, this age group consumes almost half of the sleep drugs available on the market. One theory for age-related change is that it is due to hormonal changes. Temperature General training: the increase in reading and writing occurs at dawn in the young, but at three or four in the morning in the elderly. Apart from age, it is estimated that about one in three people suffers from some kind of sleep disorder. The causes can be anything from pregnancy and stress to alcohol and heart disease. Smoking is a well-known sleep disability, with one survey showing that former smokers got to sleep in 18 minutes instead of their previous average of 52 minutes. Besides self-help therapy such as regular exercise, there are psychological treatments, including relaxation training and therapy aimed at getting rid of worries and anxieties before going to bed. There is also sleep reduction therapy, where the goal is to improve sleep quality by strictly regulating the time people go to bed and when they get up. Drugs are considered by many to be a last resort and often take the form of sleeping pills, usually benzodiazepines, which are mild sedatives. Professor Ragelson advocates the use of melatonin to treat sleep disorders. Melatonin is a hormone secreted naturally, located in the pineal gland deep within the brain. The main function of the hormone is to control the body's biological clock, so we know when to sleep and when to wake up. The gland detects light reaching it through the eye; when there is no light, it secretes melatonin into the bloodstream, lowering body temperature and helping induce sleep. Melatonin pills contain a synthetic version of the hormone and are commonly used for jet lag as well as for sleep disorders. John Nichols, a sales manager for one of America's largest healthy food stores, claims that pill sales have increased dramatically. He explains that it is sold in capsules, tablets, candies and mixed with herbs. It is not effective for all insomnia sufferers, but many users have rewarded themselves with sleeping tablets as a result of its application.

premise: The language revolution in the next decade will likely mean the new must-learn language will be Mandarin, said language researcher David Gardall, in the latest issue of the journal Science. He echoed an opinion expressed by academics and businesspeople across the Western world. English speakers did it pretty well. Modern English is the most widely studied and understood language in the world. It is the dominant international language in media, science, business, aviation, entertainment, diplomacy and the Internet. About 400-500 million people speak it as their first language and up to 1.5 billion people have basic English proficiency. Mother tongue There were of course other languages that made suggestions about the language crown. The competing world languages included, at different times and in different regions, Neo-Latin, French, Russian, Chinese, Arabic, Sanskrit, Hindu-Urdu, and Malay. Today, Mandarin Chinese, the official language of China, is the one to watch. And while the global share of English is clearly still huge, the number of native speakers is far greater than the number of those who speak Mandarin as their first language: an estimated 867 million. The sheer size of China's population and the country's growing importance in the global economy and politics partly account for its status. We also see the proliferation, for example, of government-sponsored Confucius Institutes conducting courses in Chinese and Chinese culture in many locations outside China, reflecting the increased power and security in the country. Education, too, is beginning to reflect the growing importance of the language, particularly in the US where about 24,000 young people are already learning Mandarin. When the government set up a $114 million initiative to increase the teaching of critical languages in U.S. schools, that number seemed likely to rise dramatically. And people recognize the practical benefits and role of the Chinese in business. In particular, businesses are interested in employing people who can speak Mandarin, but are not necessarily Chinese, although even those working in China can still get away with only limited knowledge of the language. Nick Harrison, a British banker based in Shanghai, has experience in the field who moved there in December 2005. Our business discussions are all in English, and the vast majority of the office management is written and spoken in Chinese. Learning the language Learning Mandarin is a big challenge. Usually we say that it takes three years of full-time study to gain on-the-job knowledge of Chinese, including knowledge of the script. If you just want to talk it out, it probably takes one year, says Michelle Hawkes, a professor at the London School of African and Eastern Studies. Maybe if we start learning at an earlier age, we might learn faster, but if you start in your early twenties, it takes a lot longer. Nick Harrison's experiences support this theory. 'I certainly don't speak Mandarin, but I have classes once a week, 'he says. My two-year-old daughter, Claudia, is progressing well and is destined to be my translator in the future.

premise: The world's most dangerous insect If asked to name the world's deadliest insect, most people would search their minds for some evil-looking spiders or scorpions, or exotic pests in the garden. However, if we define lethal in terms of the number of people who die directly as a result of the insect, one of them leads the field, without a doubt: the mosquito. As a blood-sucking pest, it transmits disease to more than 700 million people a year, killing a good proportion of them in the process. No other insect comes close to that. Although all mosquitoes are nectar feeders, females also need protein from a blood meal in order to produce eggs. To find this, they have a keen sense of smell, which detects the sweat and other organic compounds of mammals, such as the carbon dioxide they exhale. Scientific testing has proven that some people attract more mosquitoes than others, apparently having a better scent profile in fact, so adept are female mosquitoes at tracking these trails, they can penetrate buildings through air conditioning hoses and ducts as they continually move toward their victims. With the bite, they inject anticoagulant saliva into the flesh, and it is this liquid (and not their blood) that may contain the variety of viral and parasitic evils for which mosquitoes are notorious. However, even without such diseases, mosquitoes are an annoying nuisance that can occasionally cause serious injury. With the bite, the body's immune system is activated, and subsequent bites provoke antibodies that cause inflammation and itching, especially in young children. Additional bites can increase this sensitivity, resulting in pronounced swelling and blistering wounds that can occasionally become infected, especially when scratched. Two famous victims of infected mosquito bites are Lord Carnarvon, the Egyptologist who played a role in the discovery of the Tomb of Tutankhamen, and the British poet, Rupert Brooke, who died in Egypt and Greece, respectively. But the real danger will always be mosquito-borne diseases. Dengue fever, West Nile virus and some encephalitis-type diseases are all modern killers. A less deadly but more insidious example is pilariasis, a disease called thread-like parasites that migrate to the body's lymphatic system, causing body parts to permanently swell to grotesque proportions. However, as pesky as it is, in terms of its death toll, the worst disease is by far malaria. This parasite, carried by the Anopheles mosquito, causes fever, tremor, joint pain, vomiting and, if untreated, painful death. It infects over two million people a year, most of them children, killing over a quarter in the process. The Aedes Aepypti mosquito is the species responsible for that other major killer: yellow fever. It is a viral disease, but is limited to tropical regions, mainly in Africa, but also in Central and South America. After a high lever, nausea and joint pain, the virus attacks the liver and causes the hosts' skin to turn yellow (hence the name), with death following a few days later. Its toll is much smaller than malaria, with about 200,000 infections and 30,000 deaths each year, mostly in Africa. Unlike malaria, a vaccine exists, and extensive vaccination programs sponsored by the World Health Organization have had some success, while travelers to disease-prone areas are generally similarly protected. With such a number of deaths, it took a surprisingly long time for the link between mosquitoes and disease to be realized. This is exemplified in the construction of the Panama Canal the same ambitious project for dredging passage for ships through that narrow Central American country. In the 1880s, the French struggled for eight years in an insect-infested jungle, but the death toll from malaria and yellow fever made it very difficult to maintain an experienced workforce. After the loss of 22,000 lives, the work was abandoned, but soon after, a British physician in India, Ronald Ross, deduced the means of disease transmission, and identified the malaria parasite in the gastrointestinal tract of mosquitoes. He also realised that the number of mosquitoes could be reduced by restricting their access to water, providing two crucial insights that laid the groundwork for controlling the disease. Thus, in 1904, when America resumed its work on the Panama Canal, they established a multimillion-dollar mosquito abatement program, consisting of many strategies. Homes for workers were built with screens on the windows, buildings containing mosquitoes were disinfected and sick workers were isolated behind nets. Stand-water ponds (where mosquitoes breed) were sprayed with oil and insecticide, and roads were paved to eliminate puddles. For the same reason, wetlands were drained, and proper piping was used to transport drinking water and waste. All this reduced the number of deaths from disease during the ten-year construction phase to less than 6,000 a considerable number, but was still considered a great success. To this day, reducing the incidence of standing water pools, however small, remains very cost-effective in combating mosquito-borne diseases in urban areas. Many of the most dangerous species breed in accidental ditches, pots or discarded containers into which rainwater has been collected. By eliminating such sites, the number of insects decreases greatly, which limits the bites to those mosquitoes that come from farther away, but since they cannot travel far, the likelihood of being bitten (and infected) is greatly reduced.
hypothesis: Mosquito blood transmits diseases.

premise: The nature of genius has always had a keen interest in geniuses and wonders. The word genius, from the Latin gens (= family) and the term genius, which means begotten, comes from the ancient Roman worship of a deity as the head of the family. In its earliest form, genius concerned the ability of the head of the family, the paterfamilias, to perpetuate himself. Gradually, genius came to represent the characteristics of man and hence the highest qualities of an individual derived from his genius or guiding spirit. Today people still look at stars or genes, astrology or genetics, hoping to find the source of unusual abilities or personal characteristics. The concept of genius and gifts has become part of our popular culture, and attitudes are ambivalent towards them. We envy the gifted and do not trust them. In the mythology of the gifted, it is commonly thought that if people are talented in one area, they must be flawed in another, that intellectuals are impractical, that wonders burn too bright too soon and burn out, that gifted people are eccentric, that they are physically weak, that there is a fine line between genius and madness, that genius runs in families, that the gifted are so smart that they do not need special help, THAT GIFTEDNESS IS GIFTED THE SAME THING AS HAVING A HIGH IQ, THAT SOME RACES ARE MORE INTELLIGENT OR MUSICALLY OR MATHEMATICALLY INTELLIGENT THAN OTHERS, THAT GENIUS IS UNRECOGNIZED AND UNREWARDED, THAT ADVERSITY MAKES PEOPLE SMART OR THAT PEOPLE WITH GIFTS HAVE A RESPONSIBILITY TO USE THEM. The language has been enriched with terms like high brow, egg head, blue sock, smart, omniscient, boffin and, for many, intellectual is a term of slander. The nineteenth century saw great interest in the nature of genius, and produced quite a few studies of famous marvels. Perhaps for us today, two of the most significant aspects of most of these genius studies are the frequency with which early encouragement and teaching by parents and teachers had beneficial effects on children's intellectual, artistic, or musical development but caused great adjustment difficulties later in life, and the frequency with which abilities were not recognized by teachers and schools. However, the difficulty with the evidence produced by these studies, fascinating as they are in collecting anecdotes and apparent similarities and outliers, is that they are not what we would today call the norm. In other words, when, for example, collecting information about early diseases, methods of education, education, etc., we must also take into account information from other historical sources about how common or unusual these were at that time. For example, infant mortality was high and life expectancy much shorter than today, homeschooling was common in noble and wealthy families, bullying and corporal punishment were common in the best independent schools, and most of the cases studied were members of the privileged classes. Only with the growth of children and psychology in the twentieth century was it possible to carry out studies on a more objective, if not yet always very scientific, basis. Geniuses, however they are defined, are just the peaks that stand out in the fog of history and are visible to the particular observer from his particular vantage point. Change the viewpoints and vantage points, clear some of the fog and many different peaks appear. Genius is a term we apply to those who we recognize for their outstanding achievements and stand near the end of the sequence of human abilities that reaches back through the everyday and the medium to the incapable. There is still a lot of truth in the observation of Dr. Samuel Johnson, the true genius is a mind with great general powers, which is mistakenly determined in a certain direction. We may disagree with the general that we doubt that all ingenious musicians could have become scientists of genius or vice versa, but there is no doubting the accidental determination that nurtured or stimulated their gifts to those channels into which they poured their forces with so much success. Along the continuum of abilities are hundreds of thousands of gifted men and women, boys and girls. 44 What we value, enjoy, or admire in the works of genius or in the achievements of wonder are expressions of skills or abilities similar to our own, but far superior to our own. But the fact that their brains are no different from ours is proved by the fact that the hard-earned discoveries of scientists like Kepler or Einstein are becoming commonplace knowledge of schoolchildren and the outrageous shapes and colours of an artist like Paul Kelly appear so quickly on the canvases we wear. The word genius, from the Latin gens (= family) and the term genius, which means begotten, comes from the ancient Roman worship of a deity as the head of the family. In its earliest form, genius concerned the ability of the head of the family, the paterfamilias, to perpetuate himself. Gradually, genius came to represent the characteristics of man and hence the highest qualities of an individual derived from his genius or guiding spirit. Today people still look at stars or genes, astrology or genetics, hoping to find the source of unusual abilities or personal characteristics. The concept of genius and gifts has become part of our popular culture, and attitudes are ambivalent towards them. We envy the gifted and do not trust them. In the mythology of the gifted, it is commonly thought that if people are talented in one area, they must be flawed in another, that intellectuals are impractical, that wonders burn too bright too soon and burn out, that gifted people are eccentric, that they are physically weak, that there is a fine line between genius and madness, that genius runs in families, that the gifted are so smart that they do not need special help, THAT GIFTEDNESS IS GIFTED THE SAME THING AS HAVING A HIGH IQ, THAT SOME RACES ARE MORE INTELLIGENT OR MUSICALLY OR MATHEMATICALLY INTELLIGENT THAN OTHERS, THAT GENIUS IS UNRECOGNIZED AND UNREWARDED, THAT ADVERSITY MAKES PEOPLE SMART OR THAT PEOPLE WITH GIFTS HAVE A RESPONSIBILITY TO USE THEM. The language has been enriched with terms like high brow, egg head, blue sock, smart, omniscient, boffin and, for many, intellectual is a term of slander. The nineteenth century saw great interest in the nature of genius, and produced quite a few studies of famous marvels. Perhaps for us today, two of the most significant aspects of most of these genius studies are the frequency with which early encouragement and teaching by parents and teachers had beneficial effects on children's intellectual, artistic, or musical development but caused great adjustment difficulties later in life, and the frequency with which abilities were not recognized by teachers and schools. However, the difficulty with the evidence produced by these studies, fascinating as they are in collecting anecdotes and apparent similarities and outliers, is that they are not what we would today call the norm. In other words, when, for example, collecting information about early diseases, methods of education, education, etc., we must also take into account information from other historical sources about how common or unusual these were at that time. For example, infant mortality was high and life expectancy much shorter than today, homeschooling was common in noble and wealthy families, bullying and corporal punishment were common in the best independent schools, and most of the cases studied were members of the privileged classes. Only with the growth of children and psychology in the twentieth century was it possible to carry out studies on a more objective, if not yet always very scientific, basis. Geniuses, however they are defined, are just the peaks that stand out in the fog of history and are visible to the particular observer from his particular vantage point. Change the viewpoints and vantage points, clear some of the fog and many different peaks appear. Genius is a term we apply to those who we recognize for their outstanding achievements and stand near the end of the sequence of human abilities that reaches back through the everyday and the medium to the incapable. There is still a lot of truth in the observation of Dr. Samuel Johnson, the true genius is a mind with great general powers, which is mistakenly determined in a certain direction. We may disagree with the general that we doubt that all ingenious musicians could have become scientists of genius or vice versa, but there is no doubting the accidental determination that nurtured or stimulated their gifts to those channels into which they poured their forces with so much success. Along the continuum of abilities are hundreds of thousands of gifted men and women, boys and girls. 44 What we value, enjoy, or admire in the works of genius or in the achievements of wonder are expressions of skills or abilities similar to our own, but far superior to our own. But the fact that their brains are no different from ours is proved by the fact that the hard-earned discoveries of scientists like Kepler or Einstein are becoming commonplace knowledge of schoolchildren and the outrageous shapes and colours of an artist like Paul Kelly appear so quickly on the canvases we wear. This does not minimize the superiority of their achievements, which exceed ours since the miles under four minutes exceed our run. Thinking of geniuses and gifted as having uniquely different brains is only reasonable if we accept that every human brain is uniquely different. The purpose of teaching is to make us even more different from each other, and in the process of enlightenment we can learn from the achievements of those who are more gifted than us. But before we try to imitate geniuses or encourage our children to do so, we must note that some of the things we learn from them may turn out to be unpalatable. We may envy their achievements and fame, but we must also recognize the price they have paid in terms of perseverance, single-mindedness, dedication, restrictions on their personal lives, the demands on their energies and time, and how often they have had to show great courage to maintain their integrity or make their way to the top. Genius and giftedness are relatively descriptive terms with no real substance. premise: The pace of evolutionary change and heated debate has revived recent studies on evolution. Darwin's original thesis, and the viewpoint supported by evolutionary gradients, is that species change continuously but slowly and at small intervals. Such changes are almost invisible over the short time scale of modern observations and, arguably, are usually obscured by countless gaps in the imperfect fossil record. Gradality, with its emphasis on the slow pace of change, is a comforting stance, repeated again and again in generations of textbooks. In the early twentieth century, the question about the rate of evolution was answered in favor of gradation to the satisfaction of most biologists. Sometimes a closed question has to be reopened when new evidence or new arguments based on old evidence arise. In 1972 paleontologist Stephen J. Gould and Niles Eldredge challenged the conventional wisdom in an opposing viewpoint, the punctuated equilibrium hypothesis, which holds that species give rise to new species in relatively sudden eruptions, without a prolonged transition period. These episodes of rapid evolution are separated by relatively long static ranges during which a species will hardly change at all. The dotted equilibrium hypothesis attempts to explain a peculiar feature of the fossil record such that has been familiar to paleontologist for more than a century but generally ignored. Many species appear to have remained unchanged in the fossil record for millions of years, a situation that seems to contradict Darwin's model of continuous change. Mediated fossil forms, predicted by gradation, are generally lacking. In most localities a given species of clam or coral persists essentially unchanged along a thick rock formation, only to be suddenly replaced with a new and different species. The evolution of the North American horse, once presented as a classic textbook example of gradual evolution, now provides equally compelling evidence for punctuated equilibrium. A convincing 50-million-year-old sequence of modern equine ancestors each slightly larger, with more complex teeth, a longer face and a more prominent central toe seems to provide strong support for Darwin's claim that species evolve gradually. But a close examination of those fossil deposits now reveals a slightly different story. Horses evolved in separate steps, each of which lasted virtually unchanged for millions of years and was eventually replaced by a newer model. Four-toed Eohippus predated the three-toed Miohippus, for example, but fossil evidence in North America suggests a bumpy and uneven transition between the two. If evolution were a continuous and gradual process, one would expect almost every fossil specimen to be slightly different from each year. If it seems difficult to understand how large changes can occur quickly, consider this: A change of a single gene in the files is enough to turn a normal fly with a single pair of wings into one that has two pairs of wings. Now the question about the rate of evolution must be turned: does evolution ever progress gradually, or does it always occur in short bursts? Detailed field studies of thick rock formations containing fossils provide the best potential tests of the competing theories. Occasionally, a sequence of fossil-rich rock layers allows a comprehensive look at one type of organism over a long period of time. For example, Peter Sheldon's studies of trilobites, a now-extinct marine animal with a segmented body, offer a detailed glimpse into three million years of evolution in a single marine environment. In this study, each of eight different trilobite species was observed to undergo a gradual change in the number of segments usually an increase of one or two segments over the entire time interval. No significant discontinuities were observed, leading Sheldon to conclude that environmental conditions were fairly stable during the period examined. Similar exhaustive studies are needed for many different types of organisms from many different eras. Most researchers expect to find that both modes of transition from one species to another operate in evolution. Slow and continuous change may be the norm during periods of environmental stability, while rapid development of new species occurs during periods of environmental stress. But many more studies like Sheldon's are needed before we can say for sure.
hypothesis: Darwin's evolutionary thesis was rejected because no small changes could be observed in the evolutionary record.
