premise: The corn maize people are the source of life of Mexico, the history and identity of the country are intertwined with it. But that centuries-old relationship is now threatened by free trade. Laura Carlsen investigates the threat and downplays a growing activist movement. On a mountaintop in southern Mexico, Indian families gather. They chant and sprinkle cornmeal at consecration, praying for the success of their new crops, for the unity of their communities and for the health of their families. In this village in Oaxaca people eat corn tamales, sow corn plots and teach children to care for the plant. The cultural rhythms of this community, commission, ceremonies and celebrations will be defined as they have been for thousands of years by the life cycle of the maize. Indeed, had it not been for the domestication of the Teocinthal (the ancestor of modern maize) 9,000 years ago the Mesoamerican civilization could never have evolved. In the Mayan holy book, the Popol Wu, the gods create people from cornmeal. The Corn People flourished and built one of the most amazing civilizations in human history. But in Mexico and Central America today corn is under attack. As a result of the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), Mexico was flooded with imported corn north of the U.S. border. Infection of local strains with genetically modified imported corn could have significant consequences for Mexican campesinos (farmers), local biodiversity, and global genetic reserves. A decade ago Mexican bureaucrats and businessmen understood it all. NAFTA would drive uncompetitive corn farmers from the countryside to work in booming assembly plants across the country. Their standard of living will rise as the cost of providing services like electricity and water to scattered rural communities will drop. Best of all, cheap imported corn from the U.S., the world's most efficient and subsidized producer, would be an advantage for Mexican consumers. Unfortunately, it didn't turn out that way. There were not enough of these factory jobs and those that did materialize continued to be along the U.S. border, no farther in Mexico. And despite a huge drop in the price received by farmers for their corn, consumers have often paid more. The price of tortillas, the country's main food, rose nearly fivefold as the government stopped local subsidies and giant agricultural companies took over the market. Defenders of free trade such as Mexico's former undersecretary of agriculture, Luis Tellez, suggest: It's not that NAFTA failed, but that reality didn't turn out the way we planned it. Part of that reality was that the government did nothing to help the Campesinos in the so-called transition. NAFTA also did not recognize inequality or create compensation funds to help the victims of free trade unlike what happened with economic integration in the European Union. Basically, Mexico adopted a sink or swim policy for small farmers, opening the floodgates to tons of American imported corn. Corn imports have tripled under NAFTA and producer prices have dropped by half. The drop in income immediately hit the most vulnerable and poorest members of rural society. While more than a third of the corn grown by small farmers is used to feed their families, the rest is sold in local markets. Without this critical money, rural living standards plummeted. Corn is the heart of the indigenous and campsino identity. JOSÉ CARILLO DE LA CRUZ, A VICHULI INDIAN FROM NORTHERN JALISCO, DESCRIBES THIS CONNECTION: CORN IS THE STRENGTH, LIFE AND STRENGTH OF THE VICHUL. If there was change, if someone on the outside patented our corn, it would end our lives and our existence. The good news is that the free-trade threat to Mexico's culture and food security has sparked lively opposition. In Defence of Corn, a movement to defend the native maize varieties, is not a membership organization but a series of forums and actions led by Campsino themselves. This is a direct challenge to both free trade and the dictums of corporate science. THE STUBBORNNESS AND REFUSAL OF FARMERS TO ABANDON THE CROPS OF THEIR ANCESTORS IS IMPRESSIVE. But greater economic conditions continue to shape their lives. Rural poverty and hunger surged under the free trade and imposed a heavier burden on women remaining to work in the land. The battle for food sovereignty continues. Leaders of the movement insist the government will reconsider its free trade policy and develop a genuine plan for rural development.

Your treatment should include physical contact, and each appointment with your patients should last at least half an hour. Encourage your patients to take an active part in their treatment and understand how their disorders relate to the rest of their lives. Tell them that their own bodies have the true power to heal. Make them pay you out of their own pockets. Describe your treatment with familiar words, but embroidered with a hint of mysticism: energy fields, energy flows, energy blocks, meridians, forces, halos, rhythms, and the like. REFER TO THE KNOWLEDGE OF AN EARLIER ERA: WISDOM HAS BEEN CARELESSLY SWEPT ASIDE BY THE RISE AND RISE OF BLIND, MECHANISTIC SCIENCE. Oh, get the hell out of it, you say. Something invented off the edge of your head can't work, can it? Well yes, it can and often is good enough to earn you a living. A good living if you are persuasive enough, or, better yet, truly believe in your care. Many diseases improve on their own, so if you are lucky and conduct your treatment at exactly the right time you will get the credit. But that's just part of it. Some of the improvement will really be up to you. Your healing power will be the result of a paradoxical force that conventional medicine recognizes but remains strangely ambivalent about: the placebo effect. PLACEBOS ARE TREATMENTS THAT HAVE NO DIRECT EFFECT ON THE BODY, BUT STILL WORK BECAUSE THE PATIENT HAS FAITH IN THEIR POWER TO HEAL. Most often the term refers to a dummy pill, but it applies equally to any device or procedure, from a sticky plaster to crystal to surgery. THE EXISTENCE OF THE PLACEBO EFFECT IMPLIES THAT EVEN CHARLATANISM MAY CONFER REAL BENEFITS, WHICH IS WHY ANY MENTION OF PLACEBO IS A SENSITIVE TOPIC FOR MANY PRACTITIONERS OF COMPLEMENTARY AND ALTERNATIVE MEDICINE, WHO MAY REGARD THIS AS AN ASSERTION OF CHARLATANISM. In fact, the placebo effect is a powerful part of all medical care, orthodox or otherwise, though its role is often neglected or misunderstood. One of the great strengths of CAM (Complementary and Alternative Medicine) may be the skill of its practitioners in deploying the placebo effect to achieve a true cure. Complementary practitioners are better at producing nonspecific effects and good therapeutic relationships, says Edzard Ernst, CAM professor at the University of Exeter. The question is whether CAM can be incorporated into conventional medicine, as some would like, without losing much of that power. On one level, it is not surprising that our state of mind can affect our physiology: anger opens the superficial blood vessels of the face; sadness pumps up the tear glands. But how exactly the placebos work their medicinal magic is still largely unknown. Most of the meager studies done so far have focused on pain control, as this is one of the most common complaints and is suitable for experimental research. Here, attention turned to endorphins, morphine-like neurochemicals known to help control pain. But how exactly the placebos work their medicinal magic is still largely unknown. Any of the neurochemicals involved in transmitting pain impulses or modulating them may also be involved in generating the placebo response, says Don Price, a University of Florida oral surgeon who studies the placebo effect in toothache. But the endorphins are still at the forefront. This case has been strengthened by the recent work of Fabrizio Benedetti of the University of Turin, who showed that the placebo effect can be eliminated by a drug, naloxone, which blocks the effects of endorphins. Benedetti caused pain in human volunteers by inflating a blood pressure cuff on the forearm. He did this several times a day for several days, using morphine each time to control the pain. On the last day, without saying anything, he replaced the morphine with a saline solution. It still relieved subjects' pain: placebo effect. But when he added naloxone to the salt, the pain relief disappeared. Here's direct proof that placebo painkillers are mediated, at least in part, by these natural opiates. Still, no one knows how faith triggers endorphin release, or why most people can't achieve placebo pain relief simply by wanting it. Although scientists do not know exactly how placebos work, they have accumulated considerable knowledge on how to exert the effect. A rheumatologist in London found, for example, that red dummy capsules produce more effective painkillers than blue, green or yellow ones. A study on American college students revealed that blue pills produce better sedatives than pink, a color more suitable for stimulants. Even branding can make a difference: if aspero or tylenol are what you like to take for a headache, the chemically identical generic equivalents may be less effective. It is also important how the treatment is carried out. Decades ago, when the main sedative chlorpromethine was introduced, a doctor in Kansas classified his colleagues according to whether they were eager for it, openly skeptical of its benefits, or took a let's-try-see approach. His conclusion: the more enthusiastic the doctor, the better the drug performed. And this year Ernst reviewed published studies that compared doctors' bedside manners. The studies brought up one consistent finding: Doctors who adopt a warm, friendly and relaxing way, he reported, are more effective than those whose counseling is formal and offers no reassurance. Warm, friendly and relaxing is exactly CAM's strong suit, of course. Many of the ingredients of that opening recipe the physical touch, the generous time intervals, the powerful hints of supernatural healing power are just the kind of things that might impress patients. It's no surprise, then, that complementary practitioners are usually the best at enlisting the placebo effect, says Arthur Kleinman, a professor of social anthropology at Harvard University.

premise: The problem of scarce resources The problem of how health resources should be allocated or distributed, so that they are distributed in the most just and efficient way, is not new. Every health system in an economically developed society is faced with the need to decide (formally or informally) what proportion of a community's total resources should be invested for medical care; how resources should be distributed; which diseases and disabilities and which forms of care should be given priority; which community members will receive special consideration with respect to their health needs; and which forms of care are the most cost-effective. What is new is that from the 1950s onwards there have been certain general changes in perception about the finite of resources as a whole and of health resources in particular, as well as more specific changes in relation to the clientele of health resources and the cost to the community of these resources. Thus, in the 1950s and 1960s, awareness arose in Western societies that the resources to supply fossil fuel energy are finite and inexhaustible and that the ability of nature or the environment to sustain economic and population development is also finite. In other words, we became aware of the obvious fact that there are “limits to growth.” The new consciousness that there are also severe limits to health resources was part of this general discovery of the obvious. Looking back, it now seems quite remarkable that in the national health systems that emerged in many countries in the years immediately after the 1939-45 World War, it was undoubtedly assumed that all the basic health needs of any community could be satisfied, at least in principle; the 'invisible hand' of economic progress would provide. Yet just at the same time that this new understanding of the finite nature of health resources is sinking in, an awareness of an opposite kind has emerged in Western societies: that people have a fundamental right to medical care as a necessary condition for a proper human life. Like education, political and legal processes and institutions, public order, communication, transportation, and money supply, health care was perceived as one of the basic social facilities necessary for people to exercise their other rights as autonomous human beings. People are unable to exercise personal liberty and determine themselves if they are poverty-stricken, or deprived of basic education, or do not live in a context of law and order. IN THE SAME WAY, BASIC MEDICAL CARE IS A PREREQUISITE FOR THE EXERCISE OF AUTONOMY. Although 'rights' language sometimes leads to confusion, by the late 1970s it was recognized in most societies that people have a right to medical care (although there was considerable opposition in the United States to the idea of having an official right to medical care). It is also widely accepted that this right generates a duty or obligation for the state to ensure that adequate health resources are provided out of the public purse. The state has no obligation to provide a health care system itself, but to ensure that such a system will be provided. In other words, basic health care is now recognized as a “public good,” rather than as a “private good” that a person is expected to buy for himself. As he put it in a 1976 World Health Organization statement: “The enjoyment of the highest level of health attainable is one of the fundamental rights of every person without distinction of race, religion, political creed, economic or social status.” As just mentioned, in a liberal society basic health is seen as one of the necessary conditions for the realization of personal autonomy. Just at the time when it became clear that health resources could not meet the requirements imposed on them, people demanded that their basic right to medical care be provided by the state. The second set of more specific changes that have led to the current concern about the distribution of health resources stems from the dramatic increase in health care costs in most OECD countries1, accompanied by large-scale demographic and social changes that mean, to take one example, that elderly people are now large (and relatively very expensive) consumers of health resources. Thus in OECD countries as a whole, health care costs rose from 3.8% of GDP in 1960 to 7% of GDP in 1980, and it is expected that the rate of health costs to GDP will continue to rise. (In the US the current figure is about 12% of GDP, and in Australia about 7.8% of GDP.) As a result, during the 1980s a sort of doomsday scenario (analogous to similar doomsday extrapolations about energy needs and fossil fuels or about population increases) was anticipated by health executives, economists, and politicians. In this scenario, steadily rising health care costs were correlated to static or declining resources.
hypothesis: Personal liberty and independence have never been thought to be directly related to health.

The field was launched, and the term 'artificial intelligence' was coined, at a conference in 1956, by a group of researchers that included Marvin Minsky, John McCarthy, Herbert Simon, and Alan Newell, who all went on to become leading figures in the field. The phrase provided an attractive but informative name for a research program that encompassed previously disparate fields like operations research, cybernetics, logic, and computer science. The goal they shared was an attempt to capture or emulate human abilities using machines. However, different groups of researchers have attacked different problems, from speech recognition to playing chess, in different ways; AI unified the domain in name only. Thinking computers and home robots failed to materialize, and a backlash ensued. “There was excessive optimism in the early 1980s,” says David Lake, a researcher at Indiana University. “Then when people realized that these were difficult problems, there was a reduction. 'Ironically, in some ways AI has been a victim of its success. Whenever a seemingly routine problem was solved, like building a system that could land an unattended plane, the problem was deemed to be no artificial intelligence in the first place. “If it works, it can't be AI,” as Dr. Lake characterizes it. The effect of repeatedly moving the goal posts in this way was that AI referred to a 'blue sky' study that was still years away from commercialization. Researchers have joked that AI stands for 'almost implemented'. Meanwhile, the technologies that reached the market, such as speech recognition, language translation, and software to support decisions, were no longer considered as AI. However, all three of them once fell well within the umbrella of AI research. But the tide may now be turning, according to Dr Lake. In particular, the problem of information overload, exacerbated by the growth of e-mail and the explosion in the number of web pages, means that there are many opportunities for new technologies to help filter and categorize classic artificial intelligence problems of information. The implication may be that more artificial intelligence companies will start to emerge to meet this challenge. The 1969 film, 2001: A Space Odyssey, featured an intelligent computer called HAL 9000. In addition to understanding and speaking English, HAL could play chess and even learned to undress. HAL thus covered the optimism of the 1960s that smart computers would be widespread by 2001. But the year 2001 was and gone, and there's still no sign of a HAL-like computer. Individual systems can play chess or transcribe speech, but a general theory of machine intelligence still remains elusive. However, it may be that the comparison with HAL no longer seems so important, and AI can now be judged by what it can do, rather than by how well it matches a 30-year-old sci-fi movie. “People are starting to realize that there are impressive things these systems can do.” Says Dr. Lake hopefully.

premise: The Romantic poets One of the most evocative periods in the history of poetry must surely be that of the Romantic movement. In the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries a group of poets created a new atmosphere in literary destinations, discarding the styles of their predecessors in favor of a fascinating and forceful art that persists with us to this day. Five poets emerged as the main components of this movement William Wordsworth, Samuel Taylor Coleridge, George Gordon Byron, Percy Bysshe Shelley and John Keats. The power of their creations undoubtedly lies in the power of their imagination. Indeed, imagination was the most critical feature of the Romantic poets. Each poet had the ability to present incredible images and visions, though differing to some extent in their intensity and presentation. Nature, mythology and emotion were of great importance and were used to study the feelings of the poet himself. The lives of the poets often overlapped and the tragedy was characteristic of most of them. Byron was born in London in 1788. The family moved to Aberdeen soon after, where Byron grew up until he inherited the family seat of Newstead Abbey in Nottinghamshire from his great uncle. He graduated from Cambridge University in 1808 and left England the following year to embark on a tour of the Mediterranean. During this tour, he developed a passion for Greece that would later lead to his death in 1824. He left for Switzerland in 1816 where he was introduced to Shelley. Shelley was born into a wealthy family in 1792. He was educated at Baton and then went on to Oxford. Shelley was not happy in England, where his colourful lifestyle and unconventional beliefs made him unpopular with the establishment and in 1818 left for Italy, where he was reunited with Byron. However, the friendship ended tragically in July 1822, when Shelley sank in a boating accident off the coast of Italy. Somewhat dramatically, Shelley's body was cremated on the beach, witnessed by a small group of friends, including Byron. Historically, Shelley and Byron are considered the most prominent and radical of the Romantic poets. In contrast, Wordsworth appears to have had a pleasant and acceptable personality, and even received the status of Poet Laureate in 1843. He was born in 1770 in Cockermouth, Cumbria. By the time he entered his early teens, both his parents had died. As he grew older, Wordsworth developed a passion for writing. In 1798 Wordsworth published a collection of poems with Coleridge, whom he had met, a few years earlier, when he settled in Somerset with his sister Dorothy. He married in 1802, and as time passed abandoned his former political views and became increasingly acceptable to popular society. Indeed, by the time of his death in the spring of 1850, he had become one of the most sought-after poets of his time. Wordsworth shared some of the years at Dove Cottage in Somerset with his friend and poetic contemporary, Coleridge. Coleridge was born in Devon in 1772. He was a brilliant young scholar but never achieved the same prolific output of his fellow Romantic poets. In 1804 he left for duty in Malta for three years. On his return he separated from his wife and went to live with the Wordsworths, where he produced a regular journal. With ill health, he later moved to London. In 1816 he went to live with a doctor and his family. He remained with them until his death in 1834. Over the past few years, his poetry has been abandoned to other forms of writing equally outstanding in their own right. Perhaps the most tragic of the Romantic poets was Keats. Keats was born in London in 1795. Much like Wordsworth, both of his parents died in his early teens. He studied as a surgeon, and was ordained in 1816. However, poetry was his great passion and he decided to devote himself to writing. For most of his adult life, Keats was in poor health and became seriously ill in the early 1820s. He knew he was dying and in September of that year left for Rome in the hope that the more pleasant climate might ease his suffering. Keats died of consumption in February 1821 at the age of twenty-five. Sad that such tragedy often accompanies those of extraordinary artistic genius. We can only wonder about the possible outcome had they all lived to old age. Maybe even Byron and Shelley would have mellowed over the years, like Wordsworth. However, the contribution to poetry of all five writers is not measurable. They introduced the concepts of individualism and imagination, allowing us to explore our visions of beauty without reward. We are not now required to restrain our thoughts and service to that of the socially acceptable.

premise: The search for color Rarely do we ponder the artificial color of modern goods. A blue car is blue; a chair is red, red; a bike is green, green. But why does it have color? Because its surface contains pigment. If it was originally dissolved in a carrier fluid to transfer the color, it is known as a dye, but in any case, since color is the most visible element in all the objects we want, it can be said that pigments are the basis of the customer's choice, and therefore almost all difficult trades and transactions. As a result, the production of this material is a big business, which now accounts for over twenty billion dollars a year in global sales - but there was a time when none of them existed. If we go back to the mists of prehistory, objects, tools, and clothing were all dirt and bland, with nothing but their natural colors. The first pigments used were of mineral origin from natural clay dyed in the presence of iron oxides. The best known examples are the golden color of ocher, the brown of ombre and the yellow of Siena. These were ground and mixed with fat to create paint, which was used, for example, in the earliest European cave paintings. Ash, as well as charcoal (sourced from heating wood in the absence of oxygen), were also used to provide black, but in the search for colour it was soon discovered that biological material, such as plants, animal waste, molluscs and insects, could yield more interesting results. Crimson in bright red coloris a good example. It was produced from cremes, a small insect found on southern European oak trees. The pigment is a component of the ceramic acid produced inside the creatures' body, which serves to deter predation by birds or other insects. However, because the trees are large and bushy, and the sap-feeding insects are few and far between, pigment production was a painstaking and time-consuming process. This raised the price of the product, and the end result was that in northern Europe, pure scarlet has long remained a luxury color for clothing and textiles. Interestingly, across the Pacific, people produced the same dye from the same chemical inside a different insect. They were called cochineals: small scaly creatures that reproduce in abundant clusters on the fleshy leaves of a common cactus. These insects have many advantages over creams. Being so prolific and so easily seen by predators, they need to produce higher concentrations of carmic acid for protection, up to a quarter of their body weight. The resulting pigment is also stronger and durable over time. Finally, the insects are much more easily obtained, and simply obliterate or drop the leaves of the cactus, so that, after the Spanish conquest of Mexico, the cochineals replaced the creams almost completely, becoming a profitable export of Central America for the next centuries. The allure of scarlet was surpassed only by the vivid Tyrian purple, a color that has been ranked in its highest favor since ancient times. Its origin was the medium-sized Murex sea snail. With a range around the Mediterranean coast, the early cultures there soon realized that the mucus that the snail secretes when it is stabbed can be treated and nudged to produce a blue-violet color that did not fade with time. However, by needing thousands of sea snails and using a complicated (and still little known) process, all for the production of only small amounts of pigment, the paint was so expensive that only the ruling classes could afford it. This led to purple becoming associated with royalty. Roman emperors traditionally wore clothing of this color. For a less resistant blue, suitable for dyeing clothes, the indigo plant was discovered. Its leaves were fermented, then left to age, and the resulting sediment was eventually dried, treated and then reduced to a blue powder. In fact, it can be said that this pigment is the oldest used to dye fabric. This is one of the reasons why jeans were originally blue, and remain so to this day, indigo is the color used to dye them. However, it was not suitable for painting or artistic purposes. To do this, European artists used a mixture derived from grinding lapis lazuli, a semi-precious stone, whose only known origin was in distant Afghanistan. As a result, this paint was very expensive, and many artists avoided it altogether. However, others were deliberately wasteful in its use, producing proportionally more expensive paintings. The cost of this dye resulted in many experiments during the Industrial Revolution in search of chemical-based alternatives. This eventually led to the first modern synthetic pigment, Prussian blue. It was discovered in Germany in the early 18th century, and put into rapid production and export, giving artists around the world the first inexpensive but stable blue pigment. Other chemists have made similar breakthroughs. THE INTENSE PURPLE OF THE MORX SNAIL WAS ACCIDENTALLY PRODUCED BY AN ENGLISH CHEMIST, WILLIAM PERKINS, WHO SOON PUT THE MOVIN INTO COMMERCIAL PRODUCTION. In such efforts, affordable pigments were soon found in all colors. Mass production followed, bringing industrial prosperity to northern Europe, but a decline in many areas of the world where traditional organic pigments were still in production. In the Americas, for example, the purslane of the cuchinales, which had long been a Spanish monopoly and a rich source of income from exports, went into steady decline. However, all is not lost. In this modern era, there has been a shift back towards naturalness, even in pigments, and this has seen a resurgence in the popularity of cuchinales. The pigment is currently produced commercially in several countries, with Peru being the largest exporter.

premise: THE SEARCH FOR EXTRATERRESTRIAL INTELLIGENCE THE QUESTION OF WHETHER WE ARE ALONE IN THE UNIVERSE HAS HAUNTED HUMANITY FOR CENTURIES, BUT WE MAY NOW BE ON THE CUSP OF ANSWERING THIS QUESTION, AS WE SEARCH FOR RADIO SIGNALS FROM OTHER INTELLIGENT CULTURES. This search, often known by the acronym SETI (Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence), is difficult. Although groups around the world have searched intermittently for three decades, it is only now that we have reached the level of technology where we can make a determined attempt to search all nearby stars for any sign of life. The main reason for the search is basic curiosity - the same curiosity about the natural world that drives all pure science. We want to know if we are alone in the universe. We want to know if life evolves naturally if given the right conditions, or whether there is something very special about Earth that has nurtured the variety of life forms we see around us on the planet. The simple detection of a radio signal would suffice to answer the most basic question of all. In this sense, SETI is another cog in the mechanism of pure science that continually pushes the horizon of our knowledge. However, there are other reasons to be interested in whether life exists elsewhere. For example, we've had a civilization on Earth for perhaps only a few thousand years, and the threats of nuclear war and pollution in recent decades have told us that our survival may be tenuous. Will we last another two thousand years or will we wipe ourselves out? Since the lifetime of a planet like ours is several billion years, we can expect that if other civilizations did survive in our galaxy, their age would range from zero to several billion years. Thus, every other civilization we hear of may be much older, on average, than we are. The very existence of such a civilization would tell us that long-term survival is possible, and gives us some reason for optimism. It is even possible that the older civilization might pass on the benefits of its experience in dealing with survival threats such as nuclear war and global pollution, and other threats we have yet to discover. In discussing whether we are alone, most SETI scientists adopt two ground rules. First, UFQs (unidentified flying objects) are usually ignored because most scientists do not consider the evidence for them strong enough to bear serious consideration (though it is also important to keep an open mind in case truly compelling evidence emerges in the future). Secondly, we make a very conservative assumption that we are looking for a life form that is quite similar to us, because if it is radically different from us we may not recognize it as a life form, other than whether we are able to communicate with it. In other words, the life form we seek may well have two green heads and seven fingers, but it will still resemble us in that it has to communicate with its friends, take an interest in the universe, live on a planet orbiting a star like our sun, and, perhaps most limitedly, have chemistry, like us, based on carbon and water. Even when we make these assumptions, our understanding of other life forms is still very limited. We don't even know, for example, how many stars have planets, and we certainly don't know how likely life is to arise naturally, given the right conditions. However, when we look at the 100 billion stars in our galaxy (the Milky Way), and the 100 billion galaxies in the observable universe, it seems inconceivable that at least one of these planets does not have a life form; in fact, the most educated guess we can make, using what little we know about the conditions for carbon-based life, leads us to estimate that perhaps one in 100,000 stars may have a life-bearing planet orbiting it. That means our closest neighbors are maybe 100 light years away, which is almost the next door in astronomical terms. An alien civilization can choose many different ways of sending information across the galaxy, but many of them require too much energy, or they are severely weakened while traversing the vast distances across the galaxy. It turns out that for a given amount of transmitted power, radio waves in the 1000 to 3000 MHz frequency range travel the greatest distance, so all searches so far have concentrated on searching for radio waves in this frequency range. To date, several searches have been conducted by various groups around the world, including Australian searches using the Radio Telescope in Parks, New South Wales. So far there have been no 62 detections from the few hundred stars searched. The scope of searches has increased dramatically since 1992, when the U.S. Congress voted NASA $10 million a year for ten years to conduct a thorough search for life off the land. Much of the money in this project is invested in developing the special hardware needed to search for many frequencies at once. The project consists of two parts. Part one is a targeted search using the world's largest radio telescopes, the American-operated telescope in Arecibo, Puerto Rico, and the French telescope at Nancy in France. This part of the project is looking for the nearest 1000 likely stars with high sensitivity to signals in the 1000 to 3000 MHz frequency range. The second part of the project is an unintended search that tracks all of space at a lower sensitivity, using the smaller antennas of NASA's Deep Space Network. There is considerable debate about how we should react if we detect a signal from an alien civilization. Everyone agrees that we shouldn't respond right away. Apart from the impracticality of sending a reply over such great distances at short notice, it raises a host of ethical questions that the global community will have to address before any reply can be sent. Would the human race face the culture shock if faced with a superior and much older civilization? Fortunately, there is no urgency in this regard. The stars being tested are hundreds of light years away, so it takes hundreds of years for their signal to reach us, and another few hundred years for our answer to reach them. If so, it is immaterial whether there will be a delay of a few years, or decades, while the human race debates whether to reply, and perhaps formulates an answer carefully.

premise: The search for the anti-aging pill. In government laboratories and elsewhere, scientists are looking for a drug capable of prolonging life and youthful vigor. Studies on calorie restriction show the way As researchers on aging recently pointed out, no treatment on the market today has been shown to slow human aging the accumulation of molecular and cellular damage that increases vulnerability to morbidity as we age. But one intervention, consuming a low-calorie* but nutritionally balanced diet, works remarkably well in a wide range of animals, increasing longevity and prolonging good health. These findings suggest that caloric restriction may delay aging and increase lifespan in humans as well. Unfortunately, for the sake of maximum benefit, people will probably need to reduce their calorie intake by about 30%, equivalent to a reduction from 2,500 calories a day to 1,750. Few mortals could adhere to this harsh regime, especially for many years. But what if someone could create a pill that mimics the physiological effects of eating less without forcing people to eat less? Could such a mimetic for calorie restriction, as we call it, allow people to stay healthier, postponing age-related disorders (such as diabetes, atherosclerosis, heart disease and cancer) until very late in life? Scientists first posed this question in the mid-1990s, after researchers came across a chemical that in rodents appears to restore many benefits from calorie restrictions. A compound that would safely achieve the same feat in people has not yet been found, but the search was informative and raised hope that calorie-limiting (CR) mimetics could indeed eventually be developed. Benefits of Caloric Restriction The hunt for CR mimetics grew out of a desire to better understand the many effects calorie restrictions have on the body. Scientists first recognized the value of the practice more than 60 years ago, when they found that rats fed a low-calorie diet lived longer on average than free-fed rats and also had a reduced incidence of conditions that are becoming increasingly common in old age. What's more, some of the treated animals survived longer than the oldest animals in the control group, which means that the maximum lifespan (the oldest age attainable), not just the normal lifespan, increased. Various interventions, such as drugs that fight infections, can increase the average survival time of a population, but only approaches that slow the rate of aging of the body will increase the maximum life expectancy. The rat findings have been replicated many times and extended to creatures ranging from yeast to fruit flies, worms, fish, spiders, mice and hamsters. Until recently, studies were limited to short-lived creatures genetically remote from humans. But calorie-restriction projects underway in two species more related to rhesus monkeys and squirrel humans have made scientists optimistic that CR's mimetics could help people. Calories: An Index to the Energy Value of Food The monkeys projects demonstrate that compared to animals that eat normally, calorie-restricted monkeys have lower body temperatures and levels of the pancreatic hormone insulin, and they maintain younger levels of certain hormones that tend to decline with age. The calorie-restricted animals also look better on indicators of risk for age-related diseases. For example, they have lower blood pressure and triglyceride levels (signifying a decreased chance of heart disease), and have more normal blood glucose levels (indicating a reduced risk of diabetes, marked by unusually high blood glucose levels). Moreover, it has recently been shown that rhesus monkeys kept on a calorie-restricted diet for an extended time (almost 15 years) suffer less chronic diseases. However, they and the other monkeys need to be followed further, to know if a low-calorie intake can increase the average and maximum life expectancy in monkeys. Unlike the plethora of drugs defined as the latest anti-aging drug, CR mimatics changes fundamental processes underlying aging. We aim to develop compounds that trick cells into activating maintenance and repair. How a prototype of calorie-limiting mimetics works The most studied candidate for calorie-limiting mimetics, 2DG (2-deoxy-D-glucose), works by interfering with how cells process glucose. It has shown to be toxic in some doses in animals and therefore cannot be used in humans. But it has shown that chemicals can replicate the effects of caloric restriction; the trick is finding the right one. Cells use glucose from food to make ATP (adenosine triphosphate), the molecule that drives many activities in the body. By limiting food intake, caloric restriction minimizes the amount of glucose entering cells and reduces ATP production. When 2DG is administered to animals that eat normally, glucose reaches the cells in abundance but the drug prevents its processing and thus reduces ATP synthesis. Researchers have offered several explanations for why disrupting glucose processing and ATP production might delay aging. One possibility relates to the emission of ATP-producing machinery of free radicals, which are thought to contribute to aging and age-related diseases like cancer by damaging cells. Reduced operation of the machines should limit their production and thus limit the damage. Another hypothesis suggests that decreased glucose processing may indicate to cells that food is scarce (even if it is not) and cause them to switch to an anti-aging state that emphasizes preservation of the organism over luxuries like growth and reproduction.

premise: The search for the anti-aging pill. In government laboratories and elsewhere, scientists are looking for a drug capable of prolonging life and youthful vigor. Studies on calorie restriction show the way As researchers on aging recently pointed out, no treatment on the market today has been shown to slow human aging the accumulation of molecular and cellular damage that increases vulnerability to morbidity as we age. But one intervention, consuming a low-calorie* but nutritionally balanced diet, works remarkably well in a wide range of animals, increasing longevity and prolonging good health. These findings suggest that caloric restriction may delay aging and increase lifespan in humans as well. Unfortunately, for the sake of maximum benefit, people will probably need to reduce their calorie intake by about 30%, equivalent to a reduction from 2,500 calories a day to 1,750. Few mortals could adhere to this harsh regime, especially for many years. But what if someone could create a pill that mimics the physiological effects of eating less without forcing people to eat less? Could such a mimetic for calorie restriction, as we call it, allow people to stay healthier, postponing age-related disorders (such as diabetes, atherosclerosis, heart disease and cancer) until very late in life? Scientists first posed this question in the mid-1990s, after researchers came across a chemical that in rodents appears to restore many benefits from calorie restrictions. A compound that would safely achieve the same feat in people has not yet been found, but the search was informative and raised hope that calorie-limiting (CR) mimetics could indeed eventually be developed. Benefits of Caloric Restriction The hunt for CR mimetics grew out of a desire to better understand the many effects calorie restrictions have on the body. Scientists first recognized the value of the practice more than 60 years ago, when they found that rats fed a low-calorie diet lived longer on average than free-fed rats and also had a reduced incidence of conditions that are becoming increasingly common in old age. What's more, some of the treated animals survived longer than the oldest animals in the control group, which means that the maximum lifespan (the oldest age attainable), not just the normal lifespan, increased. Various interventions, such as drugs that fight infections, can increase the average survival time of a population, but only approaches that slow the rate of aging of the body will increase the maximum life expectancy. The rat findings have been replicated many times and extended to creatures ranging from yeast to fruit flies, worms, fish, spiders, mice and hamsters. Until recently, studies were limited to short-lived creatures genetically remote from humans. But calorie-restriction projects underway in two species more related to rhesus monkeys and squirrel humans have made scientists optimistic that CR's mimetics could help people. Calories: An Index to the Energy Value of Food The monkeys projects demonstrate that compared to animals that eat normally, calorie-restricted monkeys have lower body temperatures and levels of the pancreatic hormone insulin, and they maintain younger levels of certain hormones that tend to decline with age. The calorie-restricted animals also look better on indicators of risk for age-related diseases. For example, they have lower blood pressure and triglyceride levels (signifying a decreased chance of heart disease), and have more normal blood glucose levels (indicating a reduced risk of diabetes, marked by unusually high blood glucose levels). Moreover, it has recently been shown that rhesus monkeys kept on a calorie-restricted diet for an extended time (almost 15 years) suffer less chronic diseases. However, they and the other monkeys need to be followed further, to know if a low-calorie intake can increase the average and maximum life expectancy in monkeys. Unlike the plethora of drugs defined as the latest anti-aging drug, CR mimatics changes fundamental processes underlying aging. We aim to develop compounds that trick cells into activating maintenance and repair. How a prototype of calorie-limiting mimetics works The most studied candidate for calorie-limiting mimetics, 2DG (2-deoxy-D-glucose), works by interfering with how cells process glucose. It has shown to be toxic in some doses in animals and therefore cannot be used in humans. But it has shown that chemicals can replicate the effects of caloric restriction; the trick is finding the right one. Cells use glucose from food to make ATP (adenosine triphosphate), the molecule that drives many activities in the body. By limiting food intake, caloric restriction minimizes the amount of glucose entering cells and reduces ATP production. When 2DG is administered to animals that eat normally, glucose reaches the cells in abundance but the drug prevents its processing and thus reduces ATP synthesis. Researchers have offered several explanations for why disrupting glucose processing and ATP production might delay aging. One possibility relates to the emission of ATP-producing machinery of free radicals, which are thought to contribute to aging and age-related diseases like cancer by damaging cells. Reduced operation of the machines should limit their production and thus limit the damage. Another hypothesis suggests that decreased glucose processing may indicate to cells that food is scarce (even if it is not) and cause them to switch to an anti-aging state that emphasizes preservation of the organism over luxuries like growth and reproduction.

premise: Secrets of Persuasion A. Our mother may have told you that the secret to getting what you were asking for was to say please. The reality is quite surprising. Adam Dudding talks to a psychologist who has done life's work from the science of persuasion. Some scientists look at things using high-powered microscopes. Others push rats through dungeons, or mix bubbling liquids in glass cups. For his part, Robert Cialdini does curious things with towels, and believes that in doing so he reveals important insights into how society works. Bea Cialdini's towel experiments (more of them later), are part of his research on how we persuade others to say yes. He wants to know why some people have a knack for bending the will of others, whether it's a cold-phone caller talking to you about time-sharing, or a parent whose children are compliant without even threats of extreme violence. While he fears he won't be seen as the man who wrote the Bible for snake-oil salesmen, for decades a professor of social psychology at Arizona State University has been creating systems for the principles and methods of persuasion, and writing bestsellers about them. Some people seem to be born with the skills; Cialdini's contention is that by applying a little science, even those of us who don't should be able to get our way more often.\ All my life I've been an easy mark of abuse from salespeople and fundraisers and I've always wondered why they could make me buy things I didn't want and give to causes I hadn't heard of,\ says Cialdini by phone from London, where he is authoring his latest book. c. He discovered that laboratory experiments in the psychology of persuasion only tell part of the story, so he began researching real-world influence, enrolled in sales training programs:\ I'm learning how to sell cars from lots, how to sell insurance from an office, how to sell encyclopedias door-to-door.\ He concluded that there are six\ general impact principles\ and has since put them to the test under somewhat more scientific conditions. Lately, that has meant messing around with towels. Many hotels leave a small ticket in each bathroom asking guests to reuse towels thus saving water and electricity and reducing pollution. Cialdini and his colleagues wanted to test the relative effectiveness of different words in these cards. Will guests be motivated to cooperate simply because it will help save the planet, or are other factors more compelling? To test this, the researchers changed the message of the environmental relay card to the simple (and true) statement that most hotel guests reused their towel at least once. Guests who received this message were 26% more likely to reuse their towels than those who received the old message. In Cialdini's book Yes! 50 SECRETS FROM THE SCIENCE OF PERSUASION, WRITTEN IN COLLABORATION WITH ANOTHER SOCIAL SCIENTIST AND BUSINESS CONSULTANT, HE EXPLAINS THAT GUESTS RESPONDED TO THE PERSUASIVE POWER OF “SOCIAL PROOF,” THE IDEA THAT OUR DECISIONS ARE STRONGLY INFLUENCED BY WHAT WE BELIEVE OTHER PEOPLE LIKE US DO. d. So much for towels. Cialdini also learned a lot from confectionery. -Yes! Citing the work of New Jersey behavioral scientist David Strometz, who wanted to see how restaurant patrons would respond to a ridiculously small favor from their food server, in the form of after-dinner chocolate for each diner. The secret, it seems, is how you give the chocolate. When the chocolates arrived in a stack with the bill, the tips went up by about 3% compared to when no chocolate was given. But when the chocolates were tossed separately in front of each diner, tips went up by 14%. The scientific breakthrough, however, came when the waitress gave each diner one chocolate, walked away from the table then doubled back to give them another one each, as if such generosity had just crossed her mind. Tips are up 23%. It is\ reciprocity\ in action: we want to return favors done to us, often without bothering to calculate the relative value of what is received and given. Ai Jiling Ng, operations manager at Auckland's Soul Bar, says she's never heard of Kiwi wait staff using such a cynical trick, not least because New Zealand's tip culture is so different from that of the US:\ If you did it in New Zealand, when diners were leaving they'd say 'Can we have some more? But she certainly understands the general principle of reciprocity. The way to a diner's heart is to give them something they don't expect in the way of service. In New Zealand that translates to a huge smile and thank you.\ And no doubt, repeat visits. The Five Principles of Persuasion. Reciprocity: People want to give back to those who gave them. The trick here is to get in first. This is why charities put a bad pen inside an email, and why smiling women in supermarkets are handing out dolls of free food. Scarcity: People want more things they can get less of. Advertisers are ruthlessly exploiting the shortage (\ limit four per customer\,\ sale must end soon\), and Cialdini also suggests parents do this:\ Kids want things that are less available, so say 'this is an exceptional opportunity; you can only have it for a certain time'.\ c Authority: We trust people who know what they're talking about. So let people know honestly about your credentials before you set out to influence them.\ You'd be surprised how many people fail to do that,\ Cialdini says.\ They feel it's impolite to talk about expertise then.\ In one study, therapists whose patients wouldn't then do exercises were recommended to display certificates of certification prominently. They did so, and experienced an immediate jump in patient compliance. H. Commitment/Consistency: We want to act in a way that is consistent with the commitments we have already made. Take advantage of this to get a higher enrollment rate when requesting charitable donations. First ask Labour members if they think they will sponsor you in your egg and spoon marathon. Later, come back with the sponsorship form to those who said yes and reminded them of their previous commitment/ I. Affection: We say yes more often to the people we love. Obvious enough, but reasons\ to love\ can be strange. In one study, people were sent survey forms and asked to return them to a renowned researcher. When the researcher gave a fake name similar to that of the subject (e.g., Cynthia Johnson being sent to a poll by\ Cindy Johansen\), the polls were doubly at risk of being terminated. We prefer people who resemble us, even if the resemblance is as small as the sound of their name. J. Social proof: We decide what to do by looking around to see what others just like us are doing. Useful for parents, says Cialdini.\ Find groups of children who behave in a way you'd like your child to see, because the child is looking to the side, and not at you.\ More damagingly, social proof is the force that underpins the competitive materialism of\ Keeping up with the Jones/

premise: The Silk Road, stretching from China to the Mediterranean, was not a single road, but a network of trade routes. Originating from the ancient Chinese capital Chang'an, the overland routes crossed modern-day India, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Turkey, Syria, and Iran en route to various Mediterranean ports, from where the goods were transported to Rome by boat. Typically, traders did not travel the entire distance of 6,440 km, but covered one section of the route and transported their goods to another trailer for the next. As the name suggests, the Silk Road facilitated Chinese silk trade, but many other goods were transported along the route. premise: The Socratic method is a form of philosophical questioning named after the Greek philosopher Socrates. It takes place as a dialogue between Socrates and another person and attempts to explore difficult concepts like justice and ethics. In this dialogue, partner Socrates raises an opinion or thesis. Socrates then proposes further premises that will attempt to refute the original thesis. If there is opposition, it shows that the original thesis is false and that the opposite is true. In this dialogue, Socrates often showed other philosophers and thinkers how their reasoning is wrong. Some respected him for that since he was aware of the fact that his knowledge was limited and that he was only questioning everything critically. However, many people were angry that he asked questions without providing answers to these difficult questions himself. This led to him creating a number of enemies in Greece. In 399 BC, Socrates was accused of heresy and corruption of youth by three of his enemies. He was then tried and found guilty by the jury and therefore sentenced to death by drinking the poison hemlock. One of his friends, Crito, bribed the guards to allow Socrates to escape; however he chose not to flee. Many treated him as a saint when he chose to die in a position of knowledge and wisdom.
hypothesis: Socrates was the first person to use this method of investigation.

premise: The triumph of irrationality? Neoclassical economics is built on the premise that humans are rational beings who have a clear idea of their interests and strive to derive maximum benefit (or benefit, in economist speak) from any situation. Neoclassical economics assumes that the decision-making process is rational. But this contradicts growing evidence that decision-making rests on the emotions, when logic is clearly involved. The role of emotions in decisions makes perfect sense. For situations often encountered in the past, such as obtaining food and mates, and coping with or escaping threats, the neural mechanisms required for weighing pros and cons will be sharpened by evolution to produce an optimal outcome. Because emotion is the mechanism by which animals are pushed to such outcomes, evolutionary and economic theory predicts the same practical implications for utility in these cases. But does this still apply when the paternal apparatus has to respond to the stimuli of urban modernity? One of the people who thinks it isn't is George Loewenstein, an economist from Carnegie Mellon University, in Pittsburgh. In particular, he suspects that modern shopping has undermined the decision-making mechanism in a way that encourages people to collect debts. To prove the point he teamed up with two psychologists, Brian Knutson of Stanford University and Drazine Perlak of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, to test what happens in the brain when it decides what to buy. In the study, the three researchers asked 26 volunteers to decide whether to buy a series of products like a box of chocolates or a DVD of the TV show that were shown on a computer screen one by one. In each round of the task, the researchers first presented the product and then its price, with each step lasting four seconds. premise: The real price of food for more than forty years the cost of food has been rising. It has now reached a point where an increasing number of people believe it is too high, and that lowering it will be one of the great challenges of the twenty-first century. That cost, however, is not immediate cash. In the West at least, most food is much cheaper to buy in relative terms than in 1960. The cost is in the collateral damage of the food production methods that have made food cheaper: in water pollution, in soil reduction, in the destruction of wildlife, in the harm to animal welfare and the threat to human health caused by modern industrial agriculture. First mechanization, then mass use of chemical fertilizers and pesticides, then monocultures, then battery breeding of animals, and now genetic engineering The onward march of intensive agriculture has seemed unstoppable over the past half-century, as yields of produce surged. But the damage he caused was immense. In Britain, for example, many of our most beloved farmland birds, such as the shrike, grey partridge, tail and cornflower, have disappeared from huge country strips, as have wildflowers and other insects. It's a direct result of the way we've created our food over the past four decades. Thousands of miles of hedges, thousands of ponds, disappeared from view. The fecal filth of salmon farming has taken wild salmon out of many of Scotland's ewes and rivers. Natural soil fertility is declining in many areas because of continued use of industrial fertilizers and pesticides, while algae growth is increasing in lakes because of fertilizer runoff. Put it all together and it looks like a battleground, but consumers rarely make the connection at the dinner table. This is mainly because the costs of all this damage are what economists call externalities: they are outside the main transaction, which is for example the production and sale of a wheat field, and they are borne directly neither by producers nor consumers. To many, the costs may not even seem monetary at all, but only aesthetic, a terrible shame, but it has nothing to do with money. And anyway they, as food consumers, certainly aren't paying for it, are they? But in fact, the costs to society can be quantified and, when added up, can amount to staggering amounts. An extraordinary exercise in doing this was carried out by one of the world's leading thinkers on the future of agriculture, Professor Jules Ferretti, director of the Centre for Environment and Society at the University of Essex. Professor Priti and his colleagues calculated the external effects of British agriculture for a particular year. They summed up the costs of repairing the damage caused, reaching a total figure of 2,343 million. This is equivalent to 208 for every hectare of farmland and permanent grassland, almost again as much as the total the government and EU spent on British agriculture in the same year. And, according to Professor Priti, that was a conservative assessment. Costs included: $120m for pesticide removal; $16m for nitrate removal; $55m for removal of phosphates and soil; £23m for removal of the insect cryptosporidium from drinking water by water companies; $125m for damaging wildlife habitats, hedges and dry stone walls; 1,113m from emissions of gases that could contribute to climate change; $106m Soil erosion and organic carbon loss; 169m from food poisoning; 607m from cattle disease. Professor Priti draws a simple but memorable conclusion from all this: our food bills are actually tripling. We pay for our supposedly cheap food in three separate ways: once over the counter, second through our taxes, which provide the huge subsidies that help modern intensive farming, and third to clean up the mess that modern agriculture leaves behind. So is it possible to lower the real cost of food? Disengaging from industrial farming as a solution to hunger may be very difficult for some countries, but in Britain, where the immediate need for food supplies is less urgent, and the costs and harms of intensive farming were clearly visible, it may be more feasible. The government needs to create sustainable, competitive and diverse agriculture and food sectors, which will contribute to a prosperous and sustainable rural economy, and promote environmental, economic, health and animal welfare objectives. But if industrial agriculture is to be replaced, what is a sustainable alternative? Professor Priti feels organic farming would be too big a leap in thinking and practices for many farmers. Moreover, the price premium would put the produce out of reach of many poor consumers. He recommends the immediate introduction of a greener food standard, which would push the market towards more sustainable environmental practices than the current norm, while not requiring a full commitment to organic production. Such a standard would include agreed practices for different types of agriculture, covering agrochemical use, soil health, land management, water and energy use, food safety, and animal health. That could go far, he said, in moving consumers as well as farmers toward a more sustainable farming system.

premise: The truth about the environment For many environmentalists the world seems to be getting worse. They have developed a hit list of our main concerns: that natural resources are running out; that the population is growing and leaving less and less to eat; that species are going extinct in huge numbers, and that the planet's air and water are becoming increasingly polluted. But a quick look at the facts shows a different picture. First, energy and other natural resources have become more abundant, not less, since the book 'Frontiers of Growth' was published in 1972 by a group of scientists. Second, more food is currently produced for the top of the world's population than at any time in history. Fewer people are starving. Third, although species are indeed extinct, only about 0.7% of them are likely to disappear in the next 50 years, not 25-50%, as is so often predicted. And finally, most forms of environmental pollution seem to have been exaggerated, or are transiently linked to the early stages of industrialization and are therefore best cured not by limiting economic growth, but by accelerating it. One form of pollution, the release of greenhouse gases that causes global warming does seem to be a phenomenon that is going to extend into our future as well, but its overall impact is unlikely to be a devastating problem. A bigger problem may turn out to be an inappropriate response to it. Public opinion polls, however, indicate that many people cultivate the belief that environmental standards are decreasing and four factors seem to cause this disconnect between perception and reality. One is bias built into scientific research. Science funding goes mostly to fields with many problems. This may be a wise policy, but it will also create the impression that there are many more potential problems than are happening. Second, the mass media needs to pay attention to environmental groups. They also have to keep the money rolling in. Understandably, perhaps, sometimes they exaggerate their arguments. In 1997, for example, the World Wide Fund for Nature issued a press release titled: 'Two-thirds of the world's forests have been lost forever. 'The truth turns out to be close to 20%. Although these groups are overwhelmingly run by selfless individuals, they nonetheless share many of the characteristics of other lobby groups. It would matter less if people applied the same degree of skepticism to environmental caucuses as they do to lobby groups in other areas. A trade organisation arguing, for example, for weaker pollution controls is immediately seen as self-interested. However, a green organisation opposed to such weakening is seen as altruistic, even if an impartial view of the controls in question might suggest that they do more harm than good. A third source of confusion is the attitude of the media. Obviously people are more curious about bad news than good. Newspapers and broadcasters are there to deliver what the public wants. However, this can lead to significant distortions of perception. An example of this was America's encounter with El Nino in 1997 and 1998. This climatic phenomenon has been blamed for ruining tourism, causing allergies, melting the ski slopes and causing 22 deaths. However, according to an article in the Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society, the damage caused was estimated at $4 billion but the benefits amounted to about $19 billion. These came from higher winter temperatures (which saved about 850 lives, reduced heating costs and reduced spring floods caused by meltwater). The fourth factor is poor individual perception. People fear that the endless increase in the amount of things everyone throws away will cause the world to run out of places to dump waste. However, even if America's garbage output continues to rise as it did in the past, and even if the American population doubles by 2100, all the trash America produces throughout the 21st century will still occupy only one in 12,000' of the entire United States area. So what about global warming? As we know, carbon dioxide emissions cause the planet to heat up. The best estimates are that temperatures will rise by 2 to 3 degrees this century, causing considerable problems, at a total cost of $5,000 billion. Despite the intuition that something drastic needs to be done about such a costly problem, economic analyses clearly show that it will be much more expensive to radically reduce carbon dioxide emissions than to pay the costs of adapting to the increased temperatures. A model by one of the main authors of the UN climate change panel shows how an expected temperature rise of 2.1 degrees in 2100 will only diminish to a rise of 1.9 degrees. Or in other words, the temperature increase that the planet would have experienced in 2094 will be postponed to 2100. So it doesn't prevent global warming, but only buys the world six years. Yet the cost of reducing carbon dioxide emissions, for the United States alone, will be higher than the cost of solving the world's single and most pressing health problem: providing universal access to clean drinking water and sanitation. Such measures would prevent 2 million deaths annually, and prevent half a billion people from becoming seriously ill. It is important that we look at the facts if we are to make the best possible decisions for the future. It may be expensive to be too optimistic but still more expensive to be too pessimistic.

premise: The UN Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) recently approved the 1989 ban on ivory trade, despite calls from Tanzania and Zambia to remove it. Only 470,000 elephants remain in Africa today - compared with 1.3 million in 1979. While natural habitat loss has been a significant factor in dwindling elephant populations, ivory poaching has been the primary cause. Since the implementation of the ban, elephant populations have recovered in many African countries, but it is estimated that about 38,000 elephants are still killed each year. CITES approved one-off sales in 1999 and in 2008, which allowed approved countries to dispose of their government ivory stockpiles. Ivory from these sales goes out to Japan and China, where demand for carved ivory is high. Conservation groups strongly oppose further one-off sales, because much of the ivory sold is of unknown origin. Moreover, sales generated the Far East's demand for ivory. In Central and West African countries, where organized crime rings operate lucrative ivory smuggling operations, hunting remains widespread. Those interested in allowing one-off sales argue that elephants are no longer endangered, and that upholding the ban would simply inflate the price of illegal ivory, making hunting more enticing. Although the CITES decision is seen as a victory by conservationists, the future of the African elephant relies on the governments' commitment to enforce the ban.
hypothesis: Because their elephant populations are thriving, Tanzania and Zambia want to lift the ban on ivory trade.

premise: The value of a college degree The increasing cost of higher education is causing many to question the value of continuing education beyond high school. Many wonder whether the high cost of tuition, the opportunity cost of choosing college over full-time employment and accumulating thousands of dollars of debt are, in the long run, worth the investment. The risk is especially great for low-income families who find it difficult to make ends meet without the added burden of college tuition and fees. In order to determine whether higher education is worth the investment, it is worth examining what is known about the value of higher education and the rates of return on investment for both the individual and the company. The economic value of higher education has considerable support for the idea that the rate of return on investment in higher education is sufficient to justify the financial burden involved in studying a college degree. Although the earnings differential between college and high school graduates varies over time, college graduates, on average, earn more than high school graduates. According to the Census Bureau, over the working life of an adult, high school graduates earn an average of $1.2 million; associate degree holders earn about $1.6 million; and bachelor's degree holders earn about $2.1 million (Day & Newburger, 2002). These large differences in lifetime earnings put the costs of college tuition in realistic perspective. Most students today about 80 percent of all students transfer to four-year public colleges or two-year public colleges. According to a U.S. Department of Education report, Think College Early, a full-time student at a four-year public college pays an average of $8,655 for in-state tuition, room and breakfast (U.S. Department of Education, 2002). A full-time student at a two-year public college pays an average of $1,359 per year in tuition (U.S. Department of Education, 2002). These statistics support the argument that although the cost of higher education is significant, given the existing earnings gap between those who earn a bachelor's degree and those who do not, the personal rate of return on investment in higher education is high enough to justify the cost. Another benefit! Graduates of colleges of higher education also enjoy benefits beyond increased income. The A1998 report published by the Higher Education Policy Institute reviews the personal benefits enjoyed by college graduates, including higher savings levels, increased personal/professional mobility, improved quality of life for their offspring, better consumer decision-making, and hobbies and leisure activities (Higher Education Policy Institute, 1998). According to a report published by the Carnegie Foundation, the non-monetary individual benefits of higher education include the tendency of postsecondary students to be more open, more cultured, more rational, more consistent, and less authoritative; these benefits are also passed on to future generations (Rowley and Hurtado, 2002). In addition, college attendance\ has been shown to reduce prejudice, improve knowledge of world affairs, and improve social status\ while increasing economic and occupational security for those earning a bachelor's degree (name). Studies have also consistently shown a positive correlation between the completion of higher education and good health, not only for oneself, but also for children. In fact, parents' education levels (after controlling for differences in earnings) are positively correlated with their children's health status\ and an increase in schooling (and higher relative income) is correlated with lower mortality rates for given age steps\ (Cohn and Geske, 1992). The social value of higher education Several studies have shown a high correlation between higher education and cultural and family values, and economic growth. According to Elhanan Cohen and Terry Gaska (1992), there is a tendency for more educated women to spend more time with their children; these women tend to use this time to better prepare their children for the future. Cohn and Geske (1992) report that college graduates seem to have a more optimistic view of their past and future personal progress.\ The public benefits of attending college include increased tax revenues, higher productivity in the workplace, increased consumption, increased flexibility in the workforce, and decreased reliance on government financial support (Higher Education Policy Institute, 1998)... Summary While it is clear that investing in an academic degree, especially for those students in the lowest income rungs, is a financial burden, the long-term benefits to individuals as well as to society in general seem to far outweigh the costs.
hypothesis: About 80% of students attend public colleges.
label: e

premise: The coconut palm. For thousands of years, coconut has been central to the lives of Polynesian and Asian peoples. In the Western world, however, coconuts have always been exotic and unusual, sometimes rare. The Italian merchant traveler Marco Polo apparently saw coconuts in South Asia in the late 13th century, and among Sir John Mandeville's mid-14th century travel writings there is mention of 'Great Characters of Inda' (Great Nuts of India). Today, images of palm-fringed tropical beaches are clichés in the West for selling holidays, chocolate bars, fizzy drinks and even romance. Typically, we see brown cannonball coconuts that when opened provide sweet white flesh. But we only see part of the fruit and none of the plant from which they come. The coconut palm has a smooth, thin, gray trunk, which is up to 30 meters high. It is an important source of wood for building homes, and is increasingly used as a substitute for endangered hardwoods in the furniture construction industry. On the trunk rises a rosette of leaves, each of which may be up to six meters long. The leaves have hard veins in their center, which in many parts of the world are used as brushes after the green part of the leaf has been stripped. Immature coconut flowers are tightly clustered between the leaves at the top of the stem. The flower stalks can be tapped for their sap to produce a drink, and the sap can also be reduced by boiling to produce a type of sugar used in cooking. Coconut palms produce up to seventy fruits per year, weighing more than a kilogram each. The fruit wall has three layers: a waterproof outer layer, a fibrous middle layer and a hard inner layer. The thick fibrous middle layer produces coconut fiber, 'coconut', which has many uses and is especially important in rope making. The most woody inner layer, the bark, with its three prominent 'eyes', surrounds the seed. An important product obtained from the shell is charcoal, which is widely used in various industries as well as at home as fuel for cooking. When broken in half, the shells are also used as bowls in many parts of Asia. Inside the shell are the nutrients (endosperm) necessary for the developing sperm. Initially, the endosperm is a sugary liquid, coconut water, which is enjoyed as a drink, but also provides the hormones that encourage other plants to grow faster and produce higher yields. As the fruit matures, the coconut water gradually solidifies and forms the glossy, fat-rich, white flesh or flesh, for consumption. Dried coconut meat, 'copra', is transformed into coconut oil and coconut milk, which are widely used in cooking in various parts of the world, as well as in cosmetics. A derivative of coconut fat, glycerin, acquired strategic importance in a completely different field, when Alfred Nobel presented to the world his invention based on nitroglycerin: dynamite. Their biology seems to make coconuts the great marine travelers and coastal settlers of the plant world. The large, energy-rich fruits are able to float in water and tolerate salt, but cannot remain viable indefinitely; studies show that after about 110 days at sea they are no longer able to germinate. The coconut seeds are literally dumped on the shores of the desert island, with little more than sand to grow in and exposed to the full glare of the tropical sun, the coconut seeds are able to germinate and take root. The air pocket in the sperm, formed with the solidification of the endosperm, protects the fetus. In addition, the fibrous fruit wall that helped it stay afloat during the voyage stores moisture that can be absorbed by the roots of the coconut seedling as it begins to grow. There have been centuries of academic debate about the origins of coconut. There were no coconut palms in West Africa, the Caribbean, or the east coast of the Americas before the voyages of European explorers Vasco da Gama and Columbus in the late 15th and early 16th centuries. Patterns of trade and human migration from the 16th century reveal that it is likely that Arab traders and European sailors transported coconuts from South and Southeast Asia to Africa and then across the Atlantic Ocean to the east coast of the Americas. But the origin of coconuts discovered along the west coast of America by 16th-century sailors has been the subject of centuries-old debate. Two diametrically opposed origins have been suggested: that they came from Asia, or that they were native to the Americas. Both proposals have problems In Asia there is a great deal of coconut diversity and evidence of thousands of years of human use - but no relatives growing in the wild. In America, there are close relatives of the coconut, but there is no evidence that coconuts are indigenous. These problems led to the intriguing suggestion that coconuts originated in coral islands in the Pacific Ocean and were dispersed from there.
